Call it what you will, one thing you cannot call Blood Bowl is a strategy game. When the push comes to shove, this game is about little more than dice rolls. Yes, there are things you can do - using a player with X skill to attempt a particular action instead of player with Y skill, so on and so forth - ultimately though, nothing matters but the randome result of a dice roll.
Long time players tell newcomers all sorts of things ad nauseum about risk management and smart chance taking. Those players remind of the gamblers who believe they have 'a system' for winning at craps, or roulette, or keno, or slots.
There may be things you can do to slightly nudge the chances of success of failure in your favor but, in the end, nothing but the end result of the dice rolls matters and games can be won or lost on a single good/bad roll.
While that certainly fits the description of a 'game of chance' it is definitely not, a strategy game. And the dice roll essentially renders pointless any actions taken by the actual player(s). You could eliminate graphics, teams, stats etc. and just roll dice at each other for an hour or so and tally up who had the most 'good' rolls. Then have one final roll to see who won, and that's your winner.
That's Blood Bowl.

I am not recommending for immediate purchase, but perhaps a future purchase, and here is why:
To begin with, I must admit that I was excited when I first heard of the title as I am a fan of the Sacred series. I became a little more skeptical after reading about some of the changes made (no longer open world / no more signifigant variety of loot), but I figured I was up for a new hack and slash experience, and it's Sacred III after all (What could go wrong?). In the end, I am rather more disappointed in that it feels more like a combo-game of Sacred and Dynasty Warriors, in the sense that it is interesting at first, but after a while (3-4 hours) I personally find myself getting bored. Graphics are solid, gameplay is fun, and the comedic charm is a matter of personal perspective as always. However, in the end, I must admit I have little interest in playing through on all the different characters, only becasue it feels like it might be a drag. I tried them all out through the first mission (apparently necessary at this point if you want to take them into the multiplayer feature) just to see which I liked the best, and after picking a favorite have decided to complete the game (whatever that might mean) with this character and then move onto something else.
The biggest disappointment for me was how the whole image of competing with others for treasure was hyped (IMHO) and all it seesm to add up to is getting a little more gold / exp and the completion of a mission. I have no trophy display case or homebase to improve with all my glorious and hard-fought loot, rather I get a screen that is like, "Hey, you killed the most guys, good for you, here is an extra percent to add to the pile."
Now all that said, if there was a signifigant increase to the amount of RPG / Loot /Upgrading side of the equation, whether through a solid patch, or more likely an expansion or DLC, I might consider playing the game further, but for now, I would recommed a purchase only if you are a fan of the Dynasty Warriors type experience, looking for a bit of a time sink, and the game is marked down for sale (think 50% off or more).

A licensed game that doesn't suck. Makes you feel like Dredd.
Story and voice acting are simple and cheesy. Music is upbeat and catchy to match the gameplay. Visually, you can tell it's old. It kind of looks like the first Halo, perhaps with slightly better textures, but the art direction helps this a great deal. It's also filled to the brim with humor and a bit of product placement.
NPC interaction is neat. You can arrest just about anyone, for obvious crimes of course, but you can also get the people who look completely innocent and see the ridiculous sentences they get for the most trivial of crimes. When taking care of violent perps, you can shoot weapons out of their hands to see how they react. It's all pushed along very well by Dredd's commentary.
Gunplay is smooth and responsive. There's a good assortment of options on top of the various firing modes of the Lawgiver pistol, but I rarely found myself using everything available, except on hard difficulty; Still, it's nice to have an option.
The game is fairly easy. Enemies do quite a bit of damage, but the game is very liberal with its checkpoint system and lets you save anywhere you wish. Levels are straightforward, often taking place in large corridors with only one way to go. The only time a challenge really pops up is when it refuses to give health and ammunition, or when you are faced with enemies who have explosive weapons. Most of the enemies are melee-based and slow enough that you can usually just run past them.
A problem I've run into is the collision detection. The hitboxes work well enough, but trying to jump might as well be a throw of the dice. Ragdolls sometimes fly all over the place, even when the enemies are killed with the smallest of weapons. NPCs and enemies can get stuck on waist-high objects,other NPCs, or thin air, and this can get very annoying when you aren't supposed to kill said character. I had to redo the hospital level because Mortis stood still and wouldn't run away after I beat him. Not even resetting the checkpoint helped.
It isn't a very long game either. Even with the above gripes included, it only took me about 4 hours to beat the game, and I was really taking my time. There are multiple difficulties, as well as a lot of extra content to unlock: "Arcade" missions, cheats, and multiplayer skins. The Arcade missions are of variable quality, but mostly feel like they only exist because the main campaign is so short. Cheats are fun to play around with, but get old fast. Multiplayer skins are next to useless because the multiplayer is dead. The game allows you to go up against bots in a multiplayer setting, but that quickly gets old as well due to their predictable behavior.
Yet, even with its problems, the game is decent fun for a cheap price. If you like FPS, if you like Judge Dredd, if you just want to live out a power fantasy of arresting everyone and blowing away hordes of the undead, this is for you, but get it on sale.

Anyone who is a fan of Lovecraft, Fallen London, or generally the constant feeling that there are mysterious, powerful, and ultimately unknowable forces at work should buy this game.
Sunless Sea evokes uncertainty and trepidation as you pilot a tramp steamer through darkness and danger to exotic ports. Death can come at any time, even when you've got some sea legs under you after having played for a while, and even once things become somewhat understood and comfortable, there's always a nagging feeling of being at risk while your ship chug-chugs into the black again.
I think anyone who complains that this is a grind is either playing it too safe (at the beginning), or has perhaps reached a level of playing I haven't gotten to yet after many hours of play. If you're looking for a game where you can feel that you are the master, then you've come to the wrong place.

EDIT:
Well, it's been a few years and the game and expansion have been out for a while. I still find myself coming back, there's something slow and contemplative about this game that you just don't find elsewhere.
The game has had a few balance passes. Outright broken stuff has been removed (boo, I made a lot of Echoes farming sunlight!) but more variety has been added to the starting game and Zubmariner did a really great job fleshing out the mid and late game with way more stuff to do and explore.
Do I still recommend it? Yes! Wholeheartedly!
Do I have a pro tip? Yes. TURN PERMADEATH OFF. The greatest flaw of the game is they want you to treat it like a roguelike, but that means reading the same story over and over and over. Gets boring after a while.
Just turn off hardcore mode, save and load to your hearts content and allow yourself to breath in the atmosphere of the UnderZea.

Over all, I've enjoyed the game. I love the atmosphere of the Unterzee, interacting with the world is fun, and I really enjoy the way each playthrough feels like an entire new adventure with a completely different objective and character. The gameplay requires patience; a lot of it will consist of you sailing/zailing around in an effort to find something. The combat is somewhat iffy. I don't love it, but I don't hate it. It, like the game itself, is difficult and usually dependant on circumstance. In one of my playthroughs, I was low on fuel and trying to just make it to port so I could buy some more fuel, when one of those living icebergs got in my way and chased me until I ran out of fuel, which naturally resulted in my character perishing.  In another playthrough, I rarely encountered something I couldn't handle by hiding or fighting and managed to last much longer than I had before. The game is very challenging and even unfair at times, but that's part of what makes it so enjoyable. Knowing that you could meet your untimely end with a single wrong course of action really manages to keep you on your toes while also being somewhat exhilerating.
With all that being said, there is one thing I really don't like; the economy. Attaining money/echoes in Sunless Sea is too difficult, in my opinion. You get paid hardly anything for doing most things and the cost of fuel and supplies is outrageous at most ports. Best case scenario is you break even, being able to afford what you need to survive with what you've earned but not gaining any ground. Eventually, you die due to lack of ability to pay for the essentials and spend your last couple minutes watching your fuel and/or supplies dwindle down to zero. I find myself unable to explore for very long or venture too far from London thanks to the insane prices and lack of sufficient income. If the cost of essentials was lowered or the payout of doing things raised, the game would be much more enjoyable. In my opinion, of course. It could be that I'm just awful and haven't completely figured out how to actually gain ground. :P
In conclusion, I'm really having a good time with Sunless Sea. Adventuring and discovering the world is super great, I just wish I could feel like I'm actually moving up in the world instead of continuing until I eventually run out of money and find myself at sea/zea knowing full well that I have no hope of surviving due to my fatal lack of fuel and/or supplies.
EDIT: After considerable more play time (roughly seven more hours), I would like to state my renewed opinion on Sunless Sea's economy.
The economy. It's not as difficult or unfair as I said, not even close. I dunno about everyone else, but after I kind of pushed through my phase of not knowing what the hellw as going on or what to do, it all started to make much more sense. I started to get a better grasp on what was happening and how the economy worked. It's not broken or unfair. It may feel that way for the first few hours, but eventually you start to get the gist of it. Sure, it's tough. Getting ahead and making profit is not easy, but the game wouldn't be much of a challenge if it was. So if you're having difficulty, as I was, just persist. If you keep dying, try something new. Don't start every character off doing the exact same thing. And once you round that curve of difficulty, you'll find that that is where the game really starts.
Good luck my fellow/potential zailors!

(Full review follows below)
is one of the best games around for exciting open-world mayhem. Nice graphics and animations, a diverse gameworld, and an interesting atmosphere establish an enjoyable explorative experience. The world is loaded with collectibles to find, vehicles to commandeer, and things to blow up. And it is headlined with exciting, distinctive gameplay chock-full of mayhem and destruction. If you are into sandbox mayhem, this should be a sure thing for you; and even more casual fans of the genre should easily enjoy this game too, because it is just so outright fun.
Now
, as is apparent by the title, is the sequel to the first
game. The first game was decent, and I had some fun playing it. But to be honest: anything it can do, this can do better. Both games use the same core concepts for gameplay, except the ideas were certainly executed better in
. So you really don’t have to worry too much about missing anything worthwhile if you would prefer skipping over the first game entirely. Even the narrative of
is almost entirely unconnected to the first game’s story, so reading a brief synopsis should be more than sufficient for you to fully enjoy the experience. Having said all of that, though, if you really enjoy the genre, then you may want to check out the first game too.
Anyway, the strongest attribute of
has to be the riotous gameplay. You move around in an over-the-shoulder view while on foot, with various firearms at your disposal for taking out militants. And the patented grappling-hook mechanic allows some innovative ways to take down foes, bringing a distinctive novelty to the combat. Furthermore, shortly into the campaign, a wide variety of vehicles (cars, boats, helicopters, planes, and more) becomes available. These are great not only for your basic traveling needs, but also to perform ridiculous and hilarious stunts. And of course, the grappling-hook and parachute combination can be used to explore the gameworld in the signature
fashion that affords the franchise its unique identity. And with the myriad of collectibles to find, structures to destroy, statistics to record, and achievements to unlock: there is no shortage of things to do.
And I suppose if the gameplay is the best attribute of the game, then the gameworld presentation is a very close second. The graphics are pristine and the landscape is packed with diverse sceneries and environments. From mountain peaks to desert valleys, it has it all. The animations and effects are also mostly well designed, which enhances the gratification of bringing a wake of destruction through every last place you visit. And the world is humongous. Even with a jet it can take a while to cross the map. Luckily there is a fast travel system that allows you to begin a sky-dive from above any location you have visited. It integrates perfectly with the game, taking what would be tedious and flipping it into one of the most enjoyable things to do.
easily has one of the most entertaining gameworlds to explore.
But even with all of this going on, the game starts off with a very focused and linear mission that allows you to be introduced to the main narrative elements of the campaign. You will come to find, however, that the story aspects of
are minimal, and mostly mediocre. So you definitely shouldn’t go into it expecting to be told an elaborate story. But despite that, the narrative flows and the various missions are certainly enjoyable. The missions are purposeful and focused, which can be a refreshingly stark contrast to the mindless mayhem side of the game. But while there is a decent amount of total missions including the extras, there are very few main storyline missions, which does hold the overall experience back a bit. So there is some room for improvement.
Ultimately,
is a good example of what can be done in video games when great concepts meet great execution. It is such an all-around fun and distinctive experience that I would recommend everyone give it some consideration; and if you are a fan of the genre, then it should be a no-brainer.
And as an addendum: there is now a free multiplayer mod DLC. With the mod, the opportunity for hilarious stunts and mayhem is increased exponentially as numerous players can all play in the same sandbox at once. As a free bonus, it is a pretty sweet addition and can be a lot of fun if you like that kind of thing. Luckily, if it doesn’t sound like your thing, it is also easy to completely ignore since the mod installs as a separate “app” on Steam with separate statistics and achievements tracking.

I wanted this game to be good, I really did, but after trying it multiple times over the lifetime of its early access, I honestly can't recommend it. It is a really great setting, great visuals, and a really unique neat idea, which is all window dressing to a what amounts to bad, clunky gameplay. I saw the game as an exploring game, with some combat, resource management, trading and basic RPG elements thrown in, like Lovecraft does Pirates. Instead it just ends up being a frustrating confusing incoherent mess. None of the parts really work. Combat is awkward, which is unfortunate, because you get in it A LOT, or are spending all your time avoiding it, which wastes so many resources, which would not be a problem if there were other ways to get them, but you are out of supplies and fuel often before you are out of the first area of the setting. Trade is nonexistent, or rare, and exploration would seem great, but I am so busying JUST TRYING TO GET TO THE NEXT ISLAND, that I can't really enjoy it. Perhaps there is some underlying strategy I am missing, but if there is, it would have to be very convuluted and elusive. I know it is heading towards its final release, but I can't see the developers addressing the clunky gameplay by February. Even after purchasing its early release and funding its kickstarter, I will have to pass on this one.

I travelled back in time and played Warrior Kings: Battles for a couple of hours to realize again that this game is still one of the best RTS games on the market. I first played it more than ten years ago and it amazed me. Nothing changed. I tried a tons of simple RTS games during the past years, like Dawn of War, Warcraft 3, Kohan 2, Supreme Commander, Mark of Chaos or King Arthur for example and my final conclusion is, graphics means nothing in case of a great RTS game. WK:B still gives a deeper, much more enjoyable gameplay than most of today's copy/paste RTS games.
You get a city building game mixed with Total War-like battles, pure strategy, pure tactics in one game. Rushing is not an option here. Every unit is different and every one of them has it's counterparts. You should play your tactics well to achieve something in this game and you should plan your strategy carefully on what you spend your income. Build a sawmill for the peasants for more material or upgrade your heavy infantry's armor? Choose wisely!
Those minor aspects of the game, like visibly training your units, the support cart for your armies, the scouts and the spies really brought something refreshing into the genre back when the game was released. It was original.
The visible puff of the horses, the rallying of the ravens and crows during a battle to have feast on the dead bodies, the pagan demon from the wickerman, the imperial archangel from the stone statue, the praying monk knights, the renaissance musketeers totally hooked me into this game... again after more than ten years.
It's a classic! I recommend it to anyone no matter if you are not into the RTS genre. I still keep my original retail edition on my bookshelf together with the poster-sized tech and faction tree what I got shipped together with the CD and the manual.

I want to put in my first thoughts before the review section gets crazy with the buggy issues. I've played through the first episode and SO FAR the game is stellar. Incredible story telling that makes you want more BATMAN. I'm super excited for the rest. I know a review shouldn't be this early, but I wanted give feedback on some technical issues people have been having.
I will note that I haven't had any issue with framerate or resolution. Granted, I have a beefy computuer, but nothing seemed out of the ordinary. I also know a lot of people have been having bug issues, but I only encountered a small one in the first episode. This bug could be frustrating unless you know how to get around it.
NO SPOILER
The first time you start messing around with you bat computer, pretty much at the beginning of the game, you mess around with different sections including news feed, codex, and various tools. I encountered a bug trying to back COMPLETELY out of the CODEX section. It would not give me an option to back out and get to the original scene before I used the computer. If this happens to you and you're stuck in that codex screen then simply walk backwards (away from the bat computer). You will hear the footsteps of your character, meaning you have control over him even though your visual is stuck in a screen.  Walk backwards and you should hit some stairs which will put you in a new scene, taking you away from the stuck codex screen. This worked for me and I hope it works for you if you have this issue.

The game is very good from start to finish though it felt a bit short. The game has nailed many things well and because of it, it's a pretty fun experience.
Positives:
-Good controls. Whether you use a Keyboard+Mouse or a controller is up to you but regardless, the game still feels smooth. Running around is fun and air dashing feels very satisfying to pull off.
-Decent OST. The music in this game is top notch. It's well made and is pretty catchy. Same goes to the remixes.
-Memorable characters. Everyone you meet from the mafias to the goats are interesting whether it's their characteristics or their appearance. Voices ain't bad for me at least.
-Good level layout. For the most part, the levels are made well in a sense that going from point A to point B is not boring. Accompanied by the good controls, it's pretty fun to explore the areas of the game. Just don't get lost.
-The game looks beautiful. It's nice to look at the environment because of how vivid and interesting they look.
-Mods can be implemented. The good thing about this is that aside from appearance changes, it's possible to play different player made levels with their own unique functions which keeps the game from being stale. But as of now, it's still in beta so keep that in mind.
Negatives:
-The game feels short. I'm aware that the game isn't finished yet since I heard that there would be 2 more worlds and a co-op mode but as of now, it still managed to entertain but not that long.
-Bugs and glitches. Though I encountered some, it doesn't make the game unplayable but it doesn't stop it from being annoying. At least the devs are constantly patching things out to remove them.
-Some hats feel under-powered while some are too good.
-From what I remember, the lighting has some small issues in a way on how they are placed/implemented.
Overall the game is pretty good. Play it since it's worth your time.

I gave it an honest try, but at the moment it is not mature enough. And with 'mature', I don't mean 'for adults', though that is also the case, in my opinion. Where to start...
This 'free to play' constantly notifies you of buyable stuff and uprades. I suspect that you will miss out if you never buy anything in the game, so the 'free to play' is a con.
What annoys me too, is that the 'open world' is not that open. When walking outside, I expect to be actually able to walk from A to B, and not having to load new parts of the outside all the time.

The second time I played, I wasn't able to find a menu with a 'Quit' option, so I finally Alt+F4'd my way out.

The controls are far from intuitive (I play a couple of other open world games with different controls to move around, none of them as bad as this, and it's nothing to do with 'getting used to).
The reason I finally gave up, was the profanity filter in the chat. I'm going to install the game, because there are better games to fill my precious time with.

A pretty fun shooter. Don't expect a masterpiece, but it's nowhere near as bad as critics claim it to be. Most gunfights are quite fast paced and satisfying, and that's what FPS games are all about. The control and handling is smooth, and most weapons are very fun to use. Graphics might've aged by now, but they do a decent enough of a job to make a believable sci-fi setting and to make you feel like you're in it.
The game spans 10 story chapters. The first few levels have you fighting and arresting the perps, and the latter levels are more trigger happy and mostly have you fighting hordes of zombies and vampires. Some of the levels are done really well (The Docks, The Lab, The Hospital, The Undercity), whilst a few others were more of an annoyance than anything (The Training, The Smokatorium). The training level should've been completely optional and isn't a very interesting way to introduce new players to the game. However, if you can stomach it, the game really picks up from there.
There isn't much of a story there. The dark judges escape and you spend most of the game hunting each one down. The boss fights were somewhat disappointing. 3 of the 4 of them simply involved you walking around the level and pressing switches, and only one of them was an actual full-on battle where you had to shoot the baddie down. Having said that, most FPS games tend to have very badly done boss fights, so wouldn't be fair to single out this game specifically.
The game also contains some arcade levels, but they lose their appeal very fast as you realise most of them is just you vs a big group of enemies with too little health. The (5-6 hour) story campaign is the only reason to play this game really, so if you're up for some fun sci-fi gunfights, you should have a good time playing this game.

Banished is one of my favorite guilty pleasures. It's surprisingly complex and requires more attention than you'd think. Unlike most RTS games, there's no in depth tutorial, no help-at-each-click tips, and when you tip the scales just a little the wrong way, it takes effort and thought to get it back on track. The only thing I consider disappointing about it is that the story-campaign lasts about eight hours and that this game only has LAN-only multiplayer -meaning you will have to install a LAN-faking client like Hamachi, Gameranger or so on to connect with your friends online with some stablity issues. All-in-All, if you like classic shooters with some sleazy-cheesy style and have some time to kill, don't miss out on this little rusty gem.

I wanted this game to be good, I really did, but after trying it multiple times over the lifetime of its early access, I honestly can't recommend it. It is a really great setting, great visuals, and a really unique neat idea, which is all window dressing to a what amounts to bad, clunky gameplay. I saw the game as an exploring game, with some combat, resource management, trading and basic RPG elements thrown in, like Lovecraft does Pirates. Instead it just ends up being a frustrating confusing incoherent mess. None of the parts really work. Combat is awkward, which is unfortunate, because you get in it A LOT, or are spending all your time avoiding it, which wastes so many resources, which would not be a problem if there were other ways to get them, but you are out of supplies and fuel often before you are out of the first area of the setting. Trade is nonexistent, or rare, and exploration would seem great, but I am so busying JUST TRYING TO GET TO THE NEXT ISLAND, that I can't really enjoy it. Perhaps there is some underlying strategy I am missing, but if there is, it would have to be very convuluted and elusive. I know it is heading towards its final release, but I can't see the developers addressing the clunky gameplay by February. Even after purchasing its early release and funding its kickstarter, I will have to pass on this one.

Great concept and looks are undone by baffling AI.
The difficulty of this game isn't strategising your resources, but trying to counter an AI that is often infuriating. Households will hog food, starving citizens will wander past stocked barns/markets to then die, sprites will walk all the way to something only to suddenly turn around wasting a lot of time, etc
Yes, I suppose combating the AI IS the game, but rather than difficulty it brings frustation and bewilderment. When the entire goal is essentially one long end game to expand your town ad infinitum, its baffling nature wears down an enthusiasm to continue playing because plans are undone by AI stupidity.
It's a shame, because the graphics are good if you've got a decent machine, and when it does work it's a gentle and engaging game. There's real potential for a deep and complex management/strategy game here, but the game just begs to be a lot smarter.

I really really wanted to enjoy this game, atmosphere is great, premise is perfect but it is seriously lacking in fun. Grinding seems to be the only way to keep up with fuel needs and it takes all of the fun out of exploring because it is punishing to your supplies. Your terror meter ( or at least mine) is constantly headed towards full and trying to manage it will just destroy what lil stock you have in your fuel resources. If there is a tipping point due to upgrades where there is a bit more leeway in the survival aspect, I never made it there. I either was bored to tears from going back and forth to the same locations or biteing my nails wondering if I would even make it home and if I did I get rewarded 30 some odd echoes barely enough to restart a grind session.  Possible suggestion larger fuel guage, slight increase in currency exchange and adjust the terror aspect. As much as I want a suspense filled, difficult game, when I die I want to feel the urge to dive back in! Some more reward from the time I just spent running head long to my ineviatable end would also be more reassuring. This creates the hope of that 1 out of 5 runs where you finally really crush it, get some epic upgrades and then tragically die to some totally unforseen sea monster leaving you mad but proud you died an adventures life. Sunless Sea just never allowed me to get there, now either I'm an epic fail at adventuring or there still needs to be some adjustments. However,this game still might be for some people and it has a lot of promise but in the end in this state it leaves me wanting.

Once you find the sweet floaty space between F and SPACEBAR this game will be pretty comfy. The grappling hook/parachute combo is what sets this game apart from every other generic drivey shooty sandbox game.
It's a shame that one of the first few missions intentionally tries to frustrate the player. I replayed said mission a dozen times before going online and seeing the specific moves I had to make. After the mission in question (which is great fun once you know what to freaking do) you're dumped into the open world portion and perform about 20 missions before you reach anything near as complex.
The driving stinks. The handling of most cars is greasey as hell. Venturing offroad is  out of the question... and then there is the grappling hook. Sweet bliss. Once you figure out for yourself that the true joy of this game is yanking yourself around in the sky while raining death from above with your quad rocket launcher, you'll be wondering why this wasn't showcased in the first handful of missions.
To quote Mark Borchardt the dialogue is so corny it'd make the pope weep.  It's clear the devs didn't take the world they'd crafted very seriously. The humour rarely hits the target either. Without the serious drama of GTAIV or V, we're stuck in narrative limbo, where the only incentive to keep playing is the interesting parachute physics.
The fact that only 8% of people who bought this game have finished it, speaks volumes. Definitely not an all-tine classic,  but worth picking up in a Steam sale for a couple bucks.

Having played all episodes, I find it hard to review this game. Up until episode 5 I recommended this game, but now... after it all... I just can't. If you are a Batman fan, don't play this game.
Now, this game does a lot of things right. It has a great way of making you play and think about your choices both as Batman and as Bruce Wayne. But these choices are the exact reason I can't recommend the game.
You pretty much know that your choices don't actually make that much, if any, difference in a TT game. But the choices given here, with this fact in mind, are just insulting. Straight up insulting to any Batman fan.
Have to go into spoilers to explain this:
And in the end, a narrative which at the start showed a lot of potential with some interesting takes on certain established characters feels incredibly rushed just so that we could basically have the classic takes on the characters set up for Season 2. With nothing you've done having any impact on anything.
I know what to expect in TT games, and I know how the choices impact the game. But usually, those choices are related either to original characters, or at least tend to show respect to the original lore. Here, TT decided to take some "liberties" in their take on the character which just insults Batman, as well as all of his fans.
Sad to say, in the end, despite being excited and enjoying a fair amount of the season, I just left with a very sour taste in my mouth.

This game is addicting, challenging, beautiful, and has so many cool mechanics in it it is worth every dollar.

As a long time player of tabletop games related to this genre, I was drawn into this game by some fun videos on YouTube.
I wish the general community was as fun as the people who play on YouTube...
Pros - GW has a real knack for a sort of gallows humor and tongue in cheek style that somehow manages to be both dark and silly at the same time. It lends itself well to games that actually grew out of war simulations. The two narrators are entertaining, as GW characters are wont to be, and Cyanide I feel did a wonderful job capturing the flavor of the game.
Cons -
1. The UI is clunky. There is no entirely safe way to plan your moves. Misclicks result in anything from having to start all over to having your player throw the ball across the field when you did not intend it.
2. The teams are not particularly well balanced. This goes back to it being a GW game. GW, for those of you now aware, stands for Games Workshop. This is a company that just abandoned a decades old wargame franchise seemingly specifically to spite a sector of their customer base they apparently considered harmful for their sales.
We'll see how that works out. Meantime, Blood Bowl 2 sports a handful of the teams available in the semi-official (I.E. not at all supported by GW for decades now) tabletop rules. Skaven are all but unplayable. Chaos seem to rule the leagues based on the fact that they have access to an entirely separate set of upgrades that other races can only rarely access (mutations). Skaven can get them fairly easily too, but Skaven die in higher levels in truckloads with an armor value of 7 even on front line players. As the game rewards survival of multiple games heavily, Skaven and other low armor, high finesse teams find it hard to compete at higher levels of play. At least one private league now invites ONLY finesse teams into its league to avoid the devestation the high armor and high strength teams visit on their weaker cousins.
There is no cure for this imbalance in sight. My experience with GW - players and designers alike - is that making the game balanced and competative is not really high on their list of things to do. Wonder if Cyanide can break that trend? So far, the answer is no.
3. The graphics are pathetic. This game offered little in the way of graphics to begin with. It is a standard sort of top down view with very clunky camera control. But to make matters worse, players move about stiffly, often ending up somewhere other than where you aimed them only to slip into place like a loose block, and the handful of full screen animations that pop up typically sport part of one player poking through the other player because of bad positioning of the camera and/or models during the animation render.
At one point the game reversed the team uniforms between my Skaven and the opposing Skaven team...?
In short, just old fashioned sloppy graphics and animation work.
4. The community is not nearly as friendly as the YouTube videos that seem to be the main marketing arm for the game would lead you to think.
Summary: Nice idea, but the execution is predictably pathetic as GW tends to just pawn its IP off to whoever is willing to fork over the money and let the chips fall where they may. There has never in the history of GW been anything remotely resembling quality control as far as their game rules go. They make wonderful miniatures and great game fluff, but horribly horrible games. And their company is quite obviously struggling because of it.
In any event, I would definitely not recommend this game. The lack of balance between the teams and the clunky UI have left me entirely uninterested in continuing play, and like so many GW fans, the player base seems to be a bunch of rabid dogs whose main function in life is to convince people to play games with them by treating them like crap and pretending there's nothing wrong with the game's design or execution.
Caveat - There are those who accuse me of being "Sausage fingered". I seem to do well enough in pretty much every other video game I play though. I'm pretty sure this is just the typical GW fanboy reaction to anything negative you ever say about their games, but in the interest of fairness, there are apparently people who just LOVE the UI. I can't imagine why, and they are none too communicative as to WHY they think the UI rocks, but there you have it.
Maybe my fingers turn to sausages specifically for GW games.

This game is an absolute masterpiece.
First and foremost of course, the art and design. On this point, the game is flawless. Never before have I seen such an exquisite execution of artistic aesthetic: the animation is lush, detailed, wacky, fun, bouncy and exactly what you'd expect; the music is bubbly and jive-worthy; the sound effects are spot on, and the overall sound design is mastered in a way that makes the game even more immersive (for example, the sounds overpowering the music and making it quieter, which is exactly how the sounds of media from the 30's would sound). One of the lead developers said that their goal when making this game was to "make a game that
like it was made in the 1930's". I feel like they have perfectly achieved that goal.
But none of this would matter if the game wasn't fun, and it certainly is. There are enough weapon and item customisation to stop it from getting boring, every boss has unique mechanics, and because of the excruciating difficulty you are forced to learn them by rote. I can see how that might put some off, but personally I love the challenge and I'm more than happy to play each boss hundreds of times if it means I get to stretch the game out for longer. It's not a long game: I've played just under 5 hours and I'm already ~30% of the way through. But I can scarce blame the developers for that, because of the unbelievably huge amount of work that went into this game.
And that's something that is clear everywhere you look in this game. In every frame of animation, in every note of the soundtrack, you can just tell this game was made with love and care and dedication, something somewhat rare in the videogames industry these days. These people poured 3 years of their lives into this game, and it shows in depth and breadth and height.
Cuphead is an exhibition of artistic mastery and unflinching joy. For £15 (or your regional equivalent), that's far more than worth it

--WARNING--
This review represents my own, objective opinion about this game. This means, that I will not praise the game for the good things and don't mention it's flawes, but I also won't talk only bad things about the game to make it look completly worthless. As far as the review goes, it will have spoilers, so i'd recommend either reading on, if you don't have a problem with that or simply ignore this review. Viewer Discretion Advised.
--Introduction--
Five Night's at Freddy is a Horror Point-&-Click Adventure game made by one developer (Scott Cawthon).
The game reviewed alot of positive reviews by a lot of people and already was Let's Played by several big Let's Players.
--Plot--
The plot is very simple in the basic. You are Mike Schmidt who's going to work for the Freddy Fazzbear's Pizza as a Night Guard for a week during the summer from 12AM untill 6AM/ a day. Your Job is to watch the animatronics (the main attraction of the Pizzarea) as they are wandering around at night and are not allowed to be shut down or they will lock themselves.
This and many other advises and mentions about certain events are being told by a guy on the Phone, who's the only ally for the player, you reciev every night untill the 4th night. He tells right in the first night that the animatronics might come to your office and might mistake you for being an animatronic without a costume and, since this is against the rules, you'll be forced by the animatronics into a costume, which has wires and beams, and won't fit a human body in, resulting in your death. The only defense the player has are 2 doors (1 to the left and 1 to the right), the lights near the doors for the blind spots and your camera to track them down.
--Gameplay--
The game is being controlled only by the mouse and the only interaction you have are the 4 buttons in your office and the monitor, from which you can switch through different camera feeds. As mentioned earlier, you control with the buttons the doors and the light in the hallways outside the doors. To make things more "difficult" you only have a limited amout of power you can use to protect yourself. That means that closing doors, using the lights and cameras consume power. The more things you use at the same time the quicker the power depletes. If your power is completly consumed, you die unless you are close to 6AM and still have some seconds to have a chance to get to the next night. There are a total of 4 (with "Golden Freddy" 5) animatronics you have to watch for and each of them are more or less unique in their aproach. The first active animatronics will be Bonnie (the blue bunny) and Chica (the yellow chicken). They will roam randomly through the building and will sometimes aproach your office. The further you get in the nights, the more active they'll get. The next animatronic is Foxy (The Pirate-Fox) who's malfunctioning and is "out of order" in his cove. He is the most easylie predictable animatronic if you know his pattern (although that is also random which means you wont know exactly when he is going to attack). the 4th. being freddy and, in later nights, the most agressive animatronic if not dealt with. The 5th. being Golden Freddy, but there must be certain events activated to summon him, which is in the most cases very rare and can be avoided very easy.
If you die in this game, then your death will always be a jumpscare, which will be more or less predictable, and you have to start the night from the beginning. And there is no "Pause" function.
--Things I like about this game--
One thing the game is realy good at is building up tense. The feeling, that an animatronic will attack at any moment and , if you don't watch carefully you'll be punished with a Jumpscare, can happen every single moment. This works pretty good with the random mechanics, since every night is different from the previous, even on new attempts. There is also a form of balance in it to prevent abuses of certain mechanics to get through the game. The strongest element of the game is the fact, that it has plenty room for theories which can tease the player to speculate about with others.I actualy used more time to read theories and making my own theories then playing the game (which is actualy not something good, but i will talk about this later).
--Things I don't like about this game--
As I mentioned earlier that the game has random mechanics, they are not random enough (at least for me).
The biggest problem being the animatronics attacking from the same spots (Bonnie from the left door, Chica from the right door, Foxy only approaching the left door and freddy from the right. This leads to a fair amount of predictabilitie and using "strategies" which are not exactly fun in my opinion. For instance: you simply have to check the left and right door with the lights and be ready to close the door for chica and bonnie, since they won't "unexpectibly" teleport into your office. This will make the cameras for them pretty much pointless and the camera will be used for someting more simplier and more predictable. This means you will watch a total of only 2 cameras in an entire night, and you won't even look at them for long. The cameras will be used to slow down foxy and Freddy to prevent them from attacking and to check for foxy, when he is ready to attack. Another thing is the lack of "animation" in the game. all (except for Foxy) animatronics simply teleport from room to room, making the cameras to watch their position almost pointless (for chica, bonnie and Freddy) since they can almost instantly teleport near your office and before you find all of them, one will be in your office, ready to attack. If the animatronics would actualy "move" and even attack from random doors then the camera would get a much better mechanic in the game and it is more crucial to watch their positions in order to know when and WHERE they attack. The last thing the game being to short. I didn't complet the game to 100% but i got from night 1 through night 5 (with night 5 completed) in slightly above an hour and I died only once in night 1 because I was unaware of Foxy being active in the first night if you dont watch the camera at all (I was using only the lights since I knew that only Bonnie and maybe chica are active in this night). Since one night is aprox. 8min and 30 secs I would've complete the game in less then 1 and a half hour 100% using the same strategy and I would not have to replay the game again for pure "fun" in gameplay. instead I would or still am speculating about theories then, which is by far more fun espacialy with the 2nd game being out. Damn, I wanted to like this game... I really did.  As a big fan of both RTS and city-building games, the idea of survival being your primary obstacle really seemed like a fresh idea for both genres.  Unfortunately I cannot in good faith recommend anyone buy this game.  The problems are myriad, and I hardly know where to begin.  I guess I'll start by covering the good, since it's by far the shortest list.
PROS
CONS
Given what I've seen in my first couple dozen hours of play, I cannot see how this game would scale up in a fun and meaningful way.  I currently haven't made it much past ~100 villagers, at which point the game seemingly already requires autistic levels of attention.  Based on that, I can only imagine that a larger town would become an immediate and tedious grind.
In summary, I think this game concept had a ton of potential that was just impossible for a first-time developer to fully realize.  If you can get it for $2 and pile so many mods on top of it that it effectively becomes a different game, there might be some (fun) replay value there.  I've heard great things about the Colonial Charter mod, and am keeping my fingers crossed that it can save this game.  However, if you're expecting $20 worth of "fun" from the vanilla game, I believe you'll be sorely disappointed.  I'm sad to say I couldn't recommend this game at anything other than bargain basement prices.

I want to love this game, but it fights me at every turn.  I've been hoping that it would get better, but now that it's almost out of early access, I'm despairing that it will ever be fun.  I've been playing since it first was available, and this game has  never really felt like it knows what type of game it wants to be.  It's not a trading game (trading is nonexistent...most ports don't buy anything).  It's not a combat game (too simplistic).  And despite its billing, It's not an exploration or story-based game, because it's too difficult keeping yourself afloat for you to really go see what's out there.
What it is lacking is a logical sense of progression.  Perhaps with the final tweaks, it will add in some beginning quests, some tutorials, something that will let you earn money early on so that you can actually level up your ship and not die when you sail too far from home.  I like roguelikes.  I play them all the time.  This game doesn't feel like a roguelike though, because with a good roguelike the inevitable unlucky death is something you feel you at least had a hand in and you might do better next time.  This game...I never get my feet under me.  There's no sense that I made a bad decision, because I'm doing what makes sense to me but getting punished with death at every turn.  I can hardly ever get past my third outing before I die or run out of fuel.  I can't get anywhere to see all the wonderful story or the great art.
It is extremely frustrating, because I was so excited to play this game.

This is typical case of good game, bad price.
The story is very vague, and ends abruptly and with very few questions answered. In the beginning, you talk to your "friend" at the beginning and he "hands you the files" for Superhot. Who this "friend" is and how you know them is apparently not important enough for further detail in the story. Then "they" find out you've been playing this game and shut you down. Who "they" are is apparently not important enough for further detail in the story. After a few confrontations with "them", "they" eventually take you in, you kill more people, game over. The story mode can be completed and the game mastered within the span of a few short hours. Even if the story mode of the game is more of a training mode so you can learn the game mechanics before playing Endless Mode and challenges, it should make more sense and try to explain what is happening in the story, and should go into depth as to what exactly is happening instead of being a shallow, self-indulged fps. You might have found that paragraph to be fairly repetitive. That wasn't an accident, it was a metaphor.
The idea of constant bullet time is interesting, but honestly I wouldn't pay $35(CDN) for this game if I were to go back and know how quickly I would get bored of it. You can get a similar affect by playing GTA V in slow motion and 1st person. I've played Superhot for a total of 10 hours, 4 of which it was running idly, and another 1 during which I was playing Endless Mode and challenges.
The Endless Mode is self-explanatory, you play an endless run against enemies until you die. The challenges aren't all that interesting either, as the only new feature the different challenge modes incorporate is an added timer or a hinderance to gameplay, ex. only (weapon) can be used, you can only throw weapons instead of fire them, etc.
The target audience is people that use VR headsets, which is accentuated by your character wearing one whenever the PC's home is visited. This target will probably make more sense when the game is VR-compatible. But no matter what's to come, this game is currently a showpiece for a game mechanic the dev team thought of, nothing more, and is not worth its price tag in the slightest.

SUPERHOT is a game nearly entirely based on its core mechanic: time moves only when you do. When this mechanic is placed in the context of an FPS game, you essentially transform it from an action game into a puzzle game as you carefully weave through a barrage of gun fire, looking for a way to dispatch an enemy from afar. Replays occur in realtime, lending to a feeling of OP badassery.
There's some question of whether this game is worth its price point and I honestly suspect that is going to be highly user-dependent. Are you into speedruns and doing weird cost-effectiveness calculations in your head? Then you'll probably find it worthwhile. Otherwise, you might want to hold off a bit or find a friend with a discount code.

Content; believe it or not after 2+ years in "alpha" dev, the amount of content is sorely lacking. Namely endgame.
Microtransactions; exclusively costumes are pay only, while new heroes/heroines are either 20$ish or replaying the same maps hundreds of times.
Community; there are generally two types of players, those that have no clue what's going on, and those that are farmed and know what's going on. The two don't interact much and if they do the results are often less than fun.

With only 5 hours on my record for this game so far, it can be hard to adequately review it. I've yet to explore even half of the things within this game. I love survival type games, which is why I bought into Rust. Unforunately for me, I play on a laptop (which even without a dedicated graphics card, has better graphics capabilities than my outdated desktop...). They completely redid Rust, and now the graphics are just too intense for me to play the game at all. I could barely handle the original! Plus, there are a lot of things frustrating about Rust.
The Long Dark offers what Rust does not; a game where you don't have to wander aimlessly naked while other players bash you. The Long Dark doesn't currently offer a co-op, and I won't be disappointed if they never do. There's just so much in the game. I find myself truly amazed by how deep I got into it within ten minutes. I was braving blizzards, running with adrenaline pumping through me away from wolves, and giving a triumphant shout whenever I found shelter when I was just about to die.
The permadeath is something that frustrates the player, but also gives the game the sense of enjoyment that it has. You can last for weeks, months even, and have the most filled inventory with food and a rifle, and be completely prepared for a wolf attack--and then a blizzard hits, and you die. And you start over. While it would♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone off, it also provides the challenge a lot of players seek. So far playing on medium difficulty, I've only made it about three days before the cold or a wolf got me.
You're never safe, even if you think you are. I ran into this abandoned dam, and was DELIGHTED at how much food and clothing was available to me. As I was searching a locker, I heard something. A scuffle. "It's nothing," I told myself "The game wants me to think it's something and get me freaked out." Then I heard another scuffle, way closer. I peek my head out the door and this huge wolf is lunging for me. I don't even have time to think about pulling out a flare from my inventory; it's on me, and I'm dead.
I can't wait for story mode with this game, and I can't wait to see what else the creators have in mind for it. The money I paid was well spent.

The name Limbo is an honest introduction to this game as a whole.
Like limbo, for its duration the game is enigmatic, undefinable, and otherworldly with black and white graphics and a film grain, everything in the game animated as black silhouettes against a dreary, lonely backdrop made of shifting shades of gray. It has minimalist but effective sound design, think drippy water and receding footsteps, or a few flies buzzing at you. It's not full on horror, but it's a beautiful and perfect feeling of dread, wandering and isolation, all quite poetic, which is why critics just sweet talked the pants off of it and made sweet love to it in their reviews.
You'll like it mostly for these one-of-a-kind aesthetics more than for its pretty standard puzzle platforming - you might be disappointed if you are a 'gameplay first' type of hardcore indie gamer. The puzzles all come in the form of risky or deadly traps or mysterious enemies that you have to somehow negotiate or kill. This is as close as the game ever comes to horrific, with some panic of imminent death punctuating the usual thick melancholy.
If you want a short, sweet game that, if played in a dark room with headphones will really suck you in, it's definitely worth it for half or 75% off (I grabbed it for $2.50). Expect to seriously use your imagination every few levels, because though there aren't many parts to the puzzles, their solutions are not always apparent, and this adds to the game's enigmatic feeling. Plenty of puzzles you just have to die through several times to understand, but there are a ton of checkpoints, and this trial and error is intended, so don't let it get to you.
Now that I think of it, it makes sense that the development team is Danish. Its sensibility of *bleh* is very cold, very pretty, and very Scandinavian.

The Long Dark is beautiful.  Both the visuals and the sound design really make the whole game feel very desolate and lonely a lot of the time.  You'll often only be accompanied by the sound of your own breath and footsteps.  The game itself is very fun, too--a huge focus on scavenging and rationing supplies for survival, managing what gear you have on you at any given moment, finding the best place to make a base, etc.  And, the game doesn't give you a tutorial or anything, which may sound frustrating (and can be, for the first bit of gameplay), but quickly ends up giving you an almost constant sense of discovering new things.  That's what most of this game's strength is--you constantly feel like you're discovering new things, walking into new areas, etc, which is helped by a lot of obscured visibility (things like trees and hills and mountains hide a lot of distant terrain, buildings, and the like) and a lack of a map (as of writing this).
That said, there's also a constant sense of danger, either from wildlife, weather (blizzards and snowstorms sometimes appear out of nowhere and can be very problematic if you're caught off guard), running out of supplies, or just plain getting lost.  This is one of the very few games I've ever played where you can get truly lost, in the sense of "I don't know where I am relative to anything on the map".
While this game is in early access, it's fully playable and is already a complete experience out of the box.  There might be a few bugs (I haven't run into any in about 12 hours of gameplay, so at least from my experience it's very stable) and balancing issues, but you can buy this game now and play it and get a great experience.

I've always hated it when people say things like "it's not a game, it's an interactive experience" about the works of studios like Telltale or Fullbright, but if any game deserves to be called an "intereactive experience" and not treated as a game, it's this one.
In my original review, I said: "This isn't built as a game, it's built as a story.  It's a window into not one, but two individuals' minds."
I'd like to amend that statment.  This is a game about ideas, stories, and those who write them, and a story about making games.  I'm not even sure this game is about two real individuals anymore, the two characters might be different manifestations of the same person, or it could all be fictional.  This game is what you make of it, but no matter what, it's an inspiring and emotional tale about expression and creation, and not just that of video games.

LIMBO is a puzzle-platformer that raises many questions. But it is not gameplay related, it is rather yourself starting to wonder these thoughts:
Who is this nameless boy?
Where is he?
Why is he here?
What is going on here?!
The story is awfully vague, only saying "Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters LIMBO". There's not much telling where he has gone to to come to said place..or -what- he has done...or worse, what -might- have happened to him.
Or his sister.
The controls are very responsive and smooth, and smooth fits the animation work of everything in the game. The game has a touch of realism, where you'll die if you jump off from too great heights for example. He is a resilent individual, not making a single human noise from himself, but you'll hear plenty of other sounds like those of sawblades decapitating him.
The game has a very depressing color scheme being in black and white with all these horrific things that can happen to the boy. He can die some awfully brutal deaths such as impalement, crushed under and even get decapitated from giant beartraps.
The puzzles are very clever thought and brings much variety, such as using the dead for your own good or even playing traffic light with a giant bug. At some points you're even challenged to survive a situation in where the majority of your freedom is taken away from you.

Great game, great company which has supported the game through thick and thin. Cyanide has really stepped up and listened to the community for improvements and bug fixes and really improved the entire product.
Wow, it's been a YEAR since Blood Bowl 2 came out, crazy heckin' year gamers! Yessiree bob, cyanide ran a blood bowl 2 world cup, games workshop is releasing a new boxed set. Almost all the first wave dlc teams are out (and were free to people who bought the game!).
Now comes the cold hard facts: Blood Bowl is not an easy game to get into, but it is a fun strategic game. It kind of plays more like a puzzle game with lots of risk management. If you are going to hop into the game you'll definitely want to hunt down a copy of the "Blood Bowl CRP" or "Blood Bowl LRB6" since these pdfs have the entire rules which govern the game and inevitably you'll want to figure out what's going on.
That said the "campaign" mode slowly eases you into the mechanics and will teach you little by litte. I quite enjoy this campaign, it does some cool set-piece stuff with the games, but if you're a blood bowl veteran the AI just isn't challenging at all.
BUT! Cyanide has done much more than release DLC, yes! We've been fortunate to get piles and piles of free updates, tweaks and fixes. The UI has dramatically improved, including grids, skill summaries as optional display pieces, the player roster screen for editing teams was also improved. AND they added options to turn off subtitles, AND prevent the camera from jumping around during your opponent's turn, so now you can actually plan things!
However, here's the cold turkey time, is this game worth the price tag? Well let me break down your options for playing blood bowl these days:
1. You can go outside and meet a tabletop gaming club, buy miniatures and play in a local league making new friends and memories which will last a lifetime.
2. Play fumbbl, a free web-based java client which has all of the teams and over 100 fan-made teams (which are only available in fan-leagues, so you can happily play with only official teams with no fuss)
3. Play cyanide's Blood Bowl Chaos Edition
4. Play cyanide's Blood Bowl 2.
Now, previously, I mentioned that Blood Bowl 2 has more daily games than fumbbl, and this is still true, so if you want sheer number of players in your community then Blood Bowl 2 is the obvious choice.
Yes Blood Bowl 1 has more single player content, but it's been so long since I've lost a game to the AI so I'll admit I don't really care for the single player content in either game. Sure the BB2 campaign is pretty entertaining with all the fancy set pieces (and you get to use STAR PLAYERS) but beyond that, eh, I'll take my multiplayer leagues any day thank you, and boy there are a fair few to decide between!
I hope you do decide to pickup blood bowl, and if you're still on the fence I suggest you look up Cknoor's tutorials for learning the game as it will give you a good idea of whether you will enjoy the game or not.

I'm a big fan of sidescrollers/platformers, so I figured this game would be a perfect match for me. Plus I've always been a fan of this 30's style of cartoons. After several delays, the game is finally here.
As far as presentation goes, it's fantastic. It never breaks its theme, and everything ties really well together. The graphics/animations are some of the best I've ever seen in a 2D animated game, it's very impressive.
Gameplay is a mix of platforming and bullet-hell style gameplay. It's comparable to Contra and Gunstar Heroes, and I suppose a little bit of Mega Man. However, I do feel the platforming levels are a little bit uninspired. Luckily, majority of the game's levels comprise of large-scale boss battles. The boss fights are truly what stand out here, and boy are they tough. It very rarely feels unfair though, so that's a plus. Being able to finish off a boss that has been kicking your♥♥♥♥♥definitely feels satisfying. And for those who might be turned off by such challenging difficulty, there is an easy mode that you can select before each level (which, admittedly, I have not tried yet).
Overall, for $20, I feel this is a good package. The gameplay feels good, albeit with a few minor nitpicks. The presentation - graphics, sound, etc - is impressive. I haven't tried the co-op yet. Unfortunately there's no online support for the co-op, which is a bummer. But it's a really fun time even in single player, and it's a joy to simply look at. I'll be keeping an eye on these developers in the future.

Even as an early access title, this is worth the money. If you love games where you get to pilot a ship with a crew, and you enjoy good writing, this is for you. I'm having trouble thinking of other games like this that don't take place in space. It's honestly hard to place this game, genre-wise, but it shares some  similarities with a lot of ship management/trading/exploration games. If I really had to compare apples to oranges, I'd still say that this game is superior to almost all other titles in similar genres. It's not the best, but it can certainly compete with the best.
The writing is really what makes it. If you're tired of games targeted at 13-year-olds and manchildren, this is probably for you. I cannot recommend this title enough. I wouldn't call it an instant classic, but it's up there. It's close to being one.

-People who prize narrative over muscles, boob armor, and knives that make you go fast
-Anyone who loves Lovecraft
-Anyone who loves Heart of Darkness/Joseph Conrad

I currently haven't made it much past ~100 villagers, at which point the game seemingly already requires autistic levels of attention.  Based on that, I can only imagine that a larger town would become an immediate and tedious grind.
In summary, I think this game concept had a ton of potential that was just impossible for a first-time developer to fully realize.  If you can get it for $2 and pile so many mods on top of it that it effectively becomes a different game, there might be some (fun) replay value there.  I've heard great things about the Colonial Charter mod, and am keeping my fingers crossed that it can save this game.  However, if you're expecting $20 worth of "fun" from the vanilla game, I believe you'll be sorely disappointed.  I'm sad to say I couldn't recommend this game at anything other than bargain basement prices.

Graphics: By 2003 standards, this quite is kind of low compared to Rise of Nations which also released the same year. The ground looks very bland so does the units. (4/10).
Sounds: The music sometimes doesn't relate to the game and when in combat, the music can sound sometimes very awkward. (4/10).
Gameplay: Gameplay is simple, you build small settlements around a keep and your peasants farm/mine by a village, take the resources to the village and the cart will take the resources from the village to your keep (manor). You build troops to kill the other enemy. (4/10).
Level Design: Level design, for Skirmish, the maps are hideous, down right awful looking and a pain to the eye, there is very few limited maps and they all about look the same; some sand here and there, nice bland greenness for grass here and there and splotch down some random stone blobs and gold blobs as well as tree patches. (5/10).
AI: The AI aren't smart but are made simple (nothing outstanding), AI will sometimes derp out and not do what you tell them to do, and when idle, the game doesn't tell you that you have a group of villagers idle. When your troops move about they have bad pathfinding and I realized that my troops zig zagged left and right when moving to areas and controlling large amount of troops is awkward and hard to place into where you want them to perform combat while setting up their tactics. (4/10).
UI: The UI is very small but comfortable to the eye and gives you a huge portion of the map to look at, one flaw that deters me giving UI a 10 is that when hovering over what to build; it doesn't show you facts about the building and doesn't tell you what it does UNLESS you have the resources to build it. And all buildings until you build the presets for and research it, you can't see the building (it's whitened out). 7/10.
Game Writing: N/A (haven't played campaign).
Content Design: The game has quite a bit of content but it feels like it could have a lot more content because it feels so bland and feels like it has a gap with the content (for example, only about 5-6 infantry units you can build and about 3-5 cav units you can build). (6/10).

With only 5 hours on my record for this game so far, it can be hard to adequately review it. I've yet to explore even half of the things within this game. I love survival type games, which is why I bought into Rust. Unforunately for me, I play on a laptop (which even without a dedicated graphics card, has better graphics capabilities than my outdated desktop...). They completely redid Rust, and now the graphics are just too intense for me to play the game at all. I could barely handle the original! Plus, there are a lot of things frustrating about Rust.
The Long Dark offers what Rust does not; a game where you don't have to wander aimlessly naked while other players bash you. The Long Dark doesn't currently offer a co-op, and I won't be disappointed if they never do. There's just so much in the game. I find myself truly amazed by how deep I got into it within ten minutes. I was braving blizzards, running with adrenaline pumping through me away from wolves, and giving a triumphant shout whenever I found shelter when I was just about to die.
The permadeath is something that frustrates the player, but also gives the game the sense of enjoyment that it has. You can last for weeks, months even, and have the most filled inventory with food and a rifle, and be completely prepared for a wolf attack--and then a blizzard hits, and you die. And you start over. While it would♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone off, it also provides the challenge a lot of players seek. So far playing on medium difficulty, I've only made it about three days before the cold or a wolf got me.
You're never safe, even if you think you are. I ran into this abandoned dam, and was DELIGHTED at how much food and clothing was available to me. As I was searching a locker, I heard something. A scuffle. "It's nothing," I told myself "The game wants me to think it's something and get me freaked out." Then I heard another scuffle, way closer. I peek my head out the door and this huge wolf is lunging for me. I don't even have time to think about pulling out a flare from my inventory; it's on me, and I'm dead.
I can't wait for story mode with this game, and I can't wait to see what else the creators have in mind for it. The money I paid was well spent.

The Long Dark is beautiful.  Both the visuals and the sound design really make the whole game feel very desolate and lonely a lot of the time.  You'll often only be accompanied by the sound of your own breath and footsteps.  The game itself is very fun, too--a huge focus on scavenging and rationing supplies for survival, managing what gear you have on you at any given moment, finding the best place to make a base, etc.  And, the game doesn't give you a tutorial or anything, which may sound frustrating (and can be, for the first bit of gameplay), but quickly ends up giving you an almost constant sense of discovering new things.  That's what most of this game's strength is--you constantly feel like you're discovering new things, walking into new areas, etc, which is helped by a lot of obscured visibility (things like trees and hills and mountains hide a lot of distant terrain, buildings, and the like) and a lack of a map (as of writing this).
That said, there's also a constant sense of danger, either from wildlife, weather (blizzards and snowstorms sometimes appear out of nowhere and can be very problematic if you're caught off guard), running out of supplies, or just plain getting lost.  This is one of the very few games I've ever played where you can get truly lost, in the sense of "I don't know where I am relative to anything on the map".
While this game is in early access, it's fully playable and is already a complete experience out of the box.  There might be a few bugs (I haven't run into any in about 12 hours of gameplay, so at least from my experience it's very stable) and balancing issues, but you can buy this game now and play it and get a great experience.

Firstly, it is not even an Action RPG as its predecessors were.  There is no loot.  There are no towns to visit or NPCs with whom to interact.  This is a 100% Action Beat 'em Up game.  It should not have been named Sacred 3, but that is the failing of both Deep Silver and Keen Games.  They should have called it "Sacred Citadel 2" or spun it off into its own IP.
Gameplay is actually solid.  It's not inspiring or very innovative, but it is consistent and the controls are precise, simple, and functional.  A far cry from Sacred 2, this is probably Sacred 3's single most redeeming quality.
The voice acting and dialog are atrocious.  Worthless.  They would have done better to NOT record voices and include only minimal text dialog with as few in-mission interruptions as possible, or just make their own gibberish language like "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" did.
The only similarities to the previous Sacred titles are "Combat Arts" and the Seraphim, with vague references back to some of the original Sacred 1 classes (Battle Mage weapon spirit, etc.).
Don't spend $50.  Maybe $20, definitely $10...but if you pay full price for this game, you're in for a let down.

Ok so bad jokes aside here is the real review.
Cuphead has I would say three major components that make this game in my opinion great.
Number 1: The art if this game is impeccable. I would gladly pay money to watch this game as a cartoon it is that good. The devs painstakingly followed the hand draw cell methods of that era to capture an authentic feeling. This is evident in not only the visuals but audio as well. Without a doubt this is the biggest draw of the game, one worthy of great applause.
Number 2: the gameplay itself is entertaining and well thought out. It combines the simple mechanics of run-and-gun platforms of old (mega man, metroid, metal slug, Mario....to many to list) with enough depth and customization in the form of power ups that provide a feeling of character development. These upgrades are needed as cuphead is difficult...hard....challenging...so much so that this is the third component.
Number 3: It is not a stretch to say cuphead is a tough game. As a purveyor of difficult games (xcom series, dark souls, doom nightmare, etc) cuphead stands shoulder to shoulder in them with raw challenge. At the moment I can not recommend cuphead to the casual, easily deterred gamer. Most platformers are formulated as being 2 parts running and gunning enemies and 1 part bosses. Cuphead reverses this formula. The vast majority of the game is boss battles, and they are tough. Each boss has unique attacks and stages that will test your skill in every way, dodging shooting parrying at a level that requires near perfection to be successful. Each boss has multiple stages where they evolve or change into more difficult versions of themselves and the weapons they use against you. You will die a lot....a lot. You will die just to learn the rotation and garner some sort of pattern, you will die even when you know all these things because of the sheer skill required in this game. Which brings me to the final review.
Components number 1, and 2 are undoubtedly positive ones which make this game great. However number three can be the only perceived negative aspect. Based on the only negative reviews I have read (52 at time of writing compared to the 2,000 or so positive ones) the vast majority of these negative reviews come from the sheer difficulty of the game. Personally I relish the challenge but do not blame those who would avoid this game for it. If xcom had iron man mode as its only mode, or doom nightmare, etc it would be easy to see why these games would limit there audience. My only critique on this game would be to include an easy mode. While boss battles offer a simple and regular mode (I do not want to know what lies beyond regular) the only way to beat the game is to collect contracts, which can only be collected on regular difficulty. The addition of an easier mode that would allow one to still beat  the game would be a welcome addition. Further including more run and gun levels, which are both incredibly fun, and provide a way to view the amazing artwork of cuphead while serving as a nice breather between the countless bosses to be faced.
Overall this game gets a highly recommended 5/5
With the small warning.....those who are easily frustrated or defeated, look elsewhere.

This has got to be one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. Gameplay was good, the environment is literally breathtaking, and the story is magnificent.
You play as Jack, whose plane goes down in the middle of the Atlantic ocean near a lighthouse. The lighthouse is actually the gateway to the underwater city of Rapture. Or it ruins, anyway. Rapture, the brain child of industrialist Andrew Ryan, was supposed to be a paradise for the common man, but not all was well in paradise. Civil unrest, class warfare, and add unmonitored sciencetific discoveries to the mix and things got real very fast. Plasmids, tonics that give humans super powers so to speak, is powered by a substance called "ADAM". But it destroys the mind with repeated abuse and now it's aftermath roams the streets.
When you arrive, you seem to be at the tail end of the Rapture Civil War (a war between classes which quickly turned into a game of "Who Can Splice More") and you are almost immedietly contacted by a man named Atlas, who promises to help you escape Rapture.
