The game's graphics are relatively good, and the dragon designs are identical to the ones seen in the movies and from the TV show How to Train Your Dragon: Riders of Berk. However, I've noticed quite a few bugs and glitches occuring in the game- things such as when your dragon first gets fed as a baby, it may disappear and you have to enter and exit a building to make them reappear again. It also includes the quest arrow, it is indirect and doesn't point the right direction when you fly and land on the ground; another problem is one of the quests in which you need to deliver 3 black whool fleeces to Hiccup. The quest arrow immediately points to the first fleece, but you cn never find it because the arrow is constantly rotating and even when it stops nothing is found in the direction that it's pointing. (As you can see, there are quite a few bugs with the quest arrow, there are a few more problems with another few quests but this review isn't going to focus on that.) I'd also like to bring up that you simply cannot beat the game unless you pay REAL money towards the game, and almost every function in the game requires money; such as: The Fish Trap, other dragons besides the first 4, customizing your dragon after it's 'eveolved', and most items and/or decorations for your character and farm. I find this looks quite bad, if this is a children's game, why make it so that you MUST use money to finish the game- it practically tricks kids into having their parents use their credit card for this. In full, it's practically a wallet trap, it sucks the money out of your credit card because your kid wants to finish the game.
In full however, the game offers quite a few quirky, little dragons for any player to enjoy such as the Typhoomarang, the Boneknapper, and the Thunderdrum. There are many other dragons for players to choose and enjoy, and even if you choose not to pay you can choose from four of the original dragons- the Deadly Nadder, the Gronkle, the Monstrous Nightmare, and the Hideous Zippleback. You can choose 3 main colors to customize your dragon once it reaches the next of it's stages: Hatchling at levels 1-4, Teen levels 5-9, and Adult levels 10-Any. I've found the optimum gaming factor in the game is once your dragon reaches level 10, and once it can fly.
I have to say, this game needs alot of work, but since it's still a generally new game- it can still change to what it's users and players want. With this said, I hope the wallet trap fiasco gets sorted out, as well as the few bugs and such in the game. Besides this, I think the game is a game one can play as a kind of hobby. You can plant, water, and harvest plants every now and then, and you can do a few quests here and there- but even if you're a hardcore gamer you can still play because the game tends to reform to either and both. In full, I'd recommend this game to people willing to dedicate at least 45 minutes per session, money, and patience towards the glitches.

Very atmospheric, and the writing is top notch (as expected; I've played Fallen London for years now). It's an exquisite role play that always gets me thinking like a captain.
The intermittent music sets the tone perfectly, and the art style is beautiful in both its intricacy and simplicity.  The islands make it exciting to explore, while the empty expanses with only the company of the steam engine's chugging instill a degree of loneliness I never could have expected. Even with the top-down view, the sight of a pirate ship or sea monster still manages to strike fear into my heart.
The only thing that has me torn is the Merciful/Unforgiving save modes. Playing in Unforgiving mode (autosave only, with permadeath) really adds a level of intensity to the game as fuel and food dwindle. I've sat in a foreign port halfway across the sea, filled with the creeping dread that I may not make it home. The consequences seem all too real, and it's thrilling.
On the other hand, when the last mistake is made and the ship sinks, it's a drag to start over. I especially like the way you "preserve your legacy" when you die, allowing a small piece of your previous successes to carry into the next playthrough, but after the demise of my third captain I caught myself skipping over some early readings I had already seen! It's a shame, since the storytelling is integral to making this a wonderful game. Permadeath works in roguelikes, and even in Minecraft harcore mode, since the world is randomly generated and thus unfolds differently every time. It doesn't go over so well here. Imagine a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book that forces you to read from page one every time you reach a bad ending.
Regrettably, I switched my game to Merciful mode, but with the promise to myself that I may only save when I make port in London. (Perhaps a middle-ground option for a future version?)

THE SHORT
The Good:
Brilliant faction system
Unique gameplay
*A lot* of depth
Massively varied units and tactics
Many paths to victory
In depth economy system
Decent music
Satisfying kingdom-building experience
Tons of replay value
AI General Editor is excellent
The Bad:
Buggy pathfinding - can be worked around, but don't expect a fix - the game's devs went bankrupt and it's 11 years old
AI generals can be predictable
Music can be jarring, dull or downright irritating
Extremely small multiplayer community
THE LONG
This is the first review I've ever written for a game, and I usually refrain from writing them but this game holds a special place in my heart. I've played this game since it came out in 2003, and let me tell you it is one of the best RTS games there is. The level of freedom in choosing an alignment or faction is brilliant and unique, and the replay value, thanks to its skirmish mode, is massive. I have spent countless hours playing this game before it came out on Steam, building massive kingdoms and launching invasions on enemy cities with vast armies. But like all games it has its strengths and weaknesses.
The game is set in a fantasy pseudo-medieval world where all the things people of that time feared and believed in are real. The selection of units is truly vast, ranging from Barbarians, Arch-Demons and Witches to Inquisitors, Archangels and War Elephants, to Arquebus-wielding Gunners, Bombard cannons and Rocket Artillery, as well as less fantastical troops such as pikemen, knights and archers.
Of course, the game is quite old now, so the graphics aren't its strong point, appearing blocky and, when zoomed in, blurry and lacking detail and definition, but who plays games solely for graphics anyway? The art style is not as iconic as other games nor as distinct, but it's certainly not sub-par, and it creates the necessary medieval feel. Building a large and bustling city filled with shops and merchants, with carts going back and forth delivering goods from outlying farmlands and settlements is truly a sight to behold, and is extremely satisfying to just look at especially after spending a lot of time building it all.
The music is either hit or miss, with some tracks being really good and some being really bad, and the way the music jolts around at times can be very unsettling and quite disruptive. The game plays quite relaxing, serene tracks while not in combat, but when your troops start fighting the music ramps up to war-drums. This would have been a good thing if it didn't keep stopping and starting, playing war drums when your enemy sends a lone man into your base (like a scout) and you order your men to kill him. Some of the tracks are too loud as well, and play in instances where they seem inappropiate, such as epic-battle music playing when the enemy sends a small scouting force and kills a few peasants. However some tracks, namely the ones carried over from the previous game Warrior Kings, are very good, and really capture the essence of the world of Orbis.
The Campaign is not as good as the first game, being a series of rather simple skirmish-type maps, with a number of AI generals to overcome on each map. What makes it worth playing through however is the fact that you unlock the maps and the AI generals for the skirmish and multiplayer modes as well.
There are five factions, or alignments in the game (or seven depending on whether you build a Church or a Maypole while following the Renaissance path). These are the Imperial, which features zealous inquisitors and powerful knightly units, the Pagan, which features Demons and savage barbaric warriors, and the Renaissance which has access to the most powerful technology. In Skirmish or Multiplayer modes each player whether AI or human starts off with a basic Manor and several Peasants, and may choose any alignment as they go along, and the alignment is determined by which buildings you construct.
For example, you can choose to follow the Imperial path, building churches, monasteries and cathedrals and you will get access to Acts of God, allowing you to call down meteors, lightning storms and plagues upon your enemies to cause mayhem while building a solid force of troops with powerful knights and longbowmen. Alternatively you can follow the Pagan path, and doing so allows you to summon hordes of powerful demons and use sorcery and subtlety to disrupt your enemies' economy before invading with powerful close-combat warriors. Methods of doing this include possessing enemy peasants and spreading heresy, which stops peasants in a radius around the possessed unit from working until the heretic is killed.
Of course you can also eschew superstition and follow the Renaissance path, the "technological" faction which gives you access to the best economic upgrades, the best unit upgrades and the best war machines, including the truly devastating Rocket Launcher and cannon at the cost of sub-par melee troops, but with ranks upon ranks of deadly musketeers enemies will be hard pressed to actually get into combat with you!
The actual battles themselves in this game are very similar to the Total War games, following a doctrine of "combined arms" - that is, heavy infantry beat heavy cavalry, ranged troops beat heavy infantry and so on. Each type of unit is countered by another, but some units if massed in large numbers can overcome even their counter units, and if you use flanking and the right formations you can beat heavy infantry with heavy cavalry. Terrain also plays an important part in this game, with ranged units benefiting from increased range and damage when firing from on top of a hill, and suffering from greater inaccuracy when firing into forested areas. Cavalry move more slowly through forested areas and when moving over certain types of terrain such as muddy areas and through forests.
Not only are there the combat units, but also agent-type units like spies, priests and merchants. Spies can do a lot of disruptive things such as blowing up gatehouses, committing arson, stowing away on enemy carts then disembarking in enemy territory and spying on them. Priests will protect your troops from demonic influence such as Succubus powers and can also buff your troops with blessings and exorcise or banish demons, defending your kingdom from supernatural forces. Furthermore there is a Diplomacy system that, while simplistic, allows you to form alliances with other players, request for peace or declare war. You can also send tributes to other players to "buy them over".
There are ships in the game but you only get access to them in Multiplayer matches, if you can find one that is. There is no multiplayer community to speak of for this game, however there is a group on Steam that organises games every so often, but it is mercurial, so don't get your hopes up. Of course you could always play against your friends on a LAN.
While there are a few small issues like pathfinding (that is admittedly quite rubbish, but not gamebreaking and can be worked around) the rest of the game makes up for it. The way you build a kingdom, choosing your alignment as you go along is totally unique and I haven't seen this kind of thing in any other RTS, and the depth of the factions with all their little ins and outs are superb. The music could be better, or rather better implemented and the pathfinding is very weak, but the game is deep, with tons of replay value trying out the different alignments and then trying different tactics with each alignment, using pike & shot formations, artillery batteries, demonic hordes, massive formations of knights or disrupting your enemy with espionage and subterfuge.

Ah, sunless sea. How many hours have I wasted wandering from shore to shore, hauling rocks for a living?
This is a newer review, hence I would like to note early that the timed based system is now replaced with a real time attack system where most of it is sitting staring at the enemy and waiting for your cannons to equip. I would personally have prefered to have my cannons loaded and ready for fire, but such is the world of Sunless Sea. The game is very close to a horror game of a lonely little captain and the crew adriff in a vast and unforgiving ocean surrounded by monsters and being driven insane by the fact that even the very crewmate that mans the ships could simply be waiting for the right moment to rip off your face and assume your position as captain as the thing that now lives inside of your skin slowly chew away at your trusted officiers.
I recomended this game out of personal enjoyment, but I feel it also necessary to warn you about the game. The nitpicks I have with the game is simple: the game has nearly no link between narrative and gameplay.
What I mean by this is simple: you start off the game with what might as well be a bamboo raft for all the monsters and enemy ships in the game care. The world of Sunless Sea is beautifully rich in narrative, but following any threads of narratives is nearly impossible between trying not to be sunk by a brigade of crabs and trying to keep track of which islands have to be visited next, to the point where I arrive at islands at the end of the world having completely forgotten not only the story, but also what I wanted to do to get there in the first place.
The world is expansive, the atmosphere is lovely, and the music can swing anywhere from the energetic sounds of cutlass clashing atop a ship's deck to the ballard with a lovely countess in a ballgown to the raspy and bonechilling sounds that seem to rake over your very bones. All of this is lost, however, because the narrative does not reward you nearly as much as menial tasks. I made more from a single trip of hauling stones than three journeys right across the edge of the world and all I did was run across a few pirates which were barely a challenge. Trying to pursue narrative in this game is like showing up to an attack dog show with strips of bacon tied to your scrotum to get 500 bucks of betting money from your best pal. Bold, yes, and even exciting, but it will quickly turn humiliating, unbearably painful, and at the end of it all you will only be missing something important. After the second week sitting in the hospital bed you'll start to wonder whether or not the 500 bucks and the hospital bill that your insurance company refuses to pay out was worth it all when you could make about the same amount after about a week of hard work without all of the "peeing out of a tube for the rest of your miserable life" business. And that is the same thing I felt after about my 5th death and retry. Oh, didn't I mention that before? If you ever happen to die anywhere in your journey of EXPLORING THE ENTIRE WORLD FULL OF THINGS THAT WANT YOU DEAD the game expects you to start over from the beginning. I'm not talking save scumming, I'm talking losing 5 hours of playtime because you miscalculated the amount of fuel you'll need because you didn't want the game dancing on top of your hold calling you a loser.
Even after all of the rock hauling at which point I bought the largest and strongest ship in the game, the game still insisted on being annoying! After I got a boat that didn't cave into its own weight because it can't outrun a crab, the whole survival horror aspect of the game vanished because the new boat I got could ram into a living iceburg around fifty times without sinking and after it all, the one that would be ripped to shreads, broken into two, and sunk to the bottom of the cold sea would be the iceburg and not me! The cold lonelyness vanished because even the bloodless roars of all of all of the sea monsters could not make me feel fear when I'm sitting behind an arsenal that could singlehandedly sink the entire British navy and the entirety of Britain along with it!
So you may be wondering why, despite all of my compalints, I am still recomending this game. It's quite simply because its a damn good game!
The narrative, though poorly implemented, is beautifully savory. The game is beautiful as I have said and shall continue to repeat. This game is simply a gem that the souless tripple A gaming industry has become after pumping the thriteen thousanth brownish FPS shooter out of a cootch that is so overused and dried that it could be replaced by a mound of sand from the Saharan desert and, and let's be fair here, it will probably still feel fresher! Sunless sea may not have started in a good place, but I could not see a place where corners have been cut. It is a game that shows that the creators poured their sweat and heart into making their creation as good as can be even when it would have been cheaper to have gone half way and none of us would be wiser. Its clunky mechanics and ricketty conceptualization may be far from a flawless ore, but the effort and time that must have went into polishing it from there has made this game shine brighter in my eyes than any overpriced military game that has come out of the tripple A in the recent years. And for that, I'll say that they deserve your attention.

I'll be straight with you here: I'm not sure what I want next in life. I do know that I want more, that I need to keep aspiring to things, and I think life should have its fair share of excitement, of passion, of burning desires and glorious fulfilment. Inside me, very quietly, very determinedly, I strive.
So, philosophically, I'm somewhat at odds with Banished. It's not really a city-building game so much as a village-maintaining game, a game of modesty - even mundanity. Progress is slow, drama is rare and the day-to-day lives of those whose homes you watch over are mostly lives of hardship and hunger.
There are no great goals to work towards; there's no endgame or campaign. There doesn't necessarily need to be, mind, because it's often a struggle just to get by. Banished is a survival sandbox. It's harsh. The reward for success is another year scraping at the earth, chopping firewood or tending a flaming forge. Sometimes, a mother dies in childbirth. So it goes.
Each game begins with a handful of villagers, a limited stock of supplies and seeds, a new procedurally-generated map and a few months before winter sweeps in. Land must be cleared, plots laid out and those first, most critical buildings constructed. Villagers will need homes, they'll need woodcutters to supply kindling, a blacksmith to make them tools, crops to fill their aching bellies.
An interesting way to tell a story. I wasn't compelled by this story in particular but it's still worth trying out if you want to see how this sort of thing could work.

Banished is an indie town building simulation from Shining Rock Software. Banished is one of the best simulation games out there.
In Banished you play to manage some people who were banished from their homeland because of something, it doesn't really matter because what you need to do is to do everything in your power to make sure these outcast can survive and build a new society of their own. Something like that I think. Either you become a great mayor of a great town, or you just simply build a small ghost town.
Banished gameplay are so great, I can say it is quite so realistic as simulation games can get. You still can't do everything, but when you start playing Banished you're gonna realize that not everybody can be a Mayor. The citizen in Banished will age, they will grow old and die so expanding and balancing the population is important. Citizen can also die because of acccident too, for example a miner can die because of cave in or crushed by a rock, I even encounter one event where one of my citizen is murdered! Damn! Anyway, resources gathering in Banished is quite complex, there is no skill trees but production chains, and it is important to manage those production chains well or all hell break loose. To gather food we can build farms or pastures, do hunting or gathering some berries or roots in the forest, and even fishing. You can even replant the forest so you will never run out of woods. There is also trade, where you get most of your crop seeds and new pasture breeds. Then there's also disasters, a disease breakout (people will not turn into zombies however), or your own disasters because your people are starving or freezing to death. Lots can happen so keep on your toes.
In terms of graphics, Banished doesn't have very advanced graphics, but it's beautiful enough. The graphics is sufficient enough for you to enjoy Banished and forgot to check on the clock. Performances are also good, just keep in mind if you want to build a big town, you better have more RAM, just like any other simulation games.
Banished also has a workshop support for mods. Yes MODS! There are couple of mods that adds even more production chains to Banished, even more building and even more resources to gather. Some even has decoration thing for your town. The best mod for Banished currently is the Colonial Charter mods, which add almost everything to Banished that sometimes it feels like an expansion pack. You can also make your own mods that fits your gameplay.
Overall, Banished is a great simulation. If only they add at least a little combat gameplay it could be great, It doesn't have to be a war but something like repelling bandits attack, pirates, looters or something. But that's just my thought. I really recommend Banished for you all simulation gamers.

I seldom write reviews for games, but I feel compelled to write one for this stellar game.
I bought this game back when it came out originally, and I have played it frequently over the years. So while my steam hours are very low, I can assure you I have sunk a significant amount of time into this game over the years!
WK:B is/was the sorta-sequel to Warrior Kings.It's essentially just a more polished version which added better MultiPlayer options, more AI options and a Skirmish mode.
The Good:
WK:B has some fantastic concepts that still make it stand out to me today.
You don't choose a faction when you start a round. Rather as you play, you choose which tech you want to explore which opens up/removes some options from the tech tree. This is great for multiplayer because unlike virtually all RTS, you never know for certain what your opponent will be building in each round.
The variety of troops/vehicles is great, and there are some very entertaining units.
Supply lines are implemented in a way that heavily affects your strategy. In order to actually support your eventual army you need villagers working in your villages collecting goods, which are then need to be transported via wagon back to your home base for use. (Which all happens automatically). The actual wagons themselves can be attacked and destroyed/looted by the enemy. Certain troops (projectiles) will need ammo during ammo from Supply Wagons, which eat away from your resource pool.
Villagers that go and collect wood, stone and gold actually cut down trees, and eventually will remove them from the map, which not only looks cool but adds more strategy.
If you go the pagan route in the tech tree, you can build a giant wickerman and while sacrificing your peasants at its burning feet release a giant red demon (Abidos) that runs around the map hunting your opponents.
It is possible to play this multiplayer over the internet via a virtual LAN (via hamachi or something like that), which is probably why this is being listed as Single Player as you can't play directly via steam.
There is a ton of maps in the game. (They have to be unlocked in the campaign before you can play them in skirmish mode though)
The Bad:
You can't play multiplayer without messing about with a VPN.
It's old, and while there is a mod to allow better resolutions, it doesn't look good by 2014 standards :)
There are lots of little glitches in the game that can be frustrating. Mostly around pathing for your troops. There is a formation feature, but its not very well implemented.
As with most RTS, the AI doesn't have much I (intelligence). So after a while you will find it hard to be challenged unless you are outnumbered by opponents.
This one could be good/bad depending on what you are looking for, but a full game on a large map with several human opponents can last for a long long time! (On the bright side, you can save the game and return to it another time)
Bottom Line - At it's core this is a great strategy game. If you love RTS and missed this one when first came out, give it a shot! (Make sure you enable "Free Look" in the options, which allows you full camera control (mmb) rather than the silly default camera view)

With only 5 hours on my record for this game so far, it can be hard to adequately review it. I've yet to explore even half of the things within this game. I love survival type games, which is why I bought into Rust. Unforunately for me, I play on a laptop (which even without a dedicated graphics card, has better graphics capabilities than my outdated desktop...). They completely redid Rust, and now the graphics are just too intense for me to play the game at all. I could barely handle the original! Plus, there are a lot of things frustrating about Rust.
The Long Dark offers what Rust does not; a game where you don't have to wander aimlessly naked while other players bash you. The Long Dark doesn't currently offer a co-op, and I won't be disappointed if they never do. There's just so much in the game. I find myself truly amazed by how deep I got into it within ten minutes. I was braving blizzards, running with adrenaline pumping through me away from wolves, and giving a triumphant shout whenever I found shelter when I was just about to die.
The permadeath is something that frustrates the player, but also gives the game the sense of enjoyment that it has. You can last for weeks, months even, and have the most filled inventory with food and a rifle, and be completely prepared for a wolf attack--and then a blizzard hits, and you die. And you start over. While it would♥♥♥♥♥♥anyone off, it also provides the challenge a lot of players seek. So far playing on medium difficulty, I've only made it about three days before the cold or a wolf got me.
You're never safe, even if you think you are. I ran into this abandoned dam, and was DELIGHTED at how much food and clothing was available to me. As I was searching a locker, I heard something. A scuffle. "It's nothing," I told myself "The game wants me to think it's something and get me freaked out." Then I heard another scuffle, way closer. I peek my head out the door and this huge wolf is lunging for me. I don't even have time to think about pulling out a flare from my inventory; it's on me, and I'm dead.
I can't wait for story mode with this game, and I can't wait to see what else the creators have in mind for it. The money I paid was well spent.

To begin I've played the Stanly Parable and loved it. So going into this after watching the trailer I was expecting something a little off the wall. It's not that at all, not in the slightest. There are pieces here and there that are almost a little wave to being a little like a game but, inherently should be considered a ineractive movie or short story more then anything.
In all seriousness this game is really a walking narrative, if that sort of thing isn't your cup of tea I'd caution picking it up. Even if you don't find someone who has and talk about it with them. It presents itself in a really subtle way so that you begin to think; maybe not in an extremely interpersonal way but about how people interact and how two sides of a person can conflict with each other. It's a little hard to review this. I'm not sure how I feel about the experience. I feel like I need to look at and kind of reevaulate myself. Reading a bit too much into the purpose of the game? Maybe, but I think it was ment to have plently of different reactions in different people. So my experience could be completely off from someone else.
The Beginner's Guild as a game itself is actually pretty simple and that works to it's advantage. You're given the basic wasd to move around and if there is a change in controls you're made aware, which allows you to pay more attention to the story. The game is well set in way that it flows, how you unravel who made the games, who they are ment for and, what they are ment for. The whole game can be interpreted in so many diffent ways and it almost asks questions for you to answer for yourself.
The way the game wraps up sets itself in the weird limbo of not fulfilling but not incomplete. It's like I just read something personal; like I was standing in a room with someone who was reading a memoire of their life the past few years out loud while they were writing it and just stopped and walked away. Could it seem pretentious to people who play it? Yes, yes it can. Then again that's just one way of interpreting it.
In the end just slap on some headphones and enjoy your ride on the feels train.
Venture to your darkest nightmares and back. Anything's possible.

The Long Dark is beautiful.  Both the visuals and the sound design really make the whole game feel very desolate and lonely a lot of the time.  You'll often only be accompanied by the sound of your own breath and footsteps.  The game itself is very fun, too--a huge focus on scavenging and rationing supplies for survival, managing what gear you have on you at any given moment, finding the best place to make a base, etc.  And, the game doesn't give you a tutorial or anything, which may sound frustrating (and can be, for the first bit of gameplay), but quickly ends up giving you an almost constant sense of discovering new things.  That's what most of this game's strength is--you constantly feel like you're discovering new things, walking into new areas, etc, which is helped by a lot of obscured visibility (things like trees and hills and mountains hide a lot of distant terrain, buildings, and the like) and a lack of a map (as of writing this).
That said, there's also a constant sense of danger, either from wildlife, weather (blizzards and snowstorms sometimes appear out of nowhere and can be very problematic if you're caught off guard), running out of supplies, or just plain getting lost.  This is one of the very few games I've ever played where you can get truly lost, in the sense of "I don't know where I am relative to anything on the map".
While this game is in early access, it's fully playable and is already a complete experience out of the box.  There might be a few bugs (I haven't run into any in about 12 hours of gameplay, so at least from my experience it's very stable) and balancing issues, but you can buy this game now and play it and get a great experience.

Do not be fooled by this game, if you are buying it because you enjoyed Sacred 1-2 and other Diablo-esque isometrics you will hate this game. The classes and world are familiar and the combat is actually fairly decent and dynamic, however the game has changed from an open world explorer with massive character customisation to a linear scroller with almost no customisation and no loot. Some of the pathways and environments are so linear you almost have no room to move your character.
The best way to describe the change is what happened to Dungeon Siege going from 2-3, the disconnect is exactly the same. The open world with quests has become set "missions" in a bound area which you complete, get a score, cash reward and a lackluster item.
Its very pretty, production values are high, fights are fun but it is NOT Sacred.
Oh yes, it has hands down the most painful and embarrassing NPC voice acting and scripting I have heard in a game in, well, as long as I can remember. I seriously considered playing with no sound so I didn't have to listen to the idiotic banter. You feel bad for these little digital people being forced to recite lines that would cause George Lucas to kill himself.
If you have never played Sacred or Diablo and are around age 10-12 and want to bash things, you will probably like this game. I however regret the purchase. =(

TellTale's Batman, in it's first episode has shown it's promise and uniqueness compared to previous titles from TellTale. The game effectively puts you into the role of not only Batman, but Bruce Wayne, as you have to worry about the reputation of both characters. This is something key and important to Batman fans as it's always been a struggle for Batman, using himself as a self sacrifice for justice and revenge and it has effectively put that pressure on me while playing through the first part.
Here comes the catch. While I would whole heartedly recommend trying it out yourself, the game has been given numerous negative recommendations from steam players due to bugs. This may because of the hardware or drivers they have installed, but it's anyones guess at the moment. I have gone through the first episode with no bugs or crashes whatsoever, but I'm running a very advanced rig on Windows 7 so there are possibilities.
Pros: +Play as Batman
+Play as Bruce Wayne
+Characters feel Unique and not copied and pasted from the Comic thankfully.
+Deeper choices
+Story feels much bigger (Thus far)
+Unique Mechanics
+Catwoman. That's a Pro in itself.
Cons:
-Buggy for others (not me)
-Only 1 episode so far
-New QTE mechanics that need to be learned.
I recommend it to anyone who can buy it, but you may want to wait a couple weeks or so to see if there is a patch coming along for the first episode.

I have never written a review on Steam before. Until this. Let me first confirm that the game ran perfectly on my computer. I understand different hardware configurations may have been problematic, but on my Nvidia GTX 670, it was smooth as butter. Make sure you update drivers before playing the game. Now to the review.
This was the strongest first episode of a Telltale game I have played since Walking Dead season one.  The hard emphasis on the Bruce Wayne persona was compelling and necessary for the development of this character.  While the impact of my decisions remains to be seen, I felt that I truly had some difficult priorities to define.  It is up to the player to determine the level of brutality and vigilantism that Batman displays, and I felt it had a definite impact on the narrative.  The reinterpretation of many popular characters, such as Oswalt "Oz" Cobblepot, made them much more intriguing in this iteration of the Batman universe.
While the animations sometimes display the typical Telltale "uncanny valley" effect, I found them to be a definitive improvement over previous Telltale games.  This is especially evident in interactions with Selina Kyle (i.e. Catwoman). The sly looks that she gives to Bruce Wayne are significantly characterizing. Additionally, I found the voice acting to be completely on point and convincing.
The story, art design, and characterization are top notch in this game. Not to mention the very much appropriate modifications to quick time events and the new addition of gathering evidence at crime scenes.  Bottom line - this is a fantastic introduction to a new and immediately intriguing series.  If you are having hardware issues, sorry to hear it, but once those are resolved, I think you'll agree.

Review: Batman - The Telltale Series
Episode 1: Realm of Shadows
What an episode! This game throws you right into the boots of The Dark Knight and the billionaire Bruce Wayne. This game is a typical Telltale game. Cartoony ish graphics, QTEs and a lot of dialogue. But they have thrown in some "new" elements like som type of detective work where you link two evidences together as Batman.
This game has its own story and does not follow neither the comics nor the films. But I did notice some elements had some similarities to The Dark Knight Trilogy. This game is about politics and corruption that is all I'm going to say about the story.
This game is dripping with imersion everything from the characters to the music. Telltale really nailed it.
The fighting sections is again typical Telltale. It is not like the Arkham games so if you are looking for a straight action game you will not find it here.
Conclusion: A really strong start to this episodic game. A big cliffhanger at the end makes me want to play the next episodes right now. Every choice you make immediately have a major cocequence. Everything from who you give evidences to, to a small thing like to handshake someone. The only "complaint" I have is that Bruce Wayne constantly mentions that his parents are dead and it gets a little bit annoying but this is mostly nickpicking. I didn't run into one bug or chrash.
Score: 8/10 - A really strong start! Can't wait to play the rest.
Episode 2: Children of Arkham
The second episode of this series takes what the first episode built up to and continues the dark and gritty storytelling. This is probably one of the grittiest game that Telltale have made to date. This episode is more personal about Bruce and the Wayne legacy. Is the Wayne family really the family we know or is it something darker behind the scenes? This was more action-filled episode. Especially from the midway to last section of the game.
Conclusion: A great follow-up to Realm of Shadows and it really makes me want to play the rest. It continues the dark and gritty storytelling from the first episode and it brings in a new character from the comics and a new gang that I have never heard of, but looks they were a great addition to the story.
Score: 9/10 - Absolutely loved it! Bring on the next episode now please.
Episode 3: New World Order
Continuing from the second episode we see some dramatic events. We see where some characters are headed. This wasn't so action-packed as the last episode. This was more about the characters and learning more about them. Some characters did a completely 180 in terms of who they really were. But some others you could see what was going to happened. But if you know these characters it does makes sence *hint hint*.
Conclusion: After a fantastic second episode, it slows the pace down from the more action-packed stuff to a more intense episode between each character. Telltale really worked their ***** off to write each character and make them interesting.
Score: 8/10 Awesome!
Episode 4: Guardian of Gotham (Mild spoilers)
Following from episode 3 the drama is cranked up to 11. Bruce is now in an all time low. He is currently seeing his best friend changing into a completely different character. And now he is thrown in Arkham. And now he has to tema up with... Yes you guessed it: The Joker. He was in trailers so it isn't so special. I hope he gets more time in the last episode.
Conclusion: This episode is making this game even darker. Telltale is making an awsome Batman game and they are completely cranking up the drama. I'm extremely hyped for the last episode.
Score: 8/10 Awsome!
Episode 5: City of Light
Here we are the last episode of the season. And this is without a doubt the best episode. Batman challenged with his greatest challenge: taking down the Children of Arkham. Bruce Wayne has to deal with personal loss and take actions without the mask.
I'm not going to talk about the ending due to spoilers, but lets just say it has a MAJOR tease wich makes me want the second season as fast as possible.
Conclusion: The climax exceded every expectations I had for the season. The ending was made perfect and teased us about who the villian is in the next season.
Score: 9/10 As close as perfedt you can possibly get!
Overrall: I really enjoyed this game. Telltale really nailed the story about The Dark Knight and Bruce Wayne. This is one of the best Batman games made! Is it better than the Arkham games? Thats debatable, but this game is absolutely awsome and I highly recommend it to every Batman fan out there.
Overall score: 9/10 A must have!

Nevertheless, the game did its job and scared the crap out of me. That's why I'll ultimately recommend it.

A Hat in Time is one of those kickstarted games that took years to develop and release, but the wait was worth it as it completely delivers.
It's a 3D platformer-collectathon, inspired by the N64 and Gamecube 3D platformers, games like Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine, The legend of Zelda: The windwaker, Banjo kazooie/Tooie, it's all here and the similarities are as clear as water.
The star of the game is this unnamed girl with a fancy top hat, who loses the time pieces that she uses as fuel for her spaceship in a confusing accident with a member of the mafia from the planet she was flying by. After landing on mafia town she meets this red-hooded girl with a mustache, who only seeks to bring justice to this world, but this friendship only lasts until the mysterious mustached girl discovers the powers hidden in the time pieces.
A Hat in Time characters are full of charm, the mafia members are just a bunch of dummies and some of them don't even know how to react when a child confronts them. The red hooded mustache girl has a brave personality, her goal to bring justice to the world and defeat the mafia is a mentality that fits, after all she's just a child.
The characters from the next chapters are amazing too, full of personality, you just can't not love the conductor, even if he's just a prick to you.
The main character Hat Kid is full of charm, this cute "silent" protagonist shows a lot of expressions in her movements and actions, stuff like the using her finger as a gun in the detective level, her warcry agaisnt the mafia when she gets her umbrella and her reaction to the last contract in chapter 3 are some of the cutest moments this protagonist has.
The game controls are fantactic, Hat Kid controls like Mario in SM64 but with a fully functional controlled camera, you can wall jump, slide, double jump, slide after a double jump for maximum distance, you can cancel your air-slide by jumping and fix your landing, etc. The combat in this game isn't super deep, you got your close range umbrella to hit enemies and your homing glide attack, but at the end you don't need more than that as combat isn't this game main point.
The game music is top notch, they fit really well in each chapter and fight, won't go deep into this category to avoid spoilers, but themes like Picture Perfect, Crazy Science Owls, Clock Towers Beneath the Sea and Your Contract has Expired are some of the best tunes you'll find in this game, and each of them fit so well in their chapter/level.
+Amazing Gameplay, you have full control of Hat Kid and the camera around her
+Great music
+Fun levels, each with different and very unique objectives, you'll never play the same level twice.
+Devs are actively listening to the community, releasing patches and changes constantly.
+Modding support, if the main game and hats weren't enough for you then this will give you a lot of content to explore.
-Game is pretty short, two extra chapters will be released in the future, but currently the game can be easily completed in a few hours.
-The game has quite a few bugs, thankfully most of them are just graphical and animation errors
-The game ending isn't very fulfilling (This may change with the release of the next chapters, but we'll see, until then it just doesn't feel like a good end to the story)
A Hat in Time is one of the best platformers I've played and one of the best games that has been released in this year, if you grew up playing the firsts 3D platformer games from the N64 and PlayStation era, you'll love this game, definetly a must buy, and if you didn't, still, give this game a try, the cute-sie aesthetics and the character's charm is something that everyone with good taste will appreciate.
Definetly a must buy.

Okay, before I rant on about this, let me say this: This review is in no way affected by the fandom, and I do not rate a game by it's fandom.
First off, the gameplay. The controls feel awkward. This takes place in a first person perspective, right? In order to turn your head, you have to move the cursor to the different side of the screen. Which makes for poor sensitivity. Don't bring the controls of console FPS games to the PC, there's a good reason why console FPS games suck: There's a deadzone.
Also, the buttons, for the lights, are very awkward. In order to leave a light on, I'd expect to hold it, but no. You have to use it like a toggle. Sometimes, I find myself wasting power by turning and forgetting to click to turn off the light.
Oh, and the laptop, don't get me started on the laptop. In order to pull it out, you have to hover the mouse over it. Sometimes, if I move over to the other door to check, I accidentally pull the laptop out, then I "die".
The graphics look awful. Why is it that it looks like the background is just a wallpaper wrapping the inside of a tube. It looks distorted and disorienting. Also, even though the game plays in 1080p on my monitor, it looks like 480p.
One of the worst things in here is the lack of settings or pause. If you can't see crap, then too bad, you're going to have to deal with the automatic gamma correction. Need to take a crap in the middle of a game? Pressing ESC will only shut the game down.
Also, everyone says it's scary. I think the enemies look plain dumb. And if you happen to get screamed at by one of them, I don't get a heart attack, they just make me angry. It just plays the same old trope of something screaming at you from a poorly lit room. How original.
I give it a 30%. It's terrible. Save your money and buy a better horror game, like System Shock 2, Doom 3, or I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream. Those games are actually scary, and if you surgically removed their spookiness, they would still be fun.
By the way, I think the sequels are bullcrap too. They made so many of them in a short amount of time. Three games in seven months. And they all play similarly to each other. You know how people on the internet complain about Call of Duty having too many repetitive sequels released every year? Imagine if they done that for every 2.33 months. At least Call of Duty is somewhat fun compared to this garbage, by far I'd rather have CoD than FNAF. At least CoD has a redeeming factor for being a game: Gameplay. FNAF has neither of the two redeeming factors: Gameplay or story.

Banished is an indie town building simulation from Shining Rock Software. Banished is one of the best simulation games out there.
In Banished you play to manage some people who were banished from their homeland because of something, it doesn't really matter because what you need to do is to do everything in your power to make sure these outcast can survive and build a new society of their own. Something like that I think. Either you become a great mayor of a great town, or you just simply build a small ghost town.
Banished gameplay are so great, I can say it is quite so realistic as simulation games can get. You still can't do everything, but when you start playing Banished you're gonna realize that not everybody can be a Mayor. The citizen in Banished will age, they will grow old and die so expanding and balancing the population is important. Citizen can also die because of acccident too, for example a miner can die because of cave in or crushed by a rock, I even encounter one event where one of my citizen is murdered! Damn! Anyway, resources gathering in Banished is quite complex, there is no skill trees but production chains, and it is important to manage those production chains well or all hell break loose. To gather food we can build farms or pastures, do hunting or gathering some berries or roots in the forest, and even fishing. You can even replant the forest so you will never run out of woods. There is also trade, where you get most of your crop seeds and new pasture breeds. Then there's also disasters, a disease breakout (people will not turn into zombies however), or your own disasters because your people are starving or freezing to death. Lots can happen so keep on your toes.
In terms of graphics, Banished doesn't have very advanced graphics, but it's beautiful enough. The graphics is sufficient enough for you to enjoy Banished and forgot to check on the clock. Performances are also good, just keep in mind if you want to build a big town, you better have more RAM, just like any other simulation games.
Banished also has a workshop support for mods. Yes MODS! There are couple of mods that adds even more production chains to Banished, even more building and even more resources to gather. Some even has decoration thing for your town. The best mod for Banished currently is the Colonial Charter mods, which add almost everything to Banished that sometimes it feels like an expansion pack. You can also make your own mods that fits your gameplay.
Overall, Banished is a great simulation. If only they add at least a little combat gameplay it could be great, It doesn't have to be a war but something like repelling bandits attack, pirates, looters or something. But that's just my thought. I really recommend Banished for you all simulation gamers.

To begin I've played the Stanly Parable and loved it. So going into this after watching the trailer I was expecting something a little off the wall. It's not that at all, not in the slightest. There are pieces here and there that are almost a little wave to being a little like a game but, inherently should be considered a ineractive movie or short story more then anything.
In all seriousness this game is really a walking narrative, if that sort of thing isn't your cup of tea I'd caution picking it up. Even if you don't find someone who has and talk about it with them. It presents itself in a really subtle way so that you begin to think; maybe not in an extremely interpersonal way but about how people interact and how two sides of a person can conflict with each other. It's a little hard to review this. I'm not sure how I feel about the experience. I feel like I need to look at and kind of reevaulate myself. Reading a bit too much into the purpose of the game? Maybe, but I think it was ment to have plently of different reactions in different people. So my experience could be completely off from someone else.
The Beginner's Guild as a game itself is actually pretty simple and that works to it's advantage. You're given the basic wasd to move around and if there is a change in controls you're made aware, which allows you to pay more attention to the story. The game is well set in way that it flows, how you unravel who made the games, who they are ment for and, what they are ment for. The whole game can be interpreted in so many diffent ways and it almost asks questions for you to answer for yourself.
The way the game wraps up sets itself in the weird limbo of not fulfilling but not incomplete. It's like I just read something personal; like I was standing in a room with someone who was reading a memoire of their life the past few years out loud while they were writing it and just stopped and walked away. Could it seem pretentious to people who play it? Yes, yes it can. Then again that's just one way of interpreting it.
In the end just slap on some headphones and enjoy your ride on the feels train.

One of the classical overly-explosive action games, this game is a great throwback to the old 80's Rambo-esque movies and mixes traditional third person destruction derby with open world (group of islands) adventure. A tropical GTA of sorts. The basic gameplay consists of destroying evil goverment's property, i.e. water and fuel supplies in random villages, races with every medium possible and both storyline and faction quests. As mentioned earlier, this game embraces the goofy righteousness and lets you wreak havoc upon both the goverment and its civilians with little difference.
Technically this game is a port from original PS3 game, but from my experience it runs great. Even on my laptop I had stable performance on lower graphical settings and the game looks still fantastic for a game of its age (in my mind that's yesterday).
The positive points of this game lie in it's great map design, freedom of gameplay done right (main story is there to create atmosphere and not to restrict features) and a certain kind of 'comfyness' if you're weird enough to get nostalgic about games of this era. (I could also talk about personal experiences I have when this game came out and I played a ton of it w/ my friend but buzzwords are way cooler.) I think Just Cause 2 does what it does so well that I'm probably never going to buy another game that tries to accomplish the same. (For me this is a big deal, especially since the third part of the series just came out)
There aren't much negative stuff for me to say. The game has it's bugs and flaws, but for me it would be such a nitpick on stuff that didn't affect my experience. The world is so huge and detailed that finding incomplete pieces feels more like an easter egg than letdown. It does what it promises well, but for people who want a more sensible plot and structural gameplay this might be a short experience.

This review is mainly done for Red Orchestra 2's Single Player campaign. The game has the same gameplay content in multiplayer, but with actual players rather than computer controlled AI of course.
Red Orchestra 2 is set on the Eastern Front during World War II between the Germans and the Russians. One of the first things noticed in this game are the gritty depicitions of the battlefield. Graphically it's not technically amazing, but gets the mood right and looks like an accurate depiction on the actual locations. The music isn't anything to rave about, but again it sets the mood of the game by changing the music based on the current situation if you are winning or losing a game. With these two components in hand, RO2 gives some realism to war in a somber mood.
The best part about RO2 is the amount of realism in its gameplay. Weapons in the game have bullet drop and players can be surpressed from gunfire. To get through the game, using cover and the ironsights prove monumental to winning games. Correctly moving from place to place, hiding, and picking off enemies will also prevent deaths from clumsiness if these strategies are followed. While these things are not hard if the tutorials outlining the many controls in Single Player are done, it is something to keep in mind. At its core, RO2 brings a hardcore and realistic shooter that focuses on tactics than pure aim.
One of the poor parts of the game is in the Single Player campaign. In my run of the German Campaign, I had some bugs ranging from visual bugs (ragdolls acting funny like getting stuck and technical ones like lighting issues) to getting physically stuck inside the map. The AI bots aren't too great either, since sometimes the enemy or your team don't contribute to the team at times and sometimes the enemy bots can act funny with their animations being ugly and not smooth like your team. The difficulty can sometimes be wonky by being pretty easy to difficult based on the requirements and balance of the levels.
Red Orchestra 2 is best played in multiplayer with real players however. The Single Player can give a good impression of the gameplay and although it is rough in the edges, taking the game with other players can make for a great realistic FPS game.

If you want very realistic warfare based on both the eastern front and the pacific theater, check this out.
Incredibly realistic and historically accurate, this WW2 FPS uses amazing graphics, high team oriented gameplay and realistic combat statistics to make you feel like your really fighting for your life. (PTSD simulator as people like to call it)
Examples of this is a fear/morale meter, which drops when nearby allies die, lowering depending on the manner of death. If an ally is shot by machinegun fire from an enemy soldier you see, it goes down less. If your friend takes a bullet to the head from a hidden sniper, it will deplete completely. It will also go down when fired at, if artillery or mortar rounds explode close to you, if you are shot or if confronted with an enemy tank. This effects your vision and your aim.
Bullets drop due to gravity and you must deal with fixing your aim when tired out from running.
Friendly fire is always on and trauma will kill accordingly, if you take a bullet to the heart or head, you will die. If you take bullets or shrapnel to the bulk of the body, you will survive but with impairment (arm injury, less accurate, leg injury, slower movement) and can bleed out if an artery is severed or you take to much damage.
All of this can be vey daunting to a new player, so there is a very helpful training course you can take in the game to help you deal with being in a tank or using specific weapons.
This game is highly team oriented, forcing players to act differently when fighting certain factions or playing on different maps.
Certain classes are specialized, such as Commanders, who use radios placed on the map to call in aerial recon or artillery/naval strikes. Squad Leaders can be spawned on and carry smoke grenades and binoculars, which are used to cover friendly movement and set cordinates for the commander to call in heavy bombardments. Light Mortar use a mortar to clearly enemy positions when attacking or to bombard advancing americans into a red mist.
The game is insanely fun and easy to hop into, even more so with friends. Since most of my previous friends played call of duty, I didn't bother to ask them to play a realistic version of the forementioned series, so I play with my little brother, and its simply awesome.
Being realistic and having permanent friendly fire, this game is also vulnerable to griefing, although I have only encountered two so far in my 10 hour career.
Highly realistic, incredible graphics and plenty of maps makes this one hell of a game.
Personal Rating: 4.5/5

Sacred 3 is arguably one of the biggest disappointments in my personal gaming history.  The sequel to its predecessors leaves little to the "Sacred" title series, as it is far different--the "red-headed step child"--the "oddball" of the three.  Unlike the first two games in the hit series, Sacred 3 is a very linear action RPG, and the term "RPG" is held very loosely and walks a very thin line.
The graphics in the game are beautiful, detailed, and the environment rich and fairly interactive, and the combat is flowing and can bring a fun challenge, but it simply is not enough to save this game from the broken chains of what made this franchise so popular.  In Sacred 3, there is no exploration--so put away your maps, and every bit of directional video game intuition you have (or think you have).  Everything is based on a standard, linear, pre-planned map you choose from an overview screen after each level, with no way to go but "forward", and the occaisonal random dead-end so that you can loot that very special treasure chest.
Speaking of loot, this game does not offer loot in terms of items, but only health and energy (used to cast your TWO powers you are able to use at any one time) and gold.  I repeat:  Loot DOES NOT DROP from mobs or foes that you so diligently vanquish like a good little hero.  Instead, weapons and armor (you only use one of each) are "unlocked" when the game says so--usually when hitting a milestone character level or completing a specific storyline mission.
As far as storyline missions go, the story is decent and follows a logical path, but the side quests seem out of place (even for side quests), and the only objective you are ever given is "kill them all"...all of them...again...and again.  And if you are too low for the recommended level of a certain quest you want to trudge through, guess what?  Tough luck.  Keep replaying missions until you ARE able to get to that level to defeat those quests.
While I somewhat enjoy the fact that you must acheive certain character levels to unlock weapons, armor levels, and abilities, the idea in its own entirety seems hollow.  You loot gold, gold buys you skill and weapon upgrades, and you set those upgrades as active skills that you can use (you use one light skill and one heavy skill)--and normally when you find the best combination of skills, you stick with those, and the endless piles of gold you can grind out may as well be valued as worthless pebbles on the ground.
There is no character development, other than the "customizing" of your two skills, weapon slot, and armor slot--and they all fall onto a linear path.  There is no developing character stats, no adding talents, no feats, no kind of character traits, no type of roleplaying element whatsoever.  And if you have seen one area-of-effect skill, you have seen them all.  The characters, while they each have their own personalities, offer very little difference in comparison to each other.
Without a doubt, the game's strong point is its combat and its cooperative playstyle--and it gets old--quickly.  The hack 'n slash button mashing is very similar to the Dynasty Warriors style, with combos, shield breaking, knockdowns, executions, etc.  There isn't much combat variation throughout the entire game, and the fun feel you may have when starting to play the game quickly wears off after a multitude of repetitive side quests.  It's always fun to play with a buddy or three, which is what Sacred 3 offers--and is fantastic.  The difficulty scales to the number of players in the game, and while this CERTAINLY makes the game more enjoyable, there is very little synergy between characters, and it leaves you to visualize a bland series of attacks and abilities being randomly used on the map.
Another neat addition to the game is the use of "weapon shards", which is just another item the player can equip to his or her character--and these shards will add a buff to you and/or your party members, but also offer a debuff.  For example, the Vampire weapon shard gives you the ability to lifesteal on hit against most enemies you will face, with the drawback of making health orbs (health pickups) less effective.
However, these weapon shards, as well as all of the other voices, in Sacred 3, leave most normal people wanting to pull out their hair and throw on music in the background to drown out the INCREDIBLY annoying dialogue.  You are led and directed by a female named Aria, who helps you constantly on your journey--and you often wish she doesn't--as she jokes about every area and situation your party goes into.  Your weapon shards talk back to you, and after every single fight and combo you go through, you are battered with really terrible one-liners by a mage that consistently hits on you, or a vampire that has a "drinking" problem (funny, right?  not when you hear it 100 times...in one level), or a dragon that is scared of everything and literally SCREAMS in fear after every fight.
While the graphics are extremely beautiful, and the combat can be fun at most times--especially on crazy boss battles--it does NOT make up for the features taken out from the legendary Sacred 1 and 2 games...features that, according to the developers, "made the game worse", which is a sorry excuse for laziness and flat-out burglarly using generic propaganda with the word "Sacred" in their game title.
If you are expecting Sacred 3 to be a part of the Sacred games you loved so dearly, then STAY AWAY FROM THIS GAME.  It is NOT that game, unfortunately.  If you go into the game with an open mind, like I did, after reading awful previews and reviews saying this exactly, it can be fun for some hours--and then you can write a disgruntled review like I am, expressing the sadness and anger of being conned by the developers and wishing you had done a little more research before purchasing.
In short, Steam asked me if I recommend this game--Yes or No.  They did not give me a **** NO option, so a simple "No" will have to suffice.  Stay away.

Let's get this out of the way - this game is nothing like Sacred 1/2. Good, there are enough point & click ARPGs out there, and the previous Sacreds weren't all that, anyway.
The system req's should also definitely include controller(s) and a buddy. This game is made for couch co-op; there are a number of game mechanics that don't even function when playing solo.
Onto the gameplay: I found this an absolute blast. The different characters give a satisfyingly different game experience - there's the slow, hard-hitting tank, the archer / crowd-controller, and the fast-but-squishy skirmisher who excells at taking out high-value targets. Then a quite powerful hybrid who can do a bit of everything, and the pre-order bonus char, who seems a bit OP at the start but falls in line after a few levels and most resembles the skirmish character.
Combat is the main focus of this game; there's a normal melee attack that can be chained into a combo, a disabling bash that deals little damage but is absolutely crucial against certain enemies, and two 'combat arts' that require energy, which is regenerated by your regular attacks (the main similarity to previous Sacred games). Then there's a defensive move and a co-op-only battle prayer. I find it fast and fun, but I imagine it would be hell with a keyboard/mouse set-up. It is definitely not just a button masher, there are plenty of situations where chosing the wrong sort of attack spells certain doom, or at least a facefull of sword.
The game plays through individual missions, in between which you are returned to a 'lobby'. No open-world exploration. You can replay missions as often as you like, which lets you fine-tune the difficulty a bit by levelling up in easier areas if you're finding a particular mission too tough. Some of them are quite tough, you cannot simply face-roll everything in this game.
Levelling and looting is 'streamlined' by buying upgrades for gold, which is disappointing if that's not what you're after, but you still get to make meaningful choices in character builds. For example, some weapons emphasize attack area, some damage, and some special effects like knockdown or lifedrain. At some point, you will have to decide if you prefer to defend by blocking or dodging. You can experiment with everything, as the most recent upgrade in each skill line is a free buy-back, but you will not likely be able to afford to just max everything. You get to pick a new load-out before each mission.
All gear and abilities level up with your char, which means armour and weapons look progressively more bad♥♥♥♥♥ but this is mostly cosmetic.
The other major customisation is the choice of 'weapon-spirit': these come with a more or less powerful bonus, and a corresponding flaw; for example, the vampire lets your melee attacks drain life, but reduces your health recovery from health drops. They also frequently pipe up during the game...
So, to the superficials: Graphics are uniformly gorgeous for this kind of game, with lots of detail even in the non-gaming areas. The sound-track is also suitably epic. The (English) voice-acting is excellent, and there is an awful lot of it, but what the voices have to say is... not for everyone. There's a lot of goofy, inoffensive humour, like what we'd get at the gaming table after a few beers. Some of it falls flat, some of it makes me smile (I love the drunk vampire weapon spirit). The use of accents, on the other hand, just comes off as a bit racist - not acceptable and so unnecessary.
It's not a perfect game, and better suited to an hour or so of fun hack-and-slash than to day-long immersive play, but it definitely does not deserve the hate flung at it... If you liked Champions of Norrath, Untold Legends or even the fighty bits of Kindoms of Amalur, this might push your buttons; and though this is not a ringing endorsement, it is miles better than Dungeon Siege 3

Cuphead is absolutely spectacular.
I know that, as a reviewer, I’m supposed to build up to a crescendo when writing a review – but f*ck that. This game is genuinely brilliant.
There has never been anything like Cuphead before. It is a true breath of fresh air.
You honestly cannot compare it to any other game. It honestly doesn't even feel like a game (and that's in a good way). It feels more like one of those cartoons that you'd watch in the morning on the weekends on the Boomerang channel as a kid - only now, you're a character inside one of those brilliant cartoons.
Memories of Tom & Jerry, Popeye, Betty Boop, Felix the Cat, Merrie Melodies and the original Looney Tunes flood your mind when you play this game. It brought back such profound pangs of nostalgia that it honestly brought a tear to my eye.
Cuphead is proof that a game's greatness of aesthetic isn't determined by its polygon count or texture size. This game is drop dead beautiful - even at the game's max resolution of 1280 x 720. If anything, that resolution only adds to the aesthetic. Pictures can not truly convey just how beautiful this game is, it is something you have to experience yourself.
Adding to the beautiful visuals is the game’s soundtrack. Honestly, this is one of the greatest scores I’ve heard in a video game. It’s up there with Halo and The Elder Scrolls – a truly amazing feat, when you consider that this is an indie game!
It’s 1930’s music galore. Everything is covered, from folk tunes and jingles, to the brash and bold brass big bands from the golden age of swing music. The soundtrack, if you’re a fan of this sort of music, is an easy purchase. If someone had made me listen to the tracks from this game and not told me that it was for a game, then I would have honestly believed that they were genuine tunes from the 30’s. They are just as spectacular as the visuals.
And then there's the gameplay.
It plays just as good as it looks - especially if you use a controller. The controls are tight, responsive and intuitive after you play for a few minutes. The calibration is spot on and it feels like a Nintendo-made platformer with equally good run-and-gun mechanics grafted onto it.
It is seriously good. It needs to be with the game's difficulty.
The game is hard. Very, very hard - but in a very good way. It's the kind of sweaty-palmed, white-knuckled, extremely-rewarding gameplay that harks back to video games from the 90's. Super Meatboy is the only other game I can think of that offers that sort of gameplay within recent memory, but whereas the stages in Super Meatboy were your enemy; Cuphead's enemies are its many bosses.
Beating each of the bosses is excruciatingly challenging and you will curse and scream and stomp your feet until you beat that one boss you've been sawing away at and learning his moves and patterns for hours at a time - and that feeling of sweet victory when you beat that boss is pure gaming nirvana.
If you're an old-school gamer like me who grew up on games like Castlevania, Metroid and Asteroids; you'll especially love this game.
It will not be a game for everyone, to be sure. If you’re a casual gamer who likes easier games, then just walk the other direction. There is no hand-holding in this game. The only way to win is to git gud.
But for everyone else; buy it. $20 (or $30 if you get the soundtrack) is a complete steal for one of the best games to be released this decade. You will not regret it.

There has been much written about heaven and hell. The absolute paradise of the former and the absolute pain of the latter are some of only a small handful of human ideas that are immune to hyperbole; our mortal descriptions of such places will never be too much and of that we can be sure.
But what about what lies between? The concept of purgatory is a much harder one to pin down. Thoughts on the concept, both lay and philosophical, have defined it as anything from a second mortal existence to an afterlife of absolute nothingness. If the title is to be believed, LIMBO ostensibly takes place in this in-between afterlife. It may not be hell, but it is a far cry from heaven.
"Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters LIMBO." This lone sentence is the closest thing to a synopsis that the creators have given us. How the boy got to limbo is unclear. Why you must press forward is unclear. But to stand still is to both promise and condemn yourself to nothing.
But after all, LIMBO is a puzzle platformer and the instinct to move forward is natural. The puzzles are elegantly designed and make the most of your limited capability for interaction: running, jumping, and moving objects. Everything feels right and the game plays as a good platformer should.
LIMBO is not content to only be another decent indie platformer, though, as the puzzles very quickly become trials of dread and fear. Death has always been part of platformers, but LIMBO is almost eager to remind you of the pain. In your desire to move forward, you only introduce to your character more ways to die. If you miss that jump, you will fall down a pit and be impaled on the spikes below. You will have your body torn to pieces by the crushing force of a giant bear trap. You will fall into a ragdoll's seizure as electricity fries you. Even the more quiet deaths feel horrible; drowning in water is a whole process of struggling and sinking before becoming still. The screen will linger and you will sit with it until you are ready to press a button to respawn. Do you want to try again?
The hazards of LIMBO seem too much to all be manmade, but they all seem purposeful. It is hard to ignore the sense of malice that pervades this world. The colorless settings and the silhouetted character designs do some amount in making the deaths less gruesome, but only so much. You might find yourself standing still when you get that second chance. To stand still is to do nothing, but to move forward is to create your own hell.
But maybe you do keep pushing forward and maybe you do succeed more often than you fail. The purpose of this boy's search for his sister is unclear: it could be a journey of redemption, or love, or curiosity. Either way, that there is even a chance at success and a chance at relief at the other end of each dangerous trial is, in a way, a promise of heaven. There will be hard times ahead, but the pain is not infinite. To be given the chance to find an answer and reach an end is a small but merciful thing. But before that, the hard times will only get harder.
There will always be ideas about what lies between heaven and hell, life and death. LIMBO has earned its spot among the best artistic representations of such a place – not only through its undeniable dark beauty, but also the fear that a similar world might await us.

Well, a very good friend of mine gave me this for ST. Patricks day and i can say now that most of the negative reviews are fairly wrong, or are just out there to bash an old game. I personally admit the game does look pretty dated after 12 (kinda important to remember that) years. Please allow me to repeat that, this game is actually 12 years old. Give it a little slack on the graphics part. Overall the graphics arent the worst ive seen but im guessing they wanted gameplay over shiny looking walls and the like.
For actual gameplay, i quite enjoyed it actually, combat feels a little challenging, enough to keep me focused, not enough to make me feel threatened once i get use to it. Also yeah, you can only have 2 guns at a time. Would you prefer a ton of guns that are boring and poorly fleshed out or a good couple of guns that feel how one would think they would? The Lawgiver pistol in particular is a fantastic weapon you will always have with you and can do its job pretty well. Personally speaking i honestly dislike the none Judge weaponry but there is probably one that fits your play style.
Performance, my office laptop that runs on windows 8 can manage the thing so im pretty sure people having problems with it are using something the game hates. To be fair for whatever reason my laptop seems capable of running anything short of AAA titles from 2013 onwards, everything prior and after (that isnt an AAA title) it can manage with ease. Back to the game, its overall pretty good if a little short, the Civilian AI is pretty stupid and often will just stand around and get brutally murdered if you leave them there.
Finally the whole thing on the whole is dated (12 years old, i shall never stop pointing that out where relevant) but by far and away not the worst game, and certainly good for some fun, plus it has bot support in multiplayer (i think, actual multiplayer is probably long dead but you can setup multiplayer games with bots when you solo it) as i said before the guns and gameplay are great and all but sometimes you'll be a little (at least) frustrated with the civilian AI, and occasionally your team mates, had one of them get stuck on the stairs and i had to go back for him. I would rate the game about maybe 8-9/10 on the whole, only things i objectively dislike is the civilian AI, occasionally the health system as its kinda weird, and i did have the weapon ammo counter go weird and i couldnt tell whether i had ammo or not, and because i was curious (and quite stupid) i wasted my last magasine finding out, though id put this down to simply not being able to see the ammo counter clearly.

Do you like slightly janky but otherwise well-intentioned games, with a surprisingly lavish and faithful interpretation of its license? Then you've played a Rebellion game before! Dredd vs. Death is like that, it's, like, a first-person shooter by Rebellion. But it's about Judge Dredd! It's also really darkly funny in a way I wouldn't have expected a videogame of Judge Dredd to be - the comics, of course, started as outright satire, so it's always refreshing to see a humorously inept and corrupt Judge Dredd. This is probably unsurprising - Rebellion actually owns 2000AD.
It's not a fantastic game, or even a fantastic Judge Dredd game, when it comes down to brass tacks, but my oh my, if it isn't a bit of fun anyway. It's just so goddarn charming, so I can't say I don't recommend it to fans of 2000AD. If you have a fleeting relationship with Judge Dredd, you may find this is funny (and witty!) enough to lure you in. So, yeah. A tentative but heartfelt recommendation - why not.
