If you're wondering whether this is a faithful adaptation of the source material, the answer is a resounding Yes. You get to wield Dredd's famous Lawgiver gun (complete with six modes of fire) and the control scheme includes a "You're under arrest!" key that gives your enemies a chance to surrender. The game awards you for doing Judge-like things such as arresting criminals and rescuing civilians while you blast your way across Mega-City One.
The campaign isn't all that long, but completing it does unlock lots of side challenges, which in turn also unlock additional content for the multiplayer modes, which include your standard Deathmatch variations (and yes, they have bots) as well as a Dredd-inspired "Judges Vs. Perps" gametype.
The campaign had a few frustrating parts, sure, and the jump physics feel a bit floaty, and the reloading animations seem to go in slow motion, but despite being rough around the edges, I felt that it delivered on its promise of making you feel like Judge Joseph Dredd himself, almost to the point of shouting "I AM THE LAW!" at your screen.

First off, let me get this out of the way : This game is objectively bad, but the following is why I think you should pick it up anyways.
This game is an arcade shooter where the campaign is a means to unlock the more challenging ones. This game is based on the comic book dystopian future of Judge Dredd, where you play as the franchise' namesake Joseph Dredd. In this game's camaign, you fight through levels where you have to not only take down crooks by shooting their guns off or injuring them a bit before arresting them, you also have the dark Judges to contend with, as well as vampires. Exact plot details are lost on me as it gets really stupid.
The game shows signs of brilliance and potential to be a great comic book video game franchise like the Batman Arkham series, but Rebellion ran out of money, and what we are left with is a 3 hour campaign that is pretty unpolished and unoptimized, even on more modern systems. And that's where a lot of the problems with this game come from, lack of budget and time. It doesn't have any great widescreen or FoV options, the enemy AI can sometimes glitch out and do stupid things. As such, I can understand how many could be put off by this game.
On the other hand, this is a budget shooter that costs less than a Cheeseburger combo at McDonalds. Not only that, there are plenty of arcade style challenges that are unlocked when playing through the campaign, and they are actually quite fun. For a budget shooter, this one has a surprising amount to offer in terms of replayability. Not to mention, Rebellion did put in the effort to try to make it feel like a Judge Dredd game. If you are bored and are looking for something quick and inexpensive to chew through, you can definitely do worse than this game. If you are a fan of the series looking for something extra to add to your collected curios, this should at least amuse you.

I don't think I've ever played a game like this, I don't think I'll ever get to play a game like this again. I don't know that I'll ever want to play a game like this again. But that's... I guess that's why this game is worth playing.
It paints a picture. One that's seemingly easy to grasp at first. But you realize, just as you're supposed to, that you're looking at it wrong. That's how it was created. That's what it was created for. It's this step into the souls of two real, actual human beings.
Now for a video game that's unheard of. They're meant to be fake, to be pretend in some way. Video games are for the most part, the reality that could never truely exist. We don't live in a Fallout universe, we can't create building thousands of feet high made of blocks. That's what video games do for us. Most of us. They make us what we can't be. Or they entertain us. Both really.
This... it really doesn't feel like a game. For that reason. I mean it's entertaining, you learn things you'd never think you'd learn. It's not fake. It's not pretend. This game, these levels, are more real than anything I've played.
It's not a game.
I mean it is, but you don't feel that way about it. It connects with you, makes you wonder about yourself. That's what it did for me anyways.
But you arn't reading this to see how I feel after playing this, you're here to find out whether YOU should play it or not.
It doesn't end happy.
It leaves you wondering.
But that's what it's made for, meant to do. It's a journey into the minds, the reality of two very real people. And it hits you hard. It gives you an outside perspective, a view that really you can't see unless it's given to you, like it is here. It's a story. Maybe more than a story.
Some people call it a personal therapy for the creator. I mean I can see where they're coming from. But I, personally, I didn't mind that. I want to understand people, so this appealed to me. I didn't mind the personal request that was channeled through The Beginner's Guide.
So here are some reasons you should, or should not play this game.
Play this if:
You want to relate to the narrator. If you think time spent trying to understand people you'll never meet is important.
If you want to explore complex minds, understand just what pushes these people to do what they do. What makes them tick, what makes them stop.
If you love atmospheres, and want to appreciate ones created from the minds of others.
Don't play this if:
You don't wish to spend your time trying to understand people you will never interact with in all likelyhood.
If you want a world created around you, not to walk through someone else's enviroment, their trials and errors.
If you don't wish to experience a conflict that doesn't really involve you, if you don't wish to relate to the problems of others.
That's all I really wanted to say about this.

driven by their own madness then actual intelligent people.The Game has a lot problems and is by far not a AAA Game but its not THAT terrible as many people wanna make others think.
The Game itself is fairly easy to explain : Its a very simply Isometric Action Game with very little till no real RPG Elements with its focus on fast-paced Multiplayer Action.Basically you run around with a variety of very little combat skills/attacks and try to kill as much as possible as fast as possible.You gain xp and level up`s and you can collect gold(which is your only "Loot") with what you are able to buy new skills/abilities for yourself,your weapons or armor.
The Game is devided into 4 Difficulties in total and has a max level of 50.
The Storymode is not open world,its divided into Missions,which come along with a Recommendation of the level you should have for the particular mission of your choice.
Anyway you can jump into every Mission at any point(Eg. playing a lvl 25 mission with the player level of 5 and so on)
First the game is massively overprized on Steam.So like everyone smart should do with any other game aswell : Go check the Keyshops of your trust or wait for a sale...
The Game itself is pretty buggy : From Resolution bugs till Random Crashes it involves everything.
Graphics are okish but really look outdated,especially textures,backgrounds in general and the very lowres Overlays.
The Soundtrack tho is great.Really nice composed and fitting and definitely one of the best parts of the game.
The Voice acting on the other hand not so much... Partly good,partly wierd,partly really bad.
The Game itself and the way it plays out is somewhat fun.I mean it doesnt have any depth or real challenge but for a one-time run especially in multiplayer its fun to play.
Where it disappoints the most is the lack of inspiration imo.I dont care if its like Sacred 1+2 and I was 100% sure it wouldnt be on any level close to D3 or PoE and i can totally live with it being a better melee combat game but its really sad how less inspiration devs gave into the combat system.I mean when i focus a game on fast-paced action then ffs i have to take care that the combat system is more then just 4 button mash.Involve some Combo possibilites,more skills whatever to keep people challenged or motivated also in single player.
With 4 people it doesnt matter that the fight and skill system doesnt have any substance since its about having some fun but in single player it really bothers me,that its that one-sided and plain boring after a bit.
Thats btw the biggest problem S3 has overall : Long-Term Motivation.Yes you have a max cap of 50 but srsly after you beat the game once (pretty much with level 25 around) the problems with the missions are kicking in.
Basically you can just replay the whole game exactly the same way as you did before just with a higher difficulty.
Challenging/Motivating : Not so much since voiceacting,level design,waves whatever is exactly the same as you played before so that it feels like the additional 25 more XP level where added later to make the game look as it would have a longer playtime.
All in All its not a terrible game.Its a short,fun,multiplayer-focused action-slasher for a few hours.Nothing more,Nothing less.
If you want a Sacred 1/2 Reloaded or a new Dia 3 this is not a game for you and you will end up disappointed but if you can take it as it is it at least gives you some hours of fun.

I plan to create a full video review for this game, but here is a short list of my thoughts for now.  Simply put, Duskers is the BEST sci-fi rouge-like since FTL.
You are alone on your ship in the middle of space with little fuel.  The only thing surrounding your ship are ghost ships, silent space stations, perhaps even the occasional automated store.  The only option left to you is to remotely control salvage drones to explore these derelict ships in search of fuel, scrap, ship modules, and other disabled drones to add to your fleet.
To control your drones you have to type out commands into a console window, or alternatively you can take control of one drone using your arrow keys.  Typing out commands isn't just a gimmick to make the game stand out though, it is a vital tool to learn.  With the command line you can send out multiple orders to drones all at once with ease (once you learn a few more advanced commands that is).
In order to explore these ships you will need to power the ship's systems with your drones.  This will give you access to controlling various doors and airlocks on the ship, which you will need to use to avoid any xenomorphs as you scour the vessel.  Like most Rogue-likes you are going to die... constantly. But everytime you reset the game you learn more strategies about how to safely collect supplies. If you listen closely you can somtimes hear each unique sound various threats will make when they are on the other side of the room.
As you explore the galaxy you will also find various text logs on ships and stations that can be put together to find out what happened to humanity.  Your ship's computer will give you various objectives in relation to the logs you find, which you can in turn complete to learn more about what happened to the galaxy.  The logs are very well written. If the gameplay and visuals weren't already engaging me enough, the story surely sucked me in.  The only story in the game is through audio logs, and for me to say that it's a gripping story means the game has some damn good wrtting.
Overall I can safely say that Duskers is a game well worth $20.  To say that the game is light on content is not entirely untrue, but typing out commands in dozens of different ways and learning to code your own commands (yes, you can CODE your own commands) is more than enough to keep you playing.  I love this game and plan to spend much more time on it.

While the atmosphere is great and the stories are impressed (when they're willing to disclose themselves), the most of things you need to do is to collect enough money to pay bills of fuels and foods. Unfortunately, it's almost impossible to enjoy the progress to keep your ship and crew alive in the sunless economy. Because everything you need are so expensive, and you can only pay them via some few profitable lines terminated at London, your journey would become an endless London-to-somewhere routine and only at few times you can forget them and sail up to other exciting unexplored islands, as a real captions would do. This intolerable fact was discovered when I suddenly found that I spent hours in game to hunt bat swarms repeatedly, because it provides the cheapest supplies and the way to comfort crews' terrors. Trust me, it's suck to see your great journey become a journey of a bat killer, who acts like the poorest bagger to appreciate every coins given by the game system, which performs no economy mechanism but to sell expensive goods to players.
Another problem is you can only keep relations with NPCs during the story lines are opened. After that, they disappeared. You would find that after completing your jobs to convoy them from islands to islands, and enjoy the interactions with them, they would be vaporized at the final stop. Nothing continues the stories while they're actually too short for a game whom should beat other brainless 3D engine demos with great stories, and soon you're wasting your time on the supply and fuel problems again.
And the officers: while they should be your best friends who would accompany you till the end of game, they're actually only portraits. Yes, you can 'speak to them with secrets' to gain some skill upgrading, and try to waste your most precious supply to talk with them. However, they would only give you the standard NPC answers, almost like the famous arrow-in-the-knee. The boring bill-paying routines make things worse, since that means you can almost find no chances to discovery their stories when you need to travel from London to London to sell whatever profitable and report ports to the administration to earn the money. As a result, they're aboard with silence, keep silent, and also die silently with your crew and the whole ship, when you earn no enough money to reduce terrors or pay bills for fuels and supplies. They are nothing like your truly friends in Baldur's Gate or Planescape: Torment, which let you enjoy the game with NPCs' most tiny requests, lies, emotions, choices, stories and their deaths and lives.
Finally, the terrors: I think it's a really terrible thing in the game. Because you would find it's the most expensive goods to buy and the supply is even fewer than others. You can basically reduce your 1 terror with 10+ Echos, but it's so easy to be stockpiled when you're sailing on the zee. It increases rapidly while you leave shore far enough, and would stop increasing while you sail along with coasts. However, it never reduces even when you anchoring in the brightest port, unless you spend *lots of* money to buy drinks at the local taverns, if they exists. Only London provide you to reduce terrors to 50 every times you stop at the port. However, it would add your Nightmare's Strength with no cure. This basically tell you your next travel may explode because the terror would burst with the event to confront the nightmare.
So, what would you get with your $18.99? A game should become the next Fallout with the rich stories and characters, screws up with the terrible economy system and the pale NPCs and events. As an early access game I think it exposed some fatal defects that should be fixed as soon as possible, or it would be a sunk ship under the sunless zee.

Some years ago, London suffered a bit of a cataclysm and fell into massive underground caverns filled with weird stuff. Sunless Sea is a roguelikelike where you play as a captain on the underground sea - or "zea", as the game insists on spelling it.
The game's in early access currently, and I'd been aware of it for a little while but put off by the price tag. Ultimately,
convinced me to give it a try.
In the game, you steer your ship between islands in the sunless sea. You are trying to become wealthy, or gather stories and artefacts to improve your abilities and advance the game's plot. Resources are scarce: you need fuel for your ship and supplies for your crew. And every second out on the open ocean increases the terror meter as you and your crew slowly go mad from fear.
This means you die quite a lot: eaten by monsters, cast adrift by a lack of fuel, killed by mutineers. When that happens, you can retain some things for your next game - more if you got around to making a will.
On the islands, you can pursue various stories, which have frequent checks against your (somewhat esoterically named) skills. There's a lot of writing here, which is unsurprising given that this game is an offshoot from the storytelling game
. Apart from the stories, there is trade, exploration and some (fairly simple) combat.
So is it any good? It's quite fun, it's beautiful, the setting is good, the mechanics are solid. My main gripe is that your ship moves
, combat is repetitive, and opportunities for earning cash are thin on the ground, so you spend a lot of time just steering your ships and doing trivial fights on autopilot. One can hope that this can be ameliorated somewhat by the final version, but I worry that this kind of grindy gameplay is intentional.

Preserve your batteries and hide!! From what I was able to play, Outlast is so far an excellent, truly horrifying game. As you venture through the asylum you will remain cautious around every corner. Red Barrel did an amazing job with the detailed visuals of the game's models and enviroment, as well as the chilling sound design and the claustrophobic asylum that you are given full range to explore, but at your own risk. It's important that you save up batteries for your camcorder, as most of the asylum is dim or without power. This will practically leave you blind in some parts of the game, as you're unable to fully detect the grotesque looking enemies that want you dead. By forcing the player to hide from enemies, this made the game more challenging, but also increased the thrill factor as well. As I watched my enemies through closets and underneath beds, I couldn't help but feel terrified and joyful as I would evade their detection. The idea of playing as a weak character may come off as a bit unpleasent, but trust me it works quite well for this game. I mean you're not Chris Redfield or some other overpowered beast. No, you're just some journalist looking for a juicy story, who broke into an insane asylum, not knowing of the horrors that dwell from within. Unable to really fight back is such a great idea as it adds more tension and horror to the overall experiance. So HIDE!!
If you're a horror fan then purchasing this game should be a no brainer. Get it! I'd even recommend this game to casual players too! Experiance the fun and horrifying adventure that is Outast!

Dungeon Defenders 2 is a prime example of what you get when you take a good game (the original Dungeon Defenders) and try to turn it into a cash cow. A turd - and we all know what you can't polish.
If you can make it past the poorly designed menus without banging your head against a brick wall, then congratulations, you now have to deal with creating a character.
In this revolting mess, you get to pick between a whopping two characters. Don't get too excited trawling through the abundance of stale appearances, or all the other characters and their abilities, because if you want these you will have to search deep into your wallet.
The gameplay is trite and unchallenging. Tactics are few and far between. Gear is the most influential factor in determining your success with various dungeons and difficulties and most of the game revolves around grinding gear. Even the most challenging of dungeons are a cakewalk with sufficient gear. The small number of dungeons in the game are badly designed and lack variety or scope for testing different strategies. There is no challenge. In addition to this, the game is filled with too many unnecessary complications and too much garbage. For example, having to sift through a plethora of junk items after each dungeon to work out what you should sell or equip to make more bag space for the next dungeon.
The bad news doesn't end there. The endless amount of bugs, the sluggish mouse response time and the eye splitting aliasing are enough to make a kakapo question what the developers have been doing in the 5+ years this game has supposedly been in development.
Trendy have tried everything they can to milk this pathetic excuse for a game from charging for characters, pets, appearances and bag space, to equipment and upgrades. These pitiful attempts at stealing your wages would give even Martin Lewis a seizure.
The game has been in early access for years and, judging by the state of it, needs to stay there for a lot more. It showcases everything that's wrong with modern gaming. It truly is hard to find anything good to say about Dungeon Defenders 2. It pales in comparison to the original. I would not even waste your time downloading it.

First of all, the game is not as hard as the critics have made out. Anyone brought up on arcade run and gun games and other shooters shouldn't have much of a problem completing the game on regular difficulty. Getting the A-S grades and finishing the game on hard mode is much more challenging, but I'm not far from accomplishing that after a couple days of play.

As a shooter, it does have a few issues that can lead to some unfair deaths. First, bullets often fly behind other objects in the game world such as large cartoon explosions or other enemies. This is a big no no for any shmup for obvious reasons and it surprises me that the devs let this fault get through to the final game.
Another slightly unfair aspect to the game is the way the EX attacks work; your character is invulnerable while doing the animation, but the second you come out of an EX attack, you become vulnerable. Seeing as the animations often take a couple of seconds, this means that you could start one in safe space, but by the time you come out of it, an enemy or projectile could have spawned on your character leading to some unavoidable damage.
I hope these issues get fixed by the devs but even if they don't, it's very difficult not to recommend this game. Along with Sonic Mania, it is perhaps my favourite game of this year. Great stuff!

If the kind of point-and-click that you like is about gathering and combining items, plus a lot of dialogs, then this could be the game for you, especially if you played and enjoyed the first two Black Mirror games and want to know how the story ends.
My general feeling during this game was boredom and impatience. It started with a series of long dialogs and uneventful actions and I remember wondering if it would ever get interesting. Then things got a little better, but not much, and then had me yawning and rolling my eyes at the end.
Personally, I am more into games that combine gathering-and-combining with logic puzzles, deductions and not too long dialogs, which is why I (who played the previous two) felt disappointed. This game gave me very (I do mean very) long dialogs, 90% gather-and-combine and just five puzzles in the whole game. From those five, three were "remember the image you saw before  and you are done" and only two were logic puzzles. I will not say if they were easy or hard, because that varies from player to player. My problem was that they were just two!
There are a few glitches. I was forced to skip on a "puzzle" (which was no puzzle, really) because the right answer was not recognized, so I could never move on from it. I had to go to the walkthrough to find out that it was, indeed, a glitch.
Now, the story... Oh well, taste is subjective and I can only say what it was for me. Compared to how much I liked the story in the first game and how I was already sort of disappointed by the second, this one really didn't do it for me. They start, as I said, too slow and uneventful, then they try to regain the "creepiness" of the previous stories
but, for me, it was like "yeah, I saw that already in the previous two games". For the last three chapters, they take the player on a rollercoaster of Catholic fervor mixed up with a pagan ritual gone wrong and a spiritual hero on a battle for his soul, the future of mankind and even the very foundation and preservation of the Catholic Church. Religious beliefs aside, I felt that the writers aimed at doing something original and overdid the plot, cramming a lot of long dialogs and clips at the end with very little choice or interaction (save click here, put that there) from the player.
I am not toooo sorry that I got it, as now I at least know how it ends. But I wish I had waited for a better discount (I couldn't help myself and got it with the 20% off release). This was definitely not my cup of tea! But, as I said, if you are into this kind of game, this is a great one, which is the only reason I will click on "yes" recommend this game. The voices sounded very nice to me, and I have to say that I liked the images very much. I liked to wander the castle that I once wandered as Samuel and remeber events from that first Black Mirror, like the sound of the potatoes on the fire in the kitchen when I went to talk to Bates.

This game, since its inception, has been something I'd been keeping a close eye on. Judging by all the material coming out for it, I could only hope that it was as good as everything was making it look to be. And I have to say, after my first several hours with the game, it has lived up to everything I had hoped for it and more. The attention to detail with the visuals, the beautiful and boisterous soundtrack, the fluid, responsive controls, all combine into the incredible game that Cuphead is. And then comes in the difficulty. I personally enjoy a good challenge in a video game and Cuphead provides that in spades. It finds itself in the perfect position of being tough enough to force you to throw yourself against the metaphorical wall quite a few times but is certainly in no way unfair. The punishment for failure is also nothing too, well, punishing, just throwing you back to the beginning of either the level or boss fight, depending on what you're attempting. And the endpiece showing you how far you made it into the level and how many stages were left is definitely a plus. The different upgrades you can purchase also sit on the nice balance of providing you both some sort of advantage and disadvantage so that you can either feel comfortable just running exactly with what you start with in-game or choosing what upgrades might suit your playstyle better.
Overall, the game is incredible. I can highly recommend it and would definitely recommend bundling in the soundtrack because it is straight up fantastic. Everyone who can should pick up this game because it really is worth the wait and money.

Superhot is very unique and offers some fun moments, but it's far from a complete game. The story is 2 hours long, and frankly, very boring. I shrugged that off thinking it wouldn't matter much because the combat mechanics are interesting (time stands still when you're not moving, cool right!?), but sadly, the gameplay started to spread thin after a few levels.
I guess this fits the plot of the Superhot, since the protasgonist is supposed to be playing a VR game that a friend hacked into before it even hit the alpha phase of development.
Here's a short list of my gripes:
1) The AI is terrible. The majority of the levels have "waves" of enemies, so you'll start a level, clear the room, and wait for another wave or two of enemies to appear. I imagine they implemented this because the level designs are tiny and there isn't really a whole lot of room for a significant amount of enemies to patrol. The only thing indicating that a wave of enemies is approaching is a red glow that appears on doors and doorways. Most of the time you won't notice the red glow, so you're going to die a lot, and only progress through trial and error. This gets very tiring after a while.
Enemies either stand still and take a position to shoot at you from afar, or they enter a "chase mode" where they run after you, turn corners willy nilly, and find you and shoot you point blank if you're behind cover. After a while you'll learn to expect the AI to do this, and your playstyle will adapt accordingly. This causes the gameplay to stagnate and become incredibly predictable.
2) The half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥implementation of a story is terrible, but this is just my creative opinion. If you played this game and the story didn't come off as something a 9th grader wrote in a creative fiction class, then lucky you. I happen to think it completely ruins the aesthetic of Superhot.
3) There is no real progression. You unlock the ability to switch into enemies' bodies toward the end of the game, but you'll only use it 5-10 times before the story ends. That's it. You're going to beat every level in the same fashion you did with the last.
4) There is no replayabiity. It could benefit from a level timer, level scores and objectives, and a general high score counter. At least with those types of mechanics, players have a reason to return to levels and take different routes.
Conclusion:
Superhot is cool but it's not worth the price tage of $20+

For me, The Long Dark is the purest embodiment of a survival game I have played.
When I first started on my first play through, I, like you most likely will be, felt a little overwhelmed, lost, and unfairly disadvantaged against a cold and cruel world. Basic necessities of warmth, food, and water provide a constant pressure to “do something”… inaction in The Long Dark is a choice, and it is a choice that you won’t survive.
After a play through or two, I started to get the hang of the game. Part of this is due to an understanding of the mechanics; how to be efficient with calorie density in food, how to optimize your clothing for warmth and wind resistance and learning what is worth “pack-ratting” around the world with you and what you should simply leave behind.
But another part of your ability to survive will be your expanding knowledge of the Long Dark’s geography. This game is not procedurally generated and so you will slowly learn the lay of the land, though resources are randomized through the world so that you can not necessarily meta-game to instant success either.
Around my fourth play through I moved beyond surviving to thriving. It wasn’t enough to make it day to day; I wanted to be ready for tomorrow as well: stocking safe houses in obscure corners of the map or realizing that you’re low on a particular resource (like bullets, or a bear hide) and so you gear up and set out in a new direction, leaving the safety of home with what truly feels only like the clothing on your back.
Eventually you’ll make a mistake after weeks, or months, of survival. It will be something silly; not wasting a bullet on that wolf because you’re sure you’ll make to the building before it reaches you, or freezing to death in a white out because you’re positive your safe house is just a few more steps beyond your line of site.
At first you won’t want to begin another game. Starting over from nothing after you had so much seems like a heavy burden. But between the great developer updates, and the fact that there just aren’t other games that give this same level of pure man versus nature survival experience, will snare you back in for another round.
I highly recommend this game as a great escape from all of your #FirstWorldProblems

I am playing this game in early access right now, and I haven't checked for any new updates, so I might be a tad outdated. That said, I love this game. It's so atmospheric, simply in how it reads and how it moves and just how you feel.
THERE IS A LOT OF READING.
This is very heavy on reading, and for someone like me, who could play visual novels all day, that's fine. In fact, it's awesome! But I want to get that out there for those people who can't stand reading.
Earning Echo's (money) is REALLY REALLY HARD and takes time and planning. You have to know what you're doing... That, or I just haven't found the right method yet, aside from risking life and crew to capture prize vessels. Nothing pays like pirates.
The game implements some Lovecraftian horror in the most beautiful way. It's also very Steampunk, but not in the way that Steampunk has forcefully become today- meaning, brown, gears, and steam everywhere. That's literally Steampunk in a nutshell, which, if done well (I'm thinking of you, Guns of Icarus), isn't a bad thing. This game takes the concept of Steampunk0 meaning ideology, mannerisms, and presence and implements it in that way. It is Victorian London, or what's left of it, sitting in death incarnate. It is a world of darkness, filled with gods and things that you can't fully comprehend, nor will you truly ever. It is dank, it is difficult, and you will go mad. Your crew will want to mutiny, and you will have to try and get more... Or risk trying to lower their fear. It is a time when steam was the only mode of power, because it was all London could afford to get, being derelict, rotten, and nearly eaten alive. That you are alive at all has become a near miracle, and that's no mistake. Monsters in this game can be some of the most terrifying things in the world if you go too far from home, and I can't tell you how many times I've had to run screaming from some kind of horrific island turtle that looks like it's made of things no respectable turtle should be made of. Not to mention being attacked by my nightmares. NOT COOL, YO.
In all seriousness, I love the game, and the updates have all been really helpful. I hope for a little more story and a little more meat, like more pasts, but otherwise, it's fantastic, as is its prequel game Fallen London.

As you've probably guessed, this is a unique game. It's relatable to almost anyone who's been through a depression, or confusion about life, because it deals with something most of us have been through, or are going through. It showcases a very real version of someone unable to find happiness within themselves, and totally dependent on external validation. What's worse, is that the external validation is perpetuated through this game being created.
But that's okay, it's a great reference point for the rest of us. I'm glad it was made...
Though he says people will hate him for this game, it isn't necessarily the case. Because it's so honest, it's engrossing and you really feel like you're connecting with both developers at a level deeper than any game I've played.
The hardest part about after you've played this game is knowing that nothing really got resolved.
I only wish he had figured out how to truly be happy with himself before he made this game, so it could teach others how to come out of it, rather than leaving it at a depressing, non-answer to a very real problem most people today face.
If I found this guy, and he was open minded, I would give him these 3 books:
The Power of Now - Eckhart Tolle (to clear your mind of noise, depressing thoughts)
The Six Pillars of Self-Esteem - Nathaniel Branden (to better produce positive emotions from within)
The Fountainhead - Ayn Rand (to recognize why it's not a virtue to be a people pleaser)

Read this paragraph before reading anything else. The rest of my review is from when I first bought the game at the 1.0 release. I am now reviewing it a week later, and some improvements/discoveries have occured. Firstly, they seem to have fixed the door glitches, second, there actually is a way to get the same easy start every time (under difficulty settings), and thirdly, you can make the enemy types reset when you restart, too. I still think there needs to be a more in depth tutorial, because you see different kinds of dangers in the normal gameplay which appear to be environmetnal but you can't be sure (green blobs, etc.) and the effects of depressurization and flooding with radiation, as well as countermeasures, need to be discussed in the tutorial.
When you first load up this game, you're bound to be excited about the concepts, being alone in the universe with a mysterious breakout happening... What's bound to happen? Well, you'll start your first ship salvage with zero infestations, a quick resource grab that gets you moving a bit on your feet. Then, you'll have to plot your moves more appropriately as every other ship is infested and your drones are vulnerable. As you explore each ship, you may uncover a log relating to what triggered the incident, which you can look back on later. It's a very unique situation, and the gameplay style is just as unique. For the first few hours, this game is pretty enjoyable.
Once you play past the first few hours, this game quickly becomes repetetive and painfully difficult to progress in. You'll probably be very likely to use the
option to start over. It doesn't restart a salvage though... It restarts the universe right after the event. You're back to square 1 with a different drone loadout. And that safety net of an infestation-free ship NEVER returrns. For every reset, your first ship is already infested, and a lot older. The levels are a lot harder, and it's really frustrating to try and progress because sooner or later, you'll be bound to make a single mistake that ends up costing you your entire drone fleet. And there's only 1 save file. Oh, and sometimes enemies can kill your drones through CLOSED doors.
While this game would make a great short-term arcade game, I feel ripped off having paid $20 for it. There's not really a chance at progressing very far if you ever reset (which I have) and the enemies are sometimes prone to glitching (at your expense). Short summary: if it's on sale for less than $5, it might be worth your money. As for what I paid, I wish I was still in my return window.

This game is so engaging and addictive. It was worth every penny.  The trailer drew me in and I was not disappointed.
Now there are pros and cons.
Pros:
The game provides a sense of claustrophobia as you're limited to either your drone's view (which is detailed) or an overview of the entire map (but not as detailed).  You'll switch a lot to be able to see specifically where stuff is and how to position your drones.  And the times when your video cuts off, only adds to the sense of suspense and worry.  You constantly have to scavange derelicts for just enough supplies to keep you going and it's hard to maintain supplies (between repairing and upgrading drones, maintaining their upgrades, getting ammo, and much more)
Drones have to work together, sometimes swapping parts to adapt to their enviroment. You'll have to constantly be on the alert for random events (an asteroid strike, broken vent leaking radiation, a malfunctioning airlock) and sometimes you'll have to control yourself and not be greedy or stay too long.
There are moments where you'll jump in fear, such as checking a room and out of no where an enemy lunges fromt the shadows to attack you drone, killing it and destroying you vid feed so you can't see what happened. When it comes to enemies... well stealth is keep and one mistake (like leaving a door open a second too long or not closing another door) can lead to you losing either one drone or all. Best of all, the game has good replayability due to randomly generated systems, galaxies, ships, and maps.
Cons:
It can be difficult to deal with typing your commands (especially when dealing with enemies or radiation leaks or even asteroid strikes) and I've had more than once where I typed a wrong key and opened a door which lead to all my drones being killed.  Another is when you start a new game, sometimes you get bad (for lack of better term) starting equipment which makes the game harder.
Overall:
There's so much more which I could go into detail but I'll leave it to those. I found this game wonderful and despite frustrating parts, I still pressed on and was rewarded.  If you're into games with puzzles, suspense, resource management and strategy, exploration and stealth, then this is definitely the game for you.

Dungeon Defenders 2 is a prime example of what you get when you take a good game (the original Dungeon Defenders) and try to turn it into a cash cow. A turd - and we all know what you can't polish.
If you can make it past the poorly designed menus without banging your head against a brick wall, then congratulations, you now have to deal with creating a character.
In this revolting mess, you get to pick between a whopping two characters. Don't get too excited trawling through the abundance of stale appearances, or all the other characters and their abilities, because if you want these you will have to search deep into your wallet.
The gameplay is trite and unchallenging. Tactics are few and far between. Gear is the most influential factor in determining your success with various dungeons and difficulties and most of the game revolves around grinding gear. Even the most challenging of dungeons are a cakewalk with sufficient gear. The small number of dungeons in the game are badly designed and lack variety or scope for testing different strategies. There is no challenge. In addition to this, the game is filled with too many unnecessary complications and too much garbage. For example, having to sift through a plethora of junk items after each dungeon to work out what you should sell or equip to make more bag space for the next dungeon.
The bad news doesn't end there. The endless amount of bugs, the sluggish mouse response time and the eye splitting aliasing are enough to make a kakapo question what the developers have been doing in the 5+ years this game has supposedly been in development.
Trendy have tried everything they can to milk this pathetic excuse for a game from charging for characters, pets, appearances and bag space, to equipment and upgrades. These pitiful attempts at stealing your wages would give even Martin Lewis a seizure.
The game has been in early access for years and, judging by the state of it, needs to stay there for a lot more. It showcases everything that's wrong with modern gaming. It truly is hard to find anything good to say about Dungeon Defenders 2. It pales in comparison to the original. I would not even waste your time downloading it.

time for my review of this game, oh boy
this game is a very entertaining mess, what i mean by that i will explain.
this game in my overall oppinion is not really too good, but it can be very fun to play for a few hours, if you pick up this game dont let it gather dust due to negative reviews, the reason being that there is actually fun to be had in this game, the graphics are bad as hell ill admit but there is no reason to hate a game due to graphic and visual stuff, well unless it's really bad.
this game has a focus on gameplay, i know your probably laughing at that but I'm going to break down what this game is in my review for this game.
well the positives are:
the enemies, hear me out they are pigs, but its great to get away from the zombie games and have something else take the spotlight for once as a mutated mess, and pigs are a suprisingly fun idea, you can run around shooting them like regular zombies exept they generally take alot more hits than in zombie games, the reason being beyond me but its still fun
the weapon selection aint that great, but is still pretty good compaired to some other games, you have these weapons to use:

as far as im aware thats all the guns that are available to use in the game.
their is an item system to this game, and a way to purchase items during a level using pigs meat, believe it or not this is done using a grinder, of which somehow turns it into ammo and items to purchache using the ammount of meat present in the machine, this mechanic is something you dont get often, not unique but still something good to see
you can play with 2 players, and up to 4 (or 6 in the halloween update) but when this was posted this feature is still in beta, alough from my testing it so far works pretty well, i love playing with friends in this game, and when its not with friends, their is suprisingly good community with the others who you can get into games with.
the gameplay is often smooth, this game does not require a lot of processes and actually very little, meaning on even a craptop this game can reach a constant 60FPS, or more.
as their is positives their is also negatives:
their is only a single map to play on, it may be a pretty good map but it is small, and rather repetitive and dull after a while, a good map variety or progression of maps would be cool to have, but their just isnt that.
their are only 2 bosses present in the game, which you face every 10 days, the time to face them isnt bad but the variety is poor, you would expect their to be different, more cretive bosses every 10 days but it just goes back and fourth between 2, known as princess and the brother or brothers after the first 10 days, a better variety would be apriciated in a game like this.

their is no story to this game to my knowledge, a good story is always cool even for a survival game, where you can come across things that tell you about the past of the events in this game, but currently their is none, only what happens from day 1, again just a feature that would make the game better not something that ruines the game entirely
in conclusion i think this game is pretty fun, definatly good value for the current selling price, this is why i will give this game a definate up rating, even if it isnt fun forever its still a good laugh for up to 5 hours! if you enjoy it longer than that then thats great!

Cuphead is absolutely spectacular.
I know that, as a reviewer, I’m supposed to build up to a crescendo when writing a review – but f*ck that. This game is genuinely brilliant.
There has never been anything like Cuphead before. It is a true breath of fresh air.
You honestly cannot compare it to any other game. It honestly doesn't even feel like a game (and that's in a good way). It feels more like one of those cartoons that you'd watch in the morning on the weekends on the Boomerang channel as a kid - only now, you're a character inside one of those brilliant cartoons.
Memories of Tom & Jerry, Popeye, Betty Boop, Felix the Cat, Merrie Melodies and the original Looney Tunes flood your mind when you play this game. It brought back such profound pangs of nostalgia that it honestly brought a tear to my eye.
Cuphead is proof that a game's greatness of aesthetic isn't determined by its polygon count or texture size. This game is drop dead beautiful - even at the game's max resolution of 1280 x 720. If anything, that resolution only adds to the aesthetic. Pictures can not truly convey just how beautiful this game is, it is something you have to experience yourself.
Adding to the beautiful visuals is the game’s soundtrack. Honestly, this is one of the greatest scores I’ve heard in a video game. It’s up there with Halo and The Elder Scrolls – a truly amazing feat, when you consider that this is an indie game!
It’s 1930’s music galore. Everything is covered, from folk tunes and jingles, to the brash and bold brass big bands from the golden age of swing music. The soundtrack, if you’re a fan of this sort of music, is an easy purchase. If someone had made me listen to the tracks from this game and not told me that it was for a game, then I would have honestly believed that they were genuine tunes from the 30’s. They are just as spectacular as the visuals.
And then there's the gameplay.
It plays just as good as it looks - especially if you use a controller. The controls are tight, responsive and intuitive after you play for a few minutes. The calibration is spot on and it feels like a Nintendo-made platformer with equally good run-and-gun mechanics grafted onto it.
It is seriously good. It needs to be with the game's difficulty.
The game is hard. Very, very hard - but in a very good way. It's the kind of sweaty-palmed, white-knuckled, extremely-rewarding gameplay that harks back to video games from the 90's. Super Meatboy is the only other game I can think of that offers that sort of gameplay within recent memory, but whereas the stages in Super Meatboy were your enemy; Cuphead's enemies are its many bosses.
Beating each of the bosses is excruciatingly challenging and you will curse and scream and stomp your feet until you beat that one boss you've been sawing away at and learning his moves and patterns for hours at a time - and that feeling of sweet victory when you beat that boss is pure gaming nirvana.
If you're an old-school gamer like me who grew up on games like Castlevania, Metroid and Asteroids; you'll especially love this game.
It will not be a game for everyone, to be sure. If you’re a casual gamer who likes easier games, then just walk the other direction. There is no hand-holding in this game. The only way to win is to git gud.
But for everyone else; buy it. $20 (or $30 if you get the soundtrack) is a complete steal for one of the best games to be released this decade. You will not regret it.

Limbo Review
From Wikipedia: "In the theology of the Catholic Church, Limbo (Latin limbus, edge or boundary, referring to the "edge" of Hell) is a speculative idea about the afterlife condition of those who die in Original Sin without being assigned to the Hell of the Damned."
Are video games an art form? Limbo is one of those games that can answer such questions. It combines gloomy black and white visuals, low volume ambient soundtrack and chilling sound effects to produce an unforgettable experience that stays with you, much longer than it lasts. You are a young boy who wakes up in a forest, without knowing anything about your identity, where you are, where you come from or where you are going. You walk alone in the shadows, facing creatures and meeting other children along the way. The road ahead is tough and you must solve many puzzles, with the use of your brain and reflexes to keep going. There are no dialogs or cut scenes in this game, yet the storytelling is much greater than many other games. But there is death.  So much death. You will die many times in order to figure how to solve some puzzles or just to see the animation in every case. The puzzles start simple and they get more complex as you approach the ending. Oh, the ending! What an unusual way to end a game and spur so much debate over the meaning! Let’s just say, abrupt beginnings lead to abrupt endings…
Cool concept, but that's it. Poor visuals that pretend to be intentional, and the main story is 2 hours long if you die a lot.

RNG on top of RNG on top of RNG.  Once you get the basics down, which takes maybe a couple of hours and one or two resets, it becomes painfully obvious that this game is a glorified version of Solitaire, where it looks like you're doing things but in reality you never have any real choices and what happens during a playthrough is dictated entirely by the whims of the RNG.
Exploration this game gets very repetitive very quickly.  Every derelict is the same.  Some upgrades are almost absurdly more useful than others.  Find turret, shield, stealth, interface, and remote power upgrades early and you'll go a long way.   But most of the time you'll just limp along carefully avoiding enemies until you inevitably die anyway.
Eventually you'll run out of scrap, fuel, find yourself in a constellation with almost no boardable ships, find your drones stranded by radiation that cut them off from the exit, have your scouting drone get trapped in small or cluttered a room with an enemy and not be able to escape before its stealth runs out, or you'll just typo the wrong door and you'll die and it's back to the beginning.  Very few of my deaths did I feel were my fault nor did I feel I could have done anything to prevent them.  But even then there's no real progression so aside from your losing your drones it doesn't feel like much of a loss and whatever snippets of the story you've found remain.

I can't tell you how much I enjoy this game...but I'll try! Like FTL or Don't Starve, it's cripplingly hard at first (with perma-death to ensure lots of F-bombs), but once you lose a few captains you'll begin to see the sense in things like staying close to shore at first, or avoiding anything swimming around that's larger than your ship. It becomes slightly easier, then, but the enjoyment just keeps getting richer and deeper. What is the Utter Shroom? Who are the Clay Men? Why are your crew so afraid of the dark when they've lived their whole lives down here?
It's the little touches I appreciate the most. There are gender-neutral options for form of address, and you may romance men or women regardless of your stated gender (or lack thereof). There are little literary references -- Coleridge, of course, and Poe, and Lovecraft -- scattered throughout for the discerning reader. The music is haunting and the art is evocative and immersive.
And it's FUN. You guys, this game is fun. Even after...probably 30 dead captains? Let's say 30. After 30 dead, I'm still drawn helplessly back into it. It's not even finished, and it's amazingly entertaining. Absolutely recommended!

Pre-release update as of 2/4: Played it again to check out what changed since my review. Still Cthulu's Oregon Trail with great writing. Worth your money for the uniqueness of experience alone.
If you've ever played something like Escape Velocity, you'll feel right at home with Sunless Sea. It combines the neat world-building of Fallen London with a survival-ish roguelike-like. I really like this game, but I'd like anyone who buys it to understand why I like it before they make their decision.
The gameflow in Sunless Sea is surprisingly natural. All port interactions are menu-based. You'll spend most of your time at sea. Most of your time away from port will be spent managing your fuel, supplies, and terror. The concept behind the game relies on the fact that the sun makes the ocean beautiful, and setting sail into a vast, wet expanse isn't quite as romantic as our concept of the merchant marine.
Instead, you spend most of your time at sea trying to navigate between lit buoys, the shore, and trying to avoid the pitch dark that will freak the heck out of your crew. Exploring new islands and picking up quests earns you cash, new crew members, and the experience that translates into varied rewards.
Where the game really shines is in cohesiveness. You don't get on a boat in Fallen London because you're a hero. You do it because you're broke, desperate, or stupid. The game's systems support this entirely. Most of the money you'll be getting comes from military commissions looking for news from far-off ports, looting hostile ships, and any number of unique events that can occur at one of the game's many islands.
My main issue with Fallen London, gating the content by limiting the player's actions, actually translates into something really neat in The Sunless Sea. You can't try every activity a port has to offer in one visit, because being out to sea for a reasonable (a minute, maybe? probably less) amount of time gives you the "Something Awaits You" trait. This trait means that you can do something at the next port. After you've done the thing, you'll only have access to the regular port facilities. My instinct when I play games like this is to only start caring when there's a decision to be made, but making my choices matter means that I engage with the game in a much more active way.
The writing is great. Nothing else to say about it!
Finally, this game is cool because it's an early access title that will be released. Buying it now gives you a great opportunity to try a limited version of the game out, but the developer's sensical timetable should mean that we'll be getting the full version in October. The game isn't complete yet, but I think the most important thing an early access title can do is launch after it knows exactly what it is.
This won't be a different game after it's launched, there will just be more cool stuff in it.

I'm still not sure what to say about this game, but here's what I've got so far:
It's sad. Truely sad. I will not spoil anything about the game, but just know it is incredibly sad. With that being said, it is well worth playing. I will admit at $10 it's a little pricey, but I especially recommend it if you can pick it up on sale. This game tells a story that is so gripping, you need to play in one sitting. This game takes you through the mind of a struggling game designer. As someone who is in school for game design and development, I recommend this game to anyone pursuing a career in that field of study. Some parts you can relate to and others will just cause you to sit and stare at your screen.
So.. Do I reccomend this game? Yes. Does that mean I like this game?... I'm still not sure if I do. It lacks closure. I found myself sitting at the title screen, thinking "That was it? That's the end of this game!?" With that being said, the only reason I am recommending this game, is because it is a truely unique experience.

In Dredd Vs Death, YOU ARE THE LAW! Prowl the streets of Mega City One as the cities greatest judge as you punch up and arrest perps and civilians, Lay down the law on Zombies and Vampires by blowing them way with your Lawgiver and dispense justice to the sinister Dark Judges, vile undead from another dimension that fully believe life itself is a crime and that the sentence is death.
I'll say it up front, This game is really for fans of the Judge Dredd comic book seires as this little gem from the early 2000's can be described as very true to the source material. Meaning its NOT like the Sylvester Stallone movie from the 90's and it is NOT like the Karl Urban "Dredd" movie from a few years ago. Think of it a mix of both. Its cartoony and campy in some places while it still has a bit darkness to it.
As a game on it's own there isnt really anything spectacular or innovative about it when it to the point that one can easily compare it to Halo: Combat Evolved that came out two years prior. The game runs well on PC and in terms of comparison the only things i can say about DvD that's really different than Halo would be the following:
- The world itself (of course)
- A points system where if you manage to obtain a high ranking after you complete a level you will be rewarded with extra game content such as new skins for multiplayer (which has a VS Bots mode if for whatever reason you wanted to play some Dredd pvp) and mini games a for a bit of extra new game plus.
- The lack of vehicle use. There's not even a level where you can ride on Dredd's iconic Lawmaster bike.
- Your primary weapon, "The Lawgiver" is going to be your main weapon in the game. While there are some other weapons availiable to you such as shotguns and grenade launchers, you will find  yourself using the Lawgiver alot more as it multiple firing modes (e.g. Rapid Fire & Incendiary rounds) are the best response to the varity of threats in the game.
- And that you have bosses.The four bosses in the game, The Dark Judges: Fear, Fire, Mortis and their leader Death are not your regular boss battles, since they are undead they cannot be killed by traditional means and sometimes the boss fight requires you to do something different in order to win and to achive a higher rank at levels end. For example in order to defeat Judge Mortis at the hospital level with the most "brownie points" you will need to rescue all the hostages he has with him and yes they too can be killed at the slightest touch.
In conclusion. This game as i mentioned is not for everyone except for those who either are fan of the comics this game is heavily based on and those who are looking fora cheap FPS to help pass the time. I recommend this game as the former but as the latter do not expect too much from this game.

Me hice de este juego recien salio hace casi 1 par de años. Banished es un juego donde la tematica y el objetivo son simples: Sobrevivir.
El ambiente y la musica del juego hacen que Banished se sienta como un agradable juego donde pasar un par de horas de la tarde libres, jugando un apacible city builder. Pero no lo es.
Banished es un juego donde la estrategia y la planeacion son cruciales. Donde te asientas, donde depositas tus recursos, que tan lejos estan las fuentes de energia y alimentos estan de ti juegan un rol crucial para que tu poblacion no muera de hambre o frio. Donde la cantidad de personas viviendo juntas o cerca determinara que tan pronto se esparce una epidemia. Donde un mal manejo de recursos como carbon, madera o la caza de animales salvajes puede hacer que tu poblacion sufra si el invierno fue largo y las cosechas malas. Donde ser caritativo y aceptar una gran migracion nomada puede acarrearte problemas de comida, combustible, vivienda y demas.
PROS:
Ambiente y soundtrack agradable.
Totalmente enfocado en estrategia y planeacion.
Libertad para hacer tu estrategia de la manera que encuentres mas conveniente.
Un semillero de mapas aleatorios. Cada partida implica un reto distinto de terreno y recursos.
Juego drm free FTW (yo lo adquiri en Humble Store).
Graficamente impecable.
CONS:
No hay progresion a traves del tiempo. Desde el año 1 que comienzas el juego hasta el año 50 (que fue lo mas que jugue) no existe una progresion tecnologica, ni algun tipo de mejora que de la sensacion de que tu poblacion no solo crece en cantidad sino tambien en calidad. Esto ultimo puede estar sujeto a cambios y mods ya que hace mas de 1 año que no he vuelto a tocar el juego.

This is an early access review written as the game stands on 22/07/2014 points mentioned could be out dated by the time you read this.
My recommendation for this game is somewhat subjective, for people who like narrative rich adventures or the fallen London browser game I recommend this game. For those who like gothic London or steampunk-ish themed games as well as exploration and trading games I would say its a maybe, possibly you should wait for the full release. For those that like action, jump-horror or simulations I cannot recommend this.
The game play is slow and atmospheric with you piloting your steam ship around the strange and sometimes alien underzea ( the name of the setting for the game) visiting ports and completing minor missions which are usually (at this stage) simple fetch quests. There are also RPG elements with several stats to raise which can affect the success of your choices as well as combat which takes the form of a slow mini game, almost like a card game.
There are however several issues to note.
-The game is incredibly text heavy, if you're a "picture is worth a thousand words" person you may want to skip it.
-Combat is quite frankly a little dull. The developer has promised to change it but as it stands it's not a high point.
-Trading is not particularly satisfying, prices are static and profit margins are generally tiny to the point that it barely covers costs often you will have to resort to a FAQ or forum to work out how to make decent money.
-Your terror meter fills fast in the open zea (which is classed as anything more than a ship length from shore) to the tune of something like 1 terror point every 1.5 seconds its not insurmountable and it does force you to consider your routes and adds tension still, the rate it fills at plus it's cost to lower can be an annoyance.
All in all I have enjoyed the game but the number of issues makes it hard to whole heartedly recommend.

Duskers is a rogue-like dungeon exploration game where you pilot drones into derelict ships in outer space to scavenge for scrap metal, fuel, upgrades, and the answer to what caused the universe to become a giant graveyard.
Duskers sets an air of complete and total mystery. In fact, not only mystery, but horror as well. To start you off, you're taught the very simple control schemes of the game; Issue orders using a command line, and control your drones with the arrow keys. Simple, intuitive, and easy to get used to. But as soon as the tutorial is over, you dive right into the ever-expansive universe of Duskers. With nary a directive but to board what ever ship you happen to start near and gather precious scrap and fuel. Immediately you can begin to feel just how lonely this world is. How haunting it is. The only way you experience this world is through the very vulnerable camera feeds of your cute little drones as they carry out your every command, and the occasional corrupted text log that leaks to you vital, yet fragmented, information. As you begin to explore and test out the waters of the unknown, you begin to realize that though you're alone, you're not safe. Not in the slighest. Normally that realization comes from the sudden beeps, screeches, and explosions from your most favorite drone being torn to pieces by another drone or an unidentifiablly gruesome creature.
The atmosphere that Duskers sets for you is an inticing one that is hard to pry yourself away from. The sound design of the creaking ships, quiet groans and chatters, occasional whirrs from machines and drones alike. It sets the perfect environment of adventure and mystery. Duskers incites in you an exhilaration to explore and conquer these derelict space ships and stations. An ever-gratifying sense of accomplishment when you bring back a disabled drone, uncover a text log that paints you a story of it's previous inhabitants, or when you find an invaluable upgrade for your drones or ships, even when you mercilessly slay a corrupted defense drone or outsmart one of those terrifying creatures. Duskers likewise will instill into you fear as a nearby bulkhead door breaks open from a creature attacking it, or the panicked beeps of one of your drones suddenly being attacked. It will make you panic when you open a door to a room you thought was empty, only to be confronted by an enemy jumping at you from the shadows. Furiously smashing at your keyboard as you try to close doors, command your drones, and attempt to save as many of your precious little bots as you can. It will give you an air of hopelessness as you watch your last drone become disabled in the bowels of a ghost ship, its camera feed slowly failing as the last of its life drains away. It will rip your heart out when you have to seal a drone in a room crawling with infestations just to give the others a chance at survival. Regretting every keystroke as you type "exit."
Duskers all in all is a thrilling and addicting game that keeps you coming back for more. Dying, though permanent, doesn't feel like a loss. On the contrary, you feel like you're only learning more and becoming more experienced.
Seriously, after spending quite a few hours being sucked into this game, I absolutely love it. I can't wait to fire it up and play more. I can't wait to uncover the secrest this world holds. Mechanics (8/10): simple enough. The In-game controls are simple and easy to remember (for instance, if you want to open door 18, the command is d18. Easy, right? Or if you want to send some drones into the room behind door 18, which in this instance is room 7 [R7] just type in "navigate [insert drone numbers or names here] R7". And if you are feeling like a keyboard ninja and want to get all of that in one command, just type "d18; navigate  [insert drone numbers or names here] R7". Semi-colons are like spaces in this game, letting you put multiple commands in for simultaneous movements, or even in some cases for chain commands (I think there is some way to actually put in some sort of "logic" code with alias's, but I am not certain how)!
Enemies (6/10): I believe there are four infestation types in the game currently, each with their own fighting style (sentry drones just outright attempt to shoot you, "brutes" charge at you, "swarms" obliterate you (but have audio cue's as well apparently), and "slimes" continually duplicate and begin to fill rooms, possibly trapping you in a certain area! To be honest, I really don't like the whole "swarm" idea, as often when I play games I don't bother to use audio, and having enemies that do a ridiculous amount of damage and can chew through doors is just a bad idea all-round.
Modifications/Drone upgrades and repairs (6/10): the idea of modifications is great, it gives you alot of different strategies and customization with your drones. Why is my rating only a 6/10 on this area of my review then? Because repairs. Your drones constantly get malfunctioning cameras, which you will need to repair just in case something bad happens and your cameras go out (thats a whopping seven scrap too!). Your mods also degrage, giving it a "10%" chance of breaking for example (oh, by the way, breaking doesn't mean "It malfunctioned! You cannot use this item for the rest of this mission. It literally means it breakes, it is unusable and can only be salvaged for one scrap (normal mods are three scrap). That really hurts the game-play in my opinion. So if you don't spend your scrap on repairs, what do you spend them on? Well, maybe we could be able to craft mods from scrap, and not just "tow", "gather", and "generator". I am talking about every modification in the game, both for ships and drones. That way I can finally get interface and other great mods that will be less based on random chance.
Maps/Space travel mechanics (ehhhhhhh..... 3/10) I know it's supposed to make you play more strategic, trying not to run out of fuel and stuff but..... in all honestly, it doesn't add anything to the experience for me, and in a way kind of ruins it. The idea isn't bad, but trying to be strategic with your fuel implies that you can actually find fuel, and enough of it. Not to mention the "quarentine" and "transport required" mechanics, because while transport is a cool idea, it should be at least garenteed to have one target be a room with a generator.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely! It's definitely unique in its style and game-play, and because it hasn't been out long, I'm sure the dev team will do their best to balance some things and add others.

Cutscenes and animations feel smooth and despite a codex glitch at the first batcave section. This was relitively smooth sailing. Playing Bruce Wayne as an "idiot" playboy is fun while unleashing his true self as BATMAN  is so relieving...
The puzzles have been improved too. requiring more brainwork than just pressing the A button on a generator...

Fun little city-building game with a focus on survival in a pseudo-medieval setting.
You are tasked with providing shelter, food, and warmth for your citizens. If you fail, they die. Once the necessities are taken care of, you will mainly be concerned with building up supply-chains.
The Pros:
- The buildings look really cute. You are really drawn into the game while you try to set up a cozy little medieval town.
- The focus on survival aspects brings a fresh breeze to the city-building genre. I especially liked that you had to wait for a trader to trade for kettle and seeds.
- The game tracks every citizen and his family individually. The choices they make do make sense and you really feel like they are a living part of the game.
The Cons:
- There is not that much depth to the late mid-game and endgame. There are not that many buildings and industries to choose from and once you've built everything it only becomes a matter of scaling up.
- The game is hard, but not hard enough. Survival is only concern for the first winter, if that.
- The game crashes every two hours or so. I am on XP, mind you, but youtubers seem to run into similar issues.
The verdict:
Banished is a good, cute little game with a ton of potential. It is definitely a lot of fun, but if you're not a hardcore-fan of the genre, it will keep you entertained for a maximum of ten to twenty hours. Worth to pick up if you happen to find it on sale. No recommendation for the casual gamer.

I really only have one. WTF is up with the design of the penguin. instead of going with a cool design like the animated series or arkham games you went with a guy in a penguin mask? What were you thinking?

After the events of the last chapter Bruce is desperate to stop the children of Arkham. However with Harvey recovering, not knowing if he can trust Selina and losing support from his company. (Nitpicking). The only thing i would say is that it does end abrouptly. And in a way that dosent make it feel like the penultimate chapter in a story.

Limbo Review
From Wikipedia: "In the theology of the Catholic Church, Limbo (Latin limbus, edge or boundary, referring to the "edge" of Hell) is a speculative idea about the afterlife condition of those who die in Original Sin without being assigned to the Hell of the Damned."
Are video games an art form? Limbo is one of those games that can answer such questions. It combines gloomy black and white visuals, low volume ambient soundtrack and chilling sound effects to produce an unforgettable experience that stays with you, much longer than it lasts. You are a young boy who wakes up in a forest, without knowing anything about your identity, where you are, where you come from or where you are going. You walk alone in the shadows, facing creatures and meeting other children along the way. The road ahead is tough and you must solve many puzzles, with the use of your brain and reflexes to keep going. There are no dialogs or cut scenes in this game, yet the storytelling is much greater than many other games. But there is death.  So much death. You will die many times in order to figure how to solve some puzzles or just to see the animation in every case. The puzzles start simple and they get more complex as you approach the ending. Oh, the ending! What an unusual way to end a game and spur so much debate over the meaning! Let’s just say, abrupt beginnings lead to abrupt endings…

I bought this game years ago when it was just three cars and a handful of tracks. And while yes, I am dissapointed at the pace of development and Bugbears apparent bankruptcy (google it), it is still an excellent driving game.
The car physics are excellent with a lot of attention to detail. Depending on your tires and engine power you get different grip on different surfaces and it's noticable. Feedback through an xbox controller feels solid and it pays to be subtle on the thumbstick, throttle, and break. It's beautiful, too, especially at 4k. Destruction physics look great and enhance the game because your wheels, body, and engine take damage during the race which can effect your driving. Multiplayer and online are a lot of fun if you can find other plays. The game's AI is a lot better than in other racing games I've played, too. I have just as much fun playing single player as I do multiplayer.
The problem with this game is the slow development and lack of direction. It has taken a long time to add features like new cars and maps. The menu option for purchasing vehicles and parts has been there since I bought the game but only recently became a feature you need to use. Also, the game promotes destruction but the latest update penalizes you for it by adding permanent damage to car parts so you eventually have to replace them. I understand the reasoning behind this feature but it seems counterintuitive to
's nature.
I don't think Bugbear is just going to dump this game on the modding community and bail, but they raised over a million dollars on their Steam Early access campaign and have only produced half a game in two years. If they can get their butts in gear and show some direction and start updating more often this could be the greatest racing game ever. It's a risky bet, but it's sooo much fun.
Is the development process wonky? Yes.
Is the future not so bright for this game? Probably
Is it a fun game to play? You bet your sweaty palms it is.

This is what I had to say about the first Zup! game:
"To be enirely honest, I went into this with very low expectations. This was mostly due to my prior experiences with Super Duper Flying Genocide 2017, another recent title that markets itself in a similar fashion. "Short, Simple, Earn loads of achievements". And I'd be lying if I said this game is perfect, but I have to give praise where praise is due. This game really surprised me!
The very first distinction I'd like to make between this and Super Duper Flying Genocide 2017 is that unlike that dissappointment, I would actually consider this a game and a rather enjoyable and intuitive one at that! It is clear that Zup! goes for the same demographic; achievement hunters, completionists, whatever you want to call them. I consider myself part of that group, so I felt inclined to give this game a try despite my rather low expectations. Very much like the building blocks that you interact with in Zup! my expectations were blown away! This is definitely a puzzle game first and foremost, and an achievement treasure second.
Your objective is to bring the blue square onto the green tiles through the use of explosions. The red squares are explosive and clicking them will make them blow up, knocking any yellow and blue squares away in the process. It really is as simple as that. But just because the mechanics are simple it doesn't necessarely mean that the game itself is easy, in fact I'd say far from it.
The levels start out easy enough, and for the first few levels it feels like this might have actually been a bad choice after all, just another cash grab copy paste job with loads of achievements attached, but then you reach level 10 and things start to get interesting. As you progress through the game each level becomes more and more challenging and you need to both think of the right solution and make use of your reflexes and predictions to launch the blue square with the right trajectory and force to get it where it needs to be.
Soon I had forgotten about my prior pessimism and was instead joyfully exploring in how many ways I could try to knock the yellow block-towers down and with what sort of speed I could send the blue square flying in order to solve the puzzle in front of me. The simple yet addictive nature of the game had caught me entirely off guard and I was getting more and more intrigued and hopeful for the next challenge the game would provide me with...
And then it ended. Just like that.
If anything, that would be my only real gripe with the title, it is extremely short. I beat the whole thing with 100% achivements in only a couple of minutes, and I wish it would go on for a bit longer as I was actually having quite a bit of fun with it. But to be fair the game has a very low price point and the tags do describe it as "short" so I should have been expecting it to end rather quickly.
All that said, I hope you understand my thoughts about this game but in case I was too lengthy in my description of it and the enjoyment it gave me let me try to sum it up in a few short words:
This is a short but fun and intuitive physics puzzle game. I had a lot of fun with it and the achievements are a bonus rather than the main focus. I recommend this highly if you want some quick fun, and I suggest you pick up the Zup-Zup! Bundle which hosts all three games for a very affordable price. I have not yet played the other two titles, but if they are anywhere as good as this then I cannot recommend it enough."
And well, I am happy to say that after playing Zup! 2 I can confirm that this is a worthy sequel! More levels, more achievements, more Zup!
Enjoy!
