If you've ever played something like Escape Velocity, you'll feel right at home with Sunless Sea. It combines the neat world-building of Fallen London with a survival-ish roguelike-like. I really like this game, but I'd like anyone who buys it to understand why I like it before they make their decision.
The gameflow in Sunless Sea is surprisingly natural. All port interactions are menu-based. You'll spend most of your time at sea. Most of your time away from port will be spent managing your fuel, supplies, and terror. The concept behind the game relies on the fact that the sun makes the ocean beautiful, and setting sail into a vast, wet expanse isn't quite as romantic as our concept of the merchant marine.
Instead, you spend most of your time at sea trying to navigate between lit buoys, the shore, and trying to avoid the pitch dark that will freak the heck out of your crew. Exploring new islands and picking up quests earns you cash, new crew members, and the experience that translates into varied rewards.
Where the game really shines is in cohesiveness. You don't get on a boat in Fallen London because you're a hero. You do it because you're broke, desperate, or stupid. The game's systems support this entirely. Most of the money you'll be getting comes from military commissions looking for news from far-off ports, looting hostile ships, and any number of unique events that can occur at one of the game's many islands.
My main issue with Fallen London, gating the content by limiting the player's actions, actually translates into something really neat in The Sunless Sea. You can't try every activity a port has to offer in one visit, because being out to sea for a reasonable (a minute, maybe? probably less) amount of time gives you the "Something Awaits You" trait. This trait means that you can do something at the next port. After you've done the thing, you'll only have access to the regular port facilities. My instinct when I play games like this is to only start caring when there's a decision to be made, but making my choices matter means that I engage with the game in a much more active way.
The writing is great. Nothing else to say about it!
Finally, this game is cool because it's an early access title that will be released. Buying it now gives you a great opportunity to try a limited version of the game out, but the developer's sensical timetable should mean that we'll be getting the full version in October. The game isn't complete yet, but I think the most important thing an early access title can do is launch after it knows exactly what it is.
This won't be a different game after it's launched, there will just be more cool stuff in it.

This is an early access review written as the game stands on 22/07/2014 points mentioned could be out dated by the time you read this.
My recommendation for this game is somewhat subjective, for people who like narrative rich adventures or the fallen London browser game I recommend this game. For those who like gothic London or steampunk-ish themed games as well as exploration and trading games I would say its a maybe, possibly you should wait for the full release. For those that like action, jump-horror or simulations I cannot recommend this.
The game play is slow and atmospheric with you piloting your steam ship around the strange and sometimes alien underzea ( the name of the setting for the game) visiting ports and completing minor missions which are usually (at this stage) simple fetch quests. There are also RPG elements with several stats to raise which can affect the success of your choices as well as combat which takes the form of a slow mini game, almost like a card game.
There are however several issues to note.
-The game is incredibly text heavy, if you're a "picture is worth a thousand words" person you may want to skip it.
-Combat is quite frankly a little dull. The developer has promised to change it but as it stands it's not a high point.
-Trading is not particularly satisfying, prices are static and profit margins are generally tiny to the point that it barely covers costs often you will have to resort to a FAQ or forum to work out how to make decent money.
-Your terror meter fills fast in the open zea (which is classed as anything more than a ship length from shore) to the tune of something like 1 terror point every 1.5 seconds its not insurmountable and it does force you to consider your routes and adds tension still, the rate it fills at plus it's cost to lower can be an annoyance.
All in all I have enjoyed the game but the number of issues makes it hard to whole heartedly recommend.

When I first heard about this game, the Youtuber, PewDiePie had posted a playthrough of the first night. At first I was skeptical about the game, and it interested me very little. Luckily that very day, I had a friend over and they said they liked the game, telling me of the main focus of the jumpscares. I myself enjoy jumpscares, so I gave it a whirl and watched the playthrough. Throughout the time I watched it, I jumped many times and screamed every so often when one of the animatronics popped up and screamed.
Even though I was pretty shaken and jumpy after watching, I really enjoyed the game, even just watching someone else play it. This game peeked my interest really quickly, and I found myself looking up many other Youtubers play the game, I read of the rumors and lure behind the game's scenes (namely the missing children and possible haunting of the pizzeria) and I found myself hooked, which is rare for me to become so smitten to a game I just found out about.
I love the strategy and planning you have to endure to ensure you'll get to the next nights. From checking your cameras, to closing the doors and checking lights, it takes a lot of focus and knowledge to make sure you stay safe and keep power.
As for who I find the scariest, it would have to be Bonnie. Seeing Bonnie in my cameras gives me the chills. Then next would have to be Freddy. I don't find him scary, more of most threatening once he starts to roam the building, and eventually makes his way to your right door. Once he's there, I find it hard to keep composure and remember to close the door before checking cameras. I also find Chica scary once she pops up at your window. It's just unsettling for me. Foxy scares me, but I always check Pirate's cove BEFORE the hallway, just in time to close the door, and oddly I find Foxy easiest to avoid, so long as I keep my eye on Pirate's Cove.
I know I made a long review, but I just wanted to share my starting knowledge of the game, my thoughts and love for it. I highly recommend this game to those who love jumpscares and creepy horror games.

Okay first off, this does not necessarily fit into some people's idea of a "game". It is definitely not aiming to be entertaining like TSP, but rather something that might be worrying, inspiring to you.
TBG can potentially stir up your memories and emotions of a difficult time you experienced previously. Some people say TBG is tough, and it does not mean the gameplay (no, that part it actually pretty easy), but in the sense that it is "the decom inside" or "the prison within" that might get to you emotionally.
For what it's worth, I think this game gives you something to think about no matter it's the first, second, or tenth time you play it, because it is easy to see yourself reflecting back. I don't think it is suitable to be judged by the "normal" standarad of gaming community, because this game relies far less on the ability of the dev team, the creativity of the story-telling. It relies a lot on the player's own experience and struggle prior to playing this game.
In short, it's a hit-or-miss. And I don't think it's fair for people to ♥♥♥♥♥ about the "lack of gameplay" or "monotonous dialogue", because that is not the point of the game. It's not complaining how bad the plot is in Tetris.

Video Review:
A Hat in Time is a collection of my favourite classic games condensed into a small perfected package. Taking inspiration from famous 3D platformers such as Super Mario Sunshine,  this game is a masterpiece of fun, fluid platforming. This mastery combined with the personality that has been imbued into every aspect of it, creates a game that is fun throughout
Basically, you play as the adorable space faring Hat Kid, who has lost the fuel to her spaceship in a parking toll incident and now has to traverse the world to reacquire her fuel so she can fly home. During her travels she interacts a number of people on the planet, such as helping Moustache Girl in her war against the Mafia of Cooks, participating in a Bird Film Festival and signing contracts with ♥♥♥♥ing Satan.
Levels are varied in objective, only the secret levels being a simple point A-B adventure. For example, in one level you work for my favourite character, the Conductor, on his Owl Express train to solve a murder mystery, and in a another you play a remastered version of Luigi’s Mansion. The movement Hat Kid can use to traverse these levels is tight and it’s basic to learn, hard to master nature makes for engaging platforming.
And then there are the boss fights- Oh boy the boss fights. Never before did I think I would be fighting a TOILET OF DOOM to rock music in order to save the forest (A Hat in Time, sponsored by the National Forest foundation.) However, the bosses overall are teeny little bit too easy for my liking, the only difficulty being in figuring out what to do in certain battles, but the fun of the fights makes up for it.
The icing on the cake is the music; Pascal Michael Stiefel or Plasma3Music composed an excellent soundtrack that rivals Banjo Kazooie and Donkey Kong Country in amazingness. I don’t really know how to describe the music in a way that does it justice, so go to the A Hat in Time official YouTube channel and have a listen. Just do it, you won’t regret it.
So with all that in consideration; the characters, the levels, the music, my addiction - do I recommend a Hat in Time? For $30 USD it’s entirely worth it.

You are tasked with providing shelter, food, and warmth for your citizens. If you fail, they die. Once the necessities are taken care of, you will mainly be concerned with building up supply-chains.
The Pros:
- The buildings look really cute. You are really drawn into the game while you try to set up a cozy little medieval town.
- The focus on survival aspects brings a fresh breeze to the city-building genre. I especially liked that you had to wait for a trader to trade for kettle and seeds.
- The game tracks every citizen and his family individually. The choices they make do make sense and you really feel like they are a living part of the game.
The Cons:
- There is not that much depth to the late mid-game and endgame. There are not that many buildings and industries to choose from and once you've built everything it only becomes a matter of scaling up.
- The game is hard, but not hard enough. Survival is only concern for the first winter, if that.
- The game crashes every two hours or so. I am on XP, mind you, but youtubers seem to run into similar issues.
The verdict:
Banished is a good, cute little game with a ton of potential. It is definitely a lot of fun, but if you're not a hardcore-fan of the genre, it will keep you entertained for a maximum of ten to twenty hours. Worth to pick up if you happen to find it on sale. No recommendation for the casual gamer.

I do not review games very often, but this will be an exception. This game is extremely frustrating due to dumb developer decisions. Admittedly it is a "difficult" "survival" city builder. But the very extreme feedback loops that the developers built into the game spiral quickly into oblivion. Which would have been fine, if there was any way to counteract any effect of said negative feedback loop, with, say, quick corrective actions. The problem is that there are none. If you screwed up, you are usually left with two possibilities : if you have a large surplus of resources, you can take the hit and maybe it will set you back a few years back ingame (couple dozens of minute real time). If you don't have a large surplus of resources, your population will fall down fast.
Let's take an example : a small tool shortage will quickly develop into a large tool shortage. You need blacksmiths to build tools. The blacksmith himself is much less efficient when he doesn't have a tool. If you take the slow, careful approach, you will grow your town so that the supply of tools is greater than the demand, but not much more so because building tools is extremely demanding in resources (wood that you have to gather and iron and coal that you have to mine, plus more manpower to feed all the gatherers), thus manpower. Due to the extremely slow pace of the game, if a tool shortage develops, by the time you try to react (by diverting more manpower towards resource gathering and blacksmithing), half of the workers are tool-less. Which decreases the resources they gather. And then, the very dumb tool-less blacksmith will scrap enough to build tools and give the result of his production to the first newcomer (who might not even be in the critical path of tool-making chain).
There are plenty of other balancing errors like this in the game, in addition to minor bugs. (Other stupid thing : in periods of famine, people will still bonk and give birth to children like it's 1999. I'm sorry, Shining Rock Studios, but in real life, children in periods of famine are stillbirth or heavily malformed...)
So it seems that the only way to do things correctly is to amass very large surpluses and then build very carefully after that. But the game is so fracking slow that even at speed 10X you can go to the toilets and barely a year will have passed.
This game could have been SO much, but in the current state I cannot recommend it.
I should mention that all of the mods available on the workshop are built to make the game *easier*, which tells a lot about the kind of balancing that the developers did.

This game is really fun Sci-Fi puzzle game. You can say it is a rogue like in some ways as there is an element of death and having to restart. But you are often able to come back from mistakes so I don't think this is the kind of game that fits the rogue like genera as most people would define it. While you can be killed because of a mistake much later on, the game isn't so brutal as to kill you immediately unless you are really unlucky. There is an element of luck to it for certain, but you really need to think of what to do with the information you have and weigh up the risks as well. You may find that pushing to get something extra or exploring 'one more room' is not worth what it could costs you. It may sound silly, but leaving with what little you found is often the smart thing to do than risking one more room and losing a valuable drone(s) or much more.
The game is seen primarily via the terminal of your ship or through the augmented cameras of your drones as you manually control them. The only true image you have is this drone camera which also provides the sounds of the ship or station you are exploring. While normally this kind of disconnect usually reduces the impact of things that happen in the game. This limitation instead manages to genuinely make exploration tense and far more foreboding. This forced reliance on your drones for your survival makes you really fond of your drone team. At the start you'll have three named drones which you can rename if you desire. Each drone will have different equipment equipped and may vary in some stats (health seems to be the main stat difference early on). They also have different designs and can look unique amongst themselves, which helps give them 'personalities'. Making one drone your explorer and another a recovery drone will entail different levels of affection and a strange bond forms because of this. It may be more to do with what each drone has equipped and what their loss will mean initially. But after a while you'll not want to lose them, or at least I didn't.
My first exploration drone was called Anthony and he was a brave little soul. He would go delving into unknown rooms that I wasn't always sure if they were safe or not without complaint. Stupidly at one point I accidentally killed him with the defence gun of a ship I was exploring. I had forgotten to disable it before I moved him into the room to pick-up scrap and he got killed because of my input blunder. I dutifully sent in Derek who had a Tow to recover him and take him home to the ship. While Anthony wouldn’t be used during the rest of the ship exploration I was glad he wasn't lost to me. He had done his job so many times I had genuinely grown fond of him and his three friends who had been with him for so long. Perhaps it's because I am reliant on them so much that they feel like important members of the crew, and while they are fundamentally replaceable they had earned my respect. I ended up losing my entire team and failing at a later stage due to my own errors. This fondness however had changed how I approached problems and exploration and I assume from now on I may play completely different again.
The graphics are really great for what they are representing. But I don't think they will appeal to a lot of people because at a glance it doesn't look like much at all, and they may just dismiss this game. Which is frankly a real shame as it is genuinely a really unique experience to play and it manages to deliver more tension and shock than a lot of horror games have done in a while. The game sets out to do something and it does it really well, it reminds me a lot of the Alien films and games. The premise is one of real interest and lends itself to the idea of trying to survive against the unknown. All without hugely expensive graphics and effects, with really simple and well thought out designs.
The Drones are controlled via command line inputs, and while you can manually navigate you will always use the command line to interact and pick-up things. For a lot of people this will be a really annoying thing and I can imagine a lot of people will feel the controls could be changed. But I think the controls are central to how you play the game and the experience as a whole. It is very close to what the poor survivor is using and creates the feeling of having no real direct control on your fate and reliant on the drones is the key thing that makes this experience work as well as it does.

Conceptually, stylistically, and even mechanically, Duskers seems like a unique and fascinating game.  It's tense, original and compelling.  And yet, the more I played, the more the lack of progression and excessive randomness wore away at me, until eventually I gave up frustrated.
Duskers is a sort of "last man in the universe" scenario.  Everything - and apparently everyone - is dead and the player is tasked with figuring out just what the heck happened.  This involves exploring various derelict space ships via a squad of remote-controlled  drones.  It's a sort of SpaceChem meets Aliens as the player controls the drones from an overview while identifying and (hopefully) avoiding dangers.  Each drone has three slots that hold upgrade modules that serve as tools to facilitate safe(?) exploration of the ship.  These range from the subtle and strategic Motion Scanner and Lure, to the more directly useful Stealth and Teleport modules.
While controlling the drones directly with the cursor keys is necessary, the player can also type in commands from an overhead view of the entire ship.   The need to type in commands is a neat gimmick and really helps the immersion in the game, but it can also be awkward and aggravating, as a single typo could have devastating consequences.   There's no mouse or gamepad input at all.
A big part of Duskers is its procedural generation.  The derelict ships vary greatly in size and layout, yet all feel basically the same.  Each ship is essentially just a bunch of boxes.  There are no force fields, elevators or teleporters, no human corpses scattered about or locked away in stasis.  It all feels very dry.  I would have thought the setting would allow for some really unique and varied stuff in each ship, but there's only a handful of elements randomly scattered about.
There are different ship types:  a "military" ship might have more defense turrets, and a "fuel" depot might have more fuel, but these differences are so subtle I eventually stopped paying attention to what type of ship I was visiting.  Worse, the layout of the ships seems completely illogical at times.  You might explore a tiny ship with an airlock in every room, or a massive ship with only one airlock.  A power outlet might power the rooms right next to it, or those rooms might be powered by another outlet at the far side of the map.  I understand this adds to the "puzzle" aspect of the game, as you try to navigate the ship without knowing its layout, but the nonsensical ship designs really hurt my overall immersion.  The risk-vs-reward formula is so random, it's usually better to just explore a few rooms of each ship, then move on.  Exploring a very large ship can be much more dangerous, but probably won't yield more resources than a smaller, safer excursion.  I understand procedural generation is all the rage these days, but Duskers doesn't really benefit from it.  I would have much rather had a large pool of well-designed levels with a clear sense of progression than the infinite number of mediocre levels Duskers seems to be offering up.
The lack of variety affects the enemy types as well.  I found the first three types of enemies within a couple of hours of starting the game, and then after playing for a dozen or so more hours I found... one more.  There's no clear "late game" or "early game" in Duskers.  You might find the best module for your drones in the very first ship, or you might never find it at all.  Even on the easiest setting, I would often encounter enemies with one-hit-kill attacks right at the start.  Why not have a few, smaller, creepier enemies at the start when the player is just learning, then escalate things to include larger, ship-devouring "boss" enemies later on?  Duskers always felt like it was building up to something great, but that "something great" never seemed to happen.  Most of my time was spent gathering "scrap" (the game's currency), then using that scrap only to maintain the pool of upgrades and drones I already had.   I was hoping I'd eventually unlock the means to craft new upgrades or new types of drones, but that never happened.
Duskers' story plays out through a variety of text logs that are randomly uncovered when visiting the derelict ships.  While intriguing and well-written, I'm not really convinced they provide a satisfactory conclusion to the game's setup.  I never did find all of them, but replaying the game over and over to find the ones I missed didn't seem worthwhile.
There's a part of me that loves Duskers for its unique style and mechanics, but also a part of me that hates it for being such a missed opportunity.   It's a neat idea, but the lack of variety, progression and the nagging feeling that I had "seen it all" almost right from the start left me ultimately disappointed.

It's very difficult to describe this game without explaining what it is, and at the same time how *do* you even explain it? I suppose if you think of this more like an interactive piece of art than a game then you're halfway there.
The Beginner's Guide follows themes of human nature, creativity and socialization all told through snippets of small indie games that you wander through as a narrator explains his take on the creator's thought process. Very thought provoking and utterly unique, it'll leave you feeling stripped bare and unsettled without any real conclusion to comfort yourself with.
I highly recommend it, but don't expect anything entertaining in the most traditional sense of the word.

The most disappointing game I have played in a long time. A series of rather high quality in-depth action rpg's made into a simplistic, almost primitive arcade-style game I would expect as a gaming hall or browser title, not a full-price wanna-be blockbuster. An all-use ingame currency instead of diverse loot, near to no armor or weapon variation and customization. As well as hardly any attack or skill variation: light attack, heavy attack (shield breaker), and 2 skill slots with 5 alternatives to use in each, that's it, no diverse combat, just button mashing. Linear and quite limited maps instead of a living, breathing, npc-settled open world. One mission / level after the other with point recap in between, just like stages in a 90's arcade side-scrolling game.
I'm usually the last one to totally dismiss a game but I can only advise anybody to never touch this one, especially if you expected this to be a diablo / sacred style action rpg. Console port is in fact a very small excuse for (imho) destroying a (rather) popular and quite high quality game series like this.

The propsect of going all the way back to the start with randomised abilities on the drones was just too frustrating and dull to contemplate so I gave up. The experience isn't tense, it's annoying; I buy games to enjoy them not to be continually reset - where's the fun in that. At the speed it downloaded there's only about 20 lines of code and no graphics to speak of so a save command doesn't seem like too much to ask. The command line novelty soon wears off as you discover that to close a door in the face of a rapidly advancing red splodge that you don't get to see until the last minute and that your motion sensor didn't warn you about requires a down arrow plus a typed command. The most skilled touch typist on the planet is unlikely to be able to achieve that.
Take my advice - buy 3 pints of beer, it'll be better value.

It's not going for razzle dazzle in terms of visuals, but it goes for content and gameplay, and it delivers in the slow and methodical gameplay. You're playing a chess match of sorts: keep your drones safe by manipulating the environment and being 2 steps ahead of your enemies. If you're looking for something fast paced, Duskers is not the game for you. Don't get me wrong, some of the best moments of the game happen when chaos hits the battlefield: as you're scrambling in panic trying to figure out what to do. But the game wants you to take things slowly and methodically: because one wrong move will get your drones killed. This game will punish you hard for a mistake, and masochists really will love their time with this game. It's just going to take you a while to get up to speed, as the game doesn't do a good job of teaching you its mechanics, and there will be a bit of growing pains. But if you learn the walk, you'll really enjoy what the game has to offer, especially if you want to exercise your brain.

Never written a review before, but since I paid $30 for this game and am basically finished with it after only 16 or so hours, I got nothing to do today.  I give it a negative recommendation for replay value.
Here is my experience: I only ever play games on the hardest level, and on the hardest level, this game was very challenging.  But once you learn how to manage your four stats (food, drink, temperature and fatigue) the game simply becomes one of hide and seek with the wolves while you gather the very few supplies you actually need to survive.  After dying many, many times, you learn exactly where everything is, even the patrol patterns of the wolves become familiar.  I found myself planning out where I was going to go even before a new game loaded, and I think this killed it for me.  I don't know the feasibility of generating a random wilderness every game, maybe that can't be done.
And... if you choose to play this game, do NOT look online for maps and such.  They are all there, complete and accurately depicting where everything in the game can be found.  This provided a little entertainment for me as there were many areas I did not find by myself, but simply contributed to my eventual boredom with the game.
In my last game I thought maybe I would try and just survive rather than explore, so I sat in the cabin office, fishing and eating fish, melting snow, boiling water, drinking water, sleeping and foraging wood until I was practically falling asleep at the computer.  After 10 days I went out in search of a rifle and was killed by a wolf inside a building.  In one game I had two rifles and no bullets, and in that one.... no rifle.  Since it isn't at all necessary for survival, trying to craft some of the higher level stuff seemed pointless, none of it would help you in a wolf attack.  A rifle isn't necessary either, but I was getting tired of playing tag with that wolf who sits between the cabin and the fishing holes.
As far as I can tell, you can't "win" the game, which is fine, but that leaves you monotonously treadmilling along until your tools run out.  (BUG, I could not repair my hatchet) Getting achievements does not provide enough reinforcement for me to continue that.
The game is not really THAT pretty (even on the highest graphics level) compared to some I have played, so there isn't much enjoyment in simply looking around.
I thought today I would go out and try to craft all the deerskin clothing and the bearskin sleeping bag.  But then I got bored and started this review.  Plus, once you know where all the buildings are, there is no reason to sleep outside.
In conclusion, the first few hours were very exciting for me, then... nothing.  The game is about survival, and simply surviving in this game is, well, boring once you learn how to do it.

This is the first game that I've bought on Steam where I want my money back. I have dozens of games I've not even played and never plan to and I don't want to get a refund for them - I know that if I play them I'll enjoy them and that I'll have paid for that privilege. Not this though. Hell no. This game fails at every level.
Firstly, it's not Sacred 3. It's a completely different game by a completely different development house. I've heard that they have been working on this since 2010, so I don't understand how they could have failed to have any kind of focus group or input from any gamers who had played the originals in producing this item. It's not an RPG, it's has no lastability, no in-depth world, no enjoyable storyline or characters, no exciting loot drops or character builds, none of that.
Ok, so let's take it at just what it is, a new hack'n'slash rather than a sequel to an awesome game or two - this has no character variation and very little variation in the mobs, a short game world, no replayability, dreadful script spoiling good voice acting, but it does have very vibrant graphics and fair sound. Controls are poor with keyboard and mouse but fair with a controller. There's certainly a lot of action in each fixed arena you fight in, but it doesn't change, even the boss fights are mediocre. 4 hours into the game I'd given it a good try, struggling to find some nugget of gold in this midden heap. It was halfway complete and I didn't want to play it ever again.
If this was released on a phone or tablet for $2.99 I could see someone buying it and playing it once before deleting it, knowing that that was what they were expecting, but £40 or $60 or whatever it is, after 4 years in the making??? I want my money back.

I can't believe it took me until now to play this game, it's just brilliant. Has its lows like most though but I have to say it impressed me how the story develops and gives you much more than what you could get by just running through shooting things (like you do in some shooters).
It's a different shooter in most ways, let's say shooting weapons is not what you'll be doing the most in the entire game, you'll have these kind of superpower things named plasmids which are the aquired and upgraded as you advance and consume a meter bar named eve each time you use them. It's kind of easy if you ask me. I spent the entire game trying to save on everything, I mean, always have the maximum medipacks, the maximum ammo for every gun, etc. Every single bullet was important. I regret that choice as I ended up with most of my arsenal and currency unused. Yes you can run half of the game thru just using very little ammo/eve and just melee attacking your enemies with a wrench (default attack). Of course you'll have a lot more fun if you use guns/plasmids which I recommend you to. There are some unbalanced plasmids however, but try all of them so you can see for yourself which ones you like the most.
Also, if you want to get the most of the story you should try to listen as many records as you can, helps you understand the whole thing (you'll find them randomly across the entire game).
You'll definitely have a good time playing this. Worth $20? Definitely, but you can find it for $5 on most sales.

As a spiritual successor to the greatest game that has ever been made and very underrated which is System Shock, I have to say I really enjoyed the game so far...Now into the review!
When it comes to the plot here's how it goes. It takes place in year 1960, while travelling in a plane ya had a accident which ya survived in a middle of the sea, yet with a hope ya stumbled a small building with a golden statue at the top with a weird machine inside. After turning it on ya went down to the city build under the sea called Rapture, which fell due to the one man called Andrew Ryan, the owner of this city corrupted by the power created from the strange liquid called ADAM, which was never seen in the surface. Almost all of the people were addicted to it and started killing each other. While giving up hope, one man called Atlas who is against Ryan asks for your help to stop the madness.
When it comes to the graphics I must say it still holds up to this day and looks great, though like with Unreal Engine 3 ya might expect a quality change that always happens when ya loaded a game but then changes back to normal. Basically any PC ya own in and after 2007 will run it.
Now the gameplay...The most important aspect in every game. It is amazing! While the ammo and weapons may be scarce you also have another arsenal at you disposal....PLASMIDS! At the cost of EVE you can use them to either shoot lightning which can open locked areas, create a fire to melt the blocking ice or even use the telekinesis to stop an incoming rocket flying to your face and redirect it back to the enemy! There are also other Plasmids that does not require EVE and affects your status in combat or other situations.
Almost every weapon can use other types of ammunition ranging from armor piercing to the incinerating ones and ya may find Weapon Upgrade stations which you can choose only one upgrade for each weapon so choose wisely! If you are low on something but have some money you can use shopping ventsto buy stuff but if you think you don't have enough money then you can always hack them!
Hacking lets you turn any turret to turn against the enemies, lower the price for shops or change the healing station to hurt anyone except you and you do that by doing a minigame which requires you to place pipes in any order to let the cyan goo reach the end without leaking it or get to the damaged ones. Be aware that the more you progress in the game it gets more harder.
If you think that you do not understand the plot in overall then you might have missed a lot of Audio Logs. From the Audio Logs you can find more about what was the life in the city and/or even dig more about the owner and his situation.
If you liked Fallout's old styled music then you can find em here as well while sharing the newer ones and pretty much fits the game so perfectly. The sounds are also great and the voice acting is quite great.
Overall, if you think about getting the game then....Would you kindly buy and play it? It is worth 20 Euro for it!

Quick Review: This is a great game with simple mechanics that one will most definitely enjoy if they are fans of the puzzle platformer genre.
First off, I am a huge fan of puzzle platformers. This game is a bit older, but I finally had the time to give it a go and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience. LIMBO offers up a variety of puzzles with a very small number of abilities your character possesses. You can move left and right, jump, and push/pull/press objects. That's about it! It's amazing the ideas they were able to come up with for just these mechanics.
One of my favorite parts of this game is that there are no red herrings, in that, every object you can interact with in the area will somehow be used in completing the current puzzle. It's just a matter of figuring out what you need to use each object for. On the other side, one of my least favorite aspects is the use of "guess and check", where you just have to guess what it is you're supposed to do, and through a series of guesses and punishments by death, you eventually figure out what the incorrect things are, and what the proper path to completing the puzzle entails. The pain from this is a bit lessened due to respawning at the start of the current puzzle and the generosity that is offered in the number of auto-save points throughout the game.
All in all, a puzzle platformer that should not be missed if you're a fan of the genre!

I'm not very familiar with this series but as a fan of the sandbox genre I was immediately hooked by the fun gameplay and appealing graphics. It's incredibly appealing to just mess around, cause havoc and experiment with the various gameplay mechanics but the initial enjoyment doesn't last long. As you start to discover the impressively sized island with various vehicles and gadgets it quickly dawns on you that the developers went for quantity over quality here. Every design element and situation is repeated ad nauseam and there is no variety to the environments which is of course due to the nature of the game world being set in a fictional asian setting (that admittedly made me want to go on vacation in thailand and cambodia again) but I have to ask myself the question why the developers didn't choose a more intriguing setting with variety. Perhaps the idea was to get away from the genre-defining GTA series; but nowadays sandbox games have generally gone far beyond GTA clones and are rightfully recognized as a genre of its own, so much so even GTA-clones as the first Saints Row develop a completely unique identity as they progress.
The main problem with all the gadgets and functions in Just Cause 2 is that they are all introduced at the beginning of the game and while they are a lot of fun and give the game a unique flavour there isn't anything left to discover after the first hour or two. Surprised enjoyment followed by sobering grinding.
The storyline department is also severely lacking, not that these games are usually poetic masterpieces but I can't even remember a single character, as in what is their name and character. I have no investment in short-haired action man with hookshot and thus didn't continue playing once the novelty wore off. The game is too self-aware for its own good ( not self-aware funny like Saints Row alas): nameless person in nameless setting against nameless antagonists. They have names but it never matters for a second; despite the beautiful visuals you never feel like you are traversing a real world, and even a cartoonishly over the top world can feel credible/plausible if it's internally consistent and has proper world building to draw you in. This felt more like a licensed game of one of those god-awful expendables movies.
In that sense Just Cause is the epitome of a sandbox, you get nothing out of it that you don't bring yourself and you have to figure out your own way to have fun, namely smashing things together. Which is fine I guess but it comes off more like the developers couldn't be asked to do that themselves. They clearly have the skills to make all the mechanics of a sandbox game work but they don't add anything to it.
If you can get this one on sale, you're gonna have fun for a little while but don't expect a memorable experience, Just Cause 2 is a distraction more than an experience.

A Survival game with... command line elements? Yeah sounds odd, but not really bad. In fact, this helps to immerse yourself in the game, as you are directly telling the game what doors to open with more than a simple press of the E key, and either scooting your drones (Your eyes, ears, and hands in the game) by the arrow keys, or more command line entries.The only problem being, it can possibly become tedious after a while.
Several times I have sent a drone into a room only to find a angry red being stareing back, and sending the drone backwards, while typing the name of the door I need to close added a feeling of surprise and even fear. A simple slip up can mean disaster.
Add to that the looter-feel as you search for upgrades that are still intact, more fuel, new drones, and all the scrap you can get your robot claws onto, can have you playing without pause, as you jump from one ship to the next looking for your next sweet find.
That said, I only have 2 hours of play time in this game, and this is a negative review. Why? The game is still fresh out the oven and needs to cool, as it were. I enjoy it, I really do, but at this time I have had several crashes which lead to the program closing, and when reloaded, leaves you outside a ship that you already 'searched' and can not return to... thus all the loot you may have found, is lost. In a game where the looting and slow thorough searches are the games main stay, followed by moments of urgent typing, the sudden stop is painful.
So as such, I'll recommend this game after its fixed the crashing problems.  Right now I feel the crashes occur around the time that you are really getting into the game, and would possibly cause gamers to simply walk away before giving the game a chance.
EDIT: After the post, I was helped by a developer who took the time to look through the crash logs and really try to resolve the problem quickly. In the end, it was simply a graphics driver problem. The game runs great now, and the developers deserve kudos for their assistance!

This is a pretty awesome indie title that features excellent atmosphere, very unique control scheme and a challenging rogue-like elements in the game that will make you want to play this through a few times before you figure out what's really going on.
In a nutshell, it's a command line simulator that allows you to remotely control several bots that you use to board the derelict spaceships to try to scavenge fuel and resources from but also discover what happened to everyone else in the universe and why you are the only survivor.
As you go through each individual wreck, you have to not only manage your own resources, but also make sure that you scan for potential defense systems that may turn hostile or worse...increasingly creepy unusual alien creatures that may kill all of your bots and leave you stranded in space.
The most interesting aspect of the game is in how simple yet elegant it is and how great it delivers the story in bits and pieces as you go through various levels at random. It also gets progressively more challenging and as you upgrade your drones and acquire new modules for them, you get to choose on how you want to progress and complete your levels.
The main goal of the game is not entirely clear at first, but becomes more obvious after a few playthroughs and since this is a game you can play both casually and with more hardcore mentality as well, I think it will appeal to many kinds of players that don't care much about graphics and would rather focus on a complex and original gameplay design.

First, this game has almost nothing to do with the previous Sacred Universe, neither in Story nor in Gamplay.
The story is almost not present and is only an excuse to guide you over the map through the levels.
The combat System is easy to learn and not complicated. You can take 2 Abilities on the missions which you also can alter between 3-5 between missions(so not much diversity). There are 3 Weapons per Class which are only different in their special ability. There is almost no such thing as Character development except the look of your Armour every few lvl ups. The Enemy types are repetetive and the level design is like a tube. After a few missions you get the feeling,you are playing the same lvl just with other skins and in another environment (which looks very pretty i have to admit). The Bossfights are somehow challenging at first try but then rather easy to accomplish.
Sacred 3 is definitely a nice game for casuals and people who want to play with their friends a quick and simple coop game but for fans of the Sacred series and (i have to compare) Diablo like games, will be disappointed.
After 9 hours or so i completed every mission and the day one dlc missions (5 in the Underworld).
All in all this game is fun but has almost no replay vallue or longtime motivation and is never worth the 50€.

This game has so far been inspirational, unique, and personal. Far more personal than the Stanley Parable, which I also gave a 5/5. As I said though, the Beginner's Guide is unique, it is not the Stanley Parable. So even if you liked the SP, you may not get the same experience from this.

This game should be free, if it didn't also need to support the creation of more games along its line, and also compensate Davey Wreaden for his time creating it. It is the sort of game that should available to everyone, sort of like documentaries, or art funded by the government.
That's all.

Note: This review applies to both Zup! and Zup! 2
These are to my knowledge, very original puzzle games. What little there is in terms of graphics and physics is very well done. There are many things, however, that prevent me from recommending them:
- Length and Lack of Content: 20 minutes each, if you work quickly, like I did. My time played on the second one is higher because I left the game on while I went out to do an errand. The music is just a few bars that loop over and over again. Perhaps there's something in the background that I'm not hearing, but it's so quiet that it doesn't make much difference. The music doesn't go anywhere.
- Ease: There is in theory some strategy involved, but you can win most levels in a few tries by just randomly clicking. I managed to beat the final level of Zup! 2 on my first try, with only one mouse click. Perhaps this was intended as a grand explosion finale, but most other levels were like this, too.
- Broken Puzzles: On many levels, you can win by skipping large portions of the level. In many cases, there are many ways to solve each level. I don't mean that in a fun "alternate solutions" kind of way. I mean that randomly clicking will often beat the puzzle on the first try.
- No Replayability: Some games offer much less than this in terms of content, but are fun games that I would highly recommend. Tetris, for example, has much less content than this game, but is highly replayable. After you've beaten this game once, there's no point playing it again until enough time has passed that you've forgotten all the solutions (not that it would be that hard to figure them out again, anyway).
- Achievement Spam: If you're looking for achievements, this game has them. Many of the positive reviews for this game cite achievements as a key feature. I earned six within my first sixty seconds. That's one every ten seconds. I got both games to 100% completion in the short time that I spend playing them. To be clear, I earned over 200 achievements in about 40 minutes. I had to replay one of the levels, since it didn't register the achievement for that level the first time. It only took me about ten seconds to replay it, though.
- Better Options for the Money: For the same price, you can get a full-length pixel art RPG by some random indie developer. Generic? Sure. But you could actually have fun playing a game for hours on end. There are so many really good games out there for the same price, or even less. For such a low price, I don't feel ripped off by the developer, and I wouldn't really mind if I couldn't get a refund. Seeing as I can, however, I think I'm going to get something else.
Overall, I think the concept shows enormous potential, but you won't find any of it in these actually existing games. I hope the developer refines the concept in the future, and makes a more challenging and engaging game.

The user interface responds well, but everything from start to finish screams: "use controler not keyboard + mouse".
Playing the game means fighting trough an instance like zone earning points/gold which you use to buy skills with after completing the the zone. So if you are looking for "loot" to satisfy your inner packrat munchkin you are out of luck.
The playstyle is buttonsmashing in coop and is allot of fun to do with people you know. However when playing solo you will start to notice the repetitiveness of the buttonsmashing and the "rails" of this rollercoaster ride.
The game is called Sacred 3 and as such it is part of a  brand line (the 3 in it's name would be a big hint)
However where sacred 1 and 2 are open world games with multi tiered skill and loot gathering, Sacred 3 is more of a hack and slash on rails. Also the Seraphim player character which has returned in every sacred game does not look like the ones used in the previous game or even like the one used in the boxart and trailer!
The above mentioned odities really give the impression that the publisher has been abusing the name and image of a fairly populair brand to  milk some extra cash.
This does not mean it is a poor game, as it is actually a fun game in short bursts, but when you look at similar games, the pricetag of Sacred 3 is really on the expensive part of the comparison scale.
So if you are like myself who buys a game on faith and happy memories of previous installments.... then this is an excellent example of why you should always read reviews before buying.
A good game. The bones of a GREAT game are here. Once all the content is finished and some the stories are fleshed out, I'll buy it again as a gift for a mate!

Wow, Cuphead... Where do I start...?  If Nintendo or SNES games were still being made today, Cuphead would be the product of what is some of the most fine game development I have seen in a LONG time.
The art style, the mechanics, the music, the sounds...  Cuphead is sure to leave a lasting impression.  Bringing back all sorts of Looney Tunes, Disney, and other old animated feature nostalgia, Cuphead is something that should and probably WILL go down as a classic.
I think all the developers on this team may take themselves lightly, but StudioMDHR.. if you're reading this, you've all created something special here.  There are SO many people out there that want traditional animation back.. and this team pulls it off with flying colors.  But..... there is something else you must know.
THIS GAME IS HARD!!!!!!!!!!!!  You will curse..  You will have a lot of heavy sighs..
Dark Souls was born based off the classic unrelenting mechanics we all grew up with in the late 80s and 90s, where you LEARN, and then you succeed.  And that is what you will go through with the bosses in this title.
I'm sure a lot of folks will try and say that this game is the 2D Dark Souls.. but these kinds of titles existed long before Dark Souls.  This dev team took the best of platforming, bullet hell, and side shooters and crammed it all together.
(Keep in mind this game is sortof a bullet hell'ish game, so you'll encounter some cheap deaths from time to time!)
The result is fantastic though.  So, prepare yourself.. and jump back to the 30s baby... because this game will test your skill, and the beautiful art will hold you, and never let you stop until you're done.
This is Cuphead.

Bioshock is first-person shooter action game developed by Irrational Games, 2K known as Boston / Australia in 2007.
The game takes place in the 60s. The player, Jack survives a plane crash and reaches the underwater city Rapture found in decay. There he must fight against mutated humans and capture the substance called ADAM inside little girls called Little Systers that are defended by powerful Divers called Big Daddies. This substance will let the player acquire genetic improvements .
Bioshock was really surprising because it created a whole new world with incredible narrative. history is noteworthy . Despite maps are not huge, they have superlative art and there are so many things to do that you never get bored . Combat is frenetic, there are turrets and machines to be hacked that provide ammunition and resources , there are also hidden resources and tonics to search that provide a remarkable range of combat.
Instead of just owning guns, machine guns, etc. , we find tonics fire , electric rays, clouds of bees or many other forms of attack. This mixed mechanism was fairly new and fun at the time and it succeded on a very good game, Dishonored (2012), that took this concept and adapted it well .
The game has elements of stealth, survival horror and role. It also has an important political component simulating an ultra-capitalist alternative world in a city where there are no ethical dilemmas and took to end the arts , science and engineering , which led to its decline .
It is one of the top ranked games of all time . It has two sequels. The bioshock 2 showing an ultra communist character and Bioshock infinite that develops in an aerial city. In Bioshock infinite political, religious and scientific plot led to the end in a very elaborate story. It´s still a must have game in 2016.
The game was released for Windows PC , PS3 and XBOX 360. The windows version required DirectX 9.0c API.

В Batman – The Telltale Series будут рассказаны параллельно истории и Брюса Уэйна (озвученного Троем Бейкером), и Бэтмена. Обе они будут развиваться в Готэме, но не пересекутся с уже существующими сюжетными линиями, отражёнными в фильмах и комиксах. На этот раз действие развивается через несколько лет после того, как Уэйн принял на себя роль борца со злом и несправедливостью. Как и во всех играх от Telltale, здесь многое основано на выборе игроков и принятых ими решениях, но есть и существенное отличие – главный герой здесь выступает в двух образах, и обоим персонажам – и Бэтмену, и Уэйну — уделено приблизительно одинаковое количество времени и внимания.
Когда Бэтмен с кем-то дерётся, игроку необходимо вовремя нажимать кнопки (или их комбинации), дабы уворачиваться от ударов или наносить урон врагам. Никакой нелинейности и вариативности здесь нет, зато некоторые нажатия можно пропускать — я не один раз путался в кнопках, однако всё равно всё засчитывалось. Как ни крути, было бы глупо, если бы какой-то тощий бандит убивал супергероя из-за пропущенного QTE, поэтому такое решение разработчиков более-менее понятно. Да и наличие уникальной для игр Telltale механики накопления ярости немного сглаживает впечатление. Если выполнять QTE одно за другим, значок летучей мыши в углу будет заполняться, и со временем персонаж сможет нанести врагу добивающий удар.
Плюсы: хорошая завязка, после которой хочется увидеть, что будет дальше; отсутствие отсебятины и почти полное следование «канону»; увлекательные игровые моменты; большое внимание к деталям.
Минусы: скверная оптимизация; возможность безнаказанно пропускать QTE иногда всё же сбивает с толку.

This. Game. Is. Adorable.
I went in to this game expecting an indie budget title with fairly loose controls, passable graphics, and gameplay just interesting enough for a 4 hour playtime tops. What I got was so much more than that I was blown away. Not only does this game do a great job of capturing that collectathon platformer feel of old, but it does so much to stand above and beyond that. It has its own ideas, its own feel and its own charm that make it shine on its own.
I feel like the most important thing this game has is a great sense of world building. While it's 40 Time Pieces might seem small in comparison to Mario 64's 120 stars, Banjo-Kazooie's 100 Jiggies, or even Spyro 2's 64 Orbs, it's what you go through to collect these Time Pieces that make the game what it is. Every single Time Piece is its own story. Every last mission seems to have a plot connected to it. They'll take you through different sections of the level, introduce entirely new gameplay mechanics, captivate you with new characters, and charm you with all of the unique ideas this game is packed with.
Because of this the game never feels stale. You never feel like you're running through the same areas, repeating the same tasks, collecting things for the sake of collecting them. Every Time Piece is a joy to collect. From impressing millions of fans as a movie star, breaking into the Mafia's kitchen to fight the head chef, or even crawling your way through a mansion trying to hide from a surprisingly scary ghost, there's so much of this game you'll cherish and remember long after completing it.
The graphics are very cute overall. Worlds are huge and detailed with no noticible slowdown or struggle. The characters are well designed and memorable and while some corners have been cut in facial detail or animation, none of it ever detracts from the game's vivid, adorable style. The artwork that appears before every stage is another welcome addition to the game, looking stunning while lending even more charm and love to this game.
The controls are amazingly tight. Hat Kid moves exactly like you want her to. Turns and jumps never feel too floaty, special abilities are easy to cycle through and perform. Upgrades are easily equipped and never seem like a hassle to execute. Jumps and dives can be performed and cancelled out of with amazing percision. Everything from navigating Hat Kid's base to tackling the game's hardest platforming challenges never feel like the controls are holding you back. It's a welcome feeling in a genre full of hard to control indie titles.
The sound fits perfectly around the game's atmosphere, providing it with all sorts of adorable and fitting sound effects. For the most part, the voice acting is diverse and a great fit for the characters. Sound effects make collecting items, attacking enemies and interacting with the environments even more enjoyable (my favorite is hitting a friendly NPC and getting that squeeky toy sound). The music not only fits in well with the game's stages, but with the feel of the game and genre as a whole. I haven't caught myself humming any of the tunes personally, but certain songs like the beautiful Time Rift music, or the wonderfully Grant Kirkhope main lobby are a joy to listen to.
This game is oozing with charm and personality, but doesn't lean on it like a crutch. The gameplay, controls and mechanics hold up wonerfully on their own and it's nice to get a game like this that doesn't feel like you're sacrificing one poor aspect of the game to try and appreciate the others. While A Hat in Time isn't completely flawless, I'm struggling to think of any faults the game may have that's taken me out of the experience long enough to question loving this game.
Any 3D Platforming fan should give this game a shot. If you're a fan of the older collectathons like Mario or Banjo, looking for another new experience similar to (and arguably better than) Yooka-Laylee, or just think the game looks adorable and you're sitting on the fence due to gameplay concerns, jump right in and give it a shot. A Hat in Time has clearly put the effort into every aspect, coming together for a solid package that's well worth a playthrough.

This is kind of on a fine line for me.  I mean out of ten, I'd probably give it a five.  But it's getting a thumbs down for a few reasons.
The good:
Very pretty graphics
Unusual play mechanics (more on this later)
The bad:
VERY click intensive
Limited settings changes
No tutorial
Frustrating 'bonuses'
I liked the unusual game mechanics here for about the first five minutes.  Everything was bright and brilliantly spinny.  However, as I found this game under the 'idle' tag, I thought it would involve a little less hands on game-play and a little more incremental balancing. This is not a bad game, but it's probably not one I'll be playing again in the near future.

Okay, so I've gotten up to level 7 and this game just has a few problems.
1: Definitely freemium. The microtransactions are everywhere and pushed all the time. You can buy a subscription, but that doesn't make the microtransactions go away, it just gives you a bonus pack of stuff and a certain amount of microtransaction currency each month. 90% of the content is locked behind real-money purchasing.
2: Broken in several places, one being a floating fish, which rotated merrily and once I saw it, I could no longer play the fishing minigame, which is required to keep your dragon's energy up.  Also, the fireballs in the flight club game (which is one of the most enjoyable parts of the game so far) will refuse to lock onto targets, and you can't fire manually, which makes a fair few of the levels impossible to 100%.
3: Looks terrible. These aren't good graphics for a PC game. They're not even good graphics for an iPad game.
4: Controls are not rebindable. You're stuck clicking go fast and go slow buttons like an idjit.
5: Has you walk everywhere for the first several hours of the game. I don't know how long away I was from being able to fly on my dragon, but that's what was promised me. Of course, I could turn my baby dragon into an adult immediately for 500 gems. Or five dollars.
6: Is a learning game oriented towards children. Spent a half hour teaching me the scientific method as part of a required quest.
7: HAS FARMVILLE IN IT. Literally. A farming minigame where you plant and tend crops, harvest and sell those crops, and then buy more seeds to plant crops with. It is implied that this part of the game is heavily important. I didn't stick around to find out.
8: If you stand next to a cliff, then rotate rapidly, your dragon will fall off the cliff and be lost to the nether void, only to pop back into existence when you enter a new area.
9: The voice acting doesn't match the text in the boxes. Petty, I know, but super annoying.
10: The high scores on everything are hacked.
11: LITERALLY EVERYTHING ABOUT THE GAME EVER.

This game is basically what you make of it.
First, be prepared to get frustrated.  Whether it be that your most important player getting killed, not being able to pick up the ball, or failing a block or series of blocks to get that all important TD.
2nd, be prepared to jump out of your seat in dis-belief!  Sometimes you will do the most rediculous thing/s and everything (even with the worst odds) will fall right into place.
3rd, this game is based mostly on strategy and how well you can manage or minimize your risk of die rolls.  (and yes, the die are random at ALL times.  that means that anything can happen).
Concept of the game:
Think of Rugby (closest thing I can think of) that is very bloody.  Players punch each other (called blocks) in attempts to get the upper hand of the pitch (field of play).  Kickoffs, fouls, and other aspecs come into play as you set your strategy to score....
With 10+ teams available to choose from (from the time of this now edited review), you play strategies based on the way you decide to grow your team.  Do you get as many players as possible to foul the opponent?  Do you upgrade your stadium?  Or do you save your money for the big guy?
This game does have a good tutorial and can teach you the mechanics of the game.  As far as strategy though, you will have to learn that part yourself or.....(go to the next part)
"This game is what you make of it!"
I mean this part.  The greatest aspect of the game is not knowing what will happen.  You can plan a flawless strategy to only watch it fall apart because a player failed in what you wanted him to do.  The good thing is that the opponent will have the same worries and problems (although it may not be in the same match...lol).  Dealing with that frustration is the biggest thing.
Another thing is that since their is no in game chat area for people, it may be hard to find a league to play in.  You may be able to look on steam forums or other areas of the internet.  Either way, you will have to do some searching to find "groups" for league play (unless playing the AI is your thing).  The league that I am in is called "Gobbln" (that is the correct spelling).  You can google it and perhaps that will help you get started.  Great place to meet others.  TS is available for our group.  And Gobbln is always willing to teach you as well to help you be better competition.
In the older version (Blood Bowl Chaos), you got to see the difference between upgraded players and rookie players with visual differences.  However, in this version, you must either hover over the player to see what skills they have or use the control button to toggle all players abilities as there is no visual differences between skilled and rookie players.
They could have also added in more stuff to the game such as apothecaries working on wounded players, Bloodweiser Babes selling Bloodweiser in the stadiums, etc...  But the game is still pretty darn good without those added things.
And lastly, they are coming out with a legendary edition.  With this edition, they are adding in a few things and is considered an upgrade for those that already own the game.  Cost wise, Blood Bowl is ideal in keeping customers.  Its not like a "f2p" game where you get added benefits of being a subscriber.  Rather, its more like you buy the big game, then you can opt to purchase more teams and such like things.  You don't have to buy it all, even if you did, the cost is still pretty darn good overall.  I spent around 40$ to buy the original, got a few free teams when they became available, and purchased the rest at discount prices.  So the total I paid is around 55$ up to date.
What is the game worth?
It is worth what they ask for it.  If you get it at a discount, always better.  Before you buy it though, I suggest that you youtube it or even twitch it and see what the gameplay is like and see if it is your "cup of tea!"

This game denies the very basics of interactive storytelling, that being to provide some substance to the player so he doesn't become bored. It really doesn't help that the story isn't good enough to hold interest, but the story is also told to you; this means any thoughts on the symbolism will be interrupted by the narrator telling you how you are supposed to interpret it.
I understand that the idea is the Narrator looks into one man's art and tries to make conclusions about the man's personality, but you would be doing that yourself if you played the game with minimal interruptions. This idea of judging other's art is treated so blandly that it felt like a 1 and a half hour walk through an empty room while someone told me off camera how brilliant he is.
This game is a snooze-fest and I expected more from the creator of The Steven Spectacle, however if you want to pretend that you are a high-class gaming connoisseur because you understood something what was directly told to you then I do reccomend you buy this.

TL:DR - 8.5/10, the game has come a very long way, its a solid arcadey simulation with a lot of fun to be had on multiplayer, worth it for anyone to check out, especially when its on sale.
Update: The updates keep coming in and slowly but surely the game is starting to shape up nicely, if it goes on sale definitely pick this game up.
Do you remember Destruction Derby for the Playstation One? I do, and I freaking loved it. Sadly that game would be absolutely unbearable nowadays. Thats where Wreckfest comes in.
The great thing about Wreckfest is that it isnt just Derby. There are circuit tracks on tarmac, and gravel. You have a small variety of cars to choose from and with recent updates there is a progression system so you can finally start from the bottom and work your way up.
Now, Wreckfest wasn't always as good, and wasn't always recieving updates as frequently as it is now. The good folks developing this gem have spent some time ironing out their version of car physics so that racing can be exciting and enjoyable for all car classes. The damage modeling they have done is great and its extremely satisfying to see your car get wrecked up during semi-clean contact racing.
This game has come a long way and the developers truly appear committed to completing this game and having it stand on its own in a sea of racing sims. A racing sim you will not find here. This is an arcade style simulation with the flavour of real physics behind it. You can enjoy it with wheel, a controller, or even a keyboard and you will not feel at a disadvantage which to me is extremely important. Although with a wheel you could probably have a great deal of fun drifting through corners in their new Asian Drifter style car(kind of looks like an old skyline).
The absolutely best part of this game though has got to be its Multiplayer. This game is like the DayZ of racing games when you are online, its just awesome. Most of the players that stick with this game prefer a Semi-Clean racing style, so you will enjoy the bump and grind of a derby, but against the backdrop of a circuit race. Its incredible how much fun you can have when you get a server full of people to race so clean no one is intentionally hitting, but everyone is trying to get in front and you have cars going 3 wide through corners without wrecking, but instead shoving and pushing each other out of the way as they jostle for that lead position.
...And then. You might join a server with no rules at all, and you'll be wiping the tears from your eyes because for the first time ever you're in first place, and then crunch! Both your front wheels are gone, your engine is bent in half and there is a smoldering wreck of a car from a player going backwards on the track, probably giggling and laughing hysterically in front of their screens as they watch 4 or 5 more cars plow into you, turning your car into a smoldering wreck aswell.
To each their own to be sure, but man the multiplayer can be wicked fun. I hope they make it so you can play the entire game progression wise on multiplayer. Right now you simply get all the cars for free but dont earn anything, and if you choose to race with a car you do own, you don't really earn enough for it to be worth while.
Anyways, thanks for reading, this game is an easy 8/10 as it is, because it really is that fun. It will climb to a solid 9/10 by the time all the content is in and they leave early access.

What I really liked about the first Dungeon Defenders had little-if-anything to do with actually getting out there and fighting; the repetitiveness even before the Quest for the Lost Eternia Shards stuff didn't bother me, because you had multiple defense zones spread across the map to keep intact, and a solid mix of options to make it happen (with each class being unbalanced, making it worthwhile to shore up weaknesses with another class's strengths) before the DLC heroes came out, who were overall stronger, and negated the use of apprentice / squire towers almost entirely. (I still like to try with my mage / ranger mix, as if it's True Defender Mode, but I digress.) What was fun was that defensive focus: I'd use my ranger to clear a lane to protect some towers before zooming across the map to heal the other side, and running off again to face the ogre on another end. I felt like my mana spending mattered a lot, and my presence in one area could make or break the win; my towers were doing most of the killing, but *I* was their salvation and guardian while they, my army, fought the endless battle.
DD2 doesn't feel that way at all. Between the large influx of mana, the layouts (I can't explain why they're worse, but they all feel tight and close compared to any map from QftLES or later, making it that much more apparent when you don't have the right power level, as you feel powerless standing there, desperately trying to repair things.), and having one less tower per class, it doesn't feel like my tower choices are what count; it feels like I just need gear. A mage's barrier and a squire's are about even; instead of wimpy mage barriers stripping elemental resist, both do spike damage as things hit them, with health determined by gear. Instead of having lightning AoE, fireball splash, arcane haste and sniper towers, I have front cone attack towers. The class towers feel like they're supposed to be balanced. And now they don't matter.
I wanted desperately to like it, based on affection for DD1. But, DD2 has a larger focus on the action side, with each class getting four combat spells and the mana split to builder's mana and self-regenerating fighter's mana. The four spells are pretty weak if you're builder specialized, but the little bursts of balanced power are still more productive to the defenses' aid than actually standing there and healing things - making it feel that much more useless to be a builder. Honestly if you want to do well solo, it seems you should just action specialize, build tons of barricades just to slow down the waves of encroaching enemies, and wipe everything out yourself.
Honestly, it feels weird saying I hate it because it's balanced, but... I hate it because it's balanced. DD1 had clear fantasies for each of its eight classes that centered on what their towers did or didn't do (i.e., mage's glass cannon towers that hit really hard and died really fast, Squire's stocky, slow things that could murder eventually but didn't die often, hunter's tricksy traps that had to be replaced often, monk's impressive area control...) but I've tried interchanging towers in strategies for DD2 and it didn't seem to matter at all. I've tried one of the DLC heroes, the Mystic, and she just feels like she does all the things better than the core four, which is what led me to write this review. (She has one of each tower type, and her front cone attack tower has a really big front cone.) Look. I liked you guys back in DD1, Trendy. But I felt a lot smarter in DD1 because I was picking towers based on what they did, rather than how good the gear was on the guy who placed that tower. Hell; I hate to say it, but I even liked Eternia better because, even in Eternia, dungeon defending meant playing a tower defense game. If I wanted to play Diablo with cute graphics, I wouldn't be looking to something called dungeon DEFENDERS. Maybe play a bit of Kingdom Rush to clear your heads and get back to me?

Everything is available from the get-go and you can skip a lower tier (if one can call it that) car and/or part altogether and go straight for the last one from each region or group. From the first car with no upgrades to owning every car with all the upgrades took about two hours total. I even purchased two more crews at a grand each just so each of the three regions have their own crew. I don't even play the races as I didn't buy this game for that racing simulator experience ("Wreckfest", remember?). Though derby mode is a lot of fun, I often wonder why I didn't get a point for hitting another car hard or assisting in wrecking it. tldr; Give it a go if it's on sale and you really want to get that Early Access feel, otherwise wait and see if things change.

First of all, I would like to say up front that even though it is still in development, this game is awesome.  It has an interesting art style, a compelling atmosphere, decent music, and a world with a lot of depth.  Many of the characters have intriguing storylines that can suck you into the game.
That being said, the game has enormous flaws, but I am going to contradict what many other reviewers are saying.  A lot of complaints have to do with the punishing "terror" penalty from sailing in open water and the resulting "nightmare" effects.  Here's a clue: TRY NOT TO SAIL TOO FAR FROM LAND!  If you rack up a lot of terror of a long period of time from sailing in open water, you can get a nightmare penalty, which is difficult to get rid of.  Nightmares can result in paranoia and mutiny from your crew.  THIS IS INTENTIONAL, not a bug in the game.
THe economy is a bit broken, but the game devloper plans on fixing this before the game is released.  While there are numerous items currently available to buy or trade, only four can earn you a profit unless you find an item or harvest it from a quest or monster.  The four items are fuel, supplies, colonists to venderbight, and mushroom wine.  Actually, fuel and supplies can be very profitable, because you buy them in London for 10 echoes (echoes are the game's currency) and sell them for 20 echoes.
In terms of upgrading and buying items for your boat, it appears that you can only buy them in your main port of call: Fallen London.  If this is the case in the final version of the game, you might as well just grind away at the early areas around London just save up to buy the biggest baddest ship possible.  It seems silly...and it is.  The developer should (and probably will) change this).
Questing is fun, but a lot of people have complained that it is too easy to die and sometimes a "successful" quest rewards less and adds too much terror in comparison with a "failure."  So far there are really only a handful of long-term quests, but the world to explore is going to be at least three times the size of the current playable world, so I would imagine there will be quite a few more quests.  The quests are referred to as "stories." in the game.
Experience for levelling up a skill is referred to as "fragments." When your fragments bar is all the way full, you get a secret which you may then spend on a skill point by conversing with one of your officers.  Having all of your crew and officers is extremely helpful as the officers add skill bonuses, stories, and I am sure that just scratches the surface.  I have been playing for quite a while, and I still haven't discovered all there is to know about the game.  It will not be complete until the end of September, but I would encourage people to buy it now and explore the game as it develops, providing input to the developer (who apperntly DOES read reviews like this one).  Based on user input, they can improve areas of the game that need work.
All in all, I give this game 9 out of 10, but I am willing to raise that as the game is improved.
Edit:
I am very deep into the game and I am enjoying it enormously.  I love this game.  Additional interactivity and better ways to pass on traits to future generations of steamboat captains have added greater replay value.  Love it.  10/10

There are rewards for progress both in unlocking abilities, and many unlockables that don't impact the game but are still rewarding to earn.
There were occasional bugs, but they were unimportant and rare enough that I barely noticed them. Took me roughly 19 hours to 100%. In that way, the game is much shorter than the N64 bigger buget versions. Still worth every penny.
