Five Nights at Freddys is one of the most terrifying experiences i have ever gone through. The game almost perfectly appeals to people who grew up with places like chucky cheeses and people who are scared of anamatronics, but is also just generally scary. I'm not going to spoil the game for people who haven't played it yet, and actually it's best to just go in blind with this game, you are the night guard at a place called Freddy Fazbear's pizza, and the animatronics come to life at night and try to kill you. You have cameras, two doors, and two lights on each side of those doors. The game, although it has horror in much more places than just the aesthetics, does have a creepy feel to it. It's at night, the lights barely work, and the animatronics are often in very creepy positions, and of course when you die you get a jump-scare. The real horror however, is the way you play the game. The patterns of the animatronics are seemingly random, and you get the feeling of hopelessness as you play the game, trying to manage your power and the animatronics at the same time. You have to put time in and get good at the game if you want to beat it. Although the gameplay is very simple, and the cameras are a very ineffiecent tool to see where the animatronics are, this is just the first game, and it's not meant to have perfect gameplay. It's meant to be scary, which it does excellently. 8/10

Bloodbowl itself is weird to recommend. It's something you have to try to see if you like it, but ask yourself these three questions first
Do you like strategy games? If no, don't get this, this is more strategy than sport.
Are you not okay with permadeath, Don't get it, your players who are amazing will eventually die. (X-com level of trauma).
Are you not okay with losing due to bad luck? Don't get it, because chance will screw you.
This leaves the question, should you get Bloodbowl 1 or Bloodbowl 2
Bloodbowl 2 is like two steps forward and one step backwards.
Graphics are obviously better than the first one.
The UI has improved in some aspects, percentages are shown instead of forcing the player to know the rules. However grids on the field are missing, as well as the quick overview of the roles of the players. This is quite annoying since some different players can look the same.
Tutorial is also way better than BB1, it's slow but it explains the game fairly well.
The other single player content is lacking though, so you will mainly be playing this multiplayer. I recommend joining a private league though, as the normal matchmaking is flawed, due to some teams being clearly better in that format. These are easy to find in the steam forums. The community is way bigger, so you will find matches much faster, about 30 seconds, instead of the 15 minutes in BB1.
Difference in the amount of teams is quite big though. 10 in BB2 while there are 24 in BB1.
That said the ten teams in BB2 are all of relatively equal strength, with one maybe being weaker than the rest. Whereas at least 6 six teams in BB1 are deliberately weaker. The advantage of ten players however is that it is easier for new players to learn strategies against the different teams.
So, I would say that for a new player bloodbowl 2 is better, but I would still wait for a sale.

For the gameplay, its simple. You are an underpaid guard working at Freddys pizza joint & the animatronics for some reason think you need to be stuffed into a animatronic suit. Stripping off your skin and crushing your bones trying to get you inside one of those things. The game will start you off in a office room. There are two doors with buttons for closing & a security camera to check rooms with. You might be confused at first since you cannot move around, only look, click and check cameras but this is what makes the game so thrilling.
There are so many unique mechanics in this and each character does something different and will appear at different doors. This is where strategy comes into play. Duskers is a sci-fi strategy 'rogue-like' game about gathering scrap in a dead universe. You sit at a computer in your space ship controlling your drones while they explore derelict space ships, hunting for scrap, fuel and useful tech.
The game is very old-school and controlled solely via the keyboard. There are two methods of controlling your drones, either by moving them around with the cursor keys, or by issuing commands to them via the terminal. Using the terminal requires you to memorize a handful of commands like 'navigate', 'gather' etc. As with all good terminals, you can just write the first few letters of a command and auto-complete it, speeding up the gameplay a little.
While exploring the rooms and corridors of the dead space ships and stations you often come across hostiles that can damage and destroy your drones. Luckily there are several ways to avoid and/or neutralize them; one way is to just suck them out the nearest airlock. This does however have the unfortunate effect of blowing out everything else that might have been in the room with the hostile. Point being, every action in Duskers has a consequence, and often you have to outweigh the risk with the reward. I've often omitted visiting parts of space ships because I just couldn't risk losing my precious drones.
I spend a lot of the time while playing just analyzing the situation and trying to find out how best to explore the ship with the means at my disposal. Sometimes the game throws a wrench in my plans like rupturing a pipe in a room, leaking lethal radiation all over it, or perhaps temporarily breaking the video feed on my drones, leaving them blind. The game might seem unforgiving at times, but I actually think this is good, otherwise I could just learn the optimum strategy and use it every time; some randomness and chaos is good. Also, it sends the adrenaline pumping when several alarms suddenly go off and you know you have to jump ship, frantically trying to type the necessary commands to save your drones, but ending up with 'naivgaet 1 r1' instead of 'navigate 1 r1'. Great fun!
The graphics are rather simple but work very well considering the setting. It actually reminds me of the computers from Alien (the movie), and by extension, Alien Isolation. Pure 70-80's sci-fi goodness!
The audio is great, with ominous sounds being heard throughout the ship, bulkheads creaking, computers chattering, and creepy unindentified noises. Sometimes you hear a loud groan and an airlock ruptures somewhere in the ship, setting off beeping alarms and flooding the room with radiation.
This game really speaks to the nerd in me, as it has 3 elements that I adore: scifi, drones and the terminal. I'm an avid user of the Linux terminal, and this game gives me the same power at my fingertips as the Linux terminal does. I feel like I'm acting more directly with the game through the terminal than if I was using the mouse as in most games. Of course, it does help if you have a good typing keyboard, preferably one that clatters really loudly!
Duskers might certainly not be for everyone, but I think that if you like the aforementioned points, you'll love this game. At this point I've only owned the game for a few days but have already played several hours (which is a lot for me) and still find it as interesting as when I first loaded it up. It's a game I can pick up for 20 minutes or play for 2 hours as I wish, and I can easily see myself playing it for hundreds of hours over the next few years.
I give Duskers a big thumbs up, even at the current 20€ retail price. To me it is absolutely worth the price.

I played DD1 and loved every second of playing.  I was extremely excited about DD2 but when it came out as a MOBA, it bombed royally!  I was extremely disappointed with this and even paid money to support their plans to change it back into its original gameplay.  Instead of redoing the game, it appears they kept some coding and left a bit of a MOBA game play.
Here are my issues with the game.
1. Time - It’s been years and this game is still in alpha/Beta testing.  Extremely disappoint considering how much time it’s been.
2. Price for heroes - The price for heroes jumped from $2-$5 to $99!!!!!  What were you thinking?
3. Maps - The maps are just wonky to say the least.  A whole wide hallway and one blockade in the center can stop them?
4. Towers - Some hero towers are either underpowered (mage) or overpowered (Lava mancer).  One Volcano can hit an entire map from the center of the playing field.  What’s the point?
5. Gear - Your gears IPwr is off.  One level 50 green with less stats have higher IPwr levels than a level 50 Mythical with more stats.  This makes no sense.
6. Heroes - You limit the heroes to four unless you pay more money.  Not even LOL, Warcraft, Clash of clans, or other iOS games do this.  If I am going to pay money, then you better offer me something great in return not BS costumes!
7. Costumes - its overkill!  Fix the game and make it actually work instead of playing dress up with your hero.
8. Abilities - The old abilities are gone and replaced with junk abilities which require mana that cost too much and feel like a MOBA game.
9. Mana - The mana is way too small to see and having everyone run around the entire map just to collect mana that only they can see is annoying.  If Player 1 already covered an area, why does player 2 have to run that same area to get mana.
10. Mana - The amount of Mana a player receives is way too low.
11. Pets - You no longer receive pets like last time, instead you have random drops with random stats, with random eggs, and no real way to farm.  it’s all just luck.  Which really sucks
12. Bags - I have 12 bags or so with 16 slots and scrolling and trying to organize them is a pain and a hassle.  No real way to organize all your gear, instead you have to play move and shuffle just to get gear in the right place.
13. Tutorial - you really get no tutorial on anything, it all just click and figure out on your own and hope you don’t lose anything.
14. Towns - You get randomly disconnected from town because a host has left.  Why do I have to rely on a host for a town meetup, shouldn’t this be a server hosted town and not based on someone’s connection.  Does this mean that one person’s PC is hosting all our heroes at once?  Seems crappy.
15. End of map - You have to wait for all players to make a decision before replaying the map or going to town.  if a player disconnected or leaves the session before you all press G, you all have to wait for the countdown to be over before you can go to town.  Seems like a complete waste of time.
16. Hero’s orbs/Spheres - The cost is too high and the abilities are too low.
I can go on and on about how much this game is nowhere near game ready.  I recommend either waiting to even see if this game will finish or just going back to DD1.
As of right now, I cannot stand playing this game anymore.  I have four toons, all 680 ipwr levels and am bored with farming maps that have no real direction.

I bought this game 6 months ago, on Christmas sale.
To get started with, i would like to inform you that i am an old enough guy, a guy who have played all the Silent Hill and Resident evil series of games.
So, i was thinking that nothing could really scare me, till it was proven i was wrong... Too wrong actually

I installed outlast on December 2014 and after only one hour of playing, i jumped off my chair, holding my pumping heart.
And then i shouted to myshelf:  "I will never - ever play this f#%$ing S#@t again".
The truth is, i never - ever deleted this game either.
It was standing there, on my computer screen, and it was looking like a challenge...
Actually, it was looking more like an excuse to dive again, in this paranoia of a game.
So, 3 days ago, i decided to give Outlast one more try...
And finally i finished it...
After all this lengthy introduction, i believe it is time for my final verdict.
Outlast is too scary...
Maybe it is too scary for my personal taste, but i also believe, it is too twisted, loathsome, disgusting and disturbing.
To all the above, i should add that it is a little repetitive, too short, it has no strategy at all, and the gameplay is try and error, till you find the correct route.
So, why do i recommend outlast then?
I recommend it, because it remained more than faithful to its initial promise, when i bought it.
From the first minute till the last, Outlast offered me pure horror, like no other game did in the past.
Nothing more.
7/10 then and i will never - ever play it again.

It's a very cthuluesque 'Victorian-era London fell out of the crust of the earth when hell-demons invaded and set up beauracracy over the surface and now the survives eke out a living in the murky 'neath' of not-hell,' type setting, expanding on the pretty rad browser-game free RPG 'Fallen London' (formerly Echo Bazaar).
Game's pretty decent.  It's an exploration roguelike, charting the 'zee (sea) trying to keep your crew, health, fuel, supplies, and sanity in check while dodging (or farming) unterzee monsters and pirates.  Half the game you'll actually spend rolling dice checks against your stats to extract vital goodies from various events dripping in lore, and the writing's so great and every failure can yield fresh new insight into this rich setting that I don't even get mad on dying.

Superhot is the game where "time only moves when you do", and is hands down, one of the most exhilarating games I think I've ever played. As a piece of design I would go as far as to say it's pretty much perfect and executed flawlessly. I've read comments from people who think there needs to be a crouch button, or that there should be grenades in the game, but they would make it far too difficult (and the game is already pretty challenging). The time it would take to perform either of those moves would almost certainly result in you dying. Wall-running on the other hand... that would spice things up a bit.
Superhot Team have shown great restraint and given players exactly what they need. There's no extraneous fluff put in to pad it out or tick boxes. Any other weapon you choose to add to the game's arsenal would overlap with one of the weapons you already have and clash with the game's time-bending framework.
Needless to say, the rhythm and flow of the combat is immense fun and after 13 hours play time I still cannot see myself getting bored with it. The FPS has been stagnating creatively for years, and that a small Polish team with about $230,000 worth of Kickstarter pledges have managed to craft something so fresh, so exciting and so satisfying to play is something bordering on miraculous. My big worry is that AAA devs will now use this mechanic willy-nilly without thought as to what it is that makes it so special.
Superhot is my first Game of the Year candidate. I loved the story mode - however derivative - and how self-aware it was, as well as its questioning of my enjoyment of such brutal violence. The endless mode and numerous challenge modes you unlock, plus how much fun it is to play, mean I'll be playing it for many, many more hours. It really is dangerously addictive.
TL;DR: Absolutely f***ing brilliant. 10/10

I'm a huge fan of Fallen London, but when I first picked up this game, I was skeptical.
I'd seen advertisements before but never bit because... well, I'm just not that into seafaring games. Plus my biggest gripes about Fallen London had to do with an Echo imbalance (money being INSANELY hard to come by) and repetitive tasks (not to mention a crummy action bar that only lets you take a certain amount of actions per day), and Sunless Sea had the potential to carry over two of those things.
Alas, it did. But let's talk about the good things first.
The game is fun. The missions are mysterious and interesting (especially on a certain island very close to home). Although limited, you can make choices that affect the story and finding all the different sea creatures is really neat. Based on your background choices at the start of the game, you even inherit certain abilities that will make the fights more interesting.
For instance, I chose a talent for "Mirrors," which is basically perception or "Watchful" from Fallen London (more or less). This means that in combat, I can observe the creatures instead of fighting them and piece together information to learn more about them. It adds a level of tension since the monsters can continue to hit me while I do this, but the payout could be worth it.
Now, the bad stuff.
One of my biggest pet peeves about Fallen London was that Echos are insanely hard to come by. This relegates you to completing the same tasks over and over and over again (grinding, essentially) in order to obtain enough money to buy even the lower level items, which got old quick. Additionally, since Fallen London had an action bar that limited how many actions you could perform in a day, grinding was frustrating since you were wasting actions on performing the same task a multitude of times.
There's no action bar in Sunless Sea, but there is quite a bit of grinding. The Admiralty sends you on missions to find "strategic information," but the trouble comes in that you end up getting the same ports over and over again (I've lost count of how many times I've been sent to Avid Horizon, for example). Nothing new happens on subsequent visits, and it gets boring quickly, but sailing to ports and exploring on your own isn't worth it without a charter from the Admiralty since that's basically the only way you can make any Echoes to pay for your fuel and supplies. If you ignore the Admiralty and just sail about willy-nilly, you'll end up dead in the water very quickly since your crew will eat you.
In this way, the game discourages exploration, and I feel the same way about its "terror" mechanic. Terror is accrued through time spent away from home waters (basically anywhere outside of your home port in Fallen London) and rises steadily as you sail. Random encounters will increase terror too, and once you get above 80 or so, crew start to exhibit strange symptoms. If you get to 100... well, any number of bad things happen (all of them game-ending).
The problem is that terror accrues *too* quickly, and more than that, there aren't many ways to effectively reduce it (especially since you eventually lose access to one of them permanently). You can spend a night in your room for 10 Echoes to reduce a whopping 1 terror, or carouse at the Wolfstack Docks for 30 Echoes to reduce your terror by a mere 5. And though it's true that your terror gets reduced every time you return to port, it only gets lowered to 50, which means that the next time you set sail, you better hope you don't have far to go or that you run into a random encounter that actually allows you to lower your terror somehow.
Stopping at other ports doesn't help unless you're again willing to spend money, and that's a hefty price too. In Venderbight it's 50 Echoes for one night in which your terror is reduced by 5, and there are a lot of ports where you don't even have the option to take shore leave at all.
And then there's the nightmare mechanic, which is what happens after your first mission when your terror gets set to fifty back at London. The next time you leave, you'll undoubtedly rank up 70 or so terror total. When this happens, it still reduces to 50 back at your home port, but now you get a quality called "nightmare strength." Once this reaches 5, you start taking even MORE terror because you're having nightmares.
So basically, success in the game is ruled heavily by acquiring Echoes, only they're few and far between. Without them, you either go mad or starve, and much of the thrill of exploration can't be experienced because the gameplay avidly works against you, and not just in a challenging way, but in one that makes it nigh impossible to get anywhere good.
I should note at this point that I don't feel terror is a bad mechanic, just one that's heavily flawed at the moment. There should also be a way to guard yourself from it once you've been on a certain number of missions. Maybe after your first three, the rate at which you accrue terror points reduces, and more significantly after that. You and your crew are gaining experience here, after all. The game should reflect that.
Additionally, there aren't many quests at this point. I know that's coming soon so I don't judge it too harshly for that, but I do wish there was more to do.
Lastly, I'm annoyed by the fact that the mode the game was "meant to be played in" doesn't allow for multiple save files. You can't save manually and it only autosaves when you reach a port, which is all well and good, but making a new game completely wipes your previous data. The only way to bypass this is to play the game on "Merciful" mode, which removes the Invictus token and insinuates you couldn't hack it on any other level of difficulty. I wouldn't have changed the settings if it weren't for the fact that more than one person in my house likes to play the game, and instead of constantly saving over each other's files, we decided to just change the settings, but I feel like it should be a fairly basic feature to include and I'm not sure why it wasn't in the first place.
But as always, Failbetter makes a great game through storytelling, mystery, horror, incredible atmosphere, and intriguing characters. I truly do recommend it and I'm just hoping to see some of these issues fixed in future updates!

I try and keep as close to the shores as possible. Lantern-buoys and light-ships are few and far between this far North. Being within sight of land...any land...seems to relax the tension that has been building on the ship. We cross over another abyss and I take care to keep my eyes on the horizon. You learn quickly not to look into such depths. Sometimes...the abyss stares back.
I've supplemented our now meager rations with Zee-Bat jerky. Somewhere between the tomb-colonies and the Whither, we lost another crewmember. It's a shape-shifter, of that much I'm sure. It is among my crew, but all I have are baseless accusations. I can't afford to lose anyone else if I want to maintain our cruising speed. The less time we spend steaming in the dark the better. So all I can allow myself to hope is that the murderer continues to pull its weight.
I dreamt of a wind in the depths, carrying something up. I fear I've spent too much time here. London used to call me home after a long voyage; a beer in a noisy pub, a smile from my love, all helped me forget the terror. Too I felt the lure of the zee, promising fortune with the lunatic sigh of the waves breaking on the shore. The dread now calls me too. That pull of the other at the bottom. Too many nightmares. Too many dreams of the deep. It fascinates and terrifies me. What happens when I surrender to this fear? What happens when the line draws taut?

Just Cause 2 brings much needed improvement upon the first game's format. Improving in almost every conceivable way, it turned a game which was riddled with problems and a repetitive nature into an enjoyable experience. It's far from perfect, story falling into the stupid and cliche once more, but at least somewhat satirical this time, if it was meant to be taken seriously then the voice acting certainly didn't help. Just Cause 2 can also crash on systems well above recommended requirements albeit rare.
Besides those points, there's a lot to like. The soundtrack is better than ever and perfect for the game. Graphics are great and polished, assuming you can overlook the forced depth of field (developers please stop this.) The world is expansive yet detailed with various areas like mountain regions, cities and deserts to explore and complete. Quality of gameplay as a whole has improved drastically with better controls, intuitive combat including use of grapple, better side activates, missions and creative bosses.
Avalanche studios put real effort in between JC1 and 2 and it shows. It's a much more enjoyable game, sure it can be repetitive going for 100%, but I still got a solid 18 hours out of the game without completing it fully. So I recommend picking it up for anyone interested in an open world sandbox all about causing chaos then go for it.

This is very probably one of the best games ever to grace this world. Over the 20+ years of experience I've had with gaming, I have played various titles such as Big Rigs Over The Road Racing and ET for the Atari 2600, and I must admit this is an almost better experience than those two!
The graphics are amazing for a game originally meant to be played on a TI-83 calculator and the sound effects remind me of the good old days of the Atari 5200.
Some may say that the lip syncing is awful, but I disagree. This is clearly intentional. The developers were trying to pass the message that the words that come out of your mouth aren't always what your heart wanted you to say. Another example of a philosophical message passed by this game is the apparent censorship of every word you try to type in the chat, by claiming they are "too offensive". Some people may say this is due to bad coding, but yet again, they would be wrong. The developers are trying to pass the message that even if you think you are free, you are always being surveilled and observed. Perhaps it is a call to Anarchism, which would be supported by the colour of Toothless, black, but, nonetheless, it is a very beautiful, and true, message.
You have to use your imagination to completely understand the fine piece of art that this game is. This game doesn't offer you an experience, the game challenges you to find your own adventure while you read the advertisements that are on every loading screen.
It challenges you to use Marxist Sociology, and question yourself "How would the common man react to this use of capital?" when you are faced with the option to use real money to make the game proceed faster.
I'd recommend this to anyone with a fine taste in art, and I suspect that this game will, in the future, be displayed in a museum, right next to the Mona Lisa, as they are both pieces of art of the finest quality.

Basically in this game you navigate your space ship around a map of star systems containing lots and lots of derelict space ships, using drones to board and explore them. Along the way you need to gather food and fuel, upgrade your drones and spaceship, and try to figure out what caused all the ships to be derelict -- of course you don't want it to happen to you, too.
Each ship you explore is like a mini dungeon in a roguelike, with rooms and passageways and doors and airlocks.
You can navigate your drones directly/visually, with arrow keys to rotate and move them around. You can also issue text commands to cause them to move or perform various actions. The drones can carry various upgrade modules to perform specialized functions; for example a drone might have a generator used to power the dead ship's systems so you can open doors and whatnot, or a gatling gun for defense. Most of the drone modules are controlled exclusively through text commands.
The challenge in the game comes from the fact that you don't have direct experience of the ships you are exploring; all you have is the information relayed to you by your drones, which may be incomplete. Hell, it's pretty much always incomplete. So you have to infer the safety level of rooms before you enter them, and use clever manipulation of ship systems and drone upgrades to defeat the threats without direct confrontation, or in an ambush where the odds are stacked in your favor.
It can be a little challenging at first to get used to the command line interface and learn all the various drone capabilities and how to use them; but the learning curve is quite navigable and it is rewarding to get good at it. You can set up aliases for frequently used commands (or just-in-case commands that are too complicated to type in a hurry when under fire).
If you do well, you will acquire more drone upgrades, ship upgrades, food, fuel, and information.
If you do poorly, your drones will be destroyed, your ship will run out of basic resources, and you will have to re-start from scratch in a new randomly generated galaxy -- death is permanent.
It's not for everyone, but if it sounds good to you, you will probably like it.

The Coma - light and darkness battleground left me with a sour taste in my mouth. Right off the bat, it's a 3D first-person platformer, which is a type of game that often brings some inherent problems to the table. Jumps are often a bit picky, and some environment effects can catch you, even though it would have seemed you were safe.
Visually, it looks all right, but not any more special than the content that comes pre-loaded in the Unreal Development Kit (The Coma is powered by Unreal Engine 4, in case you were curious,) so I really woldn't call it "stunning." The atmosphere wasn't great as it was fairly silent and there wasn't anything tying these different environments together. In fact, I'd say that the atmosphere had to have been The Coma's weakest point, and that hurt the game overall.
Platformers are simple games because all you really do is jump over gaps and avoid obstacles. However, that doesn't make them bad, so long as you have something going on. Take an old Mario game, for example. The gameplay is simple and straight forward, but there are sound effects, infectious music, and a unified art style that develops a unique experience. The Coma doesn't do that. The Coma sits there silent, with only the 'clomp, clomp, clomp' of the character's footfalls to accompany you. By going from a surreal space environment, to a cube construct room, to a Greco-Roman temple, then to a sci-fi looking corridor, I'm left wondering 'why are these different things here?' Perhaps if The Coma had some kind of story that brings these together in some way, it would have been easier to get pulled into the experience, but there just... wasn't.
The Coma had the potential for an interesting game. We could have had some story that really delved into why this person had this vastly different concepts floating around in their head. We could have had a story evolve from the two "light and darkness avatars" debating over the fate of this individual that they're huddled around. Hell, we could have had some direction on where to go and what we were actually trying to achieve. But, this game doesn't have any of that. Instead we have silent platforming with no reason or motivation to do any of it.
Ultimately, I can not recommend this game, there just isn't enough there to justify it. It is just so lacking in content that it feels like a beta release, maybe even an alpha release, but certainly not a final release.

A small spaceship docks on the side of a long dead station and begins a process it has carried out a hundred times before. Airlock doors creak open and 3 decaying drones shuffle into the waiting dark, scanning for anything out of the ordinary. A drone heads to a nearby generator and powers up a small portion of the ship. Ancient lights flicker to life and reveal dusty, abandoned rooms to sightless machines. Nearby doors hum with their newfound power, waiting to be opened and to reveal their secrets.
The other drones begin searching for something, anything useful. A drop of fuel to make it to the next ship, a chunk of scrap to repair that long suffering drones faulty camera, maybe a destroyed drone full of upgrades or a new addition to the team.
A door is opened and a drone begins to move into the next room but there's something wrong with the camera feed, the darkness in the other room seems to be moving, pulsing and whirring.
That's no fault.
You waste no time in jumping into action, this is a threat that has been seen before. Your fingers dance across your keyboard, commanding the door to shut before the horrors from the other room are unleashed. A finger slips and instead of Door 10 slamming shut Door 19 on the other side of the ship slides open. The swarm flings itself into the room and begins to dismantle the nearest drone. Panicking now you order the 2 remaining drones back to the boarding ship, leaving the 3rd to it's fate. Maybe you can salvage something from it later.

"'The Darksouls of platformers haha. This game is too hard for the casual to intermediate gamer' Not Reccomended"
I take it back. This game has been 10x worth the asking price of $20! I love it! But, before you read the review, take note that this game is nearly unplayable with the keyboard as a controller, I HIGHLY reccommend an Xbox, PS4, or Switch Pro controller.
I feel that the people of today's society are too use to having their hands held in videogames. As a direct result, consumers retaliate and shy away from any game with difficulty; done right or not. Cuphead brings said difficulty to the table, that's for sure, but the game always brings you back in as you see yourself get further and further to the flag on the death screen. This is a big part of what makes the game so great, I never want to leave the game! The times I need to take a break to cool off is always followed by a yearn to go back.
On top of the alluring gameplay, the visual style is amazing! It's a true, beautiful homage to 1930s rubberhose animation and you can see all the hard work that the animators put in to every frame of this game. Every part of the game even has the screen crackle effect! I really like the color scheme and how the game was presented as a whole.
One of the little things that I appreciated was the sound effects. I love the clicking sounds shooting produces and the sound when Cuphead jumps as well. It gives off the vibe of a controller clacking, and it really just sends me good vibes. Not to mention that all of these effects are coupled with a nice sound track. (I like King Dice in particular)
A few tiny things before I continue onto the gripes is that I found the grading system really fair, and I loved the large array of bullet types and charms. They add a level of customablility that I feel I couldn't do without.
Now every game has some bad aspects, and Cuphead is no exception. First off, the keyboard - as I mentioned earlier - makes the game impossible, and really unconfortable. I litterally had to go out and buy a controller just to play (and I'm glad I did). The second and last problem is that the default control scheme is not the best. I personally reccommend using the Right trigger as Dash, and the Back Right trigger (ZR, R1, RT) as the lock on button, but of course, customize as you please.
All in all, this is one game that I reccommend anyone interested in video games should play and it's definitely fighting for my personal Game of the Year. Cuphead has all taught us a lesson and opened our eyes to show us how as a society we've been reduced into our safe zone of easy, mellow games and that maybe we should accept more difficult games onto our plates.
Buy it.

The game's weaker points are the repetitive tasks; enter a new area inhabited by a new enemy who walks a robotic path patrolling different rooms that you'll need to access to complete the current objective. Hide from the enemy and study his movements. Then sneak past him and advance forth to complete the objective. That's essentially what you'll be doing for most of the game.
The story is outstanding, however, so you'll likely be provoked to advance through the game even after becoming bored with the repetitive gameplay. I won't spoil the story, but I will highly recommend the DLC to experience a more complete ending. Let me clarify that I don't believe the original ending is flawed, but I do believe that the DLC ending paired with the original makes for a much better experience.
My favorite aspects of the game were the scenes I encountered. Again, I prefer not to spoil anything, but I will say that it displays some outstanding horror scenes. I'm not talking about standard gore such as blood, bodies, limbs - those things are present throughout. But there are a handful of memorable scenes that will certainly grab your attention. You'll see.
In short, the base game and DLC are worth the current price of about $30 combined, and the experience is worth your time.

SUPERHOT is kind of like Quantum Leap, where you are suddenly put into a scenerio where everyone wants you dead. You're in an elevator when three men draw their guns on you. You find yourself in front of a speeding car. Instead of having a hologram of an aging playboy and his Lego-built pocket computer to help you, you instead have the ability to start and stop time - time only moves when you do.
The whole thing plays like a first-person puzzler, the puzzle being "how do I kill everyone in the room before they kill me?" Thanks to time only moving as you do, you can dodge bullets, catch disarmed weapons in mid-air and spin around to perforate the Red Guy behind you with the gun you just liberated from another enemy.
After you finish a run, the game replays your actions in real time, which often plays out like a choreographed action scene in the best of situations, and at its worst it looks more like someone who's running an aimhack program in an FPS. But where the replays can be hit-or-miss, the mechanics are consistently solid.
The main storyline is short, maybe a few hours of gameplay at best, but the addition of endless modes, challenge runs and such give the game a life far beyond the main game. The graphics are deliberately minimalistic, which serves the mechanics well. Where these two elements (game length, graphics) have been at the center of complaints for people, I think that the story is succint, the graphics suit the premise perfectly.
The only thing on my wishlist is a level editor - I'd love to see other action movie scenerios set up, and be given the opportunity to Jason Bourne my way out of them.

Greggie was born in a very small town. He grew up just like the others as the town grew around him. When he became an adult and a vacant house was built, he occupied it. Yet, somehow Greggie stayed alone in the big stone house and this was noticed by the benevolent builder and landlord. He would stop by now and then to check if Greggie finally found his true love, but year after year Greggie stayed alone.
He saw orchards, farms and pastures built. He was there when the first  iron mine opened up. He shopped in the market across from his house and looked for friends in the nearby church. As the city expanded across the river and nomads kept coming into town he realized he was in a great city. But there was nobody to share it with.
Greggie worked as a miner, then a woodcutter, and finally as a vendor in the market across from his house. What Greggie did not know was that the builder was looking for ways (mostly googled) how to find him a spouse. Finally, at the age of 41 Greggie was not alone.
Happily the builder turned to other matters to ensure that the city kept providing for its citizens. Now and then he would still check in on Greggie to make sure he was ok.
99/10 Would stalk Greggie again :)

Pros: Disturbing, gory, intense. Plenty of suspense to go along with the jumpscares. FPP parkour done right: no start/stop, you can usually tell where you're supposed to go even when you sometimes have to figure it out while running, and it hardly ever messes up. The "found footage" style is a great idea and implemented well... the scary stuff isn't just there for the player's benefit, you're documenting it, the world will know the truth. The simplicity and linearity means you're never bogged down. Cool story, based in Norse myth. Stealth and chases work well together, and you hardly ever feel truly powerless, unlike in Penumbra and Amnesia(which I love, don't get me wrong). Creepy, memorable character designs.
Cons: Excessively gory, both in the areas that are gory, and the amount of areas that are gory(which, to be fair, aren't all of them), so you do get used to that. Length varies from 2-6(mine was 4) hours, and there's little replay value, in part due to the simplicity and linearity. Bad ending. Sometimes you do get slightly lost.
My recommendation: If the "found footage", stealth and parkour survival horror appeal to you, definitely play this.

I came into this game blindly and was blown away at everything. To start, the gameplay: Feels familiar to Super Mario 64 for me, the way the physics in the game along with how nice the controls feel is just something amazing (used a PS4 controller) and everything is very simplistic but you can do insane stuff with this. This is a game where almost everything can be done by sheer skill alone, there are things from the story that make things easier (as well as some that are necessary to progress) but you can get most things just by careful jumps and momentum.
The atmosphere feels alive, the music is very well done and complimented each area very well along with the remixed versions of the songs. The art style brings everything to life, it can appropriately set the tone with keeping the cutesy art style, the animations look very nice and gets extra points for matching characters so well. There's very small details that this game gets done and I would have definitely missed if I rushed through, this game is one where I actively took my time as it felt rewarding for exploring.
The story is very captivating as the main arc is there but you still feel intrigued with all the side characters and their stories. I should mention the voice acting in the game is amazing, each actor nailed their character and conveyed the humour very well.
This game should not be too difficult aside from a few parts for seasoned platformers, it has a fixed difficulty but there's a collectable that can make you die in 1-hit if you want to add more challenge which the game does reward. The bosses in the game suit each area very well with each having their own little gimmicks so each fight doesn't feel repetitive.
The only real downsides I have with this game is that there was a few areas where the game restricts the movement with certain walls and a few times where a very specific spot didn't work on one or two occasions. The other thing was I experienced 2 game crashes but they were minor and this game has a very good checkpoint system so I didn't really lose that much progress and for me 2 crashes in the time I played is very good.
Overall in combination with the story, the art, animation, voice acting, gameplay, soundtrack, comes together and creates an experience which I won't forget any time soon. This sets a good example of what a 3D platformer should be like and I'm proud to give this game a 10/10, you should definitely buy this game and give it a chance to impress you.

Although, i felt, that the developers ran out of ideas gradually from the second third of the game, the number of jumpscares, that this game operates with, and the atmosphere; the depressive morale and the uncertainty of "whats going on?, what will happen next?" is fairly enough to say that this game is a good horror game. The game sometimes becomes frustrating, when an enemy chases you, caches up, starts hitting you, and if you are not able to get out of his grip, its almost certain that you will die. Over, and over, and over again. It's worse, when you have no idea, where to go, where to run, what to do, and you will have lots of these events, because it's not hard to get stuck in this game, if you're playing a survival horror game of this kind for the first time. The story of the game is not much, you are a journalist, who receives an e-mail, from an insider in Mount Massive Asylum, that something is wrong, going to investigate, and find yourself stuck, amongst a bunch of mad men trying to kill you, who knows why? Later in the game you'll find out, that the cause is something (not so) paranormal, but not necessarily scientific. Feel the triviality? I did too. Thats the first twist in the story. The second one is that in the end you will feel, you know the outcome, but gonna run into the clihe of a post apocalyptic FPS-RPG. So forget the story, the point in this game is being scared. You will not have weapons, although you would need it, because of the said flustrating things above. The choice is to run, hide, press a button, turn a valve or two, find this and that, then succeed, or die trying, and being scared a few times in the process. The graphics and optimization is nice, the voice acting, sounds are almost outstanding, the character animations are an A+ work, and its a pity, that the last 1-1.5 hrs almost kills the whole feel of the game, because the whole game gets a flat, "run, find and push 3 buttons, and get out" mood, without any kind of jumpscares or any other scares to be exact. Also because of the game is no longer than 8 hrs for first time playing, you get the feeling of "not enough, i would have played more.", although you get the answers to everything, that you wanted to know, through out the game. To sum up the above: If you are looking for a good survival indie horror game, Outlast is a great choice, but not for the full 20 Eur price, try to get it from somewhere cheaper. For me the game is an 88/100 points. See you in the DLC!...

SUPERHOT has a really cool mechanic where time only moves if you move. This turns what would be an ordinary shooter into a really cool tactical simulator (almost). The story mode is SUPERSHORT, but luckily there's tons of unlockable challenge modes and endless modes.
Kind of disappointing is that I haven't found any of the cheat modes that were in the beta. Maybe they'll be patched in, in the future.
The biggest let-down is the optimization. For a game of this scope you don't really need tons of graphics settings, but for my system (which runs the newest games on close to max settings) I had to turn everything to the lowest settings in order to get -relatively- smooth gameplay. That being said, the visual style isn't really focused on amazing graphics to begin with, so running on minimum doesn't hurt what this game has achieved; a really cool shooter.

I got that game, expecting a weak Mario 64 clone, so I wasn't expecting much, since I'm not really into 3D platformer.
Long story short, I ended up liking it far more than I should. You probably don't care about my story, so I'll keep it short.
Flaws :
- controls take some time to get used to, especially if you're used to Mario. The controls are similar to these, but not identical, so until you have them down, you're going to land in a lava a few times,
- the voice acting is not that good. Some voices are nice, others are below average. Apparently, people who backed the developpement voiced the game, so it's more an issue of fanservice than hiring professional,
- a bit too short, and maybe too easy. The former is an issue, the latter is a matter of taste. Just be warned that it's not Super Meat Boy 3D.
Now, for the good parts :
- once you have the controls figured out, it's a real pleasure to jump around,
- the levels are memorable, and every one of them is unique,
- the musics are nice, some of them even good enough to be listened outside of the game,
- you have numerous interactions that serve no gameplay purpose, but help you get immersed in the game,
- the characters are charming, the protagonist's movement and poses constantly remind you that she's a kid and that she's (mostly) having fun,
- the game is quite easy, so it fits for a relaxing afternoon or after a hard day of work.
And finally, what I think is really important in a game like this : you, in most cases, have a way around obstacles. You can decide to go over it, to slide under it, or to go around it. Background:
I began playing The Long Dark a few updates ago. At first I thought only one map was playable in Sandbox, but found that there was so much to do and explore at first that it kept me entertained for a while. I can't decide if I like the lack of a tutorial or not, and kind of assume that may be what they do with the story mode. At first I could only survive a day or two because there was no in game map, which adds a flair of realism... on the other hand I ended up seeking help from the gaming community in maps that they made... which sort of feels like cheating, but I can't make it through otherwise because I would become so hopelessly lost I would not last a day.
This game cause me to really get involved with the community for the first time, because I had to look up youtube videos and things like that when I found out there was a way to unlock the other maps. I couldn't believe at first that there were gamers that had made it 50+ days in this game... but after watching videos, reading guides, and searching for suitable maps I found that I was able to unlock all the maps and make it for over 30 days.
I Survived 20 Days With No KNIFE OR AXE:
So this was the craziest game I played, and it was actually the one where I survived over thirty days. (Thus far this is my personal best.) This game spanned all maps in my search for the elusive blade. I was lousy with guns and bullets though, I had four guns and something like thirty or more bullets. It was insane... but I could not skin anything, harvest meat, or anything... Movement is life seems to always be the theme of this game and it was expressed especially in this challenging search.
Finally on day twenty-one I killed a wolf over a fishing shack and inside there was the precious... a KNIFE. I promptly went on a ten day killing spree where, by the end, I sported every craftable worn item. Finally a couple of packed up wolves took revenge upon me for killing so very many of their brothers.
Suggestions:
I really love the potential of this game and that improvements and changes keep being made to better the game play. I really love what has been done with this game so far, and if these things where never added I would still play it. However, I think these things could improve on the game and make it more fun. And it is all about using a system already in place in the game... the crafting system.
While my search for a blade made the game more challenging I feel that a knife and axe are some of the most basic of human tools. If I am able to craft a bearskin rug I really think I should be able to craft a shiv out of deer antler. I think it should be less tough then a found metal blade, and should be made from something like antler, reclaimed wood, and spare parts. As for the axe, stones could be easily added to the game and you could make a stone axe from reclaimed wood, gut, and spare parts.
I also think an interesting aspect would be adding scrap metal in with being able to search for reclaimed wood within buildings... and scrap metal could be turned into spare parts. To balance this and the addition of the bow out you can make things like guns, axes, and knives more elusive in the game.
Another thing I would love to see is the addition of maps to the game, but making them an item you can find. If realism is the key here then there would probably be area maps littered about in areas such as this. Especially in glove boxes inside of cars, which are in this game.
Another item I think would be really cool is the addition of a snow sled. Snow sleds are really basic items you can easily make from things like a cupboard door or scrap metal, gut, and reclaimed wood. It would allow the player to transport more items over long distances, such as moving from one map to another, and you can add the drawback that it will slow your character down if dragged across the road or railroad tracks.
I never played the game when this was an option, but I would really love the snow shelter option to be brought back. I really like the idea of your character slowly becoming stronger and wilder as time goes on through crafting items and actually surviving. I think adding these things will allow your player way to survive for longer without luck being such a key element. You already have things like random storms, bears, wolves, injury, ect to challenge your player. And the fact that one wrong move kills you and completely ends your game. As a player I like the challenges, but I would have more fun if there was more I could do to control my fate and survive for longer periods of time.

Imagine you’re the only human alive in the entire universe and you’re stuck inside a spaceship, how do you survive? You get your hands on little drone fellas and you send them to derelict spaceships in search of resources vital to your survival. Welcome to Duskers.
The visuals are pretty basic but do an amazing job in conveying information to the player. Still, I’m a huge fan of how the map looks, it reminds me a lot of old sci-fi stuff and it looks like something that came out from the Warhammer 40k universe. Duskers is an excellent example of how graphical fidelity isn’t a necessary condition for a game to be not only immersive but truly wonderful. The premisse of the game is pretty simple, board abandoned spaceships with up to 4 drones and try to get as many resources as you can, preferably without loosing any drones.
You can visit different systems on the galaxy map, and inside each system you can travel to nearby derelicts and then board them. As you play the game, you’ll be able to equip your drones with different modules which grant them special abilities, and you’ll also be able to upgrade said modules, as well as upgrade your mothership. These modules can be things like motion sensors, for detecting enemies in nearby rooms, or generators, which can power sections of the old ships.
The thing that really makes Duskers brilliant is its atmosphere and how involved you can get while playing. You control your drones via remote control or by typing commands on your console from your secure, albeit decaying, mothership. This allows for quite some claustrophobic scenes, if you can call it that, because when controlling the drones remotely the camera is really close to the drone. The way I see it, the game becomes more tense and a lot more fun when playing in the schematic view. Here you can see pretty much the entirety of the vessel you’re currently at, and it’s best to use when issuing commands via the console. It is the fact that you’re actually typing those commands on your keyboard that make the game so atmospheric and immersive. It is the perfect way to recreate this scenario, it is as if you were actually this lone survivor struggling to survive, if that makes sense.
At first I thought it would be somewhat confusing, being able to control the drones both ways at the same time but it is actually not. In order to move throughout the ships you must open doors and sometimes power them with generators carried by your drones. Each door is identified by a code, like d1, d2, d3, and so on. In order to open or close a door you simply type that code in the console. Simple right? The thing is, you have to be careful and slowly scan the ship in order to see if there are any monsters or defenses lurking. If you find a turret, you can disable it by interacting with an interface, which requires a drone equipped for this purpose. In order to get yourself rid of enemies, you can lure them to other rooms and then close the doors behind them, allowing you to explore the room they were originally in, or if you can also open airlocks or activate the ship defense system.
Don’t let the looks deceive you. Duskers its truly an amazing and unique game unlike anything I have ever played. It is tense, tactical, atmospheric, it requires careful planning and thinking, and most important, it is a lot of fun. I’m looking forward to see how this one develops!

So, you wanted to get scared. You wanted to play a horror game. Perhaps a survival rogue-like one? Forget your run-of-the-mill jump scare games, monsters, aliens and other nasties. Duskers will make you fear mere sounds of the ship you've docked at creaking, shudder at seeing flashing red doors and jump at simple beeps of your console.
The atmosphere of the game has to be applauded over and over. The graphical nature is simple yet complex. Simple in terms of the console view where you can see the location of your drones, the layout of the ship, the state of its doors and so on. This part is logically clean and very un-Hollywood like, where terminals will be more graphically impressive than any operating system yet look a fraction as useful. The console, coupled with the ambient rumbling of your ship's engines as well as various blips and blops, will reinforce the feeling of isolation. The feeling that you are truly alone in the cold vastness of space, desperately trying to keep your aging ship and failing drones to keep going as you attempt to figure out just what has happened to everyone.
The complex part of the graphics is the actual drone view of the ships you board. Since you're remotely connecting to your drones, you can only see what your little workers see with their sensors and cameras. This means you have a limited line of sight and a distorted representation of the corridors, terminals and generators you happen to come across. This view is both beautiful, in a way, and terrifying, as the ships' interiors are a jumble of broken pipes, floors and other machinery. Often you might barge into a room you could not probe for motion beforehand, trying to spot an enemy in order to pull out and shut the doors, but you will instead get spooked by an eerie formation of damaged equipment that might, for a moment, make it appear like you have stumbled upon a hostile entity.
The bad guys, in this case, are an unknown. You will have to progress through the story - the bits and pieces of uncorrupted (or semi corrupt) transmissions and logs of the people that had left the derelicts where they are. Your enemy will be unrelenting, unfeeling and without mercy for your drones. Should your greediness to collect more scrap, drones or upgrades get the better of you (which, with the usual scarcity of the resources it often will) and make a mistake of scouting a room you can not escape for one reason or another, the game (or, rather, the enemies) will punish you greatly. Thinking and planning ahead is always a concern and, often, you will find yourself thinking of the worst case scenario, per-emptively shutting doors and moving the rest of your drones away from the unfortunate scout and gatherer.
Later on, as you scavenge, the game will provide you with various upgrades, systems and scrap to keep your group of drones going, but never will you become complacent, as the ship you are piloting (you can commandeer some ships you clear out as well) will always have limits in terms of maximum scrap (currency) and upgrade slots. With these limits, you are always encouraged to be smart with your spending and take as few risks as possible while scavenging. However, not taking risks is simply not a part of this game.
Every ship you will dock will be dangerous. There are enemies, defensive turrets you can enable and then mistakenly run into, failing airlock doors which will, after opening for the final time, cause all the air in the exposed rooms to be blown out, including your drones, enemies and goodies. Not only that, if you manage to somehow contain the situation, exposing the rooms to space will flood the rooms with deadly radiation, which will adversely affect your drones to the point of them failing completely.
In the world of Duskers, danger is always present, risk taking is a necessity, planning is important and feelings of isolation are a constant.
And it's a world I absolutely adore.

*** EARLY ACCESS REVIEW: ***
I've played Duskers long enough to get a good feel for it and I have to say, sadly, I'm not impressed. Don't get me wrong: I genuinely _want_ to like Duskers with its fun concept of piloting your vulnerable tools around derelict spacecraft from the relative safety of your control station but it doesn't feel as though there's much reason to go looking for fuel, scrap, (possible) drones to either salvage or steal parts from, or upgrades because the chances of actually finding something useful are slim to nil - More on that in a bit. Ironically, you're required to explore in order to continue surviving so it's a catch 22.
Duskers is, at its core, a roguelike set in space with cool 80s-looking computer graphics which in and of itself is worth a lot in my book because not only does it look neat, it doesn't get boring because it works very well with the concept. The 'drone vision' with its primitive interpretation of the environment through sensors and crappy audio from drone mics are a nice touch. You genuinely feel like you're piloting a small fleet of drones. You can either manually drive the drones around (something you'll find yourself doing a lot) or the game gives you a command interface similar to a Linux/Dos/Windows cmd prompt where you 'program' your drone to move and perform tasks; essentially queueing-up tasks for it. The command interpreter, for lack of better name, is a bit dodgy though which can sometimes result in commands you queue appear to look correct (at least according to the game's limited in-game help) but actually not work correctly, or at all. This can result in not executing at best, unexpected behaviour or worse: catastrophic mistakes being made. You're actually better off manually piloting the drones for the really tricky stuff. I'd like to see the command interpreter be a bit more refined so you're not left second-guessing just prior to hitting Enter and re-reviewing the command sequence for the fifth time.
Another problem I noticed with Duskers after the initial 'coolness' factor wore off, was much of the gameplay relied on dumb luck, not skill. For example, the tools one would use to determine if going in an adjacent room is a wise idea (motion scanner, sensor, etc.) are not only unreliable but you're not even guaranteed to get any of these useful tools to 'look ahead' which means you'll be sending your vulnerable drones head-long into the unknown - As a player, where are my tools to help me choose if this is a wise idea? You're essentially left guessing. This, in turn, not only exposes the rest of your drones to danger, but is almost a guarantee you'll be one less drone going home and making next mission even more difficult due to missing tools (which are scarce as is).
Should you lose all of your drones (which can happen in a single mission!!) you're done- Game over. Time to Reset. During a play session of about two hours I reset the game 16 times because of various reasons in which I simply could not continue the game. Either my drones would be trapped in a space station, I would run out of precious fuel (even after jumping because let's face it: The fuel dispensers aren't guaranteed to give you anything) or I would lose all of my drones by sheer dumb luck (bulkheads blowing open and pulling my drones into space, doors not sealing so my helpless drones were either mowed down by some enemy, irradiated or pulled into space). The game does it's best to warn you about these types of events (mostly) but that doesn't mean you can use your skills to avoid it for every situation. The most you can do is try to get out of the craft with your drones or jump to another galaxy in hopes you'll find more fuel to carry on. Also, you're not even guaranteed to find any scrap to keep your drones in moderate working order or repair your ship or their upgrades. The readout of the craft you're going to be boarding has a 'Scrap Capacity' number which, in my experience, has been nowhere near what I've actually recovered from any of the places I've visited. Most of the time I usually find somewhere between zero and five scrap which usually I'd store for after the next mission in hopes I'd be able to repair my drones to a decent health if they made it back. This is assuming they didn't take additional damage.
The enemy types in Duskers aren't vast but they do serve their purpose. You basically have to try your hardest to slip past them (manual control) whilst giving the more menial tasks to the command queues (keeping fingers crossed you don't have to intervene whilst performing a crucial sneak which hopefully won't result in you being detected). Your options are either avoid, attempt to outrun or go on the offense against them. For two of the three entities these options work but there is a third type that is so damn fast it makes me jump every time my drone is attacked by one. This one appears to 'leap' on your drone, if it's detected (and it usually is), and is an insta-kill. But again you'd not know if this type was in the room until you happened upon it. I've tried killing this type before: Blowing it up with a mine, shooting it with a turret, blowing it out into space by opening an airlock – No joy. They are invulnerable. Worse yet, there can (and have been for me) been multiple of them on 1 ship so you're pretty locked down and may as well just pack up and leave if you can.
Duskers has an interesting back story that I'm really keen on finding more about. The story is pieced together throughout your various plays (hint: You'll restart the game a lot) and the story is cumulative so you've at least got that going for you. As of this writing it wasn't complete but from what I'm gathering it's shaping up to reveal what happened to, well, everyone, as the game developer's promised.
Bottom line- Here is some suggestions for the developers:
* Rougelikes punish the player for dumb choices BUT the player still has control to make these choices. Duskers doesn't give you any of the tools necessary to approach each (or hardly any) situation without blindly guessing if you're going to make the correct move and prosper. Best case is you'll enter an empty room but that's of no value, generally. Success through repetitive play isn't fun if you keep running out of options 'just because'.
* Drones are basically thrown into the jungle without even so much as a butter knife: They need weapons, even cheap ones that don't last long. As a player I would love to be able to get access to at least 1 weapon for one of my drones that will have an effect.
* Enemies need to do more than just sit and wait. Often times I've entered a room and there would be something just sitting there in wait, dead-centre of the room. They might do with a bit of patrolling around the room they're confined to.
* More scrap. Since the drones are mobile punching bags, it would be fair to throw in a decent amount of scrap from time to time to give the player the option to repair. Again, if the player cannot continue because their drones are falling apart and they've not had adequate scrap: How is that their fault? They didn’t choose to not repair.
Duskers is a fun game, but has potential to be something truly unique and great. I look forward to the future updates. I'm going to suggest people save their £15 but should things change in future updates I'd be more than happy to recommend this game.

As the game progresses, RNG will refuse to give you certain ship mods 100% neccessary to progress in the game. Such as quarrintine bypass or transporter to get on certain locked vessels.
The 'end game' consists of, as far as I can tell, peddling along till you have to restart because all modules are at impossibly high failure rates to destroy themselves with no ability to repair them because of the game's stingyness with giving scrap to repair things. The logs to "piece together' what happened to the galaxy are often uninteresting, and you will quickly get enough different ones to know exactly what happened to everyone. Leaving no further incentive but to peddle the RNG bike till you stop getting enough scrap for basic repairs.
You can adjust breakdown rates and scrap rates in the options, but I am leveling my judgement at the intended base balance of the game. My judgement is game balance is poorly thought out in effort to force the player to 'diversify' their tactics in a game where you have no options to diversify your tactics unless you've already had the game hand you victory several times over in the form of a wider selection of mods. I've watched developer videos, and he often conflates the game softballing him wealthpacked ships with tactical prowess.  At which point you naturally succeede if you've already had the game hand you every mod you need.
As is, the only viable tactic is gaining the ability to safely scout out rooms ahead of time for threats, but the ability to do so is limited. Even if you manage to spot a threat without endangering yourself, your ability to clear it or redirect it is entirely RNG rather than a factor of player skill.
I really can't recommend it. Which is a shame. The gameplay is fun, but the problems with balance dead end even really good runs in to pointlessness after long enough.

I wrote a full review of the released version which can be read on Christ Centered Gaming.
Below was written from a build from Steam Early Access:
TLDR: My drones are dumb and only do something when I command them to do it.  Will command console again.
Claustrophobia is an immediate feeling I get from this game.  And fear.  The same feelings Ripley had as she trawled through vents of the Nostromo listening to the creaks and clunks, wondering if terror is lurking around the corner, as the motion scanner bip-bip-bips away on a vector based fuzzy screen.
There are no aliens in Duskers.  No more alive that is.  Only drones.  Which are about as friendly as the Xenomorph in the Alien movie.  In fact the whole universe appears to be barren, made in to a junk yard, with nothing but derelict ships left scattered all around.  With no sigh of organic life, other than yourself (You’re not a robot, right?).
You are in command of a ship with limited supplies.  With a handful of drones and a limited amount of supplies there is little chance of survival.  Several wrecks appear on sensors; ready to be boarded one at a time to gather resources and supplies, to fuel your journey out in to space and repeat the process.
Your drones board a derelict ship.  It’s not the first time you have done this and you know it’s safe to move out of the airlock and in to the first room.  Lucy, Carl and Wendy sit quietly, awaiting your command.  A few resources are scattered on the floor.  You instruct Wendy to gather them up, while Lucy is commanded to investigate an open door.  As Lucy enters, your view screen flickers for a moment.  You wonder if she is being attacked briefly.  The room is empty and you know it, just a glitch on the monitor.
A generator is found in the second room and get Lucy to power it, allowing access to other rooms behind the closed doors.
Noises clang and bang around you; the sources out of sight.  It’s several hundred years old; the structural integrity is not what it used to be.  Or perhaps there is a hostile drone wandering around, lurking, deeper inside the ship?
There are 3 doors leaving out of the generator room, the one you came in from and the other two closed.  Carl has a sensor which can only be dropped and left to scan the room it’s in.  If only you had a scanner to check the surrounding rooms for movement.
You contemplate your two choices.  Turn back or open one of the closed doors to proceed further in to the bowels of the derelict.  You feel lucky today, ready to take on a bit of risk.  You flip a coin and open the door fate has determined for you.  You hold your breath for several seconds, watching the door with your eagle eyes.  Nothing appears.
You start breathing normally again.  Typing on the command console, you look away to watch the keyboard, to order Carl through the new route.  Carl chirps as he accepts the command to move through the open door, then a different chirp you hadn’t heard before.  You look up in horror.
A drone swarm has surrounded Carl, his life dropping rapidly.  You hastily command all back to the airlock.  Never have you typed so fast before.  Lucy gets swarmed as she tries to leave the room.  The swarm made quick work of their first prey and poor Lucy isn’t going to last much longer.  The airlock door slams shut behind Wendy, closest to the airlock you managed to save her before the swarm could reach their final quarry.
You breathe a deep sigh.  Two drones lost, along with their equipment.  You wonder if the supplies Wendy scooped up will be enough to fix Bob, towed out of the last derelict, to scavenge the next derelict.  It’s gotten lonelier out here.
Note: This is a preview of the Early Access Beta.  A key to the beta was kindly provided by Misfits Attic.

This game is proof that graphics do not equate to quality, and vice-versa.
While it could be argued that the asking price is just a *little* steep, I personally don't feel any buyer's remorse.  Don't let the Steam play-timer fool you, I've played this game extensively on an external hard drive off of my main computer.  With the most bare-bones of background stories given to you at the beginning, you're tasked with figuring out for yourself what happened to everyone, as well as where (and possibly when) you are as you scavenge through scores of abandoned, broken-down, dead husks of ships and space stations with skittish little drones and dilapidated equipment that insists on breaking down on you at the worst possible times.  The UI is simplistic and a bit strange to anyone who didn't grow up in the DOS era, but it's very easy to get the hang of.  The fact that the entire game is played via keyboard (no mouse input), in my opinion, actually adds to the experience.  Couple that with playing the game alone in a dark room, and you can really convince yourself that you're the one piloting these little buggers remotely from your crumbling safe haven aboard a lone starship in a dead universe.
I've seen this game described as "survival horror."  I don't necessarily agree with such a label, but more than once Duskers has had me nervously edging forward on my seat, holding my breath as I pry open a malfunctioning hatch, terrified of what I might be unleashing on the other side.  More than once the game actually succeeded in making me violently jump in surprise, slamming on the keyboard like an epileptic orangutan with a hyperactivity disorder as I desperately tried to coerce my uncooperative fingers into typing out the chain of commands necessary to save whatever drones I could, slamming hatches shut to keep the unseen horrors from getting aboard my docking ship.
After a while, once you figure things out, the game *does* have a tendency to get a little repetitive, but random mishaps keep you on your toes, disrupting your usual routine once in a while and helping break the tedium before it gets bothersome.  Airlocks may fail randomly, your drones' video feeds will cut out leaving you temporarily blind, a section of a derelict's hull may buckle and allow lethal radiation to leak into the ship you're exploring.  There are few times aboard any of the derelicts where you feel truly safe and secure.
To Misfits Attic, I say "bra-vo."  Keep up the good work.  I look forward to how development of this game progresses.
