This game is a medieval style city builder. The main focus seems to be on setting up a resource flow that can sustain your city. It's really easy to pick up (honestly, I didn't even watch the tutorial. I just watched 10 minutes of some guy on Youtube LPing it, and jumped into the game understanding the basic mechanics without a problem), and it has a very detailed and easy to understand in-game guid that explains the mechanics of the game.
It seems however, that this simplicitly is there mostly because of the lack of strategic depth in this game - there's no economy to speak of, you can't micromanage your citizens, and quite honestly, I found to be quite bored in the last few hours of playing it. I ended up even watching movies and paid more attention to them than to the game, as the game basically played itself after a certain point. Sure - needed to build more food related buildings there, redistribute the people a bit, and that's about it.
Now, as a whole it doesn't seem that bad. The engine works alright on smaller towns, but any town around 400 people or larger makes the FPS drop to around 30 or less when zoomed out even on my high end hardware. It's not unplayable, but definitely a small problem. As for crashes, it has crashed on me twice in whatever my playime currently is. While I would most definitely prefer that it wouldn't crash, the autosave feature is triggered often enough. My only wish in this regard is that you would get two autosaves, not just one.
The graphics are ~okay~, even if the weather effects make the game look a bit damp and blurry (I suppose that's the intended effect). My main problem is that it's very hard to tell the difference between some buildings in winter (namely the houses). What is even more frustrating, however, is how artificial forests (you grow your own forests in-game) make it very hard to make any sense of the ground, which makes it painful to do any city planning. Even some sort of outlines to buildings, it specially ones that haven't been built yet would help massively in this regard. Other than that, there's the little things - you can have stone houses, stone paths, but there are no stone bridges (only ones made of wood). As for the music - there's not much of it, so you'll probably end up bringing your own. UI is quite a pleasure to use as well. It's simple and rather intuitive, though I wish it didn't reuse the icons for forester and the cut wood function. (¯\_(ツ)_/¯).
Now onto the gameplay - quite a few things irk me. First of all the game speed - it's too damn slow. The standard game speed is just unplayable. 10x the standard is okay, but even that will sometimes be too slow for my taste. This game supports pausing the real-time simulation at any time, so there's no reason why there shouldn't be ways to make it any faster. Then there's the AI. Your people will hoard food, then they'll sometimes be too lazy to get their own. They will die while carrying food (farmers), and their prioritisation is quite weird; sometimes AI will also cause the workers to jump between workplaces for no reason. That said, it's not in any way gamebreaking, but most definitely annoying. There also are quite a few gameplay elements I disagree with - the way hills work (they are annoying, and will quite often make you disrupt your pretty building patterns just because of a 2x2 square hill on which for some reason you can't build even though it should be trivial to just level the place), the disasters (while some disasters such as your farms becoming infected are okay, the tornado is simply way too annoying, and is basically a trigger for the player to simply abandon their save, because they will quite often just wipe out most of your city making any rebuilding tedious) and then some. The biggest problem of all, however, is the lack of depth. As mentioned before, the only real goal of this game is to set up a workable infrastructure, or rather, understanding how to make any expansion be worth it immediately. Once you make more food than you consume, have a steady supply of iron and wool and a bit of stone, you're basically done - all you can really do is add a few buildings once in a while and watch as your city/town grows. There's no actual economy to manage, trading is very basic and I found that it's mostly useful only for getting seeds to grow your own food, but nothing much after that. I don't know, just feels way too basic for me. The difficulty isn't too high either. As long as you keep it safe and don't take any risks for no reason, you should be fine, if only slightly annoyed when an orchard infestation breaks out.
The game does have mods though, so maybe the community can fix these issues, maybe it can't. It also appears that the developer hasn't abandoned this game, as happens to many other games like these, so there might be more content for this game out some day. Either way, I wouldn't bet on it, and in the current state, I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone.
TL:DR - Simple and easy to play and understand strategy game, that sadly is too simple to be any fun after the initial moment of understanding how this game works.

The game is frightening. Jumpscares are present throughout, but a variety of elements are used to terrorize the player. I believe one of the most significant aspects of a video game is its atmosphere - one of Outlast's greatest features, and one reason why it's so much more than just a scary game. It's terrifying, haunting, and affecting.
The game's weaker points are the repetitive tasks; enter a new area inhabited by a new enemy who walks a robotic path patrolling different rooms that you'll need to access to complete the current objective. Hide from the enemy and study his movements. Then sneak past him and advance forth to complete the objective. That's essentially what you'll be doing for most of the game.
The story is outstanding, however, so you'll likely be provoked to advance through the game even after becoming bored with the repetitive gameplay. I won't spoil the story, but I will highly recommend the DLC to experience a more complete ending. Let me clarify that I don't believe the original ending is flawed, but I do believe that the DLC ending paired with the original makes for a much better experience.
My favorite aspects of the game were the scenes I encountered. Again, I prefer not to spoil anything, but I will say that it displays some outstanding horror scenes. I'm not talking about standard gore such as blood, bodies, limbs - those things are present throughout. But there are a handful of memorable scenes that will certainly grab your attention. You'll see.
In short, the base game and DLC are worth the current price of about $30 combined, and the experience is worth your time.

I really want to recommend this game, but I can't.
I only have 14-something hours invested in the game, which isn't a lot but definitely long enough for a video game...
...but not enough for a "city/town building" game.
See, such games are about replayability.
Imagine the SimCity franchise (until SC4 of course) or Cities: Skylines, where you keep discovering new things as time goes by, figure out new ways to structure your town/city so that it functions as desired and even when you're done exploring all the possibilities, there's still much more micromanagement you can do, so no new gameplay is dull.
Well, with Banished, the game starts out REALLY fun, and becomes dull very quickly. Very limited things to do in the late-game , so much so that you don't want to start another town after you're done with this one, because there is no more challenge left.
Seriously, I've built a fully-functioning and healthy town (except for a healthy amount of animals), which was completely self-sustaining. So, the 14 hours I've spent in-game include learning the game, failing 1-2 towns quickly at start since I didn't know what I was doing, starting a successful 3rd town, only to abandon it mid-way because I didn't like the map layout, and completely building a 4th town from scratch, with pretty much all the standard difficulty thrown at my face.
Too bad that it has SO MUCH potential, still!

I came into this game blindly and was blown away at everything. To start, the gameplay: Feels familiar to Super Mario 64 for me, the way the physics in the game along with how nice the controls feel is just something amazing (used a PS4 controller) and everything is very simplistic but you can do insane stuff with this. This is a game where almost everything can be done by sheer skill alone, there are things from the story that make things easier (as well as some that are necessary to progress) but you can get most things just by careful jumps and momentum.
The atmosphere feels alive, the music is very well done and complimented each area very well along with the remixed versions of the songs. The art style brings everything to life, it can appropriately set the tone with keeping the cutesy art style, the animations look very nice and gets extra points for matching characters so well. There's very small details that this game gets done and I would have definitely missed if I rushed through, this game is one where I actively took my time as it felt rewarding for exploring.
The story is very captivating as the main arc is there but you still feel intrigued with all the side characters and their stories. I should mention the voice acting in the game is amazing, each actor nailed their character and conveyed the humour very well.
This game should not be too difficult aside from a few parts for seasoned platformers, it has a fixed difficulty but there's a collectable that can make you die in 1-hit if you want to add more challenge which the game does reward. The bosses in the game suit each area very well with each having their own little gimmicks so each fight doesn't feel repetitive.
The only real downsides I have with this game is that there was a few areas where the game restricts the movement with certain walls and a few times where a very specific spot didn't work on one or two occasions. The other thing was I experienced 2 game crashes but they were minor and this game has a very good checkpoint system so I didn't really lose that much progress and for me 2 crashes in the time I played is very good.
Overall in combination with the story, the art, animation, voice acting, gameplay, soundtrack, comes together and creates an experience which I won't forget any time soon. This sets a good example of what a 3D platformer should be like and I'm proud to give this game a 10/10, you should definitely buy this game and give it a chance to impress you.

The thing about Just Cause 2 is that it's like a fabulous pie made of the most incredible golden brown pastry casing, and horrible gritty mechanically rendered filling. What at first seems like an experience you will savour for hours turns into a disgusting gristle-filled grind.
It is a pie because pies are inherently genius, and so is parachuting onto an island and wreaking havoc by any means necessary.
The delicious crust of this particular pie represents the pleasing graphics, variety of terrains, and sheer scope of movement by land, sea, and air. "Take me!" Screams the pastry. "I will melt into your brain-mouth-arms and surrender hidden grottoes of exploding delight. I will be salted with tanks and jets like chewy gravy-stained dumplings."
The problem is that, like a pie, the casing only gets you so far. The content of the actual bloody game is a repetitive slurry of increasingly hate-crazed goons. What makes it worse is that at first it appears as if you will be able to selectively disable key infrastructure and command, and leave them hilariously flailing. Instead they just get better the more damage you do. Would that have been so hard, you ****ers? Slow the response times when you blow up a comm tower? Reduce plane weapon loads when you blow up an airbase? Make the soldiers angrier and more violent to civilians as chaos rises?
Maybe the developers simply ran out of creative inspiration for failing brutal dictatorships? It's not as as if half the bloody World is doing it most of the time.
Yes, it's cheap, but I assure you that if you want the same experience for the same money, buy a bottle of Malibu and drink the lot while screaming obscenities at your neighbours until they start shooting at you or phone the police. At least you'll get a good story out of it.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad is a sequel to Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 by Tripwire Interactive, the same people that created the Killing Floor game, this review is split up into two reviews: Singleplayer and Multiplayer aspects of the game and are judged differently
I have got to say that the singleplayer for Red Orchestra 2 is the worst I have ever seen, horrible AI, tons of glitches, awful story and also the same objectives, over and over and over again. "Capture this, then capture that, then finally capture the last one, and it is the most heavily guarded!" Is this the most Tripwire Interactive could come up with!?! Let's start with the AI, the worst I have ever seen. Soldiers running around in the battlefield, not looking for cover, acting like idiots, a Soviet soldier passes by a German soldier and completely ignores him! WOW, this is what must of happened during the real war! Glitches, they are everywhere! Soldiers sinking into the ground, soldiers spinning like they are at a disco party, running on the same spot, the glitches are endless! Awful story, one of the most boring stories I have ever encountered. I understand that it is during WWII and the Germans are fighting over the Russians etc... but come on! They could of made the story much better than what it is! And the objectives, always the same... just in a different place. Do this, then do that, then take over here, then there, etc... Really gets boring after a while. Overall I am disgusted by the level of poorness this "singleplayer" has to show. But the level of realism that it shows, from the breathing, to crouching and other stuff really makes you feel like you are in the battlefield. But overall, a complete disaster!
Fun, not that fun but mostly fun, but the best is playing with your friends, as it can get very boring in a matter of a few hours. The only thing I have got to complain about is... why the hell are they advertising Rising Storm, which for me is a completely different game in this one!?! I really thought that Rising Storm is integrated into Red Orchestra 2 and it comes free, but OH NO, when I entered the game, you have to pay for Rising Storm, which I can understand, but why on earth would you integrate it with Red Orchestra 2 if they are two completely different games in two different places! And when I wanted to play one of the maps of Rising Storm in Red Orchestra 2, it did let me, but it strips away all the classes to the bare bone, what a waste. Honestly, you either make them separate games or charge for both Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm together, BUT overall the multiplayer is not bad, best with friends and family though!

21 hours played at the time of writing and the voyage is far from over.
Months have gone by, and much has changed in the Neath.
From my experience "Sunless Sea" is about discovery, intrigue, and choosing to take risks or play it safe. I've been through a few Captains. Each had a story of their own, each journey touched me and each I will remember. My first died at my own fault: I explored too far, took too many risks and they limped back to Fallen London with hardly any hope of success; no fuel, no supplies, no money; it was over and the Captain and crew were forced to abandon their dreams there in the port of London. Others I lost to battles too ambitious; slain by giant Angler Megalops, or Unfinished Pirates, or Mutiny at the hands of their own crew. Surviving a Mutiny is as terrifying as failing, which I succeeded in once; that Captain was ruthless and cold, and I truly felt the zee punished him as moments after the bloody Mutiny he was ambushed and slain by pirates.
One Captain, in particular, will go down in zee-stories for years to come. I named him William Meriwether. In the deep darkness of the zee there are many horrors and each trip needs to be planned out carefully. Captain Meriwether found profitable shipments in selling wine and honey, swapping stories with other zailors and getting lucky with the Gods of the zee. I felt such accomplishment when I managed to secure him some lodgings and a Will. From that point onwards the game changed. It was no longer about that one Captain's story; it was about the legacy that he could leave.
When I was given the option to Retire it changed how I played. Do I let the Captain retire comfortably now? Or do I risk it and keep exploring? Do I get as much money as I can to secure a better future? The longer you're in the zee the higher the Terror, the higher the risk. Journeys become further wrought with fear, the light becomes your only comfort, ports become untrustworthy and each trip has to pay off. London becomes a shining safe-haven, you let out a sigh of utter relief when you reach home. I did have a moment where I resolved to do one last trip with this Captain and let him have his peaceful retirement; but on that last trip something significantly changed in the story which led me to discover more, explore further, enquire deeper and he instead fell to the zee.
What makes "Sunless Sea" so beautifully clever is that you decide it all. You decide how you win, you decide how you make money, you decide which jobs to follow, you decide which monsters to fight.
The whole game is paced incredibly well, it gives you time to think about your actions every step of the way. Everything has a circumstance. The combat system highlights this well, as with each fight you queue up your options and you have chance to pause at any time and change those options. You can then choose what you want to do after the fight; will you butcher the creature, or study it?
I'm extremely excited about new updates, and I will say that this game is worth every penny in its current state.
There are so many stories left to weave on the deep dark zee.

A deeply immersive and bleak roguelike about a wandering omega man and his ragtag band of robo-friends.  You will leapfrog across the known universe, one derelict at a time, and haunt the skeletons of former civilization via remote control and DOS-style command prompts.  Everything you consume--from fuel to tools to repairs--will be scavanged; every piece of information you glean about your hopeless surroundings will be provided through the grainy and deteriorating sonar feeds of drones, threadbare schematics, and corrupted data logs.
At about the time you're low on fuel, running a skeleton crew of increasingly fickle drones and their increasingly unreliable equipment on dilapidated space stations and ghost ships, you'll realize the theme of Duskers: nothing lasts forever in this universe.
That being said, the game rarely feels unfair.  You're given the tools to survive as you hop from one wreck to the next, uncovering fuel and scrap to help sustain your growing cast of drones and equipment.  You'll never seem to have enough to stay on top of everything, however, and the way you prioritize your repairs and mantain your roster of robots will influence just how long you might last once the meteor storms, hull breaches, creeping radioactive crud, and consuming swarms arrive.  Maintenance and upgrades are appropriately complex systems that opens up the door for a variety of strategies, and the degree to which neglect can manifest itself in your equipment--from the way a drone might start drifting to one side. a video feed might become corrupted, or a module might begin to fail--means that you will have to cope with the hardships of the things you can't immediately fix.
Duskers is a roguelike tha provides a wealth of material and choices in a distinct format that really makes you feel like you're sitting at the controls of a commandeered vessel, picking through wreckage via command prompts.  If you've ever wanted to sit in Bishops seat and reenact the desperate moments of Aliens with cute robots for marines, this is your chance.

Much like Dungeon Siege 3, Sacred 3 has little in common with its predecessors besides a name, setting and bright, colourful visuals. It's not so much an 'action RPG' as it is an 'arcade RPG' - more Gauntlet than Diablo. Pick one of four (five via preorder or DLC) pre-made hero/ines and get down to the business of clicking stuff until it dies.
In many ways, Sacred 3 has more in common with the download-only Sacred Citadel than its heavier RPG brothers - it's a button mashing brawler at heart, with linear levels and only as much level-up and customisation option as necessary to give the player some agency. Collectibles are limited to helth, energy and gold - the latter being used to buy upgrades or new skills when you level up.
There's no denying Sacred 3 won't be everyone's cup of tea - it is practically designed for couch co-op with friends and beers, or breezy online play while you and your mates mash buttons and talk trash. It has that quirky European sense of humour that made Sacred 2 surprisingly funny, although tempered by what the developers clearly think an American audience will find funny (and spoiler alert, you probably won't). That said, it has an awkward charm about it that'll either make you snicker, or at least roll your eyes with a smile.
Performance wise, the game runs flawlessly on my machine, the first $50+ game in quite a few months to do so (Wolfenstein, Watch Dogs I am looking at you). The visuals aren't amazing and shouldn't tax most systems, but the art style is big and colourful and mostly pleasing on the eye. Playing on my 46" TV it can be a bit hard to make out what is going on when there's a lot of enemies on the screen, but it's usually only a few seconds until everything is dead from one of your combat abilities.
The music is good and the voice acting is serviceable, although leaning towards the annoying end of the spectrum. There's a surprising amount of it too, with various 'souls' you can equip for a passive bonus, and each one has its own personality and one-liners. Word to the wise: the default guy you get is super annoying, so don't forget you can switch him out after a mission or two.
All in all, Sacred 3 is a competent hack & slash adventure, one best experienced with friends and in shorter sessions. It's far from perfect, and it's a departure from its predecessors, but with Divinity: Original Sin out there to get your more traditional RPG fix, this is the perfect antidote for when you just want to switch off your brain and bash some orcs.

This game is all about the atmosphere and exploration.  Its set in the imaginative world of Fallen London (A browser based game by the same company), and the meat of the game is in the flavor text.  You can bring the not-quite dead to their eternal rest at the tomb colonies... and discover a chapel dedicated to cannibals instead!  One of the tomb colonist might awake mid way to port and empty out your larders (you can throw the cheapskate over board to get eaten by a giant crab, too!) Or you can sail out east towards and pick coral off the coast that will forever haunt your nightmares... as the sea beckons your crew into its depths.
This is definitely a game you should never read the guide for first... a huge part of the fun is setting out for teh unknown and trying to unlock the secrets of the next port... If your sanity will keep.  Along with the usual hunger and fuel, terror is your biggest drawback.  As you spend too long at sea and away from shore, your crew quickly begins growing mad as they ponder what horrors lie beneath the obsidian waves or just beyond the ships lie in the stygian abyss.  See, the Unterzee (Under-Sea) is a giant subteranean abyss where the only light is what you make.  There is no sun, no moon, no stars... just the great blackness of the zee (and the horrors she hides).  Even if you make it back home, you can find yourself gripped with nightmares that will only return on the zee.

Bioshock, what is there to say about this one.  It's probably the best of the *shock games Ken Levine made.
In briefest terms, its a First Person Shooter which uses role playing elements, such as character and item progression, in order to tell the story of a man lost and trying to escape from a ruined city gone mad at the bottom of the ocean.
The game performs storytelling fantastically.  The environments are carefully created to tell what was going on during the last moments these places were inhabited.  More so, the environments look like places that people could inhabit - an accomplishment in a day where shooters were filled with chest-high walls.  Art, scenery, the enemies, encounters, ambient noise all serve to draw you into Rapture and tell you about it without using cinematics, lengthy expository dialogue, or an "as you know bob" speech.  Everything happens because of you looking around and doing things.  What happened and what is happening leaves you thinking about the game and how it relates to you and society, further drawing you into the medium.
You are always concerned about resources, more money, more ammunition, more injectors, to stay alive.  You're always looking to progress your character either in firearms or abilities.  The guns have little to write home about, an average set of pistol, shotgun, rifle, sniper crossbow, grenade launcher, and flamethrower.  Upgrade stations make these progressively better with passive benefits and special ammunition can make them behave situationally better or worse.  If you've played a FPS you won't see anything new in the weapons.  Your abilities are where the interesting part of combat happens.  They progress by collecting Adam as you explore the city and use this to buy more abilities which let you throw fireballs, shoot lightning, make bees, confuse enemies, take more damage, melee harder, hack better along with a variety of other abilities.
Combat and moving through the story always emphasize multiple ways of doing things and at least the perception of non-linearity.  To get past a group of enemies, you can run up to them and shoot them, hack a security camera or bots, sneak past them, beat them up with a melee build, electrocute a pool of water with a plasmid, whatever you can think of with what you have.  The levels dump you off in an area with relative freedom to roam and explore with little only a little nudging to get you to the next objective.
That's not to say the game is without its problems.  To find out everything about what happened, you have to find audio logs which can be ignored its just disappointing that what they reveal can't be put in the environment and are filled with "as you know bob" speeches and long-winded exposition.  As I said before, the weapons you get are plain and very vanilla, easily out shined by the plasmids you acquire.  The combat can also get clunky as you try swapping from weapon to plasmid, changing plasmids, weapons, and special ammunition in mid combat can get tedeous without prior preparation in an encounter.  There are also some problems of balance between the plasmids and tonics.  The game also loses its steam halfway through the game.  After the big reveal scene, the game drags on for several more hours with most of the major questions answered and no new revelations to be had becoming something of an exhausting slog.  It's also an old game.  Later versions of Windows have terrible backwards compatability with older software and Bioshock is no exception.  Getting this to run on a system after Windows Vista will be a pain.
Anyway, those are my two cents for this wonderful game.

Defense Council Member, meaning I've played the game since like 2012 or 2013 when it was in pre-pre-pre Alpha as a Child's Play perk with no sound or anything, and I believe the first few days all you could just walk around in the tavern. I've played a lot, you can see the hours on record, and that's not counting any of the time before it even hit Steam. Played through every iteration, "wipe-a-geddon" last summer and beyond.
The game is just not nearly as fun as the first and it is ******* prohibitively expensive. It's kind of hilarious that in DD1 people would complain that a new hero would come out and it was five bucks or a new map and it was two bucks and you could usually get them on sale for half off. Here, get ready to shell out a whopping $15 for a character, which is beyond insane. Look at the value in that vs something like Smite, where $20 or $30 (depending on the sale) would get  you every character and all future characters which is up to somewhere around 80 characters right now. Are you kidding me? And don't say they are optional, the Abyss Lord on his own is better than all 4 starter heroes combined and it's not even close. Everything in this game needs to realistically cost half of what it currently costs.
But pricing structure aside, I have no idea why they got rid of the action wheel HUD for trap placement for controllers like the first game. It was basically perfect and now they have some weird layout that has taken almost 4 years to implement. Also, every time there is an update or a patch, the game will wipe out all your custom controls and you have to redo them every time. Neat feature.
And finally, the only gear you equip that changes your appearance is your weapon. So if you find some sweet looking armor or helm, nah... it's not going to show on your character. That's kind of unforgivable in 2016.
I used to really pull for this game but now I simply just don't care. I'd rather go back to the first one which is something I never, ever thought I'd say.

Finally, we are going to charge you 45€ for all that"

A Hat in Time is game that is a call back to earlier 3D platform collectatons such as Super Mario Sunshine. Now, I know what you're thinking: "It's a kickstarter game, it can't be good. It's just another example of devs who have half-heartedly made a game just to run away with the money." But, as someone who has 100% the game, collecting all Time pieces and unlocking the Steam achievements, I can gladly say that this is not another Yooka-Laylee which tries to sell it to you with obvious nostalgia pandering. But rather an original expereince that makes you remember how great that era was with it's amazing levels and tight controls.
- I cannot stress enough how amazing the controls are. You really need to try it yourself if you wish take my word for it. Hat Girl feels amazing to move around, with very reponsive controls and a variety of movement options to really give you a chance to get creative on how you want to move from Point A to Point B. You're giving a double jump, a dive, wall running, triangle jump, you can cancel the dive, a speed boost when you time your dive on the group giving you extra momentum, a sprint which gives you a long jump. Each and every option beautifully transitioning into the other. Its simply super satisfying to move her around and I would go as far to say it's almost good as Mario.
- Albeit, some more than others. This game has kept my attention through it's immense creativity. It has that Mario 64/Sunshine asthetic for some levels where it's just a world that changes depending on the mission objectives. However each world is a well made playground, every step of the way complimenting how Hat girl moves around. It just fun to just run around the world, sometimes straying off the path of the main goal to grab a few extra collectables or find a couple of secrets. For example:
Each world simply breaths atmosphere, never once the level felt bland. I should also mention there are levels that are similar to the "secret" levels in Sunshine, for that standard, but fun platforming challenge for added variety.
- The sound track is simply great. Each song feeling wimsical to really bring out the sense of adventure. Also there's a unique track to every world, each being vibrant and lively to fit its surroundings. If you're curious, i'd recommend looking some of the tracks yourself.
- Just as the subject says, it's fairly short. There's 40 in total time pieces to collect with 25 being enough to reach the finale. In addition, i've 100% it in a mostly leisure pace in around 14 hours. This may break it for some who wish to have a longer expereince for a $30 price. I too wished the game was longer as I wanted to continue playing, however I must say that within those 14 hours, I have yet to met a dull moment. So take it as you will
- Again, another deal breaker for some. The game plays pretty easy. There wasn't a moment in which I felt necessarily frustrated as it was mostly smooth sailing. You can make the game harder by equipping a badge that makes it so you have 1 health instead of 4, but that really doesn't excuse how easy this game was in its vanilla form. For those wishing for a challenging platformer, i'm sorry but this may be a bit disappointing for you in that department. However for those who just want a fun and sometimes challenging expereince, this game is for you.
- This part is a bit subjective, so again, take it as you will. The game really has that indie polish in a negative sense. For instance, the faces look like images that weren't properly meshed onto their models and sometimes you can see the eyes clipping out of their head and other technical tidbits. This doesn't hinder gameplay in any sense, but it just leaves more to be desired, and I wish they fixed this.

The game, is fun. Not a moment in which I felt bored while playing this. I'd definately recommend to get this game if you are a fan of 3D mario games, or wish to have a fun platforming expereince. I promise you, you won't regret it.

An excellent port of the popular and well-received turn-based strategy board game which uses the newest LRB 6 edition of the rules. Blood Bowl (BB) is the game of Fantasy Football (with Elves, Dwarfs, Orcs etc.), akin to real-life Rugby (play only halts when a point is scored) or American Football, only with excessive violence, death, secret weapons and even magic. Oh, and the ball has spikes on it. BB 2 has a new and improved game engine with awesome brutal cinematics and a cleaner UI. As well as more multiplayer possibilities than BB 1 (player trading, stadium upgrades), there's a brand new narrative single player campaign that is simple enough to appeal to new players, but with just enough variety to engage long-time fans. Lots and lots of chaos and fun.
Be aware: this game is based on dice-rolling, so luck plays a part. BUT there is also lots of strategy to it, from more basic ideas like risk management and positioning, to the more complex such as chain pushing and team builds/management/development (useful site -
. 90% of the few hundred matches I've played (that's including previous versions of the game) have felt like the better player won. Sometimes bad luck really does strike yes, but if you analyse your game-play you usually could've made some better decisions, too. Don't be put off by what seems like bad luck in your first few games, but be warned that this game requires some patience to get good at.
Online leagues are where Blood Bowl 2 really comes to life. The AI seems hard at first, but can become too easy quite quickly. Online you get the challenge of real players, can choose options such turn length (I would highly recommend 1 or 2 minute turns) and even make your own league. Matchmaking and ladder climbing in the biggest leagues is fun, but there's nothing better than playing a tournament with your friends :D

Exploring the dark, underwater world of London? In a boat? With a terrified crew? And I can eat that same crew if I get hungry?? Sign me up!!
But be prepared. You're going to die. A lot. And that's okay. You get to preserve a bit of what you got from each death, so in a sense, it less of a death and more of a restart. The greenish tint to everything is much more tastefully done than Deus Ex: Human Revolution's yellow tint to everything, in my opinion. But onto the important thing!
Do I recommend Sunless Sea? Well, yes and no.
It's going to be a great game one day. Right now it's just good. Mostly because it needs two things:
1) Balancing. A lot of balancing. You start the game with very few Echos (your currency) and the rate at which you can earn Echos is far, far too slow. It would take DAYS to make the amount of money to afford just one upgrade to your ship. (Hint: those are important) The other thing that needs balancing is the rate at which your Terror falls and drops. If you're just a little off the coast, your terror skyrockets so incredibly fast, it almost discourages exploration. And when you make port, anything you can do costs so much and reduces so little terror, that it's nearly impossible to reduce it. I understand that there's supposed to be an element of difficulty to all of this, but grinding for miniscule amounts of money while freaking your crew out to the brink of madness just really isn't worth it.
2) The fun factor. Honestly, the exploration part of Sunless Sea is quite fun. Finding new islands, getting eaten by giant crabs, and being blown to smithereens by privateers and the like is all well and good, but the combat system especially needs an overhaul. It has an FTL-like pausable strategy element to it, but not nearly to the same quality of FTL. If you're fighting an enemy ship, you can't aim for certain parts of the ship. If you're fighting a giant crab or an eel or a squid, you can't aim for the eyes to blind it. It's just different "moves" you can do like evade or attack that take time to warm up.
Basically, if you want to get this game to try it out, it's worth it. But if you wait, it'll be even better.

Zup! 2 builds on the groundwork of the first title by increasing the elements of timing and reflexes in the puzzles. The one major change to the dynamics is that the blue square is now a blue ball with rolling physics. This both increases and decreases the difficulty of levels, depending on the kind of puzzle presented: the fact the ball can roll means you've more leeway for momentum-sensitive levels, while its rolling increases the need for good timing in the sequence explosion based levels.
For this it is an improvement on the first title. If the upcoming third Zup! builds still further on the abundant potential of the concept, then the series could be a classic Achievement in the making. ;)
One idea for a future Zup! would be a level creator and/or Steam modding support. Thus the Zup! community could create  and upload ingenious levels, giving the game a whole new element and increasing its durability beyond the sub-1 hour mark.

Original review:
I really like this game, and I can see it being popular amongst coders and *nix users alike.
There is something called an alias, that at the moment behaves more like a macro. You can bring up a note pad and type in a sequence of commands divided by a semicolon, these are called from an alias you give them, thus the name.
This is an alias I'd use to call my tow drone to my explorer and pick up a ship upgrade or other retrievable salvage.
They are already fun and full of potential in their current state, but the developers are keen to flesh this system out adding variables and delays for starters. The syntax is simple (a little like tcl, partly because it's not esoteric, or overly complex but is still powerful.. mainly though because you're typing one liners, of commands seperated by semi colons.. just.. like.. in tcl :D).
There is a tutorial and starter galaxy but they just cover the basics and from there you are on your own. They have said that they don't want everything made clear and the intention is to have players discover mechanics through playing, reading logs and experimenting.
Aliases, as an example, were originally a text file in the games folder with no explanation.
The developers really care about making this as good a game as possible, while not trying to cater to a low common denominator.
At the moment the community is somewhat niche but robust and I only see it growing.
Great devs pushing boundaries with a great game that seems to attract some really great, intelligent people.. Can not recommend enough.

Okay....I've put a fair few hours into Sunless Sea and I'm still enjoying it.....can't say fairer than that. At first I died a good few times until I got the hang of how to play........like a lot of midnight gamers; I'm far more happy to have a go now than read the instructions ! A nice little feature is having the choice to keep certain assets of your dead player to take on to the next personality that you create......it's like a little doggy chance to help you get ahead which I appreciated.
Now my main character, apart from being prone to the odd nightmare and having to come to terms with hacking his own crew down twice, well let's say he's getting quite handy at knowing his way around, avoiding too many hazards, earning himself a crust and generally staying alive.....and sane!
Again, at first I was thrown by the 'terror' concept and thought it unnessesarily harsh......but the moreI play, the more I am beginning to see it as the subtle undercurrent to the whole game.....the whole point of Sunless Sea is that it's a dark and scary place which is easy to forget whilst sitting in front of a PC. The terror count makes the player pay attention much more. I've learned to pick and plan my routes very carefully, never travel in a straight line, use the bouys and take advantage of any and all possible ways to offset my 'terror'. Well done to the team responsible....I feel you've got this just right. I'd hazard a comment that without my 'sweetheart' back in Fallen London I may well have ended it all..........but of course, you'll all probably write in to tell me that you're all sleeping with her as well.......life is hard and scary; then you die in Sunless Sea !
Lastly, what do I feel would make it better?.......well, earnings are slim and a captain has to do a good few missions before he's got enough for even a decent deck gun........I suspect the boats in the ship yard are for future reference, ie when the game is finished, because the prices are totally out of reach. On a good run, if I can coincide two major missions, and I bag a booty ship on route........by the time I've offset my food, fuel and fear costs, I'll be lucky to have made 150 to 200 echos.....and that's a very good run where I don't take any damage or crew.......very hard to make dosh and buy all those lovely things in the shops. As I get tougher I'm beginning to wonder if I shouldn't just have 'The Bruiser's' other eye out and make off with his dosh except I'd only have one avenue of earning potential left and pickings are slim enough !
More importantly, every port should have an inn, shop and shipwrights......that's what makes it a port ! There's a couple of ports with totally 'nada' happening and very few ports have decent shops for trading or hull repair.......a huge missed moment here where the game could take on a wider aspect of choices of how to play the game. Let's see some more trading oportunaties or passenger movement.......in fairness, the game is still in it's starter mode and the team responsible have probably already thought of this.
All in all, I'm enjoying myself. It's a great little game with bags of potential to spend hours playing it.......my thanks to all those involved in it's creation.

This recommendation is after finishing the game. Note that is was 100% solo, coop is probably fun.
Unfortunately I don't think the game is quite ready yet, there are a few main problems.
* The first 50% of the game is largely trivial. This isn't quite what you would expect given the reputation but it is ok because it is a learning curve and it is fun and creative at this point.
* There are then two bosses which are total RNG fests. This is not ok and represents a big hump to get over. Not in a fun way either, it is incredibly frustrating and you will die a lot.
* Once you get over that hump? I one shotted 5 bosses in a row on the third island .. before finally failing against "a big robot". I got that one third time :|
In general, everything is pretty great, however it just feels unblanced. I'd hold off for a couple of days and see if they plan to fix/adjust things (nerf the charge weapon for instance). The reason is that if you are like me, you'll probably see everything this game has to offer before the game is at its best. Without a solid (but still even) challenge? It just isn't as good as it could be.
For the record, just over 6 hours to beat the game, most of that on one boss. That length seems fine once a few things are tweaked but make of that what you will. There doesn't seem to be anything else to do once you finish besides try for better scores. I can see some people trying hard to get S ranks, but I don't think it is that kind of game because that would come more down to luck in several cases.
Now problems aside, how does it play? Well the controls are great (once you remap the air dash from the absurd default) and the hit detection is mostly fair (just the flying levels are often a bit iffy). Speaking of the flying levels? They kind of suck and you'll be thankful that they basically throw up no challenge and are done with quickly.
On foot and at its best, the game is "oh I see, try again". This isn't for everyone, but it is what it is. When a boss "tenses up" you'll know they are about to do something, but you have no way of knowing what that is until they do it and you see the result. Of course that doesn't mean you can't avoid it, which is why the smoke dash probably isn't the best design choice. Even without the dash equipped, you just have to learn to dodge something once, then you'll dodge it everytime...
... unless doging it relies on a platform appearing... and it doesn't.
The parry mechanic is a bit odd. I'm not sure colour is the best thing to base it off, given a couple of "purple pinkish" enemies can't be parried but it is fun enough when it works. When it doesn't work you'll be frustrated, especially near the very end of the game. You'll know when you get there...and have to go through the same ~5 minutes again. The challenges dedicated to it are really strange as well, in a "huh is that it?" kind of way. It isn't quite a half-baked idea, but it never feels really fully baked, like the game needed something else at some point, and the designers kind of just threw their hands up and ran with it.
What these choices lead to is that the first island is the best of the game. After that you are either getting challenges that you already know how to complete or are hoping to get lucky. By and large most of the creativity after the start seems to come from the "run and gun" stages. Maybe a couple more of those in place of some of the easier bosses might have evened out the game.
Art style? I hated it upon seeing it the first time (why would you want to mimic the crap cartoons nobody wanted to watch growing up? "When's Ducktales?") but it is executed superbly and I'm now a fan. The sound is fine and the menus are functional. Load times moving around are a little longer than you would like, but restarts are instant and that is the main thing that matters.
So in conclusion, I enjoyed my time with cuphead, even if it did quickly run out of steam. A few nerfs here, a few extra boss attacks there and a couple more run and gun levels and this will probably quickly turn into a very good game and a strong recommendation.

Sunless Sea is a sort of a video game mutt. Not that this is a bad thing in the slightest. The game utilizes a mix of classic text-based RPG gameplay, Exploration, Trading and Combat.
The game itself is presented in three ways, Text-Based Screen where you handle the RPG elements of the game and are played when you reach a port, location of interest on the map or unique encounters. The second is movement across the map itself, guiding your ship across the vast underground ocean that is lovingly drawn 2-D art and textures and finally a screen where you handle combat between your ship and the various pirates, hostile navies and monsters.
Despite being a late acsess Beta it is surprisingly playable and enjoyable and the fact that the game is only going to get bigger and more polished makes me even more excited to see the finished product as well as the promised expansion pack which will introduce Submarines and exploration of the Sea Floor. And there is always the possibility of the Dev's handling the 'Castles in the Ceiling' Expansion pack which will introduce airships and allow you to explore the roof of the cave.
If you want to play a game with a rich and engaging backstory, interesting characters, stunning locales, some black humor and polished and enjoyable roleplaying and exploration gameplay this is a worthwhile purchase.

EDIT: So I eventually got the game to work and as such am editing my review.
First of all, the game is not as hard as the critics have made out. Anyone brought up on arcade run and gun games and other shooters shouldn't have much of a problem completing the game on regular difficulty. Getting the A-S grades and finishing the game on hard mode is much more challenging, but I'm not far from accomplishing that after a couple days of play.
The game itself is one of the most beautiful I've ever played, both graphically and in terms of its audio. Everything is oozing with character and I love it for that.
As a shooter, it does have a few issues that can lead to some unfair deaths. First, bullets often fly behind other objects in the game world such as large cartoon explosions or other enemies. This is a big no no for any shmup for obvious reasons and it surprises me that the devs let this fault get through to the final game.
Another slightly unfair aspect to the game is the way the EX attacks work; your character is invulnerable while doing the animation, but the second you come out of an EX attack, you become vulnerable. Seeing as the animations often take a couple of seconds, this means that you could start one in safe space, but by the time you come out of it, an enemy or projectile could have spawned on your character leading to some unavoidable damage.
I hope these issues get fixed by the devs but even if they don't, it's very difficult not to recommend this game. Along with Sonic Mania, it is perhaps my favourite game of this year. Great stuff!

For Review of the Episode 1 and 2 See EDIT 5.
For Review of the Episode 3, 4 and 5 See EDIT 6.
EDIT: Was able to fix the low FPS, but still having resolution problems (Can't go to full-screen whenever I select it, it also fezzes with Alt+Enter).
EDIT 2: Was able to fix full-screen error too, need to make your game run with integrated graphic card then select the resolution you want (while in full-screen) and then switch back to your Nvidia card.
EDIT 3: Game stopped working in full-screen again (with Nvidia Card).
EDIT 4: So, I was finally able to play the game
EDIT 5: Episode 1 and 2 proved to be a very exciting adventure. You’ll be able to experience a fairly unique Batman story with surprising twists and turns, all while feeling rather familiar, thus never kicking diehard fans against the shins. Simple game play, many story options and a high replay factor make this game fun to create your own Batman experience, or to have friends over and decide together.
EDIT 6: So, Episode 3 is a fun continuation of the story, but it’s also clear that this fragment plays itself out in the middle of the story, as there is slightly less evolution. Nonetheless, you’ll be making many interesting choices, while certain questions are slowly being answered, and new characters are being born. Certainly worth continuing your journey as the Dark Knight.
Episode 4 - This is the worst episode in a great season, but it doesn’t seem as though it’ll tarnish the entire package too much. Because the final minutes are so important it’s hard to recommend skipping it to those who have been enjoying the series so far, and it’s far from being a bad enough episode to turn people away from the series as a whole. Still, it’s a disappointing development after increasingly interesting chapters, so we’ll have to wait and see how the finale wraps everything up.
Episode 5 - It wraps up the series nicely while leaving enough dangling threads to make the possibility of a follow-up a very real, enticing possibility. This isn’t the strongest Batman episode to date (for me), but it’s nonetheless an entertaining, fitting end… for now.

This game accomplished to bring back for me the vivid experience of the early platformers, and is a throwback to the old platformers like banjo kazooie and super Mario 64. The game's graphics are very pleasant to look at, and its artstyle appears detailess. but as with many games that have proven, they aren't required to have an engine with all the bales and whistles of  advanced physics and a weather system to look good. And it's cartoonish look has a one that can withstand the test of time very well. It's difficulty, which besides it's first world that wasn't on par with the others, I would say brought quite a challenge, with segments incorporating either  precision platforming or fighting to others segments bringing them both in harmony. The pacing in the game is a little inconsistent, with a couple of levels of the same daunting run of the mill tasks of ''go send all these letters to these dead spirits'' or ''go to all these points in the map to close the lava taps'', but otherwise the game doesn't have plenty of these levels. however, there are other levels which you'd feel really engrossed in them, and would give you quite a satisfaction and a challenge for completing them, that would feel more like an adventure. Of all the five chapters, I found the fourth one ''alpine skyline'' to have kept the game at its highs, with a couple of levels with a very good set of spectacle that fascinated me, and still attaining the quite challenging platforming combined with fighting. In addition, The game's also not lacking in its collectables and hidden levels to find with all the time pieces' wonders. Though, I found the hidden time rifts levels a bit easy, considerably for the type of these levels, which are usually not mandatory in many other platformers and serve rather as a bonus for you.  In this game these bonus levels are the hard to find type and not the easy to access ones  (e.g super Mario galaxy, and its bonus levels available through the menu). The controls are responsive and precise, and are of the type I've had hoped of a game of this calibre. I liked the route the game took with its storyline, in the way that it doesn't take itself too seriously, with the good dialogues that gave me a good chuckle.
In conclusion, I think the game has done a great job at living up to the classics platformers, and could manage to influence other developers, as a proof that the game's genre is still relevant and fun. A score of 8.3/10 from me

This game will not be for everyone.  It has a pace that makes it unique and thematic but also makes it feel slow.  It has a solid base to improve on and by looking at Fallen London/Echo Bazaar you can see a company with player focus.
This is a massive step up from Echo Bazaar/Fallen London; however it follows the same ruleset, a series of stats that the system performs a test against or conditions that trigger other events and options.
The travel is new to the world but is simple and easy to pick up although it feels like you burn through fuel quickly; the world makes every turn a choice.  The well lit path is the slower but you don't take Terror that comes from travelling the quicker but darker path.
You have a solid amount to do at each port even in Early Access; you can drop off items at Ports, buy stuff you need and even complete missions.  It suffers from the classic fetch quest syndrome.
Trade is slow and painful at the moment, you have to know the areas to trade with and early on, trying to do this is restrictive as early on there is one good trade route at reasonable range.  Now this is solvable (if it is a word).  The gossip system could be used to improve trade, a hint that Hunter's Keep is running low on candles and is willing to pay double rate for candles, Clay Men running out of tools and willing to pay for them.  The Fungal company is running low on supplies and is paying the buyer's rate of London plus fuel.
As for the future of the game I see that Failbetter have the opportunity to build a thriving world.  They are not restricted by having to make 3D models for every new item; they can have text ready for an event in 5 minutes with a placeholder image and upload it to trigger in the right locations or randomly.

Well worth a go, and seeing as it's only in Early access it can only get better.  Check out eNtak or GenerikB on Youtube for some gameplay and make your own mind up.
EDIT:  After 30 hours of gameplay I'm still enthralled by TLD.  The Devs havee incorporated a lot of things that if you try to help survive do make sense.  Caught out in a gail?  Take cover on the leeward side of a boulder or tree.  Found a frozen carcass with some meat still on it?  It's faster to 'hack' up a frozen carcass with a hatchet than a hunting knife.  Need food?  Herd a deer into the path of a wolf, and then shoot the wolf after it's taken down the deer.
Just...excellent.
EDIT2:  A year has gone past since my first review.  I'm up nearly 120 hours, and yet I still come back to visit the winter wonderland.  The gmae just gets better and better.

Sunless Sea is a roguelike exploration game that throws you into a great ocean far under Neath the ground with only the light from your boat and a darkness full of terrors ...
If you would like to check out my first impressions please follow the link ...
The game itself is in early access and is constantly being updated ... yes there are areas that are empty ... you are warned with a 'this area has not been completed' message when you sail into them ... the game is hard ... and brutal ... at the beginning ... you will probably die quite quickly ... not necessarily at the claws/hands of an monster but rather from starvation, fire or mutiny ...
The art style is superb ... the darkness seems foreboding ... the many reefs under the water add a great sense of depth to the water below you ... the music is atmospheric and perfect (the album is on Spotify as well I think) ...
I played the previous verson (pre-Steam release) for several hours and thoroughly enjoyed the way the story was told ... it really relies on the player to make their own story ... to read into what is going on around them ... and I can only imagine how much more vast the story is going to become ...
Combat isn't the greatest thing at the moment ... but it is satisfying and I am looking forward to owning larger ships with more options in the future (I am sure this will be part of the game) ...
All in all a great early access title ... a unique concept that is done really well ... with a huge potential to grow ... and another game I am stoked to have backed on KickStarter

Early Access Game review (7th Aug 2014)
Edit #1 (8th Aug 2014)
I feel like I should explain why am I writing a review even tho I have only 4 hours game time on this; consider this is usually a quality/standard I rely on to judge the review writer's legitimacy. While it is true that I have not explored the mid game or late game content of this game (which is also why I did not write anything about them, this '4 hours on record' also says the game (at its current state) has discouraged me enough to stop investing time on it after 4 hours. Mostly because of the slow game pace (feeling of making no progress).
Disclaimer: This is a neutral review, not saying the game is bad or anything WHEN IT COMPLETES. It has potential, ok? (Gosh, I hate this word... 'potential'). But yea, for new players; if you are looking to enjoy a good game and pay $17.09 or $18.99 for it ... you might want to check out this and other 'negative reviews' first.
Before we go on, keep in mind this game is charging us $18.99 ... i bought it for $17.09, but still, expensive.
Especially when you compare it with Faster than Light (FTL) (10$ full price... constantly on 50% off discount coz it's an 'old game' now), which I will constantly compare this game with.
Why would I compare this game with FTL?
Both games are text based exploring RPG genre. At least 3 categories fit, why not?
Let's talk about what I like about Sunless Sea first.
1. Exploring element
You get to sail/zail, and you have full control over your sailing/zailing; something I like a lot (this beats FTL, coz FTL is one direction and multiple choice, that's all the exploring you get).
The course plotting from player, despite being provided with full freedom, is balanced by the need to estimate/calculate risk that one may encounter during the zail (strong monsters and gaining 'terror' ... a game mechancis that makes bad things happen to you if it gets too high). This creates a reasonable difficulty scaling environment for the players whlie not taking away any of the freedom of control from us.
2. Fascinating World Settings (Dark and dangerous atmosphere, fitting the title 'Sunless Sea' perfectly)
I personally enjoyed reading the text/plot a lot, even tho English is not my first language. Good read really, and helps immersion much. I don't think not knowing the plots (from another game with same world settings) before will create problem to new players. Since i'm one myself.
3. Game's art and music has done right, helps players' immersion.
Even tho I don't think they're consistent enough. As in, sometimes they show, sometimes they don't. Gets dull when there's no music (even background noise, please.) This I have to bring up FTL. The game always have music, different music for different scenario, all of them well made too. (Just my 2 cents on this, if you care less about music then just go ahead and appreciate the colourful arts).
What I DO NOT LIKE about Sunless Sea*
I'll mention something that many other players/reviews have mentioend first
1. Economy
Trading is broken/incomplete atm, grinding takes forever. This harms the fun player may gain/enjoy from exploring/zailing, also has negative impact on difficulty scaling. I.E Play time increases but you're not moving forward by much. Every now and then you get to spend 500 echo/coins on an upgrade and then you're broke again, with increasing difficulty to earn money. More importantly, getting that single piece of upgrade will not give you obvious edge against foes you previously can't defat/struggle to defeat. Meaning, you're still gonna lose a lot of hp or other resources, which you will have to pay to recover.... and then the bad cycle repeats itself.
2. Gameplay
FTL beats this game on this, hands down. FTL's combat is always engaging, timing and multitask, keeping you busy and planning multiple things all the time. This game seems to want to do the same by providing you with the same 'pause' function between planning, but there's simply no such need to have that function unless the player really wants to take it eassssssssssssyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy (as in, very very casual. No harm to have this function at all of coz.)
So, what's wrong with the gameplay of this game? To be more specific; combat.
2a. Enemy variety not enough
Only 3 enemies for early game, and then a few more 'advanced' enemies... you can tell they're advanced by their looks, but that's all you know;
2b. Not enough info on enemies
The game does not provide you with anything to let player know how strong is that thing you're fighting until you engage your enemy in combat.... and if you're unlucky, you die, start over... what's the point to punish players like this I wonder? (Looking at FTL, they provide players with options to gain info and still make the combat fun, engaging and challening. Charging almost double the price, I wonder why aren't the devs doing the same if not similar)
2c. Skill uses resources that hurt the exploring aspect of the game
You use fuels to make effective evasive moves. Meaning you're going back to London sooner if you use those moves... yep, that totally makes exploring fun.. not. Alternative/recommendation would be giving abilities starting cooldowns or adding conditions to the ability before they are available in combat (such as illumination level must be high/low enough).
2d. Weapon/attack methods variety not enough (both yourself and enemies, you have basically only 1 damaging method, and before that, you launch 2 flares.... that's basically what you do against EVERYTHING you'd fight in early game... somtimes you launch 3 flares, in another wrod, always the same pattern.... boring. I wonder why couldn't I have a skip button to skip this meaningless combat session an djust.. get the loot already. "Come on, game! You know i'm 100% gonna win and 100% my enemy will not be able to hurt me. Be a bro and don't waste time please!"
3. Exploring....after you died once.
When all the islands remain at the same place after you start over, it really feels like a big timesink for nothing when you zail, and totally takes aways the fun of exploring from players. Hell, I won't even need a map anymore. Would be nice if they can at least change the positions of islands a bit and help players to find meaning in exploring... or changes other thigns up a bit, like enemies vareity whatnot (FTL has nebula, hostile sectors and stuff like, effectively providing both level variety an maintaining gameplay/system integrity at the same time... no fun taken away, nothing is compromised).
So... tl;dr (in conclusion, as in)
Fascinating settings and stories, but not everything is completed so don't expect a fulfilling experience.
Gameplay is subpar atm. Strongest gameplay element of Sunless Sea* is exploring, but it's gimped by a broken/imcomplete trading system and BORING, BORING AND UNENGAGING SEA/ZEE ENCOUNTERS. (might as well make me dodge moving cyclones or icebergs, really, that at least tests my zailing skills). O yea I frogot to mention, the ship controling feels pretty neat, that's good... +0.5 points.
So uh, if you are seriously serious in helping the devs, do go ahead and pay 17.09-18.99 dollars for this, even for this Early Acess version, it has its perks.
BUT, if you are like me who was looking for a really fun game to play..... game is not completed, so hold your horses, 'no.' You will not get what you're looking for.
Lastly, dear devs; even for 17.09, the game really is quite expensive. I wonder if it's because of the plot writing. You'd better beef up the exploring experience or make the combat of the game engaging at least if you don't want your faituful audience throw tomatoes at you.
* = Sunless Sea at its current state (early access)

This is the most fun I've had with a game in years. A Hat in Time is a platformer that takes its inspiration from games like Super Mario 64, Banjo Kazooie, and Psychonauts, and beats them at their own game.  You play as Hat Kid, a girl on a quest to recover the time-pieces that fuel her ship so she can return to her home.  The game is pretty light on story, but it serves as a good setup to send you to exotic locations and meet charming and funny characters.  The upbeat lightheartedness of the game is a refershing change of pace from what a lot of games have on offer these days.
The level design is brilliant and varied. Each chapter throws something new at you, so the gamplay never gets repetitive.  For example, in one act, you bounce around the rooftops of a sunny island town collecting tickets to open a safe.  In another, you're solving a murder on a train full of anthropomorphic owls and crows.  Later, you're playing cat and mouse with a spectre in a haunted house.
I love the artstyle.  It's cheerful and bright, matching the tone of the game perfectly.  The graphics are very well done, with lots of options in the menu, and the game runs great on my modest system.  My PC (Intel 3570k, GTX 770, 8GB RAM, Windows 7) was able to run it in 1080p at a steady 60fps with all settings on high or max.
The soundtrack is another winner.  I'm no music connoisseur, but I can't think of a single track (and there are many many tracks) that I thought was bad or didn't mesh with the game.  In fact, I've found myself whistling or humming several tracks from the game over the last week or so. "Picture Perfect," "Train Rush,"  "The Big Parade," and "Alpine Skyline" are a few of my personal favorites.  I went ahead and bought the soundtrack so I could stop burning through my mobile data on YouTube!
As to be expected in a platformer, the controls are great.  Your jumps, wall jumps, air dashes, etc. all feel precise and in the later levels it's second nature to string them togehter to get where you need to go.  You also receive several hats and hat pins that grant you abilities such as throwing bombs, grappling hooks, sprinting, and stopping time, to name just a few,  These abilities are necessary to progress through the levels and give you access to areas you couldn't reach in previous chapters.
My only complaints about the game are fairly minor.  The camera could use some fine tuning, especially in Chapter 3.  90% of the time it's fine, but there were a few instances when I had to wrestle with it to see a jump from the angle I wanted to see it from, making it hard to judge distance / depth.  There were also times I couldn't see my shadow on a dark texture or in low lighting, making it hard to tell where I was going to land.  Some of the hats feel underused.  Particularly the time-stop hat.  You can use it as much as you want, but there are only a few situations where it's absoultely necessary to use it.  The ice hat lets you perform a ground pound, but you really only need it to launch yourself from springboards.  Hopefully these will get more use when the adidtional (free!) DLC chapters are released.
Overall, A Hat in Time is a home run, and even more impressive when you consider that this was the developer's first game.  It's definitely in my top 10 favorite games since 2010, and anyone with even a passing interest in it should check it out.  I bought it shortly after release at full price ($30 USD) and got every cent worth of enjoyment out of it, with more to come, thanks to the Steam Workshop support and aforementioned DLC!

Banished is a challenging city builder.  The idea behind the game is a small community of people are banished into the wilderness.  Your job is to keep them alive and help them thrive by managing the jobs the people are assigned to and how much of what they can store all while developing a village into a city and growing your population.  There is no story mode, just a sand box.
There are several good mods out there for Banished.  Without any mods keeping your people alive is challenging.  There are several mods to double the amount of food, wood, stone, iron, coal and fish etc. harvested per unit collected by your citzens, as well as new building and industry mods.  I recomend installing mods as soon as you figure out the basics because they make learning to play the game much less frustrating.
I like to play banished when I've got nothing to do and don't want to play a game that requires my undivided attention, but need to occupy myself for several hours.
I rate Banished a 6/10 due to lack of a story mode, and because the sandbox is really fun for a while.

For fans of the old Games Workshop game, Blood Bowl 2 is a faithful reproduction of the board game, but without depending on having a local place to set up a league night. Same rules, same gameplay, all the fun with less work.
The interface is mostly intuitive, though with an occasional misclick can be a frustrating way to lose a point. Helpful hints like coloring to indicate tackle zones, and popup bubbles to explain your chance of success on various actions tend to make up for it, though, and I imagine misclicks will happen less often as the interface becomes second nature.
My biggest complaint is that the rules documentation is woefully incomplete, with some elements like interceptions almost entirely missing from the supposedly detailed rules document available online. Hopefully, this will be completed at some point, but in the meantime, it's possible to find the boardgame's tournament rules online, and the computer game appears to mirror them faithfully.
Overall, definitely worth picking up.

Even though it has few new game mechanics to show off the game mechanics that exist is well implemented and feels good. You get rewarded for being skilled and you can have some very fast and awesome movement if executed correctly.
However, I dont find the good implementation to be the selling point of this game. This game has some of the most charming, adorable traits that make you feel like you are not enjoying an adventure FOR a child, but an advanture made BY a child. The music, the level and character design and the many small details in animation that reflect the current situation is simply fantastic. The main character is a lovable bundle of childish energy and smiles that appeal to the natural instinct of humans when seeing a normal child. The enemies and NPCs are well designed and unique with memorable personalities. I loved just watching her express herself throughout her different missions because she feels so genuine.
Finally, the story is so refreshing and authentic I could not help but smile and press on to see what new adventure she will have in the next chapter. In a game industry where grit and Skinner box gameplay allow for only generic and boring stories (Like Destiny 2) it is so wonderful to play a game with a nonsensical story that is just interesting and fun to follow.
All in all the gameplay is the weakest aspect of the game as it is only well executed. If the game was a bit more challenging and had a few more major characters to flesh out the worlds a bit then this game would easily be a contender for game of the year for me. I have not had this much fun just enjoying a game for a long time. I cannot recommend this game enough.
