Its Blood Bowl 1 with better graphics, but its less "complete" than Blood Bowl 1 was.  There are just a lot of little things that are lacking.  For example, there are no cheerleaders and no fans on the sidelines.
One of the new features is that you can build your own stadium, but the camera angles make it impossible to see if upgrading the stadium actually results in a visual change, and each race doesn't get their own unique stadium like in Blood Bowl 1.  There is also a feature where you can build addons to your stadium, but the overwhelming majority of them are things you would *never* build.  In fact, I can only think of three that you could ever want, and even then two of them you would only want as an elf team and the other as an orc or maybe dwarf team.
The singleplayer experience is also lacking compared to Blood Bowl 1.  I liked how in Blood Bowl 1 you had the league system and there was a visual representation of progression for your team in terms of which league you were allowed to join.  Blood Bowl 2 also has a league system for single player, but its just a single league that seems to *sort of* scale with your team.  Plus there are no difficulty settings (at least that I could find).
Oh, and there is a game breaking single player bug where the other team just passes its turn without doing anything that is quite frequent.
And on the topic of bugs, the game is quite buggy.  Other than the afformentioned game ruining single player bug, a lot of them are just minor interface or visual bugs that self correct.  But its just annoying to have to deal with them in a $45 game.
The game also feels like it was designed for a controller and the mouse/keyboard controls are fairly hamfisted.  Navigating the menus is more difficult than it should be, and I have a lot of instances of my players moving to the wrong square.  I'm not chalking that last one up to bugs though as, again, I just think its that the mouse/keyboard controls are bad and imprecise.
I think that maybe in a few years, once the bugs are fixed, the interface is cleaned up, and more races are added the game is probably worth buying during a steam sale.  But right now, unless you're a hardcore blood bowl fan, I would pass.

This is the first game I've started in a long time that I have absolutely no desire to continue playing.  Perhaps I'm too old, but I just don't care for the current generation of survival horror games that seem to be largely based around collecting notes/documents that paint an ambiguous "spooky" tale of the creepy environment you're exploring while avoiding and eventually running (and hiding) from enemies lurking about.
This game will succeed in startling you a number of times with jump-scare tactics but after a bit they'll continue being thrown at you and you won't even noticed since you'll have become desensitized to them (or you're just too focused on running away from whatever maniac is currently pursuing you).
Aside from not caring for the general mechanisms I already mentioned, immersion was an issue for me.  The game started out well in terms of immersion but it was broken within the first 20 minutes or so.  A little bit more interactivity with objects and the environment may have helped.  The other major problem was the heavy-handed nature of the game when it came to trying to make it a disturbing environment.  I felt like they were trying too hard in this regard and actually ended up a bit over the top with the stuff that's supposed to be disturbing to the point where it seems like a lot of it's there for the sake of being there and just breaks immersion.  A bit of subtlety goes a long way in horror.  Along the same lines, the pacing didn't work for me.  I found that there's just too much packed into too little space/time to leave much room for building up any sort of tension or anxiety.
The video/note collection mechanism is just abysmal.  The idea is that, being a reporter, capturing things of particular interest on video is important (you'll know you've recorded one whenever a new note is added to your collection).  Seems to make sense, but the things that actually fall into this category are so arbitrary that you pretty much need to run around looking through the camera the entire time to have any hope of catching them on video which takes all the fun out of trying to use it selectively when you come across something you think should be documented or recognize as important.
The platforming is nothing to write home about and certainly nothing that should be advertised as "parkour-inspired."  Are you going to be running a lot?  Yes.  Is said running anything like what can be experienced in Mirror's Edge or even Dying Light?  Absolutely not.  The extent of the parkour element of the platforming seems to be vaulting over low hurdles (with no flair to speak of) which I'm pretty sure was something done regularly way before parkour was even a thing.
There are some things the game does well.  You never know which people you encounter will be hostile or how they'll react to your presence if at all so it does a good job keeping you on edge about approaching any of the asylum inhabitants.  Also, while the stealth aspects I found somewhat lacking, the leaning around the corners mechanic lent itself well to the game.  The night-vision stuff is a bit overrated imo but it does help to build a sense of urgency and anxiety when you're exploring completely dark areas and running low on batteries.  Finally, while the graphics aren't terrific, they're pretty much on par with what should be expected of an indie game released when it was and I felt they got the job done.
So basically, if you love jump-scares and playing hide and seek (and run away) with over-the-top maniac killers or you simply have a love for all things that over-use through the lens view night-vision recording… you may just love this game.  If on the other hand you're more like me and can, for instance, remember The 7th Guest being a really creepy game, recall the tension of playing the early Resident Evil games, and remember feeling your skin crawl during parts of the early Silent Hill games… I'd say pass on this one.

Tripwire really picked up the slack on WW2 where most developers have switched to modern/futuristic shooters. RO:2 is a fantastic and for the most part historically accurate shooter that really delivers on a tactical and team based level that most other shooters can't contend with.
The combat feels quite realistic with a sometimes clunky but still very usable cover system and bullet injuries that will slow you down with a shot to the leg or even slowly fade to black when bleeding out. This makes every bullet feel like it has potential to stop your enemies even if you don't get a headshot or chest shot. Tanks are another interesting element which actually takes multiple people to control and gun. Anti tank guns make it even more interesting with the ability to shoot out treads and take out people who are inside the tank, like I said realism was key when this game was developed.
You often come across team leaders in ths game ACTUALLY BEING TEAM LEADERS. They will give commands through chat and you can see how fast it can turn the tide of the battle which isn't always easy to turn. Kills are not the focus which is a nice change from having to worry about a K/D ratio and helps most people seem to focus more on the battle.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good online shooter even if they don't care about WW2 or historical accuracy.

Oh dear where do I start with this. It's gonna be a long one!
As a long term fan of the Sacred series, cutting my teeth for the first time in the world of Ancaria back in Sacred 1 in 2004, and then on to greater glory in Sacred 2 in 2009... the news that developer Ascaron Entertainment had gone under was a massive blow. Hope was on the horizon however when Deep Silver announced they had purchased the rights and that Keen Games would be working on Sacred 3! Oh yes! More Sacred! More Ancaria! MORE LOOT!
Now in 2014 we finally get to play Sacred 3, so much time has past! Teaser videos and screenshots, discussions across forums about "what we hope for", rumours... finally we can play! Sacred 3 is here and... what the hell is this? This isn't Sacred!
Sacred 1 and Sacred 2 were "open world" action RPG's. Classic isometric camera angles, an almost free-form camera in Sacred 2. Tonnes of loot! I remember spending many hours farming for dual light-sabers on my Seraphim... Seemingly endless expanses to explore, lots of depth to crafting your own combat arts just how you like them. Stat points to build character... character customisation; want a character with bright green hair in Sacred 2? No problem!
Sacred 3 is none of this. Well apart from sharing the name and "isometric camera angle" - and I say "angle" 'cos it's a fixed camera.
Sacred 3 chooses more to go down the route of an "action game with some RPG elements". By that I mean, you will gain XP and level up - but you will have no "points to spend in stats".
You will still fight using "combat arts" - but its less about building them bit by bit as we did in past Sacred games and more a case of spending gold to purchase upgrades for them.
There is no more open world. The game starts you off with a lengthy tutorial. Once you complete that, you are returned to the menu where you can pick through locations on a map to take on individual challenges. They range from the main "story" maps - largish maps with lots of mobs and a boss at the end... stamina test maps where you have to hold off against 5 waves of mobs... and simple "clear the map of enemies" missions. After each mission is complete you will need to stand in a circle to be teleported back to the menu to choose your next adventure.
There is no apparant "droppable loot". Every so often you will kill a mob or a boss and you will be alerted that you have found an item, a sword, etc. However you will not be able to take a look at it or equip it until you have exited out of the current "challenge" and are back at the lobby/menu. Here again you can choose to upgrade your weapon by spending gold to add extra features to it. Same goes for armour, skills, and combat arts as I mentioned above.
There are no character customisation options. You can no longer tweak how your character looks before you start to play. You can't change their name either. "Claire - The Seraphim Paladin" for instance is one of the available playable characters/classes. You are stuck with the way they look. However, as I mentioned previously you can upgrade armour and weapons - and as you do so you will notice slight changes to your chosen characters visuals.
The game itself is beautiful, it plays well. The voice acting is awful. Sacred is known for tacky humour, Sacred 2's seraphim often quipping sarcastic remarks, but Sacred 3 is just over-the-top, stupid "in your face" - trying to be funny and failing completely - a miserable attempt at humour.
If you come into this game expecting a great RPG experience, either as a RPG fan or as a fan of the Sacred series, you will be disappointed. However if you approach this game without that mindset, and consider it a game of it's own accord then it can stand up - just about!
This really should have been a new IP, or a spin off from Sacred. This I will warn you now, is NOT a Sacred game - at least not in the true sense of what we have come to know. Overall however, it still falls short. To me it feels like a very hollow RPG. While playing I did mention to my friend that it felt very much like playing a Free To Play MMO, very watered down and basic. As a detective game, it fails in the most important aspect of that genre: Logic and puzzle solving. This review is a long rant just about that, nothing else.
At first, I very much liked that you can ask anybody about almost anything, and gathering much information even before you know you need it.  However, this leads to some problems, because - given that design - the dialogues, and their logging as usable hints, and their value as hints have to be thoroughly checked for consistency to avoid the following situations:
- You can get the same story from several different people, however the games wants you to pick a specific statement of a certain witness as the relevant cue in the formal puzzle soving part, though multiple ones are logically valid. That means, you either have to check every possible combination of cues hoping its the ones the game expects, or look it up in a walkthrough. Even sometimes the information you get told isnt logged / available as cue for the formal puzzle solving part though it is identical to what other witnesses said. An exact copy but cant be used as such. That means, valid information cannot be used, because the game does not accept them all, just a special subset and number of them. Seems to me like the programmers / designers filled holes in the dialogues by other dialogues, making them copies but not acepting these copies as valid in the puzzle solving. I have made the exact answer to some puzzles, but using some of the other redundant cues and not the ones which are (invisibly) formally defined as the vital ones.
- Filling dialogue holes with valid information leads to an even stronger problem: Sometimes it is the less informing cue you have to choose in the puzzle solving part. For example, for a certain puzzle, two statements were given by the same person [maybe its due to a translation mistake in the german version, however, I translate back into Englisch, but dont know what the exact english phrasing in the game is] :
1. Generally, he wears his necklace at all times.
2. I remember him wearing his necklace that evening.
So which one is the more informative if you need to know if he was wearing his necklace on that evening? Well, according to the game you have to choose the less specific version 1 to solve the puzzle... seems like the dialogue hole unfortunately wasn't filled with something irrelevant, but with something more relevant than what they thought it should be.
- Sometimes, these presumbly filled dialogues lead to situations where a witness / suspect contradicts himself very bizarre. Again, it is about the necklace again, an happened within seconds in the same interrogation:
Q: Did you remember him wearing the necklace that evening?  A: No.
Q: What happened to the necklace?  A: I took it from his neck that evening.
Alright, have fun now with figuring out how to solve a puzzle with this. In that subpuzzle, you have to pick that he took the necklace from him, along with several other persons that told you that he is normally wearing his necklace (but only the general phrase, not the specific one for that evening which one of them gives).
So, to "solve" the puzzle, you have to ignore that suspect x cannot remember if he was wearing the necklace as well as that he remembers taking it from his neck, and you choose the latter option (taking it from him), and you have to additionally add as cue his fingerprint on the necklace (which would be alone enough to answer the question the puzlle wants you to solve).
- To make this all worse, there is bar that tells you if you have all the information needed. However, it isnt correct. I had a full bar, meaning I should have all information, and was trying out all the possible combination in the hope to find the one that the game expects from me. After having fiddled a long time, I gave up and looked it up in a walkthrough. Guess what: I was still missing a cue. Thank you very, you ♥♥♥♥ing game, you are telling me that I have all the cues I need, but you won't let me solve the puzzle because I am missing a cue. Perfect. You took the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me another time.
Concluding, there is both reduncacy as well as contradiction in what you are told (resulting from presumaby filled dialogue holes and dirty programming), but absolutely no exchangeable cues, no mercy, no nothing when you have to choose the one and only exact hints to solve the puzzle part. All of the hints are identical screws, but only some of them fit. The game wants you to be exakt when it itself is fuzzy as hell.
Great design idea, but pretty much messed up by quick and dirty writing of the dialogues.

This is Sacred no more!
As a first-hour-fan of the Sacred series it was a punch in my face when i heard that Ascaron had to close its doors after they developed Sacred 2. Nevertheless i looked forward to Sacred 3, happy about the fact that the franchise will live on. However i am deeply disappointed by what Sacred 3 has become. Everything that made the original games fun and enjoyable has been ripped off in a way, that i have to call it rude.
Basically there's nothing left in Sacred 3 that we know of the former games except the Seraphim class and the name of the realm, Ancaria:
1: No open world
2: No in depth skill system
3: No character customization
4: Background / Lore
The "world" in Sacred 3 is mission based. Every mission takes place in a linear level with recurring gameplay elements:
- Fight
- Dodge
- Boss
Ok, maybe we have to fight, dodge, fight and then boss, but that's basically everything there is. The level's details are in fact beautiful i have to admit.
I remember reading, printing and studying countless class guides for Sacred 2 for hours, everywhere and anytime i could (BfG Sera, anyone?). All this has become nonrelevant in Sacred 3. You're limited to a skill system with a maximum of two choices at certain character levels. Ok, that was somewhat similar in Sacred 2, however, since you have no gear to choose from, except 3 weapons bound to your class, the skill system feels shallow at best. Your armor gets upgraded automatically at certain levels and has a more cosmetical feel than anything else. Also, there are no weapon sockets anymore, instead you unlock weapon spirits whom provide certain bonuses. Those weapon spirits, unfortunately, feel like commenting on your actions in a manner, that i'd love to play the game in an ancient, long forgotten language, i simply can't understand...
Hairstyle? Haircolor? It wasn't much in Sacred 2, but at least it was something. Combined with your hardly gathered armor set you still felt like caring for that character you played. In Sacred 3, you can't even name your figure. Everything's predefined and done for you already. Level 6? Ok, my armor got upgraded visually, automatically, done. No loot. Just gold to unlock your next skills, limited by character level and in numbers.
To this day, i listen to the audiobooks released with and around Sacred 2. I clearly remember helping Hansi Kürsch and his band Blind Guardian, retrieving their stolen instruments, so that they can do their ingame "live"-performance. I remember the conflict between elves and humans and their very own agenda within Ancaria, aswell as helping the spirit of xmas on that awesome dedicated island. In Sacred 3, all that seems to be gone. As told in the intro, all races send their best fighters to stand against that evil force, witch is noting but some totally unknown elf guy, talking slang language and somehow manages to insult you mentally speaking.
This is Sacred no more. Ironically, the original developers are working on a new ARPG title they formerly named Unsacred. Due to copyright issues, they had to rename it to Unbended. For their own good, i say, because Sacred 3 is the true Unsacred.

If you're looking for a worthy successor of the Sacred series, wait for, and support Unbended.

FULL REVIEW:
Havent played a ridiculous amount of this game just yet. But I will say, there is not anything else out there exactly like it. Which isn't bad in this case. Mostly being that if I had played something similar I would not have been as interested. The game is not something I can replay till the end of time but if the criteria fits your interest then the money is not wasted.
This game, if anything is more like a simulator for those salvage and recon expeditions you always see in movies, except instead of coming back with a magical discovery 10 scenes later, you manage them real time. At first I will admit I was a bit skeptical, but the feeling you get when watching in dread as each drone one by one be converted into spare sparts by a group of organisms, smashing its way through the interior blast doors of this dead ship you have entered in search of loot, leaves you feeling pretty hopeless.
Combining console commands and a pretty convincing GUI, the game puts you in control of not only these drones, but also the ship itself. You will slam doors as you escape, fire up gun turrets to obliterate the opposition and even sometimes yourself, flush the dirty alien scum through an open airlock you have cleverly lured them into, all while towing a dead drone back to your ship for spare parts and upgrades.
The feeling of consequence definately makes you want to watch your a**. Any drones that are left on the ship after departure, or disabled and not dragged back to the ship are left behind permanently. Your drones will become like little pet projects in which you spend your salvage parts and switch various upgrades into, in order to further your efforts to rid these adbandoned spacecraft of valuables. Improve speed or refill your trusty supply of motion trackers. Equip those new upgrades or repair that drone you rescued from the last hunt.
Not once did I find myself feeling bored, and I assume as the game progresses and my drones become further equipped and more valuable not to lose, my interest will sustain. The UI is attractive and the game is smart. The console is really cool but I already like anything console based. Pretty neat being able to generate a command to autopilot your drone to another end of the ship to hack a defense interface, while manually pilotting a drone to gather scrap simultaniously. But know what this game is before you buy it. Looking for non stop action? This has the potential to be one of the my favorite indie games ever. The aesthetic, feel, and mechanics are superb.
What I love:
The setting: The captain of my own small, vulnerable boat as it launches into the inky black underworld ocean, exploring, discovering strange places and people. Most everything I run into is the tip of a big mystery.
The art: It's fantastic. I'm not an art-critic, but jolly-good work on everything.
The game mechanics: Combat mechanics are unique and interesting. (Though I wish evasion options felt more interesting, and that disengaging actually worked)
The pace and density of the story: We only receive breadcrumbs, but I love the breadcrumbs. I can use my own imagination to wonder what the rest of the story may be, and maybe we'll learn eventually.
This game must have been written and designed by someone who is really smart and educated on quite a few aspects of the 19th century science, exploration, and HP Lovecraft. I love that time in history, and to play in a fictionalized version of that world.
Problems:
The balance of resources and resource use seems off. I understand and LOVE the feeling of beginning as a very fragile ship and crew. But I can spend hours of this game working carefully to manage my ship, only to feel like I've made very little progress in building my ship, and then see it destroyed by a puff of wind.
The Terror mechanic is fantastic, but it seems too difficult and expensive to get rid of terror. I after my crew enter some bar in some far-off island, only to spend 40 echos to lose 1 terror. That is not worthwhile.
The combat system is great, but I wish more information was readily available without mousing over bars or keeping track of the rapid-fire combat log. Most importantly: enemy's illumination and observation points. Can there be a number on top of the enemies illumination bar that constantly shows the enemies illumination? And can there be a constant display of how many observation points I've accumulated? Finally, is there a way to adjust the speed at which combat progresses? It is usually fine, but when I'm fighting the 10th zee-bat in a row, it becomes tedious. These would be wonderful quality of life improvements.

There might be a few spoilers in this comment, but nothing that would change the experience of the game.
Basically, Davey Wreden (the creator of the Stanley Parable) talks you through several small games made by someone named "Coda". Dave talks about how we can learn more about Coda from his games, but as you continue further, you begin to realize that The Beginner's Guide is not only about Coda.
The overall story is sad, but it reveals so much about expression, people, and validation. Whether or not Coda is a real person, the games are beautiful, and you will come away a different person. 5/5
The games use very simple and similar first-person controls; the jump/crouch controls are pretty much unneeded, but still allow for more interaction/fun.
Coda does a lot of interesting things with gameplay, from the recurring door puzzle to the invisible maze to the housecleaning. The individual games have vague and intriguing messages in addition to the big picture they add up to. This is not your generic game. This isn't even your generic non-generic game. 5/5
You start out with little music and generic textures, but even at the start there's the random colored blocks; Coda's artistic messages are very thought-provoking, even if sometimes negative. Despite the fact that you know it's a game the whole time, you're immersed for the full 1.5-ish hours. Towards the end, the music is very ambient and beautiful.
Like the "Wot I Think" article says, the game at times makes you uncomfortable; but that's what makes it so good. The way it forces you to acknowledge things that you've been avoiding. 5/5
The Stanley Parable addressed the in-game player's avatar and the in-game narrator. This game (which is not anything like the Stanley Parable, I can assure you) addresses the player and, primarily, the developer.

Quick Summary: Open world action shooter with a massive environment (much of which you can blow up).The game has a ton of DLC, but I don’t think any of them add anything to the game’s story, just more guns and vehicles.
You play Rico, an American secret agent sent to the island of Panau to blow stuff up and overthrow the military dictator. Integral to your mission is making nice with local factions (by performing missions), collecting money and weapons, and generally causing chaos by destroying everything you can.
The game is played in third person perspective, and similar to the Grand Theft Auto and Saints Row games you can travel the island via walking, driving, or flying in stolen vehicles. Note that the island is huge and would take you hours to walk across. Even driving from one end to another will probably take you 20-30 minutes if you follow the roads. Fortunately, the island is covered with little towns, military installations, and large cities that you can “extract” to once you gotten close enough to “discover” them. The extraction is kind of like the Fallout fast travel between points of interest, but is actually kind of time consuming (because of loading screens). It’s usually more fun to steal an attack helicopter and blow stuff up on your way to your destination.
Just Cause 2 is primarily a shooter game with a small assortment of weapons that you can find, take from dead enemies, or buy. These weapons can be upgraded as you collect weapon kits and money throughout the game, but even at the end combat can be a challenge if you’re surrounded. Fortunately you have partial regenerating health and an awesome weapon/tool that lets you escape or fight as needed: the grappling hook. With the grappling hook, you can not only zip around latching onto surfaces, but you can also grab enemies and pull them towards you or attach yourself to vehicles and hijack them. Unlike Just Cause 1, you have the grappling hook right from the start and can immediately steal even heavily armed helicopters or military tanks by doing little quick time events.
Pros:
+The game is HUGE. You can easily spend weeks trying to find all the collectibles and liberating all the cities. The collectibles can be helpful since they’re mostly used for upgrading your guns and vehicles.
+There are over a hundred unique vehicles that you can steal or hijack and use to move around the map. You’ll need them too, especially the attack choppers and fighter jets. There are a bunch of racing minigame challenges that you can take part in too.
Cons:
-The huge number of collectibles and cities can make the game rather overwhelming. Someone told me they weren’t planning to finish the game because it was “too open world.” You will not be able to completely acquire all collectibles without playing night and day for at least a month. You’ll get bored of the constant grind long before you reach even 50% map completion.
-Since the game is a console port, there are a few times when it’s not immediately obvious what buttons you’re supposed to press (like when upgrading guns).
Overall the game is a lot of fun, and as long as you don’t plan to completely liberate Panau, you should enjoy the experience.

Early access review:
After a few stumbling attempts ending in death by falling, hyperthemia, wolf attack, exhaustion coupled with food poisoning and more wolf attacks, I finally got the hang of things.
With an ever-present sense of peril, I chose to leave the forrest with all its delicious untrappable rabbits, embarking on a journey in search for better pastures and -- dare we hope? -- a gun. After a few days of scavaging, I eventually found a tunnel through the mountains, leading to a large lake. Along its shores I found a small town and was finally able to make camp on a more permanent basis. There I spent my days fishing and forraging, each day trekking back to my pleasant little homestread. Life was good. On the seventh day I finally found a gun next to a corpse and... it all went down-hill from there.
With a sense of delusional self-empowerment, possessing the means to ascend to the top of the food chain, I shot and missed a few wolves. On the 9th day, on my day home from an unusually unproductive expedition, I came upon a bear that had annoyingly blocked my path during the morning. Taking aim, I shot (and probably missed yet again) believing that I could get to a nearby house if I couldn't get it to bleed to death. And oh boy, bears can apparently sprint pretty well, for it quickly pushed me to the ground and mauled me repeatedly, leaving me for dead. Within an inch of my life, I crawled my way back to the house. The next morning, a wolf waited outside my door, making easy pray of my already wounded form. And so yet another story ended.
----------
Perhaps a little repetative with the same map every time, but as long as you're actually exploring its a very enjoyable experience.

Outlast is the perfect horror experience. Fantastic gameplay, nerve-shredding sound design, an unbearably tense atmosphere and very intriguing narrative. For best results, whack some headphones on and play in the dark; it's a white-knuckled ride that'll break you long before the end.
The Whistleblower DLC, easily more terrifying than the main game, expands the story by serving as both prequel and epilogue. It's beautifully crafted, especially nearer the end when it begins running parallel to the main game's story and you're witness to certain events unfolding from another perspective. Whistleblower's closing moments also delivered one of the most satisfying experiences I've ever had while gaming.
I've nominated Outlast for the “Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!” Award in the 2016 Steam Awards!

Possibly the most adorable game on Steam.
Basically Ghost Rider becomes a 30s Disney cartoon. They nailed the 30s Disney style, including the music. All the animations were made on paper and inked too, to give them that authentic look (I don't envy the devs, must have been a pain in the a$$).
As for the gameplay, it's pretty tough. The difficulty doesn't really come from your usual bullet hell, but smart enemies or projectiles instead - this is the mark of truly well designed combat in a 2D platformers! Enemies will sometimes zone out half the screen, while you have to dodge homing projectiles, while you have to shoot the enemie's weakspot, while you have to parry pink attacks either for energy or because there's no other way out. Yes, all of this at the same time.
There's 2 types of levels:
Run&Gun - classic  levels where you need to push through enemies to reach the end of the level. Features minibosses
Boss fights - multiple phases, and the bosses attacks are randomized too (the phases are not!). Let me explain: For example the genie boss in the first phase will always open a treasure chest, but the treasure chest will sometimes attack using swords (they charge at you) or random bling (bullet hell) or golden cats (homing swarm missiles). Every time you start the bossfight you get a different attack in that first phase (and others as well) but he always opens that treasure chest in the first phase, so the phases themselves stay in order.
There's LOADS of boss fights. More than run&gun levels, which is actually a shame. I love the run&gun levels, because those feature respawning enemies, so sometimes it's a bit more challenging. It's not about learning attack patterns like in the boss fights. You are forced to react to the enemies dynamically.
I failed a lot and tried to ace some levels too, so considering that I completed the game in 9 hours. You know this game is good when I did this in one sitting playing until 6AM. If you were to complete each level on 1st try, it could be about... 4-5 hours maybe? That's not likely to happen though, even on easy mode.
Minor complaint: coop is local only.

Well, this is a tough one to tackle. I liked it, but I'm not completely sure why - I'll present two possible reasons further down.
First, let's get the negative points out of the way: it's a bit pricey and short. I'm not sure it could have been much longer, but do get it with a good discount unless you have a very specific interest for interpretation theory as applied to/in videogames. The description says it's about 2 hours long, so keep that in mind.
I'll be one more to call on The Stanley Parable for comparison, but on a fine point: TSP achieved many (if not all) of its narrative and deconstructive effects
the structure of a videogame, it managed to do what it did precisely
it was a videogame, and couldn't have done it otherwise.
Inversely, The Beginner's Guide
videogames (and their structure) in order to illustrate something else: we can see it as an essay, a letter, a conference... At its core, I would say TBG is
a videogame, but is more efficiently presented in videogame form, just like a lecture on music may be presented in concert form - with text spoken between the pieces which must inevitably be there so you can have the experience of what is being talked about. Is the end product a videogame after all? Very possibly, just like Britten's
is, after all, a piece of music.
Both TSP and TBG are pieces about videogames, but in
different ways.
TSP managed to be, in my opinion, very nearly perfect as a videogame about videogames. The quality of what TBG achieves is... well, it depends on how you look at it and on how you're feeling about yourself.
Despite my comparisons earlier, TBG is not really an essay or a conference on videogames - it gets too personal. And that could be seen as a problem: maybe I
have liked to dig deeper, and with more references, into the method of interpretation that was being proposed. Why not? We've seen countless analyses of an author's state of mind based on their work - in music, literature, painting, choreography... It's about time we had that for videogame writing too, and that's one of the possible reasons I was pleased with this game.
But of course, TBG is a work of fiction, not an academic endeavour. So in parallel with the interpretations, we follow (sometimes unwittingly) the narrator's own narrative. Those games he interprets, the interpretations of those games, and finally the failure itself of these interpretations, all serve both as a way for the narrator to address the unseen character of Coda, and for us to discover the narrator's own doubts and troubles.
And that's where the quality depends on how you're feeling: some stuff that comes up can hit extremely close to home for some people (see Jim Sterling's review for an example), while being unexpectedly foreign to others, or simply touching-but-not-
-moving. As for me, when I saw it coming I thought it would hit me like a truck, but oddly it didn't. And I was actually pretty pleased, I would almost say proud, to see it didn't hit me. Second possible reason for liking the game.
Which of these two possible reasons is the main one? I don't know. I can honestly say I liked the overall experience, and I might replay it someday to pay closer attention to some details. If anything, it's an incredibly daring move by Davey Wreden, both because it seems to put him in such a vulnerable light (granted, all the while saying that putting oneself in such a light is in itself a trick - hello recursive layers) and because TBG is definitely
fun. It is not light entertainment, its linearity borders on the oppressive, it conspicuously hides its self-awareness in an untrustworthy way, and it does not properly end once it has stopped.
For all this complexity, you should play it. You don't get that kind of reflection and openness very often, in videogames or in other art forms.
If your teen angst is at least a decade past, there is definitely something for you in The Beginner's Guide.

Frustrating puzzles. Shaky jump controls. Platforming that often requires perfect timing. Dark lighting that is more often a hindrance than a mood-setter. And if you want to check it out as an artsy game? Don't bother. There's so little story, the title tells you more about what's going on than the events within the game.
Maybe this was the cool thing to do when this game was released. But for my recent playthrough, all I got was a pretentious art game where you'll spend most of your time dying terribly, redoing sections because you made one tiny misstep, and most often of all, referencing walkthroughs to figure out what the hell you're supposed to do.

A diamond amongst the rough. A nice little survival strategy game that is actually good.
You play as a drone operator wandering a universe filled with derelict ships. Your mission is to travel this universe and find out what happened to humanity.
-Pro's-
*Great Graphics
*Nice little story
*For an early access its pretty damn good, all the items fit together nicely.
*Actually takes some effort to keep all your stuff.
*Doesn't spoon feed you the way other games do. If you lose something you lose it for good.
-Con's-
*Game is pretty barebones, but still great!
*The degradation of your modules is way too high and really does need to be lowered/balanced.
*Not a huge amount of ways to customise your drones at this point of development.
*No mouse input (Doesn't really need it but makes it a little awkward to use).
*Clunky UI
*Would also like to see more modules, levels, aliens and overall more customisation for both drones and ship.
*Side note actually: Really not worth the $20.00 at this point in time, id wait for a sale. Maybe in the future it'll be worth that kinds of investment.
Overall I rate this game a 7/10 as it stands, I actually enjoy playing this for large amounts of time and never really get bored. Would like to see more stuff added which im sure is on the way. Can't wait to see where the game goes in the future!

I absolutly loved this game, perhaps more than even giants like Bioshock Infinite, when measured minute-for-minute, or hour-for-hour.
The art is fantastic, and music/sound fits with it perfectly.  That alone is almost enough to be worth a favorable review of this game, with so many "game that isn't really a game" things coming out lately.
On top of the amazing look and feel of the game, the gameplay itself is FUN!  Rather than just being a Mario-platformer with some enemies to jump-squish, this right-to-left platformer employs puzzles that are not only challenging enough to be enjoyable, but which also add to the "feel" of the game.  Particularly the stuff with the spider, easilly some of the best stuff in the game.
Now, it's not an exceptionally long game (assuming you don't use/watch a walkthrough, it's maybe 3-5 hrs), HOWEVER, assuming you get it at five-ish dollars that's really no cause for complaint.  That is, perhaps, the game's main but very minor flaw: simply that you're left wanting a bit more of it, like the last piece of a Delicious and Moist Cake.  Yet that's far preferable to playing into the relm of boredom and having it feel like beating the game is a chore.  In case the reference wasn't obvious enough, think Portal 1, and you get the idea of how this game feels upon completion.
All in all, I'd give this game a 9/10.  It's not 100% perfect, but it's pretty darn close.

Duskers is the next game from studio Misfits Attic and represents a huge departure from their lighthearted puzzle game a Virus Named Tom. This time around, a dark desolate future awaits you with your only allies are drones and a lone command console.
)
Duskers’ story takes place sometime in the far future, where you awaken as the sole survivor of a ship with only a few days of fuel left and no clue where you are or what happened to the rest of humanity. Your only option are derelict ships, stations and more with no signs of life for you to explore. Aiding you is a set of basic drones that come equipped with upgrade modules that let them perform specific tasks.
Duskers' universe is entirely procedurally generated when you start a new game and you are given a random assortment of drones and upgrades. The universe is broken down into systems and then sectors that have places for you to explore. How it works is that in each sector, you have a limited number of proportion jets to move within the sector. When they run out, you need to enter warp via fuel cells in order to replenish them, fuel cells are found on ships and if you run out, you will be stranded.
With a procedurally generated universe, a playthrough of Duskers can take vastly different turns
Each derelict is also procedurally generated and before you enter one, you'll be given an idea of what it is, how long it has been adrift and if there are any infestations or enemy types on board.
All this is presented using a dirty tech aesthetic; where even though you're in the future, there are basic readout screens similar to the movie Alien. The game's commitment to this aesthetic is great and it really helps to set the mood; not only that, but you can play the entire game using a keyboard thanks to it.
After selecting your target and equipping your drones, it's time to step foot into the unknown and where Duskers takes the dirty tech aesthetic even further.
The gameplay of Duskers is all about commanding your drones to explore and recover useful information and resources; however you're not going to be seeing the universe for what it is. Instead, the entire game is played through the viewpoint of your command console and all footage is fed to you via the drones' camera system. You can directly move a drone via the keyboard, but to do multiple orders and take charge, you need to use the command console.
On the bottom right corner of the screen, you have a command prompt that lets you issue orders to the ship and the drones themselves. Opening and closing doors require you to type in the door code into the console and you can command multiple drones to move via "navigate" and the drone numbers. You can view the entire schematic of the ship via the spacebar; this allows you to see all room numbers and their respective door codes. Upgrades which are attached to your drones can be used by typing their name into the command prompt and there is a help guide for more information on what they do.
Ship exploration hinges on your use of the command prompt and keeping an eye on the schematics to figure out what's going on The upgrades are very important as they are your sole means of interacting with the world. "Generator" and "Gather" are the two big ones at the start; the former allows you to turn on generators to power up sections of the ship and gather lets you pick up scrap and fuel.
Things start out innocently enough, as you find upgrade modules that you can take back and even more drones to take into a ship, but then things change. You'll soon find that the universe is filled with hostiles of a variety of types, and they are out to destroy your drones and your only means of survival.
Duskers shows a lot of promise as an up and coming rogue-like, even at this very early stage of Alpha. I'm curious to see if or how the game's mechanics will be expanded upon and what things will be added to give the game a greater plot.

This has the potential to be one of the my favorite indie games ever. The aesthetic, feel, and mechanics are superb.
What I love:
The setting: The captain of my own small, vulnerable boat as it launches into the inky black underworld ocean, exploring, discovering strange places and people. Most everything I run into is the tip of a big mystery.
The art: It's fantastic. I'm not an art-critic, but jolly-good work on everything.
The game mechanics: Combat mechanics are unique and interesting. (Though I wish evasion options felt more interesting, and that disengaging actually worked)
The pace and density of the story: We only receive breadcrumbs, but I love the breadcrumbs. I can use my own imagination to wonder what the rest of the story may be, and maybe we'll learn eventually.
This game must have been written and designed by someone who is really smart and educated on quite a few aspects of the 19th century science, exploration, and HP Lovecraft. I love that time in history, and to play in a fictionalized version of that world.
Problems:
The balance of resources and resource use seems off. I understand and LOVE the feeling of beginning as a very fragile ship and crew. But I can spend hours of this game working carefully to manage my ship, only to feel like I've made very little progress in building my ship, and then see it destroyed by a puff of wind.
The Terror mechanic is fantastic, but it seems too difficult and expensive to get rid of terror. I after my crew enter some bar in some far-off island, only to spend 40 echos to lose 1 terror. That is not worthwhile.
The combat system is great, but I wish more information was readily available without mousing over bars or keeping track of the rapid-fire combat log. Most importantly: enemy's illumination and observation points. Can there be a number on top of the enemies illumination bar that constantly shows the enemies illumination? And can there be a constant display of how many observation points I've accumulated? Finally, is there a way to adjust the speed at which combat progresses? It is usually fine, but when I'm fighting the 10th zee-bat in a row, it becomes tedious. These would be wonderful quality of life improvements.

So succeeding to the next chapter is, sometimes, pure hell (excuse my french). One might prefer to look at a walkthrough instead of constantly changing your conclusions, blindly, hoping for the best.
Beside that little inconvenient, the game is still quite addicting, with no bugs at all, and I got the chance to buy it at 2,19 CND$.
I recommend it highly.

This is one of the more promising early access games I've played so far. Yes, you will encounter "Placeholder Beasties", and some content that just isn't available yet, but for an early access game it does have quite a bit of depth to the story and gameplay paths you can pursue. The game is challenging; your fuel burns quickly, there are countless ways to meet your permadeath - that tend to sneak up on you rather quickly if you get stuck out at sea longer than anticipated, and in some cases, your fate is completely determined by chance.. I won't say that is a good or bad thing, that is for you as a player to decide based off your personal tastes, but the game has all the elements necessary to make it one of those "just one more trip" games that remarkably make the hours of the day fly by.
The bad: The game is seriously unforgiving... and can end in the blink of an eye. You might think you have made all the necessary upgrades and improvements you need to best your current enemies until they blast you with 10 zillion damage... :/
EDIT: One thing that seems to make no sense whatsoever, is that when you upgrade your ship you can't recruit past 10 crew because it's always locked at "no more than 9 or 10" so depending on the size of your ship this means you could always be cursed to move at half speed.. unless of course there is a magic fairy somewhere that fills your crew up.

This game is a shame, I love Blood Bowl. I have owned the table top Blood Bowl since 1986 and have avidly played Blood Bowl Chaos edition and with the graphics, the smoothness of play and the promise of a better AI and more management tools this seemed like it would be the best thing ever. IT IS NOT.
Blood Bowl 2 is at best ready for an extended beta-release, the number of game play bugs pile up by the day and Cyanide seems to have abandoned the support forums. There is no word on any of the many,many,many too numerous to fix bugs are being worked on and there is no acknowledgement from Cyanide that anything to fix Blood Bowl 2 is happening.
Add that to the inexplicable changes to races/players, beefed up human catchers that have no cost increase, impotent Chaos Warriors and an AI that can only win if it stacks the die rolls impossibly in it's favor and this game is a sham that shouldn't even be called Blood Bowl.
Add to that Cyanides ignoring of the LRB and their seemingly pointless tinkering at minor rules and gameplay instead of focusing on fixing the numerous bugs and this game mystifies as to why it was released.
I want to love this game, but I don't and I find myself frustrated at something that could have been so good so inexplicably ruined. I think the only thing that could save this game is to take it out of Cyanides hands, they have completely lost the script.
Unless you have never played any other iteration of Blood Bowl, or if you hated the other versions do not buy this game.

No input from Cyanide at all.

Questo gioco , è uno dei migliori titoli a cui abbia mai giocato. E ho iniziato a giocare con l Amiga 500 nel lontano 1988 , per poi passare a un 486 sx (ovvero senza processore matematico).
Quando ero bambino io, un masterizzatore cd (non dvd che non esistevano) costava circa un milione e mezzo di lire gli hard disk da 100 mb costavano 1 milione di lire e le schede grafiche ancora erano forse nella mente di chi ha progettato la prima. Internet non esisteva e i giochi erano assai difficile da reperire....
Parlando di Fps, posso dire che dopo essere stato impressionato da Wolf3d, stupito da Doom (perchè a quei tempi Doom era un passo avanti non da poco), il primo Medal of Honor, per poi rimanere coinvolto nelle ambientazioni e musiche del divino Duca altro passo avanti memorabile nel mondo videoludico..... non mi è rimasto piu impresso niente fino a Bioshock.
Per me è la storia Fps piu bella di sempre, un gioco fatto col cuore e non solo per vendere un prodotto. Curato in ogni particolare, con quei nemici malati, divertenti, particolari.... con le sfide a i Big Daddy, la trama coinvolgente al massimo. Voglio dire al giorno d oggi non c è nessun gamer che non sappia che Bioshock esiste, e se avete provato solo l Infinite (per carità bella grafica ma niente di piu) sappiate che vi siete persi LA PERLA DELLA SAGA.
Godetevi questo perchè non troverete fps piu coinvolgente neanche negli altri 2 episodi.

Playing on a Mac 10.9.5 had to turn the graphics down a little. But runs great. Super creppy, well directed horror game with very unique AI that runs after just as fast as you can. And in this game you can run pretty damn fast...vault over stuff...so can they. No weapons of any kind, just your camera wiith night vision. Battery life sucks on the camera they give you in the game, just like it sucks on your smart phone in real life. Batteries scattered about the levels and pretty easy to spot. But still its not easy pickings, this is one of the more difficult games I've ever played when it comes to horror. And I've been gaming since before Xbox (the first Xbox). When PC was all there was. Yup I'm that old gamer cat. I know my horror games, and know them well...this is by far the best. Its like being in horror movie, the graphics, grainy like and sometiimes even more scary when viewed through night vision. Like Paranormal Activity first person, holding a shakey camera style. Some of the characters remind me of something out Borderlands, or kinda Mad Max looking. Swinging baseball bats or pipes at you till you drop over bleeding. Death scenes along with scoring are stellar to say the least. This is a work of art IMO, and deserves a standing O from my side of the gaming world. You will do a lot of running in this game, then run some more. A +

This game is a work of art. Andrew Ryan is my favorite video game character that I ever came across. The speeches of Ryan and the imagery of his philosophy is beautifully displayed, such as when you first arrive and see in huge letters, 'No God No Kings Only Man', I really enjoyed all of this imagery. The environment of the game is gorgeous. The water looks so real, the music of the time era is well chosen and the game turned me into a fan of that genre of music. There were times in the game when I was being chased when I would just listen to a song play on a radio as others were seeking to kill me. The story of this game is well-made. The only minor drawback of this game is that I think the story could have been developed better. I did not get the full story when I first played this game. The fact that so much of the story relies on reading audio-recordings is a drawback resulting in a few moments of confusion about what you are doing and why you are here.

Duskers is a rogue-like, real-time strategy game based around a survival aspect where the player is expected to scavenge, build, upgrade, and maintain his or her team of drones whilst exploring the deep and recently emptied recesses of space. Dangers are plentiful, and often times lurking within your blindspots, waiting for you to make a mistake or become just a little too comfortable with your surroundings. Only by piecing together fragmented and corrupted logs from derelict ships can one find out what exactly happened and why you seem to be the sole survivor of an undefined disaster.
Is the game fun? At its core, yes. It successfully assumes the role of a rogue-like by making each playthrough somewhat different than the last with randomized loot and map, but not all the ships are randomly generated. If you're a fan of rogue-likes and find the notion of a slowly developing story to be a good reward for your efforts, this game is exactly that, and development for it is still on-going which is promising.
However, I strongly urge people who're unsure about the game to look up Youtube Let's Plays before purchasing it. It is extremely unforgiving, and sometimes even outright cruel with random, unjustified punishment - and for C$ 20, this is a big factor to keep in mind.

No loot to find. You earn gold and a limited selection of new items/item levels/skills, then must upgrade the the items and skills with the gold you earn. A dull and uninteresting system coming off of Sacred and Sacred 2.
I cannot recommend this game as a sequel to the Sacred franchise. Maybe under a different name and a lower price, it would be worth playing.

Great game. Graphics look amazing and a massive leap forward over the old version which was so ugly it was basically unplayable. A lot of time and money has gone in to the look. The engine is slick and performs OK. No CTD's or bugs for me as of yet. The gameplay is where its at though - its massively addictive. Player/team progression rocks and is faithful to the board game with a few tweaks here and there to the rules.
Two things really stand out for me from these reviews. 1. Please take all the haters with a pinch of salt. They aren't wrong, this is bare bones compared to the previous version(s), but its functional, looks good and plays great. All the extra stuff bitter vets want that isn't included isn't something you are going to miss as a newcomer. 2. Don't be misled in to beleiving you will get satisfying multiplayer on public servers. You may, chances are though you won't.
As for the game itself - its amazing. It really is. I never played the board game and I regret it now. The rules are simple (even if the strategy surrounding a play is anything but!) and you can pick them up easily enough. There's a wealth of online resources to plumb. Every single game is fresh and suitably random at times to keep your riveted. I've beated guys with 3 players left standing. I've beaten teams much higher rated due to a stroke of luck with the dice etc.
Likewise you need to be prepared to get owned. Especially by bashy teams and agility teams. You need XP to get skills on your players to make them effective against elves and stuff. Don't judge the game by the first few matches you play.
Overall, this is a well balanced, stable, beautiful update to the classic boardgame of yore. Sure there's niggles with customization, ui, online play etc. There are things we wish were included at release. Its also overpriced. All things you can live with and/or shop around to get a better deal etc.

Banished is a city builder for the thinking gamer with a lot of time on his or her hands. Starting out with essentially nothing, you scramble to scavenge logs, stones and food from the forests and streams around your wagon, desperately trying to keep your families fed and warm during the coming winter (always coming, that winter is). Because most critical resources are finite until you find a way to replenish them (e.g., replanting forests), you must provide for your population’s critical needs while ensuring there is enough set aside for future investments. Depending on your starting conditions, this can be a formidable and very enjoyable challenge.
Once you get past this stage, however, the game’s pace slows considerably as you move from trying to stay alive to simply growing your settlement and securing the means to support that growth from renewable sources. Watching your increasing population go about its business, slowly but intently, is strangely addictive and everything you see matters. It is unfortunate that after spending some time in the growth phase, the game pretty much runs out of content and all you’re left with is a perpetual but not very challenging game of resource management.
It’s an iron-age Sim City, to put it simply.  There’s no combat, no conflict at all, just growing your town while managing your workforce. If that’s your thing then you will find Banished enjoyable for hours upon hours, as I have. Considering it is available for less than €5 whenever there’s a Steam sale I see very little reason not to pick it up if you enjoy city builders. Somewhat compensating for the scarcity of late-game content is the huge amount of fan-made mods that have been created. For an indie title, the excellent sountrack and graphics deserve special mention.

So to summarize the style of game that this I'd say its a cross between Turn based RPG Combat, EVE Online, and FTL... sadly the worst of each is what is currently the game. At present the game is INCREDIBLY grindy, unforgiving, and a little bit punishing which is always a nuisance.
Now I'd say this is a roguelike or lite or whatever you want to call it but it really can't be called that because the only thing that's randomized really are the events and the enemies and the latter is in ever rpg ever so yeah, not to mention you can send something to your next character if your current one dies. The Map is static at the moment and the risk reward balance is HEAVILY skewed so that anything risky is barely rewarding and the combat is kind of slow and gets a bit dull when you have to inevitably grind. Making Echo (money) in this game is really tough, I mean Really tough, you can either go the safe but excruitatingly slow economic cargo running route but the pay off is slow and it probably takes about an hour if nothing goes wrong to make enough for a low level upgrade. If you want to fight pirates or monsters... they pay off is worse and much more risky. Something else that actually really bothered me is the lack of explanation in the explanation of how things work and what events will do, the wording is tricky and if you haven't seen an event before you may think you're getting something out of it when its taking something from you instead, you quickly get used to it though.
Having said all this I did enjoy some of my time playing like I said before but it just wasn't enough of the time I played or enough satisfaction for me to really recommend the game at the current price and state (maybe 50% off or when they address some issues). Those things aside it runs smooth and I didn't encounter a single bug, although plenty of content was missing to be patched in later. 6/10

I think The Beginner’s Guide has some very apt things to say about player entitlement and not respecting the boundaries, of projecting ones own needs and interpretations onto games and their creators. The problem is that it’s just not very fun or interesting to play. The games we’re introduced to are all quite dull, and the narration becomes very disturbing by the end. So, while I appreciate some of the messages, the game itself was repellent to me.

Well this is a weird game.
I'm not the type to play a bad game for a few minutes then quit and talk trash on it. I understand the work that could've gone into a title like this, albeit perhaps work aimed at squeezing every last penny out of a very, very young and impressionable audience. I like to get a good feel for every feature before I pass judgement.
And I must say, I have gotten quite a feel for this game.
The first problem here is that these developers are working with an IP that is very clearly targeted at a young audience. I know a lot of adults who go crazy over Toothless and I'm sure you do, too, but the game is designed in every corner to be aimed at really small kids. They'll get their parents to download it or they'll play in-browser, they'll see the shiny armor or dragons or they'll try to use the farm and lord knows that most kids aren't patient enough to wait 10 minutes for a plant to grow. So they'll get their parents to buy them gems and the money JumpStart wants is made. It's really damn grimy.
The second problem, ignoring the business model and focusing on gameplay, is that it is very buggy and prone to crashing. In the (at the time of writing) 9 hours I've spent playing, I have crashed while simply jumping around or walking about 6 times. I've frozen at a loading screen 3 times. And my menus have glitched and stayed onscreen with no way to close them about 4 times. That's just 3 kinds of bugs I've run into, and I'm sure only just 3 of many that OTHERS have had to put up with as well.
And as far as the questing goes. What the hell? It consists of walking back and forth between movie characters, getting shown a little movie clip sometimes, answering some trivia, and being told to go do the same minigames over and over. Of these minigames I've gotten to play so far, there's a target practice railshooter thing and a flying challenge. Initially you cannot use your dragon to play these, you need to use Toothless every hour for the railshooter, and you have to use another dragon for the flying challenges. For the flying nonsense, there's also a huge repetoire of dragons from the movies/show that you can use as well, but of course, only if you shell out the cash for the lovely microtransactions. And my favorite part of that is that every single one of them is 250 gems (about $2.00)..... except Toothless. He's 500! (about $5.00).
You can use your own dragon after you level it up and then age it. Teen years are good enough for the railshooter and glide challenges, and then adult is what you need for actual flying stuff. But all this takes "Energy" from your dragon, which you can only replenish by either waiting or by feeding him fish you've caught in the fishing minigame thing. Well I mean, there's also microtransactions to help with the whole energy ordeal, but seeing as so far there've been microtransactions tied to almost every single facet of gameplay, this shouldn't be any surprise at all.
There's also the farming. The way this works is you have your little plots to plant seeds and you can eventually get coops and pens for some animals like sheep, yak, chickens, and some seasonal stuff as well (at time of writing, turkeys are purchaseable. I own one because of the microtransaction gems you're given for free to start with. Gotta love turkeys, man). All of this works off of a timer. All of it. Every last bit of this is timed, and every single part of it can be "hurried" with microtransactions. Feed your sheep to get it to grow wool. Or feed it, then dish out some gems to make it instantly grow wool. Plant some cool plants and wait a certain amount of time dependent on the plant itself. OR, pay some gems and have that sucker instantly matured (just like real life). Ran out of water in your well for watering your plants? No big deal, gems are god in this land. Pay out a few of them and your well will be full again.
And my absolute favorite part about farming (and fishing, but it's not even that notable to explain or talk about in my opinion), my ABSOLUTE FAVORITE PART is that there's bounty boards tied to exchanging your farming/fishing goods for money. In every scenario where I mathed out how much I'd be getting back compared to how much gold I was putting in to producing these goods, the amount I was getting back was NOMINAL. It was like 40-50 at absolute maximum for profit, after pumping in something like 100 to begin with. I understand the MMO grind, but take note that you can spend some gems to get a big lump sum of enticing, juicy gold, and realize just what kind of game this is (if you hadn't realized already).
There are almost no redeeming factors for this game. The fishing is kind of fun (although buying new rods takes gems, and that's just.... god dammit. Just why?), the farming is okay if you're a fan of Harvest Moon-y kind of mechanics, and the flight is kind of fun even if it's really clunky and you get stuck on terrain a lot. That's it. That's all I can think of that I've had fun with in my entire 9 hour first sitting with the game.
In other words, unless you REALLY, REALLY like this series or you love to laugh at poor, greedy design at every turn (like I do), avoid this title. And honestly there's no reason to NOT avoid it. There are so many good/passable free to play MMOs on Steam now. Go have fun in one of those.

The game is stable, fun and feels feature complete. It's an indie game in the best possible way: it's a unique experience created by a small team of people.
I went into the game not really knowing what the gameplay would be. Roguelike, drones, salvaging, puzzles. There was enough of a tease to get my interest, but not enough to spell out what to expect.
The tutorial was excellent. Taught me the basics, got me into the game. Then the campaign. It starts relatively safe: in-game help messages explain new things as you encounter them, you find some scraps, extra modules, an extra drone.
You lock enemies in rooms, close the doors behind them, activate defense turrets. Bye, bye enemies. Things are going good. Then you encounter a room your sensors can't penetrate. You're uncertain: take a chance at loot, or play it safe? You open the door... Jump fuel. Nice!
You push on, looking for more loot. Another unscannable room. You take another chance, and enter. A swarm comes out! Before your drone can turn around, the swarm disables it. Your other drones are safe in another room. Eventually, you manage to lock the swarm in a room and clear the rest of the ship. You move on, minus your scout drone. You fumble along, blindly. More rooms with enemies. Some you can escape from, some you can't. Tension rises. One by one, room by room, you lose your drones, until they are all gone.
Game over. Do you want to play again? Hell yeah!
This game pushes a lot of your mental buttons. In one game, you scan everything, you're super careful and you scout everything. Next game you only have a stealth module and you're sneaking through quickly. Sometimes you can't obtain perfect information and you have to take chances. Sometimes they pay off, sometimes they... don't. The derelicts get bigger, the enemies nastier, the situations more complex.
Edit: I wrote this originally after 8 hours of playing. That was 10 beta releases ago. The game has only gotten better since then. Modules wear down over time. Your ship has things you can equip to it, but they also wear down as you use them. You are encouraged to commandeer other ships and use them to continue in your quest to figure out what happened to the universe.

I recommend the game, but I'm also biased because I'm really into programming. It's a space roguelike, proceedurally generated which means the difficulty will fluctuate depending on luck, and with a refreshingly minimalist visual style.
In some ways the game is still somewhat unforgiving; there is permadeath and on the overworld screen I pressed enter and acidentally jumped to another galaxy, which spent all of my fuel, so I wish I'd been asked for confirmation first.
Besides the unfinished aspect and an odd crash when trying to record using fraps, it offers quite a bit of charm. I'll go into the highlights first.
1. It's real-time. Turn-based games are beginning to show their age and this instead has several time mechanics; a stealth tool that drains as it is used, enemy AI that moves from room to room, radiation that damages your drones and infiltrates rooms until you close the door, time-sensitive events such as a door suddenly becoming inoperable, etcetera.
2. It's all about finding more fuel. I expect a magical fairy will not land to give you more fuel when you run out going to a rig that didn't have any more for you despite your praying, and so each jump to another node needs to be calculated in advance. While this isn't convenient, it gives the game some realism, and makes you think about what it might be like operating a real drone out in space somewhere and how to make your sparce resources work (Think Apollo 13).
3. It reminds me of the matrix. The third movie, that is, since the matrix number 1 and 2 were not really robotic but rather about virtual reality. But I suppose green lettering is really all I've got to back that up.
4. The command system is intuitive. You can type "Na 1 3" and it means navigate drone 1 to get to the room drone 3 is in. It auto-completes. It generates. It tows the husk back to the ship. This is very necessary really since nobody really wants to just play a tow-truck simluation. (Airport simulator cough cough). Instead the foundation has been laid for good things.
some gripes
The fraps crash issue... it couldn't resolve some resolution bug.
The lack of confirmation screens and/or random disasters just being a game-over scenario.
Almost painful visuals. Yes I know that it's perhaps part of the appeal, but I'd rather look at grey walls than neon lights. Having said that, textures have been done already, and so a game that provides us with maximal gameplay and minimal fuss is pretty neat.

Like my review of The Houchi Play, don't let my Steam play time fool you. I spent a great deal of time playing Maid San back on XBox 360 Indie Games.
Maid san's Caving Adventure feels like a lost Turbo Grafx 16 game to me. Back when platformer titles were king and game developers were still trying to figure out different ways to approach the subject. Maid San has two strengths available to her; the ability to jump really high and the power to cower in fear. She does so traversing a series of caves, as the title might lead you to believe, while collecting stars and avoiding the Benar - a subterranian humanoid race with a penchant for wooden clubs and cigarettes.
Avoid the Benar when you can, and tremble before them when you can't. Collect stars and clear the stage as fast and efficiently as you can (scoring is based on a myriad of factors including the number of steps and jumps you've performed).
In that regard, there is a optimal playthrough for each level.
All told the sprite graphics are very well done and serve their purpose nicely. For $2 you really can't go wrong. Its a fun, pleasant, retro game with some unique mechanics.

At first duskers seems oretty forgetable. but give it an hour or so and it soon gets complex. Tl;Dr at end.
The premise is that the galaxy is near enough void of all human life and you are to search derelict ships in order to pice together what caused this sudden end to humanity. To explore the ships you take control of a squad of up to 4 active drones and salvage what you can whilst avoiding hostiles.
Dealing with the hostiles is, for me, what makes the game great. Every hostile can be dealt with in some form or another but so can you. As an example i had a drone with a stealth upgrade and equipped with a gatling gun. At first it was great but then you find slime and your whole way of life comes to an alarming crash.
Issuing orders is done through a command line system (dont worry its pretty simple). The command line system does not allow split second actions. If your drone gets jumped on you have to type furiously to save it, as well as the others, from certain death. You will often find yourself with a drone going through a door and getting attacked because you have forgotten to take one of many precautions, before you know it the drone is dead and the hostile has promptly moved through the open door to reign havoc.
Its not all positive at this time in developement. Currently there is very little hand holding other than the starting tutorial. No database of hostiles or anything. its not game breaking but i will put this down to early access. There are very few bugs (i've not seen any).
The biggest downside though is the lack of information about the world you are in. Although i am not really that far into the game i still feel you could learn more about the world. The best way for me to describe it is by comparing this to deadnauts where you can learn every last little detail about everything. However im sure this will be remedied in the future.
Lastly The devs are very active on the steam forum. I think a dev has replied to every thread i have read!
Tl;DR
+Solid addictive gamplay
+Large choice of strategies
+Rougelike
+CMD line system is cool and adds a sense of peril to your encounters
+Simple but effective graphics
+few bugs
-Tutorial is the only help you get
-Would like more info on things like hostiles and backstory (see deadnauts)
-Some gameplay features feel like bugs when you first start out.

If you think a gothic, Victorian, steam punk, fog light, subterranean ocean hell with a dark, comedic twist sounds like a good time, you'll probably like Sunless Sea. The tone and style are both spot on, which in itself will be enough to keep logophiles like myself invested.
As with many early access games, there is a lot of rebalancing left to do, and only a fraction of the map is finished. However, the developers seem to have a good handle on what needs to be changed, and they have their plans for future updates posted online.
The biggest down side so far is the combat, which is dull and repetitive. Fortunately, it is not the focus of the game, but I hope that future versions will do something to rectify the current state of the system.
The biggest selling point of the game is the storytelling, which is truly enjoyable. But if you're not sure if that sort of thing will tickle your fancy, Fallen London will give you a pretty good idea. It's free and Sunless Sea is based on the same lore.
Signs point to a good game on the horizon, though it may be too early to tell. If the game ends up failing, it will be because the game play never managed to get out of the way of the story, but I for one have high hopes that the development team will deliver. If you believe in story oriented games, this is a good one to put some faith in.

There's something to be said for a game that captures a particular environment and atmosphere perfectly.  With the recent upgrade to Unity 5, The Long Dark presents a perfect atmosphere of cold, snow, hunger, and terror.
Think a survival game needs zombies to be fun? Think again.
This survival game features cold, snow, and good ole Mother Nature.  And once you've stumbled your way through a blinding wintry storm, clinging to life, and just barely make it through the door of a cabin and collapse on the floor, you'll realize that this is all the game needs.  There are such magical moments in playing it, whether from the life-threatening desperate-to-survive times to the peaceful beautiful serene parts as you watch the sun rise.
Who knew such a beautiful place could be so damn deadly? XD
Get it.  You'll enjoy it.  To date, it's the best money I've spent on Early Access, hands down, bar none.  The developers are constantly improving and updating the game, as well as expanding the sandbox you can play in (now up to three distinct zones with transition zones between-- tons to explore).  The community forums at
are active and friendly, with tons of fresh ideas and player feedback.  And once the game releases, there will be the Story mode in addition to the currently available Sandbox mode. It's an investment worth every penny... and more.
