tl;dr: Has promise, but isn't worth money yet. There are regular updates and a good roadmap, so i expect this review will be out-of-date in a few months.
It tries hard to feel like FTL, with back-and-forth ship combat and detailed storytelling. It has a good variety of things to do in the little docks and places you'll find, and certainly looks and feels the way the authors intended - whimsical and yet dark. There are a good amount of things to manage, from food to fuel to fragments of knowledge (which you can trade for money). It feels like it's going in  the right direction.
Unfortunately, it's just not there yet. Your ship is unbearably slow (unless you want to risk a fire by going a normal speed), the enemies monotonous and tiresome (how many rewardless giant crabs and bat swarms am i going to have to fight?), and there doesn't feel like there's a point to combat. Unless you take on a pirate ship, you gain nothing from it. A game should make efforts to provide you with incentives for your actions, not just insert filler to keep you occupied while you wonder why you're playing.
Worse, the map is static, and everything is spread far apart. Go too far to the north? Welcome to the lifebergs which oneshot you with zero illumination. Braving the south? Cool, but watch out for buoys which instantly destroy your ship (and bug out your sound) if you touch them.
Normally I'm cool with dying, but with this game, it just feels like a chore. There's nothing random about the game,  so you wind up just replaying everything you already did, then trying to find something new to do. This style of gameplay only works if you're allowed to game the save/load features, but with permadeath it's pointless. There's a "merciful mode" which allows you to save/load at will, but it still autosaves when you die - meaning that it's still permadeath.
Again, I like what it's going for; keep an eye on this one. But don't buy it until they address the monotony and pointlessness.

A far better game than RA3; the Tiberium series goes out with a big bang (I refuse to acknowledge "Tiberium Twilight").
Don't be fooled by my playtime on Steam; I played the retail disc over and over.
NOTICE: Tiberium Wars on Steam ships with version 1.09 with no option to downgrade since previous patch files are not included in the download. Single player campaign missions are NOT designed with changed made since patch 1.05 (inclusively) and beyond. The result is that the campaign is excessively and unintentionally hard when played on 1.09 (or anything beyond 1.04). Owners of the retail disc may download cumulative patches until 1.04 to experience the single player aspect of this game as intended. Owners of the Steam download version are left hanging.
This review is based on patch 1.04.
Pro:
- Engaging storyline with good acting. Very little campiness to note.
- The tone in general is darker, tenser, and much more serious than RA3. Then again, the Tiberium series has always been the more serious one.
- Generally good unit balancing, and don't get me started on "Mammoth Tank rushes". If you let the enemy build up a Mammoth Tank rush then you only have yourself to blame for not building something equally strong during that time.
- Beautiful unit and structure designs. Each faction has a unique and distinct design language, with the GDI, white and gold, blocky and rightous; the NOD, red and black, fluid and sidious; while the Scrin just looks bizarre and otherworldy.
- Infantry comes in squads instead of singles (except commando units). One rifleman or militia unit is made up of mutliple individual soldiers. The health of a unit is tied to how many soldiers are left in a squad. The firepower of a squad decreases with its health since less soldiers make up that squad.
- Excellent unit sizes and scale. Vehicles are significantly larger than infantry, while buildings are significantly larger than vehicles.
- Excellent armour types and unit countering. Riflemen will barely damage any armour unless if you have a huge amount of riflemen. Conversely, cannon and rocket-type weaponry barely do damage against infantry. A building full of riflemen will no longer destroy a tank in seconds like you would see in the RA universe.
- Cannons and missiles can and do miss against targets, especially moving targets. I personally highly appreciate this added bit of realism; EA certainly did not, and this was removed in patch 1.05.
Con:
- Bad (and very bad indeed) AI pathing. Some units and vehicles will simply give up on trying to cross a river because there is no straight line to the bridge over said river. Waypoints alleviate this problem to some extent, but some units have trouble going to their assigned waypoints! This is, however, an engine-dependent problem: Generals, RA3 and Tiberium Wars all have this same problem.
- Graphics are dated. The models and textures still look decent for a 2011(?) game, but the in-game anti-aliasing is largely ineffective. Jaggies are all over the place and is most obvious when models and textures are rendered through smoke and steam.
- No naval units apart from a few battleship props. This removes a whole dimension of gameplay; however note that the Tiberium series never had navies since the world's waters are too heavily infested in this universe.
- Few air units, though this is a common problem to all C&C games.
- Engineers can no longer repair civilian structures. Actually, civilian structures can no longer be repaired, at all.
- Building placement is excessively liberal. One can rotate buildings as much as they wish but they never seems to properly line up with adjacent buildings, resulting in large amounts of wasted space. This also contributes to the AI pathing problem because many units cannot go through some of the spaces between buildings, despite the fact that said spaces are visually much wider than the units. RA3 does not suffer from this problem since its building placement is tile-based.
- Campaigns are broken by patches beyond 1.04.

Let me just begin by stating that I am usually not the BIGGEST fan of puzzle type games; I get frustrated really easily and...ya, you get the point. However, Limbo does so many things well that I find it really easy to look past what I wouldn't normally find attractive in a game. First of all, the artwork is amazing, the simple black and white setting really highlight some of the eerie tones that the game tries to portray. Now while the artwork is simple, this is a pretty graphic game in terms of death; body parts fly off your body, guts stick on to top of roofs that smash you...its awesome.
Artwork aside, lets talk about the puzzles. The puzzles are absolutely fantastic. DO NOT look up any walkthroughs! It is so rewarding at the end and most of the time you are going to find yourself hitting your head in dissapointment that you missed such a common sense solution. The great thing about the puzzles is that none of them seem unfair, you won't ever find yourself saying "How was I supposed to know that?" The puzzles also do a great job in elevating difficulty as you move through the game, which make the seamless gameplay that much more enjoyable. 9/10

Most FPS's are bland slog fests, no fun, no colour, or vibrancy; just dull pieces of work. Bioshock, is able to capture the fun of running, and gunning your oponents down, as a game, and is able to succeed that as an art.
Game wise, fairly standard assortment of guns, early to mid 1900's themed. Interesting twist yes? Now throw in rag-tag modifcations to guns, a plethora of different ammo that does everything from explode on impact to cause massive electrical damage. Then throw in almost supernatural powers, with a wide variety of character augmentations, to help you adapt to the changing environment. Want to run at 500% speed hitting people with a wrench in the back that freezes them solid, and you can become invisable- Bioshock has that.
These augmentations to the self are not just a gameplay feature, they are a core feature of the games narrative. The game itself portrays a distopian underwater city, that, as you are forced to enter seemingly, without your own choice in the matter, forces you to see what has happened. It forces you to take on this role, and realise who the real villain of the situation is, who or what is the real monster behind sociatal collapse and anarchy. Everything in the game seemingly has a suitable purpose to back up a part of the narrative, and it works, because nothing is then ever out of place. The game is able to form a cohesive structure, that despite its debatable ending, creates a wonderful philosophical experiance.
There are those that this game is a dumbed down System Shock 2, or even a console port that is meant for lesser gamers. But until we look at games in their individuality, we cant see the shine each one brings to the table. Bioshock, as a single product is simply an amazing game, that is a must own for any gamer.

TL;DR :  Greatest game I've played in a while.  Most likely to be my game of the year, maybe even the decade.
A Hat in Time is a 3D platformer which draws inspiration from games like Super Mario Sunshine and the early Paper Mario titles.  It takes some noticable things from those games like the writing style and the slide move and also adds some things of its own, like the ability to climb up a wall for a short period before sliding down.  As the title would suggest, the game also sports six different hats with their own abilities to help you get around the levels.  On top of the hats, you can also have up to three different badges equipped at once, which all have either a passive or active effect, and are applied no matter what hat youre using.  The game controls are a bit floatier compared to Sunshine, but are ultimately alot smoother in the long run.  The game's level design is great, and offers a fair challenge in every stage.  The soundtrack for the game is very memorable, as each level will have its own tracks unique to it, instead of one theme for a world.  The game isnt that long if you're just trying to beat it (it took me roughly nine hours), but the experience is very enjoyable and memorable, which makes up for its short length.  I give A Hat in Time a 10/10, and I would highly reccomend it to anybody looking for a game that they will remember as fondly as their childhood games.

Imagine yourself walking in a forest one night. Dark, desolated, alone. You walked on, without the faintest idea of where you are heading. The forest is empty apart from the vague shadows of the leaves falling. A soft, obscured sound taps you on your shoulder.  You turned around, in hope of finding someone, something, that you can share your woes with. But no, that did not happen. All that stood in front of you are pillars and pillars of trees, looming, casting their ominous shadows onto you. You yelled, you screamed, and you cried, praying that a being, any being, will answer to your call. This is all to no avail. You have no choice but to venture on. However, deep down inside you, you know very well that someone is here, someone is listening to your calls, and that someone does not want you to be where you are. Welcome to Limbo.
Limbo is nothing more than the silhouette of a world where the protagonist venture on in desolating loneliness. Using simple controls, you will have to interact with the surroundings as the story unfolds while making sure that the protagonist lives. It's not an easy task, as everything out there wants you gone. Fellow humans, giant spiders, rocks, pipes, blades, clockworks, everything. Well, you might think that, with only two colours, this game is easy, right? Think twice, as when the colours are so monotonous, you are bound to miss something that is out to get you.

You know, it's hard to fully express what I feel about this game. It makes me so happy for so many reasons it's hard to know where to start. It is adorable, enjoyable, interesting, endlessly charming, and extremely nostalgic, in all the right ways.
It's way too common for developers to attempt to revive a nostalgic genre by exactly emulating the classic titles, qualities and flaws alike. Thankfully, the devs of A Hat in Time were smarter than that: they took the 3D platformer collect-a-thon genre, took away many of the annoying things that were characteristic to it, and delivered a lovable polished piece.
The first thing you'll notice, as you start the game, is that the music is absolutely awesome. It feels constantly fun and adventurous, with many awesome tunes that fit many different themes with something of a child-like wonder to them. It's awesome how the music changes depending on what part of a level you're in, with some instruments fading in or out, I love this kind of dynamic music.
The sound effects that accompany the soundtrack are also excellent. Adorable childish interjections, some cute short sentences like "you're free!" or "all mine" that make you go "aww <3", some ambient sounds at times that range from soothing to creepy and, of course, satisfying "slam" and explosion sound effects for combat. The voice acting is also awesome, with every character full of this caricaturesque charm and personality that I simply adore. I particularly love Mustache Girl's voice, it's equal parts rebellious and adorable.
Which brings us to the graphics, and oh boy, this game is teeming with charm in there as well. First of all, there are the characters. Hat Kid is head-exploding levels of adorable, with her silly face, cutesy outfit, precious idle animations, and a fine selection of hats. Every other character is just as cool: you get some awesomely funny mafia thugs, an adorably energetic Mustache Girl, stylish musical penguins, western train riding owls, an evil demonic queen, some cute mountain dwellers, and many other sweet, sweet characters.
The sceneries are also full of that same charm the characters have. Starting with the adorable spaceship that looks like a mix between a proper spaceship and a child's playground, moving to a very colorful town of mafia thugs, a busy and secretive movie studio, a mysterious train, a happy musical moon city, an awesomely dark and creepy forest full of bizarre things, a haunted mansion, a lovely mountain range full of villages and bushes with a wide variety of landscapes, and the absolutely foreboding final dungeon that is very... foreboding, every level has a cartoony thematic style.
Then, of course, there's the game. The controls are deliciously fluid, it's so fun and satisfying to just run and jump around, and the camera works great as well, which is rare in 3D platformers (in fact, the devs took camera development to a level many AAA games don't take). There's a great variety of special powers you can equip Hat Kid with which apply to many different situations, giving the game a bit of a "key and keyhole" aspect while providing the player with a plethora of options on how to solve a problem.
No collect-a-thon is complete without collectibles, right? The collectibles in this game come in five main types: the yarns, which are used to knit hats, the relics, that unlock certain special stages, the rift tokens that operate this crazy slot machine that gives out pretty cool cosmetic prizes, and, of course, the Time Pieces, this game's main collectible (like puzzle pieces in Banjo-Kazooie or stars in Super Mario 64). There are also badges you can buy (and sometimes find) to give you all kinds of different skills, making pons (the game's currency) worth collecting, and inviting the player to try all kinds of different stuff. I particularly adore the one that gives Hat Kid a little scooter (it's so, so adorable how Hat Kid just dangles her little feet when she's on it).
Then there's the level design. First of all, the platforming in every level is great, making worlds satisfying to jump around and explore, giving the player a selection of different paths to traverse. Even in the more linear levels, there are clever ways to skip sections if you're smart and quick enough.
This being a 3D collect-a-thon, most levels follow a "semi-open" structure where there's a handful of main objectives, but a lot of free range to run around looking for optional tokens and collectibles. Mafia Town is perfectly representative of that, with a ton of things to collect around town right away, even as you're just starting the game, headed towards your first Time Piece through the convoluted landscape of square buildings and giant-meat-rolling streets. Subcon Forest is probably my favorite, due to the amount of optional sections full of stuff to find, combined with the sweet, sweet dark atmosphere that I'm just in love with. Alpine Skyline is an awesome level overall, but it kinda falls short of its main promise: it promises us a free roaming experience, but in practice it's pretty much a glorified hub world, with a decent amount of things to explore, but with every time piece clearly contained in the "dead ends" of the paths, in which there are "tiny levels" of their own (awesome tiny levels, but tiny levels nonetheless).
In Battle of the Birds, instead of giving us one large world to explore, the game gives us a series of tinier levels, each with their own themes and objectives. The first level involves infiltrating a movie studio and retrieving some Time Pieces that are being used as props. Then there's Murder in the Owl Express, where you need to gather clues and open up new paths by solving small puzzles to solve a murder mystery, and Train Rush, which is an intense linear race against the clock to get to the end. On the other side of things, there's Picture Perfect, where you have to explore a tiny moon city getting penguin people to become your fans and take pics of you, and The Big Parade, where you run around the same moon city, but this time with a crowd on ground level that hurts you if you touch them, with a band of birds that follow you around playing a very satisfying song (seriously, that song makes me so damn happy). In the end, you get to fight a boss depending on which set of levels you were the best at. Battle of the Birds is a pretty awesome change of style.
Then there's the Time Rift levels, which come in two forms: the "blue" form, consisting of fun linear platforming challenges with a surreal atmosphere, and the "purple" forms, which have you traverse a sequence of interesting explorable mini-maps collecting "rift pons" and a set of pictures that tell a little story.
The final level is a linear challenge of epic proportions that's as hard as it is tense, culminating in an epic battle against your arch-nemesis.
Which brings us to bosses: the bosses in this game mostly follow the same formula of "avoid attacks, wait for an opening, attack", which is okay in my book. They are mostly fun, throwing deadly attacks and changing patterns as the battle intensifies, but they feel a bit redundant at times, taking way more hits than they should.
For a game in a genre that was born with consoles in mind, this game controls surprisingly well with keyboard and mouse. Accurately controlling the camera with the mouse while using the keyboard for movement feels so natural I'm impressed there weren't more 3D platformers for the PC back in the day.
So, to sum it all up, this game is awesome. It's full of heart, charm and enjoyment, bringing 3D platformers back with a cute as heck vengeance. It makes me so happy I can barely fit all my thoughts in this tiny review form. My only complaint is that the game is waaaay too short, unfortunately. Oh, how I wish this was longer :(

I still only somewhat know what I'm doing, but I was instantly mesmerized by the game.  As a prorgrammer who grew up in the 80s, the DOS-like (or bash-like if you prefer) environment, and handy features like autocomplete for text you're typing, really show a very solid attention to detail.
It does feel a bit strangely quiet at the moment right now (no music at all), and I'm not sure if that's intended or not.  It's certainly creepy.  But the sounds beyond that are quite good, although I understand from the dev progress bar thingy that more is to come.
The graphics really do make me feel like I'm looking into The Matrix in a lot of ways.  It's sort of what I imagine you might get to see as a blind person with really bad prosthetic eyes.  This is, of course, the point -- differnet of your robot guys have different sorts of vision and different sensors, and that definitely gives a varied feel to each.
I like the way that I can detect enemies in a nearby room and then do things to encourage those enemies to leave that room and go somewhere else.  I have no idea what they are or what their danger is, but either way I don't want to meet them, and I don't.  So far. ;)
This definitely has a feel unlike anything else I've played before, and I will be playing more, no question.

TL;DR: Overall it's decent, but not worth $30USD.
A good, enjoyable casual game with light-hearted humour, simple story and intriguing levels to traverse and collect things.
So why am I not recommending it? The price tag, $30USD, is expensive for how much content you get. I beat the game in just over 15 hours, and this includes 100%ing the game and collecting the bulk of the collectibles. Compare this to some other titles on steam and you'll find it's a bit lacking; I have quite a few other titles that are around the $20USD mark and I handily got 2x-4x more play time than this game.
I understand that quantity is not always better than quality, but the game is partly lacking in this area as well. It does a solid job across the board in terms of visuals, controls, gameplay objectives, mechanics and overall charm, but that's really just it. It's a solid game, but its missing that extra oomph for me to really get excited about it and say it's amazing. Decent across the board but doesn't quite hit the bullseye in any area either.
I also think it was a tad too easy. I bought this game wanting an easy-going and casual style of game to play and it certainly delivers in this regard, but the game has the two or three bright sparks where it introduces something that is unique and challenging. I couldn't help but think how much better the game could be if there were a few more of these moments and ideas, or if they were expanded upon a bit more.
If it were $20USD I'd say you've got yourself an enjoyable game for a fair price, so I would recommend it on sale. $10USD or lower would be a bargain.

I am impressed.
At first I balked at the price tag, 20 bucks seemed a little steep for an early access game of this type.  That was about 10 hours ago and I can easily see myself getting 200+ hours of enjoyment out of this game over the next couple of years.  Well worth your time and money.  Great tension, atmosphere, and strategy/management.  This is a good game to accompany Invisible Inc., another procedurally generated stealther.
Duskers is realtime, not turnbased or quasi-turnbased.  Oddly enough I found myself thinking about the old NES game The Lost Vikings while I was playing Duskers.
Perhaps more so than other roguelikes, this game forces you to press on after a failure.  If you aren't willing to accept a sub-optimal outcome, you're never going to visit more than 2 or 3 systems because of all the resetting you're going to do.  This game is all about developing your own strategy and set of best practices that constantly evolve and change with the changing conditions in the derelicts.  Just when you feel like you've got a good rythm going and you can clear out the derilicts without too much trouble...bang!  Swarm of nanobots!  Asteroid impacts!  Radiation leak!
This isn't exactly an action game, but it will keep you on the edge of your seat - and like some of the best games, it punishes you for being careless, lazy, greedy, or hurried.

*Update 04 November 2014
Dev's still routinely rolling out more story line and additional ports, Trade is better balanced now with feasible ways to earn echo's. There is still some grinding involved in order to get enough echo's for larger ships and upgrades but all in all it isn't too bad. Terror is more manageable now. Still a few bugs here and there but nothing totally game breaking. Randomly generated maps have been instated, and there's a lot more story content since my original review. Game has a much better combat system now with it being live action, more enemies both creature wise and other pirate ship wise. The story content is great, and the artwork even though it's a 2d game looks great the environmental animations bring the world to life, although I  would like to see more added. Over all game play has improved greatly. Can't wait to see and play this game in the final form.
/Update
This game has the potential to be a great game, as long as the DEV continue to update and add more content on a regular basis.
There is a lot of room for improvement as far as the Economy of the game is concerned, Trade goods pricing need to be balanced better, so you can actually make a little $ transporting goods from one place to another. With the current prices it's one hell of a grind to make enough echoes for upgrades and supplies so you can continue to play.
Terror also needs a bit of work, in my opinion. There needs to be better ways of combating terror when at sea, or at the very least, the methods that are in place currently to combat terror need to be changed so they actually help to reduce it by a more significant amount instead of only removing 1-5 points of terror at a time. Also for as fast as Terror builds up and increases when out at sea, I think by returning home to Fallen London, terror levels should be reduced more than to just the 50 level, or at least add the chance for it to be reduced further than just 50, perhaps a chance for it to be reduced to 25 or even a slight chance of being reset to 0. Getting your terror level reduced to 50 doesn't allow much room for longer journeys especially early on in the game when you don't have the echoes to purchase upgrades that can help with speed, therefore causing less terror to build up.
All in all, like I said above this game has huge potential, It's an enjoyable game to play as is, but definitely needs balance changes made in the economy to allow less of a grind when starting a new career.
Very high potential in current standings to be a great game upon the completion of the early access stage but It is still an Early Access Game that needs and will hopefully be getting updates and tweaks made regularly.
I can see how this game in its current state might turn quite a few people off, b/c it is such a grind getting started. The grind can lead to boredom (doing the same run over and over b/c it's the only way to make echo's at current) or due to the combat system in its current state (very predictable). But once again this is an Early Access Game. I can only hope that the DEV will listen to their consumers and make changes accordingly.

Duskers is in Early access, so this review is subject to change with the game.
Disclaimer - Key for this game was provided by the developer for live-streaming / Review purposes.
"Pilot drones into derelict spaceships to find the means to survive and piece together how the universe became a giant graveyard."
The description for Misfits-Attic new game, Duskers.
This game had snagged my attention from that description alone.
It also tells you everything about the game.
A. You control drones.
B. Universe is poopered all over the place.
C. Unknown Variables that tend to lead to your death.
In this game, you start with a merry band of drones. Most often named Sarah, Brandon and Matt for myself. You float your ship up to other not really working ships, stations or military facilities and then you send your drones in, and you scout. You find things to get you to the next ship, if you're lucky. And if you're unlucky there will be a monster, or enemy drone that blasts your drone(s) into oblivion.
The game has almost a puzzle like quality to it, where you have to provide power to the ship so you can open and close doors to explore. If you can funnel an enemy into a location where there is a gun and you can interface with the ship, you can kill it. If all else fails you can open an airlock and suck the thing right out. Just make sure your drones aren't in there when you do. Also make sure that you close the doors quickly before radiation floods the ship.
The coolest part of this game, to me, is that you control your drones with the arrow keys for movement. Once they're in position you then issue commands via a terminal. If using your arrow keys isn't something you enjoy you can also go to the schematic (overhead) view of the ship and move Donald the wonder drone (drone 1) into room 4 via keystrokes [Example command: Navgiate 1 r4].
The game is immersive in a surprising way, from the subtle ship noises to the drones whirring away.
On occassion mistakes were made, and I understand why they were my fault. Activating a defense turrent while Drone 1 is standing there tends to end poorly for drone 1. Opening the airlock with your drone there, as mentioned before will suck your drone out to dance with Dave among the stars.
First time I did that I forgot to move my ship to a new airlock, and I moved all the drones to the adjacent room to airlock. Opened it, had no more drones.Fwoosh. You're going to start over a lot, but when you have to do so you get to keep the logs you find from the ships, but that's all. After enough exploration or dying, in theory you'll have discovered a wonderful story.
If by some miracle you can make it out of the first area (kidding, it's not that bad) then you get to go to new and exciting locales full of things wanting to kill you too. Maybe not full, but exactly where and when you don't want them to be there.
There are ship upgrades that you can equip that give you things like better scanners, or the ability to power a point without having to leave a drone on it.
The developer is active in terms of replying, as well as when I was streaming it they came to sit in and see how I would solve problems, offering advice and tips where applicable.
At the time of this writing, this is another Indie game that caught me off guard, and I'm glad it did.
Were anyone to ask me if I would recommend this game, I would say yes. Without a doubt. It has provided me with moments worth remembering, some,  if only because I had failed.
I can't wait to continue to get lost in space.

I rarely say this about a game - especially a game in its early access stage - but Sunless Sea is ♥♥♥♥ing rad. You play as a captain exploring the underground zee around Fallen London, risking death every time you leave port. While adrift in the zee, you'll encounter pirates, monsters, nemeses, mutinies, tentacles that silently steal your crew off deck, new ports, maelstroms, new cities, new races, beautifully imagined islands, weird religions, well developed lores - the list goes on and on. And should you die and lose your ship and crew, there's always the next character who will strive to make it a bit farther out into the zee.
I encourage anyone who's a fan of roguelikes to give Sunless Sea a chance. It's a game that offers a refreshing outlook on a difficult genre, and which can only improve as the devs implement more content. Sunless Sea is tough and unforgiving, but it doesn't often feel unfair. That said, I do suggest you read the in-Steam guide early on in your travels.

A dreary, confused experience that falls awkwardly between the twin stools of half-baked trading game and under-written explore-'em-up. "London was stolen by bats!" we are informed, before immediately leaving to chug tediously around  a serious of oddly named and deeply uninteresting places while engaging in combat so predictable that it might as well take place while blindfolded and slightly dead, anaemic buying-and-selling of inexplicable items for uncertain purpose, and mysterious references to 'cards' which don't seem to exist anywhere. Which is a shame, because trying to find out who and why would have London stolen by bats and dumped underground sounds a lot more compelling than inching through a green sludge to... do stuff... for reasons.
(Imagine the Failbetter version of the Star Wars opening crawl: 'A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away...exciting things happen! But not to you, because we're off to Scunthorpe on a rainy Sunday afternoon in 1987 to get in some drying paint watching.')
'Sunless Sea' seems to depend on knowledge of a web-based adventure game (which at a cursory glance, is a deeply grindy affair) named 'Fallen London' for any real enjoyment, as the background and backdrop are detailed there rather than in situ. Random texts about 'drownies' or 'far away screams' or people chuckling on the deck serve not to build atmosphere but to undermine it as we lack context in which to place these snippets of whatever they are.
In order to improve before release, the combat needs to be reworked to provide an incentive for engagement rather than irritation, trading needs to be reconsidered to make the impact understandable, the background needs to become rather more foreground, and perhaps a hook or two could be dropped at the outset for those of us who enjoy story strands to pick up and follow (rather than tryng to avoid yet another copy and paste random encounter with unamusing monsters).
It's certainly dark - unpleasantly and verdantly dark - but at the moment, it's a horror for the wrong reasons.

is a first-person narrative-focused "walking simulator" game. It purports to be a "developer's commentary" of sorts, in which
creator Davey Wreden walks you through a series of semi-finished games designed but never released by an eccentric, reclusive solo developer named Coda. The idea is that by examining the work of the man, you gain understanding of both his personality and the circumstances surrounding the games' creation.
As has been said a million times, to discuss
much beyond even this most basic point would be to spoil the hell out of it. It deserves to be discussed—a very pretentious part of me wants to say it *demands* to be discussed—but that's a job for a critic, not a reviewer.
(The difference? To paraphrase Spider Robinson, a critic tells you whether it's Art—a reviewer tells you if it's any damned good.)
Is
any damned good? If you're the "games are art" sort who got caught up in Dear Esther and don't mind a relatively passive, linear narrative experience, you'll probably like it. If you prefer your games to be more objective-driven, stay clear. I will say that this is not
Part Deux. The jokes aren't the same, the narrator's not the same, and though both games deconstruct the ways in which games present information to their players, Beginner's Guide does it in a very different way with a wholly different tone. If you're expecting more of the same, you will probably feel enraged and betrayed by what's been done here.
Me, I liked it. Well, liked may be the wrong word to describe my feelings, but you get the idea. I appreciated my time spent with The Beginner's Guide, even though I would like to craft a strongly-worded email to the author expressing my discomfort at having my emotions raked over the coals so thoroughly. Which I suppose is the intended effect. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

I personally love the idea of rouge-likes. games that mke your actions have immediate results and consequences.
But there is a line. a delicate line, a line once drawn can make or break a game.
This line is what makes or ruins rouge-likes for players. My friends and i call this line RNG God
In FTL you can come out of warp into a sun covered with a metor shower having to fight a allready hard foe, with next to to survive it. Thats crossing the RNG line
In duskers you start off with three drones with one of a few starting set ups. this chooses FOR YOU, which tactics you will employ early in the game. you can try to do your own thing but you are extremely restricted by your starting gear.
I have had a horrible time with the RNG line in duskers, just like in FTL you can be randomly screwed over with the flip of a coin, reguardless of however skilled you are.
My worst experiance by far was a 1 hour and a 1/2 run where i tip toed through 6 ships to get another drone and an interface moduel to make raiding ships easier. EASIER, not easy.
The very next ship i go to to start employing use of the new drone and tool. i shift airlocks to deploy a drone elsewhere in the ship and suddenly : RADIATION COMING IN THROUGH THE HULL. directly into the room with all 3 of my drones who are basically keeping eyes on the entire ship.
Before this mission the ship scans said the hulls intergrity was GOOD. If you randomly change the paramiters of a mission where a constant is known beforehand to be reliable its a sucker punch. This is a prime example of Random difficulty spikes that ruin fabulous games.
I Do NOT recommend this game because of the exsistance of such extreme, random, and game breaking spikes like this.
A space bound Astroid strike give you a chance to either turn tail or continue, the enemies are fantastic, you can find them and dispose of them multiple ways, even the sudden rouge enemies deciding to open doors they dont like is fun and keeps you on your toes.
But you cannot come out of left feild with a random sucker punch.
So TL:DR
The game duskers is fantastic, from its look, to its form to its story you peice together yourself. I barely even see it being a early access game, it FEELS complete. And i will be playing it for weeks to come.
Sadly it is another rouge-like with unpredicable absolutly random difficulty spikes that players will quite likely be unready for, and it may cause undue frustration and a game over.
I do not recommend it unless you are patient, want a game like this for the sheer intrest factor or are a masochist who likes being occasonally sucker punched.

There are many ways a game can be immersive. First person games like Mirror's Edge use full-body awareness so you're controlling a body with heft and limbs rather than a disembodied camera. Gone Home, Amnesia, and The Room utilize tactile hands-on gameplay. And then you have games like Her Story and Uplink, where you're not merely controlling a character. You are the character, your computer screen acting as the in-game monitor, a direct window into the game's world.
Duskers fits in that latter category and this tactical sci-fi survival roguelike utterly succeeds at delivering an immersive, atmospheric experience,
The universe is dead. You are alone. Supplies are dwindling. Welcome to the bleak world of Duskers. As the lone survivor in a galaxy gone silent, you travel from ship to ship, derelict barges and stations and outposts now drifting through space. Fuel and resources diminish with every jump, as you desperately stave off starvation or avoid becoming stranded in the endless abyss.
But exploring vessels yourself is too dangerous because, while you may be the last human,...you certainly aren't the last organism. Death lurks everywhere, from alien horrors and active security systems to radiation leaks.
So you use the next best option, From your ship's console, you remotely guide drones through the dark rooms and corridors. You view the world through your ship's monitor and the drones' limited, grainy camera feeds, sensors and cameras that can fail or make errors. They act as your eyes, ears, and hands from the safety of your ship. And you don't guide these drones through icons or RTS-style controls, but by typing in command lines.
While it may sound archaic and clunky, the command line interface is part of what makes Duskers so brilliant and immersive. Every command must be planned and carefully considered, because if something goes wrong - and it will - you must adapt and improvise on the fly. It gives the game a deliberate, cautious pace, as you command your fragile drones to maneuver between rooms, use motion detectors, gather supplies, power generators, and so on. When you're hurriedly typing in commands as radiation is spreading through an outpost and power is failing and the creatures you had trapped in a room are breaking free, Duskers is at its most tense, thanks to that careful pacing and detached perspective.
But Duskers is also a tactical experience. Scavenged gear can be used to modify drones with lures, cloaking, motion detectors, even the rare weapon, but the best tools are the vessels themselves. You can trap aliens in a room then activate a vessel's on-board defense system, or open an airlock to suck a roaming turret into space. Caution and planning ahead are how you keep your drones intact.
Duskers mixes moments of unease and fear of the unknown with satisfying strategy and on-the-fly improvisation. Similar to Her Story or Uplink, the command console interface results in an immersive intimate experience. You are the last human, controlling your drones, from your computer.

===
The old-school is back, in all its satisfaction and difficulty.
===
- Absolutely essential purchase
- Purchase only if on sale
- Purchase only if on heavy sale
- Avoid purchasing
===
The Planet of the Vicious Creatures is an old-school themed and inspired platformer. The player will control a nameless astronaut and will have to guide him (or her maybe?) through various platform-based levels of increasing complexity.
The mechanics at the game core are pretty simple: arrow keys control all the functions you need, namely Left, RIght, Jump and Crouch. Your objective is to pass through each level from one side to the other, this though can only be done after the player collected the Oxygen Sphere present in each level, without which, the access to the next level is barred.
In each level, there will be a great variety of both living creatures and environmental hazards to impede the player's progression: space caterpillars, locusts, spiders, fire-breathing lizards, acid clouds and thunderbolts are only some of the enemies and obstacles the player will face. And each one of them will kill mercilessly, in one hit, like in the true old-school games.
You will need pixel-perfect precision in each movement and jump in order to pass each level, there is absolutely no room for mistakes.
But despair not, as there is a convenient Practice Mode, activated with the 0 key, that allows the player to try out a level without losing any life if death occurs, in order to perfect the timing and understand how to overcome that specific level's obstacles. Of course, you will not be able to progress to the next level if you complete the current one while in Practice Mode.
During the course of the whole game you will have 10 lives at your disposal, one hit from any damage source will take out one and restart the current level. If all the lives are depleted, you will have to restart the whole 60 levels back from square one. Hardcore.
===
- Graphics style is very inspired to the platformers of times past, it really looks like something thrown at us right from back in the '80s. This is exactly the style a retro platformer needs.
- Hardcore experience: 60 levels, 10 lives and ZERO room for any mistake. Each level is extremely, brutally, excruciatingly difficult, on the verge of being impossible... but it is not.
- The Practice Mode is a very good idea, it really helps players to understand the mechanics of each level andd hone their skills without losing lives, and they will lose a lot of them. It also mitigates the extreme frustration factor that derives from a game of this type.
- Decent sound design overall, nothing exceptional but does the job, some effects are pretty good and are well suited with the retro theme.

Let me get this straight: you will die on this game. A LOT.
Now that's clear, let's go into the game.
You're an astronaut transported through a portal to an alien planet, with a strange landscape, and filled with strange critters that are aggresive, dangerous, poisonous, and overall, deadly. So, basically, Australia.
Now, you need to find another portal back to earth. Sounds easy? Think again
On one hand, lower gravity allows you to jump really high to try to escape the local fauna. On the other, a toxic atmosphere means that you'll need to catch the oxigen orbs spread through the different levels in other to progress, lest you want to find your demise in a slow, agonic breathless dead (instead of the usual "killed by a giant mutant grasshopper from hell" one). Aside from jumping, you'll be able to crouch to try to avoid you impending doom, and that's basically it. Don't expect no weapons, nor powerups. You're on your own here, mate.
Upon finding your first enemy (A cute, harmless looking (don't be fooled) caterpillar), you'll learn two things: first, you can't stomp on your enemies mario style, and two, avoiding your foes is going to be hard. REALLY HARD.
And here's the gist of the game's design. Like the computer games of old, gameplay is divided in screen based levels, in which you'll need to rely on pixel perfect jumps, excellent timing, and lots of repetition in order to progress. To the point that it becomes almost like a puzzle platformer by itself.
This will be the polarizing point of the game. Let me tell you, POTVC is not a game for everyone. It's a game for oldschool enthusiasts, looking for a challenge with a classic flavour. You'll need patience for this one, or you may end with a broken keyboard.
Knowing this, the game comes with a practice mode, that will let us try the different levels in order to learn the pattern of each screen safely, without losing any of our precious lives.
Visually, the game is a gorgeous tribute to those old games, showing us some really pretty designs, along with a vibrant palette.
Sound is pretty neat too, with the usual bleeps and blops of days past, and the music really helps us get into the game, inspired by the old scifi movies, and adding an undertone of loneliness underneath it all, not unlike the original metroid.
Technically wise, the game is rock solid, and the controls responsive. If you die during a jump, (and you will) you'll know it as an error on your side, and never the case of a lousy implementation.
TL DR;
Nice old school game, evoking the classics, and with insane difficulty. Go for it if you want a real challenge, or avoid if you're not up for it.
Also, beware of those pesky grasshopers, Damn them!

“Hi friends, you have to check out this game. It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years!”
It is quite rare that a game leaves me instantly wanting to come here to leave a review, however I believe the word needs to spread about this title and more people should be encouraged to play it. The whole aesthetic design of the game from the very first time you load the game right through to the conclusion of it's, for lack of a better term, "story" is incredibly immersive. The game plays around with the concepts of self control in a way that is, to me at least, deeply satisfying.
At the time of writing this review (approx 2.5hrs of game time) I have literally just completed the initial story mode, that should give you some idea of how long the main story arc takes to complete, However once the main story is completed you progress to unlock a plethora of challenges and an endless mode to keep you coming back for more.
The core concept of the game is a first person shooter where time does not move unless you do, so moving the mouse to look around will move time forward as does taking steps and obviously engaging in combat, this mechanic is incredibly fun to explore allowing the player to set up intricate combat sequences where every movement is carefully planned to allow not only for survival against the enemy but also to create incredibly cinematic moments of finely constructed chaos.
Once a level is cleared, the game then shows you a real time replay of exactly what you did to survive. The difference between the often careful and thought out steps you took during the level, where you end up moving in small motions to make sure you don't accidentally get clipped by a stray bullet, and the end replay which always makes what you did seem frantic, is another great aspect of the game, there is also an editor which allows you to view the replay and take control of it, the replays are then going to be able to be uploaded to the aptly named "Killstagram" (This feature, the uploading of replays, currently does not work at this time however.)
SUPERHOT has a crisp, clean art style that helps draw the player into the world it tries to create. Stark lines and a lack of a colour gives it a clinical feel that I feel really helps enhance the feeling of unease as you slowly start to realise exactly what is going on around you.
If you are just looking to buy another fps shooter to add to your collection then this might not be what you are looking for, if you are looking for a new totally immersive experience with combat and puzzle elements wrapped in an insidious bow of doubt that plays on the concept of control... Well I think you will be pleasantly surprised by this gem.

Glow:
~~~~

As humans, we have no idea what it means to be part of the Lampyridae (firefly) family, and even less of the challenges they have to face day in and day out. All we know is that they glow at night.  This is going to be an eye-opener and it is going to glow!
Glow is an action/third insect shooter game where you take control of a firefly whose goal is to eliminate a specific number of spiders and slugs per level and reach the next stage.
Before you start a level, you will know what type of enemy and how many of them you will have to destroy to clear this particular stage. For the first couple of levels, your firefly will only be able to rely on the light and heavy attacks (first grade) setup. As you clear levels, you will be given upgrades for these as well as other additional perks such as minion wingmen, proximity mines and others.
As you clear levels, the difficulty will increase as your enemies (arachnids & molluscs) will spawn at very short intervals and in greater numbers.
The great news is you can customize your firefly weapons before each level; find the right combination and you will fly through that level! Otherwise, you will have to try it again.
In regards to the gameplay, Glow is fast and fun. Depending how you setup your firefly (perks and upgrades) you might clear a level fairly quickly or start it over and over.
Graphically, the game looks very good. In terms of controls you can use your mouse and keyboard or gamepad. For me, the mouse and keyboard is the way to go.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Good graphics
-	Fast and fun gameplay
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Repetitive
-	Needs more foe
Glow is a fast, fun third-insect shooter for all ages.
7/10

Fun, enjoyable game. Without story or objective other than surviving, you don't ever feel lost. After the update where they added two new maps, you can wonder around forever. The esthetic of the game makes it look and feel great. I would recommend it to anyone.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Glow is a 3D shoot-em-up featuring a firefly as the protagonist.
The game is all about the action; there's no story to speak of, although the in-game text includes some tongue-in-cheek scientific firefly lore. You play a firefly with access to a deadly arsenal of glow-based weaponry, intent on dealing death to thousands of spiders ... and a few slugs.
Graphics - Glow's graphics are somewhat mixed. The firefly and enemy models are relatively simple, with the firefly and its reinforcements seeming particularly lacklustre, but the terrain and level graphics are very pretty, and the lighting and special effects are excellent.
The game moves very quickly, so you only really have time to admire the graphics when watching someone else play, or on the levels when you have to spend a bit of time mopping up stragglers at the end.
There's a small collection of graphics options, including the normal resolution and windowed/full screen, as well as vsync, and various detail options. I experienced no slowdown in 1920x1080 with max settings on a new gaming laptop with a GTX 1070 video card.
Sound - Sound effects are acceptable, but nothing too remarkable. Music is forgettable and even occasionally annoying. I'm not sure if it's only one track or a handful of them that all sound very similar, but after the first quarter of an hour I turned off the sound and didn't miss it at all.
Gameplay - Glow is a fast third-person 3D shooter played from above and behind the firefly, which is the game's protagonist. The core gameplay involves moving around a relatively small outdoor level, blasting spiders and slugs with three different types of weapons at once, and collecting powerups to try to stay alive.
I played for about two-and-a-half hours and unlocked 11 of 19 achievements, and only saw three levels -- meadow, mountain path, and canyon -- and a handful of different enemy types: maybe five types of spiders and a single type of slug. There may be more arenas and enemy types down the track, but unfortunately this lack of variation makes Glow get repetitive fairly quickly. After not discovering any more enemy types or arenas in my last hour of play, I assume I've seen all of them.
Where Glow excels, though, other than the excellent weapon graphics, is in the number of weapons available. For any encounter you can equip your firefly with a light weapon, a heavy weapon, an ordnance (think 'bomb'), and a passive ability. You begin the game with only a single light weapon, but as you play you quickly unlock more of each type, and I found myself wanting to keep playing through another couple of levels just to see what the next unlock would bring. I can only assume that's the developers' intent.
The game includes 'partial controller support', according to the Steam page, but I only used mouse and keyboard: WASD to move, with mouse to control the crosshairs and shoot the various weapons. Unfortunately there's no controller customisation, and mouse sensitivity is set quite low.
Glow lacks some polish in some areas, too. For example, there's poor grammar and other mistakes in the in-game text, no control customisation, occasional crashes to desktop, no map or indication of where enemies are (leaving you hunting around at the end of some levels for that one lonely spider), no sound on the title screen, a sad smiley when the firefly dies, and the user interface in the menus feels a bit underdeveloped. But it all basically works, and the graphics really do look great in the heat of the action.
Pros:
+ Excellent dynamic lighting and weapon effects
+ It's a nice idea for a shooter
Cons:
- Very repetitive: levels, enemies, gameplay, music
- Lacks polish
If Glow cost any more than its current retail price, I wouldn't recommend it. It's a great demo, but there's not enough here to warrant paying more than a few dollars. Levels and enemy types are limited, and the game really has only one gimmick going for it: a lot of weapons to unlock with mostly very pretty special effects.
But it's fun for a few hours, in spite of its faults.

Steam is telling me I've played 426.8 hrs of this game at the time of this review. As you might have guessed, I am very fond of the game. I've held off on writing a review because I just don't think I can do the game justice, but I'll try.
So what do I love about the game to warrant such an embarrassing amount of hours in the game? I'll try to explain:
. They are beautiful and with the recent upgrade to Unity 5, the graphics became absolutely gorgeous. The beautiful snow-frosted branches of the trees swaying in the breeze; the stark mountains against a beautiful sometimes stormy, sometimes cloudy, and sometimes sunny skyline; The beautiful, but scary nighttime with the aurora borealis, moon, and stars smattering the sky; the bright green, glowing eyes of the wolves...er wait...more scary than beautiful those critters are. :)
. The voice actors are Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale at the time of this review. Veterans of the industry, with titles such as Mass Effect under their belts. The beautiful stinger music that signals a change in weather or time of day. The haunting, creepy music when you discover a corpse inside a house sometimes. The music is not overdone, perfectly placed, so you don't lose that feeling of abandonment. The sound effects, the creaking and groaning of the trees, the wind, footsteps crunching in the snow, the lonely hoot of an owl, the ringing in your ears when you shoot the rifle indoors, the skin-crawling sighing and muttering when in the "creepier" locations, the snarling, howling, and barking of the wolves. The sounds and music in the game are one of my most favorite aspects of the game and it's hard to list them all or describe the feelings of immersion you experience. You must experience them first-hand to truly "get it".
. You have to be careful, you have to be smart, you have to be patient or you die. I love this, it's the player in full control, how long you survive is based on the decisions you make. Plan ahead, learn from past mistakes. Unlike most video games I don't mind dying in this game. I don't feel cheated because I learn what NOT to do or how I can do it better. The saying "you make your own destiny" seems applicable to the gameplay. It's a sandbox, there's no linear path you are forced to follow, you can immerse yourself fully and explore to your heart's content. There are three modes of play: easy, medium, difficult. A fit for everyone- from peaceful exploration to death around every corner.
. The developers have always been very involved in the community on Steam and also on their own Hinterland forum and Reddit. They are AAA title veterans who know what they are doing. The updates to the game are frequent and fun. Hotfixes practically same day. They have a zero tolerance for bugs in their game and it shows in this quality product. It's hard to believe it's an Early Access title. I haven't found a more polished one.
The best part? It's like a free gift everytime there is an update. More fun stuff to check out for free! Another "best part"...the sandbox will remain available even when story mode is released for the people who enjoy it. I'm looking forward to the story mode, but I adore the sandbox survival.
TL/DR: Get this beautiful, quality game. It's Early Access with a twist - it feels like a complete game already!

I wrote my original review (included below) for The Long Dark based on only a couple weeks of play, and so I felt it was a good idea to come back and update this review now that I've spent over 85 hours with this game.
In that time, the developers successfully upgraded the engine from Unity 4 to Unity 5 over the course of a few weeks, bringing added multi-core cpu and gpu support and increasing overall performance, therefore increasing the range of computers that can support this game.  In my case, I have been playing exclusively on a custom-built rig with the following specifications:
▪ AMD K10-8750K ~3.7GHz 4-core + R7 APU
▪ Gigabyte GA-F2A88XM-D3H microATX motherboard
▪ Corsair 16GB DDR3-2400 RAM
▪ Crucial MX100 512GB SSD (Windows 7 installed)
▪ Crucial MX100 256GB SSD (Linux installed - at this time The Long Dark is not natively supported in this OS)
▪ AOC E2727SHE 27" LCD monitor w/ 1920x1080 resolution
With the above system I have been able to play The Long Dark using the Ultra graphics setting, and all effects enabled, without any significant performance issues aside from occasional, slight stuttering in certain interior environments that are using special lighting effects.  I also stream the game from this computer via Steam on my late 2006 MacBook Pro over my local network (whenever I don't feel like playing in my office) with no significant performance issues.
The first thing that you should bear in mind is that this game gets continuous attention and responsive updates from the development team.  I am confident that Hinterland Games is committed to completing this game and feel that my money was well spent, enough so that I purchased a separate copy for my oldest daughter when she expressed interest in playing.  A big plus is the rapid release of bug fixes following each new release, and special effort is repeatedly made to assist those who have lost their loot in the process of upgrading to the latest version.
The Long Dark is very immersive, enough so that I have felt it in my fingers, hands, wrists and arms when the main character sprains an ankle.  This is primarily due to the spectacular voice acting.  Some people may be a little put off by the stylized graphics, but I do not find that they detract from immersion in any significant way.
After being punished by my first few tries playing the game in Voyageur mode, I switched to Pilgrim in order to explore the maps and get a feel for how the game should be played.  Upon exploring the majority of the maps (and the new connecting area released since my initial review), I decided that I was no longer being challenged by the game and returned to Voyageur mode, which has since been a constant learning experience.  My longest run so far has been in Voyageur with 41 days completed at the time of this writing.
This is a survival game, and as such it approaches survival in a way that (in most cases) makes sense.  Some notable exceptions are the ability to carry a mug of coffee in your backpack without spilling it, the ability to craft a bow and arrows but the inability to fashion a basic spear, and the amount of food that must be consumed each day in order to survive might seem excessive.  These exceptions do not detract from my experience, however, and do not necessarily reflect the final version of the game when it is released.
That said, the player is rewarded by finding, repairing and crafting better gear, tools and shelter, all of which dramatically raise his or her chances of survival.  That said, it is still quite possible to make a bad decision that leads to your demise, and therefore every decision should be made with care.
The sense of danger that remains prevalent in Voyageur has been more than enough to keep me interested, and even though only Sandbox mode is currently available, the little stories that are created in day to day play are cool enough to share with others later.
For example, I discovered that wearing a wolf coat may surprise and frighten off a wolf, but it will come back to attack you when you are not expecting it.  After learning this the hard way (and surviving the event), I unexpectedly came upon another wolf who was frightened off by my sudden appearance.  This time I found a safe place to wait for the wolf to return, and after it failed to reach me, I successfully dispatched it with my rifle.  As I was building a fire in preparation to harvest the wolf's meat and fur, I was surprised by the arrival of a black bear.  I ran back to my safe place and shot it twice, the second time directly between the eyes.  Now I had more than enough food to last me for several days, and also the opportunity to harvest the necessary materials to make a bearskin bedroll, but I had to act quickly before the body began to decompose.
If you are at all interested in survival simulations, I cannot recommend The Long Dark strongly enough.

I am a long time player of Blood Bowl, starting with the 2nd edition of the tabletop game, through to the nineties MS-DOS computer game, to not-Blood-Bowl-honest Chaos League and finally Blood Bowl 1/Legendary/Chaos. The thing I loved about Blood Bowl 1 was the single player options, from creating a custom league, to participating in a classic competition from Blood Bowl canon, and of course even playing a proper full career, clawing your way up the rankings over the years, up against all the famous classic teams of Blood Bowl lore, winning cups and trophies along the way until eventually, hopefully, winnng the Blood Bowl trophy itself.
Now comes Blood Bowl 2; the graphics are prettier, but graphics aren't everything. The part that matters to me, the gameplay, the thing I loved in Blood Bowl 1 is... gone. The single player campaign is a shadow of what it was before. You can create a custom league, but there are no proper tournaments from Blood Bowl canon, and certainly no proper career. You play a few games in a single tournament, and then you are done. And the classic teams don't even appear in these leagues anymore. The whole thing is clearly obsessed with multiplayer, to the point that even in single player games the game still looks, feels and plays just like the multiplayer version, with randomised AI team creations clearly trying to pass themselves off as player teams. But it doesn't work. To take examples, the Broad Axes team might have the emblem of a Bugman's tankard, while Bugman's Faithful might have the emblem of an axe. Eh? It's randomisation gone mad. It makes no sense. And as I said,  there are no Reikland Reivers or Gouged Eye or Chaos All Stars. Unless you play the introductory "tutorial", or single one off matches without continuity, you will never see the classic teams of Blood Bowl lore at all. That's just not good enough. For me, without the ability to play a league or proper career with your own team against the classic sides of history, the appeal just isn't there.
And there are other disappointments. You can't improve/modify a player's armour any more. Many of the other options of old just aren't available. The font is -  to my eyes - some horrible thin eyesore - and the UI just ugly, literally not pleasing on the eyes. Meanwhile the commentators Jim and Bob now insist on actually appearing, but just get in the way. In short, while this game might be a multiplayer's paradise, it doesn't work for me. Maybe Blood Bowl 1 spoiled me, but to my mind Blood Bowl 2 is several steps backwards.
Now this might sound like I'm some kind of hater. But I am a fan of Blood Bowl and for the sake of the franchise I sincerely hope that people out there are enjoying this, and I wish the game very well. I do want this to succeed. But the single player aspect desperately needs work. The single player game is an opportunity to offer players content that multiplayer content cannot provide - such as a proper career.  But it simply doesn't. For me personally, Blood Bowl 2 is a big disappointment, and until the single player game is improved I will be sticking with Blood Bowl 1, because unfortunately, for solo play, Blood Bowl 1 remains far superior.

The ports were slated for release in April 2010.[9] Valve employed Hidden Path Entertainment to provide support on updating Counter-Strike: Source. On May 7, 2010, Valve released an update that includes new features and functionality developed in collaboration with Hidden Path Entertainment. These include 144 (now 146) new achievements, a new domination and revenge system, similar to that of Team Fortress 2, player stats, an upgrade to the Source engine and more. On June 23, 2010, Valve released the beta to the public alongside the promised OS X version.[1] On February 5, 2013, Valve released a port of Counter-Strike: Source for Linux.[10][11]

Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike conducted by the Imperial Japanese Navy against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on the morning of December 7, 1941 (December 8 in Japan). The attack led to the United States' entry into World War II.
The attack was intended as a preventive action in order to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions the Empire of Japan was planning in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. There were simultaneous Japanese attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong. The attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan. Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been strong, disappeared. Clandestine support of Britain (e.g., the Neutrality Patrol) was replaced by active alliance. Subsequent operations by the U.S. prompted Germany and Italy to declare war on the U.S. on December 11, which was reciprocated by the U.S. the same day.
Years later several writers alleged that parties high in the U.S. and British governments knew of the attack in advance and may have let it happen (or even encouraged it) with the aim of bringing America into war. However, this advance-knowledge conspiracy theory is rejected by mainstream historians.
There were numerous historical precedents for unannounced military action by Japan. However, the lack of any formal warning, particularly while negotiations were still apparently ongoing, led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to proclaim December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy". Because the attack happened without a declaration of war and without explicit warning, the attack on Pearl Harbor was judged by the Tokyo Trials to be a war crime.
Bombing of Pearl Harbor
Sixteen U.S. Army Air Forces B-25B Mitchell medium bombers were launched without fighter escort from the U.S. Navy's aircraft carrier USS Hornet deep in the Western Pacific Ocean, each with a crew of five men. The plan called for them to bomb military targets in Japan, and to continue westward to land in China—landing a medium bomber on Hornet was impossible. Fifteen of the aircraft reached China, and the other one landed in the Soviet Union. All but three of the crew survived, but all the aircraft were lost. Eight crewmen were captured by the Japanese Army in China; three of these were executed. The B-25 that landed in the Soviet Union at Vladivostok was confiscated and its crew interned for more than a year. Fourteen crews, except for one crewman, returned either to the United States or to American forces.
After the raid, the Japanese Imperial Army conducted a massive sweep through the eastern coastal provinces of China, in an operation now known as the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign, searching for the surviving American airmen and applying retribution on the Chinese who aided them, in an effort to prevent this part of China from being used again for an attack on Japan. An estimated 250,000 Chinese civilians were killed by the Japanese during this operation.
The raid caused negligible material damage to Japan, but it succeeded in its goal of raising American morale and casting doubt in Japan on the ability of its military leaders to defend their home islands. It also caused Japan to withdraw its powerful aircraft carrier force from the Indian Ocean to defend their Home Islands, and the raid contributed to Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's decision to attack Midway Island in the Central Pacific—an attack that turned into a decisive strategic defeat of the Imperial Japanese Navy (IJN) by the U.S. Navy in the Battle of Midway. Doolittle, who initially believed that loss of all his aircraft would lead to his being court-martialled, received the Medal of Honor and was promoted two steps to Brigadier General.
Doolittle's Raid
The invasion of the Philippines started on December 8, 1941, ten hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor. As at Pearl Harbor, American aircraft were severely damaged in the initial Japanese attack. Lacking air cover, the American Asiatic Fleet in the Philippines withdrew to Java on December 12, 1941. General Douglas MacArthur escaped Corregidor on the night of March 11, 1942 for Australia, 4,000 km away. The 76,000 starving and sick American and Filipino defenders on Bataan surrendered on April 9, 1942, and were forced to endure the infamous Bataan Death March on which 7,000–10,000 died or were murdered. The 13,000 survivors on Corregidor surrendered on May 6.
Japan occupied the Philippines for over three years, until the surrender of Japan. A highly effective guerilla campaign by Philippine resistance forces controlled sixty percent of the islands, mostly jungle and mountain areas. MacArthur supplied them by submarine, and sent reinforcements and officers. Filipinos remained loyal to the United States, partly because of the American guarantee of independence, and also because the Japanese had pressed large numbers of Filipinos into work details and even put young Filipino women into brothels.
General MacArthur kept his promise to return to the Philippines on October 20, 1944. The landings on the island of Leyte were accomplished by a force of 700 vessels and 174,000 men. Through December 1944, the islands of Leyte and Mindoro were cleared of Japanese soldiers. During the campaign, the Imperial Japanese Army conducted a suicidal defense of the islands. Cities such as Manila were reduced to rubble. Between 500,000 and 1,000,000 Filipinos died during the occupation.
Japanese occupation of the Philippines
Began on April 9, 1942, was the forcible transfer by the Imperial Japanese Army of 60,000–80,000 Filipino and American prisoners of war after the three-month Battle of Bataan in the Philippines during World War II. All told, approximately 2,500–10,000 Filipino and 100–650 American prisoners of war died before they could reach their destination at Camp O'Donnell. The reported death tolls vary, especially amongst Filipino POWs, because historians cannot determine how many prisoners blended in with the civilian population and escaped. The march went from Mariveles, Bataan, to San Fernando, Pampanga. From San Fernando, survivors were loaded to a box train and were brought to Camp O'Donnell in Capas, Tarlac.
The 60 mi (97 km) march was characterized by occasional severe physical abuse and resulted in some fatalities inflicted upon prisoners and civilians alike by the Japanese Army. It was later judged by an Allied military commission to be a Japanese war crime.
Bataan Death March
Japanese Occupation of China
The war was the result of a decades-long Japanese imperialist policy aiming to dominate China politically and militarily and to secure its vast raw material reserves and other economic resources, particularly food and labour. Before 1937, China and Japan fought in small, localized engagements, so-called "incidents". In 1931, the Japanese invasion of Manchuria by Japan's Kwantung Army followed the Mukden Incident. The last of these incidents was the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 1937, marking the beginning of total war between the two countries.
Initially the Japanese scored major victories in Shanghai after heavy fighting, and by the end of 1937 captured the Chinese capital of Nanking. After failing to stop the Japanese in Wuhan, the Chinese central government was relocated to Chongqing in the Chinese interior. By 1939 the war had reached stalemate after Chinese victories in Changsha and Guangxi. The Japanese were also unable to defeat the Chinese communist forces in Shaanxi, which performed harassment and sabotage operations against the Japanese using guerrilla warfare tactics. TL;DR :  Greatest game I've played in a while.  Most likely to be my game of the year, maybe even the decade.
A Hat in Time is a 3D platformer which draws inspiration from games like Super Mario Sunshine and the early Paper Mario titles.  It takes some noticable things from those games like the writing style and the slide move and also adds some things of its own, like the ability to climb up a wall for a short period before sliding down.  As the title would suggest, the game also sports six different hats with their own abilities to help you get around the levels.  On top of the hats, you can also have up to three different badges equipped at once, which all have either a passive or active effect, and are applied no matter what hat youre using.  The game controls are a bit floatier compared to Sunshine, but are ultimately alot smoother in the long run.  The game's level design is great, and offers a fair challenge in every stage.  The soundtrack for the game is very memorable, as each level will have its own tracks unique to it, instead of one theme for a world.  The game isnt that long if you're just trying to beat it (it took me roughly nine hours), but the experience is very enjoyable and memorable, which makes up for its short length.  I give A Hat in Time a 10/10, and I would highly reccomend it to anybody looking for a game that they will remember as fondly as their childhood games.

TLDR : Sacred 3 doesn't support any of the typical mechanics of the hack'n slash genre. The experience is closer to a very generic bland and mindless beat'em all. Disappointing, 3/10
In spite of all the rather poor "preview" articles, I persisted in thinking Sacred 3 couldn't be *that* bad and decided to purchase the game (pre-order, mind you...). After all, a hack'n slash IS a hack'n slash, right ? Well... not quite :/
The game does present itself as an "arcade hack'n slash", but it is actually only a brainless beat'em all.
Fantasy action games can take a wide range of shapes and forms, but let's be clear... What do people enjoy in h&s games ? Ignoring all the details, in the most abstract form it fits in 4 major points :
- Finding items, to improve their strength ; an endless gear treadmill to become more and more powerful
- Optimising their character, by leveling up, equipping armor pieces, favouring offense/defense stats choices, etc.
- Defining their experience through gameplay choices (skill tree or similar, inventory, stats, etc. or any combination of the above)
- Combat ! Well, that's the core of the action, so... It should be "fun", aka "challenging & rewarding"
Sacred 3 does not support any of these gameplay elements. The game has as much depth as Golden Axe. This is like Dungeon Hunter 4 on PC, without the (few) fun bits.
Enter a small area ; defeat a bunch of enemies (read "spam LMB", pro-tip use skills 1-2 to kill things faster) ; collect meaningless orbs ; move onto next area ; rinse & repeat. After a few times, BOSS ! Yeaah, exciti... ah, no. My bad. You can spam LMB, but can you dodge AND spam ? Oh, you can ? I guess you're too good for this game, well done, you cleared a mission ! How interesti...zzzZZZZZ...
Seriously, how can a game decently call itself a h&s without having a loot system !
I am not very far into the game myself (and probably never will be...) but I understand the base campaign can be completed in less than 10 hours on the first playthrough. The game does seem a bit overpriced for that kind of duration.
Bottomline, avoid this piece of s...oftware !
