As a previous fan of both Ascaron Entertainment's first and second Sacred game, I have to say, this game makes me very sad to experience. I was well aware of the community's warnings and disapproval, but I still got it for the sake of clarity and some itch to keep supporting a previously good developer. Even though it isn't even Ascaron Entertainment that is behind it, I still felt they wouldn't let a game reputation like Sacred slip so easily into wrong hands. (Which... It seems they might actually have..)
First and foremost, the story...
The first game was brilliant where magic was just magic, where you had to gather elements to defeat a loose Sakkara demon. As fantasy-RPG as it gets.
The second game then tried to explain how everything magical was actually run by T-energy, which had started pouring into the world and corrupt it. For the sake of the story, I won't spoil more than that, but it had enough going to keep you going to see what was behind it all.
But now with the third game, I don't see any of the T-energy or any enticing lore that keeps you wanting to progress through the story. On top of that, they made it entirely linear, even less open-worlded than Diablo.
Gameplay...
First and second game was a lovely free-roaming RPG with vast maps and plenty of quests to do along the main one. It was also hack-n-slash and focused on classic gear gathering and skill-progressing. And the combo system in the first game was brilliant, to say the least.
Sacred 3 has lost all of this, except the hack-n-slash. No excitement for finding legendary gear and enhance it, no stunning combos which they otherwise boasted about a whole lot, compared to previous games AND went to feel like a side-scroller instead of open-worlded.
Pros and Cons about the game...
To try not comparing it with the previous games, since it's obviously not; looking at it as the ARPG, hack-n-slash it tries to be, I have to admit it's still fun and challenging and accomplishes what it tries to do. I can imagine it works perfectly fine on console and I find myself compelled to continue playing just to see how powerful I am capable of becoming, but I can already imagine that it turns into a boring grind when you start up new characters after first run through. Controls feels weird when using keyboard/mouse though, so I'd recommend a controller.
So, pro is that they managed to make a decent isometric brawler, but lacks a lot compared to other brawlers.
The cons is that they went WAAAY off their usual way, making one question if they just made it to try expanding into the console and DLC world for the sake of money.
Finally, my recommendation...
If you are a fan of the previous Sacred games, don't buy this. You'll be severely disappointed and likely come to hate yourself for buying it.
If you like side-scrolling, hack-n-slash, brawlers with beautiful graphics and fairly challenging combat (If you play on the hardest difficulty) and don't mind that the price is fairly high due to the title's previous reputation. I would still not recommend it, compared to other brawlers or hack-n-slash. Bastion, Transistor and Diablo does a far better job.
Like many good games, you play this one more for its in story and dialogue than its generic yet solid gameplay mechanics.

Although still in early release, this game is shaping up to be fantastic.  If you've ever played Fallen London (and I highly recommend you do)  you'll recognise elements of that in the style here, since it's the same world.  There's a touch of Gaiman, there's a touch of Lovecraft, there's a big helping of Failbetter Games' own style, and it's marvellous.  The heart of this game is in the world and in the stories.   Plus, who doesn't want to sail a tramp steamer across a vast underground ocean full of nameless terrors? :D
Sunless Sea doesn't go easy on you, you really have to work to make progress, but this fits with the world, and once you've found your feet it does start to get...well, not easier, but you become hardier :p  You learn to follow your chart, and stay in the light where you can, you learn to keep your crew from going mad with terror, sometimes.  Risks can be worth taking, but the cost of failure is always high.
You will die.  A lot.  Every voyage into the deep dark Zee is fraught with peril.  But venture forth into the unknown, for science!  For riches!  ...to escape that giant eel that's chasing your ship!  The Underzee is full of secrets that wait to be discovered.
This is a gorgeous and atmospheric game.  The music is haunting, the visuals stunning, and it will only improve as further patches are released and more polish is added.  I definitely recommend getting in now, and becoming part of the development process.  The devs take an active involvement in the forums, and pay close attention to feedback, which is helping to shape things like combat balance and terror management.  (Check out the forums anyway, they're a great place to find some help and read other folks' feedback, everyone is friendly, and fresh sacri- er, newcomers, are always welcome.)
Also it's just a bunch of fun :D

Steam is telling me I've played 426.8 hrs of this game at the time of this review. As you might have guessed, I am very fond of the game. I've held off on writing a review because I just don't think I can do the game justice, but I'll try.
So what do I love about the game to warrant such an embarrassing amount of hours in the game? I'll try to explain:
. They are beautiful and with the recent upgrade to Unity 5, the graphics became absolutely gorgeous. The beautiful snow-frosted branches of the trees swaying in the breeze; the stark mountains against a beautiful sometimes stormy, sometimes cloudy, and sometimes sunny skyline; The beautiful, but scary nighttime with the aurora borealis, moon, and stars smattering the sky; the bright green, glowing eyes of the wolves...er wait...more scary than beautiful those critters are. :)
. The voice actors are Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale at the time of this review. Veterans of the industry, with titles such as Mass Effect under their belts. The beautiful stinger music that signals a change in weather or time of day. The haunting, creepy music when you discover a corpse inside a house sometimes. The music is not overdone, perfectly placed, so you don't lose that feeling of abandonment. The sound effects, the creaking and groaning of the trees, the wind, footsteps crunching in the snow, the lonely hoot of an owl, the ringing in your ears when you shoot the rifle indoors, the skin-crawling sighing and muttering when in the "creepier" locations, the snarling, howling, and barking of the wolves. The sounds and music in the game are one of my most favorite aspects of the game and it's hard to list them all or describe the feelings of immersion you experience. You must experience them first-hand to truly "get it".
. You have to be careful, you have to be smart, you have to be patient or you die. I love this, it's the player in full control, how long you survive is based on the decisions you make. Plan ahead, learn from past mistakes. Unlike most video games I don't mind dying in this game. I don't feel cheated because I learn what NOT to do or how I can do it better. The saying "you make your own destiny" seems applicable to the gameplay. It's a sandbox, there's no linear path you are forced to follow, you can immerse yourself fully and explore to your heart's content. There are three modes of play: easy, medium, difficult. A fit for everyone- from peaceful exploration to death around every corner.
. The developers have always been very involved in the community on Steam and also on their own Hinterland forum and Reddit. They are AAA title veterans who know what they are doing. The updates to the game are frequent and fun. Hotfixes practically same day. They have a zero tolerance for bugs in their game and it shows in this quality product. It's hard to believe it's an Early Access title. I haven't found a more polished one.
The best part? It's like a free gift everytime there is an update. More fun stuff to check out for free! Another "best part"...the sandbox will remain available even when story mode is released for the people who enjoy it. I'm looking forward to the story mode, but I adore the sandbox survival.
TL/DR: Get this beautiful, quality game. It's Early Access with a twist - it feels like a complete game already!
I hope this review helps someone. If not, drop by the forums, you'll find a wonderful and helpful community.

I wrote my original review (included below) for The Long Dark based on only a couple weeks of play, and so I felt it was a good idea to come back and update this review now that I've spent over 85 hours with this game.
In that time, the developers successfully upgraded the engine from Unity 4 to Unity 5 over the course of a few weeks, bringing added multi-core cpu and gpu support and increasing overall performance, therefore increasing the range of computers that can support this game.  In my case, I have been playing exclusively on a custom-built rig with the following specifications:
▪ AMD K10-8750K ~3.7GHz 4-core + R7 APU
▪ Gigabyte GA-F2A88XM-D3H microATX motherboard
▪ Corsair 16GB DDR3-2400 RAM
▪ Crucial MX100 512GB SSD (Windows 7 installed)
▪ Crucial MX100 256GB SSD (Linux installed - at this time The Long Dark is not natively supported in this OS)
▪ AOC E2727SHE 27" LCD monitor w/ 1920x1080 resolution
With the above system I have been able to play The Long Dark using the Ultra graphics setting, and all effects enabled, without any significant performance issues aside from occasional, slight stuttering in certain interior environments that are using special lighting effects.  I also stream the game from this computer via Steam on my late 2006 MacBook Pro over my local network (whenever I don't feel like playing in my office) with no significant performance issues.
The first thing that you should bear in mind is that this game gets continuous attention and responsive updates from the development team.  I am confident that Hinterland Games is committed to completing this game and feel that my money was well spent, enough so that I purchased a separate copy for my oldest daughter when she expressed interest in playing.  A big plus is the rapid release of bug fixes following each new release, and special effort is repeatedly made to assist those who have lost their loot in the process of upgrading to the latest version.
The Long Dark is very immersive, enough so that I have felt it in my fingers, hands, wrists and arms when the main character sprains an ankle.  This is primarily due to the spectacular voice acting.  Some people may be a little put off by the stylized graphics, but I do not find that they detract from immersion in any significant way.
After being punished by my first few tries playing the game in Voyageur mode, I switched to Pilgrim in order to explore the maps and get a feel for how the game should be played.  Upon exploring the majority of the maps (and the new connecting area released since my initial review), I decided that I was no longer being challenged by the game and returned to Voyageur mode, which has since been a constant learning experience.  My longest run so far has been in Voyageur with 41 days completed at the time of this writing.
This is a survival game, and as such it approaches survival in a way that (in most cases) makes sense.  Some notable exceptions are the ability to carry a mug of coffee in your backpack without spilling it, the ability to craft a bow and arrows but the inability to fashion a basic spear, and the amount of food that must be consumed each day in order to survive might seem excessive.  These exceptions do not detract from my experience, however, and do not necessarily reflect the final version of the game when it is released.
That said, the player is rewarded by finding, repairing and crafting better gear, tools and shelter, all of which dramatically raise his or her chances of survival.  That said, it is still quite possible to make a bad decision that leads to your demise, and therefore every decision should be made with care.
The sense of danger that remains prevalent in Voyageur has been more than enough to keep me interested, and even though only Sandbox mode is currently available, the little stories that are created in day to day play are cool enough to share with others later.
For example, I discovered that wearing a wolf coat may surprise and frighten off a wolf, but it will come back to attack you when you are not expecting it.  After learning this the hard way (and surviving the event), I unexpectedly came upon another wolf who was frightened off by my sudden appearance.  This time I found a safe place to wait for the wolf to return, and after it failed to reach me, I successfully dispatched it with my rifle.  As I was building a fire in preparation to harvest the wolf's meat and fur, I was surprised by the arrival of a black bear.  I ran back to my safe place and shot it twice, the second time directly between the eyes.  Now I had more than enough food to last me for several days, and also the opportunity to harvest the necessary materials to make a bearskin bedroll, but I had to act quickly before the body began to decompose.
If you are at all interested in survival simulations, I cannot recommend The Long Dark strongly enough.

Playing this game was a strange yet provocative experience, one that definitely lingered for a while after it was over. As its narrative unfolded, I felt as if I were moving through a contradition. While it felt intimate and personal, it also seemed cold and distant, as if it wanted me to understand yet resisted interpretation. Does such a work allow us to glimpse into the mind of its creator? Or does it lack meaning altogether? I'm not sure there is an answer. But I'd like to think it lies somewhere in the nether between these two extremes, in a post-modern place where the author may be dead but where the work can still mean something, even if this meaning is just that born out of the relationship between the game and its players.

Welcome to the game of rolling dice, a simulator where it doesn't matter who you picked or what you do, because every decision you make comes down to whether you can roll 1d6. I played 12 games of this 'game' and let me give you a rundown of how each turn plays out. You get to move your players into positions to give them strategic advantages then fight the other team to knock them down. The most common 'advantageous' roll you'll get is 2d6 to pick one depending on what you want.
So you roll 2d6.
Double skulls. Skulls knock down your player, not theirs.
So you use one of your "team rerolls" to change the outcome.
Double skulls. Your player falls over and your turn ends instantly.
You haven't moved anyone, or done anything. Your turn is done. The other guy then takes his turn, knocking down every single one of your team regardless of the odds. Heck, he can roll 2 dice disadvantaged and he'll 100% of the time score adouble knockdown that you can't avoid. Half of your team will be injured or KO'd in the first round and unable to play for the rest of the game which is IMPORTANT, as he now outnumbers you 11 to 5.
Now it's your turn again. Somehow get 2d6 to roll.
Roll double skulls.
Use a reroll?
Double skulls.
You're saying to yourself at this point "wow, this guys just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting. What a moron this never happens to me". I played 12 games and this happened at least once in EVERY SINGLE GAME. Did it happen to my opponents? NO. If they tried to make plays where they needed to dodge twice, each time at 17%, would they make it? 100% of the time, yes. Not a single person I played against lost more than 2 rolls in the entire match. By the time it got to game 10, I was so sick of this rng nightmare that I was conceding on the third turn after most of my team were dead or had broken legs and missing limbs while his players were at the line with not a single penalty.
I was under the impression that thinking about this game mattered in some way, but trust me, it doesn't, If I could go lower than 1/10 I would for this, but for the sake of it, lets just leave it at 1/10. Without reducing my settings to the lowest possible on quite a high end machine, the game crashed out constantly or took so long to register an action that a quarter of my turn was already wasted by the time people moved. On the first day I played, the servers were so broken it was disconnecting people midway through the match which forced both teams to concede a loss.
This game is -not- playable in its current state and I would not recomend any of you spend even £5 on something you could replicate by buying 3d6 and shoving them down your friends throat while their young children watched. £35 is like asking a poor man for 3 of his limbs to give him a cup of water, not even slightly worth it.
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.

Hi Folks.
To everyone new to the Blood Bowl Franchise: this is not meant to be a Single Player Game.
All about the spirit and the fun comes from fighting other Players, its all about Strategy, Tactic and a bit of Luck some times. ( Its a Dice Game after all)
But first things first - Is BB2 better than BB1?
Kind of, yes. BB2 has a much better look all over the place, the UI is more Userfriendly, the presentation of the stadiums and the teams is awesome, it plays smoother and is just more enjoyable than BB1.
And there are so cool details they added, for example if you purchase a Bloodweiser Stand for your Stadium, the crowd is much more pushed and the sound effects of your fans cheering changes aswell, more singing and Vuvuselas all over the place, nice!
The graphics are great, with cool beating animations and close up cameras if something important happens, really cool and it delivers a nice feeling of being close to the Action.
So the Game itself, the Programming and Graphics are much better than BB1.
The most common reason for negative reviews is the lack of Content it has at the Moment.
And that in fact is true, BB1 has much more Content to deliver, but you need to consider that BB1 already has 2 Addons, and compared to the Base Game the Content is the same.
A few not gamebreaking but important things missing aswell, and hopfully will be added soon.
The Game lacks in case of Informations, for example no Hall of Fame for your Team, no Player Statistics, no information about Opposing Team pre Match, no Visual change of high lvl Players and so on.
In my opinion it seems they just where running out of time to implement all those things before release, and im very confident that they will add that kind of things the next few Months.
Additional Teams will be delivered saperatly as a DLC for 6,99$ each as far is i know, what is a fair price because the teams are really looking awesome.
So for everybody new to Bloodbowl, BB2 is the better choice. Because it has a better UI and a Singleplayer Campaign wich is in fact a large Tutorial.
To the Bloodbowl Veterans out there, you want to buy and play Bloodbowl 2 for the same reasons, you played BB1 instead of Fumble. If you want all the Content the BB Lore will offer and all the Statistics and information Possible, play Fumble, its free after all.
But if you want a nice looking Bloodbowl expirience that entertains you, just give BB2 a Chance.

I'm going to start this review by admitting that I never played the original Blood Bowl. I own it, and I always wanted to like it, but the seeming overcomplexity of the system kept me from ever getting into it.
Blood Bowl 2 was pretty much the perfect game for me. The UI is clean, simple and easy to understand. The games are pegged at a nice length (usually around 40 minutes for me) and the solo league experience provides enough of a challenge for me as a new blood bowl player to be entirely engrossing. There are a large number of teams (currently eight), though hardcore blood bowl fans will probably be disappointed by the selection. More will almost certainly be released as DLC, but at the $45 price point that's frankly to be expected.
TLDR: If you're interested in a turn based strategy game with a fantasy sports twist this is certainly a game for you. If you're on the fence, or if you're a hardcore blood bowl fan you're probably better served waiting for a sale.

Maybe it's because I love the HTTYD franchise, maybe it's because I love having my own dragon to raise, maybe it's because puberty treated Hiccup well. However, I found the game to be colourful and frankly a breath of fresh air.
The graphics are outdated and similar to PS2 graphics, it's glitchy, and I've lost my dragon several times just walking around. However, this game had many more glitches before I started playing it apparently, considering I was able to input my appropriate age and I only crashed once. What we must keep in mind is this game just came out yesterday. Understandably, who would want to put a glitchy, unfinished product on the market? *cough* Ubisoft *cough* But that's the beauty of MMO's, although sometimes glitchy at first, they develop and grow over time with the right support. I think this game has a lot of potential and I'm willing to stick around for it. The cutscenes are nothing to ogle at and they play scenes from the movies for some of the quests I've done so far. Call me blinded by nostalgia, but throwing movie scenes into a computer game takes me back to the old Disney PC games. Of course, it shows laziness on development's part by not creating these cutscenes themselves, but I can still appreciate putting scenes in from the movie.
tl;dr version: I like this game. While it has it's flaws I think it has potential. 10/10 would have toothless follow my cursor in the lab again.

The developers of Zup! are back with another installment of their physics puzzler (appropriately titled Zup! 2), with pretty much everything cranked up another notch: the levels are more elaborate and there are
achievements. The objective is the same as before: get the blue block to the green zone, except now the blue block is round, which opens up more level designs thanks to the extra movement made possible by the new shape.
The amount of achievements (229) is even more absurd, nearly doubling the number in Zup!. As before, this is geared towards achievement hunters and profile decorators as there is a wider variety of symbols, with some Mandarin possible as well if so inclined.
Besides the fundamental change in the shape of the blue block, gameplay is essentially unchanged. Some levels are slightly more challenging, but the game is on par with its predecessor in terms of difficulty, and should take the same amount of time to complete. There is also no replayability as there is little reason to revisit a level after clearing it.
Overall Zup! 2 feels like an extension (or DLC) of Zup!, and like before, a big part of the game is getting the achievements to decorate profiles with. If that is worth something to you, then this game is worth considering. Zup! 3 is also in the works, and I hope something unique will be introduced this time because the novelty is wearing off.

I've enjoyed the horror genre as far back as Clock Tower 1 for SNES and am in all my glory with the ammount of indie horror games that've been flooding out in recent years. This game however, is probably the best there currently is out there as far as being the complete package.
There are jump scares, sure, but they're done well. It's not just about constantly trying to make you crap yourself. They've done an excelent job of making sure you think you're safe before scaring you. The ambiance itself, the detail, subtle sound effects and noises still scare you even when you think everything is fine and dandy.
The plot is somewhat confusing at first, because you're only given bits of information at a time, and in no particular order of importance. From random e-mails between staff at the facility, to madmens notes scribbled on a page. Often when stopping to read something you find gives you a moment of being able to breathe, but by the time you finish reading something that sheds new light on how screwed you are, it only feels worse resuming the game.
Haven't finished the DLC yet, but it's already gone beyond any expectations I could have had. Initially my thoughts were "How could they possibly top what they've already done in the original game" Yeah, they went there. So rather than being sceptical about how they could possibly top it with Outlast 2, instead I'm just excited as hell.

Summary
This game is essentially chess... in outer space... and you cant see the opponent's pieces... and the chess board is an unknown variable.
Long story short, you're some sort of researcher, setting out to try and figure out what happened in a catastrophe, and why. You're given several hypothesis, and your job is to board derelict ships left behind in the catastrophe with automated drones to find evidence to support or disprove each hypothesis. Only problem is, every ship is a massive unknown, and presents hazards, including organic enemies of different forms, hull breaches, spontaneous radiation leaks, and just plain dumb mistakes, all of which can get your cute little drones killed. To avoid such hazards, there is a progression system. Your drones are given a variety of upgrades to suit your play style, including stealth upgrades, support upgrades, and combat upgrades. Your ship can be upgraded as well, allowing you to perform drone tasks remotely. Of course, you must search derelicts to FIND these upgrades. It also requires skill with your environment. Every derelict has doors that must be powered from outlets, and then opened and closed. This gives the player the ability to lure enemies into empty or useless rooms while you get the loot. On top of all this, you, as a researcher, have been dumped here with minimal resources. You must scavenge for your fuel, and scrap metal. Worse still, much like in real life, your equipment falls prey to wear and tear, and you must keep it well maintained.
Progress and upgrade your ship and equipment, survive for as long as possible in the depths of space, prove your cunning plans against foes and obstacles, use strategy on a universal scale, and piece together murder mystery style clues find out what the hell happened to everyone. That's a pretty good combination, one this game pulls of well.
Interface
The UI is perhaps the most beautiful part about this game. It's all done in 1980's style retro computing. No mouse is used, everything is done with keys, and you control everything by typing in commands to a command bar like some sort of programmer. As for visual information, it's basically done in the style of top down false color ultrasound images. Use of this kind of technology is actually quite plausible on drones and robots, as it provides them 3d images, espescially in the darkened interiors of a derelict space ship. It has a unique combination of being high enough resolution to know what's what, and how to get the job done, while also being low enough detail to leave the interior of the derelicts up to the imagination. And rather than simply being the same overused retro pixelated visuals common to indie games, these visuals are the first like it I've ever seen, and they have a logical reason for why it might look like that in real life. If you like not only sci fi, but 1980s style retro sci fi, this is a must have.
Negatives
There are very few that I have. Being an early alpha, obviously there'll be the occasional issue, and it probably has less content now than it will later. For example, I found a glitch where the map had old ships frozen on the screen while I was looking at new ones.
The only REAL complaint I have about an actual decision the devs had on gameplay is an inability to revisit old ships and star systems. This has twice caused me problems in the 2 or 3 hours I've played the game.
For example, I ran out of fuel to continue in one star system, so had no choice but to jump to another. The problem is that you're given new fuel everytime you jump. This leads to an exploitable game mechanic, where in a player could have infinite fuel by jumping constantly. So, I understand  why they dont let you jump back to an old star system. But this essentially left me with 5/8 ships in my last system unexplored. There's a pretty simple solution here, why not just ONLY give new fuel when you jump into a NEW star system?
Another example would be when I accidentally left 2 drone upgrades (including my only tow) on a ship because I switched the wrong direction when swapping with a dead one... AAAAND of course I couldnt reboard right after to pick them up... Now THAT I see no reason for. Only thing I can think of is devs want the player to keep moving forward, probably to really feel the consequences of mistakes, but truth is, im not so sure it's possible to ONLY move forward in a strategy game. Both of these mistakes of mine could've easily been preventable or recoverable in real life had I simply gone back after the fact. But that's just not an option in this game. Anyway, I think this one particular restriction in the game is the ONE thing the devs should probably reconsider.
Recommendations
I'd reccommend this game to anybody who likes strategy games, puzzle games, management games, murder mystery plots, progression systems, science fiction, or retro sci fi technology. Basically, if you like Xcom, you'll like this game. If you're looking for something that's fast paced and exciting, then this game probably isn't for you (though it has its scary moments). This is a game you can sit down, and RELAX, playing for hours, and using your head more than anything else, much like chess.
Gameplay Suggestions to Devs
I see potential for a few cool new features.
1.) Co Op multiplayer.
Each player has their own 1-2 drones (limit to 4 drones means limit to 4 players). Sometimes players can use their own ships at the same time, allowing for multiple ships. Players can work together to solve a puzzle. This game feels well suited towards encouraging teamwork, much like the co-op in portal 2.
2.) Competetive multiplayer
I could also envision competetive multiplayer. There could be a matchmaking system that pits 2-4 players against each other on a massive ship, with 4 drones tops each. Players can either take the run and gun approach, or use stealth to do things like throw enemies out the airlock.
Door control could mainly be done through interface computers, which would make those of strategic importance. Whomever has control of the computer in an area gets control over certain doors.
3.) Finally, I'd like to see logs and clues become more of a focus in the game. Mainly, I'd like to see it be the case that players aren't just GIVEN logs upon docking, but instead, are required to search the ship to track down logs. Or better yet, even physical clues. Things like dead bodies or mysterious devices that can be towed back to the mothership for analysis. You guys could go full on NCIS with the game, and leave it up to the player to track down clues to solve the mystery. I think doing this would also provide a greater motivation to play. The main motivation now is exploration and progression. Throw in the tantalizing clues of the story you're creating, and they simply won't be able to quit. It would turn the players into a criminal investigator, who have to use their own intuition to find and determine the meaning of clues.

It's games like this that remind you what "fun" really means.
A Hat in Time is a kickstarted retro-revival 3D platformer in a similar vein to Yooka-Laylee. However, unlike that game, AHiT actually delivers on what it set out to acheive, and it does this not by riding on the coattails of its inspirations, but learning from them and creating something new and something very special. The most obvious inspiration here is Super Mario Sunshine, and that's most evident through the game's frankly incredible controls. Hat Kid, the protagonist, has a ridiculous amount of mobility in the form of double jumps, dashes, dives, wall runs, and much more that make simply moving around the levels an enjoyable experience in itself. There are numerous other unlockable abilities in the form of hats and badges, which gives the game a sense of real character progression and allows you to experiment with which powers you find most useful during gameplay.
Another aspect A Hat in Time has that gives it an edge over other similar platformers is its level/world design. There are only four worlds, but each world is completely unique in story, aesthetic, and mission design. The first world has a lot of verticality, and simple but fun platforming challenges allow you to learn the controls at your own pace. The second world takes a more story-driven approach, with a movie studio intrigue plot that bears similarities to something you might see in a Paper Mario game. The third world, probably the strongest overall, is a horror-themed plot that has you completing contracts to recover your soul from a demon, and contains one chapter so legitimately scary that I panicked and Alt-F4'd out of the game the first time I experienced it. I won't spoil the premise for the fourth world, since it was a pleasant surprise for me and I'd like it to be one for others as well. All these worlds contain interesting missions and subplots, and surprisingly difficult boss fights during the story's climactic moments. Some may complain that the game lacks focus or a central gameplay theme, but I think the variety adds a lot to the fun factor, and it kept me interested in what was in store next.
Another thing I can't fail to mention is the art and music. A Hat in Time is charming above all else, and the characters and environments certainly bring that home. Everything is very colorful and vibrant, and all the characters are extremely expressive. Hat Kid herself is the poster child (literally) for this, as her design is so adorable that found myself grinning during every scene in which she played a significant role. And as for the music... I would say that I enjoy video game music more than others, and more than should be deemed socially acceptable, and I can say that this game's soundtrack is absolutely stunning, in no small part because it has been touched by the hand of our god Grant Kirkhope.  Plasma3Music, with his help, have crafted perfectly fitting songs for every level and every boss that I find myself listening to even when not playing the game. There are even a bunch of unlockable remixes for songs that I enjoyed very much.
I've completed all 40 levels of the game in just under 10 hours, but I don't regret a single penny of the $30 I spent on this game. It's easily one of the best games of the year, and a must-play for anyone who loves platformers or simply wants a fun, cute experience to get lost in. My hat's off to you, Gears for Breakfast, you guys made me smile again.

Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars is what I consider the penultimate of the original C&C series, with Kane's Wrath being the finale before the last of the original series is crushed by the mediocre fourth installment.
While my playtime hours in this game is not what people would have spent when this game came out, believe me when I say this that C&C3 was the only game I spent thousands of hours into because of hundreds of fatal flaws that I made each time I went on dueling against other AIs. Custom maps from other community websites expands the variables of the existing battlefield into a mathematical, but explosive mess that creates a thrill of excitement.
The Campaign's story ranges between from just being good to great, and what I mean that there are some gaps within the experience you might get from this story driven gameplay, that doesn't mean it's gonna make you miss out on Kane's glorious plans that he has on this Earth, and enemies being GDI. Surely the victories of war is won by attrition? Well it surely is, and having a third faction being the technologicaly advanced Scrin threatens the entirety of RTS balance.
Yes, the traditional two factions being the global powerhouse GDI that ravels on versatile, shock and awe tactics and the sneaky but underground powerhouse Nod ( God I love Kane. ) that remains to be an expertise of guerilla and quick destruciton of it's foes with it's technologies. Now a third faction comes that being the Scrin, and the alien faction force does not mess around when it wants to destroy everything on it's path ranging from swarms to OP warships.
Remaining the traditional piece of RTS, Tiberium Wars is a game that is friendly to those who have played the previous series. With the formulas from it's predecessors, and lessons learned from C&C Generals, Tiberium Wars delivers that competitive piece everytime you go rush in to the Skirmish or even the multiplayer both local and online. Three factions are more than enough to create millions if not billions of variables and results everytime you execute each of them in the battlefield.
If you read on earlier about the multiplayer session being shut down due to GameSpy's demise, there are other alternatives like C&C Online that still have about thousands of players ( including me ) seeking for a multiplayer match. So that eliminates the worries about
You may say the balance of this game when it comes to the factions, especially the AI on the Skirmish mods being unfair. But did you know that regardless of their difficulty, you can decide their personality? Each personality ranges from being a patient AI to a very dangerous, impatient AI. Oh, I forgot the balance already? Well the game's balance isn't technically fair, but that's always the results of an RTS game.
And when I say traditional, if you played the first game on a 486 or a Pentium I, you would know that having too many units causes the CPU to crawl. Well even in a newer system, this game being capped at 30 FPS ( 60 if you used a perfect mod yet I still don't recommend ) it'll make your Kaby Lake or Ryzen CPUs crawl no matter the GPU you have if you produced, and the AI/Opposing players with thousands of units produced from factories, airbases and barracks.
And this is because of the Graphics? Well the game remains to run on the SAGE engine, which is also the engine used by C&C Generals and the latter installment of the original series being the Tiberian Twilight. The graphics does show a bit of an age, but having to just zoom out and look the battlefield from a bird's eye view eliminates that worry.
Compatibility issues? I'm currently using a Windows 10 system, and as far as gameplay goes I have no hiccups or any technical difficulties running the game. Although the resolution issue remains, unless you bought the Origin C&C Complete Collection or whatever it's name is, you'll have to use other means to fix the resolution to your desired size, or go with mods! Cause there are a bundle of mods out there.
I can't believe that this game is already 11 years old, not to mention that it still looks brand new to me due to the sparkling details it shows, but you have to make compromises now to make your gameplay smooth and fit well into your comfort and mood. I'm surprised that there are still people buying this game, both here and Origin. But I have the retail copy of the game that I bought firsthand on a local gaming retail store back in 2006, and now bought it again on Steam because the retail copy of mine had more issues adapting to the later OS systems, which is sad.
But yeah, do I recommend this game?

It's not helped that combat is intellectually uninteresting.  It's not bad.  It's just forgetable.
Which leaves you waiting long periods for a very small number of brief text blurbs that just aren't worth it.  The problem is amplified by the fact that the game rewards you for repeatedly sailing back and forth to London, so you're not even getting a regular stream of new material. I bought Sunless Sea because it reminded me of a very good comic called Leviathen and an RPG called Unhallowed Metropolis, which has some similar themes of unknowable horror in that sort of Victorian/Edwardian period.
The setting is very impressive, it is a fantastically rich world of Victorian London - spun through a dark mirror and dumped on the shores of a bleak and desolate ocean, where madness is your only companion. Which personally, sounds wicked!
I can definately see the sources it cites, the dark humour of Don't Starve, elements of the Cthulhu Mythos and it's atmosphere. All good stuff.
I've not played it, but I can see why the broswer game this is based off of, Fallen London, is such a big hit.
However. The game itself, which as I understand the progress updates is nearing completion, just isn't *fun* presently. You could perhaps argue that is the point of such a dark world, but let me point out a few things I take issue with...
1) Money making. Maybe it's the present patch, but it seems you can't trade anything with anyone. The only port I've found (Venderbight) that accepts goods in it's "shop" (all the others I have found just sell supplies and fuel for your ship and are not interested in trade goods) offer for the two goods you can sell either a paltry profit of two bucks, or 'Echos' or a loss of about 7 Echoes? At the moment, trade just doesn't seem worth it at all. Like, at all.
Even if you were to take a load of goods to Venderbight, you are coming back to London empty as there are no trade goods to buy. What the sense make?!
So the only other way of making money is doing survey missions (or hovering around the starting area capturing pirate ships for prize money), which is fine but often you'll find your profit margain getting wiped out by having to replace your fuel and crew used in the journey, as well as 'carousing' back at port.
In essence, it seems almost impossible to get any amount of money. Some two hours in and I'm still struggling to get more than a few hundred Echoes, with dreams of buying upgrades or a new boat a very, very long way off.
I appreciate it defeats the challenge if they just give you a pot of gold easily, but at the moment it's far too difficult and the grind for cash is painfully slow and not enjoyable - given the limited amount of ways you can make money.
2) Terror. What an excellent idea, as you sail the black ocean, darkness all around you, only the chug of the engine and the weak bloom of your headlamp lighting the way - the miasma of fear and paranoia starts to grip your crews minds... Bells in the distance.. Giant, squid eyes watching you from beneath the waves...
Again, all good stuff. The more terror you accure, the stranger things occur and eventually you go mad. However, given that you start at 0 and within the space of one trip (within the starting area where the terror affect is less) go up to about 50+ out of a 100! That's a big steep isn't it?! I thought these were hardened sea hands, not yellow bellied land-lubbers?!
The best way of avoiding a terror increase is planning your route so you sail through area light by bouys or remain very close to shore. Makes sense. But sometimes you have to find yourself sailing for about ten seconds in a dark area or drift a smidgen away from shore and your terror ROCKETS, I mean, it just flies up at a rate of knots!
Calm down lads, the shore is still on screen but.. - oh? Apparently that's not close enough. Even when a light ship or a bouy or land is clearly but a stone's throw from your ship your sailors still flip the f*ck out unless you are about a gnats testicle away before they calm down.
Having your own ships lights on doesn't seem to affect this very much, your terror goes up super fast regardless.
And the only ways to reduce terror are FANTASICALLY expensive. The 'best' way to reduce terror to a managble level is to return to London, where your terror is reset to 50 automatically (but you start to get nightmares), but to reduce it further you have to 'carouse' either in London or elsewhere. This costs between 40-20 echoes depending on where you are and reduces your terror from 1-5 points. Is that all?? That hardly seems cost effective given within a matter of SECONDS after leaving port you can accure those points back up again.
At the moment, you gain Terror far, far too quickly and it is much too difficult and expensive to reduce it.
3) Combat. Oh man, can you imagne! Sailing your steamer straight towards a giant Angler Crab or Lifeberg, screaming blood and thunder to your terrified crew as they struggle to bring their harpoons and deckguns to bear, shining your ships lamp straight into the beasts unblinking eye!!!!
Exciting stuff, except none of that happens here.
Combat for me so far, consists of trying to run away from an enemy I have no chance of beating (anything outside of the starting area, I am not kidding) as I have nowhere near enough money to buy better ships or equipment, fleeing into the nearest port, then having to leave port and being killed instantly by the monster who is still waiting for me. Game over.
The combat system consists of you or your opponent sailing into the other, where upon you are offerend the choice of fight or flight (or human  sacrifice, neat!) and then combat consists of a picture of you, a picture of the enemy and an 'illumination' bar for each. You want to raise their bar as much as possible, whilst keeping your own bar low. Once it's high enough, you press the 'shoot' action and then hopefully they die.
But normally they don't and kill you instantly. The amount of enemies that can kill you in one hit is daft.
There's no dodging, no position, no tactics, no *skill*. Just press the 'flare' button twice, press the 'evade' button a few times, then press the 'salvo' button. And then repeat as necessary. Again, it's not... Fun.
There is an option to 'study' your foe in the midst of combat, but this has to be done several times and leaves you open to being annihilated.
Against the easier enemies, combat is a chore. Crabs, bats (who seem to swarm near Venderbight), starting pirates can all be mostly be killed in three actions which equates to 30-40 seconds of your life you'll never see again. It's not engaging, as someone who has played many a sailing combat game over the years, it's uninspired and not enjoyable. FTL did a similar system much better.
4) Death. It's a hard game, it's a slow game, it's a game with what appears to be a great deal in it. But as such, death comes fast and furious.
After 2-3 hours of not managing to get much of anywhere, I was still mighty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when my ship glitched aground and then.. Game over. Which is fine, I mean it's a roguelike and it's not meant to be easy... But when it takes you HOURS to get much of anywhere from the start and you can die so easily by hook or by crook, it's maddening to see all that hard work thrown away.
It's almost like having to do a lap of the Binding of Isaac, without any items - and at the end of the lap you get *one* item for the next lap. But as soon as you die, that's it. Whilst some masochists would love such a challenege, Joe Muggins here thinks that doesn't sound like fun.
The 'merciful' mode helps with regards to this, as you can save on the fly. But you can either play it safe and live a long but dull life, or try the dangerous game and die fairly rapidly and see all your hard, slow, progress of upping your skills and saving your money go to waste.
At least when you die you can save a skill for your next character.
5) Conclusion.
Sunless Sea is a fantastic idea for a fantastic game. However, IN THIS CURRENT VERSION it is not especially enjoyable to play IMHO.
If it does tickle your nautical fancy, my advise would be to wait until full release, as this may leave you with a sour, salty taste in your mouth.

The game holds the name Sacred 3 upon itself, but it's a very different game from its predecessors. There is no open world here, there isn't real loot you'll find dropping from your enemies, just gold, health globes and energy globes.
The story seems silly and from the start it's apparent that the game doesn't take itself seriously at all, beginning from the narrator, continuing to what the NPCs say including even your own character and the Souls attached to your weapons.
You play in confined levels that can be pretty short or somewhat long that you pick from a map, after which you get dropped into the level and that you'll navigate until the boss fight at the end, after which you'll leave.
After certain fights (usually Bosses that I've seen) you'll find new Souls for your weapon, as well as new weapons that you'll be able to use (and upgrade if you are high level enough and have enough gold) after completing the mission.
The action is pretty hectic, with enemies attacking in droves while the player has to try and dodge out of the way of powerful attacks, break the shield of bigger enemies to be able to hurt them or stop certain enemies from casting (or interrupt althogether their spell) all the while managing the use of skills that use a limited energy resource.
Personally, I wanted this to be closer to the old games, something more akin to Sacred 2 but, so far, I have been having fun with what this game has to offer. The action can get very busy and even at the normal level of difficulty I found that dying can become rather easy if not paying attention at getting out of the way. Killing the groups of enemies coming at you and emerging victorious is also another fun aspect of the game.
The commands are responsive, the game looks quite nice and performs really well even when downsampling from something like 2880x1620.
I have found a problem with the game crashing whenever I open the friend menu in game but I'm not sure if that's the game or something on my PC.
All in all, the experience with the game so far is really positive. Probably not an experience worth 50€, but I didn't pay that much for it when I preordered, so it's more of a problem for anyone that would want to grab the game now.

Steam is telling me I've played 426.8 hrs of this game at the time of this review. As you might have guessed, I am very fond of the game. I've held off on writing a review because I just don't think I can do the game justice, but I'll try.
So what do I love about the game to warrant such an embarrassing amount of hours in the game? I'll try to explain:
. They are beautiful and with the recent upgrade to Unity 5, the graphics became absolutely gorgeous. The beautiful snow-frosted branches of the trees swaying in the breeze; the stark mountains against a beautiful sometimes stormy, sometimes cloudy, and sometimes sunny skyline; The beautiful, but scary nighttime with the aurora borealis, moon, and stars smattering the sky; the bright green, glowing eyes of the wolves...er wait...more scary than beautiful those critters are. :)
. The voice actors are Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale at the time of this review. Veterans of the industry, with titles such as Mass Effect under their belts. The beautiful stinger music that signals a change in weather or time of day. The haunting, creepy music when you discover a corpse inside a house sometimes. The music is not overdone, perfectly placed, so you don't lose that feeling of abandonment. The sound effects, the creaking and groaning of the trees, the wind, footsteps crunching in the snow, the lonely hoot of an owl, the ringing in your ears when you shoot the rifle indoors, the skin-crawling sighing and muttering when in the "creepier" locations, the snarling, howling, and barking of the wolves. The sounds and music in the game are one of my most favorite aspects of the game and it's hard to list them all or describe the feelings of immersion you experience. You must experience them first-hand to truly "get it".
. You have to be careful, you have to be smart, you have to be patient or you die. I love this, it's the player in full control, how long you survive is based on the decisions you make. Plan ahead, learn from past mistakes. Unlike most video games I don't mind dying in this game. I don't feel cheated because I learn what NOT to do or how I can do it better. The saying "you make your own destiny" seems applicable to the gameplay. It's a sandbox, there's no linear path you are forced to follow, you can immerse yourself fully and explore to your heart's content. There are three modes of play: easy, medium, difficult. A fit for everyone- from peaceful exploration to death around every corner.
. The developers have always been very involved in the community on Steam and also on their own Hinterland forum and Reddit. They are AAA title veterans who know what they are doing. The updates to the game are frequent and fun. Hotfixes practically same day. They have a zero tolerance for bugs in their game and it shows in this quality product. It's hard to believe it's an Early Access title. I haven't found a more polished one.
The best part? It's like a free gift everytime there is an update. More fun stuff to check out for free! Another "best part"...the sandbox will remain available even when story mode is released for the people who enjoy it. I'm looking forward to the story mode, but I adore the sandbox survival.
TL/DR: Get this beautiful, quality game. It's Early Access with a twist - it feels like a complete game already!
I hope this review helps someone. If not, drop by the forums, you'll find a wonderful and helpful community.

While most certainly BioShock has a unique style of an Underwater City and that enthralling 50's-60's Jazz and Blues culture, the game is not ideal...

It makes some attempts to include philosphy, allusions and metaphors in it's story. However they meet a dead end. None of them are adequately explained and thus the story lacks a certain emotional meaning, espcially when it comes to the "dilemma" of saving the little sisters or ripping their hearts out both of which lead to two rather unsatisfying endings...
I fell in love with the atmosphere and the setting, but I can't do more than just feel sad that it's just a shooter - and the shooting part feeling much more like Oblivion, the gunplay representing a very weak part of the game as a whole.
Some of the Plasmids were cool, but once again - I found myself using only 2 or 3 for the most part since a lot of the abilities they give are just either ruled out by your playstyle or simply poorly balanced and totaly useless.
The difficulty is also another issue. You litteraly have no need to put it on Hard more or Medium because you automatically respawn in a Vite-Chamber after your Hit Points are gone.
What that means is that you don't have to use your health pack  -"First Aid Kits"
because you can simply kill enemies through perseverance as it doesn't alter their health.
For this reason I found myself just rushing through the game on Easy, as the only thing that Medium and Hard consumes is your real-world time spent on the walkthrough.
I definately advise you to try it, but not at full price. And definately don't expect a revolution - it has good voice acting, unique setpieces in it's narative - which seem to be painfully familiar with System Shock 2 and rather intriguing characters - yet it's far from perfect as critics claimed it to be...

I'm a huge fan of horror, but it's difficult to find good horror. Good horror pits your desire to find out more against your desire to get yourself out alive. To do that, horror needs to appeal to your sense of apprehension; it does this through mystery. It must also appeal to your fight/flight response; it should do this through a sense of danger, real or perceived.
As much as I wanted a good scare, I was slightly hesitant to buy this game, because, watching trailers and gameplay videos, it seemed that it was jump scares. Finally, the game came on sale.
Yes, there are jump scares, but not that many, and never where I felt it was inappropriate. As a horror experience, while I wouldn't say it was anything that floored me, it did satisfy: the environments are wonderfully creepy, good combination of the supernatural with reality, there's a great sense of mystery throughout the game, although I'll say that the story is kind of stupid. This isn't really a spoiler, since this is what's hinted at from the beginning, but the premise is EVIL CORPORATION DOING PSYCHOPATHIC THINGS, exploiting crazy people for a profit . . . wait, what? How exactly does that work? Whatever.
Gameplay wise, it's very similar to Amensia: The Dark Descent (an excellent game), i.e., a limited light source, a weak man who can only run his♥♥♥♥♥away to evade enemies. Fortunately, I did feel that there was a fresh take on the mechanics: you have a night-vision camera that has zoom: you can see in the dark better than your enemies, so the game really does build up apprehension when you can see a figure in the distance and you don't know if it's hostile or not. It's a very linear game, but I don't think that's a bad thing. Chase sequences are a lot of fun, and often you find yourself ducking around corners, hoping like hell you don't hit a dead end.
Unfortunately, the majority of tasks the player is set to complete goes as follows in this formula: find obstacle that can be only lifted by two switches, run down the right hallway to flip one switch, run down the left hallway to flip the second switch, all the while having to evade an enemy. It gets quite repetitive, and once you die, your apprehension and horror are replaced with frustration.
It's quite a draining experience. I have to give the game credit for really making me put myself in the player character's position: there came a moment when the both of us stopped caring about what was going on and just wanted to get the ♥♥♥♥ out; and, time and time again, the second you think you're making some progress—whoops, the floor has fallen under your feet. Murphy's Law pushes you deeper and deeper into hell, and seems to almost laugh as it watches you pathetically scramble around.
In summary, it's a good game, maybe even great, and I'm glad I played it.

Well now, here's an interesting game. It's a strategy/management/puzzle game wrapped in a bit of roguelike with a fantastic coat of low-fi sci-fi. Other reviewers have done a far better job explaining the game, and really it's exactly what it says it is. And don't be afraid of the console/command line, it definitely kept me from jumping in immediately. While it may seem a bit gimicky, once you start playing with it you realize how much it adds to the overall ambience of the game, fitting in deftly with the theme. It's so easy to use that you'll find yourself popping off commands easily, and direct control makes you feel the claustrophobia and emptiness of the derelicts you'll be scavenging for supplies and information.
I like new ideas, and I love developers who take long shots. This game has some pretty interesting mechanics, and so far has all the trimmings to become something really special. While the price point might deter some, those who do jump in are in for a treat. Can't say I've ever played anything quite like Duskers, I just hope that Misfits Attic give us enough tools and variety to make it endlessly replayable. I do think that the gameplay alone makes for an itch only Duskers can scratch.

Probably the one and only game I couldn't keep myself from waiting for a sale.
The simplicity of the special, controlled by hats (and passives with the badges), along with air-diving (the one move I enjoyed watching, and using, a lot) really drew me to this game.
The level design probably also has to do with it - I often find myself
needing to sprint across an open area, and there's a lot of platforming that there's usually multiple ways to platform your way across anywhere.
And the music - I like how it changes instruments to suit whatever theme you're in within the same level.
Speaking of sounds, there's definitely some thought into the sound design. There's a sound when enemies notice you and when you can do an action with your left mouse button (hookshot or midair attack). The sounds fit the theme of the game; definitely wish other games implemented audio-based cues like this
Only downside so far I suppose is that the dialog could be more responsive like Psychonauts - every character usually has just one thing to say, which doesn't change upon actions I (the player) takes or later in time. And it is indeed short, but hopefully the two additional chapters coming out (for free) next year as well as the workshop fills up with a lot of good content. Speaking of the workshop, there's one well-made level in there called "The Monsoon," so if one-time time rifts aren't your thing, don't worry, there's more of the replayable "exploring"-type levels in there.
Btw, I'm glad they cut stuff from that mansion, I hate that level lol. (And yes, I learned afterwards there's a hidden skip, so I'm glad that's there when I have my siblings play lol.)

This 2D survival horror rogue-like game is the lovechild of H.P. Lovecraft (there's a terror meter and you can go insane) and Victorian Steampunk. It's very rich with content and you write your own story as you play (no hand holding). The goal is to survive as long as you can to attain your ultimate goal chosen while making your character. You can play anyway you want.  Specialize in information and be a spy. Focus on moral and healing your crew, Gun-ho and combat centric, and more to come in future patches.
As you write your story and explore the open world you will accumulate crew, skills, ships, and items. There's an ingame economy where goods are worth more on some islands than others. Figuring out how to buy/trade is vital to amounting easy wealth. You can use that wealth to upgrade said ships and even your headquarters turning it into a mansion. (one of the ways to retire and win).
Fighting reminds me a lot like Skies of Arcadia's turn based air battles. Which I think we can all agree is amazing. It might not that the 3D animation but it works well for the game's presentation and adds a lot of strategy and tension. Overall I would say this game is one that keeps on giving and no one playthrough will be the same.

This game is just plain good-looking.  The artwork and graphics are amazing, especially for a top down game.  They manage to evoke a dark , gothic atmosphere that draws you into the story.  And the story is where this game comes into it's own.  It reminds me a bit of the old choose your own adventure books.  The game is full of neat little tidbits that can pop up when you least expect it.  Some of the log entires are particularly funny if your humor tends to be a little on the dark side.  But the game rewards attention to the details.  The sound is a bit odd as the soundtrack manages to be strangely soothing and anxiety inspiring simultaneously.  The soundtrack is currently a little repetative, but the developer seems to be working on that.  Combat is simple, but requires a good deal of strategy to be successful.
As to the the developer, Failbetter has laid out a progress map and they have really done a remarkable job making their deadlines.  They continue to tweak it the in numerous ways, all of which have improved playability so far.  And the wolrd map promises to be huge, even without the planned undersea expansion. I'm particularly intruiged by the potential to link Sunless Sea to your Fallen London account for crossover playability.
Overall, I recommend the game even though it is early access.  It has so much potential and looks set to deliver.

Set in the bizarre, grim and quirky world of Fallen London, Sunless Sea is a great game for people who like exploration, text adventure-style gameplay, and randomness. Dark and Gothic but with a gentlemanly twist, its art is lavish and its music and sound effects ooze flavor. It's a surprisingly relaxing game to play too, driting through the Zee in the darkness, the waves lapping against your hull. It has roguelike qualities, can be played hard or softcore, and can be fairly punishing.
Sunless Sea as a game is a model of what Early Access games should look and play like. Visibly polished gameplay and art, a lack of crippling bugs, instability, crashes, with plenty of room for mechanical tweaks and finding the sweet spot, because the developers are active on their forums and responding to feedback. Constant updates not only fixing bugs and polishing content, but adding new content on a frequent basis.

Sailing an ocean of darkness with only your headlight and the odd lighthouse or bouy to light the way between islands, you'll always be wondering what lies in the uncharted regions of your map, just waiting to be filled. What new ports o'call await in the darkness? What new horrors sleep or lurk beneath the waves? Do you have enough supplies and fuel to make it to your destinations and make it back to Fallen London alive? Or will you have to take drastic measures in order to stay alive and keep your sanity?
So far, Sunless Sea is a great game for a late beta with a lot more still to be finished up in terms of stories and missions, but still a great game so far. Highly reccommended to any fans of FTL, any old-school RPG table-top games (since this game plays sort of like them), or even just fans of HP Lovecraft's works(I swear there is a Cthulu reference in an unmarked spot in game) or Steampunk. The game can be quite difficult if you don't know what you're doing, but the basics are fairly easy to grasp, and deaths at the start don't have that big of consequences, arguably. Cannot wait to see what else they add to this game.

In a nutshell, Sacred 3 is a solid hack and slash game that offers a no nonsense approach that's easy to pick up and play for those who want to hammer away at few attack buttons and little else for several hours. There's no menus to wade through or complexity of character progression which means players who thirst for killing can do so without hindrance.  In this regard the game succeeds, but at the same time does become repetitive quite quickly unless you're well in tune with levelling up your character, or willing to try the others classes to add some variety. As mentioned, if you're a fan of the previous games that afford more depth and exploration, then you're going to probably feel a little let down with what's on offer here as the game is Sacred by name, but certainly not in execution.

A quick "beware" warning after the first few hours of play.
If you liked the massive open world of Sacred 2 then beware that this game is very different.  There are no item pick ups.  The world is broken into a progressive map of paths to follow.  The only things you pick up are health, energy (to power your abilities) and gold.
Sacred 3 is now very similar to diablo 3 in terms of abilites.  You are given the opportunity to buy abilities and upgrades to those abilites with gold.  But you must also be a certain level to get those upgrades.  You also only get different items (weapons/armour) as you progress through the game levels.  There are no luck of drops for items.
Sacred 3 now seems to be an ARCADE style hack and slash.  I feel the focus of this game is now on the multiplayer/co-op aspect.  I dont think this is either a good or bad thing.  Just as long as people are aware that this is now a very different game to what it used to be.
So far Im not a big fan of the story for the campaign of this game.  It seems a mish mash of the same old "bad guy" out to destroy the world.  The 'cut scenes" are filled with corny lines that I assume are supposed to amuse young children.
This game is still fun, but as long as you can let go of what the Sacred games used to be.  I think Sacred game loyalists need to be warned of this before buying.  Look up game play video and reviews before buying.

As a game alone, could I recommend Bioshock?  The gunplay is floaty and 'off'.  It's difficult to explain, but the guns in Bioshock don't give as much feedback and aren't as satisfying as guns in games today.  Even comparing it to other games around the time of its release in 2007 doesn't do it much good.  Okay, so boo hoo, the "Run 'n' Gun" strategy isn't going to work in this game.  However, another mechanic balances this out - the use of plasmids.  These genetically granted powers allow you to stun, burn, and freeze enemies, allowing for a wide variety of strategies and traps. Zapping an enemy with lightning sure does make it a lot easier to get close enough to force-feed him a belt of ammo.
Exploration is very rewarding in this game.  So much so, that if you're like me, you'll end up being full of loot half the time.  While I thought that they could scale back on how much loot was lying around the ravenged city of Rapture, I really liked the map you're given.  It highlighted areas you had already explored, which meant you wouldn't spend ten minutes backtracking trying to find that one door you *thought* was where you were supposed to go, so you skipped it to keep looking for loot, but it turns out you actually went the right way and so now you need to find it again to explore the hallway and two rooms behind it.
I also really liked how fights with the Big Daddies worked.  They weren't agressive unless you attacked them, meaning you could hold off killing them until you were prepared; however, even when fully prepared, Big Daddies have a couple different attacks, making them formidable opponents.
Based on gameplay alone, Bioshock is fun, but it hasn't exactly aged gracefully.  Don't interpret that to mean I don't like the game though.  Both the story and characters are very engaging.  It's the small things, like the interactions between the Big Daddies and their Little Sisters and "idle dialouge" (randomly chosen lines spoken by enemies that have little to no bearing on the story/plot and only serve to heighten atmosphere), that really made me enjoy this game.
Having just competed the entire game a second time, I plan on going back for at least a third.

Zup! is back with its second installment, ZUP! 2, a minimalistic puzzler that has you continuing the fun with exploding blocks, moving platforms and simplistically done physics all in hopes of sending your little blue circle home to unlock the next level. ZUP! 2 adds a few new mechanics and some slightly more difficult levels this time around, all while flooding your overlay with achievement after achievement for every action you take.
With all the acclaim Steam users gave the previous installment, I wasn’t surprised to see a sequel to Zup!, but I was looking forward to some hopeful improvements to the game and some added longevity since, as anyone who has played the first game, knows it can be completed in well under an hour. While Zup! 2 adds a few additions to the level design and some time-based puzzles into the mix, the game itself can still be completed in under an hour.
There’s not much new to Zup! 2 that seemed to change, which can be construed as a good thing and a bad thing. On the one hand, it is still an amusing game with modest puzzle designs and an entertaining concept, but on the other hand this would have been a great opportunity to really excel the brand forward into a provoking puzzler that captured a lot of what the previous title left out; in that regard, Zup! 2 fell short.
However, the developers have certainly paid attention to the marketplace and know Steam’s audience, as the achievements you earn are completely geared towards profile design and showcase artwork, which shouldn’t come as a surprise to anyone who played the previous title. I even found myself conflicted on why I bought the game, undecidedly choosing and intermingling between fun and the desire for more options in my achievement showcase.
It’s hard to say anything else about Zup! 2 without putting in superfluous information. If you liked the first title, you’ll enjoy this one, if you didn’t like it then you will likely be unimpressed by its successor. We’ll more than likely be graced with a third installment in the near future and I hope the developers take some time and really put some conscious effort into it; you can only ride the coattails of success for so long.



Overall, ZUP! 2 is more of the same; a basic, physics-based puzzle game that is fun, albeit short and unembellished with overly complex level design. Play if for the fun or the achievements, but for those looking for a real puzzling experience, you’ll find Zup! 2 doesn’t fit the mold.

Okay, so people will dislike this review because it's pretty negative.
Games Workshop understands table top gaming. They know what goes into rules construction, game design, advancement methodology. But table top games don't always translate well to computer games when you make it literal.
REMOVE THE SIX-SIDED DIE. It isn't accurate, it isn't honest, it isn't true, period, the end, so long, goodbye, we're done. There are too many interconnected pieces of design, too many items that need to be weighed for this to possibly be accurate. That die is weighted, with intention, in order to reflect the other character additions of opposing teams. So stop pretending some random shmuck is going to have a 1/6 chance to get a 6 and rough up an 1800 team rank. It's complete garbage. I played 8 games as various low-level teams, maxing at maybe 1050 or so. I played another 8 games in the 1400 or so rank, and well, I declare, my rolls dramatically changed. There was a teensy tweak of strategy, but that's about it.
Remove the die. It makes people think they actually have a decent chance on plays they don't. Use a counter, a dial, something that goes to 100. That die is the most infuriating thing about this game - so infuriating, that yeah, I will give an awful review, because it acts as a carrot but is really just a big stick. Fix the die, remove the die, replace it with something that makes sense IN A COMPUTER GAME. This is a statistical game, make it some blue LED powered by Bloodweiser.
I'll likely continue trying to get better at this game, though the learning curve is not crazy, because it can be fun. But like cake, the die is a lie.
After this little deception is the artwork, which in general is great. But many times, too many times, due to the artwork meant to warn users of potential pitfalls (such as multiple dodge warnings) being opaque, they'll be hidden behind one another. You may be willing to risk an 83% dodge chance, but it's hiding a 17%. And that's when all the warnings actually appear. To say nothing of the dice rolls glitching and not displaying. This isn't a "bad" game, but it's definitely still a buggy one.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Yono and the Celestial Elephants by Neckbolt and Plug In Digital.
Yono is an indie action adventure game that puts you in the role of a young elephant god named Yono. Yono is new to the world and he was sent from the heavens for a purpose he isn’t quite sure of. To find answers, he sets out on a journey across the world to visit the races of the world and to help solve their problems.
There are 3 major races in Yono’s world, the Humans, Zombies and Robots. During his travels he meets many unique and often charming characters. Two of which join him in his journey across the world. The world also has a couple enemies that you’ll encounter as well including snakes, skeletons and goblins. There are also a few boss fights along the way as well.
The game’s main focus is on it’s many different puzzles that you solve across the world. The puzzles are largely logic based and often revolve around pushing blocks around and activating switches. They also incorporate Yono’s special abilities such as spitting water, air, peanuts, or fire out of his trunk.
There is also a bit of combat along the way but I’ll admit that it’s a bit basic since Yono is an elephant that can’t wield swords or weapons. So he simply slams into them with his face.
There are 2 stores which you can visit in major towns as well. The first allows you to turn in heart containers which grant you an extra heart on your health bar. You need to collect 4 of them before you can turn them in. The second is a tailor which allows you to change how Yono looks. There are a lot of choices and they change based on which town you’re in as well. There’s even a nod to The Legend of Zelda in one of the fashions as well.
In towns there are also some NPC’s that will have side quests for you to complete for them. The quests all take place in their town of origin and if you don’t complete them before leaving, you can always return later.
Overall, Yono and the Celestial Elephants is quite the cute little game. Yono is an interesting, if naive elephant and his journey is an entertaining one. It’s on the easy end of the difficulty threshold but this makes it a great game for older children to get into. It’s pretty entertaining for adults as well but I wouldn’t go in expecting something overly challenging. The game is also pretty short and can be beaten in 3-5 hours total.
