Greetings Everyone!  I’m back from my break and ready to play some more games in my list with the commitment of reviewing them all.  Today I have another Classic I picked up for the recent sale:  Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars.  An RTS that your father played back when RTS were RTS and chopped trees down on the weekend… eh, or something like that.  Nod is back for another war after getting romped on for 2 others and doesn’t seem to learn the lesson.  Though Kane keeps uttering “just as planned” every time everything he has built gets pushed into the dirt.  It’s a complicated relationship.
Beautiful Glow:  There are several things to love about this classic RTS; the graphics (specifically the terrain) hold up very well and the particle effects are still impressive if playing at max settings (which most computers should handle now) and I found the units themselves to be detailed enough to be satisfying.    The setting itself is more dark and grim than most RTS seem to be today; having an overall esthetic that doesn’t mind mixing in a lot of browns and blacks that most games avoid.  This shines into the narrative as well when you find out that the ‘good guys’ are basically a military state and the ‘bad guys’ are a religious zealots.
I want that:  There are some areas lacking, especially in the controls area.  Let’s be fair, this isn’t surprising as RTS continue to this day to show us controls that we never knew we needed.  The grouping is good although many units have access to special abilities that I would have liked to see a better key command (and consistent with all units, not a special one per unit) and available while commanding multiple units.
The Prophet wasn’t clear:  There is a bit of mixed bag of issues that are both beneficial and annoying from time to time.  Some missions seem to be story driven verses providing any real difficulty, thankfully this seems to happen during large turning points and does not seem to cut into the overall mission quality, though missions in general feel shorter on average.  I found myself melancholy about this as many times I welcomed the break but kind of felt cheated of the challenge.  In the vein of challengers that AI definitely does cheat; from unit deliveries from off map to knowing exactly where everything on my base but overall the game seems to pull its punches through unit selection and predicable attacks and not simulating a thinking mind.  It does try to flank and use combined assaults but unfortunately these don't really feel organic after you'd build up a few defences to counter it and it continues to attack that 'weak flank' with 3 Mammoth Tanks covering it.
Overall the game is fun and if you like RTS to a degree you probably already played this.  If you haven’t, I’d grab it on sale as a large reason many play these types of games (multiplayer) is dead.  But, I enjoy the single player experience so I’m an odd one.  One very big annoyance is the bugged intel logs; many are supposed to unlock automatically but don’t and some require very precise actions (like sending a specific unit to a specific hill for no reason!).  But if you like sending a bunch of poorly armed digital troops to their untimely deaths while you wait for your Ion cannon to charge I’d pick this up!

You play as a boy who is on a quest to find his sister for whatever unknown reason. You will face the trials of gaint spiders, ancient tribe warriors, gigantic saws and much more. All this takes place in a fluid black and white atmosphere with a soothing set of ambience in the background. However it is not without its flaws. I have two major complaints against this game, the first being that there is zero help whatsover on how to play this game. To learn the controls, I had to find which key opened the  main menu to open to the control manager. (For future players, this menu can be opened with the "escape" key and the controls on a standard keyboard are the arrow keys and the control key for interacting with an article. Also, when you are upside down, the jump key is the "down" button.) The second major issue with this game was the story. Except for the game's description, there is no way for the player to understand the story. Also, the end of the game was... open ended to say the least. I feel the developers could have done a better job explaing to the player what had happened to cause this "limbo." All in all, the game is great, but for ten dollars, I expect at the very least, a help section in the game's menu.
GENRE TYPE: Puzzle/Action-Adeventure
MUSIC: 2/5 - There wasn't much music involved with the game. A bit too quiet for my tastes.
SOUND: 4/5 - Excellent job with the background noise. You hear everything from birds to the boy's breathing.
STORY: 1/5 - This is the main issue here. The developers neglected to inform the players of the objective and the end result.
PUZZLES: 4/5 - You should be able to figure them out yourself, but an optional hint system would have been appreciated.
GRAPHICS: 5/5 - While monochrome, the game's fluid-like phsyics and detail makes the world pleasing to the eye.
DIFFICULTY: 4/5 - Simple enough at first, but it gradually increases to a fairly moderate challenge in the end.
OVERALL SCORE: 3.8/5 - Great job on physics and puzzles, but poor execution of main storyline.

-No Ads (Original Website)
-500 Free Gems Monthly*
-All Flight Club Dragons*
-20% Off InStore
-Hiccups Flightsuit

I’ll try to be clear, this game is a trainwreck. Spoilers ahead I guess, I talk about late game events but leave out character names and most details. It’s lame but I need to provide examples to show how broken the writing is.
The game’s storytelling is disastrous. The beginning is a slog where every character over explains the most basic stuff about the setting. This is a world where Malevolence (evil energy) causes pretty much every bad thing in the world, and it is a story where the chosen one of light travels with elemental spirits to gain enough power to defeat the Lord of Evil. Anything remotely interesting about the world is dropped briefly after being introduced, or comes in far too little far too late. There’s nothing complicated enough in either the world or story to justify spending so much time on redundant conversation.
Funny enough, the rest of the game has the opposite problem. Things eventually just start happening with no buildup or coherency. Scenes that are supposed to be emotionally punchy come out of nowhere from characters that have had almost no screen time. A major party member is basically written out of the game at the one third mark for no real reason, presumably this wasn’t originally planned, since you can buy equipment only they can use at late game shops, tens of hours after they’re gone from the party forever.
Too bad too, since the character in question is one of the only characters in the game that approaches being alright. Everyone else is either boring or unlikable (or both). At least half your party can be summed up as “snarkster”, leading to incredibly repetitive and grating exchanges during optional conversations. Sorey, the hero, is about as generic as it gets, being a paragon of justice with not much else going on. There’s little to no development for most of the cast, so it’s not like they change into better or more interesting people. One character seems to have no coherent characterization at all, being both a pure hearted, klutzy, bubbly waifu and cold blooded, professional murderer for hire (but only killing “evil” people of course, so the paragon of justice has no problems being around her). During one sidequest she decides to call the authorities on some children for stealing, despite their cries that they’re only doing it to survive. During a completely unrelated sidequest she defends children who have attacked soldiers of the state, saying they had no other choice to survive. The game doesn’t mention this disconnect between the two sidequests at all so it’s safe to assume its just inconsistent writing.
The game’s schizophrenic storytelling reaches its pinnacle in what has to be one of the most pathetic death scenes I’ve ever seen. Most of the character’s backstory is dumped on you in a nonsensical flashback minutes before they die. They sacrifice themselves to save another character from a ineffective monster (who can’t even move or turn around in its boss fight), and their function is immediately replaced by somebody who you have only interacted with three times in the past 20 hours. It was a complete disaster  and I was laughing the entire time it was happening.
What about the gameplay? Fighting is what you’ll be doing most. You run into an enemy on the field, an enemy group spawns in, and you transition to a more action game style setup. You have what you would expect from recent Tales Of games, two attack buttons, more moves pulled off by twisting the stick, and a stamina bar. The devil is in the details though. The game’s camera has to be one of the worst in recent memory, unlike in other games in the franchise where combat would teleport you into an empty field only vaguely representative of the area you’re in; you fight exactly in the spot on the field you engage the enemy in. This serves absolutely no purpose other than giving the camera all kinds of clutter and walls to get stuck on, like it’s a physical object in the game world. In a one on one duel, the enemy isn’t the boss; it’s the camera wildly jerking around trying to get itself unstuck off the one tree in the arena.
In addition, the combat is more limited than it has been in previous entries. You have two human party members and four elemental spirit party members, with four slots for active battling. Any human must be active at all times, and an elemental spirit is conjoined to each human. This reduces your options. There’s one point in the story where you only have Sorey and three elemental spirits, but only one spirit can join the fray because there’s only one human on the field, it’s pretty aggravating and feels needless. In addition the move pool for each individual character has seen a decrease. This was likely done because of the Armatization system. A human and their corresponding spirit can armatize together in order to become more powerful. Massively increased stats, powerful AoE moves, and access to good, easy healing, make armatization the undisputed best option in most scenarios. There’s not much reason to really learn any individual character’s moveset and combo potential because they are so limited compared to armatization, where effective play is as easy as button mashing and dodging. If you want to play multiplayer with more than two people, this also hurts that since most of the time elemental spirits (players 3 and 4) are just going to be fused into a human.
So how about exploration? It’s pretty pitiful. Overworld areas are gigantic, empty fields with almost nothing in them. The most you’ll find are optional, generic dungeons made from copypasted assets, and optional minibosses that are usually just edits of regular monsters. To add insult to injury the game makes you pay a not-insignificant amount of money to fast travel past the barren overworld. The overworld at least has a few pretty areas, which makes them preferable to the dungeons. Every dungeon in the game is made of drab, featureless corridors and 90 degree turns connecting empty rooms, if I didn’t know better you could tell me the dungeons were done by a bad procedural generation algorithm and I would believe you. Even the forests conform to featureless corridors and 90 degree turns. Sometimes the game gives you a “puzzle”, the most complex of which in the game is lighting torches that are marked by number, pretty weak stuff even for filler.
Despite the length being standard for this sort of game, it feels very barebones on content compared to previous entries. There is an end game fetch quest akin to the Triforce Hunt in Zelda Wind Waker, where the story just stops in its tracks as it asks you to do sidequests to gather gems. Most of these sidequests almost certainly weren’t originally planned to be used this way, as most of them just have the gem appear out of nowhere with no fanfare at the end of an unrelated scenario. The Coliseum, a series staple where one character or the party can fight a variety of battles and tournaments for prizes, is nowhere to be found, being replaced with a handful of one-off solo combat rooms in the field. There are more optional dungeons than other games in the series, but it doesn’t do much to help when they all pull from the same pool of assets mildly re-colored, and are about as joyless as the regular dungeons. There are a decent number of accessories, but very few costumes compared to previous entries, presumably being cut to be served up as DLC.
In short, this game offers nothing worthwhile. Combat is braindead and exploration is excruciatingly boring. The story messes up the most simplistic of concepts and characterization. Long time fans of the series or genre have played far better. Newcomers will likely be bored. I regret almost every minute I spent with the game, please don’t make the same mistake I did.

Zestiria is bog-standard JRPG with an engaging combat system that is dragged down by its wonky balance, poor AI, and abysmal storyline. Fans of the genre might still enjoy it, but I wouldn't recommend it to a broader audience.
Per tradition, start with the good. The combat is quite solid, with a rather massive number of potential combos. There's a good deal of potential variety, too; even if you play one character the whole time, you'll swap between 5 different skillsets and ultimately have access to right around 100 possible attacks. Different attacks benefit from different attack stats, so there's some room for customization and quite a bit of planning.
Unfortunately, the game has a particularly obtuse skill and equipment system. Gear comes with random bonuses attached (called skills). Some can be nearly useless, such as a water bonus on a fire character, or a guarding bonus on most anyone (the AI does not block). Some can be a great boon, such as reducing all damage taken by a flat amount, and being stackable. You're always at the mercy of RNG for that, and it can be quite grating to have some gear you can't even use for its. Skills also give vast benefits if combined with other skills in certain quantities. This means that especially on higher difficulties, the game can expect you to grind extensively, or face incredible odds.
It also struggles with balance and AI issues; many opponents will behave so predictably that you can pick a single Power Hit skill and just kite the opponent, sidestepping its tell and retaliating for a chunk of health. Rinse, repeat for a few minutes, and the most powerful bosses are easy prey. I played through on the highest difficulty available-- the two highest difficulties, Intense and Chaos, unlock as you play. I played most of the game in Chaos, where your opponents vastly outlevel you and have some silly speed boosts. I got to see bosses hit my AI teammates for 30,000 damage, where the max health is 9999. It's a pretty wide
Storytelling and characterization are a resounding miss for such an established RPG series. Characters with pivotal roles in the story often come with limited explanation, especially those who become inexplicably evil. Essentially no character has anything resembling a character arc, least of all the hero. He's a most dedicated sort of Mary Sue-- his perfect "purity" is a major plot point. There's an even worse attachment to the above which would be a spoiler to reveal, but suffice to say that you're in for frequent eye rolling episodes. It's not all bad-- some of the skits are still worth a chuckle here and there -- but it's certainly not up to the standards of the series.
The plot on the whole is clunky, with far too much coincidence and shoddy plot devices. I laughed out loud at the utter inanity of some plot developments, including some things that were intended to evoke sadness. There is literally a magical gun that shoots out people, except when it doesn't, and it's an essential plot element for much of the second half of the game. The tool never has any explanation as to where it came from, or how it works, or how it fits into any part of the world (there are no other firearms in the Zestiria universe). The liberal use of Japanese cartoon tropes can be pretty overwhelming as well.
Despite some massive amount of time not actually playing -- 17 hours in menus, plus who knows how much that I just left on and never saved -- I came in at just about 80 hours on the game clock. It's a fairly large game, especially if you try to do and see everything, but it's really hard to bring yourself to do that. In the end, I couldn't bring myself to finish a few of the final side quests. Even the combat system had begun to grate by that point, with nearly every fight boiling down to Crown Fire and Calamity Flare spam. By the end, I just wanted it over with, and a game with that problem isn't generally going to get my recommendation.

Tales is an rpg series I don't have much experience with, having neglected most of the installments (there's only so many rpgs you have the time to play!!) having only played the original SNES game (or super famicom,, whatever!) Tales of Phantasia and finishing its remake on the PS1, before getting my hands on this one. Now that I finished Zestiria as well, I must say I am quite intrigued by the other entries in the series, hearing opinions that Zestiria is considered to be a low/mediocre point and I am quite surprised as i found the game to be quite enjoyable. Not perfect though so I am interested to see what else the Tales games have to offer.
The pros have to definitely go to the amazing soundtrack with some tunes ranged from cheerful and energetic, to somber or epic battle tunes. the combat is fun and it's always exciting to use armatization and exploit the enemy's weakness.
I found the characters likeable, personally. Didn't mind the happy-go-lucky/goody-two-shoes personalities but i guess that's just bogs down to personal tastes. If there is room in rpgs for party-pooper Squall, there is room for naive Sorey!
The graphics while not the most advanced, have a certain charm, with bright colors and interesting locations. Some locations are really beatiful to look at, from the lush fields and forests, to deserts and medieval kingdoms. The world map is quite big, an open world to explore (though it might seem empty at times) and a couple of times the progression does suffer from the "but thou must" trope where you are limited where to go and what to do.
In general however, thhe artstyle of the Tales games is a nice change from more photorealistic rpg worlds and a welcome addition.
The story is not that great unfortnately but it has its moments, with some interesting themes, a really geat lore and background history and many great moments are helped by the silly personalities of the party, who can also support serious scenes when needed. So the story, yeah it's a bit average but nothing offensive. A classic tale of good vs evil. Perhaps that's one point where Zestiria gets some flack.
If there was a bigger problem where some flack is understandable and perhaps deserved in this game is the padding the story suffers from in certain points and especially during the last part. Some pacing problems arise causing minor frustration, stealing some enjoyment out of the game when it's not needed.
There are also some small problems with the camera, especially when you battle in closed rooms and corridors, making soem battles a bit more difficult to understand what's going on and to navigate easy, though most of the time i didn't have any serious problmes, the times it did happen it made it obvious that the camera implementation needed some refinement.
As for the port itself, I haven't tried the "vanilla" version at all, meaning, I immediately applied the community patch that fixes many of the problems, (now you can finally play at 60fps!) so I suggest you do that first thing! Some slowdowns/fps drops occured mostly in a couple of busy cities, if the draw distance was increased, but apart from that didn't encounter any serious problem. However, the game was a bit prone to randomly crashing every now and then. Not sure if it was the port itself or due to the 60fps patch as it usually crashed when it was loading textures and various fixes, when i entered some new areas, or when I was starting the game, but thankfully the game has an amazingly helpful "quick save-save anywhere on the map or dungeon" function besides the traditional save points so my advice is use this often to avoid losing even the slightest of progress.
Gameplay wise, for those afraid of getting their hands in a big rpg game, there is also a helpful option that allows you to change the difficulty level at any point during the game even at the most difficult of boss battles, so for those who prefer to enjoy the story and not fret over difficult battles this will defintely help. Keep in mind though that this isn't a complete "get-out-of-jail-card" and you still need to put some basic effort even in the easy mode.
The rest of the mechanics are too much to describe here, there are endless tutorials and guides within the game to guide you but perhaps some of the more convoluted skill mechanics won't matter to anyone but the more dedicated hardcore rpg fans. i personally didn't pay too much attention to it and managed to get though the story.
Overall, a prety entertaining rpg, not the best ever but quite fun and deserving your attention. If this is considered a "not-so-good" Tales game then I am excited to check Berseria (which serves as a prequel to this) because it is considered to be an improvement.
But, go listen to the wonderful soundtrack now! You will love it! It's the highlight of the whole package!

I'll start this review off with pros and cons-
Pros:
-soft body physics
-gorgeous cars and world
-good driving physics
-online multiplayer (privately hosted servers)
-good optimization
Cons:
-unfinished
-slow development
-no local multiplayer
-only partial controller support
-few cars/maps
-little in game progression
Now onto the actual review.
Wreckfest is a bit of a interesting one. I bought this game originally months ago but it felt more like just a little tech demo because there was no progression or point to actually play it. You could play as any car (of which there were few) and on any track (again, there wasn't very many tracks) so I got bored of playing pretty quickly. With the recent update, there's almost a point to play it because you have to buy the cars and there is upgrades to do to your cars. That being said, you can buy whatever car you want and max out it’s upgrades pretty quick, so again with the lack of depth. The “market”
makes it feel like you’re actually a mechanic/driver and you have to surf the local classifieds to find parts and trying to get the best value, but since there's only a couple of options for each part, you can't really customize your cars as much as I'd like. Speaking of cars, they look amazing and are incredibly detailed but the in-game world still needs some graphical improvements. The maps looked great a few updates ago, but were somewhat recently decreased for the sake of new suspension and traction simulation. According to Bugbear, it takes about three months to create a new car, start to finish, which is understandable considering how much work needs to go into each one. But it’s still a bit ridiculous. I wish they had a bigger budget and team so it could be finished sooner but I'll keep waiting for this game to be legitimately completed. Until that  day comes, I still can't recommend this game. Bugbear has set the bar for themselves pretty damn high for themselves and I see this game being one of my favorites once it's finished. People tend to give this game pretty negative reviews because they say it's been abandoned by it's developers and it's a waste of money which isn't true in the slightest. Building this game is a huge undertaking and for it to be done by just a handful of people is going to take a while. If it had the budget and team of a triple-a game I'm sure it would be a completed full release by now.
Tl;dr- Fun game, but unfinished. Looks fabulous, cars are incredibly detailed and have soft body physics, but I wouldn't recommend buying it-yet. The day it's finished, buy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.

I could talk about how great this game is, but I'll leave that to the other reviews.
What I WOULD like to address though, is how awesome the devs are.
A lot of early access games go into a lull or dead stops in development because either something went really wrong on the business end, or (as most of us assume), the development team rakes in a lot of money and decide to rest on their laurels early and just stop working on it. Examples: Day-z, Rust, Starbound, etc.
Hinterland though, CONSTANTLY pushes out updates in either the form of news or actual gameplay additions or bugfixes. This shows their true commitment to getting this game finished. Although there hasn't been a HUGE amount changed in the time I bought this game, they did add difficulty, bears, and a better UI, which is still quite a bit for fine tuning.
The most recent update for example, ported the game over from Unity 4 to Unity 5 in the form of an opt-in beta (early access for early access).
So what?
Well, there is now a HUGE performance increase (at least for me). Before, I could run the game at Ultra at around 40-80fps outside and 144+ inside. Now I get 144+ all the time. (Using a GTX 670 from 2013).
More indie devs needs to follow Hinterland's example. They show true passion in their game and actually care about the audience.

Let me start off with a simple pros, cons, and mixed chart:
Pros:
- Very vivid, beautifully detailed game. Mainly artsy and has a hand-drawn feeling to it (because it is!)
- Realistic, for the most part, has many considerations to take into account such as hunger, thirst, warmth, fatigue.
- Very fleshed out mechanics, an example would be:
You are out at night, hauling home supplies from a second base. You are freezing to death, and low on condition, so you strike up an outside fire. Little do you know, it takes time for the ambient temperature to warm up and actually provide you with warmth. You drop plenty of health waiting for the fire to gain traction and heat up, and even then, you need to huddle by until your cold meter drops.
Or:
You are out in a blizzard, and doing this absolutely shreds your clothing durability, so you must hurry. There is a home against the wind, quite a ways out, and a house a little bit farther, of the same variety. Which do you go to? The best choice would be the slightly farther one, because running with the wind, downhill, or on a snow-clear surface (or all together), you run slightly faster. Imagine you are running on a downhill road with the wind. Rather fast, right?
- Plenty of tool and clothing variety, and tiers of protection and tools
- Wildlife interaction, and many methods to exploit them for food, such as using a torch to scare a wolf away from a kill.
Cons:
- You WILL die. This may be intended, but you literally cannot live forever no matter what. It starts gradually. You run out of canned food, so you must hunt. How? With the rifle? It eventually breaks. Use a repair kit? Yeah, you can fix it until the kit breaks. Use your hands? Sure, but you will run out of materials. Magical rifle? Too bad, running out of bullets. So you decide to hunt other ways.
Fishing? Only as long as you have tools to break ice.
Snares? If they don't break, which they will eventually.
Going after used carcasses? If they aren't frozen.
Alright, you got a little bit of food, around 1.2 KG's, or 3 pounds. Use some matches to light up a fire indoors? Tough luck, they have decayed or have all been used. Firestriker? Gone. Magnifying lense? Gotta go outside bud. So, now you have a blazing fire. You manage to collect wood with your hands and keep it going, and the wolves manage to stay away. But now the deer are hunted out for a while, and you have to wait until a kill comes nearby. You are too low on food to wait, so you go out to hunt wolf.
Use the rifle? Broken. Use a knife or hatchet? Broken. You decide to fistfight it. Clothes on? They slowly get torn up throughout many hunts and blizzards, to the point you are naked and it is too cold inside. Clothes off? You prolong them slightly longer. So, now you killed a wolf, you harvest it, cook it on the same fire, but now your condition is extremely low due to being naked with no weapon. You go inside to sleep and heal, but it is too cold. You sleep until you are frozen to death. The end. So no matter what luck and abundance, you will die from some factor. This is very annoying.
- Wolves are too hostile. Yes, the game has a disclaimer, but a single wolf chasing you down and trying to eat you immediately is ridiculous, and especially considering the main male character is roughly one hundred and eighty pounds, at my guess, the wolf would be absolutely destroyed by a kick to the head.
- Wolves are too strong. Explained in the above.
- Hand-to-hand combat currently consists of clicking very fast, then clicking again to release it and damage the wolf. Then you do this is a few times or more, depending on weapon, then it runs. From there you have to chase it down. From there it is likely a second will spot you. RIP. There needs to be a better combat system IMO.
- Deer and wolf barely give you any meat, especially considering calories. You get about eighteen to twenty pounds off a deer, and fourteen to sixteen off a wolf. For perspective, to heal from 35 condition back to 100, in eight hour increments, requires about three steaks, maybe a fourth right away when cooking is done. Each steak is 2.2 pounds. So after healing, you are left with about two to four steaks with a wolf, and you can burn those calories just sleeping all day.
- I fear that story mode will not be released until sandbox finishes, which does not seem anytime soon as the game has endless potential.
- Very monotone cycle of forage, make a base, eat, drink, boil water, cook food, sleep, go out for items, come back, eat, drink, sleep, eat, drink. I know survival is realisticly just this, but a player can not get the real life feeling of constant threat of horrible death by starvation. There needs to be something to actually do.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VERDICT: I believe that game has tons of potential, and it is highly playable already, so I do recommend it as of Early Access, this April 17th of 2015. I do, however, fear it will be in Early Access for a long while ahead, and while you can certainly act as if it is a finished survival Sandbox game, there is much to be desired in the long run.

I've never been much of a fan of Mario, Banjo-Kazooie, or other platformers. But I backed it on Kickstarter anyway (the only thing I ever have) because of the great art and the devs seemed to have their stuff together. And boy, did that turn out to be a good investment - I love this game!
The art, music, writing, and voice acting are all incredible, and fit together perfectly. The atmosphere reminds me most of Banjo-Kazooie, but really stands on its own. It's a great feel-good game (with the possible exception of one particularly spooky level) but avoids cliches and remains thoroughly entertaining and funny throughout the whole story.
The gameplay is just plain fun! The controls feel really tight, and the abilities and challenges are introduced at just the right pace - no mechanic feels overused, any every level has a nice balance of all of the mechanics unlocked so far. Some elements come back in later levels in fun, unexpected ways. Most importantly (in my opinion) for a platformer, it has a perfect difficulty curve. I'm no platforming veteran, yet I rarely found myself retrying something multiple times (mostly the boss fights, and never more than twice) and checkpoints are forgiving. The level design is also great - I genuinly enjoyed exploring and looking for secrets, while I'm usually a straight-for-the-objective kind of player.
I cannot recommend this game enough. Even if platformers aren't usually your thing, the amazing presentation and story will definitely keep you entertained!

Overall I'm incredibly satisfied with this game.
If you need detailed graphics, easy tutorials, online multiplayer, or any other typical AAA studio game element you'd best look elsewhere.

It's one of those "I wish there was a neutral review option" games.
Port-wise, it's decent. You need a fix to make it run without dips but other than that it's fine.
So first off, the good things:
It's doable. It gets too easy later, but given how tanky the last enemies are it prevents you from getting frustrated.
They're fun characters, and as usual the interactions in a Tales game are cool to look at.
That's pretty much it, the bad things however...
The last part of the game takes centuries to finish no matter how much you grind. Honestly felt like they were just padding the runtime to say it takes longer than 50 hours to beat.
One of the worst cases of wasted potential I've seen. Most of the plot points introduced in the first 5 hours are completely ignored until the last 2 hours, where they rush to get it done with as fast as possible before the final showdown. And forget character development for over half the cast, they learn nothing in their journey.
Sorey is just awful and the main reason this is a negative review. The point of the story is that people aren't bad because they're possessed, they can just be bad people. This is something everyone except Sorey comprehends. You have criminals and murderers literally saying they did it just because they felt like it, but Sorey is the ONLY PERSON that doesn't believe it and keeps whining about how everyone is perfect and only hellions are evil, so CLEARLY these humans that committed a crime were just possessed otherwise they'd be perfect saints.
Over 70 hours of quests and cutscenes and he's the exact same character at the end that he was at the start.
He learned nothing, he didn't change, and it makes 90% of the interactions at the end painful to sit through because of just how stupid he is. I have no idea why people say he "has to confront his beliefs". Looking upset and not doing anything about it isn't "confronting your beliefs", it's being too stubborn to accept basic common sense.
If you have 60+ hours to waste and this is 75% off, maybe get it. It's honestly not that bad if you're into bland cookie cutter good guy protagonists or if that doesn't bother you at all.
Otherwise look elsewhere for a decent JRPG, especially if you want a decent Tales of game.

This is really charming and cool, but it's got a lot of problems from my perspective.
Controls are tight, very reminiscent of Contra. Jumping and dashing feel perfect, and actions seem instantaneous. The timing on the Slap take some getting used to, but once you do it feels second nature.
The artwork is, no surprise, amazing. Absolutely nothing looks like a sprite, which is really impressive. It all looks just like cels painted onto backdrops, which are themselves amazing.
The music is
. I was comparing it to Bendy's soundtrack, with Bendy coming across as being worse. The instrumentation is perfect, the mixing is perfect, nothing is wrong with any part of the sound design.
To round it all off, this game is excellent for couch co-op. My friend and I were having a lovely time despite the following frustrations...
The screen rapidly fills with far, far too much stuff. The game is at its best when there's just enough going on on-screen to feel exciting, and at its worst when it just throws stuff in your face causing sensory overload. Way too many things cause an explosion, and the explosion is too big and distracting. I'd appreciate it if it could be redesigned with less smoke, or with some transparency to make it less obstructive. My friend and I felt overwhelmed and overstimulated in the run and gun sections, although that's mostly due to the fact that...
Enemies spawn randomly. Mostly. It seems like there's a few enemies that are placed strategically, but there's also a seemingly endless barrage of enemies that keep spawning. It made building up a flow fairly difficult for us.
I'm sure we'll get called casual babies for it, but there really needs to be some way to replenish health. We toyed with the idea that successful parry slaps could give you some health back if timed correctly. If more strategic enemy placement were employed, this wouldn't feel as necessary, but as it is we can't help but feel that dice-roll has the potential to screw you should an enemy spawn in in just such a way that you can't do anything about it.
Our biggest gripe was that
. We considered this unforgivable. It made the boss fights way, way too stressful, with no sense that we were progressing through it at a decent pace. We had no idea how far into any one boss fight we'd gotten, and the game certainly wasn't going to tell us. Very, very aggravating.
All in all, Cuphead is a very good game, and was clearly made with a lot of passion. The difficulty can be a little daunting, but not truly beyond the abilities of anyone with sufficient grit and gumption. I hope I'm not the only one with the issues that I have (My friend and I were certainly on the same page), and I hope that some patches come along to at least give us some health bars.

This game can has two aspects that will shape your opinion of it. One of gameplay and one of story. I would love to give it a review with pros and cons and help give the best possible view, but it needs nothing else but these two things to be explained.
The first thing to know is that it is almost impossible, by design and game mechanics, for you to lose fights that are heavily stacked against you. You can defeat enemies that are 20 levels above you if you have the patience to wait it out. This comes from your ability to armatize with a seraph while dead. Yes, that's right, you can fuse while dead and then separate and have both characters alive. Combine that with the ability to swap the other Seraphs in and out of your party and they will revive while out of combat, you just have to be a bit smart and maybe a bit good on the technical side and you will almost never lose a fight and have no real reason to grind and can skip as many fights as you want. Who needs life bottles? Nobody. Just an extra safety net if you really want them.
The other thing to know is that Sorey is the most annoying protagonist you could ever meet and you will want anything and everything bad to happen to him because of how much you will hate him. Words are not enough to describe the depth of my hatred for Sorey.
If you can get past those two things, you will enjoy the game. However, I cannot give it a positive rating because of those.

Just Cause 2 is a 3rd person shooter that looks and feels a lot like GTA and Saints Row. It's main trademark is the grappling hook, that can be used to pull yourself to objects far away or pull objects towards you.
Pros:
+ Vast environment with distances that feel realistic. Driving 10 kilometers feels like driving 10 kilometers in real life. Downside of this is that the world feels a little empty and repetative at times.
+ All the major weapon classes are represented and you can upgrade your gear.
+ Pretty good story.
+ Memorable character build and rich dialogues.
+ The local propaganda radio reflects on your latest actions, trying to cover everything up.
+ Playing a villain was served in a satisfactory, humorous manner, that suited the whole story.
Cons:
- Missions start to feel repetative very quickly, falling roughly into 3 categories:
1. Go kill everyone and blow everything up in a particular place.
2. Help some gangsters get to a fortified camp and protect them until they take it over.
3. Destroy something/someone in a limited timeframe.
- A few bugs like falling through a bridge or not being able to get out of a turned over car.
Verdict
It's not amongst my favorite games, far from it. Travelling the distances was a pain and the repetative missions got tiresome quickly. On the other hand, unleashing havok has a quality of it's own and the game surely has a ton of content to keep your hands tied for some 20+ hours.
FPS, Survival Horror. RPG elements mixed with a great plot outstanding graphics for the time and very enjoyable.

This is a game in which you walk through one strange mini world after another while being lectured to by some dude who's weirdly obsessed with lampposts. It's very artsy, perhaps trying too hard at times and becoming self-indulgent (debatable whether this is intended), but I had fun playing and discovering it anyway.
If you dislike games in which your skills and actions are irrelevant (other than having to move to progress the plot), you probably won't like this one either. If you're hoping for something like Stanley Parable, be warned that The Beginner's Guide is linear, serious rather than funny and doesn't have choices/multiple endings.
Pros:
+ Atmosphere/Story: Pretty interesting "plot" that makes use of its medium in the sense that I feel like it would not work equally well as a book or audiobook.
+ Exploration: You get to see and interact with lots of surreal places.
+ Good Voice-Acting / Sound
Cons:
- Really short (90 min for me, and I took my time), I might replay it once but in general there's probably not a lot replay value to it.
- Walking Simulator: As mentioned above, you could watch someone else play it and see and hear exactly the same things.
+/- Story: Definitely not everybody's cup of tea (check out some of the negative reviews for more details), but if what you have heard so far made you curious I would recommend trying it just for the unique experience.

Hello boys and girls it's Joker here, this review/guide is primarily made for those that have experienced issues getting this amesome game to run under Windows 7, 8 & 10.. I'm currently using Windows 10 (Windows 7 up intil 4 months ago) but i know it would probably work just the same.
So, let's begin shall we..
Let me just say that installing the game caused my system to give me some kind of error message stating that the game installation could not get the required update due to it being locked after not receiving full access etc? (Err,
Anyway, i figured it out by following a few simple steps!
Step 1) Remove the contents from your library by first canceling the installation process and afterwards clearing the games cache (the game must be greyed out so to speak).
Step 2) Go over to your Windows Steam folder (Program Files x86,  Steam, SteamApps, Common,..) followed by selecting the corresponding C&C 3 file and deleting it accordingly.
Step 3) Restart your computer.
Step 4) Start Steam and install the game again, which should now work correctly..

A good game with a lot of potential. Currently lacks depth, but that is remedied little by little with each update. The gameplay cycle is long, highly engrossing and at the end leaves you wanting to jump in again to see if you can survive just that little bit longer with new tricks and better knowledge of the world. Absolutely recommended.
It begins desperate; you're woefully underequipped, with no tools and minimal supplies. You will die quickly; if the cold doesn't end you, a wolf will.
But you scavange for supplies, gather together better gear, and before you know it you've survived a week.
For a time things are good. The cold doesn't stop you exploring anymore, you've got plenty of consumables and even a wolf isn't so much of a threat - you can even harvest them for meat and materials for your trouble, if you react quickly.
But then something curious happens. You run out of places to scavange from and, suddenly, you realize that what you have is more or less all you're going to get. It is gradual, but slowly your situation gets more bleak. You run out of bullets for your hunting rifle, materials to repair your gear, your tools degrade and break. Before long you find yourself sidled up against a stove in a fishing shack that is barely keeping you from freezing, bleeding out from the last wolf to jump you at your front door, hoping that you get more out of the fishing hole than a snack. You're not going to survive heading back to proper shelter and have no choice but to load up the stove with firewood, throw down your bedroll and hope you don't die in your sleep.

This is a revamped review of The Long Dark.
Like my Darkest Dungeon review, most early access games will either remain unpolished or the state of the game will become less shape than before.
The Long Dark however is a different story, It's one of those early access games. That patches as you go along, while also providing the developers feedback along the way both good and bad. While there is no story mode, Sandbox mode provides you a glimpse as to what you will be experiencing within story mode once it's released.
You can see just how "hardcore" the game is. This is in a sense a true Hardcore Surivial game. Sure people can play it on easy, but where is the fun in that? For the true Long Dark experience play on medium or hard. And you can see why The Long Dark remains a very highly postive game. All you have is your senses and wit as you surive the candian wilderness. There is no compass, no GPS, no fast travel, no general store to trade. Just you and mother nature. And your instinct to survive
The artistic visuals in the game is amazing and detailed. Plus a very active translation steam workshop community in order to get the game out to other steam players who want to play this game but within their own native language. Hopefully, we will see somewhere down the line with more mods besides translations.
Also like with the Darkes Dungeon it's a trial by error experience, you learn as you fail and vice versa. You need to be a critcal thinker and plan ahead in a game like this. Because if you don't, you will most likely die by the hands of nature. Or become deperived of food and drink supplies which by the way are randomly generated throughout the three maps. So don't expect each map to have the same stuff in the same location. You are also randomly teleported to a part of the map, while the terrain will remain the same, everything else will be different.
There are two issues that i have with the game. The first issue is it's "struggle" mechanic. Maybe change it to tapping a particular key, instead of relying on the mouse button.
How it goes, it goes like this....
RMB (It could be LMB) is to charge up
LMB (It could be RMB) to attack
Sure you could have weapons to give you an edge, but it won't do any much good. Use your brain power, rather than your weapons, this isn't Skyrim kiddies.
The other issue is the lack of 'saves' now this question has been asked plenty of times and it is being considered. This game goes on the bases of Dragon's Dogma. Where it's one save per character, but it doesn't run like a typical Fallout or Elder Scroll game or just about any game with a mutiple save option. One save for everything basically, which sucks but that's the whole point of Hardcore survival you need to heavily rely on taking the game slowly and don't treat it like a typical RPG game.
Lastly, The game doesn't hold your hand as well. So don't expect a tutorial. The Sandbox in every sense. IS the tutorial, since story mode isn't out yet. So pay close attention to your surroundings and you will be fine. Another thing is that the steam community has been very supportive in giving the tools you need to survive. Just hit up the guide section if your lost, because i can seriously tell you. You will need those guides.
I recommend this game if you love a true Hardcore Survival Experience.

Now, I wasn't going to buy this game based on some of the negative reviews, however I loved and played BB1 and Chaos Edition so much I felt I owed it to the game to at least give it a try. I'll try and make my review unbias, however I do enjoy the game so far, so that's going to show through.
I've played around 3 matches now, and I can say I'm really impressed.
For anyone concerned that there may not be a way to do Single player tournaments, well let me put your mind at ease, as there is. You can build a team, and then choose to do a whole tournament vs AI instead of online.
With that out of the way, I was a much happier player! I spent most of my time in Blood Bowl 1 just building teams and doing tournaments, and here you can do the same thing.
Also, once you actually play it, you can see a lot of work has gone into it. Sure, there are only 8 teams + the pre-order teams, however there has been a lot of effort put into those teams, and we all know more will be released.
The game as it stands is very playable, and you can turn the commentators off. (the subtitles stay on, but they'll no doubt put in a fix for that)
So here's a quick layout for you to make up your own mind
Pros - The UI is modern and simple. It takes some getting used to but it's cleaner and I found it uncluttered and easy to use.
-The graphics are better (of course) but they have really put a lot of love into this game
-The block animations are great, I love them, if you don't you can turn them off... but I'll never get sick of my Dark Elves kicking over an opposition!
-It's still Blood Bowl, the rules are the same, they have stayed true, they haven't tried to make a blitz mode which for me is a pro, instead they have put all their effort into making a working tournament system, that you can either play online or solo. It has a home stadium you can sink spare gold into, it has an coach experience system, it feels like there are a lot of other ways to spend your cash
-The campaign is only Humans, I don't like humans, but the campaign in the last was only humans or orcs, and apparently they have put in a LOT of extras into it to make it an interesting story, so I'll try it, but I can't comment on it as I haven't yet. I think it's a pro that they didn't just leave it as tournament play, they actually put in some effort here!
-The AI is smarter... definitely smarter... which makes it a lot more dangerous
Average-
-The game takes a little longer, I am sure I could trim it by chopping back animations and gaining more experience on the UI, but the old Blood Bowl took around 20 mins a match, which was nice.
-Since the tournament is online or solo, it saves your team after a match. This stops you from loading when you lose a player. I love and hate this feature, as it could break your team to lose your star player, but then... it's blood bowl... players die... So as long as you can come to terms with this, then you'll be fine. I'm still coming to terms with it, but it's not a con.
-The team count. Who cares? Some obviously do. This in no way affected my decision to purchase this game. I have a lot of teams I enjoy playing, some are here, some aren't. It hasn't bothered me.
Cons
-To be completely honest, I bought it knowing it was blood bowl, and it is. It's better than the last in a lot of ways, it's worse in few. I don't mind the crowd is all human. The crowd in the last game was barely rendered...
-The cheerleaders are only human, this doesn't affect gameplay...  but I'll list it here, it's something they will add in.
That's about it. I just wanted to put in a review that assures people they can spend hours on the single player, just like the last game, and still have team progression. The price point is pretty good for a game I know I'll spend 100+ hours playing...
For those that aren't buying it due to the number of teams playable, well, that's a shame, but they will release more.

From publisher and developed Brad Moore, comes the indie horror game Disturbed. Released on the 3rd of October, 2016, this is a casual adventure simulation game where you go about your adventures and try not to die (although you get a lot of achievements for dying).
Play as a farmer who struggles to manage a failing farm. You come to a point where there is no more hope, and you must do something.
You figure that you will die and it is just a matter of how and where. What difference is there to make? What can a simple farmer do? Only you can answer these questions.
This game is powered by the Ren’py Engine and the visuals are 800 by 600 by default. The game runs really smoothly and there’s no connection issues (thank goodness for offline play).
I got this game around Halloween 2016, just to have a look at what it was, and found the achievements were relatively easy to get. Due to college, I abandoned my old Steam account, and forgot completely about the game. Coming back to Steam at the start of this year, I was delighted to find this again. I was really enjoying it on my old account, so to start it again and see how it went and if there were any updates was really exciting.
I found the game quite easy to remember. I managed to click most of the achievements in ten minutes of play, and then it became a lot of clicking around, seeing where my choices took me, and trying to click the last of the achievements. There was a lot to discover in this game, and it was fun to sit down for forty minutes and click around for a bit.
It was exciting to see where my choices took me, to find the horrors that waited to kill me, and to eventually beat the game.
The art style is very simplistic, however, it was still really enjoyable to look at. The sound work did well – there wasn’t much sound unless something happened, which added a tiny aspect of jump scares if you weren’t expecting them. These are easy to adjust to, however, and the jumping ceases during the game.
This game really doesn’t take too long to complete at all. As I said earlier, it only took me forty minutes (I think Steam said thirty nine minutes) to fully complete all the achievements. Achievement hunters, I’d recommend this one. It’s quite simple, although some of the achievements take a lot of time to come across, especially if you make more wrong choices than right.
I’m really glad I decided to come back to this game and give it another try. I would definitely recommend this to choice-based simulator lovers, and for achievement hunters as well. Indie horror fans would likely enjoy this one as well, so give it a try! This is definitely one of my favourite games for sure.

(Note: Though I am an amateur Games Workshop tabletop gamer, I haven't ever played tabletop Blood Bowl and I don't know if it is the same as this digital version. If not, I'd imagine it's pretty close!)
Do you have a gambling problem? This is the game for you. If you want a game that you will always win, keep moving. If, however, you want a punishing title that will sometimes make you scream for bad dice rolls, you found it. I think that's the charm of Blood Bowl 2. You could be royally screwed over on a dice roll that there was no reason to lose, yet so could your opponent. This game sometimes makes losing both fun and hilarious!
Blood Bowl 2 is a mashup between the Games Workshop high fantasy universe and American football. It is turn based and your turn continues until you are finished moving players or you make a mistake and one of your players goes down or misses a catch (a turnover.)
Each of your players has stats that determine movement range, number of dice rolled when blocking, catching, etc. The system is perfectly balanced and easy to understand. I find it very simple to estimate odds on the fly.
Want a football game where players can be injured or killed? You're looking at it! I once played a game where my opponent only had three or four players left (total is always 11 with reserves.) Best part about the injuries (or worst, depending on perspective) is that they can stick with your players permanently. Death is also permanent. It's not all bad, though, as your players level up and can pick new skills or stats. My favorite part of the game and absolutely crucial in multiplayer.
Speaking of multiplayer, there are official and user-created leagues and I haven't once found myself unable to locate an opponent. Multiplayer makes this game one of my favorites and I highly recommend it, even to people not into sports.
Single player campaign seems fun, though I was bored of playing humans so I haven't completed it. It does appear to be short, perhaps meant as a way for new players to quickly learn the game.
I give this game a 9/10. I can't wait to see some new races added to the mix. I'm also looking forward to the opening of the trading markets, where you can put players on the market and I think purchase others. Great fun! I would like to also see more lines from the hilarious commentators. (Bonus points to the devs for the Doctor Who and Game of Thrones reference. LOL!)

Superhot is *not* a first person shooter. I repeat, it is NOT an FPS. Superhot is an innovative puzzle game, using bullet time like physics to give you the opportunity to disect the levels you run through and find the path, the most efficient path, or the coolest path, to the end of the game.
The campaign lasts about 1-2 hours depending on how familiar you are with the concept, and doesn't offer too much in the way of story. It's well presented and very stylish, but is let down around the edges by some lack of precision. You'll find it takes a bit too long to learn just how close a bullet can fly past you, and you'll wonder why point blank katana swipes don't register as a hit. But aside from these minor niggles you'll enjoy the journey to the final level.
Where the game shows its hand is after you've completed the short campaign. Being able to replay the game in a number of different modes that limit your weapons, change the rules of how red guys get killed, and even measure you on how fast you can complete the levels in speed run mode (I haven't yet got to the "no restarts" mode but I dread to think how insanely impossible that might be!) The campaign may be short but it's clearly an opening salvo in a gradually increasing difficulty curve to complete all of the possible modes.
And if you're wanting something more freeform then endless mode is great for killing some time by killing red guys until you grow a bit bored of the repetitiveness and take another break.
From my gameplay so far I would assume that trying to complete the game in all its challenge modes, and exploring all the endless modes, will occupy a good 15-20 hours of your time at the very least, so I don't agree with some around that are feeling that the price point is too expensive.

This is a game in which you walk through one strange mini world after another while being lectured to by some dude who's weirdly obsessed with lampposts. It's very artsy, perhaps trying too hard at times and becoming self-indulgent (debatable whether this is intended), but I had fun playing and discovering it anyway.
If you dislike games in which your skills and actions are irrelevant (other than having to move to progress the plot), you probably won't like this one either. If you're hoping for something like Stanley Parable, be warned that The Beginner's Guide is linear, serious rather than funny and doesn't have choices/multiple endings.
Pros:
+ Atmosphere/Story: Pretty interesting "plot" that makes use of its medium in the sense that I feel like it would not work equally well as a book or audiobook.
+ Exploration: You get to see and interact with lots of surreal places.
+ Good Voice-Acting / Sound
Cons:
- Really short (90 min for me, and I took my time), I might replay it once but in general there's probably not a lot replay value to it.
- Walking Simulator: As mentioned above, you could watch someone else play it and see and hear exactly the same things.
+/- Story: Definitely not everybody's cup of tea (check out some of the negative reviews for more details), but if what you have heard so far made you curious I would recommend trying it just for the unique experience.

There is a bit of a puzzle element, especially in the speedrun challenges.  The developers knew that thinking would be an element, and begin some stages a specific way, to make you think about how you might get out of a bad situation.  You're standing in a cramped elevator, with 3 guys raising guns at you.  How do you take them all out without getting shot?  The elevator door is going to open soon, and there's more guys outside, work quickly!
The campaign is short, and can be finished in 2-3 hours.. but endless and challenge modes are unlocked, allowing you to survive against endless waves of enemies in an arena, or go back and complete stages with new rules, such as katana-only, or speedrun.  The story is interesting, I suppose.  Clever, yet not that clever at the same time.  Then again, I mainly bought this for the gameplay itself, not the game's "meh" attempt at putting the whole experience into a story, which is why I mention the endless/challenges.. that's the real meat of the game.
I'm not sure I like the body-switching gimmick.  The 7D-FPS prototype of the game didn't have it, and I don't think it's really needed.. not using it puts you at a disadvantage.   Maybe I'll get used to incorporating it into my strategies eventually.  It's not a complete turn-off or anything.. I just needed something to not like about this game, because everything else is so solid that it's hard to complain about.
I pre-ordered this game from the website for a lower price than what is asked on Steam.  Would I have paid the full $25?  I dunno.. I'd have to think about it.  It's a very cool game, and even though I'll enjoy picking it up now and then, to play through the challenges, I don't know.  It's pretty solid, but it's not perfect.  I would expect a lot for something that costs half the price of a triple-A title.
Overall, this is a quality product.  What it does, it does very well.  It deserves a place in your library, if you're looking at it long enough to be reading reviews on it.  The price at launch is steep for me, personally. but I'd certainly say it's is at least worth wishlisting.

Considering how long this game has been out, having beaten Chaos Mode, and heck, this spawned my very first Boss guide that I'd ever done on Steam, it's odd for me to write this review so late. Part of it was me debating whether this title is a "good" starting point for new Tales Of players, or whether this should be skipped in favor of something like the Tales of Symphonia Port. Others have stated that this title is an abomination to the Tales Of franchise and should be burned at the stake.
Also I've heard whether people should play this first or Berseria (the prequel) first considering it's a bit superior. To those people I must wholeheartadly say
I'll explain in the "story" category.
All that being said however, this title does have some charm to it that I couldn't overlook. That being said, let us begin.
After a brief history lesson, the scene begins with our main protagonist: an adventure-filled, happy boy named Sorey. He's accompanied by his Seraphim Companion Mikleo as they explore some ruins they discovered. Upon witnessing an "odd" storm, they fall headfirst into the ruins, but are saved by Mikleo's Artes (yes, it's spelled with an "e"). As they explore the ruins, they come across the legends of the sheperd on the walls, find a treasure, and eventually meet a human girl passed out. Eventually, after saving and talking with said human girl, before she leaves, she tells Sorey that he should attend the Sacred Blade Festavil which is held at the kingdom she's from. Why? Because she's reminded of the Sheperd of Prophecy. Thus begins a very lengthy, somewhat interesting, and enjoyable story.
There are obvious stereotypes, and many issues that arise within it. The main story is very, very bland and it's quite obvious about some things, and you'll see "plot points" before they come at you from a mile away. Some of the side stories are great though. Another thing that ticked off the fan base is the story is barebones compared to the others. There aren't any serious plot twists, no extreme mind games, but simply a boy wanting to save the world from the evil called malevolence, and battling with the concept of "evil". But in my opinion, this is one of the aspects of Tales of Zestiria that's wonderful!
Fun fact, this game is actually based off of some legends of King Arthur which is hinted at and people will notice. The characters are quite funny and interesting in their own right, several skits go over the lore, some simply have hilarious moments, and that's what I think the game is best at: It's not the end result, it's the Journey To. The overarcing plot is kinda "meh" but the parts that happen in between are wonderful. Some parts are however, questionable in their usage but further would be spoiler territory.
Voice acting is done quite nicely and all the skits are voiced. Though don't worry purists, the Japanese is still there. The English VA is not to be thrown away lightly though, and I recommend at least for your first playthrough to use English if only due to the fact that it's harder to miss some lore bits. The music is also quite nice with some lovely compositions by Go Shinna (whom you to will learn to appreciate after learning what he composed in this game), along with some other pieces.
Ah yes, that debate....I don't want to spoil, but I also don't want to be vague in this matter as Berseria IS actually superior. However, when this game came out, and then we played Berseria, people were flipping out because of the sheer amount of "HOLY CRAP! THAT MAKES SO MUCH SENSE NOW!" There are bits of lore not explained in Zestiria that are explained in Berseria that made me love Berseria and Zestiria even more! Then the question is: Why not play Berseria since it's the prequel first? Quite simply: You won't appreciate Zestiria or Berseria as much if you play Berseria first.
In my personal opinion, if you plan to play both, play Zestiria first. You'll be much happier in the long-run. If you just want to play Berseria though, then that's always an option as well.
Tales Of games all have tremendous gameplay, but the fighting can get confusing for some.
Basics are you control a character (you can hotswitch) and use four different command sequences to issue attacks. These "Artes" can all be modified to suit your need, and how you want to play. Some commands deal more damage to certain enemies then others, while some have elements (Wind, Fire, Earth, Water, etc) that deal even more damage to enemies weak against it. You also have the option to modify your AI companions. Want an aggressive support? Change it! Want someone who mainly supports hurt allies? Change it! There are many options. Though for some, it can be rather tedious to continously change commands to beat very, very specific enemies.
Various different types of "Artes" (magic in this game) can be unlocked, as well as more powerful moves, and finishing moves. All have their ups and downs.
You also have the option of using "Manual, Semi-Manual, or Automatic" when controlling your character. But for the love of all that is holy DON'T DO AUTOMATIC! That mode is more frustrating then helpful (though if you like that be my guest as it's supposed to be meant for tactical gameplay). I recommend Semi-manual first for new players (characters walk in range before doing command) then manual (instant input) when they get a feel for the expereience.
The world of Zestiria is MASSIVE and thankfully isn't completely dull. Each area has some great views but some dungeons are rather bland in taste. You will however, after several hours, want to use fast-travel unlocked decently early. A few interactable objects which is also a bit bland but not entirely bad are sprinkled here and there.
The amount of customization is staggering. From armor, weapons, to the appearance of your characters. Also for those who love it, it changes what you look like in the cutscenes as well! (eat that Shadow of Morder lol) Weapons and Armor are ENORMOUSLY customizable almost to the point of a migraine because of the amount of potential death you can create with proper crafting. I was able to create huge damage after 40 hours of crafting which was so satisfying in Chaos Mode.
You can have the difficulty catered to however you like it as well! Want something easy to merely enjoy story? Sure! Want a decent challenge? Of course! Want to be forced to grind and nash your teeth as you get frustrated that a previously low level boss can beat the crap out of you?.....I did enjoy it for what it's worth lol.
Enemies range from the standard mob (decent amount of variations though some repeats) to optional mini-bosses which give you special crystal upgrades, to the story bosses. All bosses have a "tell", all bosses can be memorized and worked on either carefully, or quickly depending on how you outfitted your characters to do what. This keeps it from getting too bland and repetative.
This is probably one of the best things about the Tales Of franchise: Variety in gameplay. Customization, playstyle, tactical or hit'em hard, you have options!
(P.S. If I missed something you wanted to know about, let me know)

An interesting premise for a game that ultimately falls flat due to pretentious writing. In brief, the game is a walking sim where the narrator - who is actually the game's creator - guides the player through a series of levels made in Source by a developer friend of his.
The basic premise appears to deal with the following two questions:
I would say that the answer to both questions is 'yes.' That doesn't mean that every game needs to be full of guns and explosions, however. The big issue I have with these walking sim type games is that they like to hide behind being 'art' when what they actually are is lazy. I love story-heavy games that have little emphasis on mechanics - visual novels, sound novels, point and clicks, FMV games, Telltale adventures etc. and these games have been around for a very long time.
Along comes the walking sim genre, which hides behind pretentious writing or accusations that players just don't 'get it' when they get bored and disengaged. I'm all for unconventional games; I don't mind if a game has barely any player interaction as long as this is made up for with a good story. This is not a good narrative. If you and I are like-minded you will have figured out where this faux-commentary is going long before the end, and when the game hits what is meant to be a crescendo your eyebrow will involuntarily be raised as if to say 'is that it?'
It thinks it is deep enough to compensate for being a cluster of boxy corridors, but it really isn't. It reminds me of another eye-rolling art excursion called 'Every Day the Same Dream' - but at least the latter had the decency to be freeware. Give this a go only if you get it on sale for €0.99 or less. Oh, and don't give this a pass because it's the same creator as The Stanley Parable  either.

So, A Hat in Time. This is a Kickstarter game that was in a development for 5 years and promised to bring back the memories of classic 3D platformer games... No, come back, please! This one is actually good, I promise!
*Ahem* So. It's surprisingly good. So far all content that the game offered me was great and it's one of the few games that I actually wanted to replay right after I completed it.
In this game you play as a girl whose name we don't know and is nicknamed Hat Kid. The game starts with you waking up on the spaceship on which you are flying back to your home. It uses hourglass thingies called time pieces as a fuel. On your way home you are flying past a planet from which a person who claimes to be a part of Mafia came to take a toll from you for passing over their town. Instead he manages to break the glass window on your ship and it results in losing all your time pieces as they fall on the planet and now you need to take them back so you could have enough fuel to fly back to your home.
The controls are good and tight. You have a variety of moves including a wall run, double jump and a dive which are pretty standart for a 3D platformer. You also have a variety of hats that have different abilities that help you to explore the levels. Also also, similar to Psychonauts you can buy and equip badges that add new abilities to your character or improve the abilites of the hats.
The game features 4 big worlds for you to explore (there are 5 worlds actually but the fifth one is just a bossfight) and they differ greatly in style and atmospere which helps to keep the game fresh and fun. For example, the first world named "Mafia Town" is a Mario Sunshine-esque world in which you are given the main objective you need to do but you can freely explore the map. The second world named Dead Bird Studio in which you are caught in battle between two movie directors that managed to get their hands on some time pieces is a more linear experience compared to the first world and so on. Each world also features bonus levels called "Time Rifts" which are pure platforming segments similar to Mario Sunshine.
The art style of this game is very good and cute, can't really say anything else about it.
The characters in this game are very good and memorable. You have the Mafia with thick russian accent who punch barrels who are dressed as old ladies to keep the town in fear, you have a scottish owl who likes to film western movies on his own train with innocent owls that just want to get to their destination on his train and a sassy penguin who is a former owner of night club who decided to film movies too, and many more.
I also want to point out the voice acting in this game. It's one of the best I've heard in a game and it adds a lot of personality to the characters and makes them much better (you also have an option to turn off the voice acting if you do not like it). Voice actors did a really great job.
The music in this game is amazing. So far every piece of music the game offered me was a delight to my ears. The game musician really needs to get an extra credit for his work.
Here's an example:
While there are a lot of good things in the game, there are some problems too. The game also brought back some cons from old platformers like strangely placed and fixed cameras which can mess with your view and thus it makes navigating the level harder, controls sometimes can be a wee bit wonky, some rough edges when it comes to graphics and animations and a story is a bit shallow in some places.
A Hat in Time is a really good and solid game that managed to bring back the feeling of the classic platformers (and some problems) while mixing in some new stuff. I highly recommend to buy this game and try it out. For me this game was one the best gaming experiences (if not the best) I had in last couple of years and definitely my favorite game of 2017.

The German/russian maps is what a we get after years of sitting through that surge of WW2 games and the fall after. It is in my opinon a great sequal to the first. I can't really say how good this game is. It really depends on how long your willing to suffer through. Can you work through getting hit by 1 shot over and over until you realize that you need to be in cover to advance? will you realize that you have no reason to be in the speacialized roles, and switch to rifleman in defeat or will you actually learn to work that class? This is nothing like CoD or BF. You are a soldier, given a rifle and through time become a killing machine. A true hero, that will be able to recover faster, go farther without tiring, and take more before giving in to the pain. They will inspire the others, and can easily sway the battles in the right moments.
Now Rising storm on the other hand is a completly different beast. You have the americans, semi auto and fully automatic rifles, heavy fire power and flame throwers. They do their job through pure strenght of arms, and hitting the enemy hard where it hurts fast. The japanese? They have normal rifles, and a full auto smg. Just one though. They also have though is they ability to plant mines with their grenades via pressure caps on them, they also can gain points by suicide running at the enemy with a grenade primed. This gives them points, and they suffer no penalty for killing themselves. they also have knee mortars so they dont have to wait for artillary to fall to blow them up at range. They also have the ability to banzai, which is their greastest assest they have. When the japanese banzai in a sufficently sized group, say 5-7 people, This causes the americans to panic HARD. They wont be able to aim, they be suppresed badly, and on top of that the japanese can take A LOT of damage during it. The japanese live and die with honor, and they won't stop until the americans are dead or going with them.
I personally think there is nothing at all like Rising storm. Nothing has ever came as close to showing what both sides did to win, and the huge difference in attitude and weapons was. This game is a must have for any person that wants a realistic, but not too realistic though there is a mode for that, shooter set in the time of staligrad.
TL;DR: This game is what you need if you're looking for a realistic like first person WW2 shooter. Buy rising storm and you get everything with it. There is no paid DLC, the only thing that is Is Rising Storm and that gets you everything though. Be prepared to be angry, and want to give up. But press on and you'll be rewarded with a gereat game.
