It's a beautiful wilderness survival game, that one) does not include zombies and two) is realistic about how difficult it would be to survive on your own, in the winter, without electricity or plumbing or grocery stores. As it's in alpha right now, so you can only play sandbox mode; and, honestly, if they had no story mode planned it would still be worth 20 bucks.
Here's the thing: even on easy mode the game can be brutal. The weather is randomized, so you could be in the middle of a nice sunny winter day, wandering around looking for food, and a blizzard hits. You're nowhere near shelter. And you only have a scavenged energy bar. And half a gallon of water. You haven't found a hatchet yet, so it takes three times as long to gather firewood. You need to find an area sheltered from the wind or you'll never get a fire going. You left your sleeping bag at your base so you can't do anything about the exhaustion setting in. Maybe you finally get a fire going, it's warm enough to protect you, you can melt snow for water, but you're getting hungry. The animals are all hunkered down, waiting out the storm, so there's nothing to hunt. You can either one, sit and wait and hope it ends soon, or two, make a run for it and hope you find a wolf's leftover deer or an abandoned building. Maybe you find a frozen riverbed and the few remaining cattails. At least those will keep you from starving; but now you've lost sight of your campfire and you'll freeze before you can get another one going. Maybe you're so exhausted you can barely walk.
You probably die.
And when you die you
. Game over, start again, better luck next time.
And I didn't even mention that the wolves are getting pretty hungry and the world-ending mcguffin-event has made them all much more aggressive than usual, and you might not be a deer but you're tastier than snow.
It's amazing.
The Hinterland team is constantly making improvements and bug-fixes alongside creating new content. I know not everyone like buying an unfinished game, but personally I love early access; I like being able to help develop a game that I think deserves it.
Also? It's gorgeous.

Disturbed is a very short Choose-Your-Own-Adventure style game with the style/technology of a Visual Novel.
I really enjoyed this game. Although some of the deaths are a little punishing (you get killed when doing something seemingly innocent), that stays true to the choose-your-own-adventure genre, so it soon becomes the type of game where you have to "save early, save often, and don't overwrite old saves!", which isn't a bad thing, it simply comes with the territory.
This trial-and-error approach added to my enjoyment as I tried to feel my way around the game and it made it really exciting when I got further into the game and started progressing more and more quickly--it made the gameplay amp up towards the end, which was very cool.
That said, this game is very linear, so once you have explored enough it becomes rather obvious where to use your items once you get them. The atmostphere is great, although I'm not sure it is quite unsettling enough to label as a "horror" game. The additional sounds like the spashing of water if you dive in the lake, or the meloncholy whine when you die are a nice touch.
I can see a lot of potential where they could have added multiple paths or ways to defeat obstacles or simply added more depth to the story, but seeing as how this game is free, these things are merely additional bells and whistles.
If you're a fan of Choose-Your-Own adventures and want to play something short with easy achievements, you should definitely give 'Disturbed' a try!

I gave this game a try on the recommendation of some of my Steam friends, and was not disappointed at all. :)
This is a sort of Choose-Your-Own-Adventure style game, where you progress through the story by making decisions about what to do next. Every decision affects the outcome (unlike some other games -
- where choice is but an illusion).
What I
liked though, was the fact that
you make those decisions, matters. For instance, you may come to a scene as yet unequipped with a certain inventory item, and if you choose to make a particular decision before you have that inventory item, you could end up losing your life.
Where the adventure gaming component is concerned, while you don't have an actual inventory that you can open and look at, the game keeps track of what items you have picked up and will automatically apply them for you when needed. This was a pretty neat system and it worked perfectly for this game.
Story-wise, the premise was intriguing enough to get me started, and the pacing & progression done well enough to keep me interested.
There is minimal atmospheric sound and no music, but whatever audio there was, was done very well. My favourite was
.
Graphics were simple black-and-white sketches, but they conveyed the environment and mood perfectly, and I have no complaints at all.
Perhaps my only gripe would be the not-so-perfect English. There were some phrasing, grammatical and eloquency issues, but none which were major enough to subtract from the overall enjoyment of the game.
"Disturbed" is a fine example of how a lot can be accomplished with a little, and that you don't need fancy art, music and whatnot to craft a good, compelling piece of work. I highly recommend this game to all old-school adventure game lovers, especially those who've been around since the days of text adventure games for 286s and DOS!
As of the time of my writing this review, "Disturbed 2" is in the works. It looks at this point to be a prequel to this game.

Alright so Banished is an oddly named civilization building game, much like Civ 5 and such, referencing the people that you control at the beginning of the game. the actual time period the game is set in is somewhere around the medieval time setting, as there is no machienes and the "Hunters"  use bow and arrow. the game is interesting ... for a while... but it does seem to get stale at some point in time, although that "point in time" seems to be randomly created and usualy related to a con mentioned below. Please do note that everything said below is of personal opinion and not to be taken in offense, or to heart. the last thing i need is hate mail because i trash talked your favorite Gatherer's Hut.
Banished is a pretty decent, but small, game to start off with, and i am in no way saying the quality of the game itself is purely negitive. i try to keep an open mind about almost every game i play. i have also spent a nice chunk of hours swimming through the game to pick it apart; i haven't just recently download and rushed to the nearest forum to spam a post with the latest "OMG THIS GAME IS AWESOME" thread that we all know too well.
Firstly, The Pro's
-Creativity
there are several types of buildings to be created that each produce special materials or goods relevent to that building, hardly any restrictions on how or where you want to place buildings (of course you can't place a graveyard or church on a mountain side) and each type of building as a somewhat realistic need for people working in that building. unfortunately, the actuall amount of different buildings could be far more, or at least more of a variety of the buildings but there are mods that add new types of buildings that you can construct.
-Economy
In-game you can build a marketplace to help distribute goods and materials among your citizens, and also build a trading post to trade with other towns or villages that you never see. it gives the feeling the the games world is larger than what your simply seeing upon your screen at the time, and the traders from other villages are mostly rythmic in there visits, about 2-4 ingame years (which i believe is around 15-20 mins per "year"). You also get tribes of nomads that visit your city and wish to become citizens, that is if you have a Town Hall built (along with two other buildings). Keeping with the idea of realism, Nomads also can bring diseases with them that can potentially be disasterous to your town.
Now, for the Cons
-Combat
there is a lack of combat within the game... no,  i correct myself, there is literally NO combat in game, your lumberjacks/hunters can't even be killed by wild animals, Nomads/Traders are 100% friendly and there is nothing like Pirates/Raiders. Following this concept, you also can not create weapons, Blacksmiths only create "Tools" or coal and there are no buildings to trade for or buy weapons.
-Resources
Yup, "Resources" is on the cons list. this concept is an "all or nothing" idea in game, you're either constantly barely scraping by or you have so much *&^% that you can't store it all. Farming in the game is nearly pointless, to the point i hardly bothered with it. For instance, building a Gatherer's Hut (picking roots and berries in the woods) produced about 3000 resources in one season with 3 people, meanwhile a 10x10 plot of farmland produced 1000 with 4 people in the same season. Wood and Stone areas are scattered around the map depending on what style of map you choose, so if you start a map and get plopped down near a bunch of lakes and mountains, you have hardly any room to build basic required buildings and the materials to even build those buildings are about a 3 minute walk for one person gather and walk back to your store building. this leads to citizens starving, freezing to death or simply ignoring their job.
and finally...
-The AI
i saved this for last because i found it to be the biggest problem that i had. on more than one occasion i have found myself yelling at my desky screen and trying to tell the little misions to construct a certain building that had been placed 3 seasons ago yet instead they went about their daily lives, probably talking about the lastest BS gossip. I have had at least 3 instances where the villagers wouldn't build either a storage building or a food generation building (while i had more than enough needed materials) yet they were complaining that they were hungry and ultimately starved to death.
the villagers will also store materials in the most random of places. I've seen a villager store a keg of alchohol in a storage barn that i had built for a gatherers hut that was on the OTHER SIDE of a mountain, yet the brewery was in town, or how about storing clothing at a fishery thats clear on the other side of town.
a personal pet peeve of mine that i found with the villagers is that they seem to "choose" when they want to work. one or two Builders will walk to a building and start construction on it but will either perform an absurdly short time of actually working on the construction and then go do something else, or they will stay at the building for days on end. When im trying to Micro-manage and plan out my village, the last thing i want is Billyjoe Jimbob heading home for a beer because he didnt feel like driving a few nails in that wall this afternoon.
All in all, Banished is a decent game for what it is, the only true bugs i have come across has been with the AI or miniscule things that i hadn't picked up on right away. the game itself is also really laid back, perfect for playing if you're allready doing something else and want this to run in the background  once you get set up to self sustainability. The graphics in game aren't award winning in my opinion but they are pretty decent for how big the game is, and if you're starting to perhaps get your feet wet with city builders as a genre then you might give it a try, but unfortuantely, gamers with considerably more skills and knowledge within this style of game will probably notice the issues and bumps in the road more than the rose covered fences lining the road.

Pester is a bullet hail arcade-style vertical scrolling space shooter and its biggest selling point is the cheap price of one dollar. For that alone, I can recommend the game, its worth the price, but looking deeper into the game, its a shallow, bare bones arcade experience that is only one step above classic Atari age retro arcade games.
The game has two modes, arcade that gives you three lives and tempest which is just a boss rush with one life. Each mode forces you to select tweaks to the mode. One of the tweaks is a duo mode where with one controller, you can fly as two ships using the left stick and trigger for one and the right stick and trigger for the other. To the game's credit there is full 360 controller support as well as keyboard support.
You can also select music, backgrounds and graphics between old school and new. I prefer old school, because I can see the pixel graphics versus the new sprites that look muddy, dark and blurry because they're stretched. In fact the entire game looks a bit blurry because of how stretched out the game is in full screen mode. Options also let you turn off the side bars with control information.
What seems to get me every time to make this a bad game is how imprecise it is. A simple tap of the analog stick or directional pad and your ship will be given a short throw rather than a nuanced or subtle movement. So I feel when flying between bullets and I need to move a bit to one direction, the controller will throw me into a bullet rather than between them. That could be the fault of the ship speed power up, but it seems to happen a lot.
There seem to be no bullet patterns or logic to the enemies. They just get shoved onto screen and you're expected to destroy them all. The screen fills with enemies and bullets rather than carefully constructed patterns. If you get stuck in a dire situation, you have bombs that will clear everything off the screen.
Other than bombs, you can collect upgrades to increase your firepower and you'll need it. Several of the enemies that stay at the top of the screen take a lot of shots and spray a lot of bullets. You collect stars that drop from enemies to fill up a power meter. Once the meter is full, use the power and you'll have a super weapon to plow through enemies and pull in stars rather than having to fly into them to collect them.
At the end of five or so waves, you'll fight a boss that's slightly larger than the bigger enemies of the game. It just feels so lackluster. Hey at least there are bosses. I will admit the game is good at preventing a boss's weakness. Such as the second boss will dive in firing missiles which would leave it open to fly behind, but the boss is smart enough to fire projectiles above it.
So the enemy design is good and I can tell the enemy logic apart from one another, but its the level design that is the problem. A giant cluster of enemies for every wave make it a game that's tough right off the bat. There is more challenge than fun.
On top of everything, the game is just ugly. The enemy projectiles are all dark green on a black background. They become difficult to see especially if you're playing in a bright room. The enemies themselves are dark on a black background too. The only bright things in the game are the player and the collectible stars. I swear that its possible for the bullets to get behind the stars so when I'm collecting a star, I run the risk of collecting a bullet with one hit death.
Pester keeps track of your high score, but there's no way to enter your name, nor any online leader boards. Its missing frills that have become a given with other games of the genre. Even arcade games in the early 80s let you enter your name as a form of glory and reward for doing such an excellent job.
There are awards rather than true Steam achievements. These awards seem to unlock new backgrounds. I'd love if the game had a random background or random music rather than being forced to chose them.
So after its all said, the choice is yours. Its worth a dollar of quarters. Otherwise, the game is unfair, jerky, imprecise, but hey its only a dollar. In an era where people buy Steam games for the cards, the price makes the game an instant hot seller, no matter how much I feel this project was rushed out the door.

Okay, so before I say anything else; this game is fantastic, and if you've never played it, you absolutely have to give it a shot. It's mechanically solid, extremely well-written, has a wonderful soundtrack, and has a setting that manages to be equal parts beautiful & disturbing. This is one of my absolute favorite FPS titles.
...sadly, the PC port could've used a little work. My first playthrough was on a console, and if you have the option, that's the one I'd recommend- no memorable flaws in that experience. This version, though, has a few issues (like mouse acceleration) that need to be addressed by editing files (as opposed to an on/off option in a menu), tends to crash instead of closing regularly, occasionally resets your video settings, and most frustratingly of all, it crashes fairly consistantly during the ending cinematic- if you try to take a screenshot to commemorate your success, double those chances. Luckily, the game's pretty affordable on whichever platform you prefer, and even if PC is where your heart is, it's still worth any grief the port might give you to experience the city of Rapture.

Few games have stuck with me as much as this, and few games are as creatively daring. Effectively utilising a "House of Leaves" like layered narrative in a way I've not previously come across in a game, The Beginner's Guide examines the need for social validation at its extremes, here in the context of the games developer and the player. Throughout it feels like a deeply personal work from its creator (whoever that may be!), and at times you almost feel like you're actually trespassing on someone else's personal space (just as the narrator is doing to Coda). Like Davey Wredon's previous "The Stanley Parable", The Beginner's Guide pushes the boundaries of what a game can be in adopting storytelling techniques not commonly seen in games. It's probably not for everyone, but at this point if it does sound even remotely like your thing - then it probably is, and I can't recommend it enough.

I mean... It's a Tales game?  Its different.
Tales of Zesterira is the Tales game that took the combat system that we had grown attached to from Tales of symphonia through Tales of Xillia 2, and turned it into a weird hack & slash-ish game.
If your new to the Tales series or looking for a good starting point in the series, Don't start with Tales of Zesteria. Ask someone else and they'll most likely hand you any of the games in the series from 2003-2014.
If your a series veteran, give it whirl. It probably could've passed for its own IP if you got ride of the Tales name (and its memorabilia). But I'll digress.
As far as visual's, its definetly on of the prettier Tales games, alot of time and detail clearly went into how everything looks in the games characters, enemies, and enviorments. Though there were one or two moments when the game did some odd things. mostly objects in the background would change shades of color when approaching them, although my personal favorite was during a cutscene around the beginning of the game that was a close up shot of Sorey (the games' protagonist), and as he began to talk his face began to stretch around his body for a moment or two before completely disappearing, leaving sorey's character model to have his black hole on his head where his face used to be. a little disturbing, but it never happened after that.
in terms of story. Imagine the RPG's of the 90's where people would tell you things like "just get past the [X amount of hours here] mark and it'll REALLY kick things off!"...But then that X amount of hours is at 12-20 depending on if you want to try and grind. Then as it goes it constatly gets interesting, then turns itself down until your finished. It doesn't make you care enough about certain story aspects that other Tales game do a great job on, and if your not speedrunning this game or doing some serious recap, alot of characters that should be important, you just forget about until they show up. Or wont remember at all just cause of how little of a role they get. I wont mention specific names, but you'll know what I mean if you try playing through it.
Another thing to note is the plot itself, again, wont go into specifics for those who want to play, but its fluffy. As in, almost all the hero's feel like marry sue's who can do no wrong. If there's an edgelord, it doesnt hit the mark. There's also this odd stance the story tries doing with topics of suicide, envy, and meanings to life, etc, but the character avoids making any statements on what should be done with these topics. It just kinda leaves you with the feeling of "I know they wanna say something, but their so worried about keeping everyone politically correct.", "almost nothing was gained from that encounter."
Last thing plot wise to mention, this game Lays it one pretty thick that tutroials are all over the place in the plot.
Now for the game PLAY. Tutorials are holding your hand for a major chunk of the game, 20+ hours in and its still feeds you pharagraphs of information. Is all of it useful? sure. In fact, I would argue the learning curves to this game are only a huge advantage to the player. But to go from a very clear tutorial, to passing it out to you until the halfway point is ridiculous. So much that the game acknowledges it when they pass tutorials off as side chats with the characters.
Combat...Its fine. Though its not what any Tales player is used to. And I would say this is the biggest turn off. Whereas I could spend hours mindlessly grinidng and farming for items in previous games since it was so fun to do, Zesteria just...makes you want to be done with it.I didn't want to grind during the last 10 hours of the game. If you take some time to learn how it works, you can be really good at it to point numbers dont matter. by the end you'll be fighting enemies 20+ (20 is the magic number apparently) levels ahead of you, and you can bop them off no sweat so long as your paying attention.
If your a Tales fan and want to give it a try, i'd say go for it. but dont go in expecting to sing praises. it's clearly got a level of love and care put into it, its not a bad game, but its different. And it shows that this game was needed to be the one to spoonfeed us when it comes to future installments.
Newcomers, give it a try, but i'd recommend a different Tales game to start you off with first.

Bioshock is a very good game but overrated in my opinion. It is the spiritual successor to the 1999 cult classic System Shock 2, which I actually played a few months prior to purchasing Bioshock. I compare these two titles closely. That might not be completely fair, but given the near identical gameplay and tone, I submit the comparison as evidence to the quality of Bioshock. Let me start off by saying Bioshock is visually beautiful and atmosphereic. The combat and RPG elements are strong and overall I had a lot of fun playing it. I DO recommend the game. However, in my opinion where it failed was the characterization and revamped gameplay directed at casual gamers. Unlike SS2, I didn't care at all about the villian and was expecting a lame ending, which was delievered. Also Bioshock suffers from the "casual gamer" elements like death without consequence and near-constant hand-holding. We all remember the good old days of 3D platformers. SM64 kicked it all off, Banjo-Kazooie brought the idea of hunting for items with much less linearity, we know the drill. Shame that they seem to be dying out now, replaced with boring old black, grey and brown shooters. A Hat In Time easily captures everything that was good about games like Sunshine, yet bolstered them further with brilliant gameplay and a charming design.
First of all, I freaking love this game's cartoony art style. It fits the game amazingly well, and makes every world a treat to look at. The diverse colour pallette is on par with Nintendo themselves, giving us everything ranging from vibrant Mafia Town to the hilariously old-school Conductor's Train to the gloomy Subcon Forest. The visuals make the game pure eye candy. Calling it 'Cute As Heck' is a massive understatement.
Next, the game is a blast to play. Hat Kid handles so well that every slip genuinely feels like your fault, and this game has probably the most cooperative camera I've ever seen in a 3D platformer, almost never screwing you over like Lakitu loved to do oh so many times in SM64. Hat Kid's moveset is beautifully diverse, giving you the run-of-the-mill basic platforming abilities like double jumps and Sunshine-esque dives, but they've been spiced with control. Hat Kid can run up walls she jumps onto, letting her pull off much longer jumps, and can cancel out of dives, meaning that you'll never overshoot your targets. Combat is surprisingly fun, giving Hat Kid an umbrella to beat the tar out of enemies with (or unleash huge lasers with if you're a Yuuka Kazami junkie like me and used the projectile badge the whole game) and pairing it with Sonic-style airborne homing attacks. Its hilarious to see a Mafia grunt block your brella swipes, only to recieve a bonk to the head and get all confused. Combine this with the brilliant hat abilities, ranging from the par for the course sprint hat (Bunny Hood flair when) to the useful Brewing Hat for chucking explosive potions at breakables and baddies alike, to the ridiculous Time Stop Hat, which literally slows time to a crawl (unfortunately, you don't get to beat people up with Za Warudo, but that's what Workshop support is for- did I mention Workshop support?) and you have an amazingly varied moveset that lets you deal with anything the game throws at you.
The stages themselves are brilliant. Dividing one world into stages is genius, as you can change each stage to fit. One level in Mafia Town, for example, has you covering yourself in mud to scare the bejeebus out of one of the Mafia until he gives you the Time Piece. Another level has you closing taps to curb a lava flow flooding the whole town, meaning you have to think about how to get to areas when your old routes are now full of child-melting lava. Battle Of The Birds has you solving a murder, getting attention from fans, defusing a bomb on a train, all sorts. And Don't even get me started on Subcon Forest. Bring spare underwear. Trust me.
Finally, the music is incredible. Smaller/Indie game franchises always have good soundtracks, the main examples being Super Meat Boy, Undertale and Touhou. This is no execption. Every track fits the game's current setting like a glove, from the calm yet uneasy Mafia Town, to the old-movie-esque Murder on Owl Express, to the blood-pumping frenzy of
(go play the game and then come back), this game's soundtrack is utterly beautiful. I'm listening to it right now, in fact. As well as that, they put voice acting in this. And somehow, ITS ACTUALLY GOOD! With The Conductor's irritatingly likeable accent, to the goon voices of the Mafia, to a very welcome cameo of JonTron in the Dead Bird Studio receptionist (also, that doesn't make this game racist, for god's sake. Stop forcing your opinions onto everyone, you whiny SJWs)  it exhumes professional voice acting, and I utterly love it.
I cannot praise this game enough. Where Yooka-Laylee tried (and failed) to re-imagine the Banjo-Kazooie style of platforming, A Hat In Time makes the perfect balance between exploration and linearity. There's usually one main path to the Time Piece, but you're free to explore the areas at your own pace. With all the hidden goodies scattered around the worlds, it's an explorer's paradise.
This game is a love letter to the days of the 3D platformer and I love it. I guarantee that you will too. Hats off to this game.

7/10 - Good game, but could (and should) have been even better.
Visually, the game is stunning.  The models and animations are superbly crafted, the indicators for tackle zones and movement allowances looks far more appealing than in Blood Bowl 1, and it's generally very clear to see what's happening on the pitch.
The game itself is a lot of fun.  There's a good amount of depth in strategy and tactics, and the variety in the available races makes every game feel different, yet still familiar.  The tutorial is a decent enough way to learn the basics of the game, and if you name your players then you have a real emotional connection to them, whether they're killing the opposing team's Big Guy or failing to pick up the ball for the third time in a row.  It makes the whole thing just that little bit more personal.
But it also has its problems.  When it comes to graphics choices, with the exception being able to turn off grass and/or spectators for fps gains, you are limited to a selection from 'low' to 'very high', with no explanation given to what these mean.  There's no way to know how detailed the shadows are, or how much antialiasing each setting uses.  For a modern PC game, this is sub-par at best.
This lack of meaningful options also extends into other areas of the game.  Veterans of Blood Bowl will want to be able to choose which skills they activate manually and which kick in automatically, but no such option exists.  Simplicity is very much at the core of Cyanide's design ethos for Blood Bowl 2, even at the expense of expected functionality.
The interface is very much designed for consoles, with lots of scrolling left to right instead of either up and down or using drop-down boxes.  This is most irritating when selecting saved formations.  You have to cycle through them one by one, and if you're too slow then you have to wait while your team reorganises itself on the pitch before you can select the next formation.  It's unnecessarily clunky and slow.
Speaking of being unnecessarily slow, repositioning individual players before the game kicks off now requires you to wait until they run into position before you can select the next player to move.  This makes setting up a formation player-by-player take far longer than it needs to.  The display for showing how many dice you will roll against an opponent also requires a short hover time now, instead of popping up immediately.  Again, it's not gamebreaking but it gets irritating.
Finally, control of the camera is often taken away from you on your opponent's turn.  Cyanide have decided that your opponent's players will take centre stage, whether you want them to or not.  It doesn't matter whether you can already see them well enough, or if you would rather look at another area of the pitch to plan your next move.  No.  Bad you.  Little Scruffy moving 3 squares is far more important than that.  Look at him.  NOW!
I'm also experiencing a lot of crashes, though I will note that I seem to be very much in the minority on that issue.  But even having followed the advice of uninstalling and reinstalling graphics card drivers, turning off all possible programs, and even reinstalling the game itself, I still get dumped out of the client on a regular basis.
But despite all this, I still have a lot of fun with the game.  I would definitely recommend it to people who want to get into Blood Bowl.  Veterans, however, may find that the differences between BB2 and BB1 are sufficient to play the older game, particularly with the reduced team roster (currently 10 teams available).

Be patient people, all the pieces are falling into place for this small development house, that has a knack for nice details and excellent atmosphere building.
For those of us who have been patient through lengthy release delays to a 95% finished produce I can tell you these facts:
1) FOR the vast majority of us, this is a far more stable and enjoyable platform than BB1 which was excellent but technically flawed
2) You get enough races at launch, really, since the whole experience is richer and deeper now (you can get more personal with your team and customize it) the launch kit is enough
3) The UI is a brilliant improvement... and I mean both the in-game UI and the menus - if the test of a good UI is that you don't notice it until you find yourself charmed by esthetics, then this one passess brilliantly
4) All the races have been a bit tweaked, the game seems better balanced now... I have had basically 9 our of 10 (I have played around 20 so far) fantastically fun games with people from the US, Europe, New Zealand and South Korea.... only a couple of disatisfied wining dolts as in in multiplayer community have been unpleasant, but even that is handled well by Cyanide
5) Connection and stability is MUCH better to BB1
6) THIS game is an ultimate strategy game with heavy reliance on dice! But the dice require a strategy of their own since they have a massive impact... the beauty of Blood Bowl is that nothing is certain, not even that 100% sure touchdown, where you are almost there.
If you are an intelligent, patient, strategy game player who wants to be massively entertained do not hesitate to pay out for this not-overpriced release (the engine makes i worthwile in my opinion)

Football. A contact sport that millions watch and love.
Blood bowl. A murder sport that millions watch and love.
The sequel to Cynanide's Blood Bowl adpation of the tabletop game of the same name.  Turn-based footbal with fantasy races as players for your team. Bashy Orcs. Agile Elves. Murder-filled Chaos abominations. Only a sample of the 7 playable races with the base game with currently two DLC races that for now were only available via pre-ordering the game. All races have their own style of playing the field and the ball. Do you want to bash and smash your way to victory? Murder the enemy team? Or just run circles around them? There's a race with your playstyle.
The game has probably hands down the best tutorial for easing new players into the core game mechanics via the single player campaign. The UI has also seen an improved overhaul from the first game making it easier to understand the math behind the dice rolling the game does to determine failures and success. It also offers both solo and multiplayer play with custom teams with a leveling system to customize them to how you see fit. Join a league and smash your way to the top.
Blood bowl does have a steep learning curve. Sure the tutorial is great at introducing all the things you need to know on how to play but learning the rest will come from practice and losing. You will lose games, players, have injuries but it's all a part of the process and makes for interesting conditions for playing each match. So read up on forums and the such for basic tactics used in the game or for team builds.
RNG is a big factor in the game so if you hate it, this game isn't for you.
A con of the current game is having DLC already when the races should have been included into the base game, not having even half the race roster the first had.

Outlast is one of the scariest games I have ever played, and yes I would say it is scarier than Amnesia. The reason why it is effective is so obvious that I'm surprised more games don't do it. Here is the secret ladies and gentlemen. PACING. Yes, it truly boggles the mind, but PACING is the key to a good survival horror game. The game doesn't just start throwing you into an attack from a murderous zombie army with a shotgun in one hand and your♥♥♥♥♥♥in the other. You start reading about a strange facility, you travel there in your car, and enter it. Even after that you aren't attacked for about a half hour. Now, keep this in mind. The game does occasionally use jumpscares, but honestly I don't mind them. They are used sparingly and the scariest part is the anticipation of the jumpscare. They are only used about 3 times throughout the story. Now, I'm not going to spoil the story, so there won't be a breakdown on what I do and do not like about the story, but it is told fairly well through documents and notes found throughout the facility. Overall, I'd give the game about a 9/10.

A number of times when being chased by... the bloke with chains round his arms (I have no care what the character names were) it was supposed to be tense, but I found it a mostly repetitive going through the motions to find where the special progress McGuffin was located before running off. It did not help that I also find the location of a run down asylum / hospital filled with THE INSANE is so utterly trite I would prefer the overused zombies of today's games rather than run through another Bedlam or Arkham (more Lovecraft, less Batman). Again, this is subjective and the mileage may vary from person to person.
So, a mechanically good survival horror game, if you can cope with the clichéd setting.

OVERALL RATING: 6/10
I would recommend Tales of Zestiria, but only if it is on sale and you have some money to blow.
The best description of this game is "okay".
This doesn't make it a bad game by any means, but it certainly doesn't make it a good game
Gameplay:
The combat in the game is an interesting thing to rate. You have a limited amount of attacks and strategies to combat oponents, which work well to their purpose but leave a lot to be desired. In short, it's sort of a button masher with grindy aspects. However, you don't get this feeling when playing it for the most part. I'd rate it about average with other JRPG games
Level and World design:
Never really a strong suit for most JRPG games. It follows the formula of designing maze like levels with numerous types of enemies. There was a large variety of backgrounds, scenery, and landscapes to explore, so I have to commend the game on that. However,  the cave areas and other maze-like combat areas don't distinguish themselves in terms of gameplay, and I consider this a missed opportunity and game mechanic flaw.
Plot:
The plot is undoubtedly the weakest aspect of the game. It's a cliche ridden bore. The whole story is very one dimensional and is not interesting for the most part. It's a classic tale of good vs. evil, with very weak attempts made at breaking this mold.
The quests and subquests were, for the most part, entertaining, but very few stood out as more than mildly interesting. In short, it's the main quest line and its plot that are the weakest parts of the game.
Characters:
The characters in Tales of Zestiria are pretty one dimensional, but likeable for the most part. This seems to be a pretty common theme in most JRPGs and ToZ is no exception. However, most of these characters play their part well, with the exception of the main character, Sorey, who is by far the most boring and uninteresting of all the characters in the game. He's given practically no personality besides being the 'hero' and the 'nice guy'. There are many times in the game, mostly during the cutscenes, where you'll just be face palming at his naivete and general cluelessness. The villains, for the most part, are also uninteresting and dull. The game makes an attempt at fleshing out their bland personalities but does a bad job doing this.
Music:
Nothing too much to say about this. The music isn't bad but it isn't memorable at all. Very bland and generic across the board.
Other areas, pros and cons:
There are a couple of other things that I have to mention when reviewing this game.
Elemental ability types and weapon upgrades:
The weapons and gear in this game follow the traditional atk, def, mag. def, etc. item attributes. This is a JRPG standard and so there's nothing really for me to say here. However, these items also have fire, earth, water, and wind elements that can be combined to increase the power of the items. These elements are mostly chosen at random for your items, and you'll constantly be frustrated trying to properly align them in order to max out the potential of your weapons. The game has remedies to help you, such as weapon fusion, but this does not help much. This is definitely a frustrating aspect of this game that was executed poorly.
Difficulty:
The game can be very interesting on higher difficulties. It can be a good challenge defeating bosses on these difficulties. It isn't too difficult but it isn't too easy, either. It strikes a good balance.
Other gripes:
You play the first 1/3 of the game with Alisha, a knight and princess. However, after a certain part in the game, you never get the opportunity to play with her again, and her character's plotline is given an unsatisfactory conclusion. It was just a weird choice for the developers of this game to wean you on to a character and then take them away from you.

Other pros:

Customization:
You get a decent amount of customization for your characters. The controls are also decent and can be customized to an extent.
CONCLUSION: This game is painfully average in many respects. It has its flaws, but despite this, I would still consider Tales of Zestiria worth playing. I love good indie games. And this one is good. Indie games basicly live from an idea, from originality. Limbo is a game that proves it. Black & white graphics, horror themed forest, little guy in the middle of nowhere and going through lots of puzzles. That's original, I bet you can't name a game like that that's already on the market.
Graphics are again black & white, that's cool, along with the "vintage horror movie grain" it really adds an awesome atmosphere. Details are presented also really well, grass, sparks, dust, everything like that. You can't really find something bad about it.
Gameplay is simple, 5 keys only. No skill needed there. But it's a puzzle game, it makes you think. So in lots of cases, you need to worry about the timing and figuring out how are you gonna get past each section.
In my opinion, a big factor in any kind of game is replay-ability. This game doesn't really offer you that. Although there's an achievement where you have to complete the game without dying more than 5 times. But it's fun to not play it for a couple of weeks, forget about all the solutions and playing it again.
Overall, it's one of the best indie games I've ever seen, it's beautiful to look at even after figuring out all the puzzles. I'll give it 8,5/10.

After a good 7 hours of playtime, I must say, the gameplay is phenoenal and unlike anything I've ever seen before, it's done well, there are verry few times that you'll die and say "Now that was just bull."  Even when it's an enemy that comes out of nowhere, this game makes you feel like you are ultimately responsible.  The only problem with the game mechanics is that some of the walls and corners seem to have inflated hitboxes, so bullets will strike against corners they wouldn't have hit.
HOWEVER, this game's story almost convinced me to give the game a negative review for two broad reasons:
1:  The story is out of place, slow, and interupts the fast paced action.
2:  The type of story was very poorly executed.
Before you read this rant, the story only covers about 2 hours of gameplay at most, so the other five hours I played at the time of writing this review was spent slicing through bullets with a katana, throwning katanas through people and catching them on the other side, and punching red dudes in the face.  Those first two hours were actually the tutorial.
As for the story:  You're playing some game you're not supposed to be playing on an old DOS terminal, you pretend to type into a box, and then press buttons you're asked to press, and occasionally you're rewarded with the sweet gameplay.  Think of the broad concept of Pony Island, except strip down all the interactive elements of the actual story and replace the pony jumping game with Super Hot's bullet hell, and make the game as condecending as physically possible.  For that type of story to work, the gameplay cannot be more engaging than the story, it doesn't have to be terrible, but it needs to be the means to the end and not the center focus of the game's value.  Not to mention that you need to let the player try to resist the system/overlord/condescending story that interrupted the awesome gameplay, or else the story is just boring.
Now, all that doesn't sound too bad, right, not nearly bad enough to bring down an otherwise amazing game and earn a negative review?  Well, it was one line in particular that nearly convinced me to write a negative review.  When I thought that this story couldn't get any more condescending, that it's tone of "We own you now, do whatever we say, slave," it uttered this line and ended the tutorial "Now go tell all your friends to play this game, tell them it's an innovative shooter and it's amazing." as "recruting."  This might work in a game about the story part of it, if it's delivered when I feel like I've won, when I feel like I've finished the game, or at the very least, have experienced the most fun part of the game and WASN'T TALKED DOWN TO BY A CONDESCENDING SYSTEM/OVERLORD/ADMINISTRATOR, but after having sat through what is by far the worst story in a game I otherwise enjoy, I really wanted to click no, I really wanted to tell people it wasn't worth their time, just to say "Hey, ♥♥♥♥ you" to the system/overlord/admin who thinks that their constant interruptons are somehow better than the act of slicing through bullets with a katana, and has the balls to not just ask me recomend it to my friends, but to say it's "innovative."  (Yeah, the game is pretty innovative, but really, don't tell me what words to use when describing it to my friends.)
So, is the game still good despite having the most condescending and pretentious story I've ever dealt with?  Do not underestimate the amount of fun you can have with a katana.
Yeah, this game is worth $15, maybe $20... but I've had more fun with this thing than most $60 games that are out now, so, not complaining about the price.

I believe that this game is the kind of RTS that focuses on the amount of units & production you have in the shortest amount of time, while neglecting the controlling units part of the RTS experience (micro, as you would normally call it)
I noticed that the easiest way to overcome my opponents wasn't to carefully maneuver my units into a great position, but rather to just make as many vehicles & units i could in 5-10 minutes and press A towards the enemy.
So if you think that managing a base & your resources is fun, then this game is great for you, this game is great for you. But if you also enjoy controlling your units intensively and getting better positioning, the game may seem a little bit dissapointing. (Although it's still a great amount of fun.)
Another downside to this game is that the FPS is locked at 30, no matter what you do, since the FPS and game speed are tied together. (Not sure how to elegenatly explain why, so just understand it's locked at 30 and there isn't much you can do about it.)
So while the game certainly has its flaws and weak points, it's still a very enjoyable and great RTS.

LIMBO is a quite simple game, but the execution is what makes this a great game. The characteristic monochrome colour scheme may look a bit gleary at first glance, but it does hammer through the glum setting and "feel", and is what makes this game beautiful and immersive.
LIMBO is what I'd call a horror-adventure-puzzle. You'll encounter a lot of creepy creatures and critters, and you'll most definitely experience some pretty gruesome deaths. The puzzles are varying and decently challenging. It's a side scrolling game, and you can never go back - this means, the puzzles are always isolated, and you don't have to backtrack to solve them.
Another interesting thing about LIMBO, is the complete lack of GUI. You just start the game, and are placed directly in the game, with no explanations or tutorials. However, the controls are incredibly simple and intuitive, so the lack of GUI/text just means better immersion.
Play the game in a dark room with a joypad in hand - does wonders for stress release.

LIMBO is an entirely melancholy, disturbing, and unhopeful experience. Blood bowl is a fantasy sports game with additional emphasis on the fantasy element.  Players create and manage teams composed of various fantastic creatures and play a game loosely based on American football in the sense that there is an inflated pig bladder and people try to carry it down a field.  Unlike American football, it is perfectly acceptable to ignore the ball and attempt to kill as many opposing players as possible.  The game is played in turn-based style similar to the X-Com games.  Each player on your team may attempt one action during your turn, but the turn ends immediately should any player fail.
Blood Bowl 2 improves upon the original Blood Bowl release with smoother graphics, better visibility, and a helpful success chance calculator so that memorizing probabilities or using a calculator is not necessary to play safely keeping the end of turn on failure rule previously mentioned in mind.
The game is tailored towards players new to the blood bowl game and it's rules.   The campaign doubles as a fun and engaging tutorial that slowly introduces the core rules in a step by step manner, then adds some challenges to the usual game modes to help build confidence and skill.  The game is not as focused on veteran players of the Blood Bowl franchise, so please bear that in mind when reading the reviews of seasoned veterans who are voicing their discontents.
The developers are extremely proactive about adding to the game and have already made two major releases to improve the game following direct feedback from players.  There is an active, and fanatical fandom for Blood Bowl spanning decades (the original game table top game was created in 1987), you are never going to be short on multiplayer opportunity if you are open to league play.  The official public league, however, is not very friendly to new players so shop around for private league communities to join if you want to sample the authentic multiplayer experience and enjoy this game at it's best.
The full playset for this game includes 24 official teams and two unofficial teams supported by the developers.  At the time of this review there are 8 teams already included in the game, two as DLC and 4 more announced as DLC in the near future.  Each team adds it's own unique take on the Blood Bowl game for an impressive number of possible match ups.  If you are a fan of sports, or a fan of strategy games, this game is not likely to get stale for you.

Cuphead and Mugman are the main protagonists of our tale of side scrolling local co-op only action (just thought I'd get that out of the way). They made a deal with the Devil on a game of craps, thinking they couldn't possibly lose, they were wrong.
The plot sets the mood from the very beginning, a game with an innocent cartoonish look and innocent looking characters but underlying adult themes are afoot... moral of the story? Don't gamble with your life.
Cuphead plays very much like the original Contra games, except the colors are reversed this go around. P1 (Cuphead) is red and P2 (Mugman) is blue. You walk around an overworld map choosing destinations to venture in to. Some are bosses, some are side scrolling levels.
There's always more than a single option available to you but in the end you have to complete every stage to progress the main story. There are side quests to embark on by talking to overworld NPC's and hidden coins to collect. There's a shop to buy different styles of shots and charms to help balance out your weaknesses as a player.
Once an area is selected you then choose your difficulty. At first only Simple (Easy) and Regular (Normal) modes are unlocked. Once you finish the game, Expert (Hard) mode becomes available.
The differences between modes are as follows:
Enemies have slower attack patterns, their attack cycle pool is a bit more shallow, meaning they won't use all of their available attacks and some phases of a boss fight will be removed entirely.
A normal level of play for above average gamers. Most boss phases are available, and most attack cycles are available, enemies attack at an increased speed over Simple (Easy) mode. Highest rank you can earn is an A+.
For true masochists. All the stuff from Regular (Normal) mode is here, except now all boss attack speeds are increased by about 1.5. Some bosses also have an extra phase added in and some even combine attacks together. It's like playing the game on turbo mode but you can now earn the coveted S Rank if you perfect the stage. Good Luck!
Once you've made your choice in difficulty you proceed to shoot, jump, parry and dash your way through some side scrolling areas (6 in total to be exact) but the meat of the game is just an all out boss brawl. There's over 20 bosses to fight all with unique patterns and looks, no two bosses are alike so you're going to have your work cut out for you.
At the end of each stage you're graded on your performance based on certain criteria:
How long did it take you to finish the fight / stage?
How many hits did you take?
How many parry attacks did you perform?
How many super attacks did you land?
Trying to get A+ (on Regular mode) or S ranks (on Expert mode) seems to be the meat of the game and where most of your time is going to be spent. You could always just breeze through stages never thinking twice about how well you did but if you want to be a Cuphead master, you'll have to practice.
Rank
hinders you from completing the game,
to your progression of the story. Once you finish a level or beat a boss, more of the map will open up to you and you can venture onward.
It's a fantastic game. As someone who grew up with Contra, it's a love letter to that game series as well as fans of a lost age of art and music. It's actually one of the only high quality side scrolling shoot 'em up games on Steam of it's kind that stays true to form. Simple yet incredibly challenging.
I would recommend the purchase if you're interested in something different for a change. Put down the mouse and keyboard and pick up ye olde game controller and go to town. I played this game for 8 hours straight and finished it in a single sitting. It took a lot of patience and concentration but it's completely do-able on Regular mode... Simple should be a breeze for the casuals. It helps to have grown up in a generation where this genre was a household name and not so niche as they've become today... If you're an old boy like me, this game should be an adequate challenge but not impossible by any stretch of the imagination.
There's a lot of stigma going on with this game right now and some gamers are saying the difficulty curve is causing them to think twice about purchasing. Rest assured there's a difficulty selection built in to the game before you access each level so there's really no excuse to be afraid... if you can't handle it, play on Simple mode. Remember you have 2 hours to refund.
The difficulty spikes fairly quickly so you know, just don't be a Dean Takahasi and take 10 minutes to beat the tutorial and you'll be able to see if the game's challenge is truly for you. Although if it does take you more than an hour to beat the first stage even, I would suggest refunding it... you're not going to make it.
Even though ratings are highly subjective and don't really mean anything, it's like an 8 / 10. An above average game and will end up being a cult classic.
It's a great game but it's not a perfect game by any means, it can be insanely unfair and frustrating at times, especially if you're going for A+ or S Ranks... this is where the game shows it's true imbalance.
The dev's could have did more with the equipment system as it seemed kind of basic. Aside from the peashooter, spread shot and chaser (homing) weapons, the extra weapons and charms we never saw in promotional videos were all lackluster and really gimmicky... I tried them all once and switched back to the basic stuff. The variety of weapons just could have been a bit better. There's also no way to upgrade your weapons either, weapons are always at the same strength level, you'll never feel over powered in this game ever.
Some bosses are a bit ridiculous in length. Some bosses can take upwards of 10 minutes to complete which is a bit crazy and defeating at times. It actually makes the first phases of the boss fights tedious, unfun and annoying to have to endure if you're only having trouble on the final phase.
I'm also not impressed you can't choose to play as Mugman in single player. You're basically forced to play as Cuphead in single player mode... not that it matters, it's just an asethetic thing but I personally perferred Mugman's design over Cuphead... options are always nice and it wouldn't have taken them much effort to throw in a character select screen before you start playing.
It only has local co-op which is also another cop-out from the developers. I mean I get it, it's supposed to be retro but please, we're living in 2017, there's no excuse for not programming some netcode in this thing just for convenience sake.
The developers claimed if the game sells well they may include online co-op.  I'm not going to hold my breath on that one. If we ever do get it, this game will be long forgotten by that point.

Pharaoh's Tomb  is a puzzle platformer and not a good one…I would have enjoyed the game if it was not for the FAST system A.K.A. bad programming.
You see every object in the game have a rectangular bounding box where its borders can be larger than the actual object on screen (the player himself, traps, projectiles and enemies).
So what does that all means you ask? It means that the hit detection is really REALLY bad since it not pixel perfect and as a result you will die by running into objects like traps and enemies that you can clearly see on screen that you didn't even touch them at all!
You can learn approximately where are the location of the borders of your main guy and every other thing in the level but you will still die because of this stupid FAST system and it's god awful hit detection…
What other problems?
Well there is the fact the sometime you wont be able to throw a javelin after landing on a tile and as a result the enemy will kill you.
There is also the fact that the momentum of your jump can randomly be stopped because you grabbed an item and thous making you fall to your death.
If not for those problems it would have been a nice short game but sadly even after finishing all 4 chapters (80 levels) I still cannot recommend it.

Yes, I'm giving this game a thumbs-up.  But let's get something straight first: this is an old-school platformer.  And I don't mean that in a good way.  Here is an idea of some negative things to expect:
- Hit detection is horrible and you *will* get frustrated by it.
- The graphics are very low resolution, even compared to other titles in the 3D Realms Pack.
- The game only uses four colors.
- The levels use the same blocks over and over.
- The levels are very small.
So why am I giving this a thumbs-up?  Simply put, I think the level designers actually did a pretty good job given what they had to work with.  Like I said, the levels are very small.  But I found them pretty interesting.  As an example, they often feature disappearing and appearing blocks that will route the player around in unusual ways.  Some of the more challenging levels require the player to carefully plan what order to get objects in to keep from getting stuck.  There are definitely some interesting ideas here, mixed in with the occasional bit of "old-school" unfairness.
I wouldn't call it a great platformer by modern standards, but I did find it an interesting diversion when I had a few minutes to burn.  The levels are so short that you can do one or two very quickly and then move on to something else.  (Note: Press 's' to save game and 'r' to restore.  I don't see that documented anywhere.)
And this isn't just nostalgia speaking, either.  I didn't play this one when I was growing up, though I did play its (much better) sequel, Arctic Adventure.  Don't get the 3D Realms Anthology for this game, but don't be afraid to check it out.
If half Life 2 redefined the single player FPS, then counter strike redefined the multiplayer online component.  Classic, fun, easy to play, hard to master.

So I bought this game while it was on sale, and I am satisfied so far. To all of those people expecting an upgraded version of Flatout, don't buy it yet. It needs A LOT of work to come close to that. But if you are look for a game that has a clear potential of being so, then this is the one to buy.
One of the best parts of the game is clearly the realistic soft body system. The metal bends according to where you hit the car and how hard you hit the car, something which you often don't see in racing games. There is a problem to this though... it is too realistic. During these few minutes I have been playing I saw 2 cars with their roof literally flattened to the point the driver should have been killed... and to the point where the steering wheel popped out of the roof so yeah, the car's soft body physics are taken seriously too far.
The game modes that are offered are vast for a game in pre-alpha. Figure of 8, plain old destruction derby, mudbowls, you name it. Although this game is meant to be a destrction derby type of game, I would really like to see tracks where you can plainly race since it would give you a relaxing breath after all the mayhem.
The car choice so far looks promising, although I hope that more are added tp the list... much more. I mean 10 cars is hardly a selection right? But the models are awesome, nothing too flashy but don't all look like rust buckets. Another interesting feature regarding cars is the ability to change its parts. For example, you can change your stock exhaust manifold to a racing exhaust manifold provided that your car is compatible with the upgrade.
Something that really sucks though is the career... because there is actually NO career mode yet. For f***'s sake why the hell didn't you include a friggin' career mode?? People, this game has been in early access for whole months and it doesn't have a simple career mode yet? So yeah, no career mode yet...
Another thing that I really didn't like is the fact that they put in the feature to repair your car's parts as they can be bought in a used condition thus not being totally efficient... but you can't use it for some reason. So the button is there, the concept is on the plate in front of you but you can't touch it cause your hands are tied behind the chair. That's exactly how it is.
Finally, I would like to talk about the game's damage system. It is total bull****. I seriously wouldn't recommend hitting the other cars, in fact avoid them. This is because you will get huge damage all the same. In destruction derby I ended up finishing 22nd but I was (according to the statistics at the end of the game) the hardest hitter... so shouldn't I have the honour of being 1st?? Especially if I wasn't hit during any part of the race but only hit other cars?? Yeah, it needs some work.
In conclusion, although I like the game so far it still isn't worth getting at full price. But if you manage to find it on sale grab it. I did have fun playing this game but some crucial details are missing, and they must be implemented fast. The developers are getting lazy as a lot of games that were in early access after it were completed before it. And honestly I don't want to feel that I wasted my money on this, it has the potential to be a GREAT game.

For all the hype this game received, I found that I was not enjoying it. The experience was plodding, with stretches of nothing bridging gameplay. The death sequences took too long to play out, breaking any sense of flow, and the correct path to take was often hard to see. The bleak color palette and lack of aesthetic left me nothing to really enjoy about the experience, and I stopped trying about a third of the way through.

If you are looking for a casual experience, SUPERHOT is a woefully brief but creative and challenging experience. Pick it up if it's on a sale if you like more puzzle-y first person shooter.
If you are one of them speedrunning folks, such as I, SUPERHOT is an incredibly execution heavy, fast paced and subversive speedgame wherein the harder you push your time the more you subvert the core design of the game. The overall dearth of glitches and exploits makes it easy to avoid bottlenecking in terms of practicing difficult skips or tricks, and the decent level of RNG puts the impetus on the runner to adjust on the fly. I was really expecting great things from BB2, but I'm sad to say I'm rather disappointed. I can't give it a positive review for now, even if I hope that if some issues are corrected and more content injected to the game, I will gladly change my review.
The Good:
- Nice graphics
- It's Blood Bowl... It's brutal, it's fun, it's challenging. But well, that's thx to the board game rules, the videogame adds little to that.
- Cool multiplayer with permadeath: it adds a sense of danger everytime you play, it's fun.
- Cleaner HUD. There has been a lot of complaints about the "player cards", but I find it not so annoying, it's rather clear and nice.
The Bad:
- The campaign is crap: you only play 1 human team, with false rules. It's utterly boring, not worth your time if you already know BB1.
- The solo content is mediocre: the solo leagues are just multiplayer leagues but with AI. It all feels too generic for me, games are chained without other things to do inbetween apart from the rare level up. It feels really empty.
- No player stats: that's the major complain for me, what's the point of playing games after games when you have no player stats (how many TD, passing, blocking, etc...) and leaderboards between all teams?? That's the basic feature missing that is the cause that I don't want to play anymore: I just don't see the point.
- No visual enhancemnent when players level up: it's not major, but the lack of all these little features makes that you don't care for your team players, because they stay the same even if they are über strong.
- Games are veeeery long: solo or multi, one game lasts in average 1:30 hours... It's too long! For just one quick game, when you don't have that much time to play anymore, you know you must reserve 2h of your time to play just a little game...
- In solo, you can't speed up turns like you could in BB1: it made the whole thing a lot less repetitive.
- The commentaries from Jim & Bob become repetitive very quick.
The Good to Have:
- It's not major, but watching the same hit animation over and over when you block someone become really dull after a while, considering that you block A LOT during a match. I would have launched this animation only on big hits like injuries.
- Where are the women? There's only 1 female player type + the duplicates pom pom girls. A strong lack of variety here, it's not made to help making women play this kind of games...
- Eye candy: different pom pom for each race, a real spectating crowd, etc... What I don't understand too, is why making a big solo campaign with a lot of animation and what not, but for kick-off events you just have one poor line of text where you could have cool animations? (like, spectators trampling players...)
SO that's that, my major complaint is that in solo, the content is very thin and don't want to make you take care about your team and see it to the top, and in multiplayer it's good but the matches are very, very long so it's a strong barrier, for me at least.
Hope the game will be updated and devs will listen to the community! It can become very cool.

I've been planing to do a RO2 review for quite some time now, but never really got around to do it...until now! This review might not be perfect or complete. But these are my thoughts about the game and yeah...here we go.
As you might have guessed from the game's title, this fps takes place during WW2. There are two parts of it: vanilla RO2 on the european eastern front, where you fight as either Germany or the Soviet Union(goodies: tanks/vehicles, OOORAAAH!), and the pacific theatre of war expansion Rising Storm (goodies: flamethrowers/katanas, Baaanzaaaii!).
Beware though: as RO2 is primarily a multiplayer title, the AI in both SP and MP is rather...sub optimal. It sucks.
Therefore, instead of buying Heroes of Stalingrad for the SP content like a friggin moron (like me...), I HIGHLY recommend buying the Rsising Storm expansion, as it also happens to have ALL Heroes of Stalingrad MP maps so...yeah. No brainer :)
But now! Enough with the theoretical nonsense and onto the ACTION! Huuza!
RO2 imo fills a very interesting niche between games like CoD (fast paced, very arcady FPS) and games like Arma 3 (veeery slow paced, big focus on realismn).
Keep in mind: I realise there are more games out there than just these two, I only picked them as represantatives of two very different game design philosophies.
So RO2 might be the perfect game for people who find CoD to be too much of the arcady bull**** it is (please excuse my Frensh here, but I really fu***** hate CoD) and Arma 3 to be too much...well, just too much. RO2 is still fast paced...you rarely ever have to walk more then 30 seconds to come within enemy contact, but one bullet can still drop you.
Other features for example are a suppresion system which makes your aim go all over the place if somebody shoots you a lot as well as weapon unlocks/improvements for all classes/weapons.
But what is it really all about? Well, there are several different game modes of which the most popular is "Territory". Ever played a round Battlefield Rush mode? Yeah, it's pretty much like that. Capture one Point (sometimes 2 or even 3 at the same time) after another and win the map! But keep an eye on both tickets and time!
Both are limited, so the attacker needs to hurry! And the defender has to play it smart, otherwise the defending team might end up stalling the attack but ultimately running out of tickets(=lives/respawns), which creates a very interesting dynamic.
I believe there are some other modes as well, but truth be told...I have never played anything else in over 400h RO2.
There are also two different types of servers: campaing or rotation. On a campaing server the victorious team gets to choose if it wants to attack or defend and which territory / map to attack. On a rotation server...well...there is a fixed map rotation :D
If you still want to know about those modes
-->

Germany and Russia are fairly well balanced. Some might say the Russians have the upper hand in CQC, but that's not really the case. At least in my opinion. There is no real imbalance.
However, some people keep saying that the fight between USA and Japan is soo unfair because US=OP. And on first glance it does seem that the US have better weapons, higher firepower etc. Example: the US rifleman gets a M1 Garand. That's a semi automatic rifle. The Japanese Rifleman however, only gets to play with either the Arisaka Type 99 or the Type 38, both are BOLT ACTION RIFLES. I could go into details of stoping power, range, accuracy yadda yadda. There are guides for this if you are really interested in stats like this(remember the 1 Bullet=Death rule?^^) . To sorta balance things out, most maps are designed for the US to be the attackers, so the Japanese have the advantage of being in the defense.
I still recommend for new players to start as the US(maybe even on a campaign server) because their weapons are far more forgiving. Trust me.
A quick guide on what makes the Japanese so uber awesome was made by WilliamTheTard-san:
Thank you, Will! When you follow his advice you "will"(get it? :D ) end up like this:
Kicking♥♥♥♥♥and chewing sushi.yummy...
Once you are ingame you will notice that there is a class system. The classes are ranging from the ordinary rifleman to extremly deadly flamethrowers.(oh, and tanks in stalingrad^^) There is a slot limit though with the majority of soldiers being said riflemen, so better be quick to grab that lovely MP40/Thompson!
There is also a squad system and a team leader, but I won't go into any details here. Suffice to say: While squadleaders are mobile spawn points for their squads and therefore are IMMENSELY important in both offense and defense, the teamleader can call in recon planes (that shows enemy locations on the map even if it's not pin point accuracy) and can drop big fu***** artillery strikes on those poor souls of the enemy team who happen to find themselfes under an arty marker.
Both SL (=squadleader) and TL (....exactly! Teamleader) get to choose from a lot of shiny weapons too. They are NOT however for storming the damn beaches of Iwo Jima on ur own, but for protecting urself from single enemy soldiers who want to kill you! SL and TL are very important for a team's success and a match's outcome is often not determined by individual skill, but by the coordination between TL and SLs.
Oh, they also get smoke grenades(1 for SLs, 2 for TL) to screen the own team's advance.
For the ordinary grunt, RO2 playes a lot like any other FPS. The controls are fluid and intuitive (WASD...), the cover system is total garbage though...don't you dare to use it. Once you get used to the increase of range (you'll find yourself shooting at guys 150m+ in the distance a LOT) and to the fact that you die every minute or so ;) there is really nothing to prevent you from having a BLAST. Except maybe teamkills...which DO happen a lot. Because, well...you fight over large distances, you have an itchy trigger finger and you DROP PEOPLE WITH ONE SHOT^^. But it's part of the game, it happens and it kinda is part of the fun too.
Here is a little tip that will safe you A LOT of frustration: Allies (Russians, Americans) sprint with their weapons in front of their chest. In BOTH hands. Axis (Germans, Japanese) sprint with their weapons in their right hands only!
Oh, did I mention RO2 has an ingame voice chat which people actually use to talk tactics and don't abuse the sh*t out of and try to be the most annoying little f**** there are?(except on Russian servers...I mean, I don't speak Russian but I recognise recordings of speeches/parades on the Red Square when I here 'em^^)  Yeah, the RO2 community is pretty awesome.
If you are still with me after this DAMN wall of text and you survived my horrible English, there is really nothing that should prevent you from buying this game.
Like right now.
I mean it...it's awesome :)
In case you want to see some ingame scenes first I picked a completly random LP from YT ( seriously...idk this guy), where you can see a defense on IWO JIMA on the Japanese side.
EDIT: He seems to be playing on an action server. Danger indicators, crosshair (only iron sights on realism) and "killed from location" are usually not in the game when you play RO2 these days.
My final verdict: 9/10
With that said, I wish you a lovely day.

If you play this game, know that you will come to know despair.
Blood Bowl is basically Football except with violence and murder (plus Orks and Elves and♥♥♥♥♥♥. You make a team of 11 players (giving them all unique names) and fight against other people. You knock over enemy players, you grab the ball, pass the ball and hopefully score and win. After the game, you get skill points for your players and level them up.
But here's the thing: When your players get tackled or hit or just generally ♥♥♥♥ up, they have a chance of getting an injury or dying. This injury or death is permenant. You may go into a game with 13 players and come out with 10. Or 9. Or 8. An injury might cause your star player might come out with a permenant unremovable stat point loss. And this handicap will persist FOREVER.
And the best part? If the dice and RNG are against you, there's absolutely nothing you can do about it. A tiny level 1 Goblin can kill a giant level 5 troll on the first turn if the dice are with it.
Every Blood Bowl team is thus a ticking time bomb that's just one game away from being destroyed forever. My High Elf team is 13-2-3 and riding high, but I know very well that the day will come. The day when I roll double 1's on a block and use a reroll to get another set of double 1's. The day when one of my Blitzers will fail an 83% success rate dodge and immediately die. The day my most valuable player is killed by a Turn 16 spite foul by some bitter Russian I just swept 4-0. I know that it'll happen.

Pharaoh's Tomb is a game I enjoyed as a child, and that child was pretty dumb.  This game is not good, and not even particularly good for the time.  There's like 80 levels or something, but about 10 levels of actual content.  There's not a lot of puzzle or enemy variety, just the same building blocks used over and over again.  I mean, it's a decent challenge, and they get a lot of mileage out of it, but...
Well, when you read the directions, the developer is excited to talk about his FAST system of animation that makes things super fluid, but makes everything have a rectangular bounding box larger than the actual guy/trap/bullet.  This really should read more like an apology for being a bad programmer because this large bounding box nearly ruins the game.  You can sort of learn to leave extra space so you don't run into stuff when clearly nothing is touching, but it's frsutrating and most of your deaths will be a result of this FAST system and it's #$%@! hit detection and oh now my heart's acting up.
Anyway, it's a bad game now, it was a mediocre game back then, and it's not worth spending more than a few nostalgic miniutes poking at it.  Almost any modern platformer will be a better use of your time even if they don't have FAST(tm)(r)(c) technology.
