I was spurred into making this review to counteract the toxic contingent of gamers that think it's too expensive.
It's not, it's worth the $25 at launch, and it will continue to be. It's certainly in contention for my game of the year and the amount of time that I have spent thusfar and will likely spend into the future on SUPERHOT make it well worth such an amount of money to me.
It's a high concept idea for a game - time moves when you move. But it elevates this fairly simple element with its stark visual presentation, its sinister narrative, and its sense of style that it maintains throughout the campaign, such as it is.
It took me around two and a half hours or so to finish what comprises the 'story', with some levels taking more tries than others. Since that time, though, I've been combing through the other modes. The Katana-only Challenge, for instance, poses an interesting break in the flow that the game has reinforced up until that point, thereby forcing you to rethink your approaches with a certain amount of caution that you might not have considered if you happened to be predisposed as I was to stealing guns from people and blowing up their friends.
Additionally, there are time-attack and endless modes, and possibly yet more that I have yet to unlock, so I think I'll be spending a bit more time yet on it.
In the end, you're going to have to decide whether the price is worth it or not, but it's not relevent to the content of the game and, as such, it can only be seen as disappointing that people are so willing to disparage something not because it isn't good, but because it isn't good
There should be no place for such a thing in this review system. The craft and time that were put into this game, stretching all the way back to when it was first conceived during the 7DFPS jam, are incredibly apparent—immanent with the cracking sound of every bullet and shattering cluster of red polygons.

I can't recommend it or not. The core gameplay is great, but there are a lot of problems. If you like the demo and would like to play with variations on it on ~25 levels, go for it. An extra gameplay mechanic gets chucked in halfway to spice things up a little.
It's a lot like Portal in that it's a small, short puzzlish game with an excellent, original atmosphere and style, but it's nowhere near as polished.
Story is compelling and fun, but only 2 hours long. Half of the challenge modes are good, half are garbage, there's about 12 in total. Endless mode is fun but you don't have any rewards or goals. Time-trial mode is the same. What sealed the deal for me continuing to play was the secret-finding exploration mode.
It's fun to start up and play one or two levels for 5mins.
Add a level editor and proper way to share them and this would be solid gold.
~~~ Here's all the problems that should be easily fixed ~~~
Endless modes and time-trial modes are lack-luster; it doesn't compare scores against friends or give rankings/grades. Stupidly, the first ~1.5 seconds of in-game time occur with the loading screen still up, so you have to begin blindly to get the best times, not that there is anything motivating you to improve your time past the single goal they give. Endless mode is fun, but the game gives you no milestones to aim for - all of the unlockables (timed endless modes) are unlocked by total kills ever rather than top score.
Irredeemable bugs:
There's a minigame that doesn't stop the music on exiting, leaving it looping over itself and forcing a restart. Some achievements are bugged, including giving me the "complete all time trials" achievement when I only did 5 of them. Worst of all, completion of the last level you do before quitting IS RANDOMLY NOT SAVED SO YOU HAVE TO DO IT AGAIN.
Graphics:
The brightness can be a bit difficult to look at sometimes.
Animations are janky, which is a bit weird because they literally only have one animated model.
It is also somehow jittery at times? VSync is broken and doesn't lock to 60fps. Level 21 is very laggy for no apparent reason.
Settings menu is pitiful, you have about 3 graphics options and can't change key bindings.
Gameplay:
Thrown objects will very occasionally bounce off or pass through enemies for no apparent reason.
Thrown objects move faster than bullets. If you shoot and immediately throw a gun, the bullet hits the gun.
I don't know why they don't have time completely stop, it makes for a much more precise experience.
When you land from a jump the screen gets a pointless and annoying/disorienting shock effect.
You can't really tell how much ammo your gun has left, reducing your ability to plan stuff.
The gun reload animation is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you can't tell how long it has left until you can fire again.
The end-of-level replays aren't quite satisfying enough, they're still too slow.
If an enemy breaks something too close to themselves they get stunned, which is a bit lame.
You are better off sticking with Blood Bowl: Chaos Edition. Other then upgraded graphics there is no reason to buy this game.

This is a good time waster. So far the only thing I can say that makes this better than the first one is their changing the game to be client side to stop the hacking of items. Though to be fair players have long since developed anti modded item servers to combat that. There are some new characters, and by new I mean only 2 so far are "new" the rest are just renamed old characters with improved skills. There have been some other changes like a public hub instead of a tavern, and the new maps are nice. The game is now "free to play" with micro transactions being used to get new characters or buy costumes that  don't affect in game stats. The game is still in "Alpha" but its has been in this state for a long time now and since you can spend money in game now and it is open to everyone I consider this game to be out for all intents and purposed. I'm tired of games using the alpha tag as a shield to hide their failings behind.
Anyway, besides that jumping is a bit wonky and you will die more because of jumping than being killed by monsters. There do not seem to be very many legendary weapons, and those are really all that matter because I had legendary weapons by lvl 7 of my first char and the rest had one waiting for them by the time they hit the lvl req for them.
So in conclusion this game is the same as the first one. It is fun to play but as of right now there doesnt seem to be a real reason to leave the origional if you are having fun. Eventually they will stop supporting the first one to force people over when they are ready. I don't know how long its going to take them to get out of "alpha" mode but the game works fine so theres no reason not to play, but theres no incentive right now to stop playing the first one if you are still enjoying it.

Battles in REDCON were sometimes frustrating at first, but after a few tweaks to my fortress, each battle felt fair and intense. It was always satisfying to defeat my opponent using various weapon and room combinations. When to use ammo types, where to shoot, what firing mode to use, and where to move crew during the battle, all added to the frantic, ever-changing strategy throughout the match. In addition, I gained passive bonuses like accuracy and healing depending on the type of rooms I added to my fortress. Luckily during all the mayhem, REDCON provides an active-pause system, which allowed me to pause the game, assess the situation, and issue commands.
If decking out one fortress wasn't enough, I was unlocking new fortress layouts while progressing through the game. Each fortress came with four different layouts which provided a lot of possibilities for experimentation and finding a play style that worked best for me.
All this gameplay is supported by powerful sounding shots, explosions, and screen shakes that make you somewhat feel you are indeed controlling a massive powerhouse artillery fortress.
If REDCON's UI wasn't adapted from mobile and instead revamped for PC screens, it would have rounded off the overall positive experience. Granted, the UI works fine during gameplay, but I would have liked to see additional options brought forth to the PC version such as grouping and keyboard shortcuts.
For such a simple game, there's a lot of depth, and strategy involved. REDCON will test your micromanagement skills, especially at later levels. At the current price of $6.49 CAD (as of July 17, 2016), I feel REDCON has pretty good value if you dig strategic-tower-defense games.
For me, despite some of REDCON's flaws, it still was a direct hit.

An addictive and frustrating game.  There's a bunch of minor UI and control issues that can be rather frustrating.  For example, if you quit a mission before taking any damage, you can reconfigure your fort without breaking a win streak, but the game never tells you.  However, underneath the problems is a game that combines puzzle and RPG ideas in a compelling way.  You have to command a fort at several levels, starting with the basic load out of structures that determines your capabilities all the way down to commanding soldiers to abandon a burning room.  The FTL comparisons are apt, but where FTL demands decisive victory and makes attrition your worst enemy, Redcon wants you to embrace the grind.  Soldiers on both sides are surprisingly hard to kill and good at repairs.  Sometimes you'll find the weak point and blow up rooms faster than the enemy can keep up, but often you'll end up in patterns of attack and counterattack that seem like stalemates until someone's lifebar gives out.  Where the game most resembles FTL is its selection of weapons, except this game has more emphasis on fire, but the battles are a little more nuanced.  One example is the mortars, which have an entirely different trajectory than other guns.  As a result, they may have different accuracy ratings versus different targets, and sometimes they can bypass enemy defense turrets just because the turrets can't rotate fast enough to change targets when they're focused gunfire from the front.  Another example is the art of catching the enemy off guard.  A mortar loaded with shrapnel will annilhate a soldier it lands on, but they have a split second to dodge.  However, some quick shots from a less powerful gun might put the hurt on them before they can leave, and you might even be able to drop your shrapnel on the location that they escape to, if your coordination is tight enough.  This game's biggest barrier aside from its UI issues is the difficulty, but, like a lot of difficult games, the difficulty curve flattens out once you get towards the middle of the game because your options go up dramatically.  At any rate, for this price it's a better single player experience than any Worms game.

I had a very, very, very long review, but it seems that steam won't let me post it. so now its just a summary.
Overall: please stay away unless you are really a fan of raining shells on people, even that, get it on discount.
- Touchscreen-like UI on a PC game
-- Very, very limited hotkeys
-- Repetitive gameplay
--- Bad story writing with barely any background information and thus no immersive feeling at all, making the whole roguelike mode look like a joke
--- Bad gameplay design and weaponry balancing, also very limited income so that you cannot really switch between loadouts effectively, meaning you are basically stuck if you choose the wrong weapons.
--- Very limited customization of fortress - You cannot hire soldiers or design your own fortress, you can only pick from templates already established and load those templates with weapons or utilities.
-- Almost no replay value, only medals that increase money and perk drop chance are carried over to later games, no perks are preserved.
+++ Well, raining explosive cannon shells on ppl is fun, that's what took me though these hours of playing
++ Some dev designed levels where you cannot use your own fortress are very challenging and interesting
Slightly longer review: I have seen a lot ppl in the comments comparing this to FTL, but this is really not a game that would fit into FTL's role, this game lacks detailed world setups, any background is barely mentioned and poorly explained, even a battle theatre map marking various landscapes and sludge seas would make this game vastly better in conveying its eternal war dystopian background. This roguelike with no background or immersive feeling is very dull and uninteresting, you can only expect so much out of it. and I see no replay value because it does not retain anything except medals that you have gained from the previous campaign. FTL had loads of ships with different playstyles, this has only a few of those fortresses with identical structure everytime, thus nothing to hope for on the second run. So overall this is far from a good game, and please stay away unless you are an absolute fanatic about shelling people.
Why you should stay away:
For lovers of immersive backgrounds, there are barely anything in detail about it.
For those who like games with lots of weapons, there are nothing really special, weapons are almost identical to what we have today, and the balancing is really off. Missiles are too slow and vulnerable, with low damage as well as slow reload speeds; lasers are only good at disrupting shield operations. Fast firing cannons are the most effective, with backup from larger cannons to take out key rooms. Basically, if you go for a combination of fast cannons, sniper cannons and have the right targeting order, there is no way you are going to lose, with other weapons you simply cannot do that.
For upgrade game lovers, there are no choice of upgrade routes, there is only one route you can follow, and that is only an increase in stats, meaning no unique abilities at the top tier.

I'm going to keep my original complaints at the bottom anyway, just so that it's on record, but now I'm going to review the game properly.
The thing about Tiberium Wars is that this was the first C&C in 3D. We'd had the studio play around with the idea earlier with Emperor Battle for Dune and Generals. But this was the first time they did it with the Tiberium series. And then they went on to include it with Red Alert, but that's a different story altogether.
I'll confess, I liked the cutscenes from Tiberium Sun a lot more, if only because of the moment when Kane returns from the dead with a big, boisterous "Kane Lives!" But y'know, any Joe Kucan munching on scenery is good Joe Kucan. And it's nice that the rest of the cast is appropriately hammy.
The Tiberium series has always been a bit more serious than the Red Alert series. It's very dour and dark as opposed to the over-the-top feeling of Red Alert. The graphics are great, for a game that's 10 years old, as is the design. The world is a "living" world, with cars and people walking around in the background (and running away when the explosions start). Unlike Warcraft, you can create properly huge armies and throw them against your enemies. Seeing as it's a sequel, you can feel that there is a progression of weapons, while keeping many of the classics.
I always enjoyed the Intelligence data, which expands on what's happening in the world, what the units are about, and the bonus objectives always have a tangible reward, from giving free units, to providing access to artillery.
So, if you can work out a way to get past the crashes on the first mission, I'd definitely recommend C&C3, on how to do a basic RTS right.

[To be clear; I do not believe that The Beginner's Guide is a game in the typical definition as an interactive piece of media, and instead I view it as a story vessel. As such, I'm reviewing it based on how well it communicates itself in this form and not from a gameplay standard.]
Without getting into the argument of 'are video games art', I am not the target audience for games that are focused on delivering a moral or a lesson instead of a gameplay-based experience. My own cynicism makes me rather numb to the emotions and feelings conveyed by the developer, which makes the whole experience fall flat, which in most cases is a fault of my own, not the developer. That said, I would be giving blatant spoilers if I explained why The Beginner's Guide struck something of a nerve with me, even if it was so heavy-handed that it ended up polarizing my feelings come the final act. The mixture of human thoughts and emotions that are channeled into game development is an interesting subject to tackle, but too many of the answers are spoon fed to the player instead of letting us sit and stew on the material.
The Beginner's Guide is a tale on the often fragile link between game developers and their players, or more specifically between Davey Wreden (developer of The Stanley Parable) and one of his friends, Coda, who makes many odd, brief games yet never releases them to the public ... Wreden acts as the narrator, putting up his thoughts and evaluations using Coda's games as the backdrop, often pausing to share his feelings regarding Coda, their relationship and what the games mean. The games in question are shuffled in and out in a timeline, most of them are  relatively brief, yet they're padded with Wreden's discussion. The longer ones require a bit more time for you to navigate their linear paths, and Wreden provides narration to accompany you. At times though, I felt that Wreden's narration bled into the scene at hand a bit too much, being more of a distraction than anything relevant to the situation.
The games that Wreden has you traverse aren't anything to write home about, but their quality isn't the focus of The Beginner's Guide; specifically you're asked to look at the design and reasoning behind the games, to analyze not the games themselves, but the process of creating them in the first place, and where Coda was coming from as he did. However, more often than not does Wreden just out and out give you the 'answers' or the meanings, leaving little room for you to come up with your own theories. Not much is left a mystery save for Coda himself, who can only be put together in the player's mind through Wreden's depictions of him and through his games. You learn more and more about Coda as you proceed through the timeline, but it's painful how on the nose some of the revelations can be; a machine to represent the thought process. Fleeing from sliding prison bars into darkness. Repetition of a known entity. Yes Wreden, the player can see these themes and what they represent, so explaining them in fine detail is simply beating them over the head with a limp fish. Even if the player doesn't immediately understand the themes, there's something to be said for showing, not telling.
It's Wreden himself that ends up souring most of the experience for me unfortunately. While he is well-spoken and keeps the script casual, like he's speaking directly to yourself as a person and not as a player, he ends up coming across as far, far too practiced in his narration, losing much of the personal touch. This is debilitating because in later acts Wreden's analysis and discussion begins to fall apart at the seams which is both unexpected and unsettling, my comfort zone feeling threatened much in the same way as Coda's, having his games released publicly against his will. The tone shifts from discussing and analyzing the games of an introverted individual to a self-admitted confessional of a man trying to understand and fix something he cannot where it's arguably not his place, or even right, to do so. The final game the player is put through is as clear cut of a personal barrier as one can create, and the big revelation in it was such a sudden, sharp punch to the gut that it rattled me more than I care to admit. But there was still that nagging doubt in my mind about how Wreden's narration here felt disingenuous due to its practiced delivery, and by the credits roll I was left feeling a bit emotionally betrayed because of this.
I can't state enough how much my expectations were subverted partway into The Beginner's Guide. I had done nary an ounce of research about the 'game' when I purchased it, and all I expected was an essay on game development done in interactive form. While I was never able to shake that doubt regarding Wreden's unnatural narration, the surprising change in tone and message was certainly welcomed, putting my fears of the game merely being a rambling tangent on video game creation to rest. A good part of the analysis is on video game creation, namely the creative process itself and not the technical development. I can't really remember the last time I was sat down, shown and talked to about what someone was thinking or feeling when they put something into a game, generally commentary like that is reserved for developer logs filled with so much technical lingo that any person touch feels artificial at that point. Your mileage with The Beginner's Guide may vary greatly from mine; in the end my sympathy for Coda became astronomical and I had to swallow my heart back down my throat during the final act. It's the tonal shift that ends up making me give The Beginner's Guide a confident recommendation, but remember: this isn't a game that's meant to challenge you or put any of your gaming skills to the test. You're going to be listening, looking and learning - If this doesn't interest you, then by all means pass it by.

Every couple decades, a popular arcade game will get a remake to a recent console. For example, you have missile Command for the PS1, Rampage: World Tour for the PS1 and N64, and Asteroids for the PS1. The graphics and sounds are updated, a small plot line is added, and minor modifications to the game are made and released as a minigame as a bundle. For the most part, the simplistic gameplay remains the same. The quality of the added content is lackluster and rushed, but it's not made to be the main part of the game, and doesn't take away from the nostalgic gameplay.
Sun Blast: Star Fighter feels like such a game. Everything about this game feels uninspired and bland. The studio behind the game seemed to have made this game to get a quick buck, and made everything out of free Unity assets. The gameplay is repetitive and lazy. Music and sounds are few and boring. Not a single part of this game seems to be original. Just writing a review for this takes a great effort, it's so bland.
The graphics are cheap-looking and bland. They look like generic assets ripped from online graphic design classes and slapped on to a game. The assets have the same quality as an early PS2 game. The music seems to be only 3 or 4 songs, and there is very little variety for sound. Overall, I'd say this has the look of a stock game you would see in the background of a TV show.
All you do is move and shoot. You can choose among 3 ships, but there is little difference among them. The weapons are the same, and the upgrades don't seem to make much of a difference. The studio tried to hide the fact that it's a lazy and simple game by modifying it slightly and calling it "levels". These include killing a certain number of ships, dodging tunnel obstacles, time attacks, and boss fights. They get old fast. The controls are unresponsive, and your ship moves too slow to avoid getting hit.
It's a remake of an arcade game I have yet to identify. I wager that none of this game was original, and everything just just taken from other games and developers and slapped together to make this uninspired game.
It gets old very fast. As of writing this review, I didn't even play an hour and got tired of it. I learned quickly that there is not much in this game. I give it two stars because it, at least, resembles a game, albeit generic.
Sun Blast is an unoriginal game, with no creativity. I the price of 90 yen is too much for this. If this is some art project for a school, then good for them. However, the fact that they charge money for this sloppy game deserves a review. I bought this game for 48 yen, with a coupon. Otherwise, I probably wouldn't have even bothered with something so unappealing. Sun Blast has no flare.

I had previously reviewed this game negatively because I couldn't find a "cancel resource harvesting" command. Such a command was added into game (or I simply found it and it had been in the game the whole time). With that issue aside, I'm happy to give a more complete review of the game.
This game can be somewhat complex. Your citizens need a lot in order to stay alive, healthy and happy. You need to keep track of overall food levels, tool levels and many other metrics in order to maintain them. The complexity of the game is not lessened by the presence of disasters. My town spent 20 carefully managed years getting to an overall pop of almost 200. Then, nomads arrived and reduced my food stores, followed in quick succession by a tornado that killed half my population, half my crops and much of my storage. With severly limited food resources, my town starved and died. The complexity involved in managing this constantly changing environment can be frustrating; it is definitely a challenge.
Gamers should take the same approach to this game as they might to a game like Crusader Kings 2. This game runs at a slow pace; it is not meant to played in one sitting. Catch up on some work and leave it running in the background, then save and later pick it where you left off. If you rush, limited resources may cause your settlement to starve and die.
If you like strategy games that are unique and challenging, but don't mind if they move at a slow pace, than this game is for you.

I'm a sim-game guy from way back - the original SimCity, Civ, etc... After reading some reviews of this game, I had very hopes, and after playing and learning the mechanics, I was not disappointed.
You know the premise - a group of settlers with limited supplies has to survive and then thrive. There is no fighting in the game, so you can focus solely on peaceful expansion. The starting conditions vary based on your choices, so there are no surprises when the game launches. The maps very in quality, so you can take what you're given or "shop around" for a reasonable map.
Food and shelter are the priority, of course, and you can do plenty right away to get them both for your small clan. The terrain usually allows for pockets of settlements or harvesting or industrial areas, and planning a good portion of the map based on the layout of the pockets before you even let a laborer move is important.
The vast majority of the buildings/structures/fields are food, resource, and shelter-related, but your people need some variety, so you can build a church, a brewery, etc... These buildings didn't have a huge influence on the games that I've played, but cumulatively they make your citizens happier. The more useful buildings are what you'd expect: Farms, Orchards, Houses, Mines, Gatherer's Huts, Forestry buildings, etc... You must assign at least one citizen to work each one (except for houses, which citizens will occupy fairly smartly, depending on the location of their jobs), and constantly manipulating the workers is crucial to thriving in this game.
How food and resources are distributed is important, and you have a few options to store things and move them around. Markets allow for the best distribution, and each house should be in the "zone" of a market. Trading Posts allow you to store a massive amount of goods for trade with merchants. The merchants show up periodically so that you can buy resources that you're low on or seeds and livestock to expand the types of food that you can produce. It is essentially how you gain "tech", but there are no new buildings or improved buildings - just new types of food.
The achievements give you an idea of the scope of the game. You can't do them all in one game, which promotes varied ways of playing. I haven't even done half of them, but I'm looking forward to trying for them all.
If you like semi-realistic and fairly logical resource/building sims, you can't do much better than Banished. One of the best tests is the "one more turn" way of playing. I've found myself playing for another hour or two after the thought, "okay, let me watch this building finish, them I'm out" passed through my head. Banished definitely passes that test. I've played about 50 hours as of this review, and considering the cost of the game, it's been worth every penny.

Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie psychological horror game. It is full of strategy, power management, and jumpscares. Lots of jumpscares... At first glance, Five Nights at Freddy's looks pretty silly and not frightening what so ever. I assure you, this isn't true. As I said, it is a psychological horror game. There is a lot of suspense, causing a lot of tension. You'll sit there for a few minutes without a single thing happening, then suddenly one of the animatronics are gone and you begin in panic as you look for it. You have to be very quick, as you don't have much time to react. And in some cases, if you make one mistake then its all over.
The storyline for Five Nights at Freddy's is very intresting, as it isn't all given directly to you. You only get pieces of the storyline, and you have to make observations in the map to learn more. For example, you'll see newspapers and such hanging on the walls that go more in depth and show the story behind the place. The story is pretty dark, and is quite sad if you think about it.
I would definitely reccomend Five nights at Freddy's to anyone who likes puzzle or strategy games while being able to enjoy a bit of jumpscares.

Great graphics, great design, great ideas, refreshing and original... with some major game-design flaws..
As you progress you buy your tower items. Unfortunately you only get so much cash and in the long run, if you spend it on the wrong equipment you will get stuck. The enemy gets so tough you can't counter them leaving you very frustrated as you try over and over again to complete something you can't complete. I like a challenge but this is rediculous.
You could restart and buy different items but the game will push various tower designs against you which go's agist the "buy the right items" design as the paper, scissors, rock design go's against you eventually.
The game should allow free item unlocks with the idea gold is just for upgrades. At least this way you are flexible enough to try various combos to beat new levels. You don't even have the ability to play previous towers to gain more gold. Unfortunately later gme requires you to do this again by upgrading weapons to a version 2. At this stage even if you buy a different weapon you now have it at a level 1 when you may need it at level 3.
The games fix? An option to skip the level if you fail a few times. Its a dodgy, frustrating and lazy fix and you can only do it 3 times totol.
Another great flaw is the AI. They seem to have far better accuracy and the ability to know where you're going to shoot them (and thats without the Defence room that allows such a thing). For the pure stratagist this is a turn off and frustrating experience as it feels like the AI can cheat.
The game has huge potential and I want to love it but unfortunately its another cheap game that will collect dust in my library. Smart gamers will push their towers to the limit beating very hard levels but for the rest of you you will feel very frustrated and most likely rage-quit.
Buy if you like a real challenge.

A crowdfunded game with a lot to live up to, A Hat In Time is a fun and basic action platformer. Controlling Hat Kid feels great in almost every aspect, and in many cases my mistakes were my own. There is a certain...light jankiness to the game as a whole, as from time to time you see the seams in the level geometry, character models, and textures. But it's actually a well-designed game and it reminds me of Psychonauts in a lot of ways. Powers are implemented well into the core mechanics, and the bosses are all fun to fight, and a couple of them provide a decent challenge. It's all on the easy side of things overall, but it's a game that doesn't treat you like an idiot while also not ever ramping the difficulty to stupid levels. The characters in it are colorful and weird, but they have a sense of originality to them as well. Even each world's level progression behaves a little differently from the other, so there's a nice variety here.
And the humor lands well in most cases, too. The second and third worlds in particular do a great job at creating a light-hearted tone.
Oh, and the game isn't super short, but it isn't exactly long. I vied for all of the time pieces in the game, and doing so on top of beating the game took me only 12 hours or so. I imagine that rushing through to the end would take only a handful of hours.
Aaaaaaaand it operates really well on my aging PC. Unreal Engine doing good work, for sure. You could probably run it easily on a wide range of systems.
But yeah, it's honestly a really fun game with a cute story. It has twists and turns and great gameplay and some decent challenge at times. It's definitely worth a look.

The review I want to leave: ♥♥♥♥ this game.
The useful review I'm going to leave:
Just because you take FTL's mechanics almost word for word doesn't mean you'll make a good game. All this piece of garbage actually does is make me appreciate the FTL team even more, because these guys don't seem to have any idea what they're doing.
This game is not permadeath (in fact, you have to go out of your way to restart the game), but it penalizes failure by denying you medals which make the game easier. So... you'll need to restart a bunch.
You can't see the enemy fortress before you start a level, so the only way to design your fortress to deal with the enemy is... to fail, which penalizes you.
Until recently, the game awarded you money for victory (more money if you beat your enemy by boarding their fortress). You use this money to unlock/upgrade room types, and then pay again to add multiple rooms. You probably see the pattern already: Yes, of course you have no way of knowing if you've researched or purchased 'the wrong stuff'. Too bad. There's no sell button, so if you've made enough mistakes, you have to restart. The game's since added an 'Easy' mode which does away with money. This certainly helps. Curiously, they didn't add a 'sell' button like most people asked for. In fact, they've made very few changes to the main game at all, implying they think this stupid design is perfectly okay.
So... what's the big deal with restarting? There are 100 levels. Most people seem to need to restart by level 30 or so.
Redcon is frustration-based gameplay. It starts off fun, then quickly develops dysfunctions that anyone can see. They're so glaring and obvious that I can only conclude the developers simply didn't (and continue not to) care. Do yourself a favor and stay away.

The combat system is very nicely done. This, along with skits are the highlights of the game. Whilst I haven't finished the game, the story doesn't seem to be anything to write about. The characters are also somewhat of a mixed bag; some characters are charming and likable while others are somewhat bland.
All in all, it is a good game and you should get it if its on sale. However, the port isn't perfect, and there is no reason for it to be capped at 30 fps.

I have, from the moment I found out about this game, been very intrigued. I've seen some short little YouTube let's plays from pre-release versions, and am doing my own series as this game is in early access. From what it used to be with merely one map segment and only wolves to think about, to now with around four or five times as much map to exlore and much better looking UI's, this game is getting more and more worth the buy.
Here's what I think, from a player's standpoint:
The good things:
-Beautiful graphics, regardless of what setting you use, and actual graphics settings which help on older or less powerful computers. (This is good for those laptop users out there, though myself is not included.)
-A LOT of map to explore (10 km^2, or around 6.5 miles^2), in three sections, all connected every time.
-Many things you have to explore to actually find, and as the game gets more in-depth and furthered along I see so much when you go back to something you thought you knew and be amazed at the changes. Everything gets better with time, so they say.
-Difficulty settings for you to pick how you want the world to recognize you: to be feared (pilgrim), a threat (voyager), or a chewtoy/plaything worth killing (stalker).
-Now even more useful UI's that look really good and function really nicely.
-Hinterland Studios, the devs who are really good at squashing bugs and recognizing community additions. (I want to see mods allowed someday, even still in early access,. And those who create them could have their ideas incorporated into the main game, with some credit on the store page to show some love to those of us fans who all dedicated time to play and support :) )
-Voice-overs that actually sound realistic to scenario, and happen at just the right moments to make you laugh or f=put the edge on the grimness of the situation. It's a roller coaster ride, this game is.
-Attachment to your character, male or female- Will or his sister (I like to think of her as his sister, or a female version from an alternate universe)- and so that when you die you not only feel sad you lost this run but you also feel said they, your character, died as well.
-You will soon realize after you start playing that it's never a matter of, "Will I survive?" It is in fact, "How LONG can I survive?" This game is called The Long Dark for a reason, and not just because it's the solar equivalent of a volcanic winter.
The negatives:
-Again, FEELS FOR YOUR LOSES :'( The one you played as before is gone. Forever. Permadeath is a guarantee. You now have another one, fresh off the crash site that doesn't yet exist, but it's never the same.
-Occasionally, you fall through the concrete. (I wish I had saved my recording, I was experimenting with software and the recording was crap so I scrapped it- sue me! Anyway, it was in Pleasant Valley, by the big steel bridge near the mine to the Coastal Highway, on the side leading to the barn.) Thankfully, the snow beneath still catches you, and you don't fall through the map.
Hmmmm....not many other negatives to speak of anymore, actually. The wolf and bear things are largely solved now, so just be cautious when ent- wait, no, spoilers. I'll let you find out about Fluffy in the basement ;)
Anyone contemplating buying this, just know: this game is not only worth buying now, but if you want to save a couple bucks, get it now. It's completely playable now, and when The Long Dark is released in full it won't be $20.00 (US) anymore. It also helps the devs know another player is interested. Why not, if you know what I mean? Plus, if you're really this far into my comment, you'll know you're serious enough to go for it. Come on- please do it, you'll loose more of what social life you have left, you wonderful gamer you :3 Earn a new one here if you haven't already, anyway.

This game is the best Early Access Game I have ever played.
I definitely recommend this game, but it requires patience. So if you're only into fast paced games, I wouldn't recommend it.
The good:
This game takes you on a journey in the Canadian wilderness, scavenging for supplies like food, clothing and tools. While searching a house you can hear the howling of the wind and the creaking of the building, sometimes you get the feeling someone else is in the house...
There's nothing like finding what you need in the time of desperation, and the game keeps on surprising you with the stuff that you can find and places you can go.
The graphics are like a mix of Borderlands, Fallout 3/New Vegas and a bit of This War of Mine - despite the sharp edges of the environment, the graphics are really charming.
The lighting and shadows are great for a game like this! Better than a lot of triple A titles.
The bad:
After surviving for almost 25 days, it was a bit disheartening to wake up to a bear mauling and killing me, because I tried sleeping until the fog went away - but hey, that's wilderness survival for you! (But It would have been nice to be able to load the game, instead of starting all over.)
There's no goal other than to survive (sandbox mode), but they say they are working on a story mode! Remember, it's early access.
Things I would love to see added (note: I don't know if some of these are/will be in the game):
- A save/load option, but with restrictions - no loading the game just because you went the wrong way! Maybe every 5th or 10th day the game should do a savepoint.
- More difference in the houses. Some houses are exactly the same, though the supplies may vary.
- More weapons. Not M16's or rocket launchers, but handguns and crossbows and the ability to use your axe on wildlife. Maybe a scope for the rifle.
- Strenght and/or backpacks. And by that I mean, your carry limit should start lower and increase as long as you are healthy, fed and moving.
Sorry for the long review and list of things I'd like to be added, but this game has so much potential I would hate see going in a wrong direction or stop being developed.

First and foremost, I do heartily recommend this game, and recommend you

Alright, well If you've read this far you might as well read the rest.
Given who developed this game, it's inevitable that it would draw comparisons to the author's previous work, namely, The Stanley Parable.  Frankly though, they are worlds apart.  The Stanley Parable is what I would term a 'Narrative Maze'.  Sure, there's a path you're intended to follow, but you still have choices, and those choices, and at times random chance, make a difference in what you see.  This game, on the other hand is what I would term a 'Walking Narrative': A linear path to follow, with a narrative accompanying it.  So gameplay-wise, it reminds me far more of "Dear Esther" than "The Stanley Parable".

Blood Bowl 2 has issues when compared to its predecessor, in a vacuum. It has 10 teams currently (Wood elves and Lizardmen just added) rather than 25, and it has a new price tag, of course, however, I feel this sells short what Blood Bowl 2 does well.
The AI has been dramatically improved, which is not thrilling for those who play in human only leagues, but for those of us that play against the AI, this is a big deal. Gone are the days of the AI, as its first action of the turn, trying to dodge through 12 tackle zones and go for it twice as a dwarf. Instead, it seems to do its turn in priority order, from most likely to work to least likely, and it seems to avoid doing bizarre and silly things unlikely to have effect. As elves, it steps out of block zones, forcing you to blitz if you are going to hit it, just like a human would.
Assuming the new races do not cost an arm and a leg, and come out at a fair clip, I think Blood Bowl 2 is going to be a great upgrade on its ancestor.

An excellent game that has a steep learning curve. In order to balance all of the needs of your population, you have to constatnly be on the lookout for expansion. Some things in the game, such as steel tools for example, are nice, but more or less luxurious. You can thrive without them, but once you have these tools, you'd better maintain their supply in the event you become dependent on them.
In short, the game takes some trial and error to learn what works at what rates and such. The game allows you to monitor these resources and other variables with in-game windows that you can move around and close at your will, allowing you to essentially build your own UI. Even then, a tornado is just going to come in and wreck it all any ways. One of the best city builders I've ever played. It has a steep learning curve, and even advanced players can make incredibly punishing mistakes. The game has also had mod support for a while now on top of random world generation, so there is plenty of replayability. If you are even considering this game, get it, especially if it goes on sale.

The original Dungeon Defenders was likely one of the best executions of an integration between FPS and Tower Defense that the marketplace has seen.  I managed to clock a substantial quantity of hours into the original game, and it was an absolute blast to play.
And then they started monetizing the game.  DLC became incredibly commonplace for addons.  New Heroes, new levels, new cosmetics, new character skins, anything they could think of.  They never directly monetized 'power', however, with the introduction of new levels with a higher level cap, it was an indirect way of power-capping new players.
The other concern out of the implementation on the original Dungeon Defenders is that as new content got released, there was a substantial amount of Gear Inflation.  +500 to a given stat, which was godly at release, was trivial a few months later.  It had a much more MMO-esque grind to the game that drove their monetization strategy.
Then we come to Dungeon Defenders 2.  When I look at this game, I realize that there were a lot of underlying engine upgrades, tons of texture updates, and they completely revamped multiple parts of the game... However, it's different enough from the original.  A lot of rehashed abilities, the same/familiar characters, etc.  The strength behind Dungeon Defenders 2 is that they have a better grasp of their monetization model going into it, and it's built that way from the ground up.
The reason Dungeon Defenders 2 is so popular right now is because it's still at it's infancy.  But even incredibly early on in the process, it really appears to be taking the same path at the original game, but by 'resetting' everything, they're opening the door for more monetization opportunies.
In my opinion, there hasn't been substantial innovation into this game to necessitate the high price tag, or recommend this game to anyone that has already enjoyed the original Dungeon Defenders.  It satisfies the same basic FPS-Tower Defense itch that can be scratched by cheaper alternatives in a more complete state.  This is much less a Dungeon Defenders 2, so much as it's a substantial overhaul of the original Dungeon Defenders.

TL;DR: REDCON is a static artillery shooter that has shades of classic Worms, and FTL: Faster than Light thrown in. Combat is real time but with the ability to pause time to issue orders to soldiers and weapon batteries all at once. Core gameplay mechanics are polished and strategy goes far deeper than simply trying to shell your opponent into submission. Worth checking out when on special.
Long review:
PROS:
1; A wide assortment of weapons for you to choose from. Do you want rockets, siege mortars, standard artillery pieces, high end energy weapons? How about incendiary or poison shells? Somewhere you'll find a perfect complement of weapons to suit your playstyle.
2; Deep tactical gameplay. You'll always have to check your threat list and retarget your weapons in order to get maximum effect. Should you go after the heavy siege weapons or the power reactors? Knock out their munitions factories to slow down their rate of fire, or just destroy the guns themselves?
3; The art style is polished and well developed. Characters on the splash screens are well detailed, and watching as your in game soldiers do a celebration dance when they survive a mission is a joy to behold.
CONS:
1; No tutorial or significant tooltip help menus mean you can spend a significant amount of time flailing about in the early game not quite sure what to do with each of the resources you have to manage. No ability to sell old weapons means you have to be incredibly frugal about buying new weapons right from the start.
2; The control scheme feels somewhat restrictive. There is no ability to bind weapons or soldiers to hotkeys for rapid access, nor is there any way to click and drag to select multiple guns. Each weapon has to be targeted individually and it can be easy to overlook one and leave it firing on an already destroyed room.
3; No multiplayer. Easily this games biggest flaw is the lack of any kind or multiplayer, be it split screen, Local Area Network, or full internet matchmaking. The game is already set up into a two player split. Having a separate multiplayer mode where you get to progress your fort from a simple two room tower into a gigantic behemoth bristling with large caliber guns and tailored specifically to your whims would help extend this game's effective lifespan. As is stands, there is little to bring you back after you finish the storyline.
REDCON takes multiple cues from other games in similar genres. Most notably, it takes combat cues from games such as FTL: Faster than Light. Your objective in each mission is to destroy or otherwise subjugate an enemy stronghold using the weapons mounted on your own stronghold. Aside from simply picking targets, you have to manage the internal workings of your own base in real time, assigning soldiers to repair damaged systems or to man the various guns or support utilities. Manning weapons gives you boosts such as bonus accuracy or fire rates, while utilities give bonuses such as extra power or improved reaction times on point defences. You'll never have enough soldiers to man everything, so you have to prioritise what you need in each moment.
Tactical strategies will soon emerge in your play style. Fire one shell to distract that point defence drone only to follow up with a full volley from all your other guns. Or maybe you could launch a flashbang stun shell, only to rapidly follow it up with a neurotoxin shell and watch as the enemy quickly chokes and dies, leaving their fort ripe for the taking.
The enemy A.I. tends to be a little precognisant at times, being able to know which rooms you are targeting and moving personnel out just in the nick of time, even when they don't have a functional radar system to warn them. It can get annoying when you just have one more soldier left to take care of, but you just can't nail him.
Money is tight right off the bat. There currently is no means of salvaging or selling off old weapons once you have bought them. Those old, outdated light artillery pieces you started off with but are no longer using will just have to stay in storage forever while that fancy mark III sniper cannon mocks you with its long range bombardment abilities. If you spend foolishly in the early game, you will find the mid and late game periods harder than they have to be when you can't afford to buy upgrades or new weapon systems.
Overall, REDCON is enjoyable and has enough content to keep you occupied for 10-15 hours or so as you progress through the core storyline. Once you are done with that though, there really isn't anything left to do as the lack of multiplayer or skirmish matchups limit replay value. REDCON is quite adequately priced for the content that you get. It plays well, the music is fitting to the situation, and nothing beats nailing that final shot on the enemy's foolishly exposed nuclear reactor. If you enjoyed FTL, you'll get some enjoyment out of this.

This is a fun game that offers superb value for money.
It requires you to have a semi-functioning brain.
It requires you to use said brain to succeed.
It requires (at times) intense micromanagement of your soldiers, prioritisation of targets for your guns, and rooms in your own tower to repair.
Careful consideration must be given to which gun platforms/rooms/upgrades you purchase and the game encourages restarting at least once or twice because of the benefits of earned medals, which apply their benefits to a new game immediately (you basically end up with more cash per medal per game).
If you want a game that offers fun, strategic decision making, and extreme value for money, look no further.

Bioshock is one of those landmark games that define what's possible with the medium, and show the industry what people are looking for. While the gameplay is interesting, challenging, and diverse enough to allow a second playthrough, the real key of the game is its storyline, though it weaves its mechanics and narrative together in an unusually graceful fashion. Bioshock bills itself as a somewhat absurdist satire of certain political topics, and videogaming in general, and several of the game's events and elements reflect this - for instance, the ability to 'buy out' any system you can hack as a riff on the idea of cynical capitalism. However, underneath the retro red-scare style motifs and other satire, the game's story is more serious and far more personal, rather than political. There's a lot of genres and inspirations going into this title, from the notable inspirations of System Shock 2 and Atlas Shrugged, to more contemporary influences from stealth games, shooters and action RPGs. I'd recommend Bioshock to anyone who enjoys a wide diversity of PC games, because it manages to be a mixture of them without losing focus.

Sun Blast is a 3d-ish, space shooter-ish, developed by OBLONE Software and released April 2, 2015. In Sun Blast you move up down left or right while shooting and dodging.
This is going to be a salty review. That being said, who knows... maybe you'll like this game more then I did. Maybe Sun Blast will capture your heart... I will admit I haven't played any other "starfox inspired" space shooter games on steam.
There is no story. Outside of the flavor text written on this game's store front.
I don't want to compare this game to star fox because Star fox is a game I actually enjoyed playing, whereas I did not enjoy Sun Blast at all. I would discourage anyone to attempt to play this game with a keyboard, and recommend you turn on auto fire (so you can spam fire while auto firing).
Lets just examine each "feature" on the store front:
1) Full gamepad support
Yes, they even have wii motion controls, for any of you on steam whom have a wiimote.
2) Three ship designs to choose from, each with unique look and behavior
One ship moves right and left a tiny bit faster the then others and up and down slower, one moves up and down a tiny bit faster and left and right slower, and the third moves up and down at a medium pace (so it's not strong in one area and weak in the other)
I didn't notice a difference between the ships in any real significant way.
3) Fight against stealthy fighters and gigantic starships
Are there stealthy fighters? Yes, there are about 2 types of star ship fighters, and 3 different types of starship "bosses".
4) Huge level selection, from planet orbits to underground tunnels to infested military bases
This is the one I have the problem with. There are only about 4 or 5 different types of levels: Survival levels, shoot down a number of ships levels, dodge and break apart rocks levels, timed levels, any mix of the aforementioned levels... and boss levels.
THEN, they reskin the pretty background, and have you do the same levels over, changing the ships on the level, and changing the "NPC" or "target" density.
In a game like starfox dynamic events would take place, even if you were playing more of a rain shooter at certin points of the game, you'd need to shoot an enemy chasing after a friendly, sometimes a friendly would save you... There's nothing which changes from level to level. It's either: shooting to get enough kills, or dodging to get through a mine field.
5) Replay levels to earn medals
Those are the challenges, and they  relate to:
6) Steam achievements and leaderboards
Most people will get this game exclusively for the steam trading cards, for the sake of trading card mills. which... I mean, if that's your goal of this game, you'll get your money's worth, but my review relates to the game itself.
Now comes my softening statements of remorse... I've clearly explained why I dislike this game... The problem: someone worked on this game. It's not pretty, it's not fun. But it's cheap, you get trading cards, and at least it's a little different.
The problem is there's no real motivation to keep playing, and I don't feel like when I die it was really my fault and could have been avoidable. I use Super Meat Boy as my go-to for samples of "difficult, but fair". It could extend to any number of classic Arcade-styled video games, like Pacman or Galaga.
If the only way to get all the achievements and to be GOOD at Sun Blast is to learn the levels like someone would learn Pacman or Galaga, then I guess I'll need to disappoint the creator because I'm not going to put that amount of time into a game like that.
Like I said at the start of this review, some people might be interested in trying this game out, and some people might like it; that's okay, I'm glad you enjoy the games you like, but I will be taking my time and playing something else.
Thanks for reading my Review. Atratzu out.

- In regards to the fewer races (which is a big debating point), some people are forgetting that the previous versions also came with fewer races. I would say that this is not a problem, the problem is that they will probably charge us a hefty fee for each one. The game is not cheap as it is, so this will make this game extremely expensive.
- Blitz mode is out! You used to be able to play the game in real time, which is not the main format to the game, but for people which prefered real time, they now have lost the type of game they liked most.
- Overall this game has very little innovation added to it. Basically it is the same game as before, just it looks better and has fewer races. Online mode is improved, but overall it is the same game.
- There is no save option during the games. Considering they take a while to complete, i have no idea why that option is not out there. It used to be there.
- The gameplay is very slow. I would love an option where i could quicksim the opposition moves in solo mode. Staring at the screen for 2-3 minutes till the computer plays pretty much sucks, you can remove the annimations, which helps, but still, way too much waiting around.
What i would have liked to see
- A LOT more stats. The history section is very limited. There should be a lot more added to beef that section up.
- Not much in terms of customization. I mean why is there no editor? Maybe i want to make a custom team or customize my players or opponents. I know that is not part of the original game, but i do not see why the developers did not add that option out there. I mean, i cannot even custom pick my own opponents in the solo leagues. I have to random pick which type of teams will be included in my leagues.
- Why is there no hotseat co-op mode! I mean that would be an awesome option considering how few games use co-op these days on the PC.
Overall?
If you have never played this game, you will love it if you like turn based sports games. There is not much which compares to this on the market. To a new player, this looks like a more polished and improved version, with the better graphics, annimations, commentary and online mode.
To a true fan of the series though, losing Blitz mode, losing 75% of the races in exchange for the better graphics (which get repetitive very early in a game like this), could be a serious drawback. I gave the game a recommended, mainly because this is an awesome game, just i feel that considering they had 6 years to make a new version, they could have added more to it, instead of removing what used to be there and charging us for everything.

To play online co-op:
"If you have Nvidia video card you can use Gamestream feature to play coop online with just ONE purchased copy of the game!
Quick guide:
1. Open Geforce Expierence and go to Settings (cogwheel).
2. Check "Enable experimental functions"
3. Enable "Share / In-game overlay" (triangle icon near settings).
4. When in-game press Alt+Z (or whatever shortcut you have to open Geforce overlay).
5. Go to Overlay settings (cogwheel) and then Stream (EXPERIMENTAL)
6. "Allow friends to join game" - "Yes".
7. Close and reopen overlay. New option will appear - "Stream".
8. Click on it and select Guest controls, then select "Play alongside me" - "Done".
9. Press on Stream again and select "Copy invite URL". Send link to your friend and he will be able to join you.
Most likely your friend will not be able to use gamepad, only keyboard. But you can workaround with software like JoyToKey or Xpadder that allow to bind gamepad buttons to keyboard keys.
Enjoy!"

I have, from the moment I found out about this game, been very intrigued. I've seen some short little YouTube let's plays from pre-release versions, and am doing my own series as this game is in early access. From what it used to be with merely one map segment and only wolves to think about, to now with around four or five times as much map to exlore and much better looking UI's, this game is getting more and more worth the buy.
Here's what I think, from a player's standpoint:
The good things:
-Beautiful graphics, regardless of what setting you use, and actual graphics settings which help on older or less powerful computers. (This is good for those laptop users out there, though myself is not included.)
-A LOT of map to explore (10 km^2, or around 6.5 miles^2), in three sections, all connected every time.
-Many things you have to explore to actually find, and as the game gets more in-depth and furthered along I see so much when you go back to something you thought you knew and be amazed at the changes. Everything gets better with time, so they say.
-Difficulty settings for you to pick how you want the world to recognize you: to be feared (pilgrim), a threat (voyager), or a chewtoy/plaything worth killing (stalker).
-Now even more useful UI's that look really good and function really nicely.
-Hinterland Studios, the devs who are really good at squashing bugs and recognizing community additions. (I want to see mods allowed someday, even still in early access,. And those who create them could have their ideas incorporated into the main game, with some credit on the store page to show some love to those of us fans who all dedicated time to play and support :) )
-Voice-overs that actually sound realistic to scenario, and happen at just the right moments to make you laugh or f=put the edge on the grimness of the situation. It's a roller coaster ride, this game is.
-Attachment to your character, male or female- Will or his sister (I like to think of her as his sister, or a female version from an alternate universe)- and so that when you die you not only feel sad you lost this run but you also feel said they, your character, died as well.
-You will soon realize after you start playing that it's never a matter of, "Will I survive?" It is in fact, "How LONG can I survive?" This game is called The Long Dark for a reason, and not just because it's the solar equivalent of a volcanic winter.
The negatives:
-Again, FEELS FOR YOUR LOSES :'( The one you played as before is gone. Forever. Permadeath is a guarantee. You now have another one, fresh off the crash site that doesn't yet exist, but it's never the same.
-Occasionally, you fall through the concrete. (I wish I had saved my recording, I was experimenting with software and the recording was crap so I scrapped it- sue me! Anyway, it was in Pleasant Valley, by the big steel bridge near the mine to the Coastal Highway, on the side leading to the barn.) Thankfully, the snow beneath still catches you, and you don't fall through the map.
Hmmmm....not many other negatives to speak of anymore, actually. The wolf and bear things are largely solved now, so just be cautious when ent- wait, no, spoilers. I'll let you find out about Fluffy in the basement ;)
Anyone contemplating buying this, just know: this game is not only worth buying now, but if you want to save a couple bucks, get it now. It's completely playable now, and when The Long Dark is released in full it won't be $20.00 (US) anymore. It also helps the devs know another player is interested. Why not, if you know what I mean? Plus, if you're really this far into my comment, you'll know you're serious enough to go for it. Come on- please do it, you'll loose more of what social life you have left, you wonderful gamer you :3 Earn a new one here if you haven't already, anyway.

Been reading the negative comments about how it was too hard and unfair and tideous and whatnot; and went ahead and bought it anyways. Have to say: this game is not for everyone. I'm on a winning-streak of 10 and counting on my first play, while others whine how it was too hard. I am missing freeplay and multiplayer. Otherwise it's a neat little game. It is not too easy and that's a good thing! You have to take a close look at the enemy and need to find weaknesses in their defense and think how to crack them best, it's by no means brainless point and click. Simple minded people might miss the myriad of strategic possibilities this game brings.
It also has a puzzle-like feel to it sometimes as different enemy castles call for different specifications of your own stronghold.
It is not for:
-people who want or need a lot of handholding (first few missions are tutorial-style afterwards you're on your own)
-people who want an easy game a 6-year-old could enjoy (seems to be the case with quite a lot of people)
-people who look for a shooter-game that doesn't require a lot of thought
It is for:
-people who like strategy games in general and would look to add another casual titel with enough depth and funny little animations to their collection
-people who like a challenge
-people who don't play long sessions but want a fun game for the coffee-break at work
People who liked FTL will like this too. The gameplay with lots of pause for strategic arrangements is similar. For this price it's ok although makes a bit small impression as there is only campaign-mode. If you don't own FTL yet i'd recommend to spend the money on that one first though, this one has better graphics while FTL had a little more depth and content, but it's not really a clone.
The broadest content in this is weapons, rooms, layouts for your stronghold. It comes short in game-modes and musical variety.
All-in-all it's not the worst game i ever bought. I expect to get 10 to 20 hours of decent gameplay out of it at least, so it's a casual titel.
On sale, below 5 bucks price it's definately a 'buy'. For this 6-bucks-price it's an 'okay' in my book.
edit: after being a few more missions in it gets really hard, but that's ok. I see this as one of those titles you repeat coming back to for an occasional 20 minutes play. So it's a 'casual game done right'.
So in conclusion: if you are specifically looking for a casual 'cofffee-break-game' this is a good buy because it does serve that type of player really well imo. After your initial 2 or 3 hours gameplay it's the ideal casual game.
If you expect an ultra-adictive game for upwards of 200 hours gameplay and long sessions this isn't it. This is just a cute little game and actually better than most 'small games' out there.
edit 2: more missions in; the game isn't really hard at all. Challenging, yes. Too hard, no.

This game is the best Early Access Game I have ever played.
I definitely recommend this game, but it requires patience. So if you're only into fast paced games, I wouldn't recommend it.
The good:
This game takes you on a journey in the Canadian wilderness, scavenging for supplies like food, clothing and tools. While searching a house you can hear the howling of the wind and the creaking of the building, sometimes you get the feeling someone else is in the house...
There's nothing like finding what you need in the time of desperation, and the game keeps on surprising you with the stuff that you can find and places you can go.
The graphics are like a mix of Borderlands, Fallout 3/New Vegas and a bit of This War of Mine - despite the sharp edges of the environment, the graphics are really charming.
The lighting and shadows are great for a game like this! Better than a lot of triple A titles.
The bad:
After surviving for almost 25 days, it was a bit disheartening to wake up to a bear mauling and killing me, because I tried sleeping until the fog went away - but hey, that's wilderness survival for you! (But It would have been nice to be able to load the game, instead of starting all over.)
There's no goal other than to survive (sandbox mode), but they say they are working on a story mode! Remember, it's early access.
Things I would love to see added (note: I don't know if some of these are/will be in the game):
- A save/load option, but with restrictions - no loading the game just because you went the wrong way! Maybe every 5th or 10th day the game should do a savepoint.
- More difference in the houses. Some houses are exactly the same, though the supplies may vary.
- More weapons. Not M16's or rocket launchers, but handguns and crossbows and the ability to use your axe on wildlife. Maybe a scope for the rifle.
- Strenght and/or backpacks. And by that I mean, your carry limit should start lower and increase as long as you are healthy, fed and moving.
Sorry for the long review and list of things I'd like to be added, but this game has so much potential I would hate see going in a wrong direction or stop being developed.

The second game I've played in the Tales series, Tales of Zesteria improves on most areas with some drawbacks. It was overall a satisfying experience that I'll have fond memories of, but ultimately the story didn't leave the same huge impression on me like Symphonia did.
First off, the cutscenes and dialogue are greatly improved, with actual camera angles and the characters interacting with body and facial expressions, which is a very welcome change. The dialogue is improved from the angle that most lines of dialogue from the characters are voiced, which is welcome too. However, the writing itself suffers a little, especially from Laila. I'm not sure if this was writing or translation, but the writing's not as good as Symphonia's.
The world is more fun to explore as there are more objects to find in a more "personal" way as you don't have a bird's eye view of everything, and the maps aren't too big to be intimidating. The dungeons and areas are clearly marked and there is even fast travel between save points, though I felt the price was a bit too high.
The combat I felt was overall better, in that you can unlock free run, which I picked up immediately. You can also check an enemy's weaknesses without having to look up your library every time either, which is great. I overall prefer the SC system to the TP system as characters aren't punished for not focusing on mana too much, however the fact that most enemies blatantly ignore my character make it difficult to pull of the dodges that regenerate the SC quickly. The camera can also be an issue if you fight indoors sometimes.
Overall there's a lot of content in this game, and I only played it once through. At least three are probably required to get all the achievements, but I left satisfied after my first run. A great game for fantasy, JRPG or anime fans.

This is without a doubt one of the best platformers I have ever played. Gears for Breakfast really delivered on this game and I can't wait to see what they do in the future! A Hat in Time offers simplistic, Banjo-Kazooie esque combat, smooth platforming, quirky characters, and cartoony, gorgeous worlds to explore and collect in. The game stars a nameless protagonist given the nickname Hat Kid by the devs as she is travelling back home on her weirdly, lined-shaped spaceship. After her spaceship slows down by an interesting-looking planet, either because the ship needs to cool down or plot, a member of the Mafia found on that same planet breaks in to her ship and accidentally releases all of her fuel (Time Pieces) out into space and then scattered on the interesting, Earth-like planet. Hat Kid must then go on a grand adventure to recover her missing Time Pieces and return home. Along the way she meets many interesting characters. From air-headed Mafia members to jazzy Moon Penguins to a soul-taking entity in the woods. They are all quirky and never fail to warm my heart and make me laugh uncontrollably. The areas Hat Kid travels through are all so unique, colorful, and filled with things to collect and places to explore. Collecting things in this game is similar to Banjo Kazooie, but not as grand and more simplified. A Hat In Time feels like Super Mario Galaxy, plays like Super Mario Sunshine and has many of the elements and dark humor of N64 era Rare platformers. I hope the things I said above have convinced you to buy this masterpiece but if you need a more in-depth look at what the game offers, I'll make a pros/cons list below.

This is a great indie strategy/survival type game. It is simple, effective and enjoyable. And the best thing is it has some amazing mods to offer more than you see at the initial installation.
There're a few downsides but let's start with ups!
- It is addictive, easy to learn and hard to master.
- It is realistic; almost spot on logical gameplay.
- The graphics are not heavy and tiring but very enjoyable and sweet.
- It lets you feel intigrated to your village/villagers because they all have names, happiness bars and individual health/hunger/education problems.
- The economy/trade system is simple yet effective, let's you craft your own economic tree.
- The advancement feeling is not through a typical research routine but rather the sense of accomplishment with your town.
But there are a few downsides and I believe the developers will nail these in their next game.
- Only the mods will give you cosmetics and diversity. For example the CC mod has almost 60-70 buildings and incredibly cosmetic items and new resources but the core game lacks these.
- The day-night cycle is barely noticeable.
- The aging of your population doesn't make sense. They age more years than you spend on your town. (a town with 10 years of history will have people that aged 50 years in that town)
- People do not share food and let their child die. But they do share heat if the winter is harsh, which is an upside.
Overall this is an incredible indie game and I spend some decent time on this thing and I still enjoy it. Which makes it one of those games that I want it to have more because I played it a lot.
Try it. You'll like it.

I purchased this game at a very low price, but actually found it is worth the list price.  I *love* the tutorials.  I have such anxiety about playing strategy games and erecting infrastructure inefficiently.  I find it paralyzing.  I'll go play something else until I read enough about the game to avoid such pitfalls (or never get around to it, which is even more likely).
But, behold!  The tutorials told me exactly where to put something.  A glowing building footprint on the ground directed me to the location, and which way to rotate the building.
Once I had played through the tutorials, I had gotten over myself.  A little trial and error is okay after all.  This game nailed me to my seat for the entire first day I owned it.  I barely moved.
A few things to note if you're a new player:
1) Make extra houses or your citizens will not procreate and your colony will die.  I learned this the slowest, most depressing way ever.
2) Citizens age 5 years per in-game year.
3) Children go to school (if available) at age 10 through 17 - if there isn't a school or teacher, they become a laborer instead.
4) When purchasing chicken from a trader - it may be live or just meat.  Make sure you know which one you're buying.
5) Farmers behave as laborers in the off season.
6) Make your pastures large enough to fit 10 animals (more than 12x12.... that fit only 9 animals for me).  Build two.  Once the herd is 10+ animals, you can split the herd and fill both corals over time.
7) Cemetaries make citizens happy, apparently. It prevents sadness (loss of productivity) when elders die.
8) It's okay to play on Medium or Easy mode at first, you wuss.  J/K.  I like Medium.
9) Food never goes bad.  You can store it indefinitely.
10) Too much stuff in your storage and stockpiles?  Increase the amount you want at the Trading Post and the trader will move it from storage and stockpiles to the Trading Post.
Excellent short adventure.

This is a pretty fun game with an interesting concept.  I've seen some reviewers suggest adding trenches or something else not "mortar related", and I think that's a bad idea.  That would take away from the uniqueness of this game, which is perhaps the best part of it.
The worst part is a pretty glaring problem:  none of the guns are balanced very well.  You can beat the game with the very first gun by getting lots of them.  Shields are poorly executed, as they are a poor mix of how much damage and how many hits they can take.  The best strategy to get past them is to synch up a lot of smaller guns to fire at the same time.  Large guns are very powerful, and perhaps the best balanced weapons in the game.  Rockets, on the other hand, are nearly worthless.   Mortar Cannons are always powerful and especially useful for taking out enemy personnel, and lasers are great for penetrating shields, although the first iteration of these weapons is grossly underpowered and shoots far too slowly to have worth.
The campaign is very long, and it does have a bit of a roguelike element to it.  Medals carry over from game to game, making it slightly easier, but not much.  As far as I can tell, there are only 6 medals which can all be acquired within 2 playthroughs very easily.
Tutorial wise, there may as well be none.  While it explains extremely basic concepts, like how to fire and what a few weapons are good for, it does very little to explain actual game concepts like scoring, the fact that it is roguelike in regard to the medals, or that the perks and nothing else will carry over.
The campaign is extremely long, so you're going to get your $6 out of it, if you enjoy the other aspects of it.
I give this game a pretty solid 7/10.
