Great game, with a fatal flaw. Money progression.
In its design, and execution, it is great. You start out a level by selecting a variety of Fort layouts, drop in the weapons and equipment you have purchased previously into the varied slots (rooms) within the layout, and then go toe to toe with the next enemy Fort in a long campaign of such levels. This is achieved through inspired layouts, the smart use of crewing rooms (that increase their effectiveness), and choosing to obliterate enemy rooms and troops in an order chosen by you, before they do the same to you.
As you progress you can spend your hard earned money on purchasing new weapon technologies as they unlock through the game, or even upgrade your existing weaponry/equipment as this comes available, making your new layouts even more powerful than those use before. But this is where this games single biggest issue begins. Money...
Although you are encouraged to customise your layout, and by extension try new things as they unlock, if you do so, and aren't fortunate enough to use your money on the right weapon/equipment at the right time, try and experiement with builds, or vary your strategy from time to time, you will eventually find yourself up against a fort that you cannot defeat, not matter how many times you try. This is because you ran out of money... with no way to ever make more.
Your only option left to you? Hard reboot and start from the very beginning again, regardless of how far you got before. Yes, you could be one of the lucky ones whose personal strategy happened to be one of the few that gets you through to the end, but more likely one of the ones who has to start from the very beginning a time or two until you realise you are severely punished if you attempt to go down various paths.
It is an issue that has a simple fix, one of many suggested by the community, but has yet to occur or be acknowledged. If any were to be adopted, I would change my recommedation in an instant.

Outlast is a horror game that is genuinely scary. This game is really ♥♥♥♥ed up. When this game is at its best, it IS the best horror game ever made. Unfortunately, there are some serious issues that highly irritated me and too frequently killed the tension and made the game a chore. The story is about a reporter investigating some strange goings-on at mental asylum. Rumor has it that there's a old Nazi doctor that has been performing mind control experiments related to the CIA's MKULTRA program. A lot of horror games these days seem like they are positively soaked in mind control imagery and themes, but ironically Outlast is one of the few horror games that explicitly mentions the program by name and it seems absent the standard disassociative dreamworld themes that are so prevalent in the modern horror game genre. Anyway, very soon after arriving the power goes out and the protagonist is attacked. The goal then changes from getting the story to just escaping. There's a running gag in the game where the main character is juuuuussst about to make it out of the front door when something happens to stop his escape. Loved that. What they did right was having most of the game be really dark. The reporter brought his video camera with night vision on it and frequently the game needs to be played through the night vision on the view finder of the video camera. The catch is that the night vision drains batteries and more batteries need to be found in order to actually see your surroundings. It was panic inducing trying to figure out where to go having to constantly make split second decisions because some Frankenstein monster was running after me just a half step behind. There are tons of scripted events in the game. Tons of jump scares. Many of the jump scares are effective, some just felt like I was in the modern version of a Haunted House ride at the fair. There are lots of NPC inmates around that give the game environment a living feel. Outlast is at its best when you're traversing through the asylum going from point A to point B running from lunatics and chaos is happening all around you. The parts that really got annoying were the way too frequent tasks of having to flip x number of switches or collect y number of  macguffins. The patrolling enemy AI would have this sixth sense for where I was at all times. You can hide in lockers or under beds to evade death (the player has no weapons) but then the problem is not being able to see anything and never knowing when its safe to leave. I understand why these parts are in the game, but they need to be DRASTICALLY reworked for future sequels. These parts almost ruined the entire experience for me In fact, I'd say just skip the Whistleblower DLC, it's jammed pack full of overly frustrating experiences and doesn't really offer anything new except for plot points. The main game took around 7 hours to finish. This game is not for the squeamish. There is a lot of brutal graphic violence. I tell you this as a hard core horror junkie. You may want to consider if Outlast is too extreme for you. Outlast is the cutting edge of scary and gory video games right now. There is lots of both in Outlast. There are some significant problems I had with this game, but at the end of the day it was an amazing thrill ride that horror fans should play.

When I first saw the screenshots, it took me right back to Tank Wars in DOS, with much improved graphics of course!
The game is artillery combat, think of Worms, but with stationary offense and defense. You need to carefully choose where to focus your assault to win the long game.
A lot of rounds will quickly turn into a war of attrition, with units repairing and healing themselves, so its critical you pick and choose your targets carefully.
The combat is similar to FTL (Faster Than Light) in that you target specific rooms, and wait for your weapons to charge. There is also the ability to pause the game to plan these attacks, just like FTL.
The graphics are very nice to look at, and I like the clever differences in the opposing sides that give a reference to how large the battle field really is.
In summary, if you like Worms, Tank Wars, or FTL, you will no doubt love this game. It's definately worth it for the price.

TL;DR - Unoriginal and unpolished. Pretty boring until mid-game. Go play Final Fantasy, and you'll have played a better version of this game.
This game does a lot of things well, but what it does best is remind me of better games. The story is slow, and generic. The action is run of the mill, and battles can be very, very boring. The game teaches you how to play pretty well, but it does it all from pop-up text windows, instead of letting gameplay mechanics develop naturally.
If you're looking for customization, you'll find next to none. If you're looking for a story that will draw you in, you'll have to trudge through a few hours of the game first before things get kind of interesting. The story plays on a lot of tropes from anime and other JRPGs, and doesn't have an original feel to it. If you're looking for fun action, then you'll be looking for a while. The combat in this game is pretty bland, and things don't get interesting until you get to higher levels. Each element of the game feels very separated from the rest, and nothing really flows together, though you can tell some parts are supposed to.
This game is lacking polish in a lot of areas, and it shows right from the beginning of the game. The characters are very one dimensional, and their dialogue can be nauseating at times. I found myself rolling my eyes plenty of times while characters rambled about themselves, and even more when they would make attempts at banter. The combat goes from button mashing to complicated in the blink of an eye, showing a lot of flashy animations without a whole lot actually happening. The plot is generic, unoriginal, and poorly contrived. It leads you on for far too long, takes an obvious twist, and is bad at explaining itself. The graphics are pretty, and the music ads a nice ambience to the settings, but it's nothing that memorable.
This isn't a bad game though, it's just not as good as a lot of other games on Steam that you can probably buy for a cheaper price.If you really love anime and JRPGs, then you'll like this game. If you're here to play a good Action RPG, look for something better.

I don't usually leave reviews for games that I play, but I feel that this absolutely needs one. First off, I'd like to say that I recommend this game with no reservations. That being said, there are some cons to consider.

Largely because this is a fairly low budget game, there are a few graphical bugs and invisible walls in inconvenient places, however these are almost entirely harmless as far as enjoyment goes. The achievements are, arguably, too easy to get. While they were by no means a cakewalk, the majority took half an hour or so of playtime to get.
The voice acting is somewhat low quality, although I'm putting this as a pro and a con because it adds to the overall experience in an amazing way.
The pros, unlike the cons, would take a very long time to list.
-The aesthetic is one of the best I've seen
-the atmosphere changes perfectly from area to area
-there is a large amount of variation in environment and gameplay based on context. This is mainly in regards switching from parkour to fighting to swinging, but there is a noticeable amount of change.
-the difficulty has a very good curve, while leaving potential to find difficulty even in the easy areas... strengthening replayability
-the controls are very intuitive, and are a very nice mix in between snappy and forgiving. Basically, they're comfortable without handholding you, and you will always go where you tell the game to go.
I had to search for the cons in this game. If it looks interesting in the least to you, I'd recommend springing for it. You won't regret it.

BioShock... Hmm, where to even begin?
It's difficult to talk about this game in non-superlative terms, but I'll do my best.  BioShock tells one of the best stories in modern gaming, and is one of only a handful of video games to fully capitalize on their unique strengths as a storytelling medium.  It tells a smart (albeit sometimes heavy-handed) story set amidst a beautifully fleshed-out, dark, crumbling underwater city.  The story is presented entirely in first-person, and the city of Rapture is brought to life by BioShock's magnificent cast of characters, art deco visual style, and exciting shotgun-and-spells gameplay.  BioShock manages to accomplish what few games seem able to: total immersion.  Every element of this game complements the others, keeping you engaged for every moment you spend within the fascinatingly twisted world Irrational has created.
I could go on at great length about the numerous other things the game does so well – its use of symbolism and consistent motifs, the depth of its story, the attention to detail – but the best way to experience it all is simply to play the game.  Even if you've played BioShock multiple times, it's worth returning to Rapture again.
BioShock really is that good.

First, I would like to give a personal thank you to BigCorporation.
You are single-handedly THE funniest, kindest developer I have ever met.
The Game:
"Hmm, Blood and Bacon; it's only a dollar and it has 'Overwhelmingly Positive' reviews...  Screw it, I'm gonna buy it."
Ten minutes later and 3 of my friends own it and we are having a BLAST!
Blood and Bacon is an experience in revenge.  The Farmer, the lord and savior, is in a bit of a pickle. So what does he do?  He recruits you and anyone else to take back the farm!  There's guns, grenades, power-ups; and BLOOD AND BACON!  Running around and shooting the crap out of dozens of pigs is just plain fun.  Play with some friends and this game is seriously a hilarious joyride.  The voice acting is absolutely my favorite part, and everything the farmer says made my group laugh out loud many a time.  Plenty of secrets exist in the game too.  There are cool little quirks and discoveries to be made, and discovering these is another little part of the "magic" that this little gem exudes.
TLDR;
This game is $.99 not on sale and is totally worth every penny, with $4.00 you can buy it for 3 friends and have an awesome afternoon (assuming you don't keep playing it every other day like we do) of blood, guts, and BACON!

If PETA was the censorship board, Blood and Bacon would definitely be banned for animal cruelty on a virtual videogame
Although I do not support animal cruelty and I fully support PETA (to a certain extent) and that I am a vegan (yes, a vegan playing a gory bloody game about boars being bloodily mutalated for no apparent reason), I am not easily offended by Blood and Bacon's setting and gameplay, in fact, I love it!
Blood and Bacon is a game developed by Big Corporation and published by Grudge Games LTD.
Blood and Bacon is a really fun Left 4 Dead type game, even as much as copying the UI from the console versions of Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 (according to console sources). Blood and Bacon was the best game I've seen for its price for a very long time, especially when playing with friends (which sadly I do not have)
You are in barn with its farmer stuck to the barn wall with a pitchfork in him and a leg chopped off (no biggy). And each day you have to try and kill the required amount of boars/pigs by shooting them, juggling them and then shooting them, electrocuting them or throwing them into a mincer. Each day, more and more boars show up
After a certain amount of days, a boos boar shows up where you shoot the living hell out of it. This happens every day in the game. The game can get boring and repetitive after a while of playing in solo, however, the game is extremely fun to play with your friends in co-op (which sadly I do not have any friends)
You can play online co-op with other people, but some of the players are so brain dead that they stay in the barn and the level doesn't play or they die too quickly
Blood and Bacon is really fun game to play. So badly made that it is good. However, Blood and Bacon's graphics are not that great. Some graphics are ugly to look at and the UI is pretty ugly to look at and the game offers a very small soundtrack. Not that much music happening while playing which is a shame
I wouldn't recommend Blood and Bacon if it was priced higher than 1 EUR, however for the price it is offering and the options the game offers and the bloody gory fun you can have while playing alone and especially with friends, I would definitely recommend Blood and Bacon to anyone

This game has a lot going for it, like the artistic style, nice graphics, an Orwellian/1984 theme, great sound (I especially like the sounds the larger guns make) and the basic idea of two forts going at it with a variety of weapons and defenses is cool and not done to death.
But in the end a game will stand or fall by its gameplay, and this is where REDCON fails. The game is a terrible grind that ends up being mostly about tedious micromanagement of getting men out of or into a room at just the right split second, manually telling 6-10 guns to fire, one at a time, after having told each of those very same guns which specific target to fire at... one at a time... Add to this an absurd amount of levels (at least 100) and an economic system that grants you a little money for completing each level, but doesn't let you replay levels or sell back guns or upgrades once bought, and you've got the perfect recipe for frustration.
You'll reach a level where certain weapons are obviously better (there's a slight rock-paper-scissors mechanism to weapons vs. defenses), but you won't be able to use those weapons, since you haven't invested in them earlier and haven't the money to do so now. No matter which weapons you chose to focus on (small guns, large guns, missiles, lasers, ICBMs), you can't have them all and they will all be clearly better for some of the entirely too many stages. So to beat the levels your particular purchases aren't suited for, you'll just have to micromanage even more than usual.
This is made worse by the defenses being annoyingly effective, so much so that even 15-20 projectiles of various size will get shot out of the air easily by 2-3 defensive lasers on your opponents fort, unless they all arrive within about a second of each other. That means telling the guns that have a faster reload to not fire while waiting for the slower guns, then when all are ready, you pause the game and tell them to fire one by one while paused and pray that enough get through to take down your target. If not, you can be sure that any damage done will be repaired by your enemy's soldiers before your next salvo is ready.
And speaking of the soldiers, while the enemy soldiers will often jump out of a room at the very last second, right before a large shell hits that would have painted the walls with their innards, your own troopers do nothing unless you tell them to. There is no way to automate them beyond having them work at whatever station they find themselves at. They will automatically repair their station if it is damaged, but even that is not necessarily an advantage, as you'd sometimes prefer the gravely wounded trooper to just get healed by the Aid Station room rather than spend the next minute repairing it while a gust of wind could end his life.
The already excessive grind of the game is in this way an many others made worse by the mechanics. You can't easily control guns and soldiers, so you have to compensate by micromanaging so much you feel like you're doing your taxes rather than playing a game. In the end, while wanting to like this game so much, it just wasn't enjoyable to me for more than a minute or two before it turned a chore again. It's like a gocart where the engine stops every 30 seconds. It promises fun, but you end up fighting what was supposed to be the source of your entertainment.

I played this directly after finishing Tales of Symphonia and Phantasia. And at first I was very disappointed. The story took my interest and the characters were interesting, but..
The pace at the beginning was so slow, the world felt"empty" (long distances of just running), the combat system was a lot complexer than the other Tales series, yet it felt more stiff and the equipment system... it took me at least 30 hours of gameplay to understand it (I still feel it is way too much trouble...)
I still recommend this game, if you can get it for around 25-30€, because it is not bad once you get used to it (after around 20h for me). The story is okay, the characters are likable (can sometimes be annoying though) and as the world gets more open there is so much to explore. You have lots of side quests, epic monsters, battle arenas, collectables to find it will take a long time to complete this game. I'm even more interested in exploring and collecting than the main story now. But when I get sick of running around aimlessly, I can do a story quest and it won't get boring.
Strong points:
+ so much to see, find, unlock (epic monsters, hidden collectables, side quests, merchant levels can be raised, seraphims can be "collected", dialogues between the characters can be unlocked, a huge world with many possibilities)
+ characters are unique and most of them likable
+ the story is interesting and well executed
+ nice soundtrack
+ japanese and english synchronization is good
+ anime cut scenes
Weak points:
- too complex in parts (fighting and equipment/fusion system need a lot of tutorials and are not self-explanatory)
- too many tutorials (Many of those I didn't read, because I was bored and wanted to learn by myself and then I had a hard time)
- some parts of the story annoyed me so much I almost quit the game, I'm glad I didn't, though.
Peronal Nagging:
# combat system of ToP and ToS was so much better, but you get used to it
# german translation is lacking

BioShock... Hmm, where to even begin?
It's difficult to talk about this game in non-superlative terms, but I'll do my best.  BioShock tells one of the best stories in modern gaming, and is one of only a handful of video games to fully capitalize on their unique strengths as a storytelling medium.  It tells a smart (albeit sometimes heavy-handed) story set amidst a beautifully fleshed-out, dark, crumbling underwater city.  The story is presented entirely in first-person, and the city of Rapture is brought to life by BioShock's magnificent cast of characters, art deco visual style, and exciting shotgun-and-spells gameplay.  BioShock manages to accomplish what few games seem able to: total immersion.  Every element of this game complements the others, keeping you engaged for every moment you spend within the fascinatingly twisted world Irrational has created.
I could go on at great length about the numerous other things the game does so well – its use of symbolism and consistent motifs, the depth of its story, the attention to detail – but the best way to experience it all is simply to play the game.  Even if you've played BioShock multiple times, it's worth returning to Rapture again.
BioShock really is that good.

Have your Lava Cake and eat it
is the line that best describes A Hat in Time. It defies the genre that it's in, whilst also being a fantastic entry in it. It manages to give you both big open collectathon levels AND keep the experience linear and guided, tell interesting stories, and provide good boss fights. And when I say "good boss fights", I mean the
bossfights the genre has ever seen! The kind you never think about when you hear the words "3D platformer".
Another thing you will notice immediately is that it does not hold back most of its movement abilities behind unlocks. Not by a long shot! The moment you start the first level, you have a double jump, which you can chain into a dive, which resets your double jump. Oh, and you also get parkour on walls, as a cherry on top. This immediate wealth of movement means you do not have to wait for collectables to make the game good. You can zip across rooftops, platforms, and enemies like a ninja mere minutes into the game, to the tune of great music and whimsy of a good sense of humor.
The only shortcoming that holds it back is that parts of it feel... unfinished. Where's the story and boss of level 4? Why is the last level so short? Why is it that most unlocks hardly ever get used as level mechanics? Oh, and no, there is no replay value in the base game - once you collect everything there's not much else to do. Thankfully, the game has good mod support to solve that.

I  wish I could recommend this game, as I enjoyed it, but in hindsight and after talking to multiple others who had played it, I realize it wouldn't make much sense to do so.
There are some things to like and love here- it's technically a multiplayer action RPG, some of the character designs are interesting (mostly your own) and switching between forms to fight is very satisfying.  Equipment fusion is a confusing but interesting system, there's the occasional troublesome boss and it's nice to see the tales series branch out and try new things.  Some of the conflicts and areas are well done, there's a decent amount of extra content and more difficulty options than previous titles to help you get that sweet spot if you suck at tales like I do.  Oh, and linking encounters is kind of cool.
All of the positives are outweighed by the bad- the camera focus on player one makes multiplayer difficult, even if you didn't essentially eat party members to change forms.  A second permament character exists early on and then slightly less than halfway through the game, but that's a long stretch of annoyance for P2.  Even when flying Solo the camera freaks out on walls and other common environmental hazards.  That connects nicely to the issue of the whole "fight where you stand" feature- it's novel that the environment is exactly the same in battle as without, but the trade-off is huge empty areas and few interesting arenas.  This isn't helped much by the mediocre teammate and enemy AI and the fact that you only have so many abilities due to how they've essentially established lines of automatic combos for you.  A lot of extra content comes down to how well you've fused boots, as well.
Those are a lot of tradeoffs, but tales has never had a perfect system by any means.  Same with the story- but I would say with little hesitation that this is one of the most insipid.  The playable cast are mostly polarizing, a major character at the beginning of the game gets dropped for the rest of it just kind of because, most of the story and plot points are actively contradicted by other story and plot points, the main villain's history is okay but their motivation is pretty uncompelling, It can't stick to its own rules at all.  There's also  some very very forced dialogue, but this is pretty much a staple of the genre.  At least the ending is alright.
In short, unless you want to play all of the tales games, you can safely pass on this one.  It has some ties to Berseria which has some similar issues but is overall much more enjoyable, but it's definitely not required to play it.

The game follows the absolutely adorable and aptly named Hat Kid who must travel from world to world in order to collect each of her 40 missing Time Pieces that have been scattered thanks to the meddling of the Mafia from a nearby planet while Hat Kid is on her way home….from somewhere?
The game follows a structure very similar to Super Mario Sunshine and Super Mario Galaxy, in which you have a basic hub that will allow you to select a world to visit alongside each mission that each world contains.
Each and every mission changes up the world in some minor or major way depending, for example in the first world of the game “Mafia Town” you begin chasing after the mysterious Mustache girl, while later on you can find yourself in a literal game of the floor is lava.
The worlds are all for the most part extremely open ended, allowing you to quite easily be able to branch off from the beaten path and explore the admittedly large and imaginative environments at your own will.
Hell the first world in particular, I am convinced it’s inspired by the hub world from Super Mario Sunshine “Delfino Plaza” simply due to how open it is alongside the general aesthetic of the place.
Now A lot of folk would be concerned however about large and vast levels in these type of games, as they can tend to be confusing to navigate in a lot of instances and even easy to lose track of your objective. Thankfully in A Hat in Time, this is not an issue, the game is very cleverly designed to the point that I never found myself lost, even after I went off the path to do my own exploring.
Not only that but via the use of Hat kids…..well….hat, you can instantly locate your objective at any time to get right back on track if you lose where you are meant to go!
The controls here are simply magnificent and very free-flowing, it’s very easy to not only make very long and wide jumps easily, you can also do pinpoint precise jumps without ANY issue whatsoever.
This is only helped through the double jump and dive abilities too which give hat kid an insane level of control, that very few platformers can reach.
On top of her basic jumping moveset, Hat kid can also pull off a basic 3 hit combo to attack enemies, and perform a Sonic Adventure esque homing attack on nearby foes, though this is a little fiddly to perform correctly I feel.
Littered throughout your adventure too you will usually come across Yarn balls, these will allow you to construct new hats to utilise, that all offer unique abilities and powers, for example you can get an ice cap to perform ground pound abilities, that also allow you to springboard from specific points in the world, or have a dwellers mask that makes transparent objects interactable for a few seconds for platforming challenges.
This isn’t even getting into the badges you can buy from a very creepy glitchy looking fellow that offer gameplay modifiers such as item magnetism or the ability to fall far without taking damage.
Hell you even get a grappling hook later in the game for spider-man style action!
The presentation here is also absolutely top notch, with some FANTASTIC visuals that are reminiscent of the gamecube era of games, all the games dialogue voice acting, jokes and music are extremely amazing through and through.
The game clearly has a lot of love put into it here, with every single part simply oozing character, whether from the shady crows that ask for personal details in the Agatha Christie esque murder mystery level(yes you heard me right) or from simple things such as Hat Kid wearing an adorable raincoat in poor weather.
I’m not even going into the boss battles which I think it’s safe to say, I think these are some of the best fights i’ve ever seen in a 3D platformer!
There’s even a number of Raw platforming challenges in the form or “Time Rifts” littered about that offer challenges very much like the fluddless challenges from Super Mario Sunshine which are all an absolute blast to play!
Sadly the game isn’t perfect, there are occasional camera issues to be found here and there (much like most platformers tbh), and sometimes Hat Kids little climbing ability can get stuck on certain objects from time to time, plus the homing attack issue I mentioned earlier in the review...but in the grand scheme of the game, these are very minor niggles at worst and really don’t affect my experience all that much in the grand scheme of things!
Ultimately A Hat in Time is without a doubt one of the greatest platforming titles I have ever played, and a game I think that any platforming fan simply owes themselves to play through!

Honestly? Meh.
The mechanic is very original, and a lot of fun when you first get started, but ultimately it feels more like a "Proof of Concept" than a fully functional game.
The enemies come in 2 flavors:
Run forward shooting
AND
Stand still shooting.
Anyone with a moderate familiarity with shooters will see the problem here.
The levels are very easy, and there aren't very many of them.
The story ... wasn't bad, but (in my opinion) actually hurt the game over all, and I would have rather skipped all story content completely as it was essentially just cut-scenes in text and ASCII that added nothing to the experience but time.
Endless mode is the worst part of the game, it's just the same terrible enemies in the same room, endlessly.
Yikes.
At least the story gave you a new room / new set-up / new surprise enemies every few minutes.
Worth $20? Nope.
Worth $15? Probably not.
Worth $10 Sure, if you've got the money and want a *short* diversion.
Worth $5 or less? Very much so, the mechanic is quite entertaining and original.
It's kind of like Portal, except murdering is your only tool to solve the "puzzles".
And it isn't funny.
And the story has less than one newton of compelling force.
And it doesn't have varying and interesting visuals and audio as you progress.
And it shouts the game's name at you constantly.
And it commands you to tell your friends to buy the game. Seriously? Desperation is such a turn-off.
Do I regret playing it? Nope, it was short.
But if I had paid for it, I would want my money back.

It is a small space shooter (...as in you shoot in space, not that you shoot spaces) with simple 3D graphics and a 3rd person "behind the spacecraft" view. The game controls using exclusively the keyboard with the arrows or the WASD keys and space or ctrl for shooting. The gameplay consists of series of levels where you have a single goal which is one of shooting enemies down, avoiding obstacles, shooting a specified number of enemies in a given time limit or taking down a big boss. When you are supposed to shoot down enemies you also get powerups, but those persist only in the level (as does your health, which resets after each level).
Generally speaking, it isn't anything special to write home about, but it is a good "time waster" - especially considering the price. Personally i also really liked the background music.
On the negative side, i'd say that the game becomes repetitive after a while (so it is only good for short bursts between other games or for your lunch break at work). Also i am not fan of saving only every few levels because of said repetition.

One of the most notable things about Blood Bowl 2 is the improved UI. The game will now display the % chance of a move, such as dodge or ball pickup succeeding while is a massive bonus for new players. Speaking of new players the Campaign is essentially a long tutorial, which is absolutely necessary in a game like Blood Bowl. The last game suffered as it wasn’t really accessible, whereas you can learn how to play much more easily in this one.
In addition to UI improvements the graphics are significantly better. The animations, particularly when blocking an opposing player, are lovely to look at. Each race also gets their own separate set of animations which really shows how much time has been spent developing each race. Everything you do has proper weight behind it and really immerses you in the experience. When a Saurus is blitzing down your lowly Peasant you’ll feel the fear.
The online leagues are easy to enter and it’s fun as hell creating a team with a silly name and theme. From my experience the community has been friendly and welcoming. It’s always nice when 2 players can both laugh at the dice rolls and unlikely moves that somehow pay off. Hopefully the community stays civil, it’s a nice change of pace from other competitive games.
The obvious downside is the lack of teams compared to the Chaos Edition of Blood Bowl 1. That’s pretty much the reason the reviews currently show as “mixed” on Steam. Personally I can see how much effort goes into every team in Blood Bowl 2, so I understand the smaller selection. More teams will come, but I imagine they will cost extra. This might put some people off, at least until a sale.
Overall Blood Bowl 2 is a massive improvement from Blood Bowl: Chaos Edition. It’s prettier, cleaner and all round more user friendly. Everything from menus to stadiums to the Skinks beady little eyes are improved. I would certainly recommend this game, especially for people new to Blood Bowl.

Here we have another game that can be summed up in a single word: YIKES!
It's cute that Sun Blast's store description not only has the gall to claim that it was inspired by Star Fox, Space Harrier, and Panzer Dragoon, but it also says that it's "the best 3d space shooter on Steam".
Sun Blast was inspired by a dumpster fire. Never before have I played a shooter with such poor mechanics, sluggish controls, and awful mission-design. Dodging enemy ships and their bullets should be a relatively simple task, but instead it's messy and somewhat convoluted. This can be attributed to the odd perspective. It's not always clear where objects are in relation to the player-ship. So this results in lots of collisions. The bosses tend to have homing weapons, and they're exceedingly frustrating to deal with. Why? Because the player-ship can't maneuver around them, and the angle makes it difficult to tell where the homing shots are heading.
In shootemups, dodging a single bullet should be as easy as breathing. The developer makes the game more difficult by increasing the speed of that bullet, adding more of them, giving them unique properties, and so on. It's the constantly building intensity that keeps these games challenging. Sun Blast somehow manages to accomplish the opposite. Dodging a single bullet is far more trouble than in any other game I've played.
The missions are exceedingly generic and dull. For the most part they're also extremely easy, except for the bosses. Whenever I had to replay the last few stages, because I died at the boss, all I could do was nod my head and think "Yep. I expected this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t."
If I spend enough time with Sun Blast, eventually I could learn to handle it's many terrible qualities.
But why? This game suffers from a total dearth of entertainment value.
Before I forget, let's take a look at this statement: "the best 3d space shooter on Steam". I can't claim to know the Steam Store's library well enough to confirm that this is false. However, I will point out that
is available on the service. While it hasn't aged well, and the frame-rate is worse than Sun Blast's, this relic from the 16-bit era is a much better game. I suppose it doesn't include enough "3D" or "space" to fit the criteria, but it might actually be worth your time.

This game was fun for a bit, but for me it got boring quite quickly.  I always hoped Banished would move beyond what it currently is, which is simply a city builder with basic resource management.  What would have taken this game to the next level is some sort of an event system that added interesting challenges and diversity.  The game desperately needs personality and unpredictability.  As it stands, it feels soulless, it's a slow churn that has few surprises.
It pains me to be negative because this game could be a foundation for an absolutely spectacular experience.  Unfortunately, the vision just isn't there.  Banished is most definitely not worth $20, but $5 and under is a fair buy.
All that out of the way, I'm going to suggest what I think this game should have been... First off, the concept is fantastic... you have a group of people banished from society that have to eek out an existence in some remote location with limited contact to the outside world.  This is brilliant, but the problem is that the designer of this game left out the most interesting parts of what these societies are all about: religion and politics!  This game absolutely needs a more robust religion and politics mechanic that ♥♥♥♥s with how you build out this society.  There should be elections, there should be religous law and it should all be dynamic.  Things should get downright ♥♥♥♥ing weird if the right conditions present themselves (witch burnings, vegan sacrifices, poligomy, etc).   There's so much opportunity to add unpredictable crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥to make you want to keep playing this game.  Sadly, like I said above the game is a clinical city builder with some basic resource management.  It's one of those games that's hard to play because you're constantly thinking about what should have been.

Early access is something of a swamp if all truth be told, too many developers use it as an excuse for poor quality or even unfinished games. Some however (Kerbal Space Program and Prison Architect being notable examples) use it as an excellent springboard to make sure that the game is not only great but also what people want it to be. FL337 however falls somewhere in the middle.
Whilst what follows is quite a negative review I must congratulate the developer of this game on thier responsiveness to feedback. I pointed out some bugs in the game when I posted this review online innitially and they were fixed in the very next patch. They really seem to be working hard to get this game up to scratch and I really do hope that Early Access is exactly what they need to help with this.
What immediately strikes you as soon as you begin to play is the jarring variation of asset quality. The backgrounds and some of the other parts look very good and emulate the classic graphic style of Shank. But then you’ll come across an enemy, or even another playable character and they’re not only done in a different style but of vastly different quality. This is also compounded by a pretty basic and ugly UI – this leads to a fairly bad impression of the game.
Ignoring how the game looks, my biggest problem with the game becomes almost immediately noticeable during gameplay. You have three attacks; light, heavy and ranged. The heavy attack takes slightly longer to perform than the light, but does a couple of additional points of damage, and the ranged does less still but can hit right across the screen. That’s your lot. I’ve played a large number of passable indie brawlers (typically developed in Japan) but all of them have focused on having a large and interesting set of moves, as that really is the heart of a brawler game. However in FL337 all you can do is increase the amount of damage your attack does. The reason this is a major issue is that it means that all the enemies are the same – and when I say the same I really do mean it. If you play the game each level after another then your power increases roughly at the same rate as the enemies meaning that every single enemy at any point takes roughly two or three light attacks and their dead. There’s simply no variation to this at all and the enemies all feel exactly the same just reskinned.
The only exception to this rule is the bosses. At the end of a level after fighting through several waves of the same enemy you reach a big boss. The first couple are defeated in exactly the same way, get behind them as they walk around aimlessly and attack them from behind. With others, you just dodge out of the way of their big attack and then hit them whilst they recover. Again, because you only have the three attacks there is no real strategy or difficulty to the fights.
The final major issue with the game is it’s animations. Each animation individually is perfectly passable, I’ve seen far worse out there in great games, however they don’t link well together. Moving from a roll into an attack is very jarring as there is little to nothing in the way of transition and enemies struggle to move from their knockback animation into an attack animation meaning that you are frequently hit without any kind of animation being visible so you just lose health. (This has been fixed in a recent patch)
Currently this really isn’t a game I could recommend that you play it’s not really got anything going for it. Whilst it has an interesting idea behind it the incoherent quality of the visuals along with the downright boring gameplay mean that there is little reason to pick it over other games out there. However I really do hope that this is one of those games that early access was made for. It’ll take some fair amount work to make FL337 a great game, but it’s one that I’ll certainly reexamine at when it’s released.

Unfortunately REDCON confuses fun and tedious grind.
On paper it looks great.  Two opposing towers covered in turrets shelling each other across the landscape whilst little men rush around manning and repairing things.  One must weigh up sacrifing available ammunution for more power and helpful utility rooms.  But there's a huge problem.
Without prior knowledge of stages it's very easy to work oneself into a position where one doesn't have enough cash to then extricate oneself.  Turrets can't be sold and stages can't be replayed so expect to be frustrated as earlier decisions come back to bite you.
If you don't google the solutions you'll need to restart the entire game often.
Worse yet the game doesn't really progress.  You'll either find youself in the afore mentioned downword spiral of bankruptcy or discover that the enemy weapons and towers upgrade at the same pace as yours; I seldom felt that I was making headway.
The men, what should have made REDCON an exciting and new experience, have no AI whatsoever.  They will cheerfully stand in flames, toxins or under falling shells.  They won't run to repair rooms near to them nor leave inactive turrets.
Orders can be given whilst the game is paused but here-in lies the tedium.  I spent far more time paused than I did playing.  And I found myself going through the same motions again and again, stage after stage.  Pause, swap injured man for uninjured man.  Unpause.  Pause, click through all turrets to find out which is firing on what and re-assign targets.  Unpause.  Repeat.
The graphics are pretty - what you see in the screenshots is what you get.  The music is a bit mediocre and there isn't enough of it cover the tens of hours of time you'd need to invest to complete this game.
The story is forgettable and can be summend up as Fat Adolf Hitler vs Evil Kaiser Wilhelm.  The only piece that really engaged me was early on, I was ordered to attack a defenseless hospital tower and I decided I wasn't going to.  Unfortunately that wasn't a win condition.
In short REDCON has an addicitve quality to it that is bad, it gives the feeling that there must be something more in the next tower or turret or layout and if you just tried that little bit harder you'd find it.  But there never is.  It's a one trick pony stretched far to thin.

8/10. Most immersive FPS I've ever played (excluding ArmA here), while still having an awesome action-packed feel to it. You can change your settings to pretty much any way that suits your play style (manual weapon bolting, Incremental tank throttle, etc.) And tank combat, although it's not used much, is fantastic because of the insanely high-detailed tank interiors. I mean, you can look through the inside of the tank, and you have to crawl to certain positions if that position's crew member gets killed. As for the infantry combat, like I said, the most immersive (and fairly realistic for what it is) combat I've seen. Getting shot in different body parts affect different stuff (Ex: if you get shot in the legs, you walk very slow until you find a safe spot to bandage yourself). And each weapon has a level cap of 50 with unique upgrades for each of them every 25 levels. As for the bad parts, the AI is... not good, to say the least. Sometimes they'll miss with 2 full magazines trying to shoot at you, and other times they'll one shot you with a hip-fired machine gun from 100m away. All in all, however, It would be more than worth the money to buy this game. And if you like RO2, definitely buy Rising Storm, because it takes all of that Red Orchestra 2 epicness to the Pacific Theatre

"It's not scary at all."
"Everyone's just overreacting to it."
Firstly,I will say that horror like comedy,is very subjective and it is very hard to please everyone with what you're trying to put on the table.Not everyone's going to think this horror game is scary.I realize that and want to share my own thoughts on the popular game.Now,let's get on with our review.
I have never been a big horro fan in general.Horror movies were all paranormal or psycho movies with boring scares to me.But,I've had a soft part in my heart for horror GAMES in particular.Playing through my character's nightmarish hell felt more immersive to me.However,like horror movies,I felt there were boring trends in them that made the genre boring,such as cheap jumpscares and Slender clones.Then I saw this game.
Five Nights at Freddy's is a little more than a survival horror game.It's a stress and situational management game as well.You play as a nightwatch guard at a Chuck E. Cheese-esque resturaunt called "Freddy Fazbear Pizza".There are animatronics there that move around at night so they continue to function.The main problem,however,is that these creepy robots will mistake you for a naked exoskeleton for one of the other animatronics and try to stuff you in one of the suits,which is full of wiring and other stuff that will kill you.Keeping the buggers away can be tricky,as you have limited power for each night and doing things such as checking the cameras for where the animatronics are,closing doors,and checking lights takes up this power.It can get really tense at times,as you never really know what trick Freddy and his friends from Hell have in store for you.
There are 4(but really 5)animatronics you need to worry about at your job at Freddy Fazbear's.There's Bonnie the Bunny,Chica the Chicken,Foxy the Pirate,and last but certainly not least,Freddy Fazbear.Each of these animatronics have specific patterns,such as moving a lot or even bolting down to your door to kill you.As the nights go on,these enemies become more and more active and will gobble your power up as you try to keep them away.
Now let's talk about the good stuff in this game:
The atmosphere is great and really gives you the feel of being in an old pizzeria,despite all of the gameplay being presented as camera footage GIFs and a main office panorama.It's dark,spooky,and the animatronics really top it off.For a $5 game,this really did give you what you paid for.A short and sweet horror game to play on Halloween or when you have friends over.The gameplay felt original and different than the other horror games I've played and it was just quite fun,in a way.
Now here comes the bad:
As you go on later into the nights,skill will not be as important as luck.The outcome of the nights are always randomized.Some nights you will have animatronics right outside BOTH of your doors,which drains power fast.Others,you will have Foxy come and bang on your door a good number of times,which also drains power.It just feels less and less dependent on skill as you go on.
The verdict:
This is a very good horror game.If you don't like it,you won't be wasting much money.If you do,you will get a horror game with great amount of atmosphere and strategy to use.It may get more dependent on luck as you go on,but Five Nights at Freddy's is still a fun ride along the way.
7.5/10-Get it and finish it,especially when its on sale.

So I finished the game yesterday which is as good a time as any to leave my impressions on it - though I haven't done the post-game content. First off, let me say that this is a good game - by which I mean directly in-between a bad game and a great game, which it is neither of. Tales Games are bound up to excellence in 3 areas - story, combat, and character relationships.
I was skeptical about the story because I'm not a fan of "messiah" stuff, but it isn't that bad, but it doesn't surprise either. Nevermind it being cliché (it definitely is) it is also rather ridiculous (and not the good kind) in a few spots. I also didn't care for the ending because I really felt if they were going to make a "shounen manga" game, they might as well have done it all the way with the ending too, which they didn't really. The story isn't bad though - by no means good by Tales standards, it is enough to keep you engaged though there are a number of gaps of hidden potential in the story to actually evolve into something interesting beyond the surface, but it never does, which is a shame.
When I played Tales of Symphonia recently I really realized how the character relationships especially through the concept of "skits" (small minisodes where the characters discuss random things) developed into commentary on some pretty heavy issues. That doesn't happen here. Just as the story is just what it is on the surface and not much more the skits never develop into that level of social commentary - they are funny though, especially the interactions between Edna (pure sassy sarcasm) and Mikleo. I didn't care much for the original companion Alisha - not that I dislike that kind of character per se, but I felt the writing (and in some cases the quality of the voice acting) really wasn't up to par to support that. On that note, The Tales series is one of EXTREMELY few where the English voice acting is at least on par with the Japanese one. You can listen to the Japanese tracks if you want to, but the English is excellent (again, Edna is amazing). So back to Alisha, I didn't feel the writing for her was all that good, but she gets replaced as a companion about 11 hours in for me for a much more interesting character (who is very well written and developed) - you see her again late-game where the writing is much better at supporting her as a character. The cast is diverse and interesting and I found myself laughing quite a bit, especially at Edna's amazing sarcasm, which they nailed like no other game.
The Combat then. Originally I had gotten myself into a frame of mind when buying this that I didn't expect too much from the story, but seeing how much I enjoyed the pure combat of Tales of Symphonia a while back, I was willing to play through a bad story. Well, let's just say that I'm very glad the story turned out to be decent and the characters interesting because the combat is actually the weakest part. For all the fact that this game throws half a dozen systems at you (and constantly reinforces it with double, triple, quadruple, infinite-drip turtorials to the point where I wondered if I would be able to fight a single battle without seeing one of the dumb things at one time) the combat is actually really simplistic to the point where it actually devolves into button mashing. There are a few things that are interesting, I enjoyed the power fantasy of transforming into a super-powered being a lot, but there isn't really any strategy involved. You can immediately see a monster's elemental resistances and weaknesses - pick artes or armatization (the super-transformation) to target that and then start attacking, doesn't matter all too much which abilities you use. The game tries to pretend it's very complex with a lot of systems, but the actual combat gameplay doesn't support it. It doesn't help that they've opted for a way that the combat takes place in the exact scenery of your regular map, but it's still limited in where you can move and the camera will I think center at the monster. This wouldn't be a problem, but if you get your back to the end of the battlefield the camera goes nuts so you can barely see anything (and even at the best of times because it is so broad you have very poor overview on how the combat is going for the rest of the characters) - and because of this "carryover" crap you can actually begin your battles with your spellcaster directly in-front of a melee monster. But you manage this problem ok, because as I mentioned all the complex systems they try to throw at you are mostly for show and can be safely ignored or forgotten and just play as you want. Even so, the combat does get tedious at times.
Oh, and for the open-world. It has elements of open-worlds, but only in the worst sense of it - meaning the overworld maps are filled with huge amounts of open space that takes time to trek through. It isn't actually filled with content. As huge a world as this is, playtime ignored it feels tiny in comparison to Tales of Symphonia or Tales of Vesperia (the other 2 tales games I've played).
So for a complete score, I'd say this ranks 6.7-7.2 as a game. I enjoyed myself quite a bit and I actually will do the post-game content (an extra ruin it seems to be) - it definitely is a game I can see myself replaying again at some point. But take it for what it is - it isn't total crap, but it isn't a great game either. Since this game regularly goes on 75% sales, I can definitely recommend it at that price.

Releasing just far enough in advance of
,
really is a beautiful game, doing a fantastic job of capturing the joy of the N64-era 3D platformer while also seeing some modern touches. It's a fairly short game, with only four worlds ("chapters") and 40 of the primary collectibles, but in that time demonstrates a huge amount of imagination, with many of the acts within each of chapter featuring a wholly unique scenario, form a train-based 'detective' sequence to arena-based boss-battles, and a wholly-freeform mountainous exploration area. While the moveset is fairly small, there's enough to do the job and controls are responsive.
The game's 'indie' roots show through at times with lack of polish in a few aspects (e.g., occasional clipping issues), but that never really detracts much from the experience, especially with the attention to detail that's frequently demonstrated (for example, I'm sure that most players won't realise that Hat Kid keeps a diary that's updated after each act!). Overall, A Hat in Time is a joy to play, and highly recommended if you have any liking at all for the genre.

I've given this game a few tries before and found it hard to stay motivated. After having played BioShock: Infinite, I decided to give it another go since that game was so amazing.
Infinite have really set the bar for what this game could've been. It's quite natural that a first game doesn't quite live up to its sequels, and that's no exception here. What's changed in Infinite compared to this one is what I always thought was lacking, even if I found it hard to point my finger on exactly what.
The BioShock games' prime selling point is the atmosphere and story. That's also what I liked the most. The atmosphere is just unique and the style is great. So is the story, if not a bit thin and hard to follow. The cinematic ending was a bit of a disappointment.
What I do not particularly like is the highly repetitive gameplay. It felt tedious at times. There's a very high variation of weapons and skills - so much so that it becomes confusing. The input configuration is also a bit clunky and gets a bit of time to get used to. Even then, I keep finding myself pressing the wrong keys in hard-pressed situation. It's quite frustrating.
These things, even though the game looks very nice at first glance, makes it a game best suited for above average gamers. Not everyone will find the motivation to enjoy this, and particularly manage to finish it. If you liked or plan to play Infinite, you might want to pick this up and give it a shot, but it's not obligatory.

+ Greatly improved graphics over previous editions
+ More intuitive interface
+ Stomping the enemy team's star quarterback into the a dead, bloody paste is still fun
+ Interesting single-player campaign/training mode for those new to the strategy in the series
+ Stayed mostly true to the ruleset
- Only 8 teams out so far, with as-yet-unpriced future DLC purchases required to get more teams
- A few issues with crashing, which wouldn't be a big deal but for the fact you can't save an in-progress game.
- Reported multiplayer issues.  I haven't had a problem, but others have.
- Fewer player customization options than previous editions
Overall, I'll give this game a reccomendation because as a standalone game it's fun and enjoyable, but It was released early and it shows.  In the end, it'll probably be a worthy successor to the other Blood Bowl games, provided they don't charge an arm and a leg for extra teams.
If you're on the fence, I'd wait to buy this product until we get to see how much they're going to charge for new teams.  If the price is too high, wait for a sale or a bundle.   Definitely worth getting, but don't be taken for a sucker on DLC.

Under promise and over deliver. That is what those who wish to win friends and influence people aim for. The problem is you are competing with others who do the opposite, profit and leave consumers with a nasty taste in their mouth, unwilling to invest.
As a result you have to try to sell yourself and your product and hope that it lives up to expectations.
I think this is what was going on with the countdown timer, a poorly executed attempt at a marketing strategy.
They are now paying for it, with many negative reviews and a growing distrust form their player base.
I believe those players are justified in their feelings. I don't condemn anyone for leaving a bad review based on that alone, as voting with your reviews and wallets is the only power you really have as a consumer.
I will though add my own some what 'thumbs up' of a review, I haven't always agreed with the devs positions but I can appreciate that they have always had their own vision and have gone to great lengths to realise it.
While I feel the timer and marketing surrounding it, such as  "last chance to buy at EA prices" etc., was less than commendable and more of a cash grab than they care to admit. It is still a very good game.
I bought it about 2 and 1/2 years ago, there was one map and not a lot to do. Gathering wood required little more than going outside the front door and clicking on a menu. The game was largely starring at stats and bars and it was still magical.
After having been swamped with zombie games (I loved the Beta days of Minecraft, DayZ back when it was a mod for ARMA 2, but after that we were all fatigued), this was a real breath of fresh air for the survival genre.
Some new players may feel the game has a lot of bar watching now, but  the devs have a done a great job in moving away from that to a place where exploration and interaction with the world is viable and even preferable to hibernation (a style of play I never liked but couldn't hate on, as there was little else for people to do.)
There are now several maps and forms of wildlife. Rabbits, deer, bears, wolves, and fish. All can be killed and used to make clothing (though the variety is wanting). You can craft snares and forage for types of plants to make medicines.
There are achievements and skills to progress in (you may well attempt to grind these out, but it certainly is a grind).
There is much to do now, though story mode is still missing, the problem being that it is all very repetitive, more so than in some other survival games where you would find a greater variety of things to do.
The price they are asking, is by their own admission not an Early access price and yet the game is still in early access.
The devs adamantly deny this, but as a PC gamer, looking out for the rest of you it has to be said.
They have been moving in the direction of console friendly features, such as a larger more clunky UI (for people sitting far away from the screen) and controller friendly input, such as 'hold' to to this and that.
The devs say it has nothing to do with that and this has always been a part of their artistic vision, which as I say I have respect for (if true in this context), but find a little hard to believe.
TLDR: To sum it up, it is imo, a little gem of a title, with a beautiful art style, well worth putting your time into, though perhaps not at this price, just yet.
If story mode comes out in a couple of months that may change, right now though, I'd say wait for a sale or grab a key from somewhere cheaper like king-uin or cdkeys.

The game is early access and still in development. This review is based on build v375 and roughly 340 hours of gameplay. At the time of writing this review, only the sandbox mode and a number of "challenges" were available. A story mode which will feature a coherent story is announced, but the release has been postponed several times, and currently no release date has been set.
It's a first person survival game set in a Canadian Winter wilderness after a geomagnetic disaster. All electric devices have ceased functioning, whether there are other survivors is unclear (NPCs have been announced for the sandbox for a future update). The player has to battle the adversities of cold, hunger, thirst, fatigue, wild animals and health issues, while exploring abandoned leftovers of civilization. No zombies, no arsenal of super-guns, no vehicles. Just the player against nature or, well, a model of nature.
The game pleases with superb art style and sound effects. Sunrise, sunset, starry night skies and the snowy landscape in general are simply beautiful to behold and have been made to look a bit like oil paintings. Everything creates an atmosphere of beauty, but at the same time loneliness and urgency. The player needs to scavenge abandoned houses, cars, forestry lookouts, factories etc. to find means to survive as long as possible. And if you learn the mechanics of the world surrounding you, it is possible to survive for a very long time.
The developers kept up a steady pace of updating and honing the sandbox mode, also adding new regions from time to time (there are now 5 major regions, each with its own "feel"), but have slowed down at some time in 2016. They are super-friendly and give feedback to even the strangest comments from players. There is a dedicated community at the developers homepage (Hinterland Games) which is worth checking out.
This game is not for everyone - it does not take your hand. You have to explore it, and the higher difficulty modes may frustrate people not used to overcome obstacles with patience. But for me, only the sandbox mode is one of the best games I have ever played. And I have basically played almost all the landmark games since 1983. I can't believe I only payed 20  € for this gem. And it's not even finished.
A number of players are becoming impatient, because the release of story mode has been postponed several times and development seems to have slowed down. However, I for one firmly believe the game will be finished in due time. Even if it weren't, I would still recommend to buy this for the full price. I think the time I have spent playing the game speaks for itself.

This game can be pretty intimidating at first and you'll probably die a lot before you even see enemy soldiers. It's really based more on knowledge than raw skill. You don't need to have good twitch reflexes (though they can help) to be a good player. You need to know how the maps work, where your team needs you most, when to move, and how to not die. Generally one side attacks and one side defends. It is crucial to coordinate with your team, especially while attacking. There definitely seems to be a strong correlation between how many knowledgeable guys on your team are using microphones and how often your team wins. If somebody says "Everybody needs to bonzai charge the cap zone NOW!" you'll be surprised how quickly 20 or so Japanese soldiers are screaming into the smoke straight into the cap. You don't need to use a mic yourself, but you'd be wise to listen at least some of the time to your teammates advice (don't worry about the crazy guy that is screaming nonsense at his computer).
Overall it's a very fun game but has it's problems. Single player is pretty much non-existent if you care about that, the movement feels a little clunky and can be awkward when a player interacts with the level geometry. They unnecessarily split up the game into "action" and "realism" modes when it's obvious this game caters to the realism audience. It lacks some polish, but it's not a $60 huge budget game so that's to be expected. There could be more maps and more vehicles, especially the latter which have been neglected since the first RO.
All in all, a good game at a good price.

I didn't know anything about the game before I played it. I usually play menu style jrpgs like Final Fantasy 7. Turns out I am really bad at this game.
This is an action RPG.  People call it a tactical RPG, I disagree. Using tactics will help you a lot. But you mainly rely on fast reflexes, being good at button combos and good eyes/perception. In a tactical RPG you can rely on your wits and do not need to rely on any physical skills on your own part.
Fights are very spammy/cluttered. Camera is all over the place. There might be a way to manage to camera manually, I don't know.
Combat is quite complex. There are several different skill types to keep track of. Three different types of Artes that are basically your attacks/spells. Battle actions (early game) are for defense, moving around in combat, manipulating team structure/control by swapping etc. Then you got your special moves(consumes battle gauge, so only usuable a few times per fight) that either transform you, perform a big attack or heal. Dodging and using Artes cost SC. You gain SC by being passive, blocking or moving on the target path. There is a lot of Rock/paper/scissor going in the combat as well. So basically, button mashing will get you killed if you bump into a decent opponent.
You can swap difficulties during the game. I have played on normal and moderate. I can't tell a difference, I am having a hard time on both as soon as there is a dangerous fight.
Story isn't bad. But I never feel an urge to find out what is going to happen next. The four companion NPCs I have found so far are typical for japanese character personalities. I like the main character most.
So far (marlind) you do not have much freedom to explore. It is common in jRPGs for the world to open up later in the game and then you can freely explore. I expect that will happen, because there is a world map with teleport mechanics in place.
As you explore you will bump into enemies who will one hit you. If you are unlucky your whole team can get wiped by one attack.
There is a quick save option that works everywhere on the map it seems. So you do not need to rely on the save points, though the save points will offer some extra functionality and will provide you with an UI for something that gives you location based bonuses.
Players who are good at beat'em up  games like street fighter etc would probably be good at this game. I have played other action rpgs like The witcher 1&2, Kingdoms of Amalur, torchlight 1&2, Forced, Devil May Cry 3, Onimusha, Ys games and a few more. Tales of Zestiria is definitly the game that has the most complicated and difficult combat.
I clicked recommended, but what I really wanted to select was Neutral.
I do not recommend this for casual players.

is the line that best describes A Hat in Time. It defies the genre that it's in, whilst also being a fantastic entry in it. It manages to give you both big open collectathon levels AND keep the experience linear and guided, tell interesting stories, and provide good boss fights. And when I say "good boss fights", I mean the
bossfights the genre has ever seen! The kind you never think about when you hear the words "3D platformer".
Another thing you will notice immediately is that it does not hold back most of its movement abilities behind unlocks. Not by a long shot! The moment you start the first level, you have a double jump, which you can chain into a dive, which resets your double jump. Oh, and you also get parkour on walls, as a cherry on top. This immediate wealth of movement means you do not have to wait for collectables to make the game good. You can zip across rooftops, platforms, and enemies like a ninja mere minutes into the game, to the tune of great music and whimsy of a good sense of humor.
The only shortcoming that holds it back is that parts of it feel... unfinished. Where's the story and boss of level 4? Why is the last level so short? Why is it that most unlocks hardly ever get used as level mechanics? Oh, and no, there is no replay value in the base game - once you collect everything there's not much else to do. Thankfully, the game has good mod support to solve that.
Old good game that still outperforms modern ones in many aspects, definitelly worth it.

I rarely write reviews. In fact, the only times that I do is when i can consider the game in question a work of art. And this is a work of art.
There's really no need to share details about the story or how you play.
All i have to say to people that are thinking about buying this is that you definitely should.
This is a game that takes the deepest truths about life and makes you discover these truths. It literally feels like it opens your eyes. And the funny thing is, the ending may always be the same, but the way that you play the game determines your interpretation of the ending. It's almost strange, honestly, and very beautifully haunting. The game becomes what you want it to be, but it will always end the same way.
I will willingly share that I have had my fair share of droughts of depression and anxiety throughout my life so far, and I think that fact made this game have an even deeper impact on me, than if I was just somebody trying to understand the story. It felt more like I was the one creating it while it was happening.
The bottom lines are these: This game will mess with your mind. It will make you question life's purpose and meaning. But it can be extremely beautiful if you just let yourself play along.

I've never had such a dramatic 180 on a game like I did with Tales of Zestiria. I went from absolutely loathing it to loving it, which was unusual considering the amount of time it took for my change to happen. I was serioiusly about 15 hours into the game and still hated my time with it, only continuing to play because of a personal disdain for leaving stories or games unfinished regardless of my opinion of them. I've only abandoned a game/story twice because it became too unbearable; this was not one of those times.
The game has a sense of humor that I don't share, which is why it took me so long to start appreciating it. And, as mentioned in my summary, the tutorials along with some of the character dialogue; I felt like I was constantly being kicked out of the world development to service some lame joke. While the jokes are still sprinkled throughout the entirety of the game, and some of the character development is questionable, once the tutorials stop the story begins to pick up.
Any other game, being 15  hours into it and not liking your time would be a huge downside, but in fairness a lot of my initial time is spent in menus, reading lore, inventory management, and reading those stupid ♥♥♥♥ing tutorials that appeared at the end of battles. On a second playthrough, or a speedrun, I wouldn't spend nearly that kind of time dealing with that crap, but first impressions are everything, and the first ones left me with a sour taste.
As I stated though, I finally came around. The meta humor is still not my thing, especially in fantasy worlds, but I learned to look past that and appreciate the characters, which won me over. I wish some were better developed: the most potentially interesting one constantly leaves your party, to the point where I thought they were building up to some awesome reunion, but nope, they're not coming back.
Not that it would ever happen, but I think the world of Zestiria could branch off to an interesting RTS game with the interesting political turmoil that crops up.
Anyway, despite my ♥♥♥♥♥ing and issues, I finally came around to whole-heartedly loving this game to the point I even went on to watch the anime and purchased some of the DLC.
I prefer how some of the story elements played out in the anime more than in the game, but I appreciate them both equally and can say I would recommend this game to any RPG fan. :)
Also there isn't nearly enough hentai of Laila and a disturbingly large amount of Edna.

A Hat in Time is a 3D Collectathon Platformer, developed by Gear for Breakfast (god I love that name)
The game follows the absolutely adorable and aptly named Hat Kid who must travel from world to world in order to collect each of her 40 missing Time Pieces that have been scattered thanks to the meddling of the Mafia from a nearby planet while Hat Kid is on her way home….from somewhere?
The game follows a structure very similar to Super Mario Sunshine and Super Mario Galaxy, in which you have a basic hub that will allow you to select a world to visit alongside each mission that each world contains.
Each and every mission changes up the world in some minor or major way depending, for example in the first world of the game “Mafia Town” you begin chasing after the mysterious Mustache girl, while later on you can find yourself in a literal game of the floor is lava.
The worlds are all for the most part extremely open ended, allowing you to quite easily be able to branch off from the beaten path and explore the admittedly large and imaginative environments at your own will.
Hell the first world in particular, I am convinced it’s inspired by the hub world from Super Mario Sunshine “Delfino Plaza” simply due to how open it is alongside the general aesthetic of the place.
Now A lot of folk would be concerned however about large and vast levels in these type of games, as they can tend to be confusing to navigate in a lot of instances and even easy to lose track of your objective. Thankfully in A Hat in Time, this is not an issue, the game is very cleverly designed to the point that I never found myself lost, even after I went off the path to do my own exploring.
Not only that but via the use of Hat kids…..well….hat, you can instantly locate your objective at any time to get right back on track if you lose where you are meant to go!
The controls here are simply magnificent and very free-flowing, it’s very easy to not only make very long and wide jumps easily, you can also do pinpoint precise jumps without ANY issue whatsoever.
This is only helped through the double jump and dive abilities too which give hat kid an insane level of control, that very few platformers can reach.
On top of her basic jumping moveset, Hat kid can also pull off a basic 3 hit combo to attack enemies, and perform a Sonic Adventure esque homing attack on nearby foes, though this is a little fiddly to perform correctly I feel.
Littered throughout your adventure too you will usually come across Yarn balls, these will allow you to construct new hats to utilise, that all offer unique abilities and powers, for example you can get an ice cap to perform ground pound abilities, that also allow you to springboard from specific points in the world, or have a dwellers mask that makes transparent objects interactable for a few seconds for platforming challenges.
This isn’t even getting into the badges you can buy from a very creepy glitchy looking fellow that offer gameplay modifiers such as item magnetism or the ability to fall far without taking damage.
Hell you even get a grappling hook later in the game for spider-man style action!
The presentation here is also absolutely top notch, with some FANTASTIC visuals that are reminiscent of the gamecube era of games, all the games dialogue voice acting, jokes and music are extremely amazing through and through.
The game clearly has a lot of love put into it here, with every single part simply oozing character, whether from the shady crows that ask for personal details in the Agatha Christie esque murder mystery level(yes you heard me right) or from simple things such as Hat Kid wearing an adorable raincoat in poor weather.
I’m not even going into the boss battles which I think it’s safe to say, I think these are some of the best fights i’ve ever seen in a 3D platformer!
There’s even a number of Raw platforming challenges in the form or “Time Rifts” littered about that offer challenges very much like the fluddless challenges from Super Mario Sunshine which are all an absolute blast to play!
Sadly the game isn’t perfect, there are occasional camera issues to be found here and there (much like most platformers tbh), and sometimes Hat Kids little climbing ability can get stuck on certain objects from time to time, plus the homing attack issue I mentioned earlier in the review...but in the grand scheme of the game, these are very minor niggles at worst and really don’t affect my experience all that much in the grand scheme of things!
Ultimately A Hat in Time is without a doubt one of the greatest platforming titles I have ever played, and a game I think that any platforming fan simply owes themselves to play through!
