Not without its issues, Blood Bowl 2 still manages to be good fun whether you prefer single player or multiplayer. Although it has less races than the previous Blood Bowls, the new version is a lot more detailed and has more races on the way (Wood Elves and Lizardmen are going to be added soon).
Pros:
- 3/4ths the price of a mainstream new release
- Most of the races offer decent customization and variety
- The way American Football is meant to be played (decapitations, rampant and egregious fouling of downed players, and the occasional fireball lobbed onto the field)
- Great depth of team and player development with persistent leagues and teams
- Flexible integration of single player and multiplayer features. Play how you want, with who you want, when you want. AI, friends, randoms, whatever.
Cons:
- D6 based game with the RNG frustrations only D6 games are capable of. Some games are spent playing against the dice instead of the other team.
- Some gameplay customization features are missing from the previous Blood Bowls. BB2 only has the core Blood Bowl gameplay and not the variant rules you could do in the BB1 games.
- Some teams like Bretonnians lack variety.
- Injury rolls are somewhat obscure and opaque to the player.
- League customization is excellent, but there is no individual match customization.
After finishing this game, I sat for half an hour staring at my monitor going "Holy s***". This game deserves every cent you pay for it.

The first thing you'll notice about Limbo is its graphics. The second is that it doesn't hold your hand. It doesn't really need to, since the controls are basic. The puzzles are not hard per se, but can take a few tries to figure out, often, by dying. And you will die a lot on your first playthrough. Death doesn't set you back very much. Stick with it, because this is part of the experience. You are, after all, in Limbo.
It's a game of two halves. The first half is quite meditative, with some horror and tension. The second half is quite the twitchy platformer. This is where the game falls down a bit. The controls aren't tight enough for some of the puzzles to be completed without a lot of trial and error.
It is an interesting game. It can, at times, feel like a very personal game. At others, it feels like the devs were trying to be clever for the sake of being clever. Don't turn down the sound - it adds a lot to the experience of the game. And it should be experienced at least once.

Banished has a ton going for it, without the need for enemies. The weather, food and population will keep you busy micromanaging that you wouldn't want to add enemies on top of it.
My first few play attempts I got "rek'd" real good, the furthest I made it was 23 years before the entire population ran out of tools.......Not something you'd think would make/break a community of roughly 200 people, but boy did it. No tools? Then you can't make jack #%$@! Tools are required to build, harvest, or even make more tools! Its small things like this that make Banished so unique in this genre.
For me, when playing Age of Empires, I'd create an awesome looking town/city/village and then BAM attacked by a whole hoard of an army. Meanwhile I'm sitting at like 50 military, and then you get demolished. All that beautiful town planning put to waste, well in Banished that's the key to it all.
If you take your time, plan each move and GROW SLOWLY then you'll see that Banished is quite rewarding. If you're a fast paced RTS kind of person though, this isn't for you. The game has the ability to speed up production time and overall game speed, however I don't recommend going passed x2. Why? Its not like anyone is going to come with an unstoppable hoard and destroy you right? True, but mother nature doesn't need an army to decimate you, just some snow, and uneducated people and you're SOL. That's right education also plays a huge factor in this game, if you have stupid citizens, you can expect them to produce significantly less than those who are educated.
Again, if you like micromanaging, great music, and a overall relaxing town/city builder, then Banished is for you..

(Rising Storm is natually included with this review)
Most people here probably have played a FPS before, but ask yourself the following question:
'' Have I ever played a FPS wherein war wasn't glorified in an ''America saves the world'' story?''
'' Have I ever played a FPS where war is as hellish as it can be as it was in reality?''
The answer would be for most of you no, and this is where Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm comes in.
Forget the modern FPS cliche shooters wherein you suck on your thumb behind a wall after getting hit and get strawberry jam to indicate that you are hurt and need to cry against a wall for a few seconds before jumping back into the fight with your laser-accuracy guns if you just press the button to aim down your sight. If you play with this mindset, Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm will personally kick your nads through your nose before calling you a massive wimp.
RO2 / RS doesn't mess around with getting serious. Not if, but when you get hit with a bullet, you will either be dead after tumbling over the floor, bleed a lot and patch yourself up with a bandage if you happened to be lucky and having dragged yourself to a safe position without getting turned into Swiss Cheese by more bullets. You get two bandages, but you will probably be dead before you get the chance to apply a second, as getting shot in a place will mean that the next hit there will probably be fatal. No bandages left, or you got shot and didn't topple over instantly? Have fun bleeding out while your soldier splurts out his last sounds in a performance which could have easily fit into Band of Brothers or The Pacific or Saving Private Ryan or other movies reminding you of the harsh reality of war. Have I mentioned yet that war is hell?
This game makes artillery incredebly terrifying, as in ''Oh lord, don't let me die so horribly''. It is not like in normal FPS'es where you just slump over or get ragdolled into a silly way, you will end up into a muliated bunch of flesh or just into red mist.  And given how long the arty can last, it is incredebly tense all the while.
Continuing with the setting, it is World War II. RO2 finds place in Russia, the area around Stalingrad of course, as it is the decisive Battle of Stalingrad. Whereas Rising Storm takes place in the Pacific, as the Americans came closer and closer towards Japan. Most of the maps are thus as close to what it was in reality, with famous locales being also as close as they were. A quick batch of examples are Pavlov's House, Grain Elevator and Stalingrad Station for RO2, and Peleliu Airport and Saipan from Rising Storm. Thereby comes that there is a distinct variety in the maps, as none of the maps feel the same.
There are maps which take place in a small ruined city block, prompting for some heavy short-range combat, maps where it is pure trench warfare, maps wherein the attacking team has to fight itself up an enemy stronghold, such as the Grain Elevator and Iwo Jima. Maps can be relatively small-scale with close combat, or they can be large, kilometres long battlefields, where a team needs to push the other all the way back. Every map is accomedated for 64 players though.  The larger maps, in RO2, also have tanks (and armed personnel carriers being released shortly), which are a whole new beast to tame for players. Controlling one has to be done in a crew, and taking one down is not an easy task. They are one of the uniquer parts of the multiplayer experience, as not everyone gets to take one out. There are specific classes who are effective against them, like the Anti-Tank Soldier (carries an Semi-auto rifle with a caliber to literally gib other players), and the Engineer (Can drop extremely heavy explosives used to destroy tanks or certain obstacles hindering their team.)
Speaking of which, the class system. It is pretty much a system of one common class and the specialists and team leaders.
Most people have to play Rifleman, and as this is the Second World War, there are no full-auto rifles for everyone, so the majority has to do with a classic Bolt-Action rifle and two grenades, and maybe a pistol if you earned one. Don't fret over not getting something flashy; The Bolt-Action rifles, such as the Moisin-Nagant M1897 and the Arisaka Type 38 are frightenly accurate at long range once you get used to bullet drop, and they are strong enough to drop almost everyone with a well placed shot in a vital part. The specialist roster gets made up by Elite Riflemen, using Semi-auto's.  Assault gets the SMG's from that time, as assault rifles as most FPS'es have didn't exist then, except for the rare German MkB42. Weapons that fire faster are nowhere as close with accuracy as Bolt-Actions after a few shots though. Then there are more specialists, like the Machine Gunner, which need something to lean their massive machine gun on, but are in the hands of a good player the backbone of the team. And as last, the Sniper, which has a limit of two per team, (take that TF2 servers) and should be in the back most of the time.
Rising Storm has a few exclusive classes for that theater of war, such as the US-exclusive Flamethrower, which does exactly what it says, and has fairly realistic physics, such as fire bouncing off walls and the damn thing actually having a dangerous range, which makes it a horrible experience to die against due to the really agonising death screams this game offers.
The Japanese get the Light Mortar Class, which is basically a Grenade Launcher class, which is incredebly deadly, but also very slow with firing, and should stick towards the back.
Lastly, we have the team leading classes, the Squad Leaders and the Commander.
The Squad Leaders are pretty much the captains of their part of the team, and basically act as an living mobile spawn point too if they kicked the bucket, but not the SL. It beats walking to the battle for a minute or so. That does not mean the SL should just hide all the time, he pretty much needs to get as close as possible to the battle and lead his squad.
They also have to set artillery marks for the Commander to be of as much use as possible too.
The Commander is basically the Team Captain, and should coordinate his team accordingly.
Stay in contact with the team as much as possible, communicate with the SLs as much as possible, and make good use of calling in recon and artillery. They can stay all the way in the back, but it is overall better to be near your team on the points. Artillery is a vital tool in attacking and defending, so don't let your team down by doing literally nothing.
Don't take it until you have read up on it and you think you can do it when nobody is taking the job.
This all sums up in an incredebly tense FPS, with a heavy dose in teamwork which I miss in other FPS'es.
Holding the other army off a vital point in the defense with your team, or going into the attack with a full team of 32 others gives a rush not too many other multiplayer games can achieve on such a scale. Seeing everything going as planned as a team is something which is pure joy. Although that doesn't happen every round, there is generally a good dose of teamwork. Add to it that this game is really immersive, and you have one of the best multiplayer FPS games of the last five years.
I now realize that I have maybe made this review a bit too long (It is about twice, or thrice as long as my Fallout: New Vegas review now I look at it.) , but hopefully I have informed whoever is reading this well on Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm.
Don't let the doomsayers saying that the game is dead to your head, it is still active, with a constant 2000 players at the moment of writing, which is not even one of the peak hours.
Furthermore, the developers are still fully supporting this game, and there are still new maps, weapons and even vehicles coming. There is also a Vietnam mod, In Country, coming out for it eventually. So stay tuned for more, and have fun!

Solid 3D-platformer with a great amount of polish and character; definitely memorable and enjoyable. Strange/dividing design choices in certain parts of the game, and with certain characters. Seems like a game that could have used another 6-9 months of QA/focus testing.
Recommended for anyone who enjoyed Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine, or Super Mario Galaxy.
Charming characters, quirky, funny voice-acting, interesting levels, and exceptional music. Every one of the four worlds feels unique.
Level pacing can feel a bit scatter-brained at times, and level design varies from excellent to poor. Expect to find glitches, bugs, an occasional stuck camera. Nothing that impedes the game, or any crashes. Strangely enough, the segregated Time Rift levels can sometimes be the most enjoyable part of play session.
Overall, a welcomed title to the starved genre. The community-created levels/mods are so far excellent, and promise immense content for the time to come. The devs are also working on post-release content for 2018.

If you'd like to watch this review instead of read it, you can find the video here:
True to the collectathon genre's name, A Hat In Time's core gameplay is based around exploration and discovery. You're given large worlds to poke around in that contain all manner of items and doodads that either make your journey easier by themselves, or can be combined into and traded for powerups. In this case, you can either find yarn to stitch new hats together, or Pons, which act as the universal currency for everything from new passive abilities and game modifiers to a way to unlock new levels. There are also the key items that are not only integral to every act, but also to beating the game itself. They're called Time Pieces here, and they're the driving motivator behind the story. Your ship uses time as fuel, you see, and after an incident, they're scattered all over this mysterious nearby planet. So, Hat Kid needs to postpone her journey home to collect them all back up and continue on her way. With great power comes great responsibility, though, and when the denizens of the planet discover what these little magical hourglasses can do, it leads to all kinds of problems cropping up. Needless to say, they're important. So important that you're sent back to the hub every time you collect one. That way, the next act can be tailored to make the quest for its Time Piece have its own set of events and storylines.
So yes, it is a collectathon platformer, but it's more akin to a Mario game than Banjo Kazooie. Specifically, World 1 feels very reminiscent of Super Mario Sunshine. And from there on, it revels in doing its own thing. The worlds just keep getting better as they go, literally reaching their peak at the fantastic Alpine Skyline. Because of the previously mentioned yarn and pons, though, it strikes a nice balance between the two styles. You get to have the fantastic setpieces and different mission types that only a customized version of the same area could have, but that doesn't mean you can't just go off the rails at any time and do your own thing. It's up to you what's important at that particular moment: do you advance the game's story, or go make your own? Do you want to add to your vault of time pieces, or hunt down some of those relics that open bonus stages? Yeah, speaking of Mario Sunshine, when you progress far enough in any given world, Time Rifts start showing up, and these come in two flavors.
The ones that pop up naturally with progression are platforming challenges that test your skills against some really cool 3D obstacle courses. They're just the right amount of difficult; never pushing you to the point of pulling your hair out, but still challenging you to approach the abilities you're used to in clever ways. Meanwhile, the relic rifts result when a time piece lands on someONE, not someTHING, and they're designed around that person's past experiences and memories. These are more like mini-collectathons, asking you to scour relatively small areas for special pons that open the hatch to the next floor, and eventually giving way to another time piece. You'll find pieces of picture books in these rifts that (when put back together), fill in the details of what the story is behind the more important characters in each area. Completing a rift also gives you a spin on a bonus wheel that rewards your skills with new color palettes and variant hats for your character, as well as remixed level tracks that you can swap out in the main hub. You can get more spins by finding rift tokens in the worlds as well, giving you one more reason to poke around in ALL the nooks and crannies.
The last big collectible item worth mention are the badges. These are equippable items that offer modifiers to either your base abilities or the game itself, such as immunity to fall damage, no bonking when you accidentally dash into a wall, or even fun things like replacing the voice acting with Banjo-Kazooie style mubling. Special mention must go to the free-roam screenshot camera (which is a wonderful addition to what is already an incredibly screenshot-able game). One weird design decision is that a key skill is tied to one of your badges. You get pins that let you equip up to 3 badges at a time eventually, but the added luxury feels a little hollow when one of those slots is always going to be taken up. It feels kinda limiting, especially when a lot of these are quality of life upgrades that make the act of playing much easier, like magnetizing pons and health restoring items to yourself. Oh, and I'm going to say this right now: prepare yourself for glitches. Plural. As in, more than one; at least two more than none. This was an indie game after all, so the coding isn't as air-tight as it could be. And you know what? I don't care.
I'm gonna sound like such an apologist tool for saying this, but I don't actually mind the glitches in this game because they're amusing. They don't corrupt my save file or make the stage unplayable or anything; they're mostly just hiccups in collision that lead to very entertaining results. I found a way to break a sequence in the very first level. I had a moment on stream where I collected a time piece, and Hat Kid fell through the universe. And this one time, Cooking Cat learned how to levitate, so not to be outdone, I sat on a chair while on top of my roomba so I could join her. Remember that camera badge I mentioned earlier? Well, if you put the normal camera between you and a wall, you can actually force the free-roam camera beyond the collision and see the level from the other side.
I mean this in the best possible way: A Hat In Time feels like it was designed by a 7-year old. What I mean by that is everything has this child-like whimsy to it; this magical perspective that comes along with that period in your life where everything is amazing. Even the hub world is a joy to explore. You can dive into a pool of candy-shaped pillows. The walls and floors are covered in bright and wonderful designs that make it look like the world's most awesome clubhouse more than a spaceship. Even the non-playable characters are fantastic and lively. They're genuinely written well, and bursting with so much personality that you could learn a lot about them just from a single box of dialogue. Some are even voiced by my fellow internet personalities. Deserving of particular mention is Yungtown's amazing performance as The Snatcher; a character who's having so much fun being evil that he actually tricks you into liking him at times. It's great! And it all retains that child-like innocence throughout. Most of the random mooks you beat up are Mafia memebers and yucky things like spiders. There's no malice behind it; they're just bad guys. You beat up bad guys; it's what you do. At least, that's what would make sense to somebody that young.
A Hat In time is easily worth the mid-range asking price. There is no doubt in my mind about that. Without any reservations, I can recommend this game to anybody who's even remotely interested in what it's got going on.

I'm doing this for the badge but at the same time I'll be writing some things about this game.
General information:
Command and Conquer 3 is a Real-Time Strategy (RTS) game that offers multiplayer and single player mode. Sadly, multiplayer is down and will no longer be up forever (that's what I know). There is still a way using certain apps like hamachi to do so but it's not public anymore.
Content:
There are many great maps from basic trainings to precision timings in the campaign. There are also skirmish maps that can be used for the multiplayer mode or practicing your skill with AI. The units in the game has a lot of different variety from infantries, vehicles, and aircrafts. These units are also splited into 3 different factions with different play style. Overall, the content for campaign is great if you compare with the expansion pack (Command and Conquer 3: Kane's wrath), but the units varies a lot more in the expansion pack. I forgot to mention that there are custom maps and mods in the game too.
Quality:
Can't say a lot of things about this, the game was created in 2007 and the expansion 2008. It actually is categorized to be a great quality during those years. For quality about gamplay, the units are balanced and are well executed in the game. Sometimes they might bug out under the map or not following certain commands but it happens quite rare. The quality for the genre RTS fits perfectly.
Weaknesses (downsides):
- There are no more updates to this game except community updates which are rarely seen.
- Multiplayer needs friends that you know since it's impossible to connect randomly to a person. Sequels are dead/ruined (Command and Conquer 4: Tiberian Twilight).
- After researching a bit in the game, Brutal AI is somewhat cheating for the economy because of its unstoppable economy even when there are no tiberiums left on his field. But if you are looking for a challenge, this AI is for you.
- Not a lot of skirmish maps other than community made maps
- Problems with certain OS like windows 10, windows 8.1, ect
The Conclusion:
This game was made about 10 years ago, so it's not perfect and even games these days are not perfect. The price is really not that worth it, I recommend you to wait for sale. The game, based on what I see, is rated 9/10.
Some stuffs:
- The campaign can be really challenging in hard mode
- There is a level editor for the game, unfortunately steam version has some problems with it. There is a fix but I'm not sure if it works for all users
- There is a fix to the crashing problems in on windows 10 and other stuff

The 'campaign' mode seems to be an extended tutorial, as far as I can tell, which for a BB vet is frustrating - but I'm not sure it has enough pointers to be useful for a novice. As far as I persisted with it, you get a series of matches linked by story, with the rules of the game being introduced a bit at a time - the earlier matches have most things work automatically, for instance, and gradually fewer things work automatically. You also get no SPP, up to the point I gave up at.
I've not tried the MP yet, so can't comment on that.
Playing SP leagues, however, works mostly better than the previous Cyanide BB games. I would say I like it, certainly. The AI seems slightly cleverer than BB:CE, though still does some really silly things (why try and pick up the ball when you literally cannot score a touchdown before the end of the half? Why not just pummel me in the hope of KOs/injuries?).
Oh, and having turn timers in SP. That's kinda annoying.
My biggest gripe, actually, is that after all the fuss of adding the ability to not use skills when you chose to BB1, that feature seems to be absent. If anyone knows how to do it, please tell me.

This is my first ever review so sorry for any misinterpretations and or spelling errors.
Starting off with what everyone has said, yes... the campaign in it's own right isn't very long, ranging from 2-3 hours depending on how you tackle the game.
However, the challenges in their own right will provide for a longer game, for me it added roughly 5 hours, almost 2 or 3 hours exclusively on the norestart mode, which means you have to beat the whole game (all levels except level 26) without dying once.
This game also brings in a few unique gameplay mechanics. Slow time, differential mental spaciation (taking control of others put in a more simple way) and bhop utilization (bunny-hopping).
If you are like me and like to fully complete games via achievements, then this game is for you. Albeit, it comes at a challenge, but overall I would say the game is both fun and challenging, providing for a great experience.
TLDR: 1. Game is fun
2. Initial campaign is short, but with added challenges and endless mode, it makes up for quite a number of hours of gameplay.
3. Game can be 100% (perfected) if you are dedicated, but it will provide a challenge (which in my opinion is good).

Nothing new to add here. A masterpiece. It's full of character, of smart gameplay(no run'n gunning here folks! Use your head or prepare for a lot of Vita Chambers!). Memorable characters, memorable story(with a satisfying conclusion, no less!)... I mean, is it asking too much for a happy ending these days?
Also gotta say: character growth is amazing. Comparing the early game where you're worried about wasting pistol bullets to the late game where you're settling elaborate traps and lighting multiple enemies on fire makes you feel powerful.
Graphics are one of a kind. No, really, they are really good to this day.
Rapture is... the most belieavable setting I can remember. It's interesting. What happened here previously? How did these people get to where they are? This is a game that is heavy with political and philosophical questions, and it does them right! You'll meet conflicting ideas that are hard to grasp and even harder to judge. This game treats you like someone who can think for himself. It doesn't point and say: this guy is right, that guy is bad. Hell no, the beauty here is people fully dedicated to ideals that the game will deconstruct and expose any flaws it can find.
Only two gripes, though: presentation of the story throughout audio diaries, while immersive, is a wasted opportunity. I get it Bioshock, you're trying to avoid imposing your story on me. But give yourself more credit: it's not because I didn't scrounge every corner for collectables, nor made every link between characters, that I'm not interested. Give me, and yourself, a chance.
Also... controls. Couldn't find an appropriate mouse sensitivity throughout the entire game.

(Rising Storm is natually included with this review)
Most people here probably have played a FPS before, but ask yourself the following question:
'' Have I ever played a FPS wherein war wasn't glorified in an ''America saves the world'' story?''
'' Have I ever played a FPS where war is as hellish as it can be as it was in reality?''
The answer would be for most of you no, and this is where Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm comes in.
Forget the modern FPS cliche shooters wherein you suck on your thumb behind a wall after getting hit and get strawberry jam to indicate that you are hurt and need to cry against a wall for a few seconds before jumping back into the fight with your laser-accuracy guns if you just press the button to aim down your sight. If you play with this mindset, Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm will personally kick your nads through your nose before calling you a massive wimp.
RO2 / RS doesn't mess around with getting serious. Not if, but when you get hit with a bullet, you will either be dead after tumbling over the floor, bleed a lot and patch yourself up with a bandage if you happened to be lucky and having dragged yourself to a safe position without getting turned into Swiss Cheese by more bullets. You get two bandages, but you will probably be dead before you get the chance to apply a second, as getting shot in a place will mean that the next hit there will probably be fatal. No bandages left, or you got shot and didn't topple over instantly? Have fun bleeding out while your soldier splurts out his last sounds in a performance which could have easily fit into Band of Brothers or The Pacific or Saving Private Ryan or other movies reminding you of the harsh reality of war. Have I mentioned yet that war is hell?
This game makes artillery incredebly terrifying, as in ''Oh lord, don't let me die so horribly''. It is not like in normal FPS'es where you just slump over or get ragdolled into a silly way, you will end up into a muliated bunch of flesh or just into red mist.  And given how long the arty can last, it is incredebly tense all the while.
Continuing with the setting, it is World War II. RO2 finds place in Russia, the area around Stalingrad of course, as it is the decisive Battle of Stalingrad. Whereas Rising Storm takes place in the Pacific, as the Americans came closer and closer towards Japan. Most of the maps are thus as close to what it was in reality, with famous locales being also as close as they were. A quick batch of examples are Pavlov's House, Grain Elevator and Stalingrad Station for RO2, and Peleliu Airport and Saipan from Rising Storm. Thereby comes that there is a distinct variety in the maps, as none of the maps feel the same.
There are maps which take place in a small ruined city block, prompting for some heavy short-range combat, maps where it is pure trench warfare, maps wherein the attacking team has to fight itself up an enemy stronghold, such as the Grain Elevator and Iwo Jima. Maps can be relatively small-scale with close combat, or they can be large, kilometres long battlefields, where a team needs to push the other all the way back. Every map is accomedated for 64 players though.  The larger maps, in RO2, also have tanks (and armed personnel carriers being released shortly), which are a whole new beast to tame for players. Controlling one has to be done in a crew, and taking one down is not an easy task. They are one of the uniquer parts of the multiplayer experience, as not everyone gets to take one out. There are specific classes who are effective against them, like the Anti-Tank Soldier (carries an Semi-auto rifle with a caliber to literally gib other players), and the Engineer (Can drop extremely heavy explosives used to destroy tanks or certain obstacles hindering their team.)
Speaking of which, the class system. It is pretty much a system of one common class and the specialists and team leaders.
Most people have to play Rifleman, and as this is the Second World War, there are no full-auto rifles for everyone, so the majority has to do with a classic Bolt-Action rifle and two grenades, and maybe a pistol if you earned one. Don't fret over not getting something flashy; The Bolt-Action rifles, such as the Moisin-Nagant M1897 and the Arisaka Type 38 are frightenly accurate at long range once you get used to bullet drop, and they are strong enough to drop almost everyone with a well placed shot in a vital part. The specialist roster gets made up by Elite Riflemen, using Semi-auto's.  Assault gets the SMG's from that time, as assault rifles as most FPS'es have didn't exist then, except for the rare German MkB42. Weapons that fire faster are nowhere as close with accuracy as Bolt-Actions after a few shots though. Then there are more specialists, like the Machine Gunner, which need something to lean their massive machine gun on, but are in the hands of a good player the backbone of the team. And as last, the Sniper, which has a limit of two per team, (take that TF2 servers) and should be in the back most of the time.
Rising Storm has a few exclusive classes for that theater of war, such as the US-exclusive Flamethrower, which does exactly what it says, and has fairly realistic physics, such as fire bouncing off walls and the damn thing actually having a dangerous range, which makes it a horrible experience to die against due to the really agonising death screams this game offers.
The Japanese get the Light Mortar Class, which is basically a Grenade Launcher class, which is incredebly deadly, but also very slow with firing, and should stick towards the back.
Lastly, we have the team leading classes, the Squad Leaders and the Commander.
The Squad Leaders are pretty much the captains of their part of the team, and basically act as an living mobile spawn point too if they kicked the bucket, but not the SL. It beats walking to the battle for a minute or so. That does not mean the SL should just hide all the time, he pretty much needs to get as close as possible to the battle and lead his squad.
They also have to set artillery marks for the Commander to be of as much use as possible too.
The Commander is basically the Team Captain, and should coordinate his team accordingly.
Stay in contact with the team as much as possible, communicate with the SLs as much as possible, and make good use of calling in recon and artillery. They can stay all the way in the back, but it is overall better to be near your team on the points. Artillery is a vital tool in attacking and defending, so don't let your team down by doing literally nothing.
Don't take it until you have read up on it and you think you can do it when nobody is taking the job.
This all sums up in an incredebly tense FPS, with a heavy dose in teamwork which I miss in other FPS'es.
Holding the other army off a vital point in the defense with your team, or going into the attack with a full team of 32 others gives a rush not too many other multiplayer games can achieve on such a scale. Seeing everything going as planned as a team is something which is pure joy. Although that doesn't happen every round, there is generally a good dose of teamwork. Add to it that this game is really immersive, and you have one of the best multiplayer FPS games of the last five years.
I now realize that I have maybe made this review a bit too long (It is about twice, or thrice as long as my Fallout: New Vegas review now I look at it.) , but hopefully I have informed whoever is reading this well on Red Orchesta 2 / Rising Storm.
Don't let the doomsayers saying that the game is dead to your head, it is still active, with a constant 2000 players at the moment of writing, which is not even one of the peak hours.
Furthermore, the developers are still fully supporting this game, and there are still new maps, weapons and even vehicles coming. There is also a Vietnam mod, In Country, coming out for it eventually. So stay tuned for more, and have fun!

One of my favourite games of all time. Not only was it a absolute blast back when it came out it is still one of the best real time strategy games made to date.
First of all, the three sided campaign is masterfully made with a great story and fun missions to back it up, it’s not just a campaign you will love the first time around but for many many more playthroughs. The live-action cut scenes work amazingly and really draw you into the universe that was made in the earlier games. Not only where they well-made but well-acted too and with a well-known cast aswell.
The game play is fluid and fun, with a user interface that is easy to get used to and fast to use, it's easy to command your armies and produce new units on the fly. The three factions are well balanced, each with their own unique strengths and weakness like GDI’s slow moving but hard punching pace and Nods quick guerrilla war hit and run tactics. This gives each faction a real reason why you should play them and not just a simple reskin with a few different abilities.
If you get a few friends the game really shines, from massive wars with brutal AI’s to making the best defended base you can while keeping the enemy locked away on one side of the map its really a blast.
It also has a great modding scene! With mods like
which brings in units from the older games,
, a completely new campaign that is well made with its own life-action cut scenes as well and many many more, some still being made to this date, there is definitely plenty to do!
Not only this but they are many new maps to download and a great although hard to get working map editor.
All in all if you like real time strategy games I can’t stress enough how much you should try this game and I doubt you will be disappointed, and with prices being so cheap here on steam and on Origin it’s a game you can have many hours of fun on without hurting the wallet.

I really wanted this to be an improvement to the first game(s), but so far, only the graphics have improved. The AI and player customisation are actually worse.
8 races is not enough for a varied experience. I'm sure more teams will be added as DLC down the line, but releasing a game at full price and adding essential elements for more money is just not okay.
Note: I have not had a look at multiplayer yet.
General comments on the AI:
- The AI still doesn't know what turn it is. It'll risk players Going For It to get closer to the End Zone in turn 8 or 16, even with no chance of scoring.
- If the AI manages to pick up the ball in an opponent Tackle Zone, they'll stop moving. No atttempts to dodge out.
- The AI will dodge out of the enemy ball carrier's TZ in order to make irrelevant blitzes or assists elsewhere.
- The setup is randomised. Yes, really. The AI doesn't set up according to your setup, it just picks a random formation. Furthermore, setting up your players is a very slow and dull affair; you have to wait for each player to run to the designated spot, one at a time. There is no need for this whatsoever.
- The AI really likes standing (or setting up) next to the sidelines. Jim and Bob are talking about why this is a really bad idea, but apparently, the AI programmers didn't listen to them. On that note, Jim and Bob look like they've been dubbed from another language; their mouth movements are just generic animations that go on while they're talking.
- Even with the improved graphics, it's harder to tell the difference between the players. The only difference between players in the same position is the head. With identical helmets, this does very little to make them stand apart.
I am very disappointed. :/

Releasing just far enough in advance of
,
really is a beautiful game, doing a fantastic job of capturing the joy of the N64-era 3D platformer while also seeing some modern touches. It's a fairly short game, with only four worlds ("chapters") and 40 of the primary collectibles, but in that time demonstrates a huge amount of imagination, with many of the acts within each of chapter featuring a wholly unique scenario, form a train-based 'detective' sequence to arena-based boss-battles, and a wholly-freeform mountainous exploration area. While the moveset is fairly small, there's enough to do the job and controls are responsive.
The game's 'indie' roots show through at times with lack of polish in a few aspects (e.g., occasional clipping issues), but that never really detracts much from the experience, especially with the attention to detail that's frequently demonstrated (for example, I'm sure that most players won't realise that Hat Kid keeps a diary that's updated after each act!). Overall, A Hat in Time is a joy to play, and highly recommended if you have any liking at all for the genre.

How do I begin with A Hat in TIme? I was not there when they revealed their idea to the world, nor did I donate to the kickstarter, nor did I even know what it was exactly until I saw it on here and watched the trailer. But it struck home, even disregarding me not knowing a thing about it. I had grown to be sick and tired of my grind games, and the barren wasteland that is steam's library as a whole, but as  soon as I saw what was offered, I was immediately hooked. If there was one thing I needed, it was a well polished platformer where you could feel the developers putting their blood, sweat, tears, and love into it.
A Hat in Time follows a silent, but plucky young girl and her hat through an adventure on a large, gorgeous looking planet. You explore this planet using your space ship as the main hub world, with the space ship itself holding many interesting nooks and crannies for you to explore and re-explore as the game goes on. The game itself looks good, the animated style coupled with the top notch platforming who's design allows for play styles of all speeds (I personally started off a little slow but eventually I was zooming through as if I had never stopped playing platformers) all while exploring a world with plenty of NPC's to talk to, hidden things to find, and collectibles ranging from humorous souvenirs of the planet to yarn balls that will let you create more unique hats with their own special powers, all the way to coins to attempt to play a slot machine for various hats skins, song remixes, and alternate costume colors. There are also badges you can buy ingame that also increase utility for the hats, but sadly there are too few for myself, with about 12 or so, but in this case the number is plenty to go through your adventure.
The story itself is simple enough. You as a plucky hero have lost through certain means the ability to make it back home, and when the going get's tough, you get going. For a platformer, this is perfectly fine, especially as the colorful cast and voice acting really bring the story home. The voice acting makes everything endearing and through the gameplay makes you really want to complete and collect everything. Every level has it's own little story line and, this was a nice touch to me personally, it's own artistic preview of what you're going to be doing for every level. This touch was great to me as it really made me feel like the Devs cared about their game. Add in bonus levels, the ingame backstory goodies to collect in them, the great music and intersting concepts for each level, and an enjoyable final boss fight, and this game easily becomes one of my favorites of this year.
My only gripes is getting used to certain controls, which honestly was a learn to play issue on my part (certain actions require getting used to, for instance press the jump button when you climb up something will make you vault over it, unless I'm actually wrong, but pressing forward allowed you to climb up just fine) and for any hitting your face into a wall (which actually causes recoil, which I'll get a bit more into in a second but also  has a badge that gets rid of this feature) is quickly overcome and just not getting enough game for myself. The latter part will apparently be answered for with free DLC for two additional chapters, which makes me more than happy to hear.
As for the praises I can only begin to shower on this game, where do I even start? The music is great, with various remixes to spice things up, the platforming is great, your character has weight, and has trouble hitting things early on (hitting a large enemy will cause you to recoil until you get your actual weapon or use a particular jump atttack). When you hit a wall, you will not just stop in place, your girl will hit the wall, recoil and fall a distance away from said wall, depending on how hard you hit it. The boss fights are great, often done in different styles, the levels are beautiful, each one being more fun than the next, and your character and everyone else in it have their own great personalities, even regular run of the mill npcs.
And what sucks is that I know I'm missing more and more praises to give this game. This game is great, heads and shoulders above others, and certainly will get rid of any bad taste Yooka-Laylee might have given you. This is the kind of game that really restores your faith in game developers to deliver fun, quality games without ridiculous pay to win garbage, grind, or subpar, shallow  gameplay under the excuse of, "People will still buy it, right?". And like most anything good, it's over far too soon. If you get the chance I highly suggest picking it up, especially with the DLC on the way.
To the Devs: Thanks for making a game that doesn't suck. Keep up the good work

Ok.  Now here is a good game.  The big question people seem to ask is, is it worth the asking price?
To me, yes.  If you are someone who gauges their dollar spent on games based upon hours, maybe not.  It cost me $20, but for me, there will be plenty of replayability here.  Maybe not for you -- it is completely subjective.
The story is very "meta" and is of course short.  Now you do unlock modes.  But it might be worth waiting for a sale, if you think 20 bucks or so is too much to ask for your time.  I don't judge that and I understand it.
However, I will say that I got a TON of enjoyment out of the ~2 hour story mode, and know that I can spend quite a bit of time in the unlimited mode.  You can play slow and methodical, taking advantage of the time stop, or try to go full on twitch FPS.  The very simple, but highly polished mechanics mean that you can get a lot out of each level.
Do yourself a favor, if you really want to play this, avoid letsplays and twitches.
I completely understand why some folks would not recommend this title at price.  No argument, that's a reasonable and subjective opinion.  I however think it is easily worth the asking price, especially given other games at that asking price.  I think I'll be able to pick this up a few times a week just to fart around and see different ways of completing levels.  That is TOTALLY DEPENDENT upon what kind of gamer you are.  If you want an epic, well written story for your dollar - no, stay away.  If you want something along the lines of THEY LIVE in a video game, that reminds you constantly you are playing a game, you might enjoy it.  And again, the mechanics are ROCK SOLID.
If you like shooters, but also like turned based games where you can weigh your  options, this is an awesome little hybrid with some very cool mechanics.  It runs smooth.  If you want a 40+ hour adventure for your dollar, with a polished story, no, I'd say wait for a sale.  But overall I recommend it.
I mean, the game makes you literally exit to windows and restart to continue the story, it is so "meta".  Contrived?  Sure.  But it adds to the immersion (whatever that really means).  It's a solid title.  I'd really like to see more from these guys,
It's farily unique and might surprise you.  If you have any doubts, *wait for a sale*!!!  But otherwise, dive in.

Hat in Time is a lovably crafted, adorable platformer about the equivalent of an alien girl getting into Hijinks recovering her time-altering ship fuel. It can be completed in about a day or two if one were to sit down and mainline it, longer if they go after the bonuses. $30 might be a bit much to ask for with its short span, but anything less would be a bargain.
Hat in time is a platformer game that sees its roots from platformers of similar Genre's such as Psychonauts. It follows a young girl often referredd to as just 'kid' who, after a run-in with the mafia; has her fuel scattered across the planet. Time-altering hourglasses, making your journey to recover them and the people you meet along the way. A girl with a mustache, a possessive contract demon. Even two warring 'bird' movie directors.
------------------------------------
Incredible soundtrack. Boss music sounds energized and upbeat, stages fit their music thematically. And even through challenge stage prizes you can earn remixed versions of songs you can have play instead.
Adorable artwork. Each of the stage Act's come with their own splash artwork that portrays Hat kid and her situation in appealing light. This shows up especially in Chapter 2, I'd like to believe.
Level Variety. Chapter one gives you the sense that things are going to be open-world hunts similar to how Super Mario Sunshine may have done, but later on the type of game each stage illustrates changes that fact dramatically. Chapter 2 has sidescroller segments, Chapter 3 has a hide-and-seek Clock tower Horror segment. And so on.
Extensive mod support. Coming from modded routes, the devs havee every intention to let one create and insert content for just about everything available in the game. Levels, hats, color palettes, you name it.
Great subtext humor. "THIS IS INSULTING! IM GONNA SUE!" and many other comedic bits exist in things in all stages as well as your ship, providing comedic quirks that'll get a chuckle or two out of most.
However, there are a few nitpicks.
Performance. While the game does have fantastic settings options - enough to make even people on an awful HD3000 like me - run the game playable, some places can't quite escape the framerate drops. VFX in Chapter's 2 and 3 were especially bad at this, resulting me having to take some serious measures to get playable framerates for important boss fights.
Controls. While sharp and responsive, they can also be deemed the most hindering example for when wall climbing/jumping. Numerous times have I died in a challenge run because the wall that I was auto-jumping on top of was instead hurdled over with too much zeal. Unless you can train yourself to stop touching the movement as you're making the hop, you will
nine out of ten times.
Hitboxes. While on the topic, hitboxes for certain things such as tightropes can be a bit nitpicky. Sometimes you land on them from a meter away, and sometimes they'll ignore you entirely screwing up your whole flow. There's also an occasion where people with abyssmal FPS (7-15) will have pickups bugged, making you need to pause and unpause the game to make them valid for picking up.
Short. Regrettably, with five chapters and a 25 (of 40) hourglass minimum to complete the game. It won't take you much longer than me (About 6-8 hours) to complete the game if you aren't trying to shoot for absolutely everything everywhere. Atleast more content is planned!
Hat in Time is definitely worth the money if you can't wait for a sale - if it is on sale, there's literally no reason to not get it if you enjoy platformers such as Psychonauts or Mario Sunshine.

You know what my first review was not good enough to really detail what I think of this game, so let me get it out there. Also I'm updating the review so that I can get the steam awards stuff.
Tl,dr;
This game is fun. You should get this game. It's fun, satisfying, and just charming in every aspect of the word. I want more. (This is basically every review out there reworded like you do with a High School  history essay.)
For Funny Points and so when you actually do play the game you can laugh at this:
I once had a friend. This mafia guy warned me about her, but I thought she was chill. Then time broke. The end.
Actual review:
I would buy this game 3 times over if I could, no scratch that 4.
Basic Summary:
You play as the adorable Hat Girl (yes that is her name, there's really nothing else to it) going around Super Mario Sunshine/64 style collecting the main collectable of the game, Time Pieces. If you're even considering buying this game you should've known that by now. If you even have seen one review you would know that this game is by far one of the most cutesy/charming 3D platforms out there, and you can tell Gears for Breakfast put so much damn love into this game it almost is like it was their own child. Now onto a basic Pro's and Con's List.
Pro:
- Art Style (and yes that is my own objective opinion)
- Hat Girl is the most satisfying thing to control ever, it's like a combination of the best parts of 3D Sonic (being the homing attack she has), and the movement control of 64/Sunshine Mario. The moveset is also very forgiving and quick to pick up; you can probably learn the entire control scheme on a controler within minutes of playing the game.
- She might even be more satsifying to control than Mario in Super Mario Oddesy (which is a
really bold statement but her moveset is simpler so it could just be the symplicity over the
variety and motion based commands of Mario)
- Level Design is fun, and is very clear and consise when it wants to be, or open and free when it lets you. The levels also don't feel copy-pasted, and each protrays it's theme very well so I never get bored going to different areas.
- Grant Kirkhope and Plasma3Music are wonderful composers and really have brought a lot of life into this world through the sounds, I cannot tell you how much I've just listened to the soundtrack in a level over and over again.
- Tons of little dialoge and actions that really just bring life to the world. It's so refreshing to find little tiny details everywhere.
- Speedrunning stuff is accsessable and really satisfying due to the simple control scheme that can be used to do more complex manuvers.
- Active modding community makes it so that the game, even when you beat it 100%, will never become dull.
- Did I mention cute characters? I think I did. They're cute, and have good interactions.
Neutral Points:
- Voice Acting is kinda a mixed bag, you go from annoying girl to really funny and enthusastic soul stealing ghost. But if you don't want Voice Acting you could always buy the plug your ear's badge or just turn off the volume for character voices.
Negative (more like nitpicking) Points:
- Some animations aren't really that polished as they could be (i.e. theres one scene when Hat Girl closes her eyes and you can still see her eyes in the eyelid).
- Hats overall feel somewhat gimicky (besides the speed hat, which actually is quite nice) and somewhat hinder fluidity from time to time. Other times it's perfectly fine though because they serve the purpose of blocking off a section until you have propper equipment.
- I want more of this game, that's the real nitpick here, I JUST WANT MORE OF THIS STELLAR GAME.
In conclusion, A Hat in Time is a stellar product that is fun, charming, and just overwelmingly a great game. Gears for Breakfast obviously put love and care into this game and I hope they recieve the goal they wanted when they released this game. Also hopefully they have enough funding to make more games like this or free content updates or DLC for it or SOMETHING.
Also if someone at Gears for Breakfast is out there can you just tell us if you plan to bring this wonderful game to the Nintendo Switch? It just seems like such a perfect platform to do this cause playing this game on the go would be great.

This is a unique experience. If I had to put it into a category, it would definitely fit the "walking simulator" one, the kind of games where instead of mastering challenges by skilled shooting, puzzling or strategic resource management, you wander through different areas and discover a story.
In The Beginner's Guide, Davey Wreden, author of the acclaimed The Stanley Parable, invites us to explore a bunch of experimental games (really all walking simulators) made by his purported friend "Coda". He shares his thoughts on them and talks about the kind of person Coda is and how their friendship developed. If this sounds boring to you, maybe this really is not a game for you. I did like how TBG invites you to listen closely and question what Davey relates, to think your own thoughts about what you find and how it all fits together. It's an experience that left me with a strange calmness and satisfaction, and something to chew on for days after having finished it (in fact I'm still analyzing all its facets at the point of writing this).

There's also the issue of whether or not the story of the game is real or not.

If the story is fake, then we go back to the laziness, predictability.

I'm gonna add my own reflection in the form of a review, like other people have been doing.
Right now I am mildly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. There is no point to this "game". It just exists for the sake of itself. You never know what to believe, or how to interpret what you are actually experiencing. The narrator imposes his own interpretations constantly. It is tempting, even reflexive, to accept and believe his conclusions because the "games" themselves are so inconclusive and vague that the meaning he draws on them is the only thing that holds them together. This is the case both figuratively and literally, as you the player are helpless as you are guided along his narrative path. This has the effect of being both disconcerting and comforting, as you have trust that he will be with you in the end to fit the big puzzle together like he promises in the beginning.
About mid-way or so you find yourself in a lecture hall where the roles reverse themselves. You start out as the observer being lectured to about perfection by a confident person, then you become them and you see their own imperfection and vulnerability.
[skipping a bit ahead on my train of thought] This is what the game comes down to for me. It is, among many things, a meditation on discomfort, loneliness, and uncertainty. The narration itself cuts out, and presents itself in a way where it is impossible to be sure whether or not this is some elaborate and convincing fiction, or disturbing real life story. You yourself are challenged by the game to question the narration, while you attempt to parse out the objective Truth, destination, or "lamppost" amidst the vaguery of the experience.
For the final ending you are on your own, as the narrator has given up his search for answers. This time you do not get a lamppost like before. Instead, it goes back to the glitched first ending, and you float upwards to see an infinite maze stretch out around you. In the first non-glitched version of this ending, the player is supposed to throw themselves into this light to sacrifice themself and save humanity. In the non-glitch version the sacrifice is death. However, in the glitched version you float up and leave your sense of self and control, your sacrifice is surrendering yourself to your smallness.
In the game before the final ending the narrator is confronted by a distant coldness and rejection. This stuns him to the points where he stops talking over the thoughts of the player, and Coda. A few other people mentioned the feeling of violation from the way he narrated before. He finally surrenders his well-intentioned but narrow-minded quest to analyze and understand his friend. He relinquishes his desperate control of the narrative, seeing the damage he had inadvertently done. In his effort to understand and "help" by taking over Coda's narrative he stopped genuinely listening to Coda, and even to his own emotional reality.
The narrator leaves to work on himself, and the player is left to follow an unknown path alone. Finally, the player arrives at the same sacrificial ending, without any lamppost or answer. The lampposts felt unsatisfying anyway. But the metaphor is complete. As you levitate upwards you have no choice but to let go of certainty and sit in discomfort, which is ultimately what is required to grow as a human.
I don't think the narrator is narcassistic, I think he is human. He did a thing that most people have done or will do many times in their lives. I know I certainly have. But there we go. In the spirit of the game I will say that there are many possible interpretations and subjective truths. I see how my emotional and intellectual response reflects whats going on in my own life. So beyond not giving you anything to hold on to, this experience has been a good exercise.

Over all I like this game, but I still have some mixed feelings about it. I'm not sure whether to recommend it or not because it completely depends on who the person. This game requires a LOT of patience as the puzzles become extremely challenging. There is much trial and error involved. I would sometimes spend a half hour trying to find a solution to a puzzle just to stumble into another one ten minutes later that stumped me. As you can imagine, I grew very frustrated. It did feel highly rewarding to over come each section and to finally figure it out, but there came a point where I just wanted to beat the game. There were a small handful of puzzles that I couldn't seem to figure out on my own no matter how hard I tried, and I was at the point where I was so eager to get it over with that I eventually looked up the solutions for a few of them. I hated to cheat, because there's no better feeling than figuring something out on your own, but I had just ran out of patience. And the demo, I felt, was very misleading. I was given the impression that it was all about platforming. There weren't any puzzles in it or at least, if there were, they were very benign and not noticeable. I get that games raise in difficulty, but the difficulty in puzzles had escalated to a shocking height to me. I will give it a lot of credit though. The puzzles are extraordinarily clever and well thought out. I haven't seen a game where the puzzles were designed so great, except for Portal. And maybe the problem lies in me. I have never enjoyed puzzles that much. I have a lot of patience in life, but not much in puzzles.
You're also thrown right into the game, with no dialogue or spoken plot or cutscenes or instructions. For the most part, it's executed well, but I was upset to know that I had to actually look in the options menu at the controls to see that ctrl was the action button, mostly to pull and push things which is a large part in this game.
I will still recommend this game, if only you are prepared for the difficulty. It looks to be a simple game, and the demo makes it out to be a simple game, but be prepared to invest more time into it than expected, to die a load more than expected, and possibly even to look up a guide when stuck.

SOLVED! Command & Conquer 3 Tiberium Wars AND Kane's Wrath not launching/working on Windows 10. after soo long trying to figure out some way to get the game to run on Windows 10, I FINALLY found a solution just when I was messing around in the display driver settings. First of all my laptop is the late 2016 Razer Blade with the GTX 1060 and Core i7 6700HQ. Okay here's how I got it to work on Windows 10, first, make sure the game is not running as an administrator and all the compatibility mode/settings are disabled, I know most people probably enabled these trying to get the game to work (including myself). Okay next, open settings, in the search bar type "device manager" then select it, next select "display adaptors" then "Intel HD Graphics" then go to "driver" and select "Roll Back Driver..." then just give it a minute, the screen may turn blue for a second or whatnot, and that's it! the game should run perfectly! you can adjust it to whatever graphics or resolution you want and you can use a dedicated GPU (if you have one). if this helped you please like this comment so others will see! :)

Well, this game is the definition of one step forward, two steps back.
So, this is what we get after almost a year of delays. Well, let's get to it, then.
Stepping in the right direction:
+ Better UI.
+ New Race: Brettonians.
+ Better Graphics.
+ Easy to invite Steam friends to a friendly match of Blood Bowl.
Retreading same old footsteps:
= The announcers are back, and they are just as fun to listen to.
= Solo Old World League is as close as you'll get to the original Campaign.
= It's Blood Bowl.
= Customization ups the ante with choosing uniform patterns instead of just a single colour, but scales it back again by letting you only change the players' heads.
And, of cousre, the backsteps:
- No mid-match "quit and save" option in single-player, except in the campaign. As clumsy as the old SaveBetweenHalves/Drives->AbandonMatch->QuitWithoutSaving routine was, there was, at least, a way.
- The Campaign (Story Mode) is just an extended tutorial utilizing the Reikland Reavers (Human).
- Blitz Mode is gone. No more custom gear for you.
- Back to 8 teams? Are you joking? Chaos Edition had 23. 23!
- No team-specific cheerleaders. Human cheerleaders for everyone!
- Very limited graphical options (Resolution, Quality presets, Grass, Spectators).
Don't bother. Wait for the Legendary Edition.

Brilliant. Truly brilliant.
Gameplay-wise, it reminds me quite a bit of 8 and 16-bit era platformers like Contra and Super Contra, Gunstar Heroes, or a sped-up Mega Man. The only way to win is to practice, and learn, and get better. Learn how the bosses move, learn when you're safe to move, and learn the entire sequence of the boss battle. It's difficult but very compelling -- you want to try again right away, because, ah ha, now I figured out his pattern! But the boss stages have multiple "waves," so you don't learn their one trick and it's over. You have to remember the tricks to each wave of the boss stage. It's the perfect balance between challenging and frustrating. You can do it, you'll just have a good number of fun, failed attempts along the way.
If Cuphead were just about the gameplay, it would be a solid title but not exactly groundbreaking. But that art. Oh my god, that art. I was already a huge fan of old cartoons from Warner Bros., Fleischer Studios, Disney, and others, so even if Cuphead made a mediocre attempt at the style, I would have loved it. But I'm thrilled to say the art style, the humor, the little touches here and there: PERFECT. The game is a visual delight, and it's not just the style that's compelling, it's the black humor throughout, like characters shooting Craps in an empty coffin. It's like the bleakest Betty Boop or Porky Pig cartoon, where every animal, vegetable, and mineral is an anthropomorphic nightmare.
While Cuphead is a combination of 1980s platform gameplay and 1930s cartoon stylings, it feels like one of the freshest experiences I've had gaming in quite a while. Very warmly recommended.

I came into this game expecting to be in for a great time.  Instead I got disappointment and frustration.
The Good:  The atmosphere and setting are great, the bad guys are pretty good, thankfully the game is short.
The Bad, Major issues:  I only played the game on hard, so that might be the reason for some of these problems.
1.  The camera light.  On hard, you get 5 batteries and the camera goes through them like crazy if you leave it on.  Most of the areas are so dark, that you're probably going to play through most of the game with the camera up so you can use the light.  That means most of the game you're constantly hitting the F button over and over again, just so you can get a brief glimpse of the area and then move through it without wasting your battery life.  It gets old after awhile.  Having the camera up is also the only way to obtain the 'notes' that you find and there's no real indication that you should film that spot, so if you don't have the camera up the whole time, you'll miss them, though I wouldn't really say you're missing anything by not getting them.  There comes a point where the camera gets cracked, so you have to put up with that for the last 1/4 of the game.  It's pretty annoying.
2.  The game lacks any interesting discovery because there's only 3 things you'll ever find:  Batteries, documents, and notes (if you have your camera up).  It would have been nice if there'd been some interesting reason to actually explore areas.
3.  You have no actual weapons, so your only real weapon is stealth.  The problem is that the stealth mechanics are broken, at least on hard difficulty, which is very frustrating.  All being stealthy does is get you killed.  Enemies seem to make no sound whatsoever if they're more than 10 feet away from you.  When they do make sounds, it's incredibly difficulty to pinpoint where it's coming from, and whether it's coming towards you or away from you.  It gets real annoying when you figure an enemy must've walked way down the hallway away from you, so you pop out the door and he's right on the other side walking towards you.  Also, enemies seem to have some sort of sixth sense about your location.  They don't have to actually see you go into a room, they just know you're in there.  Also annoying is that almost every 'switch' objective you hit causes the patrolling enemy to automatically come to that location.  If you hit a switch, just pop into a locker or under a bed right after, because 80% of the time, an enemy is going to come running into the room.  The enemies also appear to have supersonic hearing.  It doesn't seem to matter whether I'm crouch walking, regular walking, or running, they hear me no matter how far away they are and start walking/running towards me.  This got real annoying during the doctor segment.  He was patrolling some hallway and you have to get to the end of it and push some box out of the way of a door so you can get through it.  Every time I'd step out into that hallway, he would immediately turn around and start walking towards me.  Eventually just brute forced my way through that part because I got tired of seeing him spin around and start walking towards me again.  Also annoying is that our hero can't close doors quietly.  Instead, he has to slam them shut for some reason, which goes completely against the idea of being stealthy.
You'll figure out that brute forcing your way through parts is a much better plan than trying to be stealthy.  That pretty much destroys most of the horror and intersting gameplay in the game.
Minor Quibbles:  While there are a few surprises, most of the time you can predict when there's going to be an enemy around.  This destroys a lot of the tension and sense of dread.  Also, the game is extremely linear most of the time.  There aren't any puzzles to be solved and most rooms just lead to dead ends.
Also annoying is that there are parts where you run away from enemies, and doors you've previously been through are now boarded up or locked.  The game often expects you to notice vents in random locations to hop up into to get away, which is somewhat counterintuitive.
This game reminds me of a bare boned version of Amnesia.  Essentially, if you strip away everything interesting about Amnesia, you're left with this game.  The only things it does that match Amnesia are the atmosphere and the enemies.  Sadly, I spent the majority of this game being dissapointed and just wanting it to end.

In Five Nights at Freddy's you play as a security guard working late shifts in a restaurant filled with animatronics. The restaurant is very much like the American diner "Chuck E. Cheese's". The games is scary, I couldn't even survive two nights. This game is by far the best horror game of this year. The great aspect of it is that you're isolated, trapped in one position. In most horror games the goal is to run away from the ghost or monster or creature or whatever the scary villain be in the game. However, in this game, you can't run, making it even more scarier...
Yes, plenty of jumpscares. Honestly, I really don't like the stereotype of playing a horror game in the dark alone. Yes, it makes it creepy but it's honestly better to play with a friend sat next to you. You just have to trust me on that one! There's also a few easter eggs you can catch a glimpse of in the game so that's good for all you easter egg hunters. Overall one of the best horror games of 2014, a must-have for horror fanatics. Be warned though, most of the fanbase is obsessive and irritating and most of this game's sequels are awful.

Welp, this is Five Nights at Freddy's
You are a Night Watchman at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a Chuck-E-Cheese style establishment, Singing Animatronics, pizza for kids, and so on. Whilst it's a place where kiddies go during the day to have fun and party, you aren't here during the day, no, you're the Night Watchman After all, you gotta sit the night shift through to get your meager living, how else will the bills for your crappy apartment get paid?
What are you watching for? Burglars? Teenage no-do-gooders? No, you're keeping an eye on the Animatronics themselves, Now, the Animatronics are left in Free-Roaming mode at night so they don't break down more than they already have, they used to be able to during the day, but that ended up with one of the Animatronics being decommissioned and some poor soul without a frontal lobe.
This wouldn't be a problem, but the animatronics will stuff any naked endoskeleton (I know there are theories that they're just murderous, but I'll just go with this for now) into a Freddy Fazbaer suit, it won't damage an endoskeleton, but with all those wires 'n crap in the suits, imagine what they would do to a person? Speaking of a person, guess what the Animatronics think humans are? (hint: An Endoskeleton)
The establishment is in decline, after multiple lawsuits and events (including an infamous event where a man dressed up in a Freddy Fazbear costume and kidnapped and murdered children) it's low on funding, kids and their parents aren't as willing to come to if after the public events, and the whole thing is expected to be closed by the end of the year.
Because of this state, they have a limited nightly electricity budget meaning that you have only a limited amount of energy with which to do things such as check the cameras, light up the hallways that lead to your office, and close the doors to prevent the animatronics from stuffing you into a suit, with limited power comes with the fact that closing the doors would mean you're wasting it, and you thus need to leave yourself exposed if you don't want the power to go off as Freddy sings to you his Toreador music box before he ends your night abruptly.
The game has a dark setting, a terrifying atmosphere, and is a great title, everything from the dark hallways to the animatronics themselves, everything about this game is great, you're going to be blown away by the subtle yet terrifying world this game is set in, with rumors still circulating about its mystical yet dark plot and background of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, you're going to love Five Nights at Freddy's.

While you may be expecting a casual game to waste the hours with, and you can easily jump in and out, the tactical depth and finding that winning combo to get past that one irritating level bring enough depth to keep even a toughened stratergist occupied.
Currently I'm at about 38% complated for 9 hours of gameplay. Going by that I've got at least another 10-15 hours to go. So £5 for 25 hours of gameplay? You really can't complain at that.
My only real complaint is that a campaign map would have been nice so you can pick and choose your battles and what equipment you can find and aquire. Other then that though there is very little wrong with this game, though a more indepth tutorial as to how certain weapons work would have been nice. As would be a sandbox mode which the dev's have said they're going to work towards adding.
Overall, its a solid 4 out of 5 gamescore. The lost point is for the added mode and complexity that could add to the games lifespan an fun.
Ignore the negative reviews. Most of them are complaining about this game being a mobile/flash port and for symbology they claim looks Nazi in origin... Both of which don't bear anything towards the gameplay.

DD2 is without question the best tower defense game that I have ever played. I have invested well over 600 hours and that number will grow significantly. The game literally never gets old. If you enjoy loot collecting games like Diablo, and Path of Exile then this game is for you.
Pros
* Beautiful graphics and environments
* Unique maps, heroes, pets, bosses and other enemy types
* Incredibly diverse and addicting loot & and upgrade system
* Tons of unique defensive towers, traps, and walls
* Awesome passives that allow you to create devastating tower and weapon combos
* Nearly infinite amount of defensive build strategies
* Creative weapons and abilities for DPS characters and pets
* Game Server list with friendly lobbies (create your own match or join others)
* Teamwork (many of the endgame maps require good teamwork and planning)
* Development team is active and involved with the community
* New content and challenges are added often
* Nice controls, can also be comfortably played kicked back on the couch with a controller
* F2P game that can be fully unlocked and experienced with spending a dime of real money
Cons
* Occasional server lag which results in some rubber banding.
* Limited amount of loot storage bags. The game is capped at around 12 storage bags and that simply isn’t enough for the amount of content that is offered in the game. Won’t be a problem early on, but gets annoying managing your inventory after you invested a 100 hours or so.
I originally had some concerns with the microtransactions model, however, do not let this influence your decision at all because this team has somehow actually managed to create a fair model for everyone. It is not like other F2P games that try to nickel and dime you to death.
Everything in this game besides a few cosmetic items can be unlocked with in-game currency called Defender Medals that you accumulate by just playing the game. It doesn’t matter if you fail a map or not, they still award you with the in-game currency. How awesome is that?
There are also daily and weekly challenges that allow you to earn even more of the in-game currency and other awards such as unique pets or salves. Once you start learning the mechanics of this game, you will almost certainly get hooked and this will lead to you having more Defenders Medals than you can ever spend. I now use all my extra medals now for gear and pet upgrades.
I still occasionally buy something with real money just to support the team and its development because it is fantastic game. IMO, it is better than most $50.00 AAA games so I don't mind dropping a few buck to show my support since it has brought me countless hours of entertainment. Thank you Trendy for this fantastic game.

It's a good, somewhat completed game, that's fun in LAN. :) It's free to play, and there's no real "pay-to-win" need, either. I love how you can collect items throughout, reminding me of Borderlands and Diablo. None of those wussy items like in Secret World and Age of Conan, either. ;) Tons of small gimmicks, like pets and skills. Later in the game you can change some of the effects on the other towers.
A few downsides, though: it's buggy (it's alpha, so no surprise there). You'll be thrown out of the game and have to rejoin the match at times (fortunately you don't have to wait for the match to finish before you can rejoin), sometimes the weapon-animations suddenly stop showing, or trying to carry more than 1 gold/crystal during the Kobolt Challenge will simply delete the other, sometimes you just can't connect with a friend and both gotta restart the game...
I do wish there'd be a few more towers to chose between for each character, though, but at least you can change character ingame as often  as you wish, and use several types.
Yeah, there are downsides. It's a free alpha though, so can't complain and let it prevent me from giving a recommendation, because we (four of us) had a lot of fun. Some even bought the hideously expensive Hero/Costume packs - not worth it in my opinion.
My tip? Download it, play it for free, enjoy it a lot (or not, and no money lost). If you like it enough that you'll buy pretty-coloured things for lots of real money, well - all power to you, I suppose.
Enjoy!
