Part 1: REVIEW FOR PLAYERS FAMILIAR WITH BLOOD BOWL
This is just another BB client. Some pros, some cons in comparison with BB1.  The most noticable differences:
1. Much better online than BB1 in public leagues. Private leagues will need some time to evolve to the level of BB1, but I believe it will happen soon enough.
2. Interface is different and will require some time to adopt, but is of about the same level.
3. Less number of teams, others will probably be in DLCs.
4. AI is betterm but still good only for newcomers, it'll not hold vs experienced coaches.
5. Some optional and obligatory homerules and some rules are bugged, but nothing gamebreaking if you can live with some changes from the rules.
6. Better graphics.
Part 2: REVIEW FOR NEW PLAYERS
There are several BB clients on the market: Fumbbl (the worst GUI and graphics, the best content), BloodBowl2 (the best GUI and graphics, most differences from original board game rules), BB1 is somewhere in between. There is no point in buying BB1 now as the number of players in online is bad. If you are not a diehard board gamem fan, the differences with the rules should not matter much for you, so get BB2.
Most negative reviews are coming from experienced coaches who are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off with some differences with the board game rules and low number of teams. In fact it doesn't affect the core of the gameplay and present teams are enough to represent most aspects of BB and are balanced well. Teams that can come as DLC later are not going to be much better, the balance is quite good here, so if you are not going to try them all you'll not have to spend money on them. So do not be afraid of poor ratings or ranting in the forums. Haters gonna hate, but it doesn't really make the game worser for new players.
I would recommend this game to you if you like turn-based risk-managment games or warhammer universe.

Bioshock is one of the best games I've ever played. It's the creepiest game I've played since the original Silent Hill on PS1. The underwater city contributes to a claustrophobic environment. The enemies in this game aren't just mindless grunting zombies. You often walk in on them talking to each other, arguing or fighting with each other, working on some machine. Even though they clearly have a psychotic monster mentality to them, they still seem to go on about their business at times. It's creepy when they sing. Anything the Little Sisters say is especially creepy.
The art style is fantastic. Really good graphics for a game from 2007. And I enjoyed the music selection for the game. It gives age to a science-fiction style underwater city full of genetic experimentation. The best is when you turn on a jukebox and it plays "How Much is That Doggy in the Window" because it's so completely inappropriate for the setting. It just adds to the strangeness.
The game controls great. I'm not a big fan of first-person games, but climbing, jumping, pressing buttons, collecting items, and simple navigation like walking and crouching are all perfectly executed. Most enemies don't sprint around you, which makes it easy on the stomach for those who suffer motion sickness. I found the game to be more about slow exploration than fast-paced shooting.
There is a good variety of weapons and "plasmids" which are basically superpowers. You can easily switch between plasmid and weapon with the right mouse button. As in most games you can mouse-scroll to change weapons or click the corresponding number on the keyboard. There is a "damage research" system that lets you take photographs of enemies to build up research points, which turns into bonus damage as you complete the research tiers. You can upgrade your weapons at upgrade stations and you upgrade your plasma by spending Adam, which is acquired from Little Sisters. You can choose to harvest or rescue the Little Sisters. I recommend rescue. The rewards were sweet.
Bioshock is more than just combat. The more you explore, the more tape recorders you find, which reveal more of the story. There isn't much in terms of puzzles. The game points you in the right direction with a flashing arrow. Items of interest are obviously highlighted. Hacking is the main "puzzle" side of the game. You can hack vending machines, security bots, and safes through a mini-game. Hacking security bots and turrets makes them work for you.
I played on easy, because I really don't play FPS games and my backlog of games is too large to get hung up on a single game too long. Easy setting was EXTREMELY easy. I never died and the final boss was a joke. As I progressed, I needed to buy less and less supplies. After a while I couldn't even collect money anymore before my wallet was full. Using the invisibility plasmid also makes the game significantly easier. You can hide from monsters and more importantly security bots. If you trigger an alarm you can just stand still (and invisible) until the timer ticks down.
The best part of this game is the story. It is interesting with an amazing plot twist. I'm not going to say much about the story. No spoilers on that one.

Banished has been a wonderful experience. As a fan of the "Age of Empires," "Command and Conquer," and "Total War" franchises, it's been strangely theraputic to play a game where there is absolutley no military action or presence of any kind.
Battling against the wits of mother nature, and her arsenal of cold weather, poor crop harvests, and devastating tornadoes and fires has proven to be a worthy challenge.
That being said, I will echo what many other users say. The game loses it's appeal once the town reaches a certain size. To me, the enjoyment comes from the strategy on what buildings to build, and when to build them, coupled with the doubt you'll make it through the winter. Once you have a large enough town, and are producing more than enough food, the threat really seems to subside (this is the stage I am used to building a military force, but cannot in "Banished.") And the enjoyment wanes. Still, it is fun to restart on a new map.
I recommend this game, but really only if you can catch it on sale. I paid approxamately $5 USD for it, and love it. If I paid $20 for it, I may not love it so much. When 1.0 is released, i'm hoping theres more depth, or some sort of end game.

Video Review:
Ever wonder where your chicken nuggets come from? This platformer is Super Meat Boy slid his double quarter pounder into Flappy Birds and gave it his secret sauce. That is Chicku. BTW, do yourself a favor and play this game with a controller.
WARNING: The game is graphic in that is has copious amounts of cartoon blood. If you are with PETA, move along, this is not the game you were looking for.
ON TO THE REVIEW!
Sound: 7/10
Graphics: 8/10
Gameplay: 10/10
Replayability: 7/10
This platformer does have integrated multiplayer. Co-Op and Deathmatch. Nothing like playing a suicide bomber chicken to take out your friends.
SOUND:
Basic sounds and music that doesn't annoy you after 4 straight hours of gameplay.
GRAPHICS:
Cute cartoon mayhem within this slaughterhouse of horrors. Every death allows for another layer of blood to wash over the background with each subsequent death (as long as you remain on that level obviously).
GAMEPLAY:
I feel this game is well worth the $10 it is going for, for its coming out of Early Access sale price. Even for the regular price of $12.99, I would still pay that much for this game. (***Note, publisher provided a game key for review purposes, but in no way has influenced my personal or professional feelings on this game***). If you mess up slightly and barely nick a hazard, it is not always game over! (YAY!) That is because it is possible to loose your wings, legs, and even head, and still be able to complete the level. I really really enjoyed this little perk of game play, so you can literally run around in game as a chicken with it's head cut off.
All in all, there are 3.5 world types with over 120 levels to beat. After certain levels, you get to unlock perks to add to your multiplayer death match, like Zero Gravity. The levels occasionally will have multiple paths to take to beat them, depending upon your play style.
Co-Op consists of local players dropping into game by pressing 'A' on their controller and helping you to clear the level.
REPLAY:
This game has decent replay as you go back through and attempt to beat your previous level clear times. There are a total of 3 coins per level to be obtained, which can then be used to purchase custom hats and headgear for your chicken. There is nothing like running around blowing friends up while your chicken wears a bloody Jason Hockey Mask!
Overall score: 8/10

Very fun game with plenty of strategic depth.
1. Equipment selection. (There is a limited number of equipment slots available.) Do you go for maximum offense or countermeasures to prevent them from striking you? Heavy hitting artilery that's slow or rapid fire rounds? You'll also have to contend with munitions and power.
2. Equipment placement. Decide which equipment to protect since equipment in the back ranks are very difficult to hit (accuracy is a big factor).
3. Decide which stations to man (You have limited number of soldiers). Stations that are maned have special bonuses, such as reduced reload time, or improved accuracy.
4. Actively move soldiers to stations where they are needed (ie. put out fires, repair damaged stations, or to recover health in a medical bay.
5. Decide which high-value target to take down. Do you focus fire? Or simultaneously strike multiple targets?
6. Micro managing each weapon's fire is available should the need arise. Since countermeasures have a cooldown, it is possible to send out a coordinated strike.
Based on game completion percentage of 21% for 5 hours, there's around 20-25 solid gameplay here. Highly recommended.

No, you're keeping an eye on the Animatronics themselves, Now, the Animatronics are left in Free-Roaming mode at night so they don't break down more than they already have, they used to be able to during the day, but that ended up with one of the Animatronics being decommissioned and some poor soul without a frontal lobe.
This wouldn't be a problem, but the animatronics will stuff any naked endoskeleton (I know there are theories that they're just murderous, but I'll just go with this for now) into a Freddy Fazbaer suit, it won't damage an endoskeleton, but with all those wires 'n crap in the suits, imagine what they would do to a person? Speaking of a person, guess what the Animatronics think humans are? (hint: An Endoskeleton)
The establishment is in decline, after multiple lawsuits and events (including an infamous event where a man dressed up in a Freddy Fazbear costume and kidnapped and murdered children) it's low on funding, kids and their parents aren't as willing to come to if after the public events, and the whole thing is expected to be closed by the end of the year.
Because of this state, they have a limited nightly electricity budget meaning that you have only a limited amount of energy with which to do things such as check the cameras, light up the hallways that lead to your office, and close the doors to prevent the animatronics from stuffing you into a suit, with limited power comes with the fact that closing the doors would mean you're wasting it, and you thus need to leave yourself exposed if you don't want the power to go off as Freddy sings to you his Toreador music box before he ends your night abruptly.
The game has a dark setting, a terrifying atmosphere, and is a great title, everything from the dark hallways to the animatronics themselves, everything about this game is great, you're going to be blown away by the subtle yet terrifying world this game is set in, with rumors still circulating about its mystical yet dark plot and background of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, you're going to love Five Nights at Freddy's.

The game has its merits mostly based on its intricate battle system. The combinations you can make are pretty abundant and a lot to take in at first, but using your Blast Gauges and Hidden Artes always feel satisfying. The combo system is complicated enough to make you think your button presses in advance in order to have better results in your battle. The anime-style art is high quality, with some nicely done cutscenes and good animation.
However...
The story and characters are just not well written enough to make me care about them. The story seemed promising near the middle of it, but sadly crumbles down at the end with no real tension other than "beat enemy x". The cardboard-y characters can sometimes have some interesting banter but lack any sort of edge to keep things interesting and ambiguous. All of it feels like a safe and traditional approach at a fantasy story with the typical tropes you'd find on any RPG. The grinding turnout is also lacking, where battles can sometimes feel a tad repetitive with no real reward other than leveling up.
All in all, if you're a Tales fan, you might find this enjoyable. However, the magic only lies in the battles, not the story. Maybe you can play this game to lower expectations, then play Berseria which is miles better on all aspects from the get-go.

It's a good, somewhat completed game, that's fun in LAN. :) It's free to play, and there's no real "pay-to-win" need, either. I love how you can collect items throughout, reminding me of Borderlands and Diablo. None of those wussy items like in Secret World and Age of Conan, either. ;) Tons of small gimmicks, like pets and skills. Later in the game you can change some of the effects on the other towers.
A few downsides, though: it's buggy (it's alpha, so no surprise there). You'll be thrown out of the game and have to rejoin the match at times (fortunately you don't have to wait for the match to finish before you can rejoin), sometimes the weapon-animations suddenly stop showing, or trying to carry more than 1 gold/crystal during the Kobolt Challenge will simply delete the other, sometimes you just can't connect with a friend and both gotta restart the game...
I do wish there'd be a few more towers to chose between for each character, though, but at least you can change character ingame as often  as you wish, and use several types.
Yeah, there are downsides. It's a free alpha though, so can't complain and let it prevent me from giving a recommendation, because we (four of us) had a lot of fun. Some even bought the hideously expensive Hero/Costume packs - not worth it in my opinion.
My tip? Download it, play it for free, enjoy it a lot (or not, and no money lost). If you like it enough that you'll buy pretty-coloured things for lots of real money, well - all power to you, I suppose.
Enjoy!

Undoubtedly my favorite 3D platformer since 'Super Mario Sunshine'. I 100% recommend anyone who loves platformers, or anyone who loves well-made games period, to check this out. I don't buy many games at full price, but I'm glad I did here. There are hundreds of well worded positive reviews out there already (that I totally agree with). I'm not sure what else I could add to the chorus there, so I'm going to do something unexpected for how much I love this game: I'm going to gripe about a couple of minor things.
1- This one is just personal: I genuinely disliked almost all of one world, the Alpine Skyline (except 'The Windmill'. That part was awesome). I found it tedious, stressful, and nausea-inducing. The camera did not work nearly as well in this area as it did in the rest of the game.
2- I wish there were a LOT more of the 'Time Rift' levels, these were by far my favorite part of the game but there's only a few, and they are quite short.
3- The game gets frequent 1.5-2 gigabyte updates, apparently due to the way Unreal Engine 3 updates work (if they update one small thing, an entire large chunk has to be re-downloaded). This is no fault of the devs, but still, if you have slow internet or data caps, watch out. I've gotten 10 gigs of updates in 2 weeks. Additionally, every update resets your in-game settings, potentially leaving you with a lot of adjustments to make every time.
This game is as good as, or possibly better than Super Mario Sunshine, and I think I would label it the BEST 3D Platformer ever (keeping in mind that I haven't played Super Mario Odyssey yet, which of course looks outstanding). This isn't another 'Yooka-Laylee' disappointment. Buy it immediately.

Command and Conquer is a legendary franchise that is much beloved by people all over the world. A franchise that unfortunately has remained dormant for some time and most likely will continue to do so. But most of the games contained within it are extremely great, and this one is no exception.
C&C 3 takes place in the Tiberium Wars arc that began with the original game. The world has prospered under the control of the GDI. A sort of United Nations military force, that combats terror threats. However, a quasi-religious cult known as the Brotherhood of Nod reappears to try and take control by force. The thing I like the most about Command and Conquer is it feels the closest to present day warfare compared to other RTS games such as Starcraft. It features a very well funded military symbolizing "peace" and "order" against an anarchistic anti authoritarian movement. And the entire conflict revolves around the accumulation of a resource known as Tiberium.
This also ties into the general gameplay of the series and this game in particular. In Command and Conquer there aren't any worker units and buildings are queued similar to units. Your units tend to be squads of footsoldiers, tanks, jet fighters and so forth. Even though it is a very sci-fi game with aliens, lazer beams and so forth. It still feels much more down to earth. Infantry units die very quickly to units carrying rifles, but are useless against buildings and vehicles. Wheras vehicles have lots of health and can carry other units but are weak against explosives. It's a game where you have to pay very close attention to what units you're controlling and which ones are attacking which.
C&C 3 in particular takes a few cues from other RTS games like Starcraft. It adds an alien race known as the "Scrin". Who have their own unlockable campaign. Although there are very few surprises when playing as the Scrin, they queue their units the same and their buildings are mostly similar. But there are statistical differences to playing it. Which unfortunately only become really prominent at higher levels of play.
My favorite aspect of C&C 3 in particular is it's skirmish mode. Specifically how customizeable it is. You can set a particular AI opponent to have different mannerisms. Like you can set an AI opponent to turtle, meaning staying in his base and preferring to not attack. Or you can set an AI opponent to be a rusher, who will attack at the soonest moment. It's one of my favorite RTS games to play exclusively in singleplayer for this reason. Multiplayer is also available however you will need to use third party methods to get connected as it ran on Gamespy which has been shut down.
Solid RTS, one of my favorites. Easily recommended if you're a fan of campaign and skirmish.

To start off this review here is some background. I used to play and very much enjoy the first Red Orchestra and honestly was really excited for RO2 - when it was released I was unfortunately very dissapointed with the game. I knew the bugs would eventually be ironed out but it just felt different...smaller maps, no fluid controls, no tank maps at the start - little things that added up to being flawed game and I'm sure this wasn't experienced by just myself.
Now I've come back to it following the release of Rising Storm and I have to say through Tripwires hardwork and persistance the game is where it should have been in or around the release - the game has been jigged around, tweaked and smoothed to a thoroughly enjoyable experience.
I'll start off by saying the gameplay is relatively slow for a FPS, those of you that have played the predecessor will be used to this. The controls are fluid to suit the style of play with a good intuitive team communication feature to ensure the best possible teamwork out of essentially a game of up to 63 random people.
Aiming, shooting, gun mechanics etc. take a while getting used to but honestly are far easier and far more responsive than that of RO1; this may deter some hardcore sim enthusiasts but if you're looking for a competitive game then this suits perfectly.
Maps are smaller than RO1s, this does have it's pros and cons - pros being it suits competitive games more as you'll realistically not need so many players as the original game did to make a viable game. Cons are from a perspective of a single player really - large maps had a sense of immersion which is missing in RO2 and I hope to see some good community made maps turn up soon. The original had very large tank maps and I have to admit my experience in a tank on RO2 so fast has been extremely limited - however RO2 won't win any prizes if you're looking for a bigger better version of what RO1 did for the tank lover...honestly if you've never played RO1...well lets say it had one of the best tank simulations and this was purely a side part of the main game.
Whilst this review is blunt and to the point I urge anyone who is into FPS to try this, especially if you haven't tried an FPS sim before. They are relentlessly fustrating at the start as you get adjusted to the gameplay speed and die from places unknown in an instant, however it adds to the immersive gameplay, one that is rewarding, team based and skillful.

One word describing my adventures with Banished: ADDICTIVE.
I used to play vanilla Banished for a super long time until recently I began exploring mods to enhance my gameplay. Ever since, I haven't looked back, especially since I can have LLAMAS! And build fancy houses! ...And I guess more ways to keep my people alive.
So, when I originally began to play Banishd, I actually had zero interest in city-building games. Pretty much all "Tales of" games deliver on interesting combat and characters while faltering somewhat on pacing and/or story. Tales of Zestiria seems to have faltered more and delivered less than some other Tales games, but it still provides enough fun for me to offer my recommendation (with some reservations).
The active battle system plays more like a combo-oriented brawler than it does a traditional RPG, and it has just enough depth and enough split-second decisions to keep things interesting, but the game has to teach you about this combat system for effectively the entire first half of the game to ensure you can see all of its depth. If you can get past the tutorializing, there's a lot of fun to be had from mastering combat, ramping up the difficulty, and seeing how stylishly you can finish off enemies.
In typical Tales style, the narrative experience feels comfortable while still providing a few surprising twists to established story archetypes. Even with a smaller cast and shorter run time than most other games in the series, you're bound to bond with at least a few of the characters through their earnest depictions and genuinely funny reactions.
Unfortunately, many of the game's design limitations hold this game back from being truly excellent. The expansive maps are often sparsely populated, and you'll never experience some of the depth of the game's content without gratuitous grinding. The story feels as though it could have used a bit more polish in places, and some of the dialogue feels as though it could have used another few passes by the localization team to make it feel less stilted to an English audience. At points, it also feels as though they were building up the story just for the sake of making a sequel.
This was a great game to come back to after a hiatus from the series from many years, but it is certainly is not my favorite Tales game. Newcomers to the series would find a fairly good entry point here, especially on PC, but long-time fans may not be too impressed.

Outlast is a fantastic horror game. The ambient noise added to the creepiness that existed already from just being in a mental asylum with all of inhabitants off the wall is topped off with the feeling that you are always being followed... always being watched. The game isn't jump scare dependant like many of the modern day horror games it is able to sustain itself throughout the course with its story, environment, and NPCs both hostile and those not trying to kill you. While the game is very good overall, the system of which you record your events through the video camera is very overpowered. The night vision on the camera makes any blackness have rather clear images, something that a camera's vision tends to not have. And if the camera was a more accurate depiction, the asylum has a very linear movement system for you to go through, there's no real good opportunity to explored anymore than very small section. Outlast is very impressive and the story that is in it is very deep and takes more than just a quick runthrough to find out all that you can. I highly recommend playing the game if you're into horror and aren't off put by lots of blood and gore.

The Beginner's Guide asks the question wether or not we can engage in a conversation with an author through their work.  While the answer it reaches is "no", perhaps it's just a poor communicator.
The game can either be seen as a character study, or a larger critique on the nature of art.  It doesn't really work as either.  A few moments of thought as to character actions and motivation both muddles the central relationship of the drama to the point of incomprehensibility, and paints the true author insert character, Coda, in the most irritatingly narcissitic way possible (when a few moments of though gives Coda a number of flaws the game glazes right over.)
If we view it as a critique on the other hand, it's sloppy, inconsistent, and I find it's message just a little bit gross.  Sometimes it argues for death of the author: the work doesn't indicate the authors mental state.  But it also champions the idea that any sort of interpretation is impossible, even of the more straightforwardly symbolic games, because we're not the author, and only the author knows the meaning.  It's Schrodingers Author!  Are they alive or dead?  The game also has the incredibly self serving "tortured artist" narrative, not so much in the process of creating art, or the nature of being an artist, but in having to deal with an audience.  That contempt, and sense of inflated self worth permeates the entire game.  It's also undermined: Sure, Davey (audiences in general) is stupid, and flawed, and selfish, but he's also RIGHT: Should art be distributed, it will have an audience, and an aritst is essentialy a communicator.  An artist tries to get an idea into someones head by creating something, a code, that they hope will be decoded.  If the art can't ever be decoded, it's ineffective art.  If an artist doesn't show his art to anyone, sure, he can take pleasure, in creating, but that's it.  That's only half of the artistic process, and typically leads to lazy, self indulgent art.  Of course, theres a place for art as a personal escape, but the game conflates that with all of game design, a field almost always with an audience, and commonly with a commercial element (as this game has.)  Hell, THIS game attempts to encode a message to be decoded by the audience.  It's an inherently self destructive work.  If it had more of a sense of humor, and was this self destructive on purpose, you could call it Dada.
I can't really wholeheartedly reccomend it, not on any complaints of gameplay or structure, but merely because I don't think the ideas were fully fleshed out.  I had high hopes for this game, and I can certainly see where a lot of good ideas started, but to me at least, the game failed at telling a message not worth expressing.

Blood Bowl 2 is one of the best games I have played in a while. I think we can all agree that running around a football field with teams full of fantasy races bashing each other while trying to score touchdowns is simply an awesome premise. The game is turn based, which I love, and it involves quite a bit of dice rolling, which makes each match unique and unpredictable. The "turnover" mechanic is brilliant. If you fail an action during your turn and one of your players gets knocked over, then your turn immediately ends.This leads to nailbiting choices like: "Yes, if I make this risky block, I'll score a touchdown. But if my player falls over instead, then my opponent will be in a good position to score. Do I wait for a better opportunity next turn? Or do I go for it now?"
There is real strategy to be had here. Manage your odds. Do everything that is safe first in case your rolls go south and end your turn. Learn how to set up block strings and use the all-important once-per-turn "blitz" move. Don't make unnecessary dice rolls. Your strategy will also vary greatly depending on which race you choose to play. Dwarves? Bash up your opponent's players and watch as they are carried off the field on stretchers. High Elves? Look for tiny openings in your opponent's defense and exploit them with your high agility, speed, and passing skills.
The art direction and graphics are first rate. I don't think I'll ever get tired of seeing my ogre (I named him "Slurple") smack down the opposing players. I still laugh out loud when someone fails a "Go For It" roll and goes tumbling to the ground and fumbles the ball. The prat falls and the accompanying sound effects are *perfect*. The person who designed this really knows their stuff.
The two commentators in the game (Bob and Jim) make me chuckle as well. When my ogre is lying prone on the ground, tries to get up, but misses his "intelligence" roll and goes nowhere, then one of the announcers might claim "I've seen *mushrooms* that look smarter than that."
The game is rock solid stable. I have not seen even one crash or freeze up during the 63+ hours I have been playing. I did encounter two bugs involving player lineups and gold inducements, but these were fixed very quickly.
In the future, I think I would like to see more robust league creation options, as well as an easier way to see what skills players have on the field. The negative reviews I have read are written either by veterans of Blood Bowl 1 who dislike the fact that some of their favorite features are not in the game, by people who do not understand how randomness works, or by people who feel the game is too expensive. Note that there will be additional teams added to the game, but you will need to purchase them at about $7 each if you would like to play as them. The base game comes with eight teams.
In any case, I am very happy with my purchase and would highly recommend Blood Bowl 2 to anyone who might enjoy turn-based strategy with RNG meshed with football in a high fantasy world.

Over all I like this game, but I still have some mixed feelings about it. I'm not sure whether to recommend it or not because it completely depends on who the person. This game requires a LOT of patience as the puzzles become extremely challenging. There is much trial and error involved. I would sometimes spend a half hour trying to find a solution to a puzzle just to stumble into another one ten minutes later that stumped me. As you can imagine, I grew very frustrated. It did feel highly rewarding to over come each section and to finally figure it out, but there came a point where I just wanted to beat the game. There were a small handful of puzzles that I couldn't seem to figure out on my own no matter how hard I tried, and I was at the point where I was so eager to get it over with that I eventually looked up the solutions for a few of them. I hated to cheat, because there's no better feeling than figuring something out on your own, but I had just ran out of patience. And the demo, I felt, was very misleading. I was given the impression that it was all about platforming. There weren't any puzzles in it or at least, if there were, they were very benign and not noticeable. I get that games raise in difficulty, but the difficulty in puzzles had escalated to a shocking height to me. I will give it a lot of credit though. The puzzles are extraordinarily clever and well thought out. I haven't seen a game where the puzzles were designed so great, except for Portal. And maybe the problem lies in me. I have never enjoyed puzzles that much. I have a lot of patience in life, but not much in puzzles.
You're also thrown right into the game, with no dialogue or spoken plot or cutscenes or instructions. For the most part, it's executed well, but I was upset to know that I had to actually look in the options menu at the controls to see that ctrl was the action button, mostly to pull and push things which is a large part in this game.
I will still recommend this game, if only you are prepared for the difficulty. It looks to be a simple game, and the demo makes it out to be a simple game, but be prepared to invest more time into it than expected, to die a load more than expected, and possibly even to look up a guide when stuck.

Limbo is an Inde Puzzle Platformer that is mostly standard in the sense of its mechanics (aside from a couple of shiny moments in the "late game"), but that has a strong point in its artistic choice and the way that the whole aesthetic of it is. It is a very interesting idea that I haven't seen in a lot of other games of this class (if at all really, I can't remember any other game that has done that before).
The mechanics of it, as I said, are very standard in comparison to any other puzzle platformer: you jump, you move stuff around, you try to find a way to keep moving forward and not to fall to your dead. The interesting thing about the game comes to play when you are confronted with some of the "enemies" of the game, but then again it is more of a time pressure in the puzzling than an actual fight against the AI of the game. Other special things that might happen in the game that changes the mechanics a little bit are some of the puzzles (I cannot explain them without spoiling a bit of the game though).
The game can be completed very fast. I finished it in about 3 and a half hours. I did not finish it to a 100% because that includes looking for little "light bubbles" around the world that are meant to be collectables or achievements, but these do not affect the game in any way. And again, I cannot imagine that finding all of them might extend the game all that much. The game itself in a mechanic point of view is okay. Maybe a little bit about average, but not much more than that. Challenging at moments and has some interesting ideas. You can be sure that you won't get trough a whole are without dying a couple of times, but it has nothing to do with skills, it has to with the game being a♥♥♥♥♥♥and setting you up to some traps you CANNOT see coming at all. I guess dying is just a part of the game, which actually makes sense considering the artistic view of it.
The artistic view and aesthetic of the game are the most attractive elements of this game. The way I would describe it is a black and white world (light and shadow kind of thing) that looks beautiful, but has a creepy and impressionistic element to it. It made me feel a little bit uncomfortable at some points because of the impressionistic nature of the art style. It is not "gore" in any way, but it is something that get's close to it in a 2D shadow-like graphics. Nothing to worry about, though; just a dark game. The world is very well made and it pays attention to little details, which is weird considering that you are basically seeing shadows of the world in a 2D view. A very good thing that I have to point out is that the game makes a very good work of letting you know what is actually a platform you can jump on and what is just a part of the background/fordground.
There is a story element to the game that, as far as I am concerned, is left to free interpretation throughout the whole game and up to the very end as well, not giving you any answers to any of your questions. Where are you? What/who are you looking for? Why is there other people here? The game has no dialogue at all, but it manages to get across just as much story as it wants to, leaving you with just enough questions for you to keep pushing forward and looking up theories in some forums after you have finished the game.
Warts and all, this game is good. It is an experience that I enjoyed. Short and simple, but worth some of your time. Get it if you care more about story than about mechanics.

The idea of the Confederates gaining the naval strength to go toe to toe with the Union navy is one of my favorite What Ifs of the war and there as so few naval foused games, especially set in this period, that it seemed like a match made in heaven.
Where things went wrong.
1: You can only control the flagship of a squadron directly. In fact you can't give any orders to the other ships at all and can't even order your ships into battle formation as far as I can tell.
2: The flagship's controls are far too clunky and the flagships will sometimes switch their engines to full reverse for no apparent reason.
3: Battles take forever even with the turbo speed option engaged. I played one battle for almost an hour. Not only was the battle not over but none of the 13 ships involved had been sunk or surrendered and the most heavily damaged had only taken around 65 percent damage. This ship started fleeing at 60 percent damage but fled through the heart of my nearest squadron guns blazing rather then running away and soon rejoined its squadron for their next pass.
4: There aren't enough ship classes in the game. There are six ship classes but each side only has three warship classes to choose from. Though I will say that I was pleasantly surprised when I realized they didn't just have both sides using the same ship classes they really need more choices in fleet makeup,

One word describing my adventures with Banished: ADDICTIVE.
I used to play vanilla Banished for a super long time until recently I began exploring mods to enhance my gameplay. Ever since, I haven't looked back, especially since I can have LLAMAS! And build fancy houses! ...And I guess more ways to keep my people alive.
So, when I originally began to play Banishd, I actually had zero interest in city-building games. I am terrible with strategy games and micro-management, but the more I understood the game play (which will take a while to understand), it became easier for me to play, and led me to trying more difficulties.
The downside to Banished though, is that there really isn't an end-game; when you reach a certain number of townspeople, it becomes repetitive, and less about survival (since you literally have everything covered in terms of food, health, amenities, etc.) At that point, that's when I switched over to the Colonial Charter mod that gives a wealth of new objects, buildings, decor, food, animals, materials, etc. to the game. There is also an (optional) addition of Natives you can trade/war with, new professions, and new objectives (Adam and Eve, if you think you can do it!)
Overall, I enjoy this game more about its process and building my towns, rather than focusing on the end goal. Because I am such a casual player, I don't really focus on the achievements for this game (since they're a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ half the time), but that is also an option if you start to get bored.
I'd say if you like games such as Anno (which inspired Banished), or SimCity (a colonial SimCity!), then you'd enjoy Banished. :>

RTS these Days have two Problems: Rush and Pomp.
First of all, all Strategy Games have become Starcraft-like Rushers, you have a set build cue and the winner is the one who's faster. My fondest Memories of Age of Empires or C&C were Games that could take hours. As a result, I've come to dislike Combat RTS in the twenty-first century.
Previously, it wasn't hard to find economic city builders and simulations where combat was optional, or not in it at all. And if it was, like in the old Anno Games, it was mostly combat for supply lines, not blind destruction. "Strategy", as it's called. But these games today come in flashy graphics and marketed so strongly to the mainstream of which they became part, that they have been dumbed down so that losing isn't an option anymore even if you're dumber than the planks of your ships in Anno 1503 were.
It is in this environment that Banished shines. It's a Sandbox Citybuilder in a harsh Environment where every mistake, every failed adjustment, and mistakes in planning ahead can be your death sentence. And even if you do it right, your town of 500 People can be devestated by a single Tornado. This game is out to get you, but it's that challenge that makes it so fun to play and gives such a great sense of accomplishment. Games like Banished don't need a set build cue, because every map is different and common strategies won't work on certain maps. They don't need photo-realistic graphics, they need to serve a purpose and that's that.
What's more, the game changes significantly, with three very distincts phases. First, you start a game with a lot to do and always too few people to do it. You have to shift workers around to where they're most needed, prioritize and show strong micro management. As your town reaches its first 100 People, you have some workers to spare but now have to make sure they're fed and have all ressources available, bringing the game more and more towards macro-management. You atomate supplies, trade becomes crucial. And towards the end, it'll be space you'll seek most desperately, every map only has so much buildable ground available, and every tile becomes an invaluable ressource later on. But stop expanding, and the next generation will be short several hundred people, disrupting all your supply lines. It's always a challenge, but the challenge itself changes greatly.
Banished is in equal parts a casual, relaxing experience as a challenging example on how perfectionism should be employed in strategy games. Everything I loved on the Eco-RTS of 15, 20 years ago, is present, everything serves a purpose, is easy to handle and looks good enough to not fail that category either.
If you are hasty, if your tank armies are huge and if you often reload games, stay away from Banished. If you enjoy the challenge of an economic city builder which, in all simplicity, can never be completely mastered, then this is a game for you. I can't get enough of it.
It needs a bit of polish, but overall it's pretty good.

The concept is really good and the dev team's ambition really shows. However, there are a few things about this mod that bring down the whole thing. Pros and Cons to follow.
Cons
- unable to load any saved games. According to the forums this has been something that the devs are aware of but have not mentioned in forums since december 2016. I really cannot understand how this core mechanic was broken/disabled.
- constant crashing. If saved games could be loaded I would not hold this against the mod.
- Tanks cost way way to much for either side to produce/ maintain anykind of armored presence, the chinese suffer from this more than the japanese. Ex: a tank that costs 500 MP, 55 fuel and 10 population should be able to stand more than 3 shots from a light AT gun and not be damaged at all by infantry gunfire. At the very least, it should be easier to replace when lost.
- visually units look impressive up close but at any kind of zoomed out distance they become really monotone, lose thier head or turn invisible.
- Some of the doctrine unlocks are too expensive for what they offer and a match can be over before you get a chance to unlock them.
Pros
- when you can actually see the full detail that was put into each unit, they are very impressive and well done.
- the devs clearly did thier research and implemented what they found quite well.
- many of the balancing and AI issues that ruin the skirmish games can be ignored in online play
- with a reasonable amount of work I expect that this mod could (and one day should) be up there with Great War or Eastern Front as a must have, right now its not worth having if you dont have a committed group of friends to roll online with.

I love Banished. This game is where I turn when I want something like "Don't Starve", but don't want to micromanage everything. What's nice about Banished is that after a certain point, you don't have to do all that much unless you want to expand. You can sit back and watch your community do its thing, while occasionally making adjustments as the situation calls for. You can leave the game running while you go to the bathroom or get a drink, and be reasonably confident that everything will still be fine when you get back. (If you tried to do that in "Don't Starve", you'd probably come back to find your character dead or in a hopeless situation.) This also means Banished is not too taxing on the brain. Sometimes I want something to fill the hours and challenge my brain a little, without making me feel mentally or emotionally exhausted. Banished is the perfect answer to that need.
The graphics, though simple, are stunning, and the music is very enjoyable. My only complaint is the UI, which could do with some improvements; but that's far from a deal-breaker.

Tales of Zestiria is a very good JRPG game, with a very interesting world and a lot of things to explore there. With a good story and many cool characters to play as. Also the combat system is quite different from previous Tales of games.
You got many cool and interesting characters from the main and side one's.
Battle mechanics are confusing at first, feels like it has too many things to care about, but the more you play the better and more interesting it gets.
There is many cool looking attacks and super moves, many different combos you can do and unlock more by progressing through the game.
You have many waifus Alisha, Rose, Lailah, Edna, Symonne and maybe more. Or husbandos if you like guys. And of course Edna is top tier waifu :3
You have lots of skits(which are chats between characters), some are very funny, that should should not miss or skip.
You can find many outfits and other fashion stuff, to customize your characters and make them look better, funnier, cooler, etc. Like sunglasses, cat on head, mustache, funny glasses, cute or cool outfits, etc.
There is many interesting moments in the story, related to different characters of your party.
Many different maps with lots of NPCs and chests to open, and quests to do.
You can play not just as the main hero but also as other main heroes.
A good amount of well done trailers of important story moments.
You got many optional quests, places, things to collect or beat.
After you beat the game you have Dungeon EX with many cool bosses to fight with or continue exploring or doing side quests. Or you can do NG+ for more options and increased monster level and rewards, and difficulty.
Sorey was kinda a boring main hero, because he prefers to avoid killing his enemies and fight in a more justice way that he feels is more right.
You can't have Alisha in your party almost the entire game.
While story is good, but sometimes it gets boring and many times you are "ok I don't even give a ♥♥♥♥", and it doesn't give you an option to deal with some bad guys you would like to kill, makes you play the "good guy".
Exploring optional ruins and caves eventually gets boring, because they tend to look the same, they take you too much time to explore because normally they are large.
You can't fast travel to very far places, making you waste time going to one town to then find how to fast travel to the other town or close to it.
When doing quests many times you can't even use fast travel because you need to see some special story related interactions, this is understandable, but not to this level, because is not fun having to walk 1-3 big maps or stupid ruins or caves just to get to your destination, and many times you walk a lot just to see some pointless interaction between characters that are just random non story related NPCs. And there is not a way to move fast, you can only walk, since as I said previously fast travel is not available at those moments.
Game has a lots of "cheap" bosses, which are not optional, who have tons of HP, aren't really hard mechanic wise, but hit very hard, and make you waste many resources and time.
Many times it feels like game is done like this just to make you waste more time and artificially increase the playtime.
Also I was tired of being called Shepard and savior, from any casul NPC in any town.
PS: if you feel like increasing the 30 fps cap to 60 fps, and give the game more performance options you can install a fix mod that can be found on guides section.

When I asked about the DLC, and whether it was going to be present with the Steam release, the moderation team banned me from posting any further. To my knowledge, this happened to others as well.
It's too bad that the moderators for this game's page are such objective ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, because the game itself is pretty cool. Locked at 30FPS, so the port is questionable, but it runs smoothly enough and is scalable enough to play on mid range PCs.
If you liked all other Tales games, there is no chance you won't like this one at all. You may find the beats to be familiar, but then again if you've made it this far into the series, you've already been dealing with the same clichés for a decade and it likely won't start bothering you now.
I do have to mention that the DLC in fact is NOT present with the base version of the game, which strips out a fairly major character at the start of the game. The way she leaves is completely incomprehensible and her presence was clearly just waifu baiting to push players to purchase the DLC to see more of her. That's kind of unacceptable but I think they stopped doing it in subsequent games, at least.
All of this considered, it is still a fantastic iteration on the Flex Range Linear Motion battle system and the story this time around is a bit more inspired than your tired "You good guy, this bad guy, this cute girl, go be hero". Which makes it feel at least a little bit fresh -- but admitedly, only as fresh as a game that's basically fodder for a shounen anime can get.
There's some camera issues, since battles now take place in the open world rather than in instanced arenas that just magically appear. This means that you may sometimes run into fights in a closed-off area and the camera jerks and jumps around a little bit until you settle on a comfortable angle. If I remember correctly, I think mods have fixed this, however. The PS4 version got ♥♥♥♥ed in the process, sadly.

City builder with a challenging early game, and a horribly non-existant late game.
There are many things Banished got right. I believe above all else, its market timing was perfect for being a worthy city builder during a long drought - you may find that you're reading this review when this isn't applicable - that's important to consider when reading other reviews. Learning it is challenging, but fair - winter is harsh. The music, interface, sound, graphics, and overall aesthetic appeal is all very good for the price point. In fact, I'm not sure I can think of a single city builder that has done a better job with the interface.
Where Banished really falls short, where most of its competition doesn't, is late game content. Getting a population to around 300 is pretty much the game, and you can easily get there in ~15 hours of gameplay. There are no new structures to build, and your only real choice is to just tile the map using the same carefully constructed methodology of your first group of economic buildings. I think the optimism that the modding scene will pick up this slack is wearing out, too. Some of the achievement hunting may give reason to start a few new towns if that's your thing.
Despite that shortfall, to say that I didn't have plenty of fun while it lasted would be disingenuous. This is the type of game that is enjoyable for its novelty factor, but not the kind of game that you'll keep on playing once the novelty wears out.

So, if you can pretend the ceaseless tutorials don't pop up every three seconds (there's even even collectables that's are tutorials!), and the somewhat needlessly complex equipment system, you'll find a pretty good JRPG here.
The characters are all charismatic and likeable, the combat system is very enjoyable (though also really needlessly complicated, oi), and the world itself is varied enough that it doesn't feel bland. For some reason this game gets a bad rap, but I don't get why. I've only played Symphonia however, and maybe the other Tales games are just that incredible.

Ok, so this game has a few flaw, but overall it is an enjoyable experience. I myself am a huge fan of the shmup genre, with Starfox (the original for SNES, not 64) being the first game I ever played to completion, and this game definitely deserves a spot on the shelf with other shmups. Let's get right into it, shall we?
Pros:
- MUSIC! This game has some of the most up-beat, driving, and overall motivating music I've heard in an indie shmup for a while
- Variation: This game doesn't just ask you to shoot everything. It requires you to master all forms of gameplay presented.
- Well paced. This game doesn't have a difficulty wall. It gradually eases you into the harder and harder levels. And even as the levels progress, it is preparing you for what's to come.
Cons:
- Control... No matter your ship, you control like you're flying a blimp
- Graphics: The graphics are lacking a bit. I gather that this is an indie game, but everything looks a bit too flat and uninspired. There's no real art direction other than "Standard space shmup."
I rather enjoy this game and can see myself playing it quite a bit in the future. That said, it's not the best game I've ever played. There is certainly better, but for $2, I'm not going to complain.

Game feels very inconsistent with its mechanics, which leads to issues when the game wants very quick reflexes on some of the enemies. It wants to represent a run and gun game, but it has an off-center gun and platforming segments that slow the pacing of the level down. It wants to have semi-bullet hell levels, but it has dark projectiles that blend in and objects in the foreground that obscure your view. It looks good, sounds good, and runs well on my PC but it also serves as a distraction when the game requires focus.
You can trade off coins to get more health, but that also reduces your damage and prevents you from getting better weapons; which you're going to need when going through levels where enemies and bosses have more health. You have to collect the coins in each level, which means you're either going to be trying to dodge enemies or unloading bullet after bullet into them.
It's a rather unforgiving game, but I feel it's more unforgiving due to its inconsistent gameplay and less of the enemies themselves. Unlike other games which rely on memorization or mastery of a game's specific control scheme, there's only a few ways you can approach each level and repetitive losses on the same stage just turns montonous. The game draws you in with its unique visuals that set it aside from your typical 8-bit platformer, but shoos you away with its gameplay.
If you're a fan of games that require either memorization of patterns until you can perfect levels or quick reflexes, this might be the game for you; however, the game's controls aren't smooth enough for me and the gameplay doesn't strike me as unique enough to hold my interest. Some may find a better experience with this game than I have.
EDIT: After beating the game on Normal, I still feel the same way; there's 27 "main levels" and about 9 boss rush levels near the end in the entire game, with 6of those being regular run and gun levels and 4-5 being bullet hell airplane sequences. Despite the 1930s aesthetic being unique, the character designs themselves are not very captivating or interesting; usually just a generic character drawn in the 1930s way of having an exaggerated smile or sneer. The stages do get overbearing at some points with the backgrounds and foregrounds, especially in one of the airplane levels near the end. Controls didn't really improve with experience; I still had some times where I struggled with movement or the parrying.
My favorite stages were probably from World 3; I liked Cala Maria, Werner Werman, and Sally Stageplay. World 2 is a very forgettable world.
My least favorite stages were the Phantom Express due to its "parry to move cart" mechanic, and the final boss being rather anticlimactic.
King Dice's theme song is a really good track.
Overall, it's probably not for everybody but if you're interested you should get it at a discounted price of $10 or lower. There's games that do the gameplay better and the design isn't captivating enough to be worth the admission fee - the game's fast pace also doesn't let you appreciate a lot of the graphics due to having to focus on random projectiles and enemies popping out of places.

Spooky, alien, simple. Three words that come to mind when playing LIMBO. A strange, minimalistic game, LIMBO puts you in control of a little boy who is searching for his little sister in a hostile, seemingly abandoned world. The art style is eerie, and persistant throughout the entire game with almost next to no music.
What remains is it's gameplay that consists of two buttons. Jump and grab. While it might seem limiting, the game is in fact one big puzzle game hidden in a 2D sidescroller. The limited amount of actions are just enough to make every puzzle new and challenging. So challenging even that you will die with every new problem presented to you. Every death leaves an impact on the player, because the ways the little boy gets killed are gruesome to put it lightly, and you are responsible.
Clocking in at just over an hour for skilled players, and two hours for first time players it might not seem like it's worth the money, and looking at that way, you would be right. But this isn't just a game, but a lonely and eerie journey.

NOTE:  I want to thank Gatling Goat Studios for reaching out to me and giving me a Steam key to play this game to make a review and record some game footage before the game launched in Early Access.  As always, this has no effect on my review or my scoring for the game.
This game is really, really fun and makes you want to play again and again.. But I warn you now.. it's isn't easy!
Prepare to die, and to die often!  Prepare to watch your poor chicken carved into chicken nuggets in all sorts of bloody, gory ways!  ..And that's a big part of the lure to this game!
While you can use a keyboard and mouse, a controller is definitely recommended.  You have a total of 3 maps, each with 40 levels, so 120 total levels in all to try and get your chicken to break open a crates with little trapped chicks inside.  Flying past all the spikes, spinning saw blades, and many other hazards is where the challenge comes from, each level progressively getting harder and harder.
There is also a local multiplayer mode where up to 4 local players can all duke it out for the claim to the most brutal chicken ever!
The ability to play each of the 120 levels and earn coins to equip your chicken hero with "cool cosmetic gear" adds to the addiction of this game and it really is a game that is a ton of fun to play!
Heres my scores for this game based on my own unique scoring system:
Value:  33 out of 40.
Fun:     28 out of 30.
Controls & Bugs:  20 out of 20
Graphics & Sound: 8 out of 10
-----------------------------------
MY TOTAL SCORE:  89%
The price of this game is the biggest reason this game didn't score higher.  Even though there is a ton of levels and replayability, I just feel that if this game were priced a little lower, it would be much more appealing, so if you can catch this game at 50% off or better from it's $12.99 asking price, then my score for this game rises into the mid 90's!  That shows you how awesome I think this game really is!

Clearly they put in a lot of effort into the art style and animation... guess they forgot about putting in gameplay.
This is probably the first serious review I've ever felt the need to write, I was super excited for this game... I mean this is a launch day review! Unfortunately though, it did not meet up to any expectations.
So how does this game fail? It's not fun or rewarding. Rewarding experiences = Fun; I'd like to talk about how Cuphead makes you indifferent to your own actions, and thus... indifferent towards playing the game.
This is something that's overlooked WAY too often by developers, how does the game tell you you're doing something good VS when you do something bad? In Cuphead, you start out with the Peashooter; your standard weapon against runaway toons. This is clearly the main part of the game right? You shoot stuff. However when your peas hit your target, the effect is a puff of smoke and a barely audible sound... I know that the relevance of that might be hard to comprehend but it's a HUGE deal. Think about a game you played with an enemy that was guarding; how does the sound differ from when you strike their guard, vs when you land a clean hit?
you know you shouldn't keep spamming.
Cuphead doesn't give you that feedback with its sfx and hit animation; its a poof of smoke... as if your bullet just... disintegrated without doing anything. It's so strange? Because everything else feels perfect? Jumping, parrying, CROUCHING... the game clearly conveys that those actions are meant to do something... but for what!
Let me segway into another related point...
If you have any experience with these sort of games, you'd know that there's not THAT much more to it... its super simple really. The hit sounds they have are only slightly different, but effective. Enemies explode in a satisfying way giving you confidence that you dispatched them for good... but even without that? THE BOSSES HAVE HEALTH BARS. The simplest way to amp up Cuphead would just be to add a health bar to your foe. You see... there aren't any stages that you have to get through to have "Contract Matches". You walk around on a map and then you start a boss fight. SO why is there no health bar if it's just you against ONE enemy? Seriously every other game does, and that's why they work.
Let me tell you why it's such a detriment.. even with the issues I've stated, it wouldn't have mattered that much if you
how much dmg you're doing; that would have been sufficient. Instead... I feel like the match is on a timer, and it doesn't really matter what I do, it will just end after a certain amount of time.. as if I'm just existing next to this beautifully animated creature while it does it's thing.
There's different guns and EX moves that you can buy at the shop with descriptions like.. "Auto Aim but less damage" or... "Short range but great damage" .............is that true though?? That's what the TEXT says but the game doesn't make me FEEL like that's true. How could anyone know?? No health bar.. tsk tsk.
Had this been part of the game, it would have vastly improved the experience. Players would feel like they're doing something.. when you die, it does let you know how far you got; and while that's great.. I'd rather not have to die to feel like I'm making progress. Change the sfx, maybe add something else to the hit animation? Have the enemy SHOW you that its hurting and how much damage youve done to it? DEFINITELY add a health bar. The game NEEEEDS it.
SO let's say that it got all that right... would it be worth playing then? Well... yeah I guess so!! But it won't be great.. it doesn't have a gameplay mechanic that increases depth or complexity. Everyone is playing the same game the same way. What does Touhou have? If you stay at the top of the screen (where the most danger is) you absorb all pick ups. You are rewarded for staying alive with a MASSIVE increase in atk power. Don't even think about going for high score runs if you die just once; What does Ikaruga have? A BEAUTIFUL AWARD WINNING BALLET ROUTINE, where your perfect execution is rewarded with more enemies, more dance numbers, and MORE FUN. What does Cuphead have? Parry... let's talk about that.
So what is Parry? Basically there are pink projectiles from your opposition which you can press A on to... jump off of them? The projectile is then nullified and of course you don't have to worry about it... ANd THATS IT. Does that sound like fun? YOu do get a small boost in Cards which let you perform EX moves... so I would imagine that the idea is to Parry, Gain Cards, cause mayhem.. but you don't really feel the need to do that?
First off, those pink projectiles are HARDLY ever a threat... so it's not something you do to avoid damage. Their location is a little tricky though.. theres a risk of punishment for going for it. Let me give you an example: Theres a pair of brawling frogs and one of their moves is to fire projectiles at you... a low to make you jump, a mid to make you crouch, and a high to catch you in the air. Every 3rd or 4th one will be pink! Were you to Parry one, the position you would be in would be... disadvantageous. More challenge right? THE PROBLEM IS THAT IT IS A PLAYER CREATED CHALLENGE.

Here are some ideas that I'm sure you would agree would be fun. Maybe a succesful parry would result in a clear board? Giving you a chance to deliver a strong counterattack? Or maybe instead of the board, only within a certain radius? I would have loved it if within that certain radius, every projectile would be reflected back at its deliverer. A more radical fundamental change would have been if the parry jump could propel you to a high reward/ high risk location? AN exposed weak spot that you could shoot but also receive more flak? Or honestly?? If it just played more of a role in avoiding damage in general? Like... sure you COULD try to make your way through that onslaught of attacks, or you could try to nail this high skill parry to avoid it completely? Just saying..
IN CLOSING, I never thought I'd be the kind of person to write such a negative review but.. this is for the love of what it COULD be.. I sincerely hope that some changes are made, this was a fantastic idea.. its just that the execution needs a little work. I hope that theres a reason for me to buy this game again in the future but for right now.. I have requested a refund and I would not recommend this title to anyone.

Chicku's influences are clear: Flappy Birds, Angry Birds, Super Meat Boy... even the film Chicken Run. The result is a simple, amusing game that's charming enough to keep you playing for a good session or two.
The selling point of the game is the simple but annoying control system, based on rotating your chicken around 360 degrees, and tapping a button to flap in that direction. There's also a button that freezes you for a second, then fires you in the chosen direction, taking you safety past obstacles such as blowy pipes.
These controls result in genuinely funny (and gory) moments of chaos, and while you do get better with practice, the fact your chicken is so prone to gravity means you're never far from death.
Gameplay highlights video:
Chicku's campaign mode consists of LOADS of short, spiky levels. Almost too many - the game spreads itself quite thin and you might be waiting quite a while before something genuinely new turns up. But the levels are so short (some can be completed in a couple of seconds) that it's got a great sense of pace, urging you onwards.
Most levels are just "get to the end", but occasionally you'll need to collect stuff over the course of as many lives as you need. For completists, each level has a one, two or three coin award depending on your best speed. The coins can currently be spent on randomly allocated hats.
There are more unlockables (that seem to come after a certain number of levels or coins, I wasn't entirely sure) that can be used to modify the game with crazy disco balls and the like.
The multiplayer versus mode, which I haven't tried yet, puts you in a choice of arenas of similar size to the campaign levels. A variety of weapons and tools spawn for you to collect and use to kill the other player. Time limits can be changed, silly modifiers (once unlocked) can mix things up.
So it's one of those games you jump in, get confused by for a few minutes, get into the spirit of it and blitz through half of it very quickly. Beyond that, it'll be worth a few more goes, plus waiting to see what is added over the course of early access. If you can sort out local multiplayer, the battle mode does look fun, although these days it's up against a LOT of arena games that offer more complexity.
* Version reviewed: 1.01 (Early Access)

Having put over 150 hours into Blood Bowl 1, and a little over 50  hours into Blood Bowl 2, I think the game is well worth the upgrade. The graphics are better, the UI is vastly superior, and it's far easier for newer players to pick up the game and learn. There was an issue with the end turn button being in an awful place, but that's been fixed.
All that said, there are a few downsides. I do wish the DLC had launched with the game, as it seemed to me they marketed it that way. I also wish the league settings and stat tracking were a bit more in depth, but that's something that could get patched in down the line.
Overall though, the game is solid, and I've had a ton of fun playing it. Some might say it's not worth the price, but I've played this game far more than a lot of other games I payed the same, or more, for. If you love sports, turn-based strategy, and fantasy, you'll love Blood Bowl 2.

Take the core concepts of FTL (room management, single item selection and movement, upgrades and customization) and apply it to a post-apocalyptic world who's warfare tech has stagnated to forts and artillery (and the occasional laser...). The game is pretty fun and quickly becomes frantic in the later portions of the game. At first I was disappointed because I thought the game didn't have any customization (the first 3-4 missions doesn't allow you to customize your fort) but once I realized that you actually can, the game became much more fun.
The actual gameplay itself is simple. You target the enemy fort using your own guns and try to blow it up. Forts have "rooms" or emplacements that can be target to disable guns or utilities like med bay etc etc. You have Operators who repair the rooms and man the rooms which provide passive bonuses to the item they are manning. Operators are limited so try not to let them die. You win when you bring down your enemy's health bar to zero. Later stages of the game gets particularly difficult. Guns have different special abilities like stun or shred etc etc. And you can get some serious firepower in the later stages as well. Still a really hard game.
In summation, it takes the things that made FTL fun and applies it to artillery and forts. Works really well and for 5.99, it's not a bad price. Definitely recommend this one.

Outlast is a fantastic horror game. The ambient noise added to the creepiness that existed already from just being in a mental asylum with all of inhabitants off the wall is topped off with the feeling that you are always being followed... always being watched. The game isn't jump scare dependant like many of the modern day horror games it is able to sustain itself throughout the course with its story, environment, and NPCs both hostile and those not trying to kill you. While the game is very good overall, the system of which you record your events through the video camera is very overpowered. The night vision on the camera makes any blackness have rather clear images, something that a camera's vision tends to not have. And if the camera was a more accurate depiction, the asylum has a very linear movement system for you to go through, there's no real good opportunity to explored anymore than very small section. Outlast is very impressive and the story that is in it is very deep and takes more than just a quick runthrough to find out all that you can. I highly recommend playing the game if you're into horror and aren't off put by lots of blood and gore.

I have found it to play out more tactically than some other run'n'gun bunny hopping games out there and you get more of a feel that you are a part of a team than an individual.  Its mostly accurate portrayal of World War 2 characterizes the brutalness of that war.
The game does not capture the intenseness of Red Orchestra Ostfront (the first game).  There is a
other than the two current tanks, although they are done well.  Good armoured combat and combined arms battles are almost non-existent.  The game is also dressed up with completely unnecessary frilly perks and leveling, and at least one annoying weapon that should not even be there at all but was probably put in to appease the more casual run'n'gun crowd.  Except for Classic mode (a slightly slower tribute mode more reminiscent of Ostfront), the game is plagued by olympic speed sprinting and unrealistic snap shooting that almost eliminates firefights.
As said, the game is more gritty and real feeling than other mainstream shooters out there and it does shine more in Classic mode.  The weapons are done fairly well and the game does look great on Ultra settings without having that overly bright contrasty blue/orange look of a couple of mainstream games we know.  Servers are fairly configurable so you can run different game modes or a combination of your favorite features from them.  The tanks, while only two, are well done and suppossedly we may see more in the future although I wouldn't say anytime soon as of March 2014.  AI is better than in the first game Ostfront, but certainly nothing to brag about.  Community mappers and modders have contributed to this game with free content and I highly recommend you check that out.
A Note!  This game includes limited access to Rising Storm.  If you want full access, buy Rising Storm instead because it includes Full Heroes of Stalingrad Multiplayer (but not the single player).

Disturbed is an adventure/choose your own adventure type of game. You are traversing a map trying to solve the riddles. The events are fixed per scene so once you figure it out then you know to avoid it or to trying to fit it in properly in the sequence of events. It takes about an hour to beat.
I found the game fairly mediocre overall, but decided on giving an upvote since it is free. I was not a huge fan of the art, but that is a matter of personal taste. I also found there was not enough variety in the scenes, with the story too linear. First decision A or B; try A, die, so restart and choose B; next decision C or D; choose C; die; so start again, choose B, then D, etc. It is very linear and you basically go from scene to scene and trial and error. After you are a number of choices in, you have to repeat a lot of scenes just so you can arbitrarily die in some decision.
I see this as a poor man's version of "The Forest of Doom." Very similar plot of being in a forest, but much nicer graphics, better decision tree, but costs about $2 on sale.
Another free alternative to this game is "The Bottom of the Well" - a grim adventure tale, but where the story is actually very interesting and complex.

Having put over 150 hours into Blood Bowl 1, and a little over 50  hours into Blood Bowl 2, I think the game is well worth the upgrade. All that said, there are a few downsides. I do wish the DLC had launched with the game, as it seemed to me they marketed it that way. I also wish the league settings and stat tracking were a bit more in depth, but that's something that could get patched in down the line.
Overall though, the game is solid, and I've had a ton of fun playing it. Some might say it's not worth the price, but I've played this game far more than a lot of other games I payed the same, or more, for. If you love sports, turn-based strategy, and fantasy, you'll love Blood Bowl 2.

Chicku is the love child between Super Meat Boy and Flappybird creating a game that is a well-designed and unique take on the platforming genre. Your goal is to fly your chicken through the maze avoiding grinders, grills, and other obstacles dangerous to chickens. There are 120 unique levels in the game and an additional 120 nightmare levels. The nightmare levels are the same layout as the original levels but with a TON more obstacles and traps. Best of all you can play the entire game with your friends, as every level in the game can be played local co-op. While the game can be frustrating at times overall it’s a silly, rewarding experience that has more than enough content to be worth the $13 price tag.

When I saw REDCON, it had "Mixed Reviews" - apparently due to a few bugs. I've played about an hour and I havne't seen even a glimpse of these, so perhaps those are fixed now.
