I should say outright that I really wanted to like this game and say something positive about it, because I can tell how much effort the moderators put in to it and how good the models are. It's a beautiful, well crafted game, but it's realism detracts from balanced gameplay, and ultimately makes it almost unplayable. The Japanese can beat the chinese really easily, and that makes the game incredibly unbalanced. It's saving grace is that it can be modded in corsix *if* you make your own attrib file folders, and that it's actually really fun to play for the first 15 minutes until the poor balance kicks in. 8/10 grapics, 9.5/10 realism, 2/10 gameplay.
As for the actual gameplay, the game has horrible balance to the point of being almost unplayable and is incredibly slow and tedious. You have to research upgrades just to do the most basic things, like build a machine nest, and in the end no matter what strategy you go with the AI always knows the exact opposite and due to how long it takes to create any kind of challenge to it, you basically lose. Even playing the Japanse who are clearly superior to the chinse sucks, because of just how damn tedious it is and how omnipotent the AI is. You basically end up having to trick the game by spamming certain units to throw off the AI or overpower them early on, which just ends up kind of not being very fun even if you win, which is unlikely.
It doesn't really matter how good you are or what strategy you employ, unless you get lucky or are extremely fastidious you will lose. One tiny slip up and you lose literally all your units in a single hit from a mortar or a single machine gun, and yet it takes 30 minutes just to be able to use the most basic functions of the game. It should also be noted that one faction, the Japanese, is just 10 times better than the other, which practically makes it unplayable. Even when you win, it doesn't feel like you did well, it just feels like the creators have no understanding of balance. Robs you of a victory both ways. I tried like crazy to get the game to become playable but to no avail.
2/10, the graphics are good though, like an 8/10 if not a 10/10 for the graphics. It's honestly a real shame that such good modders can't fix a few basic gamepay and balance issues. There's a reason the original company of heroes isn't this tedious and ridiculous. It's extremely frustating to see a game really well made in some areas, and completely horrible in others. But it is a free mod and the mod team is not proffesional so I have to get them a pass. I was sad to see it be so horrible, though.
EDIT: Through some finagling I was able to get corsix to work on it. If you do want to mod the game yourself for better balance and to expedite things without needing the research or starting off at higher resources etc., then download the Corsix mod editor, go to the gamefile in your company of heroes or company of heroes reluanch folder, and then add the appropriate folders, and say "extract all" to all of the gameplay files so they can be edited in corsix. These file folder names are Archives, Data, DataAttrib, DataSoundHigh, DataSoundLow, Locale, Movie, and OPS. With these file folders, you should be able to get corsix to work after extracting all of the game files (but make sure to make the file folders first or else corsix will crash without a properly named destination folder), and then you can mod the mod.

So picture this, a house with a 75 year old person in it, fully stocked with firewood, coal and food. The house next door has a family of 6 and they freeze to death, the family next door to them has a family of 4 and they starve to death. With this game mechanic you will lose lots of people, over and over again when it is not necessary, and there is no mod to correct it.

I really liked this. To me it's the logical extension of the Telltale Games "drama told through gaming" games (Walking Dead, Life Is Strange, Wolf Among Us, Tales From The Borderlands). It starts like a documentary (another idea I really like - documentary told through gaming) and then turns into something different - an introspective journey of self evaluation. Really thought provoking and tons of themes and symbolism to chew on for long after it's finished. I sat afterward for quite a while and mulled it over. I didn't have the emotional catharsis some have said they had, but certainly an intellectual one.
I can see where it's not going to be some people's "cup of tea". If you're into games simply as entertainment and don't want to have to figure out what the "point" is, or if you're looking for something to challenge your skill, you'll hate it. The challenge here is purely intellectual and psychological. In that respect I think this game is going to be a bit of a Rorschach test.

This is a blast to play. Many games include short Bullet Time as a perk or something to give you a temporary edge over your opponents. Super Hot is all about Bullet Time. The mechanic builds suspense and adds a layer of strategy as you play through it. There were a few levels that I found myself repeating over and over until I found just the right string of actions needed to finally kill all the enemies. While the game was difficult at times, it was never really frustrating. The only time I found myself annoyed was at the very end where I spent a good 5 minutes trying to see if I could defy the final orders given to you before the story ends.
Pros:
- The game is satisfying. Dodging around, cutting bullets with the sword, and blocking bullets with random objects you throw around makes you feel like a badass from the matrix.
- The game FEELS great. The controls are responsive and in a game that requires precise timing, that is everything.
- Just enough difficulty to give you some trouble every now and then without becoming discouraging.
- The body swap feature you get later on leads to some hilarious moments. I found myself waiting to get shot at, throwing a gun at the red guy that's firing at me, swapping bodies, catching the gun I threw at my future self in mid air, turning around, and mowing down a group of enemies quite a few times xD.
Cons
- Short story. VERY short story. You can finish this game in 1 sitting quite easily. It would only take about 2-3 hours.
- It's hard to judge exactly when a bullet flying at about head level will actually hit you. I found myself thinking "Hey, that will probably miss me. I should be fine if I just let it fly over my...never mind then >.>" a few times. It's a minor issue, but it still throws you off a bit when you see a bullet kill you even though it looks like it will just harmlessly fly over your head.
That's about it. If you don't feel like spending $25 for a short game, wait until it goes on sale. It's a great experience and I hope they add more in the future. (I could be wrong, but I think the developers hinted to more content coming out in the future in one of the final screens)

It combines old elements (side scrolling, platformer puzzles) with new elements (complex physics, beautiful animations, high quality 3D graphics, etc...). It presents this with a novel visual style, as if you're looking at an early 20th century movie, that really boosts its creepy atmosphere. The sparse but great sound effects and cues enhance its atmosphere even further.
The puzzles are easy enough not to be frustrating, and hard enough to be a challenge, I loved most of them.The learning curve was just right for me too. Some puzzles force you to die and retry or have lightning reflexes though, since you don't always have a view on the entire puzzle while you're going through it. For the hardcore puzzlers the real challenge is collecting the secret eggs, I only found 2 without a walkthrough,
Highly recommended, it has been a long time since a game impressed me this much. I don't even care that it's short (although I wouldn't want to pay a high retail price because of that). 9/10

Awesomely replayabe survival game featuring hunting, scavenging and fishing.  Brutal save and load feature that will not let you reload your game once you've died cause..you know..you're dead and there are so many ways to die.  Freezing, bleeding to death, illness from uncooked meat or unpurified water, wolf, bear, stepping on a campfire and burning to death and good old dehydration and starvation.  Three very different and interesting areas to explore with impressively randomized items in the scavenging locations from game to game.  A tip to all who might buy this...killing a wolf that is on top of you involves left clicking to build up power and then right click to strike.  And don't try to kill the bears unless you're tired of playing the game you are in and want to restart.   Clothing and tools wear out with use and must be repaired or replaced.   I could go on forever.  This seems like a complete game to me and I can't wait to see what else they might throw at us in the future.  Definitely cool. - Gameplay stays true to vanilla CoH, except maybe the infantry dies easily.

Cons

TLDR: Feels like an early access game. Lots of fun in the beginning but gets boring pretty quickly. Not worth it for 20 (21for us canadians) dollars.
I got this game a while ago around the time when I believe it was early access, or just leaving it. The game, I thought, was wonderful. It was the type of thing I loved: building and managing a medieval city. It was great. My only problem with it, though, and this will be a problem at any stage in the game, is that the developers mistook punishment for difficulty. The game will, at the slightest fault on your part, begin into a massive death spiral. Did you not get /quite/ enough farmers? Well now the entire city is starving, congratulations, have fun completely restarting. The problem with the game is that as soon as you run low on a resource, the entire town will collapse. But, that's the only challenge. If you amp up the supplies just a bit with a mod or something, the game gets so boring that there's not even a point playing it anymore. This fault is only amplified by the fact that there really isn't much to do in this game. You never feel like you're progressing. Got steel tools? Congratulations. They do nothing more than break rocks a bit faster. All you have to do is replace the tools when they get broken. Just in the process of writing this review I realized many of the mistakes this game has. For example, the lack of difficulty beyond material losses could have been fixed by having random events (besides wildfires that no matter how close you are to the river, you can't stop from burning down your entire town) such as, say, a bear breaking into one of your barns. The problem of death spirals could be solved by having more states for villagers besides "fat and happy" and "starving to death in the manner of literal seconds". Like really, if I go without a snack for 10 minutes I don't literally die of starvation. Or maybe you could actually get some things of *value* from trading? Which really brings up another problem. You are /one/ village. There's no other villages, there's no competition. There's no reason for you to keep playing besides "let's see how big my town can get" which would be fine, if you could actually have some /diversity/ in your town. For a city builder, there's a pretty big lack of buildings to choose from. And even worse is that there is literally only two map types: Mountains and mountains with bigger gaps in between. It's all the ♥♥♥♥ing same every play through. There are never deserts or plains or swamps. Your villages don't feel unique they just feel like every other village you've made. There's so little character in it that eventually you just give up.
I give this game a 5/10 for being painfully average, with nothing to do later on. Don't bother getting it unless you get it /really/ on sale. It will  provide you a few hours of entertainment, but don't expect to get hundreds of hours playing it.

I really enjoy this game. In fact, it's almost the perfect formula for a city-builder/civilization simulation. It's got a unique feel to it and a strong sense of accomplishment when you do things well, which is accompanied by subtle challenges in decision-making that can make or break your town. That said, it's freaking difficult, which I love, but may not be for everyone.
Let's break it down:
• Game looks wonderful, graphically
• Game has a pretty solid soundtrack
• Can be relaxing and almost meditative at times
• Provides for a difficult challenge with high rewards and steep risks
• Very good and responsive AI
• Very clean and adjustable in-game UI, and simple menu
• Very open and immediately immersive
• Has a sense of realism that many games lack (via seasons, disasters, and the general sense of urgency when things go wrong)
• Creative and active community running the Workshop
• Can be frustrating at times, and until you get the hang of it you may find yourself restarting frequently
• Lack of specific goals, other than to survive (for those "What now I've done everything" players)
• Not much in the diversity of music or graphics, but what is there is beautiful
• Not much in the diversity of base-game content after playing for awhile- but I feel that mods add a lot to the value of this game, if what you need are more decisions to make.
Overall, this game is very enjoyable and has a lot of replay value to the right people. But the problem seems to be that it is designed specifically
those people, which is both a blessing and a curse. If you crave a difficult city-sim and want to take on a challenging learning experience that can prove to be both frustrating and rewarding, this game is for you. If you're a point-to-point, objective-driven player who wants something less sandbox and more railroad, then this game might be worth skipping. If you have no idea what you want, give it a shot. You'll know after an hour of playing.

Just Cause 2 is an open world third person shooter. You go around completing missions, blowing things up, and collecting items to increase the chaos within the country called Panam. (tbh, mostly blowing things up)
There are a lot of good points about this game as well as some bad ones. First off, the world is beautiful (open world! :D ) and there are so many locations to discover which really adds to the atmosphere of the game. There are also a ton of different modes of transportation that you can use to get around the island which are all unique in some way. The fun in this game came from exploring and completing missions. The grappling hook is probably the best part, I mean, come on, who wouldn't want a grappling hook to get to place to place? The Just Cause Series is known for this fun style of movement for a reason.
Now one of the irritating aspects of the game is that when you save, it doesn't save the location of where you actually are. Once you load up a file, you will not spawn the location you were last but instead the nearest base/stronghold from where you last saved. It is a bit annoying that an open world game doesn't save where you actually were last, forcing you to re-travel back to whatever you were doing before.
There is a story in Just Cause 2, but it wasn't extremely interesting. (I definitely had more fun blowing things up and killing people) I mean, it does teach a lesson about the state of the real world which I thought was very insightful, but could be crafted better in my opinion.
The price for this is alright, but I would recommend getting it when on sale or in a bundle. It is pretty fun, but not really the "best game ever".

Got this game even though the store page said the reviews were "mixed" for this game. The game was on sale for 19 cents and has steam trading cards, so for that price I couldn't resist.
The game is very fun. It is basically an on-rails arcade shooter, that starts off really easy but quickly ramps up in difficulty when you get to the boss battles. I was stuck on one of the boss battles but felt really good after I finally beat the level. The music is great and although I think its the same 2 or 3 tracks, It dosen't become annoying. There are pickups on the levels that make it easier to blast enemies, like a faster gun and a shield.
The graphics are pretty bad for a game released in 2015. To be honest it looks like a PS2 game and for some reason the game Is locked at 45 fps. Also, when you first launch the game and try to run it in 1920x1080 you'll notice that the screen is cut off. However, if you go to the folder where the game is installed, there is a tool that will fix the problem.
My biggest gripe with the game would be the User Interface and Presentation. There is no real indication of how far along you are in the campaign. When you beat a level it just tales you to the next one. There's no screen that says how many more levels there are. Also there is no way to easily change to another ship, (the game lets you choose from 3 at the beginning of your campaign).
These problems however do not negate the fact that the core game at hand is very fun. At full price I don't know if I would feel like I got a value.  There is only about 2-4 hours of gameplay, but for 19 cents I cant complain.

SUPERHOT is an FPS puzzle game where time moves when you do (which is by the way not entirely true, because even if you do not move - time does advance very slowly).
It's really that simple - move carefully, dodge bullets, plan your moves and kill red guys.
By now you'd probably already read a bunch of reviews that smacked the game for short story.
That's totally true - it took me about 1.5h to beat the campaign.
But in my opinion story is nothing more than a tutorial (and a nifty William Gibson-esque cyberpunk-y explanation of what's going on).
The cool stuff starts with challenges and replaying the same 34 levels with different rulesets.
And here's the main question - are you the person that enjoys the story or a person that like game mechanics and gameplay?
If you are into stories, then I'd suggest waiting until this game is discounted. 10$ or sounds about right for the story only.
But if you like mechanics - then grab this game right now, it's bloody amazing.
Especially awesome moments of slicing bullets, changing bodies and catching your own weapon mid-air included.
Developers joked about it in-game, but I'll say it anyway - It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years.
And definitely one of my favourite games of 2016.

The retail version of Counter-Strike: Source also includes Half-Life 2: Deathmatch and Day of Defeat: Source

At first I felt like it's an experiment in leveraging word of mouth to sell an abstract meaningless creation by telling people it's deep and meaningful and watching them repeat that nonsense just so that they themselves do not seem shallow.
But in the end it's not just that. It's an exercise in solving problems you do not have for the narrator you do not care about by making forced choices that do not matter whenever told to fo so by the narrator. There's no gameplay, no meaningful win condition and, in the end, no aesop to be made.
The creator should have taken some effort to make the player care about the narrator or the narrator's obsession or, at least, to explain why the "games" make any sense from a sane person's point of view and, thus, should be played by the actual customer.
P.S.: Now that I think of it, the game takes less than 2 hours to complete and, technically, can be refunded upon completion. Not refunding it would be an act of paying up for your own mistake of buying it on faith.

I've played every mothership Tales released in North America since Symphonia except for the Vita games. This is by far the worst.
Never before have I played a game with such an inflated ego. Never before have I played a game that demands so much unnecessary work from the player. It actually expects you to go out of your way to study its overwhelming number of overcomplicated mechanics, even going so far as to make fun of you for possibly forgetting about one. It just isn't fun. Battles don't take place on a separate screen anymore - you fight exactly where you encountered the enemy. Under the right circumstances, which is nearly all of them, the camera just gives up.
The fields are too big and you can never fast travel when it matters which leads to constant downtime as you run from point A to point B. Often times you'll reach your objective just to be told to go somewhere else. The dungeons are absolutely atrocious. The game is a hallway simulator.
The characters are one dimentional and unlikeable (except for Zaveid). Somehow it manages to have worse villains than Vesperia and even Legendia. The story makes no sense at all. Every major cutscene left me dazed and confused, forcing me to read the synopsis to get anything out of them. Unfortunately that never once helped.
This game is also riddled with strange technical errors that the Tales series has managed to avoid in the past. Sorey always goes into his T pose when you use his mystic arte and characters will occasionally teleport into position at the start of cutscenes.
The only reason I finished this is because I want to play Berseria. At least the music is great, when Go Shiina is writing it. Sakuraba's is as boring as ever.

I would recommend buying this game at full price if you're a die hard tales fan. If you're just a person who enjoyed playing Tales of Symph/Vesperia, I wouldn't recommend buying this game for more than $15. If this will be your very first tales experience, I would suggest purchasing Symphonia first as I feel its a better experience and a whole lot cheaper.
Lets start with what you get right out of the box. Your standard combat from every tales game is perfectly set in place, combos and artes feel fluid, item usage is easy, and enemies have a resistance and a weakness. You get a full range of characters, from the dark yet alluring Edna to happy yet mysterious Lailah, and the cocky and cool Dezel. There is a lot of loot, custom skins for each character that is customizable, and a ton of side quests that usually have a nice reward for your troubles.
But in that, lies the problem with Zesteria. For a game that is packed with decent content, it never really did grab my heart or made me excited to play it. The combat, while nostalgic of its predecessors, actually feels dated. Even with the addition of armatizations, the fights just don't seem much more than a brawler with "ice beats fire" strategies. The characters never really grow, either, in terms of emotional states/basic connections. For example, early on in the game you meet Alisha, and the game hints that there will be a potential love interest in it for your main character with her (as most tales games usually included), but there isn't any. There is no build up between friendships for any of the characters either, its almost as if they all are just happy to be together for absolutely no reason. Even the customizable skins, at first I was under the impression that there will be certain skins I will obtain/unlock throughout playing, but theres literally only one unlockable skin for your main character, and its obtained at the end of the game, and its literally just a color change. I was super dissapointed in that.
The biggest gripe of all things, though, was the fusion system in this game. The story may feel sluggish and lazy, the characters may be bland, but for the most part, you're literally fighting for like 95% of the game from battle to battle. So the one thing you look forward to is loot, and boy, in this game does it suck. First off, weapons do not "scale" in this game. Instead of varied statistics, weapons have what you call "runes" on them. There are 50 different runes, and each weapon can only hold 4 of them. Certain combination of runes can hold powerful bonuses that will make your character more fun to play, however, you have no control over which runes you can obtain. You may get lucky and somehow fuse a strong rune set at some point in the game on a weapon, only to have that weapon be replaced just 5 seconds later by a normal weapon. The fusion system does not allow you to carry over the rune sets, its either you just guess and ruin your weapons, or it gives you a good rune set but it doesn't scale.
God I hate the fusion system.
If you're willing to accept that this is a tales game and nothing more, then we can go on and rate it.
The story: 6.5/10 - Unpolished, Lazy.
The characters: 7.1/10 - Unoriginal and stale.
The combat: 6.1/10 - Standard Tales combat, horrible loot system.
The gameplay: 7.5/10 - It manages to meld a lot of its mistakes, but some are just too visible.
The music: 5/10 - Like come on.
Final Score: 6.6/10 - I hope future tales games that release on steam will improve from this one. Buy on a steep sale.

Limbo is a charming game. Its atmosphere, sound and visuals are very well done and really pull you into the eerie, morbid world of Limbo. Limbo is a simple puzzle platformer at heart and while the puzzles are intriguing, most are not intuitive. Expect to die a couple of times as you figure out where all the traps and objectives are in each puzzle. The environments are a pleasure to explore and you'll encounter various landscapes including jungles, swamps, cities and underground caverns. Each of these landscapes introduce interesting puzzle mechanics, keeping the puzzles fresh. Limbo is a short game (around three hours for a basic playthrough), though the visuals and sounds make for a memorable experience.

I really enjoy this game. In fact, it's almost the perfect formula for a city-builder/civilization simulation. It's got a unique feel to it and a strong sense of accomplishment when you do things well, which is accompanied by subtle challenges in decision-making that can make or break your town. That said, it's freaking difficult, which I love, but may not be for everyone.
Let's break it down:
• Game looks wonderful, graphically
• Game has a pretty solid soundtrack
• Can be relaxing and almost meditative at times
• Provides for a difficult challenge with high rewards and steep risks
• Very good and responsive AI
• Very clean and adjustable in-game UI, and simple menu
• Very open and immediately immersive
• Has a sense of realism that many games lack (via seasons, disasters, and the general sense of urgency when things go wrong)
• Creative and active community running the Workshop
• Can be frustrating at times, and until you get the hang of it you may find yourself restarting frequently
• Lack of specific goals, other than to survive (for those "What now I've done everything" players)
• Not much in the diversity of music or graphics, but what is there is beautiful
• Not much in the diversity of base-game content after playing for awhile- but I feel that mods add a lot to the value of this game, if what you need are more decisions to make.
Overall, this game is very enjoyable and has a lot of replay value to the right people. But the problem seems to be that it is designed specifically
those people, which is both a blessing and a curse. If you crave a difficult city-sim and want to take on a challenging learning experience that can prove to be both frustrating and rewarding, this game is for you. If you're a point-to-point, objective-driven player who wants something less sandbox and more railroad, then this game might be worth skipping. If you have no idea what you want, give it a shot. You'll know after an hour of playing.

You are Miles Upshur, a journalist who has come to Mount Massive having received an email from someone within the facility (the main character in Whistleblower) which raised concerns about the safety of the facility and Murkoff, the company who run it. +Intense chase scenes
+Outstanding voice acting adds to the immersion of the game
+Some very interesting characters

+/-You don't have time to catch your breath as there are no parts of this game where a scare isn't lurking around the corner
-Very little replay value
-You're gonna need more underwear

9

Solitaire Ultra is simply what it says, solitaire.
Although solitaire is fairly simple, this game does have a few pros and cons, as any game would have.
The visual effects of this game are quite nice, the glow around the cards when you get a combo and just the overall space aesthetic is quite visually pleasing.
The music is very nice. Synthwave is one of my favourite genres of music and the music in this game is quite reminiscent of that genre. Very nice.
The sound effects are very satisfying too. If you reveal a card a sound will be played and it seems to come from slightly to the left. If you move a pile from the right to the left, you'll hear it get picked up in your right ear, and placed down in the left. A nice feature that is quite immersive. For solitaire at least.
I'm going to be honest, these things annoyed me quite a lot when I was playing.
You can't move cards down from the foundation, a fundamental feature that actually made me lose a game because I hadn't arranged the cards correctly from the start. I'm not that great at solitaire, so this is a feature that I would like to see implemented. Whether it be a toggle or just a standalone feature that is always there.
(Devs have said they intentionally removed this)
The cards can also be quite hard to read at times. Although the neon effect is nice, It doesn't help that the glow can make cards difficult to read. I have to concentrate for a short while because I can read the card I am looking at. Maybe skins could be added, weather it is creating your own and putting them into the game, or they are unlocked by playing. Something to make the cards easier to read would be nice.
There is also no double click to move cards. If I reveal an ace, I have to manually drag it into the foundations, same with all the other cards that need to be moved there too. I don't think a double click to move feature should be global (moving cards without thought) but just something simple to make the game more relaxing rather than having to waste time doing things I shouldn't have to.
Auto solve. Simple. I don't want to have to drag the cards into their respective piles. They're hard enough to read as it it.
Once a combo starts, if you constantly rearrange your piles with kings on them your combo multiplier will rise. I got to about x57 by doing this.
Overall I think Solitaire Ultra is a fun game, it's solitare. The things I pointed out were things that instantly caught my eye and because of this I can't rate it higher than a 5/10. This game lacks features that can be found for free in other variations of the solitare genre. With bug fixes and some skin redesign it could become better than the competition.
Back to Windows Solitaire it is.

I would recommend buying this game at full price if you're a die hard tales fan. If you're just a person who enjoyed playing Tales of Symph/Vesperia, I wouldn't recommend buying this game for more than $15. If this will be your very first tales experience, I would suggest purchasing Symphonia first as I feel its a better experience and a whole lot cheaper.
Lets start with what you get right out of the box. Your standard combat from every tales game is perfectly set in place, combos and artes feel fluid, item usage is easy, and enemies have a resistance and a weakness. You get a full range of characters, from the dark yet alluring Edna to happy yet mysterious Lailah, and the cocky and cool Dezel. There is a lot of loot, custom skins for each character that is customizable, and a ton of side quests that usually have a nice reward for your troubles.
But in that, lies the problem with Zesteria. For a game that is packed with decent content, it never really did grab my heart or made me excited to play it. The combat, while nostalgic of its predecessors, actually feels dated. Even with the addition of armatizations, the fights just don't seem much more than a brawler with "ice beats fire" strategies. The characters never really grow, either, in terms of emotional states/basic connections. For example, early on in the game you meet Alisha, and the game hints that there will be a potential love interest in it for your main character with her (as most tales games usually included), but there isn't any. There is no build up between friendships for any of the characters either, its almost as if they all are just happy to be together for absolutely no reason. Even the customizable skins, at first I was under the impression that there will be certain skins I will obtain/unlock throughout playing, but theres literally only one unlockable skin for your main character, and its obtained at the end of the game, and its literally just a color change. I was super dissapointed in that.
The biggest gripe of all things, though, was the fusion system in this game. The story may feel sluggish and lazy, the characters may be bland, but for the most part, you're literally fighting for like 95% of the game from battle to battle. So the one thing you look forward to is loot, and boy, in this game does it suck. First off, weapons do not "scale" in this game. Instead of varied statistics, weapons have what you call "runes" on them. There are 50 different runes, and each weapon can only hold 4 of them. Certain combination of runes can hold powerful bonuses that will make your character more fun to play, however, you have no control over which runes you can obtain. You may get lucky and somehow fuse a strong rune set at some point in the game on a weapon, only to have that weapon be replaced just 5 seconds later by a normal weapon. The fusion system does not allow you to carry over the rune sets, its either you just guess and ruin your weapons, or it gives you a good rune set but it doesn't scale.
God I hate the fusion system.
If you're willing to accept that this is a tales game and nothing more, then we can go on and rate it.
The story: 6.5/10 - Unpolished, Lazy.
The characters: 7.1/10 - Unoriginal and stale.
The combat: 6.1/10 - Standard Tales combat, horrible loot system.
The gameplay: 7.5/10 - It manages to meld a lot of its mistakes, but some are just too visible.
The music: 5/10 - Like come on.
Final Score: 6.6/10 - I hope future tales games that release on steam will improve from this one. Buy on a steep sale.

Jesus, this one brings back some memories. I remember actually being on the forums as this game progressed. I remember some of the EA forum members as well and all the drama that happened both from the forum members and the EA staff, like EAApoc being "kidnapped" by Nod to keep the third faction a secret, thus mysteriously EALAPredator made an appearance to take his place and he totally isn't the same guy behind the username.
Regardless, I was too poor at the time to buy the game on release. I got it a bit later when it was $30 to buy the special edition thingy that came both with this and Kane's Wrath.
With that said, I hold Command & Conquer series very dear to my heart. Red Alert 2 was probably one of my favorite games of all time for a long time... Hell, it probably still is. However, Command & Conquer Generals was a huge slap in the face to fans of the series. Command & Conquer Generals is a great strategy game, but it's an insult to the C&C fanbase to call Generals a Command & Conquer game, an even bigger insult to claim the whole series connects to Generals somehow (I bet EA doesn't make those claims anymore).
EA has a history of not doing Command & Conquer series justice, especially today. I will say that this game, as well Kanes Wrath, is probably the LAST true Command & Conquer game with quality gameplay. The game is great.
For any strategy gamer that is unfamiliar with C&C base building, it's simple. You have different factory types, just like any other strategy game, but you do not need any form of constructor unit to build structures. You have a construction yard, you build around the construction yard, you can no longer build structures if you lose said construction yard, etc. All the newer C&C games don't implement this any longer, which is a shame because that is what made this series so special. There is only a small handful that implements RTS in such a way, so it's strange for them to basically change the formula from being unique to being generic.
With that ramble nonsense said, this game has proper C&C base building and it works great. It's fluent, it's easy to understand, it's great. What makes this different from the old school C&C games is it implements upgrades in a way similar to C&C Generals, which is great because it's much more flexible and clean unlike the older C&C titles that implements upgrades.
The resources gathered in this game comes from a source that is typically never ending, making it necessary to take over strategic points on the battlefield. The maps design that comes with the game is generally well crafted, making it possible to attack enemies by multiple points. The great thing is how many maps you can download from the community using the "World Builder" tool, which is a map editor/creator. The only bad thing is how this game doesn't use workshop like it easily could.
The single player campaign is great. It's not too cheesy, it's just good quality B-Movie material. The game has great live action scenes, which the C&C series is famous for, that tell a great story in a creative way. They're not directly telling a story, you are told a story by being given orders and playing the missions. Rarely, there's an exception to this chemistry, but it's a good system that worked well for all the other C&C games and is oddly pretty unique to C&C how it's implemented.
Online is dead. However, when it was alive, it was good. You can still play LAN, which I'm sure you're aware can be used through programs like Tunggle or Hamachi. The gameplay is great with other players.
The AI in the game is greatly challenging. It's fun to play against both humans and computers alike.
Overall, the game is fantastic. Kane's Wrath is a great addon to consider if you enjoyed this one.
Pros-
Great single player
Simplistic and easy to learn gameplay, but rewarding to master
fast paced, fluent, and the battles are overwhelmingly satisfying
great variety in maps, especially with community based maps
Cons-
Not a whole lot of variety for playable faction choices such as sub factions (this is addressed in Kane's Wrath expansion)
Online is dead, you'll have to use LAN
$15 is pretty high for a game of this nature and age
Replayability for singleplayer is not overwhelmingly high
8/10

This is a difficult game to write about, but a few hours after playing it, I was left with several thoughts and feelings still floating around about what I’ve experienced. There’s a lot to process and possibly more than I think I’ll be able to get to here. I’ll be interested in replaying it and seeing where things stand from there, but for now this is what I’ve taken away from the game.
I heard good things about The Beginner’s Guide but not any details about what it was. At first I assumed it was a video game about being a rogue leftover part of a game in the middle of being made (The Magic Circle, I think) so as it turned out I knew even less than I thought about the game. It’s by Davey Wreden who made The Stanley Parable, a fantastic game which my brother introduced me to the demo of by insisting it was entirely different to the game itself. It was and the game is something fantastic to experience. This is a little along those lines as far as using the mechanics of a video game to tell a story.
The game stars one speaking character; Davey Wreden. He narrates the games which make up The Beginner’s Guide, acting as a kind of documentary of the works of a person called Coda. Coda’s a character whose personality and backstory is only provided by the commentary of Davey and the designs you walk through. I guess in a way you are the third character as the audience member walking through Coda’s world, curated by Davey.
To start off with, you’re wandering a Counter Strike map designed by Coda and right away there are things wrong with it, only visible once you start moving within the world. I knew a few people who tinkered with CS back in the day and it places this designer firmly in the era of people modding games that I know of. The errors look like they could be due to a first-timer learning what they’re doing but Davey tells us of recurring themes in the work of Coda. There are floating boxes, strange cubes and dead ends. It’s alienating and within or without the fiction it’s entirely on purpose to set the tone. We are not a person in the world, we’re a witness to a game being designed.
Once you have had a bit of a search and heard what Davey has to say, we skip ahead in time to the next project of Coda’s. It’s a space game with a non-working gun and an actual maze. Again, it’s something an amateur or an artist may have made and Davey has his own insights. The look of the levels are oddly charming in the same way that I find using the old graphics as to see how the original looked back in the day. There’s a moment where you die and Davey talks about Coda’s intent simply be that you die, only he experienced a bug which he replicates. You’re elevated into the air and can see the maze, the ship, all without a ceiling and the edges of the game world. There are sharp corners on the background and space itself is just a box you’re in. This is important, this change of perspective.
The narrative of The Beginner’s Guide is presented through the game’s mechanics, but on several levels. One of the next games is one where you play a character who can only move backwards through a level. This section is something which I could imagine standing on its own easily enough and has messages unique to the game as well as to the greater narrative. It reminded me a little of Passage which was a game asking whether you want freedom with loneliness or companionship with restriction. There was no right answer in that game. This one the restriction’s a little more linear and you switch between the ability to see what’s ahead or the ability to move without seeing to navigate. Again, this is important. All of it is. There are puzzles, but not many, this is more of a journey than anything else, but a ‘walking game’ which uses the minimal mechanics of the game to its’ advantage. In games like Dear Esther, you would be in awe of a heavily detailed world but at a loss of what exactly to do between chunks of narration. Here, the worlds are small and bite-sized, the worlds can be as small as a single room or massive and awe-inspiring.
Davey talks of the grander designs being experimented with and the meaning behind it all, as well as his experiences with Coda in real life. His interpretation of things like the series of small prison games, the domesticity of one game. There are recurring styles presented and some aspects evolve which reflects Coda’s growth as a person. His voice is only really experienced by little floating circles in one level and the dialogue options in a handful of games. Otherwise we’ve got the mechanics and Davey’s accounts as all you have to go on.
It’s fascinating to see and for ninety minutes as a documentary, fake or otherwise, it makes for a great use of the medium. The games themselves are fairly small and definite works in progress, but there’s something which has inspired the narrator and hearing his analysis of it helps drive us through. And this is where we get to the spoilers.
I don't know how this community is with spoilers, so I'm going to link to my site where the rest of the information is. There are a couple of flips in the narrative where it made me think deeply about one thing, then turned it round and made it all new again, all in a really short game. It's impressive and sticks with you. As I said, this all goes to spoilers. I hope you don't mind being shielded from them by me linking to my site here.

Dark and brooding, the 2D platformer that is LIMBO is a journey into the vast world of unknown dangers. Advancing through  each section of the game requires learning from numerous grisly deaths that illustrate the frailty of the player character, a boy who is trapped in such a world.
LIMBO is minimalistic in its approach to immersing the player into the game. Without much of a tutorial or guide, the game's compelling black-and-white visuals and simple yet effective controls embrace experimentation, allowing the player to make sense of the task that has been handed down.
Sublime in its atmospheric presentation, LIMBO is a work of art that mimics the seeminly Sisyphean challenge that is human life itself. The story is relentlessly fatalistic but through its brutal punishment of its player's mistakes, pushes the character to breathe life into and advance through the hellish depths of its world, before finally revealing a glimpse of the human condition that complements the fatalism: hope.
Amazing artwork, fun and tough gameplay, definitely a must buy.

This is a weird game for me to review because I feel so conflicted about it. I'm sure you know the story of Five Nights at Freddy's already and you know how the game works due to the countless 'let's plays' on youtube (cough cough Markiplier & the Completionist), so I won't go into too much detail about that and I'll dive down into what I like and dislike about the game. What I dislike about the game is that it's main mode of scaring people is by using "jump scares".  To me, a horror game shouldn't have to rely on jump scares to say "i'm a scary game, and you should be scared". A scary game should rely on story telling and creepy atmosphere to get the message across about what it is, and that's where FNaF really shines. It doesn't use storytelling in the conventional sense, but it lets you piece together the story based on little snippits that the player recieves from the pre-recorded messages and based on posters that the player can see in the hall. Knowing why these things are happening in the pizzeria makes it that much more scarier. Overall I'd give this game a 6/10. I like it, but it could have been so much better. With a $5.00 price tag, it's worth it to play with a group of friends on a weekend and see how far you can get. Hopefully the sequel doesnt dissapoint.

The Long Dark excels at what it has set out to do so far. Even at this stage, the game rarely feels like an early access title. The future may hold even more greatness for this game, and with the developers' commitment, is unlikely to be abandoned like so many promising concepts are these days.
Pros and Cons:
+Lots of areas to explore.
+Complimented by the simplistic graphics where things are easily distinguished and weather is not jarringly of lower quality.
+Grand vistas of unique sights.
+Looting is a fun activity, and thoroughness is encouraged and rewarded.
+Functional crafting/cooking system that is easy to use.
+Hunting is greatly rewarding, and challenging.
+Bears.
+The game is not easy, but not so unforgiving that it isn't fun.
+ Some degree of random generation aids in replay value.
=Inventory is okay though moderately clunky.
=No multiplayer. This would disrupt the game's purposes, though.
=Lacks tutorials sufficient to guide players through the steep learning curve, though individual discoveries are joyous.
=Rifle is difficult to aim, I'm not sure why.
=Luck is an essential factor. Unlucky starts can lead to quick deaths while lucky ones can set you up for mid-game easily.
=You wait for your character to do many things through time compression. This is not a bad thing though one mistake while choosing how long to sleep can essentially murder you.
-Sometimes deer take a rediculous amount of time to bleed out from rifle hits. Chasing them gets tedious.
-No end-game goals aside from continuing to live, making animal clothing, and looting all the things. But once you've been just about everywhere, the only thing to do is consume stuff until you die from lack of ammunition, for example. This might change, and will certainly be different in the story mode.
-No in-game navigation aids, though these are anticipated to come in the near future.

My first few attempts met with disaster and I quickly realized that it's also a survival simulator.
Building a healthy colony that will prosper over the years requires planning and careful, moderate growth.  Early survival sometimes is balanced on a knife edge. While all buildings are unlocked immediately in the unmodded game, overconfidence is a killer, and many folks may find this a harsher, less forgiving simulator than most.
However, once one works out the mechanics one soon has a colony up and running and carefully building up a surplus while not over-expanding can lead to an addictive game for those that are detail oriented.  Hours and even complete afternoons may quickly disappear while managing one's colony.
The game is visually pretty great. It runs smoothly and without any difficulty on my Windows 8.1 set up. While  there is some minor lagginess when running at 10x speed with a population over 800, that's NOT really a problem most of the time. I understand that the game is the work of one single developer and I find that amazing. It's an incredible achievement.
I've currently got 94 hours in game and have collected 27 of the Steam Achievements associated with the game. So far I've NOT played with any of the mods though I have watched a couple let's play series using them and mods add a whole extra level of awesome to this game. And that brings up one of my few complaints...
Achievements cannot be earned if any mods are enabled. Of course that includes the mods that allow non-English speakers to play the game. (Guess one of the hidden challenges is that one must master English in order to earn any achievements)
Several of the achievements aren't conducive to earning in the same game. These include building a colony without any agriculture , or building a colony without educating one's populace, or even building an isolationist colony that doesn't trade with the outside world.  While I THINK that I could now earn any of these in separate replays (and I''m planning on trying) I'm more interested in exploring how the game plays with some  great mods that are available.  If only there were a mod (like the one in City Skylines) that allows you to earn achievements with Mods enabled...
For a game that costs less than a movie in Manhattan this game was a GREAT investment. (I got it in one of Steams frequent major discount sales)
if this sounds like your kind of thing I'd check it out.

To get the most important thing sorted right off the bat: This is a good game, you should buy it, you will enjoy it.
In more detail, the enjoyable parts are the fun writing, the great art, the ABSOLUTELY INCREDIBLE MUSIC, the wonderful boss fights and the platforming which manages to make a platforming casual like myself to not throw his controller while yelling.
Oh wait hang on, that's everything about it that's enjoyable, isn't it? By and large, yes. There are a few parts that could be criticized, though, mostly that the game lacks a bit of polish here and there in the actual platforming that makes up most of the levels. The game sometimes doesn't want to grab ledges, a few jumps are punishingly pixel-perfect(though really only a few) and the game sometimes helps you, sometimes ignores you and lets you plummet to your doom. Conversely, the boss fights are all amazingly well-done.
It's like someone inverted Shantae, which has tons of mood and good writing and art, well-polished actual levels, and then kind of hits its head and waddles around in confusion when you say "boss fight." Hat In Time, on the other hand, could've done with about another 500 boss fights without boring me, while I could see a few places to tighten up the levels themselves.
It's also a bit short on content, about 12 hours of play for me, which involved just toodling around Mafia Town for about an hour because I was enjoying jumping on things, wearing hats and listening to the music. But supposedly we're getting another two acts in the start of 2018, so I think that's a bit of a minor thing to pick on. Besides, 12 hours of very solid entertainment is good value for money considering that it's a game with essentially no random generation at all, everything about it being hand-crafted.
I'd say that the SubCon Forest and Dead Bird Studio both feel like they could've had another couple of stages in there, though. But if I had to choose, I'd rather that they stopped while I wanted more and felt like they could've done more, rather than another eight stages down the road where I groaned every time I saw the Conductor or DJ Grooves(not the Snatcher, though, good luck ever making me tired of him, nerds.).
Ultimately I'd give it a 9 out of 10. It would've been 11 out of 10, but I have to subtract two points for the ending. Very minor spoilers ahoy.
So if you're still reading this review: BUY THE DAMN GAME ALREADY. OH, AND DON'T BE CHEAP, GET THE SOUNDTRACK, TOO. YOU WILL NOT REGRET IT.

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Sun Blast with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.
Sun Blast was presented to me in one sentence as “like Starfox 64”. Prior to even redeeming the key I found this an unfair way to represent a new game because Starfox (in my opinion) is the best of the best for that third person arcade shootem’up genre. Putting expectations at that level means that a fully competent title could easily be harshly critiqued or condemned for not being absolutely perfect.
Fortunately, this is not the case for Sun Blast; it is anything but competent. Right from the start the controller mapping is atrocious. O(PS4)/B(360) is NOT the select button, it is the back button. Period. To be fair, that’s nothing a quick remapping would resolve right? Wrong. Attempting to open the remapping section of the options menu hard crashes the game. Every. Single. Time.
At that point I figured I might as well try out the actual game to see if troubleshooting would be worth the effort. Spoiler: it wasn’t. The ship you pilot is MONSTROUS; at any given moment over a fifth of your screen is obstructed by it. Shooting can hardly be called that, when you fire the only feedback is a pitiful streak of blue moving awkwardly towards the center of the screen. And yes I mean the center; the depth of the playing field is so janky that it is almost nauseating trying to figure out where your ship is relative to the debris you’re attempting to shoot or avoid. Not a good experience at all.

Outlast is a survival horror game that takes place in the Mount Massive Asylum. You are Miles Upshur, a journalist who has come to Mount Massive having received an email from someone within the facility (the main character in Whistleblower) which raised concerns about the safety of the facility and Murkoff, the company who run it. You will not encounter any scary monsters in this game, those who you run from are men, twisted by Murkoff.
A word of warning, this game is extremely graphic and contains some very disturbing scenes, this game is absolutely not appropriate for a younger audience.
+Gorgeous graphics which help add to the immersion of the game
+Interesting setting
+Truly terrifying and not just because of the jumpscares but because of the atmosphere of the game
+The game's sound design is fantastic and helps contribute to the above point
+You cannot fight what you come across in the asylum, you can only run and hide
+Unpredictable enemies makes the game even more scary
+Intense chase scenes
+Outstanding voice acting adds to the immersion of the game
+Some very interesting characters
+The 'people' you come across in the asylum who were once patients feel very real, mainly due to their unpredictability and the voice acting, and it really helps add to the immersiveness and atmosphere of the game
+/-Some very graphic and disturbing scenes, some may find these too much but I feel they help to add to the realism of the game
+/-You don't have time to catch your breath as there are no parts of this game where a scare isn't lurking around the corner
-Very little replay value
-You're gonna need more underwear
Verdict:
9
An outstanding horror experience made great by its atmosphere and characters more than anything. A must have for survival horror fans.

I've been following SUPERHOT for a while now. Played the demo countless times.
While I applaud the developers for their innovative ideas in gameplay and the fact that the game was released as a completed title I have mixed feelings for recommending this title. My original post was going to be a NO but I changed it at the last minute. So, this YES review will likely read as a NO.
The largest overwhelming issue is the length of the game. Not only is the whole game easily beaten in a single two or three hour sitting but the levels themselves are small and short. You spend as much time in the menus and 'cut scenes' as you do fighting. Some of the beginning levels are so basic and short that they take less than a minute to finish.
Difficulty was also a bit of a let down. Unlimited mode gets a bit more exciting but the story itself (which you have to finish to get unlimited mode) was extremely easy for me.
While some may like the visual aesthetics I can't help but wonder what this game would have been like with a graphical overall. This is minor as the game did not pretend to be something it wasn't, but I can't help but feel a little frustrated that I built a powerful gaming PC to play 'indie' titles. Again, this is more of a personal complaint though.
Speaking of difficulty and personal complaints, I really disliked the 'hot switching' function in the game. This single handedly made the game insanely easy for me. So much so I just decided not to use it. I understand it's reasoning within the game's story but I just wasn't a huge fan of it.
Lastly, the biggest reason I can't suggest this game, is the price. At nearly $25 (or $22.49 as of right now) it's just not meaty enough. The levels are short. The mechanics are amazing, but simple and not really explored much throughout the game.
However, after typing all of this up and thinking of the experience I had and that fact I've been playing it on and off as a quick fun game on breaks and inbetween work, I have to say I enjoy it quite a bit. Yes, it's kind of shallow in a lot of ways, and it's probably not worth the money for the amount of content it has in it, but I would recommend people at least look into it. So, I'm going to go back to the beginning and change it from a NO to a YES.

While this may look like a fairly standard, if gimmicky, FPS at first glance, you'll find it's actually more of a first-person puzzler: There's always more than one way to complete a level, sure, but there's plenty more ways to fail.
The core of the game is the story mode. From a technical point, the campaign is very well structured – a mix of tutorial and difficulty curve that proves that the developers know what they’re doing, but oh man, that narrative!
It's one of those rare instances of Sci-Fi done well – dark; intelligent; futuristic but rooted in the modern world.  It takes 2-4 hours to complete, depending on your skill level and how solidly you play, but that doesn’t mean it's lacking in any way. People will be discussing this for years.
Once you've completed the main game, there's also a whole bunch of challenges - they're levels lifted directly from the main campaign, but with a tweaked rule set, such as completing the level in the least amount of steps, or having more portalable surfac- Wait. No, I'm reviewing the wrong game here.
Look, i'm not saying SUPER HOT is the new Portal, but I find it very hard to agree with reviews that put it down for being too expensive or not having enough content. The story length and quality are comprable, and even the price isn't too different when you consider the companies involved. The wealth of challenge modes put Portal to shame, and reddit is already pouring over the game for hidden material.
Don't dismiss it just yet, okay?
If you like dark sci-fi, and I mean actually dark, you’ll love the story, and you should get on it before the spoilers come out.
If you like speed-running or ARGs, there's a whole swathe of goodies for you here.
If you like unique games with strong mechanics, and want to see more risks being taken by smaller companies, then you should totally consider paying full price.

Great game for the survival genre. I have enjoyed it so far. I actually pirated the game before hand to try it out and ended up buying it on here. Once the game gets bigger, I suggest a demo or something.
Pros
-Graphics - really nice artistic type look instead of the usual gritty realistic visuals

-Constant updates- The devs are constantly updating the game which is good to see for Early Access. Keep it up guys!
Cons
-Realism - it would be nice to have actual animations when doing things in the game instead of just loading bars. this disrupts immersion some for me.

Overall, I enjoy the game. Is it worth 20 dollars? Maybe. Once the game is released, yes. Of course with Early Access, you're usually investing in the game instead of buying the finished product. I made the investment and am happy so far. Can't wait to see how much more the game evolves!

This game doesn't really know what it wants to be. The title says Wreckfest, the cars are bangers, there are demolition derby's and figure 8 tracks, so, you would think this is a game where hitting other cars isn't optional. And the title sounds kinda like an arcade game, not an simulator, so the handling will be pretty easy and forgiving too.
Well, none of that is really true. Ofcourse you can hit other cars, but the damage you get is pretty high, so in no-time you are a burning wreck. A good strategy on a Figure 8 track is braking hard if you think you gonna hit a car. The best tactic in demolition derby is: don't hit any cars, And if you got to hit them, do it slow. Hitting a car at full speed feels like more damaging to your car then to the opponent. Clean driving is the way to go, that just doesn't feel right in a game called Wreckfest
The fact that the opponents are pretty are pretty agressive doesn't help either, they don't really know that it's better to drive clean.
The handling isn't much better too, it feels just pretty bad, not really diffucult or simulator like, but it isnt arcade either. It's a strange middle of the road way of handling, Throw in the agressive AI and your car sometimes spins completly out of control, but sometimes it does not, and just keeps going.
The damage models are pretty bad, cars crumple in really wierd ways, and damage hardly affects handling, even if 3 cars ploughed in your side, making your car a bit U shaped, it still drives wonderfully. Engine damage? Well, the panel says my engine is red and that's problaby not a good thing, but there is no decrease in power, problems shifting gears, strange clunking noises. But, one hit and it's in flames.
Sound is pretty good, but nothing special.
Graphics were pretty good, but time doesn't stand still, and now it's just meh. Not bad, but nothing too good either.
But, all those things aren't the biggest problem.
The biggest problem is that updates are slow. The last update was in July IIRC, and that was a small bugfix. New tracks, new cars? Well, there were a few, but they got added 6 months ago, nothing new since then.
"Get instant access and start playing; get involved with this game as it develops", well, in this case, it's more like "...if it develops". Yeah, there will be a real track, but, honestly, who cares? It is, or was, a game where you crash cars, i don't care if i do that on some real Finnish circuit, or on one that doesn't exist. I bought this game for some fun racing, racing that includes ramming, smashing, crashing, T-bone'ing, and some more smashing. If i wanted to race clean, i'd play Dirt Rally or PCars.
For now it is a bit of a frankenstein game, a part of it really wants you to smash right in that car because it is Wreckfest, and another part will punish you for that, because it is a clean racing semi-simulator.
Really can't recommend this game for this price.

What exactly triggered the extinction of the 3D platformer? Like survival horror games, there seemed to be no real catalyst – right up until the end of the PS2’s life cycle they were still relatively popular, and then they just disappeared overnight, destroyed by a digital meteorite or possibly evolving into the feathered grey sludge that is the modern AAA game.
Resurrected with some fossilised code found in amber, A Hat in Time is a pure bred, exploratory 3D platformer and almost by default is the best of its kind made in the last decade. I say almost, as A Hat in Time is not the first game this year to try to put the paddles to the unbeating heart of the 3D platformer – Yooka Laylie launched in March to rapturous shrugs, and while it wasn’t horrible it was somehow worse than the 20 year game it was slavishly imitating.
Thankfully a Hat in Time is very much its own man, and it is far better for it – while it obviously takes inspiration from earlier games (notably Mario Sunshine), it also appreciates what DIDN’T work, especially in those later bloated Rare titles. Banjo Tooie, Donkey Kong 64 and by extension Yooka Laylee all suffered from enormous, empty worlds that were frankly a chore to navigate. A Hat in Time is much closer to the smaller, tightly designed levels of Banjo Kazooie and Mario 64, and the fluid controls and carefully calibrated difficulty curve make those worlds a joy to play around in.
The four worlds themselves are largely very well designed and have an admirable degree of variety, though the quality of individual missions and challenges can be variable. There’s definite improvement as the game goes on – the 3rd world, the obligatory Haunted House level is definitely a high point as it’s here that the exploration, challenges and humour all come together perfectly – whoever played Snatcher, the fabulous soul stealing tsundere ghost just sells the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it. The early game as well as being less interesting to play also suffers from some dubious acting and writing, and the whole “Mafia island resort” gag just doesn’t land with any conviction.
In addition to the main areas, there are also “blocks in space” levels that are inspired by those in Mario Sunshine, in the same way that Chinese toy factories are inspired by the moulds that mysteriously go missing. Those were notable high points in the otherwise lukewarmly received Mario Sunshine and they’re just as welcome here, pure linear platforming challenges that are a nice counterpoint to the broader exploration in the main levels.
It should be pretty evident that I kind of loved a Hat in Time –thanks to its amazing controls it’s just a joy to play, despite its flaws. Really the biggest concern is that it’s possibly a little pricey – I personally found the 23 quid asking price to be very fair for the 12 or so hours I got out of it, but if you put a bigger priority than I do on hour/dollar it might be worth waiting for a sale. If that’s not a concern for you, then I totally recommend pulling the trigger, if just to support an incredibly promising and talented dev team. Speaking of triggers (of the squishy clicky kind), the game natively supports gamecube pads with correct on screen prompts if you have an appropriate adapter, which is almost worthy of a recommendation by itself.

Rising Storm is a standalone expansion pack to Red Orchestra 2, an online, first person, war world 2 shooter. Red Orchestra 2 featured battles on the eastern front of WWII, Rising Storm changes the scenery and focuses on the pacific theatre of war.
Teamwork is crucial, and it really makes the game something special. Rising Storm is not a game that encourages Rambo's or lone wolfs. If you try to be the hero and run off on your own, you are going to be killed.
The team based game-play provides experiences and intense action that just isn't found in other titles. There is nothing like the feeling of pulling off a full team banzai run to capture a point with 32 of your teammates The game's sound is amazing with everyone screaming BBAANNNZAAIIII as gun fire screams by your head and your friend is blown into bits by an artillery shell. Tripwire really deserves credit for the sound in this game, everything sounds amazing! With a nice headset, or a good sound system, this game will blow you away.
Don't get me wrong, I love this game, but the graphics don't even come close to competing with the completion, such as graphically impressive Battlefield, or even the somewhat dated Call of Duty engine. The graphics, at best, are adequate. If graphics are important for your experience, you may want to consider skipping this title.
Your ping is going to be ugly as well. Throughout my games I've noticed my average ping to be about four times higher then a game of Team Fortress 2 or Counter Strike GO. The strange thing is, I haven't found it to impact the game-play much. Either the game's net-code is constructed to handle high ping, or I'm personally not sensitive to it.
With the realistic sound, and the horrors of war occurring all around you, this is not a game to play if your looking for a relaxing experience. Most of the populated servers are well administrated, which encourage balanced teams, which lead to close intense matches for the majority of games I've played.
The game features the usual classes such as rifleman, assault, sniper, etc, and contains a large amount historic American and Japanese weapons. New to rising storm is the flamethrower class for the Americans and the Mortar class for the Japanese. I personally found the flamethrower hard to use, but in the hand of a skilled player, it is great at clearing out choke-points and buildings. I found the mortar much easier to use and it is great at spamming explosives down range at bottlenecks on the map the Americans are trying to push through.
The game community is not large, and with the small player-base, the player community tend to be enthusiasts and provide good team based games. On the downside, as a new player, playing against these experienced players, you are going to die... a lot. As a newb, it will be frustrating as hell, but if you stick with it, you will start to learn how to play, and the game will reward you for being patient.
So... should I buy it?
As mentioned above, the game has a few problems, the graphics could be better, the difficulty can be very unforgiving, and the small player-base can make finding/joining good servers difficult. If you can look past these flaws, you won't find a better shooter, period. The guns are amazing, the game-play is great, and the sound is epic. I can easily recommend this title at its current full price. If the flaws cause you to be concerned, wait for a sale, and pick it up cheap. I promise you that you won't be sorry you did.

I've been following SUPERHOT for a while now. Played the demo countless times.
While I applaud the developers for their innovative ideas in gameplay and the fact that the game was released as a completed title I have mixed feelings for recommending this title. My original post was going to be a NO but I changed it at the last minute. So, this YES review will likely read as a NO.
The largest overwhelming issue is the length of the game. Not only is the whole game easily beaten in a single two or three hour sitting but the levels themselves are small and short. You spend as much time in the menus and 'cut scenes' as you do fighting. Some of the beginning levels are so basic and short that they take less than a minute to finish.
Difficulty was also a bit of a let down. Unlimited mode gets a bit more exciting but the story itself (which you have to finish to get unlimited mode) was extremely easy for me.
While some may like the visual aesthetics I can't help but wonder what this game would have been like with a graphical overall. This is minor as the game did not pretend to be something it wasn't, but I can't help but feel a little frustrated that I built a powerful gaming PC to play 'indie' titles. Again, this is more of a personal complaint though.
Speaking of difficulty and personal complaints, I really disliked the 'hot switching' function in the game. This single handedly made the game insanely easy for me. So much so I just decided not to use it. I understand it's reasoning within the game's story but I just wasn't a huge fan of it.
Lastly, the biggest reason I can't suggest this game, is the price. At nearly $25 (or $22.49 as of right now) it's just not meaty enough. The levels are short. The mechanics are amazing, but simple and not really explored much throughout the game.
However, after typing all of this up and thinking of the experience I had and that fact I've been playing it on and off as a quick fun game on breaks and inbetween work, I have to say I enjoy it quite a bit. Yes, it's kind of shallow in a lot of ways, and it's probably not worth the money for the amount of content it has in it, but I would recommend people at least look into it. So, I'm going to go back to the beginning and change it from a NO to a YES.

While this may look like a fairly standard, if gimmicky, FPS at first glance, you'll find it's actually more of a first-person puzzler: There's always more than one way to complete a level, sure, but there's plenty more ways to fail.
The core of the game is the story mode. From a technical point, the campaign is very well structured – a mix of tutorial and difficulty curve that proves that the developers know what they’re doing, but oh man, that narrative!
It's one of those rare instances of Sci-Fi done well – dark; intelligent; futuristic but rooted in the modern world.  It takes 2-4 hours to complete, depending on your skill level and how solidly you play, but that doesn’t mean it's lacking in any way. People will be discussing this for years.
Once you've completed the main game, there's also a whole bunch of challenges - they're levels lifted directly from the main campaign, but with a tweaked rule set, such as completing the level in the least amount of steps, or having more portalable surfac- Wait. No, I'm reviewing the wrong game here.
Look, i'm not saying SUPER HOT is the new Portal, but I find it very hard to agree with reviews that put it down for being too expensive or not having enough content. The story length and quality are comprable, and even the price isn't too different when you consider the companies involved. The wealth of challenge modes put Portal to shame, and reddit is already pouring over the game for hidden material.
Don't dismiss it just yet, okay?
If you like dark sci-fi, and I mean actually dark, you’ll love the story, and you should get on it before the spoilers come out.
If you like speed-running or ARGs, there's a whole swathe of goodies for you here.
If you like unique games with strong mechanics, and want to see more risks being taken by smaller companies, then you should totally consider paying full price.

Along the playthrough I found myself really touched, but I want to make clear one thing: The Beginner's Guide can be more appreciated by specific people, and it's not about beeing a game developer as someone stated, I mean it's not only for devs, but I can say for sure that it's requested an experience in some sort of creative field -no matter if professional or not- to see the heart of the game.
That said, this is what I found in The Beginner's Guide:
You can be lucky enough to have inspiration, and you'll get curious to what it brings, you'll try to polish it, to use it for first works, and then you'll maybe recieve some approvation, so you'll try to change it, to force it in another direction, but here comes the hard lesson: the more you put inspiration in a cage of rules, expectetions and will to have success, the more that it will fade away, you won't be able to catch it, you will see just its distant ghost in some early works, and then just silence.
