Played several games now and I don't know what to think. It's sure prettier than Chaos Edition (Blood bowl 1, all add-ons), and the client seems more usable. But there is so much in it that just irks me. This product doesn't seem to deserve its price bracket:

It also makes some teams indirectly weaker, with all but one of the current teams being relitively tough, or having easily available tough units, this makes a block/injury focused team less affective.
-Lack of assets, there are only 2 spectator models, ork with drum and human in armour. Stadiums are all identicle until leveled up with small differences that have nothing to do with their starting theme. Players have only one model and sometimes an alterable face (per unit type obviously).
-Poorly thought out UI. For the most part better than BB1 but with a host of new flaws that I'm hoping will be fixed dispite being identified early in testing and still being there now. For instance, team purchasing, in which you ask players to purchase units without allowing them to pick extras. This means that new players will end up spending all their ingame cash on units without getting vital re-rolls, because re-rolls are purchased later.
-Poor single player experience. Yes it is a 2 player board game, but we were promised a decent single player experience. But the "Campaign" mode is a drawn out and frackly dull tutorial, while league mode doesn't even attempt to hide the fact that its just a bot game generated at your teams current point value. Combine this with a bafflingly inconsistant AI, and I can't see why I should play this over Chaos Edition right now.

First, let me totally clear. This game is now nothing like the Flatout Racing games that they sold it as back in 2014. As it stands today, it's a playable mess. The only thing worthwhile I've gotten out of was the Sneak Peek 2.0.
Graphics are solid, but dated despite the new engine and performance is dreadful across the board. The confusion of an arcade destruction racer drunkenly switching to a clean racing sim style game in late development has left the game playing like crap. Gone is the delightful destruction, but the physics are sub-par for a clean racing sim, and the change in collision physics mean you can be t-boned and then pushed around the track for entire laps incapable of escape except by reseting.
And about those big engine changes and the updates to clean racing sim. They're weak excuses at best, and damned lies most likely. Around the time of my first major review, the excuse was major overhauling because people wanted the final game to keep the 24 person races featured in the earliest releases. This developers have adopted a 'take the money and wander off drunkly' approach. They haven't utterly abandoned the game, they were prepared with a shameless cash grab upate announcement for the Steam Summer Sale.
Don't hold out hope and don't make excuses. The game has been in development for four years. In early access for two years. It only took two years to make Flatout 2. I have decided to edit my review to reflect the changes and fixes that have been made to the game.
Before, i did not reccomend the game because of the frequency of gamebreacking bugs and lack of features at Launch. these have since been fixed and the 2 races that were developed before launch but sold seperatly as DLC or preorderbonus have now become part of the main game.
The developers have recently announced that the next 4 races will also be free DLC wich of course is great for people that play the game, i dont think it is neccesary though since DLC that is developed after Launch has the right to cost money.
The Good
+ The graphics update is amazing, a few minor things like race specific cheerleaders are missing but overall its a HUGE upgrade
+ The multiplayer has been Improved significantly, ever since the first few bugs have been swatted i have not disconnected from a single Multiplayer game. there seem to be no Desynchs or Ping issues at all.
+ A few balance changes have been made to the game that are very close to the custom rules developed by the remains of the bloodbowl tabletop community
The Bad
- Sadly there is no more campaign feature for all races. There is still a campaign but that one is only for the Humans and functions primarily as a tutorial.
- The ammount of races and available customisation options for your Players is lower then in the blitz campaign of "Bloodbowl Chaos Edition".
However 2 new races have already been added to the game and 4 more have been anounced as free DLC.
- My last point is a Matter of personal taste, i would have very much enjoyed a few more customization options for your Team.
Unlike the progression for your players, the progression for your Team is rather unintuitive.
Buying more then 4-6 rerolls (depending on your race) and an apothecary is actually detrimental to your team as it inflates your teamvalue and gives an opponent an advantage (through petty cash) that far exedes what having the additional cheerleaders or coach assistants gives you.

I've played Just Cause 2 originally on xbox 360 and put more than 20+ hours into it. Panau is a big beautiful island with lots to see and as Rico AKA The Scorpio as your tour guide. Rico is a mercenary looking for someone on the island and is drafted to help local gangs reign chaos in an attempt to complete his own personal mission.
Just Cause 2 follows somewhat of a GTA game play scheme. Notable differences include driving and the obvious attachment of a hook shot / grapple. This grapple is what makes Just Cause, Just Cause. This thing can literally attach to anything within a certain distance. This includes automobiles, helicopters, buildings, boats, trees, mountains and literally anything you can think of. Upon grappling onto a car, Rico can perform "stunt jumps" in which he is able to maneuver himself on and around the car. This comes handy in case you are being fired at and need some extra cover. When attaching oneself to a helicopter, Rico can chill underneath or just like a car, attempt to hijack it.
There are a few QTE (quick time events) that need to be performed in order to successfully high jack any moving vehicle. You can also grapple enemies if you're really feeling it. Alternatively, Rico can attach his grapple to two objects. Say you want to shoot at an explode-able object but it's not quite close enough to the enemies. Rico can shoot his grapple at the barrel and then attach it nearby or on the enemy. Once the barrel is shot and starts flying, the grapple will pull it towards the enemy. It's an extremely cool feature but with a few flaws. If you're trying to get cars that pass by to run into it, it doesn't really work. For one reason or another the game made it so you cannot simply have people running into the grapple. What you may do though is use it against cars or helicopters. Being chased? Not a problem. Attach to the car then attach to the road or any tree that's nearby and watch them flip.
Driving is sort of it's own unique thing in the game. When the car is flipping over multiple times I like how they did that effect, but I do not like how they made the driving scheme. It seems a little stiff and controls sometimes don't react as you want them to. Shooting is quite basic in the game and auto-targeting seems welcomed.You may zoom in while shooting and even dual wield certain weapons. Weapons can be swapped for different weapons and three slots are available to fill up. Smaller automatics and pistols can swapped out for one another (one slot). Bigger shotguns or automatics can be switched (second slot). The third slot consists of grenades or C4 (both which can be carried at the same time). Shooting is decently fun but can get old. You can crouch and roll to evade fire from enemies but there is no real cover system. It would have been nice if they added something like Gears of Wars has in regards to taking cover. What is notable in this game is that lots can be blown up. Sadly, it's not on a Mercenaries 2 : world in flames sort of demolition (which I think to this date is still the best) but JC2 still has it's moments. There is fun in mindless violence of blowing entire enemy bases up (from radio towers, electrical stations, gas tanks, enemy vehicles and towers).
What you can do damage to is sort of limited. In Mercenaries 2 you could blow up an entire oil rig. In JC2, that oil rig has only certain aspects you can take out. Whether this is good or bad is determined by you. By pressing down on the D-pad you may call up "the sloth demon" aka your personal distributor of weapons, vehicles and extraction if needed. They really gave the player a chance to enjoy a wide variety on their menu but most unlock only after a certain amount of progress has been made (be it collecting crates, completing missions or blowing government equipment up). Anything here also costs a pretty penny!
The game is known for it's beautiful graphics especially demonstrating the beauty of being able to encapsulate the entire island in the background. Even though it's not the next gen sort of graphics, it still provides for an enjoyable sight to see. The display for the weapon meters are excellently done. Even though you may run out of ammo a lot, you'll know exactly how much you have left.  Sounds are varied (explosions are finally sounding different) and comments are made by either Rico, enemies and even civilians. They organized the map in a way that is extremely easy to figure out where you are and where you want to go. They were even kind enough to indicate where potential hidden locations could be.
Overall, a fantastic game. Even with a few minor flaws the gamer is sure to enjoy Just Cause 2.
RATING : 7.9/10

This game is quickly becoming a favorite of mine. It's by no means perfect, but it's very well-crafted and I find myself constantly impressed with its graphics and its level of detail.
Pros:
- It's incredibly immersive. Pop on some headphones, turn off the lights, and it becomes almost impossible to fathom that you
freezing to death in northern Canada.
- Graphics are lovely. Like a moving painting, as many have said. Even on its lower settings it looks pretty nice.
- The devs haven't skimped on detail, like I mentioned above. Your speed depends on whether you're walking into the wind or not, the game gets hazier-looking when you're dangerously low on health, you can see and hear your own breath, etc.
- There's lots of content. Three maps, lots of places to explore, plenty of cabins to loot.
- This game is a great way to eat only candy bars for 30 days and somehow not die of malnutrition.
Cons:
- The wolves. They're infuriatingly unrealistic. I wish there was an option to play in a higher difficulty, but toggle off wolf attacks. The easy difficulty, where the wildlife won't attack you, is too easy to live through, but with anything above that, your face will be ripped off by a wolf every time you turn a corner. I'm glad that this isn't a zombie game, but the wolves may as well be the "zombies."
- Clothes fall apart very quickly. Actually, everything falls apart very quickly.
- I don't see how a single human being can carry 66 pounds worth of firewood and canned peaches and not eventually keel over from exhaustion.
Overall, great game, I really enjoy it. I don't expects it to be without flaws, since it's still in early access, but it does have some issues.

I've known about a Hat in Time for maybe a few months, thinking it looked like a decent platformer, and that I would check it out as I'm a fan of the genre.  The last actual platformer I played (off the top of my head) is Super Mario Galaxy 2.  Going in with little to no expectations, I was given something else entirely than what I expected.  This game grabbed me from the get go, from it's colorful and bright setting/art, to the fluid animations and controls, and dare I say, how god damn adorable it is.  Everything about it, the level design, the platforming, collecting items, the hats, just everything oozes charm, and a passion for this forgotten genre.  And the music is one of the best OSTs I've heard.  The more you play, the more it ramps up in terms of quality.
Of course there are flaws, but the shear quality, thought, and passion put into a Hat in Time completely overshadows those flaws.  It's a little too easy, the geometry of the levels can mess with you a little bit, some bugs.  But I consider these mere nitpicks rather than actual flaws of this otherwise fantastic game.
In short, I love this game.  It completely took me by surpise and blew me away.  I had an absolute blast from start to end, its just pure fun.  I know there is mod support and new chapters/levels coming in the future, but I sincerely hope Gears for Breakfast considers a sequel.  If you are fan of platformers or just like games that are just fun, I cannot recommend this game enough.

Imagine the lights go out, never to return. Bright aurora flare across the sky, and all humanity’s technological might is laid to waste, neutralized in a kind of quiet apocalypse. Everything that has shielded humanity from the disinterested power of Mother Nature is suddenly wrenched from us, dropping us a few links down the food chain. Food and water are scarce. The roads are no longer safe. And winter approaches..
The Long Dark is a survival adventure that challenges single players to try and live for as long as possible in the Canadian highlands following a worldwide extinction event that killed off most other humans. The game will eventually feature an episodic story mode the focuses on a crashed bush pilot, but for now, there is only a sandbox mode and three maps to explore. That may not sound like much, but it is more than enough to keep me entertained for hundreds of hours. The fact that game is in first person really gives it that “What would I do in the same situation?” type of feel that I’ve not experienced in this type of quasi-realistic simulation before. The fact that this is a perma-death type of game also makes the struggle for survival even more intense.
There are no zombies in the game or aliens or monsters – though the magnetic disaster has apparently made the wolves extremely aggressive. It’s really one man or woman against nature. But don’t worry, there are plenty of things out there in the real world to kill you. Your biggest enemy is likely going to be the cold. Weather patterns are randomly generated each game, but the land is always covered with snow. I’ve played where there was a stretch of good weather that lasted for a couple days and I’ve played where blizzards ravaged the landscape. The game takes into account the type of clothing you are able to find and uses that as a sort of armor against the cold temperatures. It also factors in the wind, so if you are decked out in something like fleece, you might be good if it’s calm and cold, but will be in trouble if the gale force winds start blowing.
Going inside a building will get you out of the wind and the cold. There is everything from fishing shacks to forestry service outposts to abandoned cabins and houses to industrial areas like dam control rooms. Finding a nice place to get out of the cold for a while is one of the highlights of the game. Not only can you turn that place into your base of operations, using it to store food and medicine you’ve found, but most places are packed with at least a couple useful items that you can find by carefully searching cupboards, boxes and containers. A few rare buildings have pot-belly stoves in them, allowing you to light a fire to get even warmer, as well as doing necessary things like cooking raw meat and fish or melting snow to create drinking water. Most skills like fire-building, cooking and sewing are skill-based and will increase over time with use – and quite a few failed efforts.
One of the most impressive things about The Long Dark is the number of factors that it takes into consideration. Wind works against you when factoring in temperature, but so does the condition of your clothing or whether or not you’ve managed to get them wet. The game also lets you remedy those negative situations, by for example, using a sewing kit to repair your clothing or finding a nice wind-proof top layer jacket to put on over your wool sweater. You can even catch diseases by doing things like drinking from unclean water or eating raw meat, and you can get hurt by falling over a steep edge at night. Thankfully you also have a full first aid kit, stocked with whatever you can scavenge and a nice interface for treating your various injuries. The developers have stated that they are not trying to make a realistic survival simulation, but The Long Dark comes closer to anything that I’ve played along those lines before.
Graphically, the game looks really good, with stylized cartoon-like graphics. It really reminds me of a Telltale Games title in terms of the art work. The sound is also pretty good, with nice little touches like squeaky floorboards in abandoned cabins and things like wolves barking out a warning when you get too close. Most of what you will hear though is the howling of the wind, which is a deadly reminder of the danger when you are outside, and more than a little comforting once dulled by the walls of your warm, makeshift fortress for the evening.

At €2.99 original price (although I've never seen it go on sale), you get an almost 3 hour game that is creative and easy on the eyes. The story is deep and contains a fair share of twists. Some you see coming, others you don't.
I usually understand confusing stories immediately, but a number of things weren't so obvious to me at first. After watching a 9 minute explanation of the game on youtube, though, I got all the hidden messages. I'm sure I would have picked up on everything if I played through it again, anyway. The story has a number of twists and hidden messages that make it quite deep. It's sad, too, to put it lightly. Some people say they cried at the end. The script was surprisingly powerful in that regard, and the sad parts were caused by something rather intense. Hidden messages and metaphors are found constantly in this game, but it's hard to appreciate them on the first playthrough, giving that all the knots are tied together and everything starts making sense only in the end. Until you reach the last "level", the game is an abstract piece of art with hidden meanings you don't understand and can not truly appreciate, and that is why Stray Cat Crossing is worth at least a second playthrough, even though it does not have any achievements.
I would say that my only complaint with this game is that the last "level" is very repetitive. This is not accidental, and the repetitive aspect is explained and justified well within the story. That said, it doesn't make it any more fun to do the same thing, and read the same dialogue over and over. Something I really liked up until that point was the fluidity of the game, and that I never felt like any part was dragging on until then. Then it dragged on big time.
Anyway, I don't want to end on a bad note, since I really did enjoy this game and I'm glad I forked out the €2.99 for this experience. It's not spectacular, but it's very well worth it.

So. I first bought The Long Dark during the 2014 Christmas Sale way back when because I saw a video from a YouTuber saying it was good and had far, far too much money to waste. (which was all wasted in that very same sale. DAMN YOU GABEN.)
On March 8th, 2015, I finally decided to make my first attempt at playing this game. I had been binging on a number of other games recently and finally decided "Eh, I'll see what this whole thingamabobber is about."
Now, I was essentially going into this thinking "indie survival simulator" and getting terrible flashbacks of all the BAD attempts at the same genre that the indie community (and even the professional community) have made in recent years. Yes, the screenshots looked pretty and stylized, but I wasn't about to judge a game by graphics alone; if I did, then most entries of Call of Duty would suddenly jump above everything else from the very bottom of my list.
I was going into this expecting to laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off at a poor attempt at gameplay and quality and tension in general.
I was so, so, SO wrong.
This game. This. F***ing game. This game is AMAZING.
My first sandbox playthrough lasted about a day and a half, at which point I had run out of resources, was stuck in the middle of a blizzard with no firewood or starters, and was freezing my♥♥♥♥♥off. I decided to go quietly, laid down my bedroll, went to sleep, and never woke up.
In that moment, I felt a part of my soul die with my character.
This is not a game to be laughed at. This is not a game where you play it and look for all the bugs and errors to make fun of. This is a game that, within the first half-hour, will have you so incredibly and undeniably hooked that you care about your character in such a way that the game over screen reads like a gravestone of a close friend.
Three pieces of advice for new players:
First, expect a challenge. Even on the lowest difficulty where the wolves DON'T attack you, this game is punishing for your mistakes. As stated above, my first playthrough lasted about a single in-game day because I failed to account for resources properly. My second playthrough has lasted about five days, but I still don't see myself living past fifteen. This is not a game to mess around with: make EVERY MINUTE COUNT. Otherwise, you won't last very long at all.
Second, expect to be surpised and stunned by the visuals. This is not a game that has ULTRA-REALISTIC 3D where EVERY SNOWFLAKE IS RENDERED AND DRAWN DOWN TO THE ATOMIC LEVEL. No, this is a low-poly, low-res-texture game, even on ultra graphics settings. And yet, despite ALL of that, the style alone makes up for it. During my first playthrough, one of the very first things I did was climb the tallest mountain I could reach. I made it up there at sunset and... well, I just stood there. I broke my very own rule of making the time count, because I was so shocked at how GORGEOUS this game can be. In my second playthrough, with even more time to explore, I have had my mind blown over and over and over again as this game delivers stunning view after stunning view. Despite not having AAA ultra-complex graphics, I can easily say that TLD is more beautiful than any AAA game on the market.
Third, expect to become attached to your character. Seriously, you WILL come to care about your character. And THIS is why I truly love this game so much. In my ENTIRE GAMING CAREER, there are less than five games to EVER make me shed a tear. But when my first playthrough ended and my character passed away in his sleep, I did indeed shed a tear. I shed MANY. This game forges such a strong emotional bond between player and protagonist that I simply can't praise it enough. You have to play it and EXPERIENCE it to understand.
So play it. For the love of every god I can think of and/or name, fictional or otherwise, PLAY THIS GAME. In an industry filled with parody games and vanilla, generic copies of old classics, The Long Dark delivers such an original, strong, and emotional presence that it simply cannot be ignored. So, to Hinterland Studio Inc., I applaud you for creating an experience unlike anything else I have ever had the pleasure to enjoy.
You will not be wasting your time playing a poorly-concieved indie game here; you, as a living being, DESERVE this game. Do not deny yourself this experience. Enjoy The Long Dark in all its frozen glory.
Now, with that said, I'm going to go back inside my fishing hut and eat some more delicious rainbow trout.

Cuphead is a game of the year contender for 2017, hands down. The art design is beautiful and wholly unique to the gaming industry. The soundtrack is wonderfully vintage. The environment is hand painted. When you see how much work went in to crafting Cuphead's aesthetic and feel, you'll see how this game took over 3 years to come out.
Cuphead is also a hard game. Very, very hard. This would be a bad thing if the game wasn't fair, but thankfully it is. When you die in Cuphead, you die. It's not because the game is necessarily cheap, but it's because you may not have timed your jumps right. You were too slow to dodge. Things like that. You become a better player by playing, not be cheesing the game. That's why it's so rewarding to finally clear a fight with one of the brilliantly designed bosses.
If you like platformers, buy Cuphead. If you like the style, buy Cuphead. If you're looking for a great value, buy Cuphead.

It's a fairly simple, straightforwards RPGMaker-esque game at it's heart - balanced, progressive, steady story, that kind of thing.  What makes it stand out, though, is the combat system it utilises.
You gradually are taught Hiragana symbols - 5 or so at a time - and you encounter monsters that look like those symbols.  You 'attack' by choosing the correct phoenetic pronunciation of the targetted symbol, or else your attack misses.  There's something about the environment in which this act of recognition and repetition occurs that actually makes it an effective memory tool!
I'd advise playing through it in a few long sessions, rather than a little bit here and there, to optimise the retention process.  It's a fun way to learn!

So far Blood Bowl 2 is living up to all of my expectations and surpassing more then a few. First a word of warning to those reading reviews there are two bits of misinformation i have seen on this steam page and i want to point that out real quick.
1. Blood bowl 2 does not have fewer races it has the exact same amount has blood bowl 1 so watch out for dishonesty there as they both started with 8.
2. Blood bowl 2 does not have day one dlc the lizardmen and wood elf teams were not finished when the game was (also they are not part of the originial BB2 8 bringing the total to 10 whenever they are added)
Anyways now that thats out of the way here is my take and first the good.
•Graphically this game is a massive improvement it is absolutely gorgeous in comparison to the graphics of the rather aging blood bowl 1.
•The UI though is bar far the biggest improvement and in ever way both the games menu system and the in match ui are simply astounding i think it would not be unfair to call it a 100% improvement over the originial where the UI was the most dodgey aspect of the game.
•The information, this may sound odd but blood bowl one wasn't always that good at telling you what was going on. Blood bowl 2 gives you easy to find data and critical info like the chance to dodge or pass or catch.
•The next big mention is the multiplayer in blood bowl 1 getting into and setting up leagues was a hassle and now it is rather seamless.
•It is also worth mentioning this game performs exceptionally well in fact it strangely enough peforms better then blood bowl 1, i get a more steady framerate from it then i did from its originial at the time. (not to mention you can actually alt tab thank god...)
•Lastly the attention to detail is really good, everything feels visceral from the animations to the quality work of the models and the envrioment.
Now for the Bad.
•There is some missing fluff, the biggest place i have seen this is in the lack of race specific cheerleaders. I would consider this a minor con as to be honest in all my years of playing blood bowl i rarely ever cared about cheerleaders they often aren't worth the investment. So i can understand why the dev team put less of a focus on them given that the playerbase largely ignores them. Its also worth noting you get to have your own stadium which helps to replace that home team feel that the cheerleaders sometimes provided.
•I have also heard there is no visual progression outside mutations for leveling up players though i cannot confirm that yet  and that is about all the bad i have found.
Now the iffy.
•Bretonians instead of Goblins. It's hard to say if this is a good thing or a bad thing. On one hand goblins offered a unique style of play centered around cheating. Currently no team really offers that in the same way (except for the dwarfs but that is a stretch). The other side of the coin is the fact that goblins are not a competitive team but a "fun" team where as Bretonians are clearly a competitive team.
•So im tossing this one up to opinion, if you wanted more competitive teams in the initial roster then goods news for you! If you were hoping for more "slapstick" teams in the roster then i am sad to say you will have to wait for anything beyond dwarves.

UnnyWorld is a new competitive MOBA game with a twist.
It's tough to be a third party games publisher these days but the developers of UnnyWorld decided to give a interesting twist to the MOBA genre.
UnnyWorld adds a unique touch to a world full of established ideas, and it's a fun new take on the MOBA genre with cute 3D visuals. They really could do no wrong.
In the game you build a base on your own planet with various crystals. It has cute, colorful characters that everyone will fall in love with.
UnnyWorld tries to seperate itself from the pack with interesting features. There are lots of fun upgrades and things to buy through the game's easy to use purchasing system, but players will find that they can easily progress in the game without spending any money at all.
The main mode of play is Bang Bang Party, a quick 3v3 deathmatch with two lanes that have a tower each before the core structure that must be destroyed to win.
The graphics are adorable, especially if you love cute cartoons. But don't that mistake you UnnyWorld is very competitive and all for the E-Sports community.
You can max out all graphics settings and run at maximum resolution without too much worry. Not only that but it's also for iOS and Android so there's always friends to make and play with.
The game is actively developed and growing FAST so there's always fun new features to look forward to. Honestly it's my new favorite game and i'll be playing it non-stop. Also I'm making a guild if anyone wants to join send me a friend request. Look forward to seeing you all in UnnyWorld!

There's no challenge to it.
I played the original Dungeon Defenders a while back, and I'll admit I don't remember much about it aside from
1) The number of hackers I had to contend with.
2) The challenge of the maps and how freakin' impossible it could sometime get.
and 3) how much fun I had all while getting rofl-stomped by hordes and hordes of minions.
I bought this game mostly because it was free to play, and because it had the Dungeon Defenders name on it. What I got was a watered-down, no-effort sequel that sucks all the fun out.
Basically, this tower defense game is completely brainless. The sprawling maps have been greatly reduced in size, meaning it's easy to address any lane at any time so you'll never worry about leaving one uncovered.
The heroes are all overpowered, the STANDARD heroes, never mind the premium ones, to the point where the towers themselves become little more than roadblocks to hold off the hordes until you get there and smash through them.
The towers are overpowered, to the point where I can sit on my hands and occassionaly jump in to combat to stop my AFK timer from running out.
The bosses are a complete joke, lasting about 15 seconds if they're lucky, which they're often not.
Top-tier chests were all I got at the end of games, to the point where I was GLAD to see worse loot, just to break up the monotony.
Trendy seems to have gotten it in their heads that handing players victories and rare loot on a silver platter makes them happy. Not when the victory was earned by me staying still and OCCASIONALLY tending to my towers. Not when the rare loot is constant. Not when the bosses die without so much as threatening the center. There's no challenge at all. I'm told there's a challenge later, but if you'll not my time up top, I shouldn't have to sink 16 hours into a game before it becomes challenging. In all those 16 hours and several dozen games played, if not more, only once did I lose, and only because the game I was on was on a timer. And some jerkwad kept taking his sweet time to ready up. I played the challenge again immediately thereafter, and it was a wash for the bad guys, just like the rest.
My recommendation? Go play Orcs Must Die: Unchained. It's another F2P tower defense game that's challenging. Plus, it has a greater variety of towers, heroes, gear and maps, actual strategy is required, and when you get enough loot to upgrade your stuff, you'll feel like you've earned it, regardless if you spend money in it or not.

UnnyWorld is an independently developed MOBA by Unnyhog. The game gimmick is instead of casting spells with the keyboard, you need to draw special shapes with your mouse.
There's not really any story to report on: when you make your account you get a tutorial mission with some character known as "Evee" whom you see once, and I haven't seen again since.
There might be more coming with the story as the game matures, but so far... nada.
As said in the Quick Review, the gameplay gimmick is that you draw special shapes instead of pressing number keys to cast spells. You do still move with good 'ol WASD though.
There are several maps and game modes mainly the mode is a 3v3 5-10 minute control point match, however there is a type of payload hybrid map too. As per usual with MOBA's, it seems like there aren't nearly enough maps to keep me interested.
Something I did really like about UnnyWorld and would love to see them expand upon, is some Tower Defense themes. You get your own planet which you can construct creep houses, turrets and defenses. Unfortunately other then invading random people's plannets this idea has fallen between the cracks.
UnnyWorld is Free to play, so you can download and play it yourself. Unfortunately I have my suspicions that there's a bit of Pay-to-win going on in the background...
...At earlier levels of the game you're quite capable of holding your own against other players. If you're curious about how that is done, do watch the unscripted thoughts video where I try to cover all points of the game at this time.
As it stands... UnnyWorld has potential, but really needs a lot of refinement and work. Clearly the developers have passion for their game, and I hope they succeed with it, just be-careful of the tightrope line you must walk in the Free to Play market.

I highly recommend Blood Bowl 2.  My experience is based on the beta and will be updated after a bit more time with the launch version. I also have a ridiculous # of hours logged with the previous game.  While I'm no expert on the game, here are some changes I've noticed in comparison to BB1:
- Gold in your treasury adds to the TV once you have more than 150K.  Initially I didn't like this, however now I find myself much more willing to purchase inducements that exceed petty-cash values in matches, and this truly adds to the gameplay.  More importantly, I am no longer afraid to fill out a team roster with reserves. I think this was a great decision from the developer.
- Team management is more robust. You have an upgradeable home-stadium. Player transfers / market is a feature (was not live during beta). All in all, teams feel like they have more of a life and identity.
- Chances on action success are shown in a % tooltip. This will help players that don't initially understand the dice system (hey, I'm sure they exist). But moreover, it just helps with making quick choices in context.
- The league system / interface appears to be better designed.
- The standard grid overlay (which you could toggle on and off in the last game) is gone. In its place, there is a contextual grid on each player you select. It's not distracting and functions perfectly well. You now see a numeric indication of stacked tackle zones on any given tile.
- Animation and gameplay feels more life-like / brutal, and fun!
- The controls will feel strange at first. There is an option to toggle BB1 controls, and the BB1 camera (I recommend). Though the BB2 controls may work just fine for some, and the BB2 camera is actually enjoyable once you're comfortable with strategy.
- You're no longer tied to your opponent's cutscenes. For those that remember from the first game, an angry player would remain idle at keyboard while you were spamming 'Esc.'.  This is handled much better.
- The dice / roll log was limited. You see current roll results at the bottom of the interface. Hopefully a full log will be visible in the future.
- The visible armor changes that occurred when a player leveled up, seem to have been cut. I thought it was a neat feature of the first game. (Not to be mistaken with mutations, which are visible after acquired).

BioShock is gaming as high-art. The graphics are excellent. The environment and characters are compelling. The music and sound effects are interesting and immersive. The gameplay is that of a top-shelf first-person shooter with role-playing elements skillfully blended in. As with any sufficiently meritorious work of art, no review, no matter how articulate the language, can adequately convey just what this game is. The only way to do BioShock the justice that it so sorely deserves is to experience it for oneself first-hand. This is not hyperbole. Even if you don't particularly appreciate FPS or RPG games at the genre level, you simply have to play THIS one as its value is much, MUCH greater than that of the sum of its parts. I've attempted numerous times to identify another game that can go toe-to-toe with BioShock in terms of sheer artistic merit and respective success in fully realizing an original, visionary game world. I've come up empty-handed every time. Consider that this game was released about 6 years ago (as of the time of this writing). That's an awfully large window for a worthy, comparable contender to emerge.
BioShock is what some might refer to as a "masterwork" or maybe even a "magnum opus". If it were a painting, it might be the Sistine Chapel. If it were a movie, it might be Citizen Kane. Sometimes during development, once in a great while, the various components of a game end up coming together in such a way that something very special is produced... Something that exceeds possibly even the creator's expectations. This game is one such instance. In the near future, there will come a time when video games in general are afforded the respect which they deserve. Perhaps by then BioShock will be recognized for what it is: A significant achievement in the field of human artistic expression (and most definitely NOT merely an entertaining distraction to be consumed and discarded).

I have been a strategy game player all my life, I and can honesly say this is one of the worst. Sure there are great graphics and the cutscenes that glorify you, the commander, with well known science fiction actresses playing the rolls are certain to make you feel like a conquering hero. But beyond that the gameplay is nearly unplayable unless you are an expert. I was playing on normal up until act 5 when I just got way to tired of having to restart. Because once you make a mistake, there is no recovering.
The tiberium crystal economy is always too slow to keep up your war machine with the constant enemy advances. And the worst part of it is that you are basically on a timer. Because once you are out of the initial crystal piles, there is no way to keep up production because the crystal piles grow out of the ground at a slugs pace.
On top of that, there seems to be no way to build up defences to use a 'turtle up' strategy, even while you are trying to build up your initial forces. And because of that, enemies are constantly getting inside of your base and wreaking havok on your very weak structures that cost more than an arm and a leg.
On top of that, there seems no other way to win than to build up a massive force and then sweep the map. Because there is no real use for scouting and no long range siege abilities except on the absolute most expensive units, when it would be a much better idea just to build up a lot of mammoth tanks. You can forget about skirmishing as the enemy will always either have a large number of base defenses that will wipe out any small force or their troops will be in constant production coming out of their buildings so you wind up doing no real damage and lose everything.
I do not recommend this game to anybody, even if you are already bord of all your other games. Stick with the good old Age of Empires or Starcraft series for a much more enjoyable experience.

I have enjoyed the Tales franchise for years since I first started with Tales of Symphonia. Sadly, this game is a Tales game in name only. It is too much of a departure from what makes the series great that I just cannot recommend it to anyone who enjoys the Tales franchise.
The story is way too simple and is unable to evoke motivation on a grand scale as the previous games have done. There are no real earth-shattering surprises in this story that turn it on its head, either. The villain is also completely cliche and boring. Further still, the game itself does a poor job of portraying a sense of scale on the level of previous games. You explore a part of a continent instead of exploring a world - and the inclusion of teleporting instantly between save points only makes the world seem smaller.
Add the inclusion of extremely complex and completely unnecessary mechanics to buff combat performance and you're left with a game that really doesn't know what it wants to be. On the one hand, you have a major simplification on the story and the world, but a major complexification of the combat and item mechanics.
And, to top it all off, you will need to mod the game to get it to run past 30 FPS, which also adds a bunch of physics and other graphical bugs. There is no way that I, in good conscience, can recommend this game.

When I heard a lot of criticism about this game, I went into with caution that I might not like it. I was pleasantly surprised to find that I don't really agree with a lot of people's criticism. I thought it was one of the better Tales games, especially recently. However, I do have some thoughts of my own, and I'll break it down into pros and cons.
Pros:
- This Tales game's story is a lot less convoluted than previous ones. Tales games have that reputation of having overly complex stories that can be difficult to follow, but complex doesn't inherently mean "good." Of course, people want depth and layers to a story, but some Tales games were taken to ridiculous levels of complexity. I'm glad that they toned it down a bit and made this story simpler. There is little room to be confused about anything in this game.
- I love the introduction of armitization. There are some who don't like it, and I really don't understand why. I thought it was a unique, interesting addition to the gameplay. Armitization is when Sorey or Rose (the human characters) "fuse" with one of the seraph (elemental beings of fire, water, earth, & wind) to combine power/strength/HP and more. It was really handy in boss battles in particular. Additionally, it was quite stylish and fun.
- I like that the traditional elemental beings in the Tales games were actually turned into characters and not just beings to be summoned when needed in this game. In previous Tales games, these beings were known as Sylph (Wind), Undine (Water), Efreet (Fire), and Gnome (Earth). They were merely summoned in battle momentarily, then would disappear for the actual story plot. In Zestiria, these elemental beings are called seraphim ("seraph" for singular), and they're actually people. There are hundreds of them (NPCs) and 5 of the main characters of the story choose to be in Sorey's (the MC) party. Sorey's best friend Mikleo is a water seraph, for example. I thought this development made things a lot more interesting rather than having a party completely of humans.
- Traveling is made simple. In previous Tales games, usually there was a flying animal or ship or whatever that would take the party around the world. Sometimes, this could be annoying. I remember specifically being frustrated in trying to find a specific spot on the map needed to find a certain place in previous games. In Zestiria, traveling is done through save points. The simplification of it comes at a price though -- gald to be exact. Not a big deal though if the player fights enough enemies. Gald isn't that difficult to come by.
- (Some) Villains are humanized. What I mean by that is, the villains are actually developed and not just some disconnected concept character. The player gets to find out why the main villain is being evil. The player gets to find out why the main villain's sidekicks are doing his biding. They have/had hopes and dreams just like any other people.
- The epilogue "Alisha's Story" was enjoyable. I do find playable epilogues to be fun though, so I guess this might be more subjective. Alisha was absent for a lot of the game, so finally being able to see her having more significance in the story was nice.
- This
is a treasure.
Cons:
- Dezel wasn't developed enough, and so
I still thought that the scene was good and
. I just feel like the player should've gotten to know him a bit better. His flashbacks were kind of vague as well.
- The epilogue "Alisha's Story" shouldn't have been DLC. It should've been a mandatory part of the game, because without it, the player has no idea what happened at the end of the main story.
- Heldalf's (the main villain) "everyone is suffering and so am I, so I should just kill everyone" motive is way overdone and not particularly interesting.
- Katz Korner was lackluster. There wasn't much to do there other than shop and fight an optional boss. I mean, if I go through all the trouble of getting Katz Korner to appear and be accessible, it should be more worthwhile.
- Just like with a lot of Japanese games (and anime), there is a blatantly obvious lack of dark-skinned characters. I don't think I even saw one. Not even a NPC.
- I really hate that some enemies can just phase through the player and disappear to surprise attack a moment later. Annoying.
I'm probably forgetting stuff, but I feel this got most of my feelings across. Overall, I really enjoyed this Tales game. It wasn't a disappointment like I thought it would be. I definitely recommend it to JRPG fans.

This particular cat is a little on the fence, as far as this game goes. On one hand, it's rather lovingly and competently scored and animated, with its own crazy little "Alice in Wonderland" style - as cliche as that is. The downside, speaking of which, would have to be the cliches. The story takes the path traveled over and over again.
It features essentially a very simple, even mundane, story, and simply slops buckets of symbolism (and a fair amount of distracting nonsense) over it until it's sufficiently thickly coated to obscure the rather shallow real plot beneath all the whimsy. No one is really a "character" in this game. Even down to the protagonist, every individual is more of an archetype filling a pseudo-horror-game storytelling cliche slot, rather than a true personality.
The puzzles are maybe a little too easy, aside from one that's simply obtuse and another that's frustratingly repetitive. Yet, for all these complaints, I can't say I didn't enjoy making my way through the game, or that I wasn't impressed by its presentational flair - even if the tiny animated sequences, a real highlight of the early game, just peter out after a while. Tales of Zestiria is as middle the road you can get with a modern jRPG, which is probably the game’s major malfunction by the end of it. Mediocrity. In this day and age where giving a game a 7/10 score makes it bargain bin material where does Zestiria fit in?
- The narrative is as basic as it gets, an energetic and sheltered country bumpkin is suddenly confronted with an ancient evil where he learns he’s the chosen one to bring light to the darkness. Expecting something grandiose? Tough luck, you’re not going to get it. In all seriousness, a generic story doesn’t bother me much as long as the game built around it is good. In the end what separates video games from other media is that it’s interactive with many different facets to enjoy, it’s just a shame that Zestiria didn’t bother to innovate much on generic fantasy tropes when there are plenty of games -- even jRPGs -- that do.
- Characters are a mixed bag, there are some that I genuinely like while there are others that feel a bit inconsistent or even underdeveloped. I think a prime example that a lot of people like to point to is Alisha, who is arguably the poster-girl of this game yet she’s not even active through half of it. Without any spoilers, the gist of it is that a portion of the characters are either one-dimensional and/or riddled with tropes. This is honestly the most painful detriment to this game considering how the journey for most RPGs is dictated by character arcs and character interactions. While Zestiria excels at having believable character interactions there are a couple of characters that really needed fleshing out.

- The skits are good, not really much to say. They keep you entertained and are generally very cozy. I feel like a good majority of the writing budget went into the character skits rather than the actual characters themselves. While it helps make the characters more likeable the skits don't really make up for the lack of character depth. Overall the largest positive this game has going for it.
- I
prefer turn-based gameplay more than the ARPG hybrid most modern jRPGs are shooting for. Zestiria can definitely be satisfying to play, but it’s not perfect. Things that really hamper my enjoyment of the combat system would include:
- Don’t even get me started on equipment fusing. Sure, it increases the longevity and replayability of the game, but it’s too dependant on RNG and grinding to be feasibly useful outside of NG+. The whole skill chart system makes getting loot a pain in the butt, you’ll get some really cool looking end-game gear but later you realize the stats don’t coincide with your build. Throughout the entire game I stuck with the same sword for 40+ hours simply because the bonus stats I got from it were too useful to ditch. This really hinders the ecstasy you get from acquiring new loot in RPGs.
- Port quality is garbage, it feels like I'm emulating the game rather than playing a proper PC game. Most of the issues disappear with the community fan-patch, however some of the cutscene physics can glitch out. Either way, simply because there's a patch that makes Zestiria playable doesn't mean I should give the devs a pass on this one.
- English voice acting is extremely meh, stick to the original Japanese dub if you don't mind playing the game in a foreign language.
- Too much localization, this is mostly an issue during the less serious moments of the game where the localization team thinks they have free reign to "westernize" some jokes. Immersion breaking pop culture humour isn't funny, stop it.
Zestiria is OK and will entertain you if you have the time to invest into it. The main crux is that there are a lot of better games and/or better jRPGs to play than Tales of Zestiria. If you're playing Zestiria to get into Berseria in the future then I think it's a fine investment, if not then your money is better spent elsewhere, if you're already a Tales fan... then I can only assume you already own this game.

Very enjoyable game if you're looking for a blend of WW2 FPS with some realism. I definately recommend this to anyone fans of FPS's. However, personally there are a bunch of things I dislike about this game compared to the original, which was the main reason I bought this one. Here's my list of opinions that I personally dislike about the game:
1. The weapons upgrades can be interesting and I've had fun unlocking them, however are totally unrealistic. It seems soldiers bring their own personal weapons to the battlefield rather than using standard issue service weapons.
Some guns though that I expect to have an interesting upgrade such as the flamethrower or p38 pistol, actually have no or boring upgrades.
2. Iconic german weapons not in the game; being the p08 luger and the mg42. Why aren't they in this? The p08 was the standard german side arm, while the p38 was meant to eventually phase them out, usually only being possessed by officers, and the Mg42 is probably one of the most notorious machine guns of all time.
3. Bayonet is always on the gun if selected, which you also have to unlock? I'm sure that all riflemen were issued bayonets for their rifles, why couldn't they have kept the bayonet system from the first Red orchestra?
4. Grenades are underpowered. Completely useless for clearing rooms unless they land on top of the enemy.
5. Weird quiet sound effects, grenades being an example.
6. Magical medikit that heals all, causing bullets to pop out of their entry wound. IMO any wounds taken should remain until the player dies, but can be treated by the soldiers field medikit for injuries in non vital areas, with impaired aiming ability or lowered stamina after. A medic class should be implemented to heal vital area wounds and be the only ones to significantly heal players.
7. Lack of vehicle variety. I've gotten pretty sick of driving the T-34 and Panzer IV over and over. I remember the developers saying something about introducing half-tracks and different tank models. Seems that is never going to happen. The new tank immersion system would have been great in a Tiger tank, or an IS-2.
8. Small maps: Probably part reason to why there is a lack of vehicles. Compared to RO1 these maps are tiny.
9. Ping issues. Always had this problem with this game. Local servers are usually between 80-200. Sometimes jumping up and down frantically. It seems other people have this problem too.

GREAT GAME, ABYSMAL COLLISION DETECTION.
(You die when you shouldn't, enemies don't die when they should, and the environment has invisible extensions)
Firstly, let me say that SuperHot is actually a really good game. It’s unique, it’s innovative, and it’s damn good fun. The developers have a wonderful game idea here and they deserve our support for their work and for their achievement. I’m very happy to have supported SuperHot during its beta phase, and I’ve already put in 11 hours of game time and with the possibility to invest many more hours into this brilliant twist on the first person shooter genre (depending on the devs course of action).
So, after all that praise, why am I not giving it a thumbs up? Simple: the game has some glaring faults that seriously interfere with enjoyment of the game, the worst of which is the collision detection. Let me explain...
Carefully lining up a shot so the bullet passes in between two shelved pieces of glassware thus hitting the red man behind them, the game instead decides to make the bullet collide with one of the glasses which then acts as a shield for the enemy. Said enemy then goes on to kill me because of the inaccuracy of my “missed shot”.
Conclusion: bad collision detection.
A thrown katana races elegantly towards the centre mass of a red man. Just as it's about to connect I feel pleased and confident with my well-aimed throw. The elated feeling, however, quickly turns to horror as I watch the sword touch the surface of my adversary and pass completely through the chest cavity with no effect whatsoever. I'm then unarmed and left at the mercy of a man wielding a rapidly-firing assault rifle.
Conclusion: appauling collision detection.
An enemy has fired a bullet at my head and I move out of the path of the bullet far enough for it to sail straight past me. Once I’ve reached a safe distance from the trajectory of the incoming bullet I stop moving to slow down time to its minimum value so I can plan my counter attack strategy. While I’m standing there weighing up all of my options, the bullet gracefully glides through the air over towards the far left hand side of my screen. As the bullet is just about to pass me I’ve made my decision for my counter offensive, and I’m about to put that plan into action when BAM - the stray bullet magically manages to hit my head despite me being nowhere near it. I then lose my 100 kill streak in endless mode and start muttering curse words under my breath.
Conclusion: really poor collision detection.
Sadly, these aren’t random occurances, as they’ve happened to me many times during my 11 hours. It’s because of this sort of nonsense that I don’t play Battlefield 3 or 4 anymore. SuperHot's main fault is that it seems to treat your character as a human-sized cardboard box. An issue which needs fixing if people are to continue playing the game - and there are a lot of us with this grievance.
Very quickly, other collision issues include: bullets hitting walls even though the gun and the crosshairs are well away from them, and thrown weapons inexplicably exploding in mid air in front of you despite there being plenty of clearance for a successful weapon throw.
Another problem with which SuperHot suffers is a very short campaign. The game boasts having over 30 levels. The trouble is that most of these can be completed in about one minute - even on your first attempt. So a 30 level story mode took me just over an hour to complete leaving me sat there thinking, “Was that it?”
To make matters worse, these short levels are then punctuated with annoying story sequences that interfere with the flow of the levels and the action. However, it is worth noting that the vast majority of the enjoyable gameplay is to be found in the endless mode and the challenges - and these are genuinely fun. Manipulating the accelerating or deceleration of time by varying the velocity of your motion is a great bullet-time mechanic that allows you to overcome the odds despite your being outmanned and outgunned, and I have genuinely enjoyed the bug-free moments.
Pros:
- A really fun first person shooter with a unique mechanic that brings good puzzle work and strategy to the genre
- A lovely art style that dazzles the senses without ever cluttering up the screen
- Very nice sound effects that really immerse you in a world where bullet-time rules
- Watching red glass men crack, crumble, fall apart, and then disintegrate in front of you at what ever speed you choose is wonderfully entertaining
What we need from the devs:
- More levels
- A level editor so that the community can create and share its own maps and campaigns
- More variety in enemies and weapons to increase the game's longevity
- Greatly improved collision detection
I will be giving this review a thumbs up when and if the developers fix the game’s problems.
As always, leave your questions below and I’ll get back to you.
Until then, I’ll see you in the matrix...

Other than that if you know nothing about Hiragana coming in then this will teach all the basics you need to know. The encounter rate is fairly high, of which it needs to be, and should give you enough encounters per area to memorize each set of characters. Once you reach a certain point of the game some of the characters that are introduced will stop appearing in favor of newer ones. Use the wrong translation and no damage will be dealt. Fighitng every battle will let you breeze through the game so long as you also did the sidequests.
When each of the lessons are presented the stroke orders of each of the characters will be, as well as sounded out, drawn out and then further allowing you to hear, and see, the sound and stroke order as many times as it takes. Some of the lessons will even give you some introductory grammer lessons in how they are used as is the case with や, つ, ゆ, and よ as well as a few others.
As with any learning endeavor, the journey does not end here just because you beat the game.
Final rating is 5/5

My biggest complaints with the game are in the features the game is missing as opposed to Chaos Edition. For example, there is no real-time mode, there is no World Cup mode or tournament mode. It really focuses on the League mode between players. Essentially, if you have no friends or don't like playing competitively, there isn't much for you to do. It would also be nice if there were more animations overall.

Pros:
- Mixes RPG and Tower Defense together which diversifies and gives the game a unique playstyle.
- Unlock 4 classes for free.
- 2 playstyles which you can build each class the way you want. (i.e. building or fighting which the game will explain).
- You can switch classes based on how they are built. (i.e. At the end of a wave switch to a class that you have specialized to be a builder, then switch to a class you've built to be a fighter after you're done building.
- The stat points and the equipment also support the way you want to specialize your classe in.
- Simultaneously gain experience and levels for all the other heroes when only using one, this helps for grinding.
- Afraid that you're alone or it's too difficult? Worry not, you can play multiplayer or go off to be a lone wolf.
- Has an auto collect system where it does the equipment collecting for you.
- You get 4 bags which hold equipment.
- Dying doesn't punish besides respawn timer.
- Challenging for those who want it.
- You can play with friends.
Cons:
- VERY grindy
- Requires you to use your brain as does every TD game
- Not very F2P as grinding and playing a lot will only be the way to advance
- Time consuming
- Only 4 main classes are available as free, (Squire, Monk, Huntress, and Apprentice) the others you must grind a lot for or buy with gems.
- A LOT of things require gems such as costumes or skins for your characters and getting pets.
- NO guilds or clubs for people looking to socialize and work with others.
- Gets quite boring after grinding for many hours.
TLDR; Don't play if you don't have a lot of free time and don't expect the game to be full F2P as it requires gems for a lot of things, otherwise the game is unique, thrilling, and challenging.

Blood Bowl 2... oh man, what a game it is and a wonderful one at that too!
So what is it?
Well it is the digital version of the Table Top game called Blood Bowl of American football set in a Warhammer fantasy setting where murder is appriciated.
It is a very complex game so it can be a bit daunting at first glance but it is a hell'a'lot of fun and the UI and tooltips are clean and clear as to what each thing does even if it takes a bit of time to fully understand everything.
Think of it as a strategy game where your opponent's most lethal weapon is you screwing things up - it is a risk management system relying on RNG to do most things; yes, just walking a bit too far (doing a so called 'Go for it' - going additional squares outside of one's own movement range) requires of you to roll a dice to see if your character dies or not and this is how you play the game for the most part - reduce risk as much as you can and prepare for worst case scenarios.
Going onto the buisness model:
Alot of people aren't going to like it but here's what has been done, Cyanide puts the standard game out for a set price and you get 8 races with that. After that instead of doing what they have done in the past to re-release the game again for the same price, they will sell the different races as DLC so you can handpick exactly the ones that you want (don't worry - as a new player you get all the races you need from the start to play a ball game, a punching game or a pretty standard well balanced team that can pack a bit of a punch and pass around the ball at the same time; YOU DO NOT NEED ANY ADDITIONAL RACES TO ENJOY THE GAME this is for when one is more experienced and wishes to dedicate more time and money to the game) for a reasonable price.
Can I recommend the game? The game seems to be without any glaring bugs that made it darn difficult to enjoy Blood Bowl 1 Chaos and Legendary Edition, the UI is clear as a blue sunny day, the gameplay inputs feels responsive and direct (no excessive amount of clicking necessary as this games uses a mouse and keyboard in other words), excellent models and amazing graphics...
I will say this much: this is a good time to be a Blood Bowl fan or someone who's interested in Blood Bowl as I can full heartedly say that this is an EXCELLENT digital version of Blood Bowl! If you like management games but just wished you could punch that annoying fellah' who makes it more annoying... welcome to Blood Bowl where the ball is a secondary objective (still required to score to win tho') and punching people to death is a fun and viable tactic!
Get the game! xD

Very challenging, makes you seriously think before every action and prioritize everything. You need to make a fire, you have to melt some snow and purify it because you are dying of thirst, but you also need to cook the raw venison because you are starving but you only have one single piece of reclaimed wood and a wolf is outside your door and you are wounded and have no ammo left and are borderline hypothermic and then suddenly you fail at building a fire, you search your surroundings to scavenge something to burn but fail so you go back outside to try to make a run for it from the wolf to another cabin but oops, you die. This is normal and almost everytime you play.
Graphics: Beautiful and not too demanding on lower end computers like mine. I have a GEFORCE 750 ti and 60fps consistent no matter what is going on with high settings. The world and objects are sort of like Borderlands, not as cell shaded, but sort of like that in appearance, I don't know the name for such artistic styles in gaming.
Combat: you can't just swing a weapon or fist like a typical FPS, everything is delibrate. Use a torch to frighten off a wolf or light a room, throw a flare, use iron sights on a rifle, but you are not going to weild a hatchet like Skyrim here.
Crafting: little hard to grasp with a steep learning curve at first, but easy to grasp. You can scavenge anywhere at any time for things like wood or tinder, and at any fire you can melt snow, purify and cook food. You can fish and make traps for things like rabbits.
Simulation: It does a very good job at creating the desperation and fear of finding food, warmth and shelter you would expect in the Canadian winter wilderness, but much like any game it is slightly unrealistic, like the fact that you can technically go without solid foods for days, and that hypothermia would set in within minutes and you would most certainly die without immediately being dried and placed in warm dry shelter after falling in icy water, or the fact that technically you don't need to purify the melted snow since it is perfectly safe to go outside and eat all the snow you want as long as it is not yellow snow lol. But hey, its just a game.

My first Long Dark Experience:
I played through this sandbox mode a few different times on hard. I wasn't too used to it yet and kept losing at life early in the game, so I decided to try the easiest mode where I figured I could survive for longer than 24 hours to get a real understanding of the game. Just after spawning I stumbled upon a Logging Campsite where I found a few essential items like pop and canned food, as well as newspapers and firewood. After warming up and resting for a while I left with every intention of finding high ground to see if I could see any other man made structures I could venture off to. High ground was reached where I saw something that looked like a cabin sitting on the top of a mountain in the distance. I made it over there in just ten minutes or so of running, It was a lot closer than It looked. At the base of the hill the cabin was sitting on, I sprained my ankle so I was slightly immobilized and had to walk rather than sprint to the top. At this time I thought freezing to death would be a problem. Luckily for me, it wasn't. I made it to the top where I found a hunting rifle with 5 rounds, plus some more essentials like food, and firewood. I rested until 7:30 the next morning. My ankle felt better so I ran down the mountain, shot a deer and a wolf. I skinned, gutted, and then I took the meat. I made a small fire, accidentaly burned myself, and then ate. At this point I ran further and found some train tracks. I followed them and found a frozen lake with little fishing shacks on it and a cabin on the shoreline. I went inside the closest building which was the cabin, where I started a fire, crafted a snare, line, hook, and a few more items at the workbench. Then I went upstairs, where I searched a dead body and found a candy bar, started a fire, and went to bed. I died in my sleep of dysentery... That burn I recieved when I made the fire became infected because It wasn't properly treated. All I had in my medical kit was a bandage, which was useful but I also needed antibiotics. Of course I did not have any... Little did I know I had Inflammation of my Intestines accompanied by bloody diarrhea. What a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ way to die... Over all, the gameplay is excellent. I like the non-realistic look to the game and everything you have to accomplish to survive. Only complaint, is that it doesn't have multiplayer.
11/10 Would get dysentery again.

, rated for what it is in the first place, would be a 6/10 game to me.
But after optimizing the game via community mods/patches, this bad PC port plays like a charm and is definitely a great and interesting experience for any RPG fan, or those who want to become one.
+ Graphics and visuals are pretty
+ Character design is beautiful and unique
+ Storyline is interesting
+ Cutscenes, story dialogues etc. are simply amazing, have great humor and have unexpectedly logical responses
+ Many features and mechanics (Transformations similar to "Bankai" from Bleach, party AI strategy settings, automatic crafting...)
+ Equipment can be upgraded and by that enchanted with special effects
+ Dynamic combat system (not as fast paced like in a hack and slash game, but it's at least not another turn based RPG!)
+ Challenging boss battles & difficulties
+ Most of the normal battles can be avoided (not forcing you to fight)
+ Costumes / little character customization (some unlockable without DLC)
+ English / Japanese character audio by choice at every startup, but subtitles are english only
+ Side Quests
+ Controller support
~ You are not required to grind to play through the story, but in order to unlock all achievements or to play on higher difficulties, really good equipment is needed (and you can only grind for that)
~
, but quickly becomes repetitive (
)
~ The best looking costumes can only be acquired through DLC (and those are a little overpriced imo)
~ Has the classic "come back later to open this treasure chest with the right key" feature - personally not a fan of it
~ Equipped weapons/armors don't change character visuals. Most RPGs don't do that, so this is OK, but would have been nice in this case, since you actually have some customization options for the characters.
- The PC port is really bad and probably unplayable for some people, without using mods/patches.
- The "Fusion" system is badly implemented and requires you to farm a lot of money and weapons for achievements. Luckily it is not required for story-only playthroughs.
- Camera in battles is sometimes really bad because of obstacles or the battle area limit.
- You walk around a lot, even once you've unlocked fast travel, it's still a lot of walking (big areas)
- Gameplay mechanics are somewhat hard to grasp for starters and seem overwhelming at the beginning
- Keyboard+Mouse controls are wonky and annoying in some situations
- The community fixed bugs better than the developer, which is very dissapointing

Banished is possibly the most challenging city sim. That i have ever played. The game is extremely punishing to those who go in there thinking "Oh it's just like Sim City" lol. No, it isn't. This game is very detailed in almost every aspect to how your town is from the overall health of your citizens, happiness, and, how many jobs are there avaiable as well as citizens.
I mean seriously this game has a graph to keep track of progress of every little thing from resources, to population, to supplies. This game is very well informative. Plus the tutorials are also a big help. The developers really put a lot of hard work into the game. Just make sure you keep your citizens happy and use critical thinking skills in applying to the needs of your citizens and you should be fine :)
Plus this game has a modding community behind it. To make the game better or slightly easier for newcomers to the game.
The only downside to this game is the overall "disasters" In this game it's either natural (tornadoes, fires) or medicial (diseases, and such). With that being said, The game doesn't have any bandits, wolf attacks, or neighboring towns for you to take over. Lol, yes i know what your thinking "But um this is a building city simulation. Not some sort of RTS conquest" and yes i get that. However the disasters happen rarely. Sometimes not at all. This game is a great time killer. But that is actually the problem. Lol, i want to be more active with my village. Maybe trade it with other villages that I have created, or defending my town from bandits and wolves, or take over other towns that are randomly generated on the map. Perphaps share the world space with a friend who has the game as well?
If the developers are going to make a second Banished game. I sincerely hope they add more "disasters" in the game. It's a great start, plus the game overall should keep you busy. Not everyone will like this game because of these elements or lack of certain elements. But hey who knows maybe a modder will make something like this in the near future? So don't get your hopes up
All and all. If you like delicate city building simulations. This game is for you.

Overall, with the time I spent, I feel I got my money's worth out of it, and had a great story, and even literally laughed out loud a few times at some of the conversations.  The devs put a lot of work and thought into the game, and despite the combat misgivings, it was still worth sticking it through to the end.  Although I haven't done it yet, I would advise getting the Alisha storyline DLC (if you want the full story).  That will be my next purchase at the next sale.

GREAT GAME, ABYSMAL COLLISION DETECTION.
(You die when you shouldn't, enemies don't die when they should, and the environment has invisible extensions)
Firstly, let me say that SuperHot is actually a really good game. It’s unique, it’s innovative, and it’s damn good fun. The developers have a wonderful game idea here and they deserve our support for their work and for their achievement. I’m very happy to have supported SuperHot during its beta phase, and I’ve already put in 11 hours of game time and with the possibility to invest many more hours into this brilliant twist on the first person shooter genre (depending on the devs course of action).
So, after all that praise, why am I not giving it a thumbs up? Simple: the game has some glaring faults that seriously interfere with enjoyment of the game, the worst of which is the collision detection. Let me explain...
Carefully lining up a shot so the bullet passes in between two shelved pieces of glassware thus hitting the red man behind them, the game instead decides to make the bullet collide with one of the glasses which then acts as a shield for the enemy. Said enemy then goes on to kill me because of the inaccuracy of my “missed shot”.
Conclusion: bad collision detection.
A thrown katana races elegantly towards the centre mass of a red man. Just as it's about to connect I feel pleased and confident with my well-aimed throw. The elated feeling, however, quickly turns to horror as I watch the sword touch the surface of my adversary and pass completely through the chest cavity with no effect whatsoever. I'm then unarmed and left at the mercy of a man wielding a rapidly-firing assault rifle.
Conclusion: appauling collision detection.
An enemy has fired a bullet at my head and I move out of the path of the bullet far enough for it to sail straight past me. Once I’ve reached a safe distance from the trajectory of the incoming bullet I stop moving to slow down time to its minimum value so I can plan my counter attack strategy. While I’m standing there weighing up all of my options, the bullet gracefully glides through the air over towards the far left hand side of my screen. As the bullet is just about to pass me I’ve made my decision for my counter offensive, and I’m about to put that plan into action when BAM - the stray bullet magically manages to hit my head despite me being nowhere near it. I then lose my 100 kill streak in endless mode and start muttering curse words under my breath.
Conclusion: really poor collision detection.
Sadly, these aren’t random occurances, as they’ve happened to me many times during my 11 hours. It’s because of this sort of nonsense that I don’t play Battlefield 3 or 4 anymore. SuperHot's main fault is that it seems to treat your character as a human-sized cardboard box. An issue which needs fixing if people are to continue playing the game - and there are a lot of us with this grievance.
Very quickly, other collision issues include: bullets hitting walls even though the gun and the crosshairs are well away from them, and thrown weapons inexplicably exploding in mid air in front of you despite there being plenty of clearance for a successful weapon throw.
Another problem with which SuperHot suffers is a very short campaign. The game boasts having over 30 levels. The trouble is that most of these can be completed in about one minute - even on your first attempt. So a 30 level story mode took me just over an hour to complete leaving me sat there thinking, “Was that it?”
To make matters worse, these short levels are then punctuated with annoying story sequences that interfere with the flow of the levels and the action. However, it is worth noting that the vast majority of the enjoyable gameplay is to be found in the endless mode and the challenges - and these are genuinely fun. Manipulating the accelerating or deceleration of time by varying the velocity of your motion is a great bullet-time mechanic that allows you to overcome the odds despite your being outmanned and outgunned, and I have genuinely enjoyed the bug-free moments.
Pros:
- A really fun first person shooter with a unique mechanic that brings good puzzle work and strategy to the genre
- A lovely art style that dazzles the senses without ever cluttering up the screen
- Very nice sound effects that really immerse you in a world where bullet-time rules
- Watching red glass men crack, crumble, fall apart, and then disintegrate in front of you at what ever speed you choose is wonderfully entertaining
What we need from the devs:
- More levels
- A level editor so that the community can create and share its own maps and campaigns
- More variety in enemies and weapons to increase the game's longevity
- Greatly improved collision detection
I will be giving this review a thumbs up when and if the developers fix the game’s problems.
As always, leave your questions below and I’ll get back to you.
Until then, I’ll see you in the matrix...
